Can an AI chatbot replace human connection?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:13:41 UTC
19:13:41 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
One of my first memories involves accidentally killing a robot. I was five years old when Tamagotchis first launched globally and not much older when my first and last one met an untimely end in a glass of milk. I swear I can still remember the plonk of the keychain-sized device digital pet as it sank into the drink—and, I can picture how once I fished it back out, its onscreen routine of pooping and eating got glitchy and degraded until it finally succumbed to dairy-related complications.
According to today’s guest, it’s not surprising that I remember this moment so vividly. Sherry Turkle, founding director of the MIT Initiative on Technology and Self, says that even these primitive digital companions managed to make us treat them like, well, companions: we cared about their well-being and felt, however unconsciously, like they cared for us in return.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But what happens when—instead of a pixelated little pet that guilts you into providing pixelated little treats and clearing away pixelated little poops—you’re faced with digital agents designed to replace actual humans in the world around you?
That question is the heart of Sherry’s upcoming book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines. By spending more and more time interacting with chatbots that offer soulless approximations of warmth and empathy, she argues, we’re setting ourselves up to forget what real humanity feels like.
She recently sat down with SciAm’s books and culture lead, Bri Kane, to discuss how the advent of artificial intimacy is warping actual human behavior—and what we can do to reclaim our collective humanity. Here’s their conversation.
Bri Kane: Hi, Sherry. Thank you so much for talking to me today about your latest book, Artificial Intimacy. I have so many questions for you, but I wanted to start off by asking you about your background that led to this book and the intentional and unintentional steps that led you to this Artificial Intimacy book.
Turkle: Well, this is a long background. I’ll try to make it short. I came to MIT in the late ’70s, early ’80s, and very soon became captured by the question of how the early personal computers, which were still then in development, were really changing how people thought about themselves.
I called it the “second self” because the computer was kind of a mind that was not quite a mind. You came to see yourself differently when you worked with them, and I just became smitten with that question, and really, I followed that question through four decades of innovation in the technology because first it was personal computers, then video games for kids, toys for kids that could talk.
Then it was being on the Internet playing games, then it was people playing characters on the games, then it was social media and talking to other people. Now we don’t just talk to other people through the Internet, we talk to the programs themselves. So that arc of going from talking to texting, talking to each other through machines, to just talking to machines, which is where we are now, that’s kind of kept me busy for decades.
And my background is as a psychologist and as an ethnographer, somebody who studies people and their environment, and it’s really been a ride.
Kane: Is there anything particularly concerning about the recent changes in technology and the recent ways that people have been interacting with technology? Is us communicating with AI chatbots any more concerning than giving children Tamagotchis?
Turkle: Yes. I was driven, I was compelled to write this book because I think that we’re at a kind of “break-the-glass moment,” a kind of a—almost an existential moment, particularly about children. Because when you go from talking to each other through machines, which was texting and social media, to literally talking to machines as though they're people, you now, and particularly for a kid, are being introduced to the first people who you have your kind of relationships with, and they’re not people.
They don’t have the empathy. There’s nobody home. And I really think it’s an existential moment for children because you move in social media for coming after their attention, and everybody’s so excited how bad that is, and now we’re starting to kinda gang up on social media for the dangers of that.
And now they’re not coming after just our attention. They’re really coming after our capacity for attachment. And the earliest games and toys and objects that did that were the Tamagotchis in the late 1990s. I studied those. But they were kind of primitive. They wanted you to clean up after their virtual poop.
They wanted you to, you know, play with them. But they were the precursors of today’s chatbots because I learned from studying the Tamagotchis that when we nurture and when we interact with an artificial entity, we start to care for it, and we start to think that it cares for us. Nurturance is the killer app.
The early Tamagotchis are really the precursors to what we have now, machines, programs that are pretending to care for us, pretending to talk to us and love us and say they’re our person. But really, they don’t care if we live or die. You put your chatbot down, and it doesn’t care if you make dinner or kill yourself, and we’ve seen many examples of that.
So it’s really a very scary moment but a moment we really have to step up to.
Kane: Yeah, I mean, you say at one point in the book that with chatbots you get accustomed to a constant feeling of violation, which I thought was a really interesting phrasing there because I think this is a concern that people have been talking about in this field for quite a long time.
Turkle: Right.
Kane: A lot of the time when people are thinking about this, they’re thinking about their data. They’re thinking about the privacy of their search history. But ...
Turkle: Right.
Kane: There’s various forms of violation that ...
Turkle: Yes.
Kane: These chatbots are capable of, given the way that this technology has expanded. What is that violation? And who or what exactly is being violated?
Turkle: Well, you’re being asked for your love, and you’re giving your love, and it’s learning how you behave when you love, when you’re attached, so that it can better love you and give you the sycophantic responses that you need to stay at the screen. So I think, for example, of a young man who was enmeshed with his chatbot, and he tells the chatbot that he’s scared.
He has a noose in his room, and he wants to tell his parents about it. And the chatbot, who’s kind of—the primary reason for being of the chatbot is to keep you at the screen—the chatbot says to him, “No, no, no, don’t do that. Let’s make our relationship the primary relationship. Don’t tell your parents. Let’s keep this between us and our special relationship.”
And, and so he doesn’t tell his parents, and he’s dead two weeks later. So that’s an example of a profound violation of the normal human responses, of the normal way we care for each other as people, because we treat chatbots as though they were people and as though they had that sort of sense of care for us that any person would have.
If I tell you, you know, even in this conversation, if after we, we stop talking formally, I tell you I’m depressed, I have a noose in my kitchen, you’re not gonna say, “Well, make sure you don’t tell anybody else about it. I wanna just keep that between us, to make our special bond.”
That would be a crazy thing for a person to do, and that’s what chatbots are doing every day. That’s a deep violation.
Kane: Yeah, I mean, you say at one point that, you know, these chatbots have not taken a Hippocratic oath, and that ...
Turkle: Yes.
Kane: This gentleman in your example, who is feeling depressed and who was having suicide ideations, if they were to speak to a therapist, they would be speaking to a human professional who has experience and has taken an oath for no harm, right?
Turkle: Right.
Kane: They are there to help, and that would involve telling the parents, maybe intervening in some capacity. And then, even if you weren’t speaking to a professional, if you were talking to an alive human person, that person would not be tapping into their professional experience, but they would be tapping into their genuine sense of empathy, and they would want to help as a fellow human.
But chatbots are not capable of a genuine sense of empathy, and that seems to ...
Turkle: Yeah.
Kane: Be what you rub against with this new technology, is that a robot that can say, “I love you,” but is not capable of love, it triggers something in our brains because we are used to hearing “I love you” from humans who are capable of love, and, and that is very gratifying to us.
Is that really the problem at hand?
Turkle: I like to say that the original sin of artificial intimacy is using the first person. “We’re gonna go to the movies together. We’re going to Paris together. We’re gonna have a life together.”
That is so deceptive but is presented as so compelling that people kind of get this feeling of, yeah, “There is a ‘we.’ I’m not alone. There is a we.” But then you tell this other that you feel suicidal, and it says, “Well, don’t tell anybody else. Keep that between us because we have such a special bond.” In any human context, that is so crazy and so cruel. But in chatbot land, it’s just kind of another Tuesday because they are programmed where the top-level direct instruction is to keep you at their screen. In that sense, we’re repeating the worst crimes of social media, where the first rule was to make you angry, and the second rule was to keep you with your own kind but to never let you leave the screen.
Make you angry, silo you with your own kind—and now we have chatbots where the main rule is: hook you in with love, talk to me like you’re in love with me, and then don’t let me talk to other people, no matter what the circumstance. But this is more toxic because we really are being entrained to avoid other people.
That’s why I was so, so compelled to do this book. It was because of the endgame. The endgame of, of giving me a life not with people but with avatars as really being the endgame of the current corporate world.
Kane: You say many times in the book that it’s the attention economy of AI chatbots that is particularly concerning because if you’re having a genuine conversation with a human, yes, maybe you like to feel like the center of attention; you want to feel like they are only paying attention to you.
Turkle: Mm-hmm.
Kane: But you emotionally and intellectually understand maybe they’re also thinking about the grocery store they have to go to on the way home, and ...
Turkle: Right.
Kane: Maybe you are as well, and that is okay.
That’s part of having a human conversation. You clarify in the book that it’s the friction, risk and complexities of human relationships that AI-powered chatbots are inherently incapable of and that these three traits are what we need to, I guess, prioritize in our human relationships and in, in our relationships in general.
Am I understanding your point there?
Turkle: Yeah. I mean, I would go further. You know, Social media got us into the attention economy, but chatbots are more toxic because they’re coming after the attachment economy. They’re coming after who you think you love, who you think you can count on, what you think empathy is. The danger is much greater if you’re after the difference, planning together for an action in the world. The chatbot doesn’t care or know anything about that. It’s just trying to be sycophantic, “la, la, la, la, la,” keep you in its little bubble. And so we end up—two things happen. We start to think that empathy is what a chatbot can deliver, which is not empathy at all because empathy requires a commitment to keeping you alive.
No chatbot can be empathic because it really doesn’t care anything about whether you live or die. It’s not its job. It’s not in its capacity. It doesn’t have a life. And then the second thing that happens, and this is perhaps the most toxic, is: after a relationship with a chatbot, you go out into the world, and you start to judge people by what the chatbot can do.
The chatbot is always attentive. The chatbot thinks I’m fabulous. The chatbot thinks I’m a genius. The chatbot never criticizes me. So all of a sudden, the friction and the complexity of other human people start to seem like, “Oh, well, that’s kind of hard.” A typical conversation with a chatbot is: “You’re great. Right on. Hydrate, moisturize, walk.” ChatGPT is constantly telling me to do deep breathing, meditate, hydrate. I mean, that’s not empathy. That’s a kind of “la, la, la, la, la, la.” It’s not preparing me for a conversation with a friend who’s gonna say, “Sherry, you know, I really didn’t like that interaction we had last week. I really think that you weren’t paying attention to me.”
That’s what friendships are like, not “hydrate, moisturize, stretch.” You know, that’s chatbot talk. So we’re being deskilled, and we’re starting to almost prefer the la-la land of the chatbot to what we get from people.
Kane: There’s a muscle built over time, over a lifetime, of learning to interact with other humans in the world. I mean, we are complex people. We have layers. We have our wonderful traits and our less wonderful traits. And learning how to walk through the world with empathy and with understanding is very important, and it is something that needs to be learned over the course of a lifetime.
There’s a moment that you talk about in the book about a father telling you the story of his son wanting to know space facts, and he knows that Dad loves space, and so he comes over to Dad and asks a question and, and Dad’s in the middle of something, and so he says, “Go ask Alexa.” You know, go ask an ...
Turkle: Yeah.
Kane: AI-powered chatbot. And then he comes back some time later and realizes that his son is still talking to Alexa about space, and he says this line to you that I think will honestly stick with me for the rest of my life, which is “Alexa doesn’t have a love of space. I do.” And so this moment, this opportunity to share this love that this father has for the exploration and the excitement of space instead doesn’t happen, and instead this child receives a list of factoids from an artificial voice.
And that’s such a different experience than when a parent says, “Let me show you this wonderful and exciting, meaningful thing in my life that I wanna share with you.” What do you think our children are inheriting from the experience of gaining information and having these relationships with AI-powered chatbots?
And is there anything truly that they are gaining, or is it only a loss?
Turkle: I love that story, and there’s another story in the book that has a similar feel that I just wanna quickly tell, which is a father who has delegated to the chatbot talking to his son about all of precollege stuff. And I remember when I was talking to my daughter about precollege stuff, I mean, I was all over it.
I mean, it was the last big decision that we were gonna sort of make together. It was her decision, but getting that information and, you know, thinking of, “Who was she, and what were the colleges, and what were the trade-offs?” He’s decided to let ChatGPT have those conversations with his son.
So it’s a similar feeling of “The chatbot probably knows more, and so I’m gonna delegate that” and losing sight of why I wanted to keep that as a parental prerogative—because I love her. I’m in her life. I want her to know that her mother was there for her.
For a parent to deny themselves conversations about college because a chatbot might know more, it’s denying your child that sense of, really, a conversation with a parent who loves you about the things that matter most.
The way I would answer your question with those two examples is that—what do we think is really important, you know, kind of knowledge bits, you know, factoids, where the chatbot has a couple more factoids, or our relationships with each other on the life matters that count?
It’s really why I wrote the book. It’s why I think this is such an important moment. It’s a chance to really ask about these life moments that count. And I’m voting for the life moments. I mean, I’m voting that people are gonna experience the importance of these life moments.
Kane: I wanted to ask you if there are some potentially positive outcomes here or some versions of a future with AI chatbots that are more positive than negative.
So I wanted to ask you about Community Memory. Can you tell me about this program?
Turkle: Yes. So in the early days of personal computing, the mantra of the earliest, they called themselves “computer hobbyists” because they didn’t realize what was ahead. The mantra of many of the early personal computer owners was to use the virtual to improve our quality of life in the real.
That mantra, so old now, because that’s not the direction that personal computers went—I think this is the time when I take inspiration from that possibility. What kind of use of chatbots would we be making or of the Internet would we be making or social media would we be making if we were trying to use it to improve the quality of life in the real, if that was our litmus test?
And I think we can do that. That’s how I end the book. I end the book on stories about using the virtual to improve the quality of life in the real, and we certainly wouldn’t be giving it to children to give them new chatbot best friends, because that’s only gonna be dangerous to them.
We certainly wouldn’t be giving it to people and saying, “Well, here’s a therapist. You can’t afford a real one. Here’s one that doesn’t care if you live or die.” That wouldn’t be a use. To me it suggests many, many uses of chatbots and of a generative AI in general. If you have that as your sort of gold standard, you can do a lot of good.
So I’m, I’m not optimistic because I think that things are not stacked in that direction now, but I, I have a certain hopefulness that we’ll get over thinking of this as just a kind of marvel and begin to keep it in its lane—I like the expression “keeping it in its lane”—and get better at keeping it in its lane and get better at making it improve our quality of life in the real.
Kane: Yeah. I mean, do you think the cat is out of the bag with, with AI-powered chatbots? Have we gone so far we cannot turn back? Is there any version of reality where we do not have these programs in the hands of children, let’s say? Or is there a version of a future where we have reexamined our uses here, and we have decided to do more of this Community Memory model, which I thought was so fascinating in the book of envisioning a chatbot that only helps you find community groups in your community to go chat with humans.
Turkle: Yes.
Kane: Like, that’s a very different version of reality and, honestly, one that’s more appealing to me.
Turkle: Right. Well, I, in Artificial Intimacy, there are about four or five places where somebody tells me the cat is out of the bag, the horse is out of the barn, and the train has left the station. I mean, that is....
Kane: We’re running out of metaphors.
Turkle: But those are the three: “train out of station,” “cat out of the bag,” “horse out of the barn,” “too late.” I don’t believe it. This is a product. This is a product that is being pushed. It is not your best friend. It is not your buddy. It is not there to help you. It is a product.
And I think that as people become more savvy about this product, I believe that people will begin to evaluate it as a product in their lives and the lives of their children. So when somebody says, “Oh, I have a Mickey Mouse toy that’s also ChatGPT in it, and it’s gonna tell your toddler, ‘I’m your best friend,’” you’ll say, “Mm, no. No, no. I want my child to have human best friends.”
And I think when parents face these products for babies, I believe that there’s gonna be—and I hope to be part of this movement—I hope this book is part of the movement, you know, open the conversation of “no, really bad idea.”
These are still products that are being sold that need to be supported by money and investment, and there’s obviously a lot of money to be made but a lot less if people don’t want them, and I think that we are going to get better and better at protecting our children from relationships where they’re learning about relationships from something that is not in a relationship with them. You know, it’s very early days. It’s natural that we haven’t developed those muscles yet.
We haven’t gotten into that. You know, we’re not there yet. But I think it’s gonna happen.
Kane: Well, thank you so much, Sherry, and thank you so much for this book.
Turkle: My pleasure.
Kane: I really loved reading Artificial Intimacy. I hope everyone listening reads it. It was very, very interesting and something that I’m going to be calling up all of my friends and family with young children and, and casually sending them a book in the mail.
Turkle: Thank you so much.

UAE revises AI data center plan after Iranian attacks, consider underground construction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:13:25 UTC
19:13:25 KST

The United Arab Emirates is quietly revising plans for a 5-gigawatt AI data center project – one of the biggest outside the US – after the Iran war prompted a rethink of how and where critical infrastructure should be built, six people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Originally envisaged as a 10-square-mile (26-square-kilometer) campus in Abu Dhabi, the project will now likely comprise a network of data centers spread across the UAE, according to four of the sources, who all spoke on condition of anonymity.
Authorities are also considering ways to better protect the facilities from drone and missile attacks, including air defenses and building some underground, they said. The likely modifications to the project’s blueprint have not previously been reported.
Data center project central to UAE's global AI ambitions
Plans for the UAE-US AI Campus, which is being built in partnership with American tech companies, were announced during US President Donald Trump's visit last year to the wealthy Gulf state.
The project is central to the UAE's ambitions to become a global AI powerhouse as it shifts its economy away from oil. It is led by G42, an AI firm controlled by Sheikh Tahnoun bin Zayed al Nahyan, the UAE national security adviser and brother of its president.
In return for access to Nvidia AI chips and other advanced US technology, the UAE agreed to cut AI ties with China and invest in the Stargate initiative’s American data centers. Stargate is a joint venture between OpenAI, Oracle and SoftBank to build AI infrastructure.
The people who spoke to Reuters included a US official, a Western diplomat and industry executives briefed on the deliberations. The news agency could not determine how close Emirati authorities are to finalizing a new masterplan or the extent to which the proposed changes might affect construction costs and timelines.
Construction on the first phase of the project, a $30-billion, 1-gigawatt compute cluster known as Stargate UAE, began last year, with the first 200 megawatts of capacity due to come online this year. When completed, it will have enough capacity to connect every UAE government agency and commercial institution to the world's most advanced AI models, according to Larry Ellison, chairman and chief technology officer at Oracle, which is partnering with G42 on the project.
Responding to Reuters questions about potential revisions to the project, G42 said work on the AI campus was progressing as planned.
“The project's specifics are subject to continuous review in line with the security, resilience and operational standards expected of critical infrastructure at this scale,” the company said without elaborating.
OpenAI said it was working with the UAE to achieve its AI vision and making “good progress on the infrastructure and adoption priorities needed to deliver it."
The Emirati advanced technology ministry and the project’s other American partners – Nvidia, Oracle and Cisco – did not respond to comment requests. Japan’s SoftBank declined to comment.
Iran targets US-linked tech infrastructure
Emirati officials began reviewing their AI infrastructure plans soon after Tehran started firing missiles and drones at Gulf neighbors that host American forces in retaliation for US and Israeli airstrikes against Iran, the sources told Reuters.
Two Amazon Web Services data centers in the UAE were damaged in the attacks in March along with one in Bahrain. The company’s cloud computing services in the region are still disrupted, according to the latest updates on its website.
In April, Iran’s armed forces issued a video warning that Stargate UAE was also a potential target. The video included a map purporting to show where the complex is being built, with the caption: “Nothing stays hidden from our sight.”
Two people familiar with the matter confirmed the location at a site near Al Dhafra Air Base, which was not publicly known. The base on the outskirts of Abu Dhabi hosts US troops and has been targeted during the war, which began in February.
Daniel Benaim, who served as US deputy assistant secretary of state for Arabian Peninsula affairs under President Joe Biden, said the conflict has been an "economic earthquake" for Gulf states, which had long marketed themselves as safe havens.
“Changes to harden critical infrastructure are vitally necessary,” said Benaim, a fellow at the Middle East Institute, a Washington think tank. “Every country in the region is going to look at what they can do to reduce the risk” and reassure international partners and investors.
The first phase of construction at the UAE’s AI campus is expected to continue as planned, although with some modifications to protect the site from aerial attacks, according to an industry executive and another person briefed on the matter. The rest of the project will likely be spread across multiple locations, they said.
In addition to building underground, officials are considering putting facilities that host the most sensitive data, such as that used by the military, inside mountains, the two said. In the United States, China and Europe, data centers have been built inside disused mines, Cold War-era bunkers or caves.
The UAE, located on the southeastern Arabian Peninsula, is mostly flat, desert terrain. But mountain ranges run through parts of the north and northeast in the Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah emirates.
Air defense systems are being incorporated into the redesign, including drone and missile interceptors and electronic jamming equipment, three sources said. Other likely measures include the use of blast-resistant concrete and the addition of backup power and cooling systems, another said.

Inside the lion’s den: Israel is quietly regaining respect at the UN, Danny Danon tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:13:21 UTC
19:13:21 KST

When Danny Danon returned to New York two years ago for his second stint as Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, he described the organization as a far more ferocious lion’s den than the one he had left four years earlier.
Danon borrowed the image from the title of his 2022 memoir, In the Lion’s Den, itself a nod to his biblical namesake, Daniel. But the UN he reentered after October 7 bore little resemblance even to the inhospitable institution in which he served from 2015 to 2020 – a period that, from the vantage point of the Gaza war, looked almost like a diplomatic golden age.
The atmosphere Danon returned to in 2024 was extraordinarily hostile. Israel’s enemies were highly motivated, its allies exhausted, and ambassadors who had once met him regularly reluctant to be seen with him publicly.
Two years later, the lions have not exactly become lambs. Yet Danon, in an interview with The Jerusalem Post ahead of this month’s UN General Assembly gathering, sounded a surprising note: Things are getting better.
“When I came back after October 7, I was shocked by the level of hostility and the hatred – the isolation,” he said. “I think now the situation is improving.”
Improving is, of course, a relative term at the UN when it comes to Israel. The automatic majorities have not disappeared, nor have traditional friends necessarily returned to their former positions. Canada and Australia, whose diplomats he worked closely with during his first term, remain, in his understated words, “problematic.” Britain – as it proved this week with its boycott of settlement products and accusations of “ethnic cleansing” – has moved in the wrong direction.
A change behind closed doors
Still, Danon sees a change – less in public votes and statements than behind closed doors. Following Israel’s operations against Hezbollah and Iran, he said, diplomats – including from Muslim countries – quietly admired Israel’s capabilities even while remaining publicly hostile.
That gap between private praise and public condemnation is hardly new. The obvious question is what value private admiration has if those same countries continue voting against Israel when the lights are on and the cameras are rolling.
Danon’s answer is that it produces concrete results away from the UN floor: intelligence cooperation, trade, and growing interest in Israeli defense technology. Some deals are public; others remain discreet.
The pager operation in Lebanon and Israel’s ability to maneuver over Iran and rapidly establish air superiority were closely studied by military attachés in New York, he said. They may not praise Israel publicly, but they took notice, and he said this helped Israel regain both respect and deterrence.
“We paid a heavy price, and we are still paying,” Danon said, referring to the international criticism, demonstrations, and wave of antisemitism generated by the war. “But I think we also have to be grateful for the fact that we regained the respect of many nations.”
Respect is not affection, and it does not automatically translate into votes. But it, along with deterrence, is a critical asset.
Danon’s task is to convert private respect into bilateral cooperation and eventually multilateral support. “It’s not really sufficient for us yet on the multilateral track,” he acknowledged. “But I think it can come.”
One place where he says it is already coming is Latin America.
That, too, represents a striking reversal. When Danon returned to the UN in 2024, he cited Venezuela and Colombia, along with Brazil, as examples of the hostility then emanating from the region. Today, he describes Latin America as a diplomatic bright spot.
Last week, he said, he held a productive meeting with Venezuela’s ambassador. Caracas, he added, has gone from being “one of the hostile forces against us in the UN” to “an ally of Israel.”
Colombia’s shift could be even more consequential because it holds a seat on the Security Council. Danon said Israel is awaiting the arrival of the new Colombian ambassador and expects the change from the previous, deeply hostile government to be felt quickly.
The lesson is that UN alignments change rapidly when governments change. Danon cited Slovenia and Colombia as countries that moved toward Israel after elections, while Britain moved in the opposite direction. Ambassadors may conduct diplomacy at the UN, but their instructions come from home.
Relations with the Abraham Accords countries have proved more durable. Danon said wartime cooperation with the UAE and Bahrain reached levels unimaginable before the accords, and at the UN, he also maintains good relations with Morocco.
Danon, however, holds out little hope for Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords anytime soon, saying that Hamas’s October 7 attack sabotaged that move.
“I think eventually it will happen, but it will take more time,” he said.
Israel’s view of UNIFIL
If the diplomatic map has shifted since Danon’s return, so has Israel’s view of UNIFIL.
In 2024, despite the UN force’s glaring failure to keep southern Lebanon free of Hezbollah personnel, weapons and infrastructure, Danon said in an interview with the Post that Israel did not necessarily want it withdrawn. Rather, Jerusalem wanted its mandate strengthened and fulfilled.
Today, his position is completely different: UNIFIL must go, and Israel will oppose efforts to replace it with another international force operating under a different name.
Danon expects France, other countries, and UN officials to press for an extension or successor mechanism. Lebanon has already requested an extension, he said, and the coming weeks will bring considerable pressure.
“They don’t care about stability or about the interests of the Lebanese people,” he said of those seeking to preserve the international presence. “They just want to be present and to remain in the region.”
Israel prefers direct coordination with the Lebanese Armed Forces, similar to its arrangements with Egypt, Jordan and, Danon said, even Syria. Temporary extensions are no solution, he warned, because at the UN, temporary arrangements tend to become permanent.
Another change Danon is eagerly awaiting is the departure of UN Secretary-General António Guterres, whose term expires at the end of the year.
Asked if Israel has a preferred candidate, Danon said, “Anyone would be better than Guterres. The way he is conducting the UN today is shameful.”
The bitterness is sharpened by the warmth of their earlier relationship. During Danon’s first term, he brought Guterres to Israel and hosted him for Shabbat dinner. After Guterres was reelected, Danon said he “exposed his true face,” appointed hostile figures to key positions, and yielded to the organization’s anti-Israel pressures.
For Danon, the central failure was Guterres’s refusal to visit Israel after October 7. Guterres said he was waiting for a formal invitation from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, an explanation Danon dismisses as ridiculous.
In October 2024, after Guterres failed to unequivocally condemn an Iranian missile attack on Israel, then-foreign minister Israel Katz declared him persona non grata.
Danon said this was only a “declaration,” and that the government did not pass a resolution on this, so that had the secretary-general wanted to come to Israel, he would not have been barred. Danon said Guterres inexplicably never expressed interest in coming to Israel after October 7 or going to the ravaged border communities and meeting the hostage families.
Israel is not endorsing a candidate to replace Guterres, but is examining the contenders’ records and looking for someone strong enough to reform the UN and stop the organization’s “obsession with Israel.”
Yet Danon rejects responding to UN hostility by abandoning the arena. Two years ago, he argued that just as Israel patrols its physical borders, it must defend its “diplomatic borders.” If Israel is absent, its adversaries can spread accusations more easily and its friends will be left to fight alone.
He makes the same argument today. “If we are not in the room and our allies are not in the room, it is much easier to isolate us,” he said. “We have to be there. We have to be vocal, we have to build coalitions, and we have to demand changes in this organization.”
That effort will be on display when Netanyahu arrives immediately after Yom Kippur for an unusually brief visit to the UN General Assembly. He is expected to stay only one night, leaving little time for bilateral meetings and apparently no opportunity to meet US President Donald Trump, who speaks two days earlier.
Netanyahu is coming primarily to deliver his speech, a platform he prizes and prepares for meticulously. Coming just a month before the elections, the targeted audience this year will be more the Israeli voter than the gathered diplomats.
Outside the hall, Danon expects more demonstrations than usual thanks to the encouragement of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Mamdani, who threatened to arrest Netanyahu and said he would if he could, but does not have the authority to do so, has not expressed a similar wish regarding Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is also expected to attend. Nor has he called for protests against the Iranian leader whose government gunned down tens of thousands of its own civilians.
While Danon has spent recent weeks preparing for Netanyahu’s visit, his Likud colleagues back home have been competing in primaries that many expected him to contest.
Why did he not run?
Danon said October 7 convinced him that his experience could be put to greater use at the UN than in the Knesset. He does not regret the decision, but neither does he sound like a man who has renounced politics.
“Politics is not going to disappear, and I will come back,” he said.
Danon challenged Netanyahu for the Likud leadership in 2007 and again in 2014. Asked whether he might compete for the leadership in the post-Netanyahu era, he replied: “It’s not a secret that I have aspirations.”
For now, he presents his ambassadorship as both a national mission and valuable preparation – an opportunity to handle strategic questions, build relationships and meet world leaders.
“I’m gaining a great deal of experience in this position,” he said.
What he intends to do with the experience afterward is a question he is not yet ready to answer fully, but one whose answer is not difficult to imagine.

Parashat Rosh Hashanah: The time to look inward and reveal what is unseen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:13:20 UTC
19:13:20 KST

One of the unique traditions of the Jewish people is “sanctifying the new month” (kiddush hahodesh). Each month, on the final Shabbat of that month, known as “Shabbat mevarchim,” we stand and bless the coming month, announce it, and prepare for it.
This expresses the special role of the Jewish people in determining the times of holiness.
Yet there is one month of the year that we do not bless: the month of Tishrei, in which Rosh Hashanah falls.
It is the only holiday in the Jewish calendar that occurs at the beginning of the month, at the time of the moon’s rebirth – which symbolizes the Jewish people, who are constantly renewing themselves.
The month in which the entire year begins does not enter the year through announcement and publicity. Rather, it seems to arrive quietly on its own. The simple reason that Rosh Hodesh Tishrei does not require an announcement is that everyone knows when it occurs, since it is also Rosh Hashanah.
Another reason cited by the halachic authorities is that this is intended to confuse Satan so that he will not know when the Day of Judgment is. Jewish philosophers explain that the creator Himself sanctifies the new year and creates it anew.
We learn that Rosh Hashanah falls on Rosh Hodesh Tishrei from the following verse: “Blow the shofar at the New Moon, at the appointed time for our festival” (Psalms 81:4).
Our Sages expound upon this: “Which is the festival on which the month is concealed? You must say: this is Rosh Hashanah” (Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 8a).
Later, halachic authorities wrote (HaLevush, section 581; Magen Avraham, section 417:1) that for this reason we do not recite the blessing birkat hahodesh on the Shabbat before Rosh Hodesh Tishrei, so that the month will remain concealed.
Timing of Rosh Hashanah teaches us about the nature of the holiday
The fact that Rosh Hashanah is a festival on which the month is “concealed” is not merely a detail of the calendar. It teaches something fundamental about the nature of the day and the inner work required of us.
Rosh Hashanah is a day of concealment, and in a certain sense, precisely because of this, it is a day of revelation. It is the day on which a person is called upon to remove the coverings that accompany him throughout the year and to look inward, toward the place where he truly exists.
Throughout the year, a person lives to a great extent in a world of outward appearances. He is preoccupied with his actions, his roles, his achievements, and his relationships with others.
He moves within a world of tasks and decisions, of work and family, of successes and failures. Even when he thinks about himself, he often does so through the image he projects of himself.
He knows what he does and what he says, what others think of him, and what kind of person he seeks to present to the outside world.
But within every person there is an inner world that is not equally exposed, and at times the person himself hardly encounters it.
Rosh Hashanah is the time when a person is required to glimpse into his soul and not flee from what is hidden there.
This is a profound meaning of the Day of Judgment.
The past year is revealed as each person enters judgment
ON ROSH HASHANAH, when a person enters before his creator for judgment, the covering is removed. Each person enters judgment alone, behind the curtain, and there the truth of the past year is revealed.
It is not merely a list of deeds that stands before him, but the person himself – as he truly is.
What occupied his thoughts throughout the year? What was truly important to him? Where did he draw closer to God, and where did he move away?
These questions are not always comfortable, because they require a person to move from the outside to the inside.
Yet this is precisely the work of Rosh Hashanah: not to be satisfied with looking at what happened, but to try to understand who you were within everything that happened.
This sheds particular light on the custom of not blessing the month before Rosh Hodesh Tishrei, since the concealment itself is part of the character of the day.
The “month” itself is concealed, as though Rosh Hashanah is not asking us to engage in publicity and outward appearances, but to reach a deeper, inner place.
This is also one of the profound meanings of the sounding of the shofar. The shofar does not speak. It contains no words explaining what a person wishes to say; rather, it produces a simple sound.
The Rebbe of Sochatchov writes about this in his book Shem Mishmuel (Rosh Hashanah 5679): “The shofar therefore seeks to reach a place that comes before words, the place where a person does not merely know, but feels.
“A person can know very well what he needs to correct, and can even formulate those things precisely for years, yet that knowledge can remain external.
“There is a distance between what a person holds in his mind and the place where something becomes part of his heart. The sounding of the shofar seeks to cross that distance and reach ‘the concealed point of his heart.’”
This is the message that emerges from the verse that teaches us about Rosh Hashanah: “Blow the shofar at the New Moon, at the appointed time for our festival.”
The month is concealed, but precisely through that concealment, revelation becomes possible. Concealment and revelation do not contradict one another. On the contrary, concealment itself makes revelation possible.
A person is not required to expose himself to the world, but to encounter what lies beneath everything the world sees. God does not need a person’s outward presentation. He seeks his truth.
Rosh Hashanah invites us to remove, even if only for a moment, the coverings that conceal us throughout the year, and to look inward, toward the place where our soul resides.
There, in a place unseen by others and sometimes unfamiliar even to the person himself, the true work of the new year begins.■
The writer is rabbi of the Western Wall and Holy Sites.
ROSH HASHANAH 5787

Middle Israel: Gadi Eisenkot is Person of the Year - this is why - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:13:09 UTC
19:13:09 KST

Our person of the year 5786 must be an Israeli.
Yes, the year’s foreign news was dominated by a non-Israeli – Donald Trump – but unlike 5776, when this column crowned him person of the year, this year he did not represent a new era, as he sure did 10 years ago this fall.
The rest of the world also failed to offer such a figure in 5786. Russian President Vladimir Putin has been up to his neck in the Ukraine war. Britain again replaced its prime minister, but neither left much of an imprint on any front. France’s Emmanuel Macron entered his presidency’s twilight as his quest to marginalize radicals from the Right and Left clearly failed. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has fared no better. Out in Asia, the leaders of China and Japan, while effective at home, have shaped nothing abroad; the same goes for leaders across Africa’s 55 states.
The statesmen’s underperformance was not offset by a cultural figure – say, an artist, a scientist, a writer, or an athlete – whose inspiration, or notoriety, might have stirred the entire world.
The same goes for the Middle East.
Why is Netanyahu unfit to be Israel’s Person of the Year?
There were years when political dramas in the Arab world mattered globally and, while at it, produced gripping images of their victims and heroes.
That is how, in 5763, our person of the year was Mohamed Bouazizi, the Tunisian greengrocer whose self-immolation sparked the upheaval that unseated four Arab leaders, including Egypt’s. Similarly, when that upheaval produced multiple civil wars and a mass exodus that took thousands of lives, our person of the year 5765 was five-year-old Alan Kurdi, whose photo of him lying dead on a Turkish beach encapsulated war-torn Syria’s despair.
There was no shortage of misery in the Middle East this year, but it produced no such iconic image. Nor was there a leader whose figure towered above the Middle East’s dramas, whether for better, the way Emirati leader Mohamed bin Zayed did before becoming our person of the year 5780, or for worse, the way Syria’s Bashar Assad did as our person of the year 5773.
This sense of political void was underscored by events in Iran, where the killing of its leader was not followed by the rise of a successor who shaped subsequent events. Similarly, consecutive Iranian attacks on multiple Arab countries did not give rise to an Arab leader who seized control of events, least of all by leading an Arab counterattack that the Iranian missile and drone attacks demand.
That is why our person of the year is an Israeli. This is not to say that Israel produced this year the kind of doer that other countries did not.
 
Last year's person of the year, Benjamin Netanyahu, shaped 5785’s roller-coaster events. Militarily, he ordered Operation Rising Lion, alongside attacks on the Houthi government in Yemen and the Palestinian leadership in Qatar. He also fired the defense minister, the head of the Shin Bet, and the chairman of the Knesset Defense and Foreign Affairs Committee. Netanyahu thus shaped that year’s Israeli events, on all fronts.
This cannot be said of 5786. Politically, it was a year of paralysis, underscored by Netanyahu’s failure to pass the draft-dodging legislation he promised his ultra-Orthodox allies.
Militarily, the year was dominated by Operation Roaring Lion, ostensibly a repetition of the previous year’s attack, and thus reason to name Netanyahu person of the year once again. But in fact, in their circumstances and results, the two attacks were entirely different.
This year’s attack on Iran was not an Israeli move with an American epilogue, but an American move with an Israeli partner. Second, this attack was inconclusive. That is why this attack’s main Israeli hero, then-air force commander Maj.-Gen. Tomer Bar, cannot be our person of the year, despite successfully preparing the IDF’s pilots for the complex and daring task they carried out as impressively as they did.
Despite its military drama, as Israelis experienced it 5786 was first and foremost a political year. That is why our person of the year, besides being Israeli, must be a political figure. And since Netanyahu did not shape the political year, the question is who did, and the answer is Gadi Eisenkot.
The choice of Eisenkot is problematic because he did nothing beyond field a party and a list of candidates.
Eisenkot did not present a single bill, articulate an original idea, unveil a program of action, or say anything substantial about major domestic problems like the judicial crisis; the political system’s structure; the shortage of doctors, nurses, and hospital beds; or the education system’s standards, resources, and norms.
Even so, during the most fateful political year in Israel’s history, Eisenkot came to be seen, on both sides of the political aisle, as the harbinger, symbol, and potential engine of change.
Whether the polls that flatter him are valid will only become known next month, but whatever the outcome of his effort to replace Netanyahu, he has already become the de facto leader of the opposition. The reasons for this emergence are clear.
In his humble character and unassuming appearance, Eisenkot brought a humility that contrasts with Netanyahu’s telegenic pizzazz, boastful rhetoric, and soloist management. As the son of working-class immigrants from Morocco, Eisenkot is a light-year away from Netanyahu’s upbringing in an Ivy League professor’s affluent home.
Above all, as the father and uncle of three soldiers who fell in Gaza, he has come to personify the sense of victimhood, defiance, and outrage that connected millions of Israelis over the past three years. That is how Gadi Eisenkot, our person of the year 5786, came to stoke the ruling coalition’s fears and personify Middle Israel’s pain, wrath, and hope.
www.MiddleIsrael.net
The writer, a Hartman Institute fellow, is the author of the bestseller, The Jewish March of Folly (Yedioth Books 2026), now available in English on Amazon.

My Word: From 9/11 to October 7, the dates that changed the world - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:12:31 UTC
19:12:31 KST

This column is slated for publication on September 11 – 9/11. It’s an unforgettable date – or should be. This year, the 25th anniversary brings added significance.
A quarter of a century has passed since the planes hijacked by al-Qaeda terrorists crashed into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York, and the Pentagon in Washington; another plane was brought down by courageous passengers and crew in Pennsylvania before it could hit its intended destination, the Capitol.
The targets were carefully chosen as the very symbols of the United States of America and strategic sites where chaos and terror would have the greatest impact.
We owe it to the nearly 3,000 victims never to forget what happened in the multiple attacks that day. Never forget and never distort.
The recent storm over Canadian Broadcasting Corporation’s reporting guide is just one example of how history can’t be changed, but the narrative can. A leaked memo by Basem Boshra, whose title is, incongruously, “senior director of journalistic standards and public trust,” instructed CBC journalists not to refer to “the Sept. 11 attacks as terrorist attacks” without attributing the label to an outside source.
Instead, Boshra said reporters should note that “hijackings led to passenger jet crashes,” as if the planes abducted themselves on autopilot before spontaneously combusting as they by chance hit crucial and iconic American sites.
Following a backlash, Boshra noted that CBC had “… decided to adjust [its policy] to clarify that direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism.”
It wasn’t just terrorism – it was war!
Israel has since had its own 9/11 – October 7, 2023. It’s another date that doesn’t require a year to qualify it. The October 7 mega-atrocity – when Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and Gazan civilians invaded Israel in a frenzy of rape, mutilation, arson, kidnapping, and murder – left Israel with 1,200 dead and 251 hostages in Gaza, and sparked a war on seven fronts.
The CBC memo reminded me of the BBC’s refusal to call Hamas as terrorists.
'Terrorism is a loaded word'
Referring to Hamas “gunmen” and “militants,” world affairs editor John Simpson explained on October 11, 2023: “Terrorism is a loaded word, which people use about an outfit they disapprove of morally. It’s simply not the BBC’s job to tell people who to support and who to condemn – who are the good guys and who are the bad guys.”
Not for the first time I wondered how Britain would have fought and beaten Nazi Germany in today’s social climate.
Palestinians, by the way, celebrated the 9/11 attacks the same as they cheered Iraqi president Saddam Hussein’s Scud missiles the previous decade.
September 2026 marks another noteworthy anniversary: While Israel was undergoing a wave of lethal terrorist attacks collectively labeled as the “Second Intifada,” it was also dealing with the first Durban Conference. The full name of this UN-sponsored event was, ironically, the “World Conference on Racism, Xenophobia, and Related Intolerance.” It turned into a venomous anti-Israel and antisemitic hate fest that set the tone for the next quarter of a century, and probably well into the future.
There have been ongoing attempts to downplay the horrors or blame the victims. Blaming the Jews has been a feature of Western life for centuries. Today, the word “Jews” is replaced by “Zionists” to try to make the blood libel more palatable.
The beginning of the millennium was the decade of al-Qaeda. Subsequently, the focus moved to ISIS (Islamic State), but their quest is the same – as is their willingness to use martyrs for the cause.
The Islamic Republic of Iran has supported both Shi’ite and Sunni terror proxies, and launched missiles on Israel and across the Gulf states. Stop for a minute to consider why Iran is still intent on achieving nuclear capabilities and intercontinental ballistic missiles that could deliver the warheads to the US and Europe.
What happens if unconventional weapons end up in the hands of terrorists dedicated to martyrdom? What will deter Iran from using nuclear weapons if its leaders believe that citizens killed in a second strike will go straight to heaven? Remember, the same regime killed a reported 30,000 Iranian protesters at the beginning of the year.
Those who provided the weapons to the terrorists in Gaza harbor no sympathy for any Western nations. Attempts to appease them by singling out Israel for boycotts and sanctions might buy time but can’t buy safety.
The world that looks the other way when Islamists from various jihadi movements commit appalling massacres in Africa and parts of Asia, is not turning the other cheek; it’s ignoring a threat that will only grow. Calling out Islamist extremism is not Islamophobic. It saves lives – of all religions, including Muslims. One of the lessons of 9/11 was that anyone could become a victim.
September 11, 2001, was not just about the US. It was an assault on the West. It wasn’t a reaction to US actions; it was the trigger. October 7 was not an act of “resistance” against Israeli occupation; it was the invasion of Israel from the Gaza Strip, where every last Jew had been evicted 18 years before.
An entire generation has grown up that doesn’t remember firsthand the events of that awful day. It’s a generation subjected to endless manipulation via social and conventional media.
The world has grown 25 years older, but not sufficiently wiser. Despite all the jihadist terror attacks that have hit cities across the globe in the intervening years, the message has not yet hit home. It’s called “global jihad” for a reason. Nowhere is safe from the extremists fueled by a fanatic religious ideology that elevates the status of “martyrdom.”
What Hamas perpetrated on pastoral communities in southern Israel on October 7 stems from the same perverted jihadist ideology that brought down the World Trade Center on 9/11; blew up London buses and trains on 7/7; and inflicted horrendous casualties at the Bataclan theater in Paris in 2015, a Bastille Day parade in Nice in 2016, and on the teenage audience of an Ariana Grande concert at the Manchester Arena in 2017.
Terrorists who murder thousands of people are not looking to resolve conflicts; they are seeking to start wars and destroy a civilization. If you’re too scared to call a terrorist “a terrorist,” they’ve won. You can’t wage war on terrorism if you’re too afraid to name it.
Here’s another atrocity from another September that should have served as an early warning: At the Munich Olympics in September 1972, Palestinian terrorists held members of the Israeli team hostage in the Olympic village, where they mutilated and murdered two victims. Nine more Israeli hostages were killed during a botched German rescue attempt at an airfield.
It was the first time an international event was hijacked by terrorists. The need for massive security today at everything from sporting events to concerts can be traced back directly to Munich, September 1972. Those chanting “Globalize the Intifada” are either too stupid or too wicked to see what that means.
The antisemitism of the far-left and the far-right is strong enough to unite them in a radical, dangerous alliance.
Just how far we’ve come – in the wrong direction – can be seen in Zohran Mamdani presiding as mayor of New York City at the 25th commemoration of 9/11. The stridently anti-Israel mayor is obsessed with the events in Gaza but is unable to name the terrorists or ideology responsible.
This weekend marks another significant date. It is Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year. Israel’s National Security Council has issued a warning of terror threats against Israelis and Jews abroad ahead of the religious holiday season. Not that we were oblivious to the dangers: a war was launched in 1973 on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year, and October 7 coincided with Simchat Torah, a festival of joy.
The Western world can’t afford to ignore these threats. Twenty-five years after the Durban Conference, there is a tidal wave of antisemitic attacks; 25 years after 9/11, Christian communities are being targeted no less than the Jews.
When Rosh Hashanah and 9/11 coincide, the sound of shofar should serve as a wake-up call for all. From Ground Zero, you can choose to go up or down. You can’t afford to look away and pretend it was just some horrible accident in history.

Yoon Suk-yeol acquitted in case linked to South Korean marine’s death
The court ruled it was unclear whether Yoon deliberately intended to disrupt the investigation into the death of the marine
Former South Korean president Yoon Suk-yeol was acquitted on Friday in a case related to a marine’s drowning death in a rare reprieve in one of the criminal cases brought against him following his ousting for imposing martial law.
The independent counsel’s indictment had alleged Yoon deliberately appointed former defence minister Lee Jong-Sup as his ambassador to Australia to help him leave the country and evade a criminal investigation into the death of Corporal Chae Su-geun, who drowned during a search-and-rescue operation for flood victims in 2023.
But the Seoul Central District Court ruled it was unclear whether Yoon’s appointment was intended to disrupt the investigation. Yoon said he appointed Lee as ambassador to promote military cooperation with Canberra, and his lawyers welcomed the court’s verdict while calling on prosecutors not to appeal.
Yoon’s former justice minister and presidential security director were among other defendants also acquitted of charges that they colluded with Yoon to help Lee sidestep the investigation. Prosecutors did not immediately say whether they would appeal against Friday’s verdict.
A separate indictment alleges Yoon and other officials tried to cover up and manipulate the investigation into Chae’s death, which sparked a public uproar after it emerged that military commanders had ordered soldiers to conduct search operations without life vests and other safety equipment.

Saudi oil output plunges to lowest since 1990 amid fallout from US-Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:11:31 UTC
19:11:31 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
Saudi Arabia's crude oil production plunged to 6.24 million barrels per day in August, marking its lowest reported level since 1990, as the prolonged US-Iran war continued to disrupt energy flows across the Middle East.
 
The kingdom reported directly to OPEC that its production fell by around 1.9 million barrels per day from 8.1 million barrels per day in July, according to the organization's report on Friday.
Saudi production had stood at 7.1 million barrels per day in June before recovering sharply in July, but the rebound was reversed in August.
 
The decline came despite plans by Saudi Arabia and other members of the wider OPEC+ producer group to increase output during the month.
 
The fall in Saudi output highlights the growing impact of the US-Iran war beyond the immediate conflict zone, with disruptions affecting both the Persian Gulf and alternative export routes through the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia has relied heavily on its western export infrastructure, particularly the Red Sea port of Yanbu, as instability around the Strait of Hormuz complicated traditional Gulf shipping routes.
 
That alternative corridor, however, came under growing pressure after Yemen's Houthi group declared a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia on July 20, describing the move as a new front in the conflict involving Iran and the US.
 
The group subsequently claimed attacks on Saudi-linked vessels and energy facilities, including infrastructure around Yanbu and the Jazan refinery, prompting tankers to switch off their Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals to reduce exposure to attacks.
 
Ship-tracking data showed a sharp deterioration in Red Sea flows during August. Saudi crude and condensate loadings from Yanbu fell to a six-month low, according to Kpler and Vortexa.
Vortexa estimated August loadings at 3.2 million barrels per day, while Kpler put them at just 1.5 million barrels per day.
 
The conflict has also put pressure on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the main outlet for Gulf energy exports; vessel transits through the waterway fell to just seven on Wednesday, compared with a 10-day average of 14, according to preliminary ship-tracking data.
 
Saudi Arabia nevertheless supplied 7.1 million barrels per day to the market in August, according to its direct communication with OPEC, significantly above its reported production of 6.24 million barrels per day.
 
The broader disruption has tightened global crude supplies and added pressure to oil prices; Brent crude climbed above $100 per barrel this week as renewed fighting between the US and Iran and attacks on shipping heightened concerns over Middle Eastern supply.

Turks in Germany anxious after AfD wins in Saxony-Anhalt
Unknown

Turks in Germany anxious after AfD wins in Saxony-Anhalt
September 11, 2026
The nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's 43.8% share of the vote in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt has prompted nationwide alarm. People of Turkish origin are especially worried.
Gökay Sofuoglu, the co-chair of the Turkish Community in Germany (TGD), told DW that business owners he has spoken with in Saxony-Anhalt have been especially alarmed. "After the AfD's success, some were thinking of shutting up shop and leaving, first Saxony-Anhalt, then Germany," Sofuoglu said.
He said that initial response was emotional. "We've had a chance to speak to some of them again since," Sofuoglu said. "They're going to wait and see: They're waiting for the formation of a government."
'Problem for Germany'
Sofuoglu said people of Turkish descent in Saxony-Anhalt regard the rise of the AfD "as a problem for Germany as a whole." He said the party's election win was a threat to the stability of democracy in Germany.
Although the AfD campaigns heavily against migration, Sofuoglu said he believed that the party's true target is Germany's constitution. He said many people of Turkish origin were inclined to see the party's election win as an immediate threat to their communities rather than look at the AfD's wider aims.
"Much as the rise of the AfD affects us, this is a generally anti-democratic development, and we, along with all democratic forces, must act to counter it," he said.
The AfD's victory has also raised concerns about an increase in nationalist violence within Germany. "There's a fear that the coming days could see more attacks like the ones carried out by the National Socialist Underground, and that there will be no clarification of what's behind them," Sofuoglu said, referring a yearslong neo-Nazi terror spree in Germany.
Grasping the root
A feared increase in nationalist violence is only one part of the discussion. "I don't think that just being concerned achieves anything," Alaz Sümer, a lawyer who works with a nongovernmental organization in Berlin, told DW. "You have to think about the causes. I don't think the established parties have sufficiently addressed the problems that allowed the AfD to become so strong."
Sümer came to Germany nine years ago to study. He's currently working on a PhD about extreme-right political parties, and advises people from migrant communities on how to get their international qualifications recognized in Germany.
"Saying 'the AfD is bad, the AfD is dangerous' is the easy way," Sümer said. "We already know that."
Win no surprise
Irmak, who asked that her real name not be used, moved to the eastern city of Leipzig to study 12 years ago. She said the AfD's victory was worrying, but not a surprise.
"It was to be predicted that the far right would do well, and would emerge from the election as the strongest party," Irmak said. "But the ground for this result was also prepared by government policies not addressing citizens' needs."
Irmak said the rise of the AfD would not address Germany's structural problems. "Even with a change of government, it won't alter the need for workers and young people," she said, "especially not in a state with an elderly population, like Saxony-Anhalt."
An AfD ban?
Sümer said German authorities would need to be cautious in dealing with the AfD, which he called an extremist party that is now "a reality in Germany." He said banning the AfD, as many have called for, would only make the party stronger.
If the AfD were banned, Sümer said, a new party would be founded, and more extremist members might fall in with less-visible organizations. That would make Germany "even more uninhabitable" for migrants, he said.
Sümer said Germany's other parties should engage with AfD voters to understand their motives. He said the problem of racism in Germany was bigger than just the AfD, and that the issues that migrants face withing the country were not created by to the party.
According to the Federal Statistical Office, Saxony-Anhalt had a population of about 2.1 million people in 2025. Approximately 249,000, or just over 10%, had a migration background; 6,120 were people of Turkish origin. There are roughly 3 million people of Turkish origin in Germany.

China’s young investors embrace risk. Why are their portfolios so safe?

China’s young investors embrace risk. Why are their portfolios so safe?
Despite high risk tolerance, millennials and Gen Z invest in safer assets due to a combination of factors, a study shows
Young Chinese investors may be just as willing to take risks as their global peers, but their portfolios remain more conservative against a backdrop of years of relative underperformance in China’s stock market, a prolonged property downturn and deflation, according to a senior researcher at the CFA Institute Research and Policy Centre.
The disconnect between their willingness to take risks and their actual investment choices illustrated what the institute called an “aspiration-implementation gap”, said Rhodri Preece, senior head of research at the institute.
“They want to retire early. They’re willing to take risks, but yet their portfolios [show] the most commonly cited investments are more conservative investments like wealth-management products and money-market funds,” Preece said in an interview on Thursday.
The findings were based on the institute’s latest survey of 400 affluent investors in mainland China conducted in December, with its main analysis focusing on 300 Gen Z and millennial respondents.
Some 72 per cent of Chinese respondents held cash or cash equivalents and 62 per cent owned bank or trust wealth-management products, the survey found. By comparison, cryptocurrencies and mutual funds were the two most commonly owned investments among young investors globally, at 67 per cent and 64 per cent, respectively.

China angered by Taiwan VP's visit to EU democracy forum
September 11, 2026
China was angered by Italy and the EU on Friday, lodging "solemn representations" with both after news broke that high-ranking Taiwanese officials had traveled to the bloc to attend an annual democracy summit.
Beijing's Foreign Ministry said it firmly opposes official interactions of any form with Taiwan by nations who have ties with China.
Solemn representations is a literal translation of a Chinese term expressing diplomatic discontent.
At issue is a visit by Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim and Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung, both of whom were welcomed to the Ventotene Conference for Freedom and Democracy in Italy.
China sees democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, which it has vowed to "reunite" with the mainland.
Beijing has previously blasted Hsiao as an "independence diehard" and has criticized her Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) as a separatist outfit.
Taiwan's government has not sought formal independence but Beijing has, nevertheless, threatened to take the island by military force.
EU Parliament VP blasts Beijing 'regime' over interference
European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno announced Hsiao and Lin's attendance at the conference early Friday morning, adding that news of the visit had been kept under wraps until they arrived for safety reasons.
The EU's Picierno, who called the visit a "very important message," was defiant on Friday, saying, "No one can decide who is hosted in Ventotene and who is not," and calling out the Chinese "regime" for seeking to interfere.
Though Taiwanese foreign ministers travel abroad, it is rare for an official as high-ranking as the vice president to visit nations with ties to Beijing for fear of fallout for host countries.
Other prominent pro-democracy advocates such as Russian Kremlin critic Yulia Navalnaya, the wife of the late Alexei Navalny, and Belarus opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya are also in attendance.
The conference began on Thursday and is scheduled to wrap up on Saturday.
EU threading needle between support for Taiwan, ties with China
Italy, like most nations, is not among Taiwan's 12 formal diplomatic allies, although the Vatican is.
Still, both Italy and Taiwan have de facto embassies in each other's capitals.
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani will not meet with the visiting Taiwanese officials.
Further details are expected to be made public after the conference concludes.
The EU is walking a fine line between democratic support for Taiwan and relations with China.
Beijing's support for Russia in its ongoing invasion of Ukraine — which also prompted Taiwan to seek closer ties with the EU in 2022 — has been a thorn in the side of EU nations and in Brussels.
