The national average for a gallon of diesel has risen to $6.05, up more than 60% from $3.71 a year ago, according to data from AAA.
- Yemen's Houthis seized the key Red Sea port of Mokha on Thursday, according to numerous reports. If confirmed, the move would make it easier for the Houthis to target ships transiting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial waterway for Saudi Arabian oil exports.
- Iran's government on Friday called for an end to Saudi Arabia's blockade of Yemen and the immediate resumption of talks, in its first public statement since Iranian-backed Houthi rebels entered Mokha, intensifying their threat to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a key global shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi airstrikes hit rebel-held Mokha airport in Yemen, Houthi broadcaster says
Saudi airstrikes hit the rebel-held Mokha airport in Yemen on Friday, an Iranian-backed Houthi broadcaster reported, a day after the Houthis entered the key port city on the Red Sea, bringing them closer to the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Their advance further threatens commercial shipping on an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier Friday, Iran's government called for an end to Saudi Arabia's blockade of Yemen, throwing its support behind its ally, the Houthis. In its first statement since the rebels entered the port, Iran's Foreign Ministry also called for a return to negotiations between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
The rebels' capture of Mokha, overlooking tanker routes out of the Red Sea, could boost Iran's strategy of driving up world oil and gas prices to pressure the United States, experts say. It also raises concerns of a new front opening after more than six months of war in the region - one in which Saudi Arabia is forced to respond.
Experts say the developments in Yemen could give Tehran more leverage in any negotiations with the United States. On Wednesday, the spokesperson for Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guard called for any negotiated settlement with the U.S. to include Yemen, the first explicit reference to that front.
Iran seeks end to Saudi blockade of Yemen after Tehran-backed rebels take key port
Iran's government on Friday called for an end to Saudi Arabia's blockade of Yemen and the immediate resumption of talks, in its first public statement since Iran-backed Houthi rebels entered a key Yemeni port – according to sources speaking to the AP, AFP and Reuters news agencies – and intensified their threat to a key global shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement carried by the state-run IRNA news agency, Iran's foreign ministry said Yemen's sovereignty must be respected and its problems cannot be resolved through a blockade or military alliances.
Iran also said it was ready to help support negotiations. Meanwhile, experts say the developments in Yemen could give Tehran more leverage in any negotiations with the United States after over six months of war.
The Houthis' entry into the Red Sea port of Mokha on Thursday brings them within 50 miles of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important alternative for global shipping as Iran targets vessels on the Strait of Hormuz. It's the rebels' biggest territorial gain in years.
CBS/AP
At U.N. meeting, Yemen seeks international support in its conflict with Houthis
Yemen's special envoy to the United Nations called on support from the international community after the Iran-backed Houthi militant group seized control of the Red Sea port city of Mokha.
"This renewed war should alarm us all," Hans Grundberg, the U.N. special envoy for Yemen, warned at an emergency meeting of the U.N. Security Council on Thursday.
"It effectively marks the end of the relative calm that Yemen has experienced for over four years since the U.N.-brokered truce," Grundberg said.
He called on the international community to address this "new and more dangerous phase – one whose consequences, if left unchecked, will not stay within Yemen's borders."
The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels have entered Yemen's strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha, two local residents told The Associated Press on Thursday.
A Yemeni military source told the AFP news agency earlier on Thursday that the Houthis had taken the city. Four government military sources made the same assertion to the Reuters news agency.
Yemen's U.N. Ambassador Abdullah Al-Saadi said a single Yemen state with a monopoly on weapons that has sovereignty throughout the country, which the government is seeking, is "a fundamental guarantee" for security for Yemen, Saudi Arabia and the region.
He called on the Security Council to condemn the Houthis' military escalation and to implement measures "prohibiting the supply of arms, components, technology, and military expertise to the militia" which are fueling the conflict.
Saudi U.N. Ambassador Abdulaziz Alwasil said that the kingdom remains supportive of peace in Yemen but that it would "take all measures necessary to deter Houthi attacks."
Alwasil warned that "the kingdom's commitment to de-escalation and to supporting a political solution must not be allowed to become an opportunity that this militia exploits to continue its attacks and to threaten the security of the kingdom and the region."
CBS/AP
Diesel prices top $6 a gallon for the first time ever
Diesel prices in the U.S. have passed a painful new milestone for the transportation industry: $6 a gallon, a surge experts said is likely to have ripple effects for consumers as businesses pass on their higher energy costs.
The national average for a gallon of diesel rose to a record $6.05 on Thursday, up more than 60% from $3.71 a year ago, according to data from AAA. Diesel is widely used in trucking and rail, affecting the cost of transporting goods around the U.S., as well as in construction and farming.
Diesel had already surpassed $6, according to GasBuddy, which tracks changes in gas prices in real time.
Iran destroys U.S. sea drone in Strait of Hormuz, IRGC says
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Thursday that its navy targeted a U.S. unmanned surface vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.
"The Navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted a Saildrone Explorer-type unmanned surface vessel in the Strait of Hormuz area," the guard said in a statement carried by its Sepah news outlet under the headline "Destruction of a US Saildrone in the Strait of Hormuz."
The ideological arm of the Iranian military added that the sea drone had been used in the region by the U.S. Fifth Fleet stationed in Bahrain.
Washington has previously used Saildrone Explorer USVs to gather data and images in the Gulf. The sea drones are driven by solar and wind energy and can be deployed on missions in the ocean for up to one year.
This isn't the first time Iran has seized a U.S. Saildrone Explorer. In September 2022, Iran seized multiple drones, but later released them at the United States' request.
Iran on Wednesday said it captured an unmanned U.S. submarine drone, providing video of the drone being pulled out of the water. The U.S. military said one of its underwater drones had "malfunctioned."
CBS/AFP

Adalah clashes with Israeli universities over alleged discrimination against Arabs after Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:34:30 UTC
18:34:30 KST

The Adalah organization, the Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, clashed with Israeli universities after it published a harsh report on Monday titled “Apartheid in Israeli Academia: Arab Students After October 7, 2023,” which claims that Israeli higher education institutions have implemented discriminatory disciplinary policies since the start of the war.
Adalah claimed that the universities effectively created two separate tracks: a stricter track for Arab students, referred to as “Palestinian” students in the report, most of whom are Israeli citizens, and a more lenient track for Jewish students.
The report, authored by Adalah attorneys Lubna Touma, Adi Mansour, and Mai Diab, and edited by Dr. Fadi Khoury with assistance from Tom Mahager and Dr. Hassan Jabareen, reviews proceedings against Arab students at around 40 academic institutions, primarily over posts published on their private social media accounts.
Adalah said that international supporters contributed nearly NIS 1 million to provide legal representation and assistance to dozens of students following the proceedings. According to the report, the Galilee Foundation provided support that enabled its writing and publication.
According to the report, on October 8, 2023, less than 24 hours after the massacre carried out by Hamas and other armed groups in the Gaza border communities and the start of what the report calls the “war of extermination of the nation over the Gaza Strip,” the University of Haifa issued its first decision to suspend Arab students from their studies.
Adalah claims the university’s then rector made the decision without prior proceedings or a hearing, based on posts students had uploaded to their private social media accounts in the hours before the decision. Within days, additional academic institutions followed.
“By mid-October 2023, a broad pattern could already be identified: immediate suspensions of Palestinian students from their studies, the opening of disciplinary proceedings against them, and the classification of their posts as expressions of support for terrorism or identification with Hamas’s attack,” the report states.
The organization said it received 132 complaints from male and female students at nearly 40 institutions, in what the report describes as “large-scale suppression of Palestinian students’ freedom of expression in Israel.” According to the data presented in the report, 76% of the students who faced disciplinary proceedings were young Palestinian women.
Arab students suspended prior to hearing, Adalah claims
Adalah provided legal representation or advice to 100 of those who contacted it. In more than 80 cases, the report claims, temporary suspensions were imposed before a hearing took place. In 20 cases, students were expelled permanently or suspended for periods ranging from one to five years. In some appeals handled by the organization, the decisions were overturned or the punishments were significantly reduced.
The report links the measures taken against students to political pressure from state officials, including the education minister, who called for student suspensions and expedited disciplinary procedures. According to Adalah, in several cases institutions also reported students to police, leading to arrests.
The range of content that led, according to the organization, to complaints or proceedings was broad: criticism of government policy, the IDF, or the war in Gaza; references to the October 7 attack; sharing reports about the humanitarian situation in the Gaza Strip; Quranic verses and prayers; and symbols of Palestinian identity. The report claims that in some cases, merely liking a post, displaying a Palestinian flag or the word “Palestine” on a profile, sharing a news report, or praying for Gaza residents was sufficient to trigger action.
At the center of the organization’s argument is the claim that the burden of proof was reversed: instead of the institution proving that a post constituted a disciplinary offense, students were required to prove that their statements did not constitute support for terrorism. According to Adalah, institutions expanded their authority to cover private posts unrelated to academic studies, almost exclusively in relation to Arab students. At the same time, the report claims, they avoided taking similar action against Jewish students who published racist or inciting content.
The report’s conclusion follows from this argument: according to Adalah, Israeli academia has shifted from being an institution that regulates conduct related to studies into one that monitors private expression and determines which expressions of Palestinian identity, religion, solidarity, or political criticism are legitimate.
The organization describes the track applied to Arab students as an emergency “administrative track,” involving expanded authority, reduced procedural protections, and the use of vague tests of loyalty and “enemy” status. In contrast, it claims that Jewish students have retained a “constitutional track,” in which limits on institutional authority and freedom of expression are more strongly protected. Adalah warned of a “chilling effect” that would lead to self-censorship and “harm the sense of security and belonging of Palestinian students on campuses.”
Haifa University denies report of Arab student discrimination
“The Adalah report presents a partial, biased, and highly inaccurate picture,” the University of Haifa said in response to the allegations against it. “The correct picture is this: the proceedings against students who were suspended following October 7 publications were conducted in accordance with disciplinary regulations, and the students were represented by attorneys.”
The university added that “following the recommendation of the panel that heard the disciplinary proceedings, the parties agreed to pursue mediation before a retired judge, a former vice president of the Nazareth District Court, in which the students were also represented by attorneys. At the conclusion of the process, during which agreements were reached with the assistance of the mediator, two students were expelled from the university, five apologized and carried out community service at nonprofit organizations according to an agreed number of hours, and two students were acquitted.”
The Education Ministry did not respond to the allegations and referred the inquiry to the Council for Higher Education (CHE). The CHE declined to comment on the report.

Emma Bonino dies at 78 after decades of political and human rights activism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:32:55 UTC
18:32:55 KST

From the fight for abortion and women's rights to her commitment to Europe and human rights: Emma Bonino's political journey.
Emma Bonino has died aged 78.
The founder of More Europe, a longtime leading figure in Italy's Radical Party and former government minister, passed away after her health deteriorated in recent weeks.
Bonino had recently been admitted to the Santo Spirito hospital in Rome after a respiratory crisis. She arrived in critical condition and was transferred to intensive care so that her condition could be monitored. After an initial improvement, on 10 September, she left the ward and was moved to a private facility.
In 2015, Bonino revealed she had a tumour in her left lung. She underwent treatment for years while remaining active in politics. In 2023, she announced that she had overcome the disease.
In the following years, however, new health problems emerged. In autumn 2024, she was admitted to hospital in Rome for respiratory issues and, in November 2025, she suffered another serious episode that required admission to intensive care. On that occasion, doctors ruled out a recurrence of the cancer, instead identifying a metabolic problem.
A life devoted to Radical Party causes
For more than half a century, Bonino was one of the most recognisable figures in Italian radical politics. From abortion to contraception, from the liberalisation of drugs to the fight against the death penalty, she became closely associated with many of the country's major civil rights campaigns.
Born in Bra, in the province of Cuneo in 1948, she joined the Radical Party as a young woman and in 1976 was elected to the Chamber of Deputies. Even before entering Parliament, in 1975 she had founded the Information Centre on Sterilisation and Abortion (CISA), working to make safe and accessible abortion available in Italy.
Her activism also involved putting herself directly on the line. She deliberately risked arrest to draw attention to the dangerous conditions faced by women who sought illegal abortions. Such campaigns helped make Bonino a leading figure in Italy's feminist and radical movements.
From Italy to Europe
She entered the European Parliament in 1979. From Brussels, she focused in particular on human rights in Eastern Europe and opposition to authoritarian regimes.
In the late 1980s, she supported the Solidarność movement in Poland and was arrested and expelled from the country. In the years that followed, she was also arrested in New York during a campaign for the distribution of sterile syringes, and in Afghanistan, where she was detained by the Taliban after photographing women.
At the same time, her work broadened to major international issues: war crimes in the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda, the fight against the death penalty and the construction of an international criminal justice system. She was also among the supporters of the creation of an International Criminal Court.
From 1994 to 1999, Bonino served as a European Commissioner, with responsibility for humanitarian aid, fisheries and consumer policy. During those years, she followed the crisis in the Balkans closely and spoke out about the responsibilities for, and consequences of, the violence in Bosnia.
Her support for Western military intervention in the Balkans was one of the most controversial choices of her career and brought her into conflict with part of the peace movement.
Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, she continued to work on women's rights, supporting campaigns against female genital mutilation and for the protection of women in Afghanistan while also working for the recognition of the rights of African women.
Minister and key player in Italian politics
Bonino returned to Italy's government in 2006 as minister for International Trade and European Affairs in Romano Prodi's second government. In 2013, she was foreign minister in the government led by Enrico Letta.
Over the course of her career, she was elected seven times to the Chamber of Deputies and twice to the Senate. Her parliamentary experience spanned different political camps, although her political path remained above all linked to the radical, liberal and pro-European area.
In 2017, she was among the driving forces behind the creation of More Europe, a liberal and pro-European political movement that became a party in 2019. Even in her later years, she remained an active voice in public debate on civil rights, Europe, and international affairs.
A radical voice spanning five decades
With her death, Italy loses one of the most influential political figures during the second half of the twentieth century and the first decades of the 21st.
Alongside Marco Pannella, with whom she shared decades of Radical Party campaigns, Bonino brought issues into the streets and political institutions that, when she first championed them, were often still on the fringes of public debate.
Over time, she became an enduring part of Italian political history: combative, divisive for some, but hard to ignore.
From the battles over abortion to the death penalty, from Afghanistan to the Balkans, through to her pro-European commitment, Bonino built a political career around a conviction that never changed: rights are only truly rights if they can be defended even when doing so is uncomfortable.

MOSCOW, September 11. /TASS/. Oil production by OPEC+ countries participating in the output reduction agreement fell by 980,000 barrels per day (bpd) in August 2026, which is still significantly behind planned levels, the International Energy Agency (IEA) reported.
The targeted level for OPEC+ countries within the agreement stood at 34.27 mln barrels per day (mbd) in August, while real production reached 27 mbd, according to the report. This brings the volume behind the plan to about 7.26 mbd.
In August, among the seven OPEC+ nations Algeria increased output by 10,000 bpd, production went up by 240,000 bpd in Kuwait, by 980,000 bpd in Iraq, down by 2.27 mbd in Saudi Arabia, and up by 40,000 bpd in Oman, according to the IEA. Russia’s output fell by 200,000 bpd. Meanwhile, Kazakhstan boosted oil production by 340,000 bpd in August.
Production by all OPEC+ countries decreased by 1.46 mbd last month to 33.11 mbd.

Bush communities are begging for more budget airfares even as regional airline Rex warns that stiff competition in small markets is pushing the airline to the brink.
Isolated and aging populations are being let down by expensive ticket costs, Madeleine Lawler, chief executive of Regional Development Australia on the Mid North Coast of NSW, warned.
Her comments came during the latest public hearing into the state of Australia's regional aviation sector.
Flights from Coffs Harbour or Port Macquarie cost about 71 cents per kilometre, but from Ballina, where budget flights are available on Jetstar, the average is 12 cents per kilometre, Lawler told the inquiry.
"When I first moved to Coffs Harbour, I was able to get a Bonza flight for under 100 bucks, or Tiger Air was in there for a while, and I was able to get around in a really affordable way," she said.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We are slicing demand out of our economies by not having those lower price points available in the market, and that means our tourism economies suffer as well."
But half-empty planes could not cover the costs required to run a flight, so Rex shared the burden with travellers from the bush or cancelled services, the struggling airline's network strategy general manager Warrick Lodge told the hearing.
"You end up in a situation where ... carriers are forced to charge each of those passengers more to try and cover their costs," he said.
In July 2024, Rex entered voluntary administration only to be kept afloat with a taxpayer-funded package of $40 million before being bought by American company Air T in December 2025.
Despite this, it was forced to end its Melbourne to Albury route.
Rex had already provided 40,000 seats a year to a market that only had 22,000 passengers — then Qantas added another 31,000.
The airline chose to redirect services to the Melbourne to Devonport service.
Now, no airline flies Melbourne to Albury, while Rex pulled all services to Devonport in June.
Across the business, some Rex routes barely covered operating costs, while others were forced to contribute to overheads, Lodge said.
The airline has deals in place with the Queensland and WA governments, which subsidise operations in those states.
The Royal Flying Doctor Service told the hearing that regional airlines are critical to their operations.
Adequate air travel supported early intervention and helped patients avoid emergency treatment.
"Many of these flights will be to retrieve Australians who are critically ill and need urgent medical evacuation," federation chief executive Emma Buchanan said.

Emma Bonino, Italian politician who fought for abortion rights, dies aged 78
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:30:35 UTC
18:30:35 KST

Emma Bonino, Italian politician who fought for abortion rights, dies aged 78
Bonino was a passionate advocate for social justice and gender equality who deliberately courted controversy to advance her many causes
Emma Bonino’s life in politics began with a crime. In 1974, at a time when abortion was illegal in Italy, she travelled to a clandestine clinic in Florence to terminate an unplanned pregnancy.
“Coming back by train at night, I decided that never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation,” she later recalled. A year later, determined to drag abortion out of the shadows, she handed herself in to police, turning her private “offence” into a public act of defiance.
The arrest made headlines, fuelling a campaign that eventually led to the legalisation of abortion in 1978. It also launched Bonino into parliament with the Radical Party, a small but relentless force for civil rights.
Direct and diminutive, Bonino was a passionate advocate for social justice and gender equality who deliberately courted controversy to advance her many causes at home and abroad.
“I have been fighting for rights all my life, warning people to defend them, because they don’t last forever,” she told state broadcaster Rai in 2024.
In a dynamic career spanning five decades, Bonino won repeated election to both the Italian and European parliaments and served as a foreign minister and European affairs minister in Rome. She was also a high-profile European Commissioner in Brussels.

KOSMOS transforms mallorcan townhouse by giving old materials new roles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:30:17 UTC
18:30:17 KST

kosmos architects turns mallorcan residence into a reuse study
On the steep hillside of Banyalbufar, overlooking the Mediterranean in Mallorca’s Serra de Tramuntana, KOSMOS Architects and Blanca Gardelegui transform a traditional village townhouse through repair, adaptation, and reuse into a family home. Dubbed Amor de la Isla, the project works with what the house already contains, as well as leftover construction materials found in local storage, turning the limitations of the remote site into the central design strategy of the project.
The architects begin by looking closely at what is already there. Broken tiles, an old door, roof tiles, oil funnels, a discarded manhole cover, and even rebar caps are all reconsidered for their potential.
Banyalbufar is a village shaped by its difficult terrain. Houses climb the hillside between the mountains and sea, connected by narrow pedestrian routes and flights of stairs. Moving materials through this landscape is not straightforward, making conventional construction particularly demanding.
For Can Amor de la Isla, this problem becomes a reason to work differently. The team repairs existing elements wherever possible and gives materials that might normally be discarded another use. The approach is practical first, but it also gives the finished house a character that could not have been achieved through a conventional renovation.
KOSMOS Architects and Blanca Gardelegui repair the existing windows and facades, preserving traces of the previous life of the building. Inside, broken ceramic floor tiles are cut and recomposed into a large terrazzo surface. What was once a collection of damaged pieces becomes a continuous floor, with the irregularity of the fragments remaining visible. An existing timber door undergoes a similarly simple transformation. Cut in half, it becomes a folding door that better suits the compact interior.
The reuse continues through the smaller details of the interior. Oil funnels are used as lamps, ceramic roof tiles become lampshades, and a discarded cast-iron manhole cover forms the base of the stove. Rebar caps are used as door handles.
In the kitchen, traditional Mediterranean chain curtains are used in place of solid doors to screen the appliances and storage. They keep the space visually open while adding a familiar local element to the interior. Paint is used as the main new material. The architects use color to reshape the existing rooms and establish different relationships between the spaces.
the renovated townhouse sits within the stone houses and terraces of Banyalbufar
a pulley becomes part of the facade
One of the few new additions is a pulley attached to the facade. It was installed to move construction materials and supplies up through the narrow, vertically arranged house, where carrying everything by hand is difficult. A spherical light sits above it, giving the simple mechanism a second function. At night, the light makes the pulley visible from the village and sea, turning a practical piece of equipment into a small marker on the facade.
Much of the renovation follows this same approach. The architects repair the existing windows and facades, reuse the original tiles, and adapt objects and materials that were already available. New elements are kept to a minimum, while the things that remain are altered to suit the needs of the house. Its original materials remain visible, alongside pieces that have been cut, repaired, repurposed, or given an entirely different function. The renovation allows the existing building to change without losing the traces of what it was. At Can Amor de la Isla, the remote setting makes reuse a practical necessity, but it also shapes the character of the finished house.

Gaza documentary ‘NAZA’ wows Venice and breaks standing ovation record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:30:17 UTC
18:30:17 KST

'NAZA', the new documentary by 'No Other Land' filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, earned a record-breaking 24.5-minute standing ovation following its premiere – the longest-ever ovation recorded at the Venice Film Festival.
The only documentary selected to this year's Venice Film Festival main competition premiered yesterday and has emerged as a serious Golden Lion contender.
NAZA, the new film from Israeli No Other Land directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis.
The 80-minute hot-button doc, shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv during the ongoing Gaza war, features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whitleblowers. They discuss how Palestinians are targeted – hence the title of the film, a military acronym used offhandedly by Israeli Military Forces referring to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike in Gaza. It stands for "Nezek Agavi": collateral damage.
The film builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian.
NAZA earned a record-breaking 24.5-minute standing ovation following its premiere – the longest-ever ovation recorded at the festival.
Previously, the record was held by Tunisian director Kaouther Ben Hania’s Gaza-set The Voice of Hind Rajab, about the death of a 6-year-old girl killed by Israeli military fire while attempting to flee Gaza City with her family. The film, which premiered last year in Venice and was one of Euronews Culture's Best Movies of 2025, elicited a 22-minute standing ovation.
Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's No Other Land was released in 2024 and followed Israeli settler violence against Palestinian communities in the West Bank. It won the Oscar for Best Documentary.
Speaking at a press conference yesterday, Abraham said: “We just told these officers and soldiers, please describe to us what you did. Of course there were other questions that arose but the principal question was a question of detail - sketch it for us, we want to know how it worked. And sometimes just asking the question, you get answers.”
In an interview with Variety, Abraham added: “As Israelis, we found ourselves wanting to use the kind of position that we have - the access that we have to people in our own society who went into the military - to look at that system as it carried out what all human rights organizations are saying is a genocide.”
NAZA is produced by The Guardian, as well as James Wilson and Jonathan Glazer - the Oscar-winning team behind the film The Zone of Interest.
Considering Venice comes to an end tomorrow and the raptuous reaction to NAZA, the question remains: Will it become only the third documentary to win the Golden Lion, following 2013's Sacro GRA and 2022's All The Beauty and the Bloodshed?
NAZA will screen in Spain at San Sebastián International Film Festival on 23 September and then at New York Film Festival on 26 September. As of writing, no official theatrical release date has been announed, but French distribution company MK2 Films is handling world sales rights.
This year's Golden Lion winner will be announced on Saturday 12 September.

9/11 families to gather at World Trade Center and Pentagon to remember victims on 25th anniversary – US politics live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:29:01 UTC
18:29:01 KST

It is the 25th anniversary of 9/11, as Americans come together to remember and commemorate the devastating effects of the attacks, which claimed the lives of 2,977 victims.
Today’s milestone anniversary will bring memorial rituals – wreath-laying, flag-flying, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names - and volunteer projects in tribute to the day.
“In the course of history, there are a few moments that divide time into, really, what came before” and after, president Donald Trump said at a 9/11 remembrance in Washington this week.
The Republican, who was in New York on 11 September 2001, has often recounted his memories and said he plans to attend the Pentagon’s anniversary ceremony later today.
Vice-president JD Vance is expected to attend the observance at the National September 11 Memorial in New York, while other administration officials are headed to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania.
Planned remembrances extend far beyond the attack sites, from beams of light projecting from New Hampshire’s Mount Washington to a stair climb at Mississippi State University’s football stadium to a ceremony at Honolulu’s 9/11 memorial.
In other developments elsewhere today:
Donald Trump doubled down on his pledge to pay all US adults $5,000 if Republicans hold on to control of Congress in the midterm elections. He’s one of the few people to actually mention the pledge tonight, as many lawmakers and officials – including his vice-president, JD Vance – avoided mentioning the so-called “dividend” altogether. Trump defended his plan: “We can do that because our country has never done better. We’re taking in trillions, trillions of dollars.”
In a shorter address to voters than his nearly two-hour speech on Wednesday, Trump again pleaded with voters to “pretend I’m on the ticket” in November. In an improvised pledge of allegiance to himself, Trump directed the audience to commit to voting in the midterm elections at all costs. The president asked Republicans in the arena to repeat: “I don’t care if I’m registered or not. I’m going to try. And cheat like hell like they do.” Trump also told those gathered in Dallas that they would “go to hell” if they didn’t vote.
Earlier, JD Vanceurged Republicans who may oppose parts of the Trump administration’s agenda not to abandon the party in November’s congressional races. The vice-president pointed to Charlie Kirk – the conservative activist killed a year ago today – to argue that voters shouldn’t “throw the baby out with the bathwater” over “a policy issue here or there”, an apparent nod to dissent over the Iran war that he avoided naming.
Vance’s speech, in many ways, was an audition for a possible 2028 presidential run. He spent much of his time on stage setting out the threats of the so-called “far left”, listing the administration’s greatest hits and slamming Joe Biden’s tenure in office.
Meanwhile, dozens of demonstrators gathered outside the arena to protest Trump’s policy agenda. Dallas police said that two people were taken into custody after an alleged assault involving a counter-protester and for blocking a roadway.
It’s been 25 years since the terrorist attacks of September 11, and during this time Muslim Americans have learned how to live in that dangerous space between other Americans’ fears and their ignorance.
The fear was clear from the beginning. Immediately following 9/11, Muslim Americans faced what Human Rights Watch called “a severe wave of backlash violence”.
A tide of hate rose up against ordinary Muslims and those who appeared to be Muslim, including at least three murders in the immediate backlash after the attacks.
The federal government, for its part, began targeting Muslim immigrants in a massive surge of repression that legal experts soon compared with the Palmer Raids of the 1920s.
The ignorance was just as evident. Even Oprah Winfrey did her part to allay it, dedicating an episode of her show in October 2001 to “Islam 101”. The Qur’an leapt on to the New York Times bestseller list that fall.
Yet despite these early efforts at education, most Americans still learned little about Islam and Muslims.
One 2006 study found that only a third of those polled realized that Muslims worship the same God as Christians and Jews do. Close to 10% of respondents thought Muslims worship a “moon god”.
Trump to commemorate 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks at the Pentagon
President Donald Trump is set to observe today’s 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks by attending a ceremony at the Pentagon.
It’s the second year in a row for Trump to mark the day at the Pentagon. The president, who is originally from New York, last attended the ground zero ceremony there in 2024.
During last year’s commemoration at the Pentagon , Trump delivered remarks recounting moments from the day of the attacks, including snippets of conversations from passengers who were aboard the hijacked airplanes.
At a Tuesday event at the Ellipse just outside the White House, Trump vowed to “never forget” victims, noting that the attacks were one of few moments in history that “divide time into really what came before” and after.
For the first time, this year’s ceremony will add a silent moment to honor people who were exposed to the clouds of toxic dust released by the twin towers’ collapse and have since died of cancer and other illnesses.
Questions remain about how many people developed health problems linked to the dust.
It’s a reminder of how the attacks’ long shadow has reached into many corners of life in the US and beyond.
Police officer Casey Kloepfer plans to spend time today at the Brooklyn station house where his father, officer Ronald Kloepfer, reported to work that day before being called to the World Trade Center. He didn’t make it home.
Casey Kloepfer was only four, but he grew up hearing about his father’s affinity for helping people and for a job that enabled him to do so. He became an officer this past June, AP reported
“It’s big footsteps to fill, but it’s definitely something that I take very seriously and want to continue to honor him and be the best police officer I can,” he said by phone this week.
The 29-year-old wears his father’s badge number and even has joined the New York Police Department lacrosse team, which his dad founded.
As clear as that cloudless September morning, Jenna Jacobs McPartland remembers the moment everything changed. “I was cleaning the bathroom and watching the Today show in the background and nine months pregnant,” the 52-year-old recalls by phone. “I think they were showing ‘Today throws a wedding’ when the news broke in.”
A plane had hit the north tower of the World Trade Center in New York. McPartland did not know that her husband, Ariel Jacobs, was attending a conference at its Windows on the World restaurant.“I called his office to say, ‘Hey, turn on the TV. Do you guys know what’s going on?’ His assistant said, ‘Oh my God, Jenna, he’s there.’ The whole world disappeared and there was this sort of hollow collapsing feeling.”
Ariel Jacobs did not live to see his son, Gabriel, born six days after September 11, 2001. McPartland, then living in Briarcliff Manor, New York, would marry twice more, set up a grief support charity, and become a chef and restaurateur. Each 9/11 anniversary, she has a picnic at the cemetery where a few pieces of bone from her late husband are buried.
Speaking from Fairfield, Connecticut, McPartland says: “Ari was an incredibly joyful person who cherished his life. I made a conscious choice to honour him by living as joyfully as I can. It’s not always easy. I still cry pretty frequently. If there’s a movie with a building getting blown up, or if I’m reading a book and they casually mention ‘post 9-11 this’ or whatever, it catches me off guard. The grief finds a place to live in the heart, and you visit it.”
McPartland and other victims’ families have learned to live with that grief over the past 25 years. But America writ large has struggled to carry the weight of the worst terrorist attack in its history. The world’s most powerful nation responded by inflicting terror of its own, betraying its history as a safe harbour for immigrants, and pitting Americans against one another. The initial heroism, goodwill and unity of 9/11 gave way to discord at home and diminished moral authority abroad.
McPartland adds: “It makes me incredibly sad and bordering on angry that the death of my husband has been invoked to cause more violence. It is the othering of people that got him killed in the first place and, when we Americans fail to learn that lesson and choose collectively as a nation to other people, whether it’s immigrants or other nations, that is a deepening of that tragedy that is sickening and unfathomable to me.”

The vice-president pointed to Charlie Kirk – the conservative activist killed a year ago today – to argue that voters shouldn’t “throw the baby out with the bathwater” over “a policy issue here or there”, an apparent nod to dissent over the Iran war that he avoided naming.
Vance’s speech, in many ways, was an audition for a possible 2028 presidential run. He spent much of his time on stage setting out the threats of the so-called “far left”, listing the administration’s greatest hits and slamming Joe Biden’s tenure in office.
Meanwhile, dozens of demonstrators gathered outside the arena to protest Trump’s policy agenda. Dallas police said that two people were taken into custody after an alleged assault involving a counter-protester and for blocking a roadway.

Balkan truck drivers’ protest to block EU borders
On September 14, truck drivers from Serbia, North Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Türkiye will stage a new protest following similar action in 2025 over strict rules on stays in the Schengen area. They plan to block traffic at border crossings with EU countries, including the largest in Europe, the Kapitan Andreevo–Kapıkule crossing on the Bulgaria- Türkiye border.
The protest is against an EU regulation that allows drivers to stay in the EU for up to 90 days within any 180-day period, birgun.net reported, citing a statement by two of Türkiye’s largest truck drivers’ organizations, KATAŞ-SEN and Uluslararası Şoförler Derneği.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan has rejected speculation that Bucharest is preparing to send troops to Ukraine to take part in the war. In an official statement posted on the presidential administration’s Facebook page, the claims were described as a “false narrative.”

Albania and Türkiye show strong results in PISA 2025
Albania ranks first in the Balkans in science and mathematics in the PISA 2025 assessment. Its students recorded average scores of 435 and 433 points, respectively, Shqiptarja.com reports. However, the country lags behind in reading, where Albanian students achieved an average score of 408 points.
The international assessment conducted by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) measures 15-year-olds’ ability to use their reading, science and mathematics knowledge and skills to meet real-life challenges.
Students in Türkiye improved their PISA performance, scoring 494 points in science, 472 in reading and 462 in mathematics, Daily Sabah reports. Since Türkiye first took part in PISA in 2003, its scores have increased by 64% in science, 60% in reading and 52% in mathematics.
Greece recorded a decline in student performance in PISA 2025. One in two secondary school graduates is unable to perform basic mathematical reasoning, while four in 10 cannot understand simple physical phenomena or basic texts, ekathimerini.com reports.
In Romania, 48% of 15-year-old students are unable to understand a moderately long text, identify its main idea and find the requested information, according to the 2025 PISA results, Digi24.ro reports. In 2022, their share was 41.7%.

In science, the figure for North Macedonia is 36%, compared with 74% across the countries participating in the assessment.
In Serbia, 43% of students perform below Level 2 in science. In mathematics and reading, 53% and 48% of those tested, respectively, fall below the benchmark, danas.rs reports.

Healthcare is driving Sweden's election: Big promises, few easy fixes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:26:53 UTC
18:26:53 KST

At the core of Swedish elections this Sunday is fixing the healthcare system — something that matters to voters the most. The political parties from the left to the right wing are making promises, but health experts say none of them cut to the core of the issue.
Long waits, staff shortages and poor primary care quality due to low staffing have become familiar features of the Swedish healthcare debate since the pandemic, turning the health service into a test of whether the country’s welfare model is still delivering what voters expect.
Political parties across the political spectrum are promising solutions for the issue that matters the most for Swedish voters, but doctors and nurses question whether the changes are what the system actually needs, pointing to improving working conditions and staffing, as well as strengthening primary care.
Getting it right could grant political parties many votes, as some 64% of voters named healthcare among their most important political issues in an August poll, up from 55% in May, followed by education and crime and public safety. Some voters are ready to even change a party that pays attention to healthcare, according to separate polling by Novus for pharmaceutical industry group Lif, which found that 34% could consider changing parties.
With that in mind, parties are pitching increasingly ambitious campaign pledges for fixing the healthcare system ahead of the 13 September election.
The political proposals
The most ambitious overhauls of the system are coming from centre-right parties.
To ensure faster access to healthcare, something that has become a headache for many Swedes, the centre-right Moderate Party, currently third in polls, wants to cut the statutory healthcare guarantee, which limits how long patients should wait for specialist care, from 90 days to 30. However, currently some patients have to wait even beyond the 90 days.
According to Sweden’s National Board of Health and Welfare, 27% of patients were waiting for planned specialist surgery or treatment beyond Sweden’s 90-day healthcare guarantee in April 2026. The Moderate Party is offering that if a region could not provide care within 30 days, the patient would have to be offered treatment elsewhere, with the home region covering the cost.
Meanwhile, the Christian Democrats, the second-to-last party in the polls, are offering an overhaul of the century-old system. They want to replace the country’s region-based healthcare system with a state-run model, arguing that regional boundaries create unequal care and prevent Sweden from making efficient use of capacity across the country and, in turn, reducing waiting times.
Social Democrats, who are leading the polls, are after the primary healthcare system — pledging that at least 80% of Swedes should have a named doctor by 2030. Centre Party also promises to introduce named doctors, while the Liberals want to create 4,500 more general practitioner positions.
No silver bullet
However, none of the reforms pitched by political parties in Sweden is a “miracle solution” to fix it all, Fanny Nilsson, an internal medicine doctor, board member of the Swedish Society of Medicine and an author who travelled across Europe comparing healthcare systems, told Euronews Health.
Experts Euronews spoke to argue that politicians, while focused on cutting the waiting times, are missing the core of the issue: workforce shortages, poor retention, excessive administrative burdens and an under-resourced primary care system.
“If those issues are not addressed, waiting lists will persist,” Hanna Kataoka, president of the Swedish Medical Association, told Euronews.
The Swedish healthcare paradox
A lack of primary care professionals and a lack of continuity, with patients often unable to see the same doctor over time, creates a paradox at the heart of Swedish healthcare, Nilsson said.
“We are very strong and good at very specialist advanced care. We are quite advanced in research and adopting new technologies and new pharmaceuticals,” Nilsson said.
“But how can we have the best healthcare in the world when you cannot get hold of your GP?” she added.
The numbers are backing her words. In 2024, some 7% of Swedes reported being unable to get the primary care they felt they needed, more than twice the EU average of 3%, according to OECD data. Meanwhile, seven in ten primary-care doctors were responsible for more patients than recommended, according to a 2026 Swedish Medical Association report.
While parties such as Social Democrats, the Liberals and the Centre Party vowed to fix this issue, Nilsson says that it lacks a concrete long-term vision for delivering it.
The proposed fixes for the healthcare system are “just dumbing the debate,” she said.
“It just makes all of these questions too shallow, too dumb, and that is, I think, also why the voters in Sweden are having difficulties following the healthcare debate,” she said, urging politicians to look at healthcare systems beyond their four-year terms.
Will parties’ campaign pledges work?
The same goes for the promises from the Moderate Party and Christian democrats.
The 30-day guarantee could expand the role of private healthcare providers concentrated in large cities such as Stockholm, as rural areas, particularly northern Sweden, lack enough staff and could be forced to send patients elsewhere.
“Then the patients are going to be flown to Stockholm, get surgery there, and be flown back,” Nilsson said.
Leaving staffing issues in regions unsolved and instead relying on private healthcare providers is not a good way to look at healthcare,” she said.
As for the Christian Democrats’ ambition to completely upend the century-old system, experts are sceptical that changing the level of government responsible for healthcare would itself solve its problems.
“A major structural reform risks consuming years of political attention without addressing the issues that matter most: workforce shortages, working conditions, primary care capacity and long-term planning,” Kataoka said.
Nilsson says the Christian Democrats are “right in saying that the state should be more involved”, but argues that changing who runs healthcare is not the same as fixing what is wrong with it.
Sweden’s hospital-bed shortage
Nilsson points to another problem she sees at the heart of specialist care — Sweden’s exceptionally low hospital-bed capacity, with only 1.9 hospital beds per 1,000 people in 2023, the lowest level in the EU.
She says poor working conditions are a major reason behind it, with only a third of Sweden’s healthcare workforce not doing overtime and just one in ten able to take a break during the working day.
This leads doctors to discharge patients earlier than they would like or spend large amounts of time trying to move patients between wards and hospitals because beds are unavailable.
“It’s causing a lot of ethical stress. ‘Who to discharge? How do I clear a bed?’,” she said.
“It's awful work that we are doing that many doctors are very upset about.”
A 2024 investigation by medical publication Sjukhusläkaren found that bed, staffing or resource shortages and high workloads were contributing factors in 100 of the 237 hospital deaths it examined from 2023.
Kataoka said the biggest improvement to doctors’ ability to treat patients would be “more time for patients”, requiring better staffing, stronger continuity of care, less bureaucracy and better-functioning IT systems.
“A major structural reform risks consuming years of political attention without addressing the issues that matter most: workforce shortages, working conditions, primary care capacity, and long-term planning. These problems require sustained action regardless of the governance model.”

Hassan Hajjaj: The Andy Warhol of Marrakech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:26:53 UTC
18:26:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Hassan Hajjaj's colourful world of Moroccan art, fashion and London rockstars
Tucked away on a quiet street in Shoreditch is LARACHE, Hassan Hajjaj’s shop, studio and general hangout space.
It’s a Sunday, and the Moroccan artist and photographer has just finished shooting two families when I arrive. Inside, there is a lot to look at. Colourful clothes, sunglasses, shoes, bags, cans, tins and plenty of Hajjaj’s trademark patterns and prints fill the space.
His photographs are hard to miss. Traditional Moroccan djellabas, caftans, headscarves and babouches sit alongside Nike, Gucci and Versace-style logos, animal prints, stripes and bright colours. His sitters might be sitting on an overturned Coca-Cola crate, leaning against a motorbike or holding a football or musical instrument.
Even the smallest details are very Hajjaj. Tomato paste tins, olive and harissa tins, and Coca-Cola cans are stacked around his subjects, while colourful plastic mats and Moroccan fabrics serve as backdrops.
Looking around LARACHE, there are clearly many different influences at play. But Hajjaj says he has never been able to point to one person or one particular moment and say, "That’s where it all started."
"I think there are too many influences to name, and I don’t have one particular person," he tells The New Arab. "It could be a film, a book or travelling. I’d say it’s probably more about the journey of my life and what I grew up with."
That mix has been there for a long time. Hajjaj says his work has grown by trying things out, picking up new ideas and then bringing them into what he was already doing.
"I wouldn’t say it was something that happened from day one," he says. "It was more of an evolution, doing things, experimenting and seeing where they took me. Each thing happened and added another layer to the next."
One of those early influences was fashion. In the 1980s, Hajjaj ran a shop called R.A.P, selling clothes that would now be described as streetwear, including T-shirts with fake Chanel No. 5 and Gucci branding. He was also influenced by New York designer Dapper Dan, who became known for using luxury logos in his own designs.
"I used to have a shop called R.A.P., which stood for Real Artistic People, back in the 80s. I was selling clothes, which we now call streetwear,” he says. “We used to sell a lot of counterfeit versions of brands like Chanel No. 5 and Gucci and stuff like that."
It was not just about the clothes themselves. Hajjaj was interested in how these brands, logos, and products could be taken apart and played with.
"I grew up on Dapper Dan from New York,” he says. “He was really one of the people who helped make counterfeit fashion even bigger."
More than meets the eye
This approach of taking something familiar and placing it somewhere unexpected is still evident throughout his photographs. A designer logo might appear next to a Moroccan slipper, while a tin of tomato paste can become part of a carefully arranged portrait.
The tomato cans, tins and other everyday objects also take Hajjaj back to Morocco. They are not simply there because they are colourful; they come from the world he grew up in.
The same goes for the patterns. Growing up in Morocco, Hajjaj was surrounded by mosaics, tiles, calligraphy and repeated shapes, which eventually became a big part of his own work.
"Growing up in Morocco, which is an Islamic country, we’re not really supposed to have figurative images and things like that," he says.
"So a lot of what’s traditionally considered art is, like you said, mosaics, different kinds of patterns and calligraphy."
He adds, "The repeated patterns come from things I grew up with, like the repeated patterns on djellabas and the tiles on the floor and stuff like that."
But for all the clothes, colours, cans and patterns, Hajjaj’s photographs still come down to people. He started taking pictures of his friends because he wanted others to see the people and places around him.
He does not, however, want to tell viewers exactly what they are supposed to take from an image.
"I’m not really trying to convey too many messages," he says. "I always let the viewer make up their own mind about what the message is."
For Hajjaj, that can mean the same photograph is interpreted in completely different ways depending on who is looking at it.
"It could be because I’m Moroccan. Sometimes they see a picture and might look at it as Islamic, while sometimes I look at it and just think it’s cool. It could be the same image," he says.
"That image can be seen in five or 10 different ways by different people."
Finding his Rockstars
That freedom has become particularly interesting in London, where the people around Hajjaj come from all sorts of backgrounds.
His 'Rockstars' series grew out of this side of his life, with the artist photographing musicians and creatives he met around the city.
"A lot of my friends are from London, but they could be of Jamaican, Nigerian or Brazilian background," he says.
There was no big plan behind documenting this mix. Hajjaj was simply photographing what he saw around him.
"I wasn’t really trying to do something political," he says. "It was just something that was happening around me, and I was trying to capture that moment."
The 'Rockstars' series has been developing for around three years and has included a younger generation of musicians and artists. Central Cee is one of them.
For Hajjaj, the appeal was partly personal. He recognised something in the people he was photographing and wondered what he might have been doing if he were their age now.
"I was just sort of lucky enough to capture this new wave of, let’s say, creative people in London, and I saw myself in them," he says.
"I thought, if I were their age, hopefully I’d be part of that kind of scene."
His relationship with his sitters has not changed much, even as the names have grown larger. Some shoots come through major publications, while others happen because somebody happens to walk through the right door at the right time.
His photograph of Billie Eilish came through Vogue. Hajjaj was asked to photograph her for the magazine, but the shoot turned into an opportunity for her to wear some of his clothes too.
"Billie Eilish was actually a shoot for Vogue, so I was asked to do a Vogue cover shoot with her," he says. "When I finished shooting her, they had their own stylist, makeup artist and hair team, and they asked if she could wear some of my stuff."
Central Cee was much less planned.
"He’s a friend of a friend of mine," Hajjaj says. "He happened to come to Morocco and came to my place. It was just the right surroundings, and something that happened naturally."
Then there was football. Hajjaj was asked to design a boot for Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi for AFCON, giving him another chance to bring Moroccan references into something completely different.
"I wanted to keep it Moroccan, with a North African style," he says. "So I used the kind of patterns you normally see on djellabas and incorporated them into the boot to keep that Moroccan feel."
For him, there is no need for every project to follow exactly the same formula.
"So each one really had a different avenue, different thoughts and different relationships," he says.
Taking over Sotheby’s
That idea of putting different people and places into spaces where they might not normally appear also carried over into his Hassan Hajjaj: My London Rockstars, Ends to Estates exhibition at Sotheby’s.
Hajjaj had originally been looking for somewhere a little different to show the work. He did not want to simply put the photographs into another gallery and call it a day.
"I didn’t want to really do it in the gallery," he says. "I was trying to find like an offbeat, interesting space to do it."
When Sotheby’s offered him the chance to show there, he decided it made sense. The photographs would not just be hanging on a wall; they would be bringing a group of people into a space they might not normally enter.
"The reason was to have these kinds of people hanging on the wall, taking over a space where they normally wouldn’t be invited or might not have the confidence to go inside," he says.
The reaction from his friends was telling. Some congratulated him because they saw the show as proof that he had “made it” at Sotheby’s. Others had a much more straightforward reaction: they had walked past the building for years but had never actually gone inside.
"There were a lot of people saying, ‘You know, Hassan, I’ve always walked past here, but I’ve never been inside. And my answer to them was, ‘That’s the reason you’re here. That’s the reason for this show.’"
Making a space his own
Away from exhibitions, Hajjaj speaks about his Shoreditch shop. When he first got the space, he did not have a clear idea of what he wanted it to become.
"I didn’t know what I was going to do with it because it’s a dead street anyway," he says.
"But because I was already doing product, I needed a space to work from and somewhere to put my stuff, so I kind of opened it up to the public, but also use it as a studio."
Over time, it became a bit of everything: a shop, studio, office, meeting place, and a place for people to drop in.
"We use it as an office, as a meeting place, and really anybody’s welcome to come in as well," he says.
"It wasn’t really a plan from the beginning, and I’ve kind of kept it like that."
That lack of a strict plan seems to be part of the appeal. People come in because something catches their eye, and sometimes the conversation carries on from there.
"It gives me a chance to meet new people here," Hajjaj says. "Sometimes people just come in off the street, and because of the style of things I’m doing here, they’re often quite interesting people. They’ve taken an interest in something inside the shop, and I’ve met some great, great people here as well."
Who’s next?
After photographing friends, artists, musicians and some of the biggest names in music, there is still no particular person Hajjaj is desperate to get in front of his camera.
When asked about his dream subject, he immediately throws out a couple of names.
"I could say Bob Marley, James Brown. I could name loads of people like that," he tells The New Arab.
"But I don’t really have a dream list. I just love shooting people when it happens naturally."
Nevertheless, for Hajjaj, there is certainly no shortage of new things happening.
He is preparing for an exhibition at the Philharmonie de Paris, opening on 21 September and running until April 2027, focused on musicians. He also has a group exhibition coming up in Parramatta, Sydney, as well as projects in Qatar and collaborations planned for next year.
But sitting in LARACHE, surrounded by the clothes, tins, crates and photographs that have become so recognisable as his, Hajjaj does not make his work sound particularly complicated.
"It’s really everything that I grew up with," he says. "That’s really me in that frame, in a sense, and my journey."
Zainab Mehdi is a British Iraqi journalist and the Associate Features Editor at The New Arab. She holds a BSc in Modern History and International Relations from the University of Essex and an MA in Near and Middle Eastern Studies from SOAS

Delay tactic or genuine solution? Carbon capture under fire again as EU invests in ‘unproven’ technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:25:30 UTC
18:25:30 KST

Carbon capture and storage has been found to be “technically uncertain and very high cost”.
CO2 emitted by a fertiliser factory in the Netherlands will be stored underneath the seabed in Norway, in what the owners are calling the “largest commercial carbon capture and storage (CCS) project in Europe”.
At an opening ceremony this week, the ammonia and fertiliser plant announced that it will capture 800,000 tonnes of CO2 a year then liquefy it to be sent by ship to Norway.
Having funded the project, the European Commission was keen to promote its investment – with the Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth attending the inauguration alongside the Prime Ministers of both countries.
While the Commission says the Sluiskil plant, run by Norwegian chemical company Yara, is a “strategic investment”, opponents say it is “risking billions in taxpayers’ money to fund a dangerous distraction that delays climate action”.
As one of the most divisive topics in climate action, we look into the facts about carbon capture and how the EU came to be funding this experimental technology.
What is carbon capture and storage?
Carbon capture and storage (CCS) refers to technologies designed to prevent CO2 from entering the atmosphere in the first place and/or to remove it after it has been emitted.
As is done at the Sluiskil plant, most projects use a liquid to chemically remove the CO2 emitted from the production process, where it is then compressed into a liquid-like state and transported typically through a pipeline to a storage site. At that point, it’s either stored deep underground or is transformed into things like building materials or synthetic fuel. In the case of the latter, this technology is referred to as CCUS, where the ‘U’ stands for utilisation.
As of February 2026, there were 75 operational CCS projects around the world, according to climate change publication Carbon Brief. Almost all of them are at fossil-fuel extraction and processing sites, according to the IEA’s database. Together, these projects capture 62.5 million tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2) each year. This is equivalent to 0.2 per cent of total global emissions in 2025.
While Yara’s chief executive, Svein Tore Holsether, said in a statement, “The carbon capture facility in Sluiskil proves that large-scale industrial decarbonisation is possible today”, the cumulative emissions saved are a very, very tiny drop in the ocean.
US non-profit the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) has conducted in-depth research into CCS. Their Energy Finance Analyst, Andrew Reid, says: “Despite the political and financial support that has been pointed to CCS over the past three to four years, it remains technically uncertain, very high cost, and reliant upon huge subsidies to move from feasibility to construction and operation.”
CCS: To help the fossil fuel industry to extract and sell more oil and gas
To understand its uses, it’s important to understand where carbon technology originates from. According to Carbon Brief, it “was originally rolled out at US and Canadian oil wells in the early 1970s as a way to achieve “enhanced oil recovery”. This involves injecting captured CO2 into depleted wells – a process that stores the gas, but also helps to extract more oil.” This is by far the most significant use for carbon capture worldwide, with three-quarters of it used for this purpose.
This means that “the majority of CO2 that is both captured and used today helps the fossil-fuel industry to extract and sell more oil and gas,” according to Carbon Brief.
How did the EU end up funding carbon capture and storage?
One of the arguments against CCS, which campaigners have been making for years, is that it is a way for polluters to keep polluting, rather than emitting less of the gases which are heating up the planet at alarming rates.
“All capture and storage projects suffer from the same problem: they distract attention and resources from cutting emissions at source and give polluting industries like fertiliser production a pass to keep on polluting,” says Rachel Kennerley, Senior International Carbon Capture Campaigner at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL).
Belén Balanyá, researcher and campaigner at Corporate Europe Observatory (CEO), has been tracking the lobbying efforts of the fossil fuel industry for 25 years. She has recently focussed on lobbying by the CCS industry. The outcomes of annual COP climate talks are known to be influenced by lobbyists representing industry. Balanyá found that around 500 CCS lobbyists were at COP29 in 2024. A year earlier, at COP28, CCS proponents (largely tied to fossil fuel industries) scored a significant win with the endorsement of “abatement and removal technologies” in the agreement.
Referring to fossil fuel industries, Balanyá says, “You look at what’s on the agenda and it’s always escape hatches to stay in business,” she tells Euronews Green. “It’s where they move when they’ve been forced to – when there’s more knowledge and more acceptance about climate change and their role and that they have to decarbonise.”
CCS being endorsed in a COP agreement may have contributed to its legitimacy in political circles within the EU. The CCUS Forum (now the Industrial Carbon Management (ICM) Forum), set up by the European Commission in 2021, is an annual event with working groups that feed directly into EU policymaking. CEO found that every group has been co-chaired by the fossil fuel industry or associated organisations.
A newly released report from the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) details the risks of overshooting 1.5°C of warming and how we can limit them. It assessed what it called Carbon Dioxide Removal and found that many issues remain with the technology, such as whether it can scale sustainably (due to costs, land and energy use), whether it would actually keep CO2 out of the atmosphere permanently and who’s responsible for regulation and leaks.
CCS: Good or bad?
Wherever commentators stand on CCS, there is some agreement that for some industries, the technology can be useful. Yara’s project targets emissions from ammonia production which “provides a relatively concentrated CO2 stream, making this one of the more straightforward industrial applications of carbon capture rather than an example of the very hardest emissions to abate,” according to Domien Vangenechten, Programme Lead in Clean Economy at E3G.
“The lesson should therefore not be that Europe needs CCS everywhere, but that we should pragmatically deploy it where it can cut substantial emissions today.”

F1: Madrid Grand Prix debut at the Madring circuit
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:24:51 EEST
18:24:51 KST

F1: Madrid Grand Prix debut at the Madring circuit
Kyiv • UNN
Madrid is hosting the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring circuit, featuring 22 turns and speeds of up to 340 km/h. The contract runs until 2035.
Formula 1 will make its debut this weekend at the new Madring circuit in Madrid, which will host the Spanish Grand Prix for the first time. The hybrid track combines public roads and private sections, features 22 corners, and on some straights the cars will be able to reach speeds of up to 340 km/h, UNN writes.
Details
What makes the new Madring circuit special for the inaugural Madrid Grand Prix
Formula 1 is debuting a new circuit on its calendar. The Spanish Grand Prix has moved from Barcelona to Madring in the country's capital, and a contract to host the event at the new Madring circuit has been signed through 2035.
Madrid hosted Formula 1 races around 40 years ago at the Jarama circuit, located 30 km north of the city. Madring is located much closer to the city center—a new complex built specifically for this purpose and quickly accessible by public transport.
Using both public roads and private land plots, the Madring circuit will combine features of a street circuit and a permanent circuit, similar to the Miami International Autodrome. Its 22 corners will vary in character, while on the straight sections the cars will reach speeds of up to 340 km/h.
Practice, qualifying and race schedule
Today, September 11, the first free practice will take place from 14:30 to 15:30. In the evening of September 11, the second free practice will take place from 18:00–19:00.
On Saturday, September 12, the third free practice will take place from 13:30 to 14:30, and qualifying will take place from 17:00 to 18:00. The race itself will take place on Sunday, September 13, from 16:00 to 18:00.
Why Madrid replaced the traditional Spanish Grand Prix in Barcelona
Madrid was awarded the right to host the Spanish Grand Prix thanks to a more attractive commercial offer, a long-term 10-year contract, and the new concept of the hybrid urban Madring circuit around the IFEMA exhibition center.
At the same time, Madrid has not completely removed Barcelona from the calendar. In the 2026 season, Spain will host two races due to overlapping existing contracts.

The St. Petersburg Metro plans to adapt nine stations for use as civil defense shelters amid growing concerns over potential emergencies and attacks, Russian media outlet Fontanka reported.
The project also covers four underground sections and around 35 kilometers (22 miles) of metro tracks, according to documents published on Russia’s government procurement portal.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On Thursday, the metro began looking for a contractor to prepare a feasibility study for the planned work. The contractor will determine which facilities need to be built, upgraded with additional equipment, or converted into protective shelters.
The study must also assess risks including changes in groundwater levels, ongoing urban development, and aging equipment.
Two emergency scenarios must be considered: an industrial disaster and a fire.
Particular attention will be paid to ventilation systems. If contaminated air enters the shelters, they must be capable of filtering out radioactive dust, aerosols, and toxic substances.
The St. Petersburg Metro had already conducted a similar price-monitoring exercise in March, suggesting the shelter preparations have been under consideration for months.
The city is also carrying out a broader inventory of civil defense shelters. Authorities inspected 2,633 sites in 2025, including standalone shelters and facilities located inside residential buildings. Officials said most required repairs.

Indonesia seeks to repatriate five baby orangutans found in Odisha; trafficking network suspected
Unknown

File photo: Five baby orangutans were discovered in a Balasore forest, baffling wildlife officials
Indonesia is working to bring back five baby orangutans found in a forest in Odisha, as authorities investigate a suspected international wildlife trafficking network that may have brought the animals thousands of kilometres from their natural habitat.The five orangutans were found by forest department officials patrolling the Jaleswar range in Balasore district on September 8. They are believed to be between one and 1.5 years old and have since been moved to Nandankanan Zoological Park in Bhubaneswar, where they are being kept in quarantine.Indonesia’s ministry of forestry said preliminary observations suggested the animals could be Sumatran orangutans, but stressed that their species and genetic origins would be confirmed through DNA testing.“Based on preliminary observations of their physical characteristics, the five animals are suspected to be Sumatran orangutans,” the ministry’s head of public relations and foreign cooperation, Ristianto Pribadi, said in statement quoted by Antara news agency.The ministry said it was coordinating with Indian authorities, including India’s CITES Management Authority, as well as diplomatic missions in Jakarta and New Delhi, Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency and its agriculture ministry to expedite the animals’ return.
The presence of the orangutans in India has raised suspicions of transnational wildlife trafficking because the apes are native only to the islands of Sumatra and Borneo. Odisha’s environment minister Ram Singh Khuntia had earlier said investigators suspected an international racket could be involved.International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under CITES, the global agreement regulating trade in endangered wildlife.Indonesian conservation groups including the Leuser Ecosystem Foundation, Indonesian Wildlife Network, Center for Orangutan Protection and Indonesian Orangutan Forum have also offered to assist with the repatriation.Once returned to Indonesia, the orangutans are expected to undergo health checks, quarantine and behavioural assessments. If they are found fit, they could enter a rehabilitation programme aimed at eventually returning them to the wild.
The case comes as orangutan populations face mounting pressure from habitat loss and other threats. The World Wildlife Fund estimates that about 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.A third species, the Tapanuli orangutan, is classified as critically endangered, with fewer than 800 believed to survive in the wild. Its entire known population lives in the Batang Toru forest in North Sumatra, an ecosystem threatened by mining, palm oil plantations and a large hydropower project.The discovery of the five infants has now prompted authorities in India and Indonesia to investigate how the animals entered India and whether they were victims of a wider international trafficking operation.

NestAI expands operations in Latvia to advance defence AI on NATO’s eastern flank

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
