====================================================================================================

The Israeli fashion empire Hollywood can’t stop wearing: Galia Lahav’s rise to the top of global bridal couture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
05:15:04 UTC
14:15:04 KST

At 37, Galia Lahav, today one of the hottest fashion designers in the world, was still teaching arts and crafts at a school in Ashdod. She was married to Natan Lahav, CEO of Yehuda Reshatot (Yehuda Welded Mesh), and raising two children.
“I was a happy woman, satisfied with what I had,” she says. “Natan and I got married very, very young. I was 20 and he was 21, and we had just completed our military service. By then our children were already growing up, and we felt it was time to slow down at work and finally start enjoying life.
“But one day I suddenly got it into my head that I wanted a third child. I told Natan, ‘Osnat is already 17 and will soon enlist in the IDF, Rani will enlist after her, and then what? You and I will be left alone in this big empty house.’ I said, ‘Let’s have another child.’ I wasn’t sure he’d be thrilled.”
Why?
“Because getting pregnant at 40 wasn’t common then. It was even considered dangerous. But Natan answered, ‘Another child? As far as I’m concerned, let’s have two more.’ That’s how Idan was born.
“During maternity leave I sat at home with him, I had time to think, and then another idea entered my head. I told Natan, ‘We’re already established, we don’t lack anything in life, so this is the time for me to fulfill the dream I’ve had since childhood.’ I told him I wasn’t going back to teaching arts and crafts and wished instead to open a fashion house.”
Four decades later, Lahav, 78, is ranked second on a global list of five leading bridal couture designers, behind American designer Vera Wang, who recently sold her brand, and ahead of Monique Lhuillier.
“All the biggest names are on that list, and among them is little Galia from Ashdod, the first and only Israeli,” she says. “Every now and then I have to say it out loud just to remind myself that this is real. Sometimes even I can’t believe how far I’ve come. I dreamed of designing in my own style, selling my work and succeeding, but I never imagined the brand would grow to this scale.”
Beyoncé, Jennifer Lopez, Sydney Sweeney, Christina Aguilera and Gal Gadot have worn her evening gowns onstage, in photo shoots and on red carpets. Paris Hilton, Millie Bobby Brown and Simone Biles chose Lahav for their weddings, as did Israeli celebrities including Eden Fines, Yuval Caspit, Naya Federman and former hostage Sapir Cohen.
Lahav herself will not volunteer the names of Israeli celebrities who spend weeks or months sitting face-to-face with her as fittings evolve into intimate conversations. Discretion, she says, is part of the job. Not every local star bothers to credit her. “It’s a shame. A compliment costs nothing,” she says. 
But perhaps the name is no longer necessary because the dresses themselves have become recognizable. When Israeli singer Netta Barzilai released the video for “Nana Banana,” for example, it seemed obvious who could have put her in a short, pink ruffled tulle dress.
“Every time I receive a photo of a bride wearing one of my dresses, it moves me,” Lahav says. “I don’t want to sound sentimental, but there really is a piece of me in every dress. Seeing the finished look fills me with pride and joy, and that’s what keeps driving me to move forward, stay ahead and create what comes next.”
The interview takes place at Lahav’s fashion house, four floors of luxury tucked among the garages of south Tel Aviv. The building has an elevator, naturally, but Lahav races up and down the stairs in heels. That is her daily workout.
During a trip to Kyoto, Japan, for the opening of another store, she slipped in the rain and broke her leg. She was flown back to Israel on an emergency flight. Five days later she was back at work, using the elevator to reach her small office in a wheelchair.
Four decades after reinventing herself from arts-and-crafts teacher to fashion designer, Galia Lahav has grown from a one-woman operation into a family empire.
Two of Lahav’s children, Osnat and Idan, had already built careers of their own in entirely different fields before leaving them to join the family business as co-CEOs. Her husband, who recently retired, also comes in once a week, she says, “bringing new ideas and initiatives.”
Their middle son, Rani, who served in an undercover Israeli military unit, later became religiously observant. “His son from his first marriage, the oldest of my eight grandchildren, has just enlisted in a combat unit,” Lahav says. “We celebrated with a good meal, and I made him the soup he loves. That’s what grandmothers do.”
There is something else many people do not know about Galia Lahav. Her blond hair may occasionally appear at fashion shows, or at a ceremony where President Isaac Herzog presented her with a lifetime achievement award marking 40 years in the fashion industry, but she rarely gives interviews.
Why?
“Because in Israel, people don’t know how to give credit.”
Galina Nimoy was born in Pinsk to Sonia (later Sarah), and Yaakov, young Holocaust survivors who clung to one another and to the hope of building a new life. “A week after they met, my father proposed to my mother. Two and a half years after their eldest son was born, they had twins, my sister Tamara and me.
“My father, who had grown up in HaShomer HaTzair (Jewish socialist-Zionist youth movement), helped Jews leave the Soviet Union and make their way to Israel illegally. Someone informed on him, and when I was a year and a half old, he was sentenced to 24 years in a harsh Siberian prison where visits were not allowed. He simply disappeared from our lives.”
“Until then we had lived in a big house. My father worked as a forest manager and earned good money. When he went to prison, they threw us out of the house and my mother was left alone with three babies, without knowing when she would ever be reunited with her husband.
“Friends urged her to place us in an institution, warning that she would never be able to raise three young children on her own. But my mother was a lioness. She told them, ‘Even if all I can feed these children is potatoes, I’ll be the one to raise them.’ She found work as a bookkeeper at a children’s home, where we were given a room to live in, and she raised us there with love.”
“We grew up poor, never knowing whether our father would come back, and surrounded by the vicious antisemitism of the postwar years. On the way to school, people would hurl slurs at us and say, ‘Why are you Jews still here? Why didn’t the Nazis finish the job?’
“It was brutal. We learned how to survive. My mother, who was incredibly strong, would always tell us, ‘One day your father will come home, and we’ll move to Palestine.’ But year after year passed, and eventually I stopped believing that miracle would ever happen.”
“When I was eight and a half, my mother received a telegram from Siberia. After Stalin’s death, some political prisoners were released, and my father was among those chosen to go free. Years later, he told us that when they informed him, he fainted. He simply collapsed from the shock.”
The reunited family then made their way to Israel. “My father arrived already fluent in Hebrew and trained as a wood engineer, a profession that was well developed in the Soviet Union because timber was widely used in construction. My mother learned Hebrew quickly and found work in bookkeeping. Compared with many new immigrants, we settled in relatively well.
“During our first year, my parents sent us to live with my father’s sister in Petah Tikva so we could improve our Hebrew. At school, a teacher asked whether I wanted to replace Galina with a more Israeli name. I told him it depended on what he had in mind. My twin sister Tamara became Tamar, which was an obvious choice. When the teacher suggested Galia for me, I thought it sounded nice.”
When her father took a senior position at a plywood factory in Ashkelon, the family moved south. “Ashkelon was very good to us. It took me about two years to fully understand what was going on in class, but we loved Israel, grew up alongside kids who had been born here and settled in well.
“After finishing high school in Ashkelon, I received a deferment from military service to attend a teacher-training college in Givatayim, where I studied arts and crafts. By the time I graduated, Natan had finished his army service and said, ‘Let’s get married.’
“It wasn’t that I was in any rush to get married at 20. And contrary to what people whispered behind my back, I wasn’t pregnant either.”
Then give me one good reason to get married at 20.
“We’d already been together for four years. Natan was my first boyfriend. When I was 16 he saw me at a party in Ashkelon and didn’t leave my side for a minute. That same evening, when he told me, ‘You’re going to be my wife,’ I replied, ‘Wait until I even agree to go out with you.’
“He began his military service in a pilot training course and had to Hebraize his last name, Lindner. As his girlfriend I told him, ‘Natan Lahav is an amazing name,’ without even imagining that it would one day be my surname too.”
Lahav began her career as a designer in the basement of the family home in Ashdod, but soon realized she needed to move closer to the Tel Aviv area. “We were looking for a house in Ramat Ef’al, near a childhood friend of mine. Then Natan took me to see a plot of land nearby, in Kiryat Krinitzi, and I pinched him hard to signal that he should put down a deposit.
“A year later, the house was ready and the basement became my kingdom. I didn’t start the business just to make money. That was never the dream. I wanted to create something of my own and enter a completely different world. If money is the only reason you work, eventually the work itself stops exciting you.”
She learned the foundations of the profession from her mother. “She was an excellent seamstress, and that was what she did to supplement the family income. By 12 I was already sewing beside my mother, and sometimes instead of her, and I was exempted from sewing classes at college.
“I always had nerve. I saw that my hand could leave a unique signature on fabric, and I knew what kind of fashion I wanted to create. I never dreamed small. My first designs were oversized sweaters, which were fashionable at the time, with fur, leather and bead appliqués. I marketed them to stores in the area that were willing to take a risk and sell something unlike anything people had seen in Israel.
“After about a year, I moved into evening gowns with appliqués, which became part of my signature style. With the help of a sales representative, I was soon selling them in about 200 stores across Israel. A few years later, the sewing room in our basement could no longer keep up with demand, so I rented a villa nearby and turned it into a studio where I could work around the clock, including on custom designs.
“That’s where I made my first wedding gown. A longtime client brought in her engaged daughter, who told me, ‘I don’t want just another white dress.’ That sentence stayed with me. At the time, Israel had bridal salons and beauty parlors catering to brides, but there was still no real destination for distinctive, fashion-forward wedding gowns.”
She unveiled her first bridal collection when Idan, her youngest child, was about 10. “I had always loved the polished, tailored French aesthetic, and my first gowns had a very romantic feel. “Then I traveled to Rome and Paris with a friend whose taste I trusted.” 
“We visited all the major couture houses, and I came back to Israel obsessed with corsets. Everyone was shocked. A corset on a bride? But I knew it could work.”
When Lahav moved the business to Tel Aviv, opening what she describes as “a huge store on Dizengoff Street,” she committed fully to couture and meticulous hand craftsmanship.
“Every dress was made by hand from start to finish. I had two or three women whose sole job was to embroider pearls, stones and beads onto the gowns. It was painstaking work. Sometimes the embroidery alone took more than two weeks, but that was what set me apart, and I loved it.
“Fashion journalists at the time didn’t understand what I was doing. They told me no sane woman would wear a voluminous princess-style wedding gown with petticoats and a corset. On the rare occasions they came to the boutique, they would say, ‘That isn’t the Israeli style. You’ll never sell it here.’ “I took the criticism quietly. I realized they simply couldn’t see the level I was trying to reach.”
What was the most insulting thing anyone said about you?
“Someone said he couldn’t write about me because I didn’t know how to read fashion. Obviously that isn’t pleasant to hear, but I never gave up.
“The vision I had in my head pushed me forward. If there are brides who love my dresses, and there is already a waiting list for upcoming events, why should I be influenced by criticism from small-minded people who don’t know how to give credit?”
Her breakthrough came when she designed evening gowns for Israel’s 2007 beauty pageant. A year later, after dressing contestants on the Israeli version of “Dancing with the Stars,” she was marked as a designer to watch.
“They finally discovered me when I was approaching 60,” she says with a laugh. “I dressed Anna Aronov and Rotem Sela in gowns with sheer looks and exposed backs, and everyone talked about the three cups I had sewn into them, at the bust and crotch.
“I felt appreciated, and even though my heart nearly burst with happiness, I couldn’t help asking myself why they had ignored me for 20 years. 
“In the bridal world in France at the time, the princess look was popular. When I brought it to Israel, people laughed at me and asked, ‘What is this?’ They only praised Shenkar graduates. Thank goodness I didn’t let the criticism influence me. I stayed true to myself.”
By then, two of Lahav’s three children had joined her at the fashion house, working alongside her from the fourth floor of the white Tel Aviv building the family calls “headquarters.” Twice a day, FedEx shipments leave from there for clients around the world, a routine that has continued even during wartime.
“When the business began to take off, I worked day and night. Nothing could slow me down,” Lahav says. “Natan supported me every step of the way and was an incredible father. Our three children grew up with a mother completely consumed by her fashion dream, because when you love what you do, there are no real working hours.
“When you’re doing what you love most, the hard work doesn’t feel like a burden. You don’t get tired of it. Even today, I can sit and sew for 12 hours straight and enjoy every minute.”
Her eldest daughter, attorney Osnat Lahav-Malkin, 56, married with one child, made a career change 20 years ago. “One day Osnat called me and said, ‘Mom, I’m tired of fighting with people. I’m tired of the office.’ So I told her to come by and see what we were doing. I said, ‘Why go work somewhere else when we already have a family business?’
“She came in with no real idea of how the fashion house worked, but quickly found her place on the business and development side. I was thrilled. I’m much more of an artist, while Osnat brought structure to the finances and schedules. We started traveling together to source fabrics, and by then I was already thinking about expanding abroad. I had no idea how to do it or where to begin, but I knew I couldn’t grow the business alone.”
Idan, 41, married with three children, joined the family business 13 years ago, almost by accident. “I definitely wasn’t planning on it,” he says. “I studied computer science at the Interdisciplinary Center and worked at several startups, including Soluto, which was later sold in a deal that also benefited Naftali Bennett. After that I launched my own startup, eventually shut it down, and one Friday afternoon I stopped by my mother’s store on Dizengoff Street just to say Shabbat shalom.
“My father was there and asked me to help him with an email problem. When I opened the inbox, I saw a flood of messages from overseas that no one had answered. I couldn’t understand why. So I replied to a woman in Canada, and suddenly we had sold a $7,000 wedding dress. It was crazy.”
The price of the dress?
“That was part of it. In the startup world, you can work endlessly, raise money from investors and still not generate a single dollar in revenue. Then, almost by accident, we discovered there was real demand for Galia Lahav dresses overseas.
“We started exploring international markets. Australia was our first stop because we were seeing a lot of online traffic from there. Our expectations were far too high, and the trip was a disaster. We didn’t sell a single dress. Then we tried England, and that didn’t go much better. At that point we were ready to give up. We thought, ‘Maybe this just isn’t going to work abroad. It’s disappointing, but it’s not the end of the world.’ Then we decided to give it one last try and went to New York. That’s where everything changed.”
All four of them went to NY. “My father was part of it too,” Osnat says. “We knew there was demand because we could see the online traffic and customers were finding us through Facebook and Instagram. We were also studying the competition. The United States was the biggest market, but much of what was available there felt fairly conventional. We were bringing something genuinely different.”
What do you mean by conventional?
“A classic gown, white or cream, weighed down by layers of petticoats. In a word, boring,” Lahav says. “Then I came in with sexy wedding dresses, open backs, halter necklines and fitted silhouettes that emphasized the body, all of them handmade.
“It took me time to understand that weddings are shaped by culture too. An American wedding might mean a reception and some dancing, something relatively short. An Israeli wedding can go on for hours, often with an after-party, so the bride needs a second, more comfortable dress for dancing, and sometimes even a third. I like to think I helped introduce American brides to sexier, lighter gowns they could actually move in.”
Ten years ago, Idan also helped take his mother’s designs to the Paris couture stage. “One day he asked me, ‘Mom, can you see yourself showing in Paris?’ I told him, ‘I’m not sure they’ll accept me. No Israeli designer has ever shown there.’
“He began corresponding with the couture federation, and we put together the fashion house’s credentials. I flew to Paris for an interview with Sharon Sever, 55, the designer I work with, who speaks French. Years earlier, he had actually been my student in elementary-school art class, and when we met again after his military service, I encouraged him to study fashion in Paris.
“A month after the interview, we got the answer: We were in. We opened champagne at the office, and for nights afterward I could barely sleep from excitement. I felt as if I had reached the very top, stepping onto the same stage as the giants. Dior, Chanel, Valentino and me. The first and only Israeli.”
Lahav prepared a spectacular collection and was greeted with applause when she stepped onto the stage at the end of the show, held at the Grand Palais, which she describes as something out of a fairy tale. “We continued flying to Paris Fashion Week every year until COVID ended the tradition.”
As social media gained power, celebrity stylists began approaching the fashion house. The stars generated valuable exposure by tagging the brand and helped elevate Lahav’s international profile. But the queen of couture herself remains surprisingly removed from the glamour.
She has never met Beyoncé or Jennifer Lopez. She did meet Simone Biles, “the tiny gymnast,” who ordered two wedding gowns. “I was in New York when Simone Biles came for a fitting, so obviously I went over and we hugged,” Lahav says. “I don’t remember whether we took a selfie.”
One celebrity with whom Lahav did form a more personal connection is Sydney Sweeney. “A few years ago, I designed a white dress for her for an event,” Lahav says. “The event was canceled before the dress was finished, but she still paid for it and kept it.
“More recently, she contacted me directly and asked for two dresses for the premiere of ‘The Housemaid.’ For one of them, I went for a timeless Marilyn Monroe look, with a sculpted bust and a pleated skirt that emphasized her waist. Everyone went crazy for that dress. Honestly, I had a feeling it would get that kind of reaction.
“I also designed a little black dress for her, but that one didn’t attract the same attention. There’s just something about Marilyn Monroe.”
The international reaction still excites Lahav. “At shows around the world, the audience treats me like a star,” she says. “Brides cry with excitement. People ask to shake my hand as if I were Oscar de la Renta.
“Israel is a young country that doesn’t have heritage brands like Mercedes, Lego and IKEA,” Osnat adds. “Our strength used to be almost entirely in high-tech, and suddenly there is a startup here made out of fabric. That is anything but obvious.”
So you became your mother’s bosses?
Osnat laughs. “Does it look like it?”
Idan adds: “Mom is the boss of everyone. She’s the real deal.”
Unlike his sister, Idan eased into the family business gradually. At first, he was drawn to the technology side, introducing new software systems and building up the company’s in-house development capabilities. “We have our own development team. Everything is done in-house,” he says.
Over time, he also came to enjoy the travel and the opportunity to meet people from around the world. But what ultimately convinced him to stay was something simpler: hearing from a satisfied customer. “There’s nothing better than getting feedback from a client,” he says. “When I read the words, ‘You made me happy,’ I realized that beyond creating beautiful dresses, we were also doing something meaningful.”
Under Idan’s leadership, five Galia Lahav flagship stores opened in Los Angeles, New York, Miami, North Carolina and London. Each store covers about 1,000 square meters and includes a bar as part of the hospitality experience.
The online system he developed supplies merchandise to about 100 stores around the world, and he is now expanding the company’s European sewing operations as it looks for ways to produce outside Israel as well.
“The world is big and Israel is small,” Galia explains. “In the 1990s, immigration from Russia brought couture seamstresses to Israel, and those who came to work with us continue sewing, sometimes even after retirement age.
“Today I search everywhere for high-end seamstresses, and there are none, just as there are hardly any shoemakers or farmers left. All the young people go into high-tech. A couture seamstress is a respected profession, and she can earn as much as an engineer.”
Today, about 90% of the company’s work is destined for customers abroad, and roughly once every two months Lahav flies to a fashion show or the opening of a new store. “I, at my age, with my terrible English, fly to Japan and China and Moscow because the distributors want to meet me,” she says.
“We were the first to identify the potential of the East. We also have our own method of working. We don’t mass-produce and we don’t have rows and rows of dresses hanging on racks. There are several samples, and we manufacture remotely according to each order.
“Every bride in the world orders according to her body measurements, in the design she imagines, and receives exactly what she pictured. We recently made a wedding dress for Millie Bobby Brown, who ordered it and had her fittings in New York. 
“If a bride imagines a dress that doesn’t appear in the catalog, we’ll offer her a custom design. And if necessary, we’ll fly anywhere in the world to dress her. ‘We’ means either Sharon, our designer, or me. Couture dresses demand couture service.”
And the price?
“Overseas, we have two lines. Galia Lahav Couture dresses range from $12,000 to $20,000, while dresses from the Galia Lahav line are priced between $5,000 and $10,000. It’s the more accessible of the two, but both perform well internationally. A dress from the regular line requires at least a week of work, while a couture gown can take two weeks to complete.”
Twenty thousand dollars for a wedding dress is...
“It isn’t cheap, but there are plenty of affluent brides around the world who want a lavish wedding and are willing to spend accordingly. Many of them also want something distinctive rather than a conventional wedding gown. They often keep the dress afterward, sometimes with the idea of passing it down to their daughters. Paris Hilton, for example, kept hers.”
And what does a Galia Lahav wedding gown cost in Israel?
“Israel is the only place where my wedding gowns are available for rent. I won’t quote a price because it depends on so many factors, but renting makes it possible for many Israeli brides to have an additional dress for dancing.
“The price goes up if a bride wants a custom design that isn’t in the collection. Put it this way: When I design for an Israeli client, I’m not doing it for the money. It’s part of the prestige of the brand. I’ve largely stopped designing evening gowns because I simply don’t have the time, but I can’t turn down a longtime client who has been coming to me for years. My Israeli brides let me into their world, into their love stories, and that brings me enormous happiness.”
What does the name Eden Fines mean to you?
“Eden has a provocative image, so everyone expected her to choose something very revealing. That was exactly why she came to me wanting a classic, more traditional and modest gown for the ceremony. She wanted that to be the surprise.
“We created a dramatic princess gown in silk taffeta, with a handmade overlay of flowers and leaves. I think she helped bring classic bridal styles back into fashion.
“After the ceremony, she changed into a cream-colored feathered gown with a swan-like look. It was sheer, with real feathers placed over the body, and she looked incredible. Later she changed again, this time into a completely sheer jumpsuit for dancing. To me, that was the look that best matched her personality.”
There is nearly a 50-year age gap between you and Eden. Did you find common ground?
“Before our first meeting, I wasn’t sure she was really our kind of client. But after seeing the sketches and after meeting with several other designers, she chose us. Why? I think she felt that we understood her vision and could make it a reality.”
And Yuval Kaspit?
“She came to me and said, ‘Galia, I want to be a bohemian bride.’ I paused. Bohemian isn’t really our style. Eventually I told her, ‘I’ll go with it, because I went through a bohemian phase myself once.’ Sharon and I traveled to a trade show in Paris, found some unusual fabrics and sent her photos. Once she approved them, we brought them back. She walked to the Chupa barefoot.”
For a designer whose business is overwhelmingly international, the impact of the war that began with the October 7 attack is an unavoidable subject. Lahav, however, says the business has largely carried on as before.
“There’s no connection between a wedding dress and a war,” she says. “When a bride falls in love with a particular dress, nothing is going to stop her. My name is displayed prominently in all five of our flagship stores, and anyone who looks me up online can see that I’m Israeli. There may be women who don’t want to buy from Israelis, but I wouldn’t know, because they simply don’t come to us.
“In the first year of the war, when flights were severely disrupted, our shipments got stuck. Somehow, we found ways to get them out of Israel so that no bride would miss her wedding day. As far as I could tell, the pace of business never really slowed.”
Osnat agrees. “If someone looks into the brand, discovers that we’re Israeli and has a problem with Israel, she probably won’t buy a wedding dress from us. But thankfully, we have enough stores and retailers around the world that we haven’t felt much of an impact.”
Lahav and her husband, who have already passed their golden wedding anniversary, live in a penthouse in Tel Aviv’s Kokhav HaTzafon neighborhood. On Saturday mornings, the grandchildren, “except the ultra-Orthodox one,” arrive with friends to use the rooftop pool.
Today, Lahav says she cannot imagine having built her life anywhere but Israel. “We had opportunities to move to the United States. When the children were young, Natan was offered a very good job managing a factory there and flew over to consider it. When he came back, he said, ‘We’re not leaving Israel.’
“I can’t see myself living anywhere else. And how could I have built the business into what it is today without my children beside me? I’ve seen colleagues with major businesses forced to shut them down because there was no next generation to take over.”
Osnat says the family’s decision to remain in Israel is deeply rooted. “My grandfather was a Prisoner of Zion. We are a Zionist family. We came here to settle the country and build industries here. That is what my parents did for years, each in their own field, and we are continuing what they started. Right now the situation isn’t amazing, and obviously we could earn more somewhere else, but money isn’t what drives us.”
Idan agrees. “Galia Lahav never went into fashion for the money. She wasn’t thinking about how much she could earn. That was never what drove her. What she had then, and still has today, is a genuine passion for designing wedding dresses. When you love what you do and can also build a successful business from it, that’s the perfect combination.”
After 30 years in bridal couture, is there still anything left to invent?
“Of course,” Lahav says. “My mind never stops working. Sometimes I dream about a completely new dress at night, and by morning I’m in the studio telling everyone, ‘This is the next collection.’
“One night I dreamed of a completely sheer dress with tiny shorts and structured cups, and I said, ‘This has to open the show in New York. We’ll put a dramatic coat over it, and at the end of the runway the model will open it.’ I had never heard a reaction like that. People were shouting ‘wow.’
“Then I started dreaming about princess gowns again. I felt fashion was circling back, so I created a collection with volume and crinolines, and it was a huge success. We also began playing with color beneath traditional white gowns, using linings in powder pink, blush and lilac. Our Chinese clients especially loved the pale blue.
“This year we introduced burgundy, with a burgundy corset and matching floral details. And I already have another surprise in the works. That one will be revealed soon. Every morning I wake up with an open mind and look for ways to speak to the next generation, to get into the heart of Gen Z.”
How?
“How did I miss Taylor Swift?” Lahav says with a laugh. “She didn’t come to me for her wedding dress, and I would love the chance to dress her someday. I may not know all her songs, but there’s no question she has a huge influence on what younger generations wear.”F

Dozens of draft dodgers arrested at border crossings ahead of Rosh Hashanah Uman pilgrimage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
05:11:08 UTC
14:11:08 KST

More than 60 draft dodgers have been arrested at border crossings since Sunday, many of them haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men attempting to travel to Uman ahead of Rosh Hashanah. Most of the arrests took place at Ben-Gurion Airport as the men attempted to leave Israel, while additional arrests were recorded at the Taba border crossing.
The IDF confirmed that dozens of draft dodgers were arrested at border crossings over the past two days but did not provide an exact number or details about the detainees. According to the military, enforcement is carried out routinely in coordination with the Population and Immigration Authority, and preparations for arrests of those who have failed to report for enlistment are adjusted based on situation assessments.
The IDF emphasized that those required to enlist can regularize their status and report for service.
The “I Entrusted Guards” hotline has meanwhile issued a warning to haredi youths at risk of arrest, urging them to avoid arriving at border crossings. The hotline warned that the risk is not limited to Ben-Gurion Airport and that attempts to leave Israel through land border crossings could also result in arrest.
The hotline claimed that young men who had already attempted to leave the country were arrested and transferred to military prison, warning that some could remain imprisoned during Rosh Hashanah. The warning comes as police continue preparations for increased activity at border crossings ahead of the annual wave of travel to Uman.
Pilgrimage has become an especially sensitive issue
Every year, tens of thousands of Breslov Hasidim from Israel and around the world travel to Uman, Ukraine, to pray at the grave of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov. This year, amid enforcement against draft dodgers, the pilgrimage has become an especially sensitive issue within the community.
Senior Breslov rabbis called on those who could face arrest not to arrive at Ben-Gurion Airport and not to attempt to resolve their status solely for the purpose of taking the flight. At the same time, an unofficial initiative has emerged within the community to hold Rosh Hashanah prayers in military prison if the trip cannot take place, in an attempt to create public and operational pressure on the IDF.
'I am willing to sacrifice my life for this'
A Breslov Hasid in his 50s who is in Uman with five of his sons told Walla: “There are boys who have been traveling every year since they were five years old. For them, getting to Uman is in their soul.”
He said some young men are following the rabbis’ instructions and will remain in Israel, while others say that they are “willing to sacrifice their lives for this.”
He described attempts to leave through various border crossings, including Egypt and Jordan, based on the assumption that screening there is less predictable. “Everyone has their own ideas. It is a game of cat and mouse,” he said.
One of his sons, 24, remained in Israel due to his military status, while two of his other sons serve in the IDF.
Military Police activity is carried out in cooperation with the Population and Immigration Authority and according to situation assessments. Enforcement takes place routinely, but forces have been reinforced ahead of the holiday.
Those who have been absent from service for a significant period are generally brought before a military court judge, and some are imprisoned. The IDF did not provide a figure for how many of those arrested were transferred to prison.
A Population and Immigration Authority official explained that the authority handles anyone who appears in the system as subject to a travel restriction, without knowing in advance the source of the order.
“If it is a military order, the army is called to the scene, and it decides whether to arrest [the person],” the official said.
According to the official, a technological change implemented during Passover now allows authorities to identify people with travel restrictions during check-in, even when the process is carried out online.
A 19-year-old traveling from Poland to Uman told Walla that the arrests have become the main topic of conversation among travelers.
“Dozens of young men are not a drop in the ocean. It is probably most of the draft dodgers who were supposed to arrive,” he estimated.

"The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests – such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea – while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges," the official said.
This comes a day after the Houthis struck the city of Mocha on the Red Sea, potentially leading to bringing the Iranian-backed Houthis closer to closing the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the same way that Iran has attempted to close the Strait of Hormuz.

Coalition strengthens as People of Israel crosses threshold, despite Likud dropping one seat - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
05:10:29 UTC
14:10:29 KST

After the submission of party lists ahead of the Knesset elections, the coalition bloc has strengthened by three seats to 50, following People of Israel’s crossing of the electoral threshold. This is according to a Maariv poll conducted by Lazar Research, headed by Dr. Menachem Lazar, in cooperation with Panel4ALL.
However, Likud has lost one seat, falling to just 19, its lowest figure since May 29, 2025. As a result, the coalition bloc has gained only three seats overall. The poll also found that after the previous survey showed the Reservists and Economic party crossing the threshold while Ofer Winter’s party did not, the two have now switched roles: People of Israel crossed the threshold, while Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha’s party did not.
The Zionist opposition bloc holds 58 seats, while Arab parties receive 12 seats. The poll also found that the number of undecided voters dropped significantly following the closing of the party lists, from 11% to 7.5%.
In response to the question, “If Knesset elections were held today, which party would you vote for?” respondents answered: Yashar 25 seats, Likud 19, B’yachad 14, The Democrats 10, Yisrael Beytenu 9, Otzma Yehudit 8, United Torah Judaism 7, Shas 7, Joint Arab List 7, Ra’am 5, Religious Zionism-Zehut 5, and People of Israel 4.
The Reservists and Economic party (3%), Blue and White (1.3%), Noam for Israel (0.7%), and the Haredi Public party (0.4%) would not pass the electoral threshold.
Eisenkot maintains double digit lead over Netanyahu
Gadi Eisenkot also maintains a double digit lead over Benjamin Netanyahu this week in terms of suitability for prime minister, with 50% saying they see him as the more suitable candidate, compared with 38% who chose Netanyahu. Naftali Bennett also leads Netanyahu in the prime ministerial suitability question, with 45% compared with 40%.
The poll also found that an overwhelming majority, 79%, said that even if the party they vote for does not become part of the country’s leadership after the Knesset elections, they would remain in Israel. In contrast, 9% said they are considering leaving the country in such a scenario, while an additional 12% said they do not know how they would act.
Among voters of opposition parties, around 15% are considering leaving in such a situation, but only 2% said they are certain they would do so.
The poll was conducted on September 9–10. A total of 4,329 people were invited to participate, and 601 respondents answered, a 14% response rate. The sample represents Israel’s adult population aged 18 and older, including both Jewish and Arab citizens. The maximum sampling error is 4%.

BJP national president Nitin Nabin, Uttarakhand CM Pushkar Singh Dhami interact with youth in Haldwani
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
05:07:03 UTC
14:07:03 KST

Uttarakhand CM Pushkar Singh Dhami and BJP national president Nitin Nabin interact with youth in Haldwani, Uttarakhand, on September 20, 2026.
HALDWANI: BJP national president Nitin Nabin and Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami took part in a youth interaction programme in Haldwani, where they discussed careers, employment, entrepreneurship, skill development, technology, sports and the future of Uttarakhand with young participants.During the interaction, participants raised questions related to the development of the state and the country. They also shared their experiences of various government schemes and offered suggestions on employment, self-employment and access to better opportunities in Uttarakhand.
Nabin cites central schemes, emerging opportunities
Nabin said that under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership, the potential of India’s youth was being given a new direction while new opportunities were being created for them. He said initiatives such as Digital India, Startup India, Skill India, Make in India and Khelo India had provided young people with platforms to advance according to their talent, capabilities and skills. He added that young people were not merely seeking employment but were also emerging as creators of jobs and new opportunities.He said the role of youth was increasing amid a rapidly changing economy and advances in technology.
According to him, new avenues had opened up in areas such as artificial intelligence, startups, innovation, digital technology and entrepreneurship. He said Uttarakhand’s young people had immense talent and potential and that connecting their energy and capabilities with the state’s development could help take Uttarakhand to new heights.He said that in a mountainous state such as Uttarakhand, it was important to expand opportunities in local employment, self-employment, tourism, skill development and entrepreneurship. He added that the ideas, suggestions and aspirations of young people could play an important role in determining the future direction of the state. He called on the youth to turn future challenges into opportunities and actively contribute to building a developed India.He also described social media as a powerful medium and said young people should use it positively for the development of society and the country. He said all 1.4 billion citizens would need to work together to realise the vision of a developed India. He also urged young people to enter politics and public life and contribute to nation-building. He stressed the importance of time management, saying effective use of time was essential for success.
Dhami highlights recruitment, self-employment
Dhami described young people as the country’s greatest strength and said India’s large youth population was providing the nation with new energy, fresh ideas and capabilities. He said the growing use of technology and innovation was also opening up new opportunities for young people.The chief minister said that after assuming office on July 4, 2021, his government began working with the resolve that “the youth and water of the mountains should both serve Uttarakhand.” He said recruitment to vacant posts in government departments was accelerated and that around 34,000 young people had so far been appointed to government services. He also referred to action against irregularities in recruitment examinations, saying members of cheating rackets had been sent to jail and that a crackdown had been launched against those attempting to jeopardize the future of young people.He said the government was not limiting opportunities to government jobs and was also focusing on self-employment, startups and entrepreneurship. He cited the Chief Minister’s Self-Employment Scheme, skill development programmes, homestays and the Chief Minister’s Udyaman Khiladi Scheme as initiatives through which young people were being provided opportunities.
Sports infrastructure, technology and investment
The chief minister said Uttarakhand was establishing a new identity in sports and that sports infrastructure was being expanded across the state. He referred to work towards setting up a Sports University in Haldwani and a women’s Sports College in Lohaghat. He also cited Uttarakhand athletes winning more than 100 medals at the National Games, describing it as evidence of the state’s growing sporting talent and changing sports environment.He said opportunities were being created for young people in tourism, local products, science, innovation, artificial intelligence, robotics and other emerging technologies. He also referred to the Investors Summit, saying it had been organized with the objective of generating new investment and employment opportunities, while efforts were under way to expand industrial activity in the mountainous regions of the state.
The chief minister said the government was also providing free coaching facilities to young people preparing for competitive examinations to help ensure equal opportunities. He added that the talent, hard work and potential of Uttarakhand’s youth were among the state’s greatest strengths in its effort to build a developed Uttarakhand.BJP state president Mahendra Bhatt, MP Ajay Bhatt, public representatives, party office-bearers and a large number of young people were present at the programme.

Quick hits: NFL goes AFL, Jonas Brothers rock, and 100k fans see rare sight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
05:02:12 UTC
14:02:12 KST

NFL MCG quick hits: Jonas Brothers sing John Farnham classic as 100,000 fans watch 49ers beat Rams
The NFL's first match in Australia lived up to the hype, with more than 100,000 fans packing the MCG to watch the San Francisco 49ers defeat the LA Rams.
There was more than just football on the field, with the Jonah Brothers rocking out at half-time and belting out one of the great Aussie anthems.
The NFL brought American flair to the MCG, but the game had a little AFL flavour.
Here are the quick hits from the historic season opener.
1. An anthem so nice he sang it twice
With the NFL playing its first ever match in Australia, it also meant that our national anthem was sung before an NFL game for the first time.
The honour of singing Advance Australia Fair was given to singer, and Commonwealth Games swimmer, Cody Simpson, and our man did us proud.
Simpson even gave the anthem a little twist at the end, this was a special occasion after all.
After completing the anthem, Simpson then sang the final two lines again, as planes flew overhead at the G.
2. A little AFL flavour at the 'G
Melbourne was getting a taste of America with the NFL.
The pageantry of pre-game, tailgates outside the MCG, and plenty of NFL fan fare.
But the NFL made sure to add some Australian flavour to its game as well.
The first points of the match belonged to San Francisco 49ers kicker Eddy Pineiro, who kicked a 20-yard field goal in the first quarter.
Officials raise their arms in their air to signify a successful kick, but for this field goal, the action was a little different.
The officials extended their arms and made the same gesture for a goal in Aussie rules, a fitting touch for any game of footy played at the MCG.
3. 100,021 fans witness a rare sighting in the NFL
The NFL came to Australia with the intention of drawing a huge crowd, and putting on a spectacle.
That was achieved, and then some, with an official crowd of 100,021 packing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground. The official capacity of the MCG is 100,024, meaning the NFL was just three shy of claiming that every seat was filled on Friday.
And those 100,021 fans got to see something that most Americans never will: the centre catching a pass.
The centre is the player who snaps the ball between his legs to the quarterback at the start of the play.
The centre has two jobs:
- Get the ball to the quarterback
- Protect the quarterback or running back
But on a historic day in Melbourne, 49ers centre Jake Brendel became the hero of big men everywhere.
Midway through the second quarter, Brendel snapped the ball to quarterback Brock Purdy, and then protected his QB by blocking Rams defensive lineman Kobie Turner.
When Purdy threw his pass down the middle, Turner was able to jump in the air and get his hand to the ball.
As the ball hung in the air, threatening to be intercepted by the Rams, Brendel quickly reacted and caught the pass for a two-yard gain.
Frankly, it was a pity the MCG crowd did not get to see Brendel cut loose for a big run, but seeing him claim the first reception of his career was a moment that would not have been on any NFL bingo cards.
4. Jonas Brothers tribute to John Farnham
The superstars at the MCG on Friday were not restricted to footballers.
American pop rock band Jonas Brothers were the headline act at half-time.
The performance, albeit short, had all the the style and chorography of the half-time show at the Super Bowl.
And there was a nice touch to an Australian legend during the performance.
The American stars sang one of the great Aussie anthems, You're The Voice by John Farnham.
The capacity crowd at the MCG was in full voice for the famous song, a great nod to one of Australia's greatest artists.
5. Kittle wants a shoey, and to go home
There are few better personalities in the NFL than star San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle.
His interviews are always a highlight, especially after a 49ers win over their rivals in LA.
Following his side's impressive 27-7 win over the Rams at the MCG, Kittle gave a trademark interview with American broadcaster ESPN.
He was asked about the Australian tradition of a shoey, which the American star claimed he wanted to try.
"Are you trying to set me up to get in trouble?" he asked the reporter when quizzed on whether he would want to try a shoey.
"Wherever I can do one, I'm gonna try to find one in the stands."
Kittle finished off his interview in similarly entertaining style.
He said how much he was excited to leave Melbourne and head home, before appearing to make sure his comment did not come across like he, and his teammates, did not enjoy their week down under.
"We embraced going to Australia — 15-hour flight, we were here the whole week — it was a grind but we did it," he said.
"We'll see you guys back in America, I can't wait to go home. I did love Australia though, this place is awesome."
We loved having you George, bar the Rams fans here who have gone through a painful defeat.

Gliders return to world stage after spell in wheelchair basketball wilderness
Australia's women's wheelchair basketball team has returned to the world stage, two years on from missing qualification for the Paris Paralympics.
It has been a lean decade for the Gliders, once considered amongst the world's best, failing to qualify for the 2016 Paralympic Games as well.
But a new dawn appears to be breaking for the team, which, anchored by an experienced core and energised by an exciting group of tournament debutants, has begun its tilt at World Championship glory in Canada.
The tournament serves as an important stepping stone for the Gliders, with the side having already set the goal of a podium finish at the Brisbane 2032 Paralympics.
Meanwhile, Australia's men's side, the Rollers, are gunning for a third World Championship title, after missing the medals in Paris.
Taking the long way around
While the Gliders have been plotting their return to the top of the international game, China has emerged as a true powerhouse of women's wheelchair basketball, having medalled at the 2021 and 2024 Paralympics, as well as the 2022 World Championships.
So, a first-round tussle with the Asian powerhouse was always going to be a tough task for the Australians, and something of a baptism by fire for their three tournament debutants.
The Gliders went down by 11 points in their opener on Wednesday night, but it was a game of real promise for the Australians, according to emerging star Katelin Gunn.
"We haven't played as well as we have against China in quite a few years," Gunn told ABC Sport from camp in Ottawa.
The meet is Gunn's first major international tournament, but she has been in and around the Gliders' set-up since making her international debut in 2022.
She was a member of the side that qualified for the tournament by the skin of its teeth late last year, triumphing in a gruelling repechage in Madrid after missing direct passage to the competition.
Head coach Jeremy Symot, who was appointed Gliders boss last year after a highly successful stint in the Australian domestic league, named the same 12-player squad for both the repechage and the World Championships.
The roster includes team legends Shelley Matheson and Sarah Vinci, who boast 40 years of international experience between them, as well as superstar centre Georgia Munro-Cook, fresh from her 3x3 bronze medal at the Commonwealth Games.
Gunn believes the squad is as strong as she has ever seen it, and that the shared experience of last November's repechage has pushed it to a new level.
"We took a lot of learnings from Spain and we will build more and more on them," Gunn said.
"In the few training sessions we've had together as a group, we have just connected more than ever."
Destination Brisbane
A 73-30 loss to Canada in their second game on Friday morning means that the Gliders now face an uphill battle to progress from Group A, with the Australians likely requiring handsome victories in their remaining pool matches.
But regardless of whether a knockout-round berth does prove elusive for the side in Ottawa, the tournament is a vital next step on the road to Brisbane 2032.
Gunn, who will be in her late 20s by the time of a potentially career-defining home Games, is aware it will take time for her team to reach its potential.
"It's all about building each game, each benchmark event, getting closer to where we want to be," she said.
"It's a slow process, but hopefully we'll be closer to where we want to be by the end of this competition."

When it's time to wash your pet's bed and how to do it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
05:00:08 UTC
14:00:08 KST

Is it OK to clean your pet's bed in the same machine as your clothes?
Have you ever run a pet bed through the family washing machine and found your favourite jumper covered in hair after a later wash?
About 64 per cent of Australians live in a household with at least one pet — mostly dogs and cats — and most of them have their own comfy beds that can get pretty funky.
Our experts say it's generally OK to clean pets' bedding in your washing machine, but there are simple ways to make sure the bed, the machine and your clothes are not ruined in the process, as well as detergent considerations for your fur baby's comfort.
Is it a hygiene problem?
While pet bedding can get quite dirty and smelly, associate professor Rietie Venter, who works on the traditional lands of Kaurna people at Adelaide University's School of Pharmacy and Biomedical Sciences, says running it through the home washing machine is low risk from a hygiene perspective.
"If you wash it separately [from your clothing], by itself, that should be absolutely fine," she says.
"If you have a heavy-shedding dog … you will have to remove the hair first, otherwise it just clogs up your machine."
Dr Venter says most of the oil, dirt, dead skin cells and microbes on the bedding go down the drain, so you're unlikely to pick up any problematic nasties if you wash your clothes in the same machine.
And while pets carry lots of microbes, she says when you cuddle them or allow them on your bed, you're exposed to the same germs anyway.
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
How to wash pet bedding in a machine
Before putting pet bedding through your washing machine, Ngunnawal and Ngambri country/Canberra-based appliance repairer Tait Leaney agrees you should brush as much hair and debris off as possible.
He also recommends doing your own washing before your pet's.
And while it may be tempting to use scented washing products to cancel out odours, University of Sydney veterinary dermatology lecturer Tina Baxter urges pet owners to avoid them, particularly when laundering dog bedding.
"[Dogs'] noses prefer smells that are often quite off-putting for us," says Dr Baxter, who also works as a vet at the university's teaching hospital at Camden, on the traditional lands of the Dharawal, Gundungurra and Dharug peoples.
"When we make decisions around washing bedding in something that smells lovely to us, the dog may very strongly disagree."
Dr Baxter recommends using enzymatic washing powders designed for humans that are "very mild" in smell.
Pet beds with removable shells can simplify the process, Dr Venter says, as the covers can be washed and dried regularly with ease.
But some beds can actually be put into the machine whole.
"Our dog … has one of those foam ones that you can just put in and … actually, it works quite well," Dr Venter says.
If you're washing a whole pet bed and you don't have a dryer, Dr Venter recommends doing it on a warm, sunny day with no rain, as the bedding needs to dry quickly so germs can't multiply in it while it is still wet.
In terms of what washing machine settings to use, Mr Leaney says it is best to follow the instructions on the bedding.
"As long as the pet bedding can withstand a hot wash, that's always going to be more hygienic," he says.
"But the hotter the wash … the harder it is on the [item being washed] and the less energy efficient it is."
Will pet bedding damage my washing machine?
Putting your pet's bedding through the home washing machine is generally fine, Mr Leaney says.
But he has had one or two pet bed-related repair jobs during his time in the trade.
"The main ones are … bedding with stuffing inside," he says.
"The washing machine will rip those up a little bit and then the stuffing ends up all through the machine."
However, if you follow the bedding's washing instructions, Mr Leaney says this scenario is unlikely.
When putting pet bedding through the dryer, as with human washing, it's important to clean the lint trap afterwards to avoid creating a fire hazard, particularly in older machines.
If you want to keep your washing machine sparkling between pet washes, Mr Leaney recommends wiping out any seals, throwing in two basic dishwasher tablets (yes, dishwasher tablets) and running a cleaning cycle (or the longest, hottest cycle you can), followed by an empty cycle to flush it.
If you've got big dogs or lots of pet bedding, he also warns not to overpack your machine, and says to check its capacity (usually in kilograms in the user guide), as it can become unbalanced, stop running, and leave you with a wet, smelly mess to deal with.
And for people who don't fancy sharing a washer with their pets, some laundromats have machines specifically for pet bedding.
How often should you wash your pet's bed?
If nobody in your family, including your pets, is immunocompromised or has allergies (for example, to dust mites, which are everywhere but can accumulate in bedding), Dr Baxter says dog bedding only needs washing "when it smells", but this will vary between animals.
She says the sniff test can also be applied to cat bedding.
"Cats are, by nature, fairly clean creatures," Dr Baxter says.
"It can probably sit there for some time without that causing any health problems."

====================================================================================================

The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills | Nils Pratley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

It’s an open secret in the energy industry that “the great grid upgrade” – the £70bn programme to rewire the nation’s electricity transmission network to enable clean power by 2030 – is running over budget and behind schedule, and may end up costing consumers and businesses more in their bills than advertised.
How far behind? How much more? It is impossible to get straight answers from the bodies overseeing the massive spending programme, which may continue at an even greater scale into the 2030s. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (Desnz), its in-house body, the National Energy System Operator (Neso), and Ofgem, the supposedly independent regulator, publish acres of information on narrow matters, but none provides a clear big-picture assessment: how is the grid upgrade really going?
Thank goodness, then, for Friday’s National Audit Office (NAO) report. The watchdog has unearthed a few hard statistics and demanded far greater official transparency. Prime minister Andy Burnham, in cost-of-living mode, should take note: trouble is brewing.
Of the 88 grid upgrade projects originally identified, 12 have already been completed (good news) and 12 have been subsumed into newer work (fair enough). But of the 56 deemed “essential” for meeting the government’s target of clean power by 2030, the NAO says 50 are “forecast to be delivered after their optimal date”. Of those, only 22 are forecast to be less than a year late; the rest are further behind schedule, with one put at between six and seven years behind.
The “optimal” date, in this context, is the date required not only to fulfil the 2030 clean power deadline but also to keep a lid on the maddening “constraint costs” – payments to Scottish windfarms to turn off when the grid can’t handle their output, plus payments to southern gas-fired generators or interconnecters to France to start supplying electricity.
On one windy day alone this week, such constraint payments reached £29m. The tally for the whole of 2026 is virtually guaranteed to top £2bn. The big worry is that the upper end of Neso’s forecast for 2030 – a colossal £7.8bn, all going on bills – might be realised if the delays worsen.
Therein lies the reason why a grid upgrade is needed in the first place: the transmission network suffered from a lack of investment, even before the switch to renewables started. The transition makes the work more urgent. But what is also revealed is a state failure, going back decades, to expand the grid to keep pace with additional generating capacity. The suspicion now is that the same mistake is being repeated.
Many construction delays can be explained, it should be said. The NAO report cites standard stuff such as acquiring land rights, obtaining planning consents and legal challenges. But then there are procurement headaches caused by the need to wait for project‑specific signoff from Ofgem. There is also global competition for equipment as other countries expand their electricity networks. According to the report, the government estimates that some kit has risen up to five times in price from 2022 levels, with delivery times becoming extended. In short, the whole thing is taking longer and costing more.
But nailing down what it implies for that original £70bn figure, and thus bills, remains impossible. Nobody, it seems, is willing to put the numbers together. This passage from the NAO report is damning: “Publicly available information gives a partial and inconsistent view of progress towards upgrading the grid. Coverage is incomplete and key delivery risk metrics are missing. As a result, the available datasets cannot be reconciled with each other or the data we received from Ofgem, Neso and Desnz, and they do not give a clear view of overall portfolio delivery status.”
The watchdog calls for Ofgem and Neso “to deliver critical projects on time and provide transparent reporting so parliament and the public can hold them to account”.
On-time delivery may already be out of reach, but the demand for greater transparency is spot-on. Ofgem should publish medium-term forecasts for electricity bills, as this column has regularly argued, because the “network costs” element – what we’re talking about in this context – is capable of being forecast. Or it should take up the excellent idea from EDF, one of the big generators and retail suppliers, for “a live, publicly accessible tracker” to “radically increase transparency on cost and ongoing construction progress” and allow a strategic review.
The political danger for the government is that, sometime around 2028, the delays and cost inflation will become impossible to ignore. Even some pro-renewables enthusiasts, who fully back the government’s stance that the upgrade is the only way to bring down electricity bills eventually, warn of a backlash if £70bn becomes a much larger number. Ministers should do themselves a favour: be open.

'The game is up': Aussie professor at centre of AI maths controversy speaks out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
04:53:36 UTC
13:53:36 KST

Racing to solve maths problems now 'pointless', says Australian at centre of OpenAI controversy
In short:
Melbourne-born Tristan Buckmaster was at the centre of a controversy this week involving one of the world's top AI companies and a previously unsolved mathematical problem.
He told the ABC the human-led academic pursuit of mathematics had now changed forever and warned of AI companies' increasing recklessness.
Professor Buckmaster says he will step back from racing to publish breakthroughs and it is time to "re-evaluate what math is".
Artificial intelligence has made the race to publish mathematical breakthroughs pointless, according to the Australian professor at the centre of a bitter dispute over a claimed solution to one of the world's most difficult unsolved mathematical problems.
"I think it's pointless. Like, I think the game is up," Melbourne-born Tristan Buckmaster told the ABC.
The New York University professor also warned Australia about the centralisation of resources into the hands of a small number of privately owned foreign companies, which were now publishing solutions to maths problems that had puzzled people for decades.
"Australia needs to think about protecting our own national interests in this world where the resources are so skewed," he said.
Professor Buckmaster said AI had become a crucial tool for research, but he had grave concerns about the recklessness of the companies building it as they competed for attention and commercial advantage.
"They have zero respect for the scientific community. I mean, it's appalling, honestly," he said.
This week, leading AI company OpenAI claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven fiendishly difficult Millennium Prize problems that come with a US$1 million reward, using AI tools.
The moment of triumph for OpenAI and the artificial intelligence industry was sullied by accusations and criticism of the company's conduct by Professor Buckmaster.
He published a public statement this week accusing the AI company of trying to gazump him and his research partner Levent Alpöge, from OpenAI's rival Anthropic, after hearing they were close to solving the problem.
Professor Buckmaster also said the company offered to let him write up their solution if he took his partner's name off the research.
Professor Buckmaster said he and Dr Alpöge had more research they could publish but questioned the point of racing ahead with it when AI could perform work that had previously occupied researchers for years.
He said there needed to be a discussion about how mathematics should operate in this new environment.
"What do we do about credit? What do we do about hiring? What do we do about PhDs?"
Professor Buckmaster said some mathematicians had stopped publicly sharing what they were working on to avoid tipping off AI companies about their plans.
He has called on academics and people from OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepMind to discuss ground rules for how they worked together.
He said the companies' power carried responsibilities that went beyond competing to solve problems before their rivals.
Credit controversy
Professor Buckmaster and Dr Alpöge both used tools from OpenAI and Anthropic as they pursued solutions to mathematical problems about how fluids move.
After months of work, Professor Buckmaster became convinced the technology could make substantial contributions to the field of mathematics.
He said AI was like a "whole team of PhD students that don't need to eat and don't need to sleep".
Building on the work of mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa, the pair found a solution to the Euler problem, a stepping stone to the Navier-Stokes problem.
Professor Buckmaster said he spent weeks checking and improving the "slop" proofs generated by AI.
OpenAI then claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes problem. It said the company's researchers guided AI agents to come up with its own solution to the Euler problem and, then, Navier-Stokes.
The company said it began its effort after hearing rumours two Millennium Prize problems had been solved, later realising the rumours related to Professor Buckmaster and Dr Alpöge.
After hearing rumours that OpenAI had started to work on this, Professor Buckmaster said he contacted OpenAI to explain their work was a personal project and that the rumours had incorrectly identified the problem they had solved.
During calls between Professor Buckmaster and representatives from the company, Professor Buckmaster said OpenAI proposed he and Dr Alpöge publish their result before the company released its Navier-Stokes result.
He said another proposal would have involved him writing OpenAI's result under his name, acknowledging the company's model, but leaving out Dr Alpöge because he worked at Anthropic.
Professor Buckmaster said he refused because he believed it would be unethical to publish the research without acknowledging both the contributions of his partner.
Loading...
Time to 're-evaluate what math is'
OpenAI's lead researcher Sébastien Bubeck previously told The New York Times the offers were intended to help Professor Buckmaster, including by providing computing resources or allowing him to write up OpenAI's proof.
He acknowledged expressing not wanting to publish a paper with an Anthropic employee.
Professor Buckmaster questioned whether OpenAI's research had benefited from their unpublished work, which they had been using OpenAI's Codex tool to help write up.
An OpenAI spokesperson denied that was the case.
"We can say categorically that it is impossible for Dr Buckmaster's Codex prompts over the last two months to have influenced the system in any way, including training," they told the ABC.
"In addition, since the completion of Navier-Stokes we have made substantial progress on another Millennium Prize problem. We are working through how to share these results thoughtfully."
For now, Professor Buckmaster said he wanted to finish existing work and support his PhD students and postdoctoral researchers, rather than chase another Millennium Prize.
"I think it's more important to re-evaluate what math is," he said.

Unknown

2026-09-11

13:52:35 KST

In brief
- Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor have commemorated the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.
- John Howard, who was prime minister at the time and on US soil, has also reflected on the tragedy.
Twenty-five years ago, the world watched with horror as two hijacked airliners plunged into the Twin Towers at the World Trade Centre in New York, part of a catastrophic attack that would kill 2,977 people and change the world forever.
A quarter-century on from the disaster that claimed lives from more than 90 countries — including ten Australians — tributes have poured in from Australian leaders and agencies.
In a video posted on social media, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called for a pause to reflect on "that darkest of days", and for Australians to think of the people across the world whose lives were changed forever "in scenes so confronting that they remain seared into our collective memory".
Albanese said that while it was a day that changed the world, the bravery seen amid the horror showed "the greater side of humanity".
"From New York to Washington, to Pennsylvania, so many people responded to terror with extraordinary courage, compassion and defiance," he said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"And together, they defined the spirit of a nation. We hold on to that, and we remember everyone who never came home from what should've been just an ordinary day in September."
Coinciding with the historic date is a new event in the relationship between Australia and the United States: the first NFL game played in Australia, held at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) on Friday.
During the game, the Australian Defence Force teamed up with its US counterparts in a flyover to commemorate the lives lost 25 years ago.
"In a powerful display of unity and skill, the Royal Australian Air Force Roulettes will fly with the US Marine Corps Ospreys, in a mixed formation above the MCG for this historic event," the ADF said in a statement, adding that the defence force would provide additional ceremonial support at the NFL match, including a Flag Party.
Opposition leader and former PM reflect
Leader of the Opposition Angus Taylor said it was "hard to believe" that the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks had arrived.
"It is hard to fathom that an entire generation of young Australians have reached adulthood who were not born on 9/11. And yet, they have grown up in a post 9/11 world — a darker world. My four children are among them," Taylor said in a statement.
"We all remember where we were, and how we received the shocking news ... Of course, this was the pre-smartphone age, and many Australians would not see the news until the following morning. I was one of them ... The entire situation was unfathomable and surreal."
Taylor went on to describe his appreciation for then-prime minister John Howard's actions.
"In America’s darkest hour, Australia heard America. Australia stood by our ally and dear friend ... It was right that Australia took the fight to the terrorists in the Middle East, regardless of the shortfalls of those campaigns," he said.
Howard was on American soil during the attack. He told ABC Radio on Friday he was preparing for a press conference in Washington DC when he was told by his press secretary a plane had hit the World Trade Centre.
"We knew then it wasn't an accident, it was something worse," he said.
The former prime minister was in the US for a visit that included talks with President George W Bush on 10 September 2001.
Howard said the significance of the event soon became apparent.
"It meant a lot to the whole world, and it certainly meant that I quickly came to realise just how important our association with the Americans was, because this powerful country had been attacked in an atrocious, cruel manner," he said.
"It meant that the world would never be the same."
Howard said the decision to follow the US into wars in Afghanistan as a result of 9/11 was the right thing to do.
"I was unhappy with aspects of the ultimate withdrawal from Afghanistan. It did look rather chaotic at the time ... overall, I don't have any regrets," he said.
It's estimated that nearly a million people were killed by post-9/11 war violence in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan between 2001 and 2003, including more than 400,000 civilians, according to research compiled by Brown University.
Taylor acknowledged the hard work of Australia's defence personnel in the wars that followed the attack, and called for a "reckoning" on present-day Islamist extremism.
"As we mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11, an atrocity committed by terrorists, and in memory of all those murdered, it is time we had a reckoning with Islamist extremism," he said.
Howard said the September 11 attacks were an unparalleled event of his prime ministership, shattering long-held notions for many around the world.
"That was the beginning of it ... That shattered the illusion, if it existed as an illusion, that we lived in a world free of terrorism," he said.
"It was an entirely new and different and horrifying and terrifying world."
— With additional reporting from the Australian Associated Press.

Russia now importing fuel from South Korea, Turkey because of Ukraine drone strikes, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
04:51:50 UTC
13:51:50 KST

Russia now importing fuel from South Korea, Turkey because of Ukraine drone strikes, report says
Russia has had to expand the number of countries it imports fuel from as Ukrainian strikes continue to hammer at the foundations of Moscow's economy, according to a new report by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) think tank published Sept. 11.
Media reports in August indicated that Russia was importing gasoline from India for the first time, but the latest report by CREA mentions that Moscow has also had to rely on South Korea and Turkey for imports.
Oil imports surged to 172,000 metric tons in August, "more than seven times the previous monthly high," reads the report.
"Russia was forced to import fuel from South Korea and buy back gasoline refined from its own crude in India," the report notes.
Turkey "appears to have started shipping gasoline to Russia, with the first cargoes arriving in September 2026."
The report mentions that Ukrainian strikes on Russia's energy industry have "turned the tables on the world's once largest oil product exporter."
In recent weeks, Ukraine has launched successful attacks against Russian energy infrastructure on a near-daily basis.
"Russia's need to buy gasoline from a refinery it partly owns in India and ship it halfway around the world using the same fleet that carries its exports has demonstrated the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on its domestic refining capacity," reads the CREA report.
According to CREA, Ukrainian strikes on the port at Novorossiysk in southwestern Russia interrupted exports for nine consecutive days, "the longest disruption since Russia's full-scale invasion began."
The oil-export Black Sea port at Tuapse, Russia's fourth-largest before 2022, "did not load a single cargo of oil products for the third consecutive month" after being struck by drones in May.
But even with some 40% of Russia's oil-refining infrastructure taken offline, Ukrainian military intelligence estimates that Russia can keep waging war through 2028.
