Five big takeaways from Trump's midterm convention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
03:31:02 UTC
12:31:02 KST

Five big takeaways from Trump's midterm convention
Sept 10 - President Donald Trump and his Republican Party wrapped up an unusual convention in Dallas on Thursday hoping to strengthen their midterm election prospects, gambling that a high-profile show of party unity will energize supporters and help Republicans defy historical midterm losses.
Here are five takeaways from the two-day convention.
RUNNING AGAINST A 'SOCIALIST HELLSCAPE'
The Republican National Committee had billed the convention as a chance to refocus voters on Trump's political agenda and tout the party's policy successes.
But Trump and many other speakers on the convention stage focused most of their time on attacking Democrats as left-wing extremists and dangerously un-American. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Democrats of wanting to turn the country into a "socialist hellscape."
The tactic of attacking political opponents and injecting fear into an election campaign is a strategy deployed by both parties for decades. Trump has long made issues such as crime and immigration central to his political appeal.
The focus on Democrats underscored the political challenges confronting Republicans as they seek to defend their congressional majorities. With dissatisfaction over high prices and the war in Iran weighing on Trump, speakers repeatedly argued that Democratic control of Congress would pose the greater risk.
IT'S THE ECONOMY, STUPID
The gathering took place against the backdrop of growing unhappiness over Trump's stewardship of the economy and his inability to bring down high prices on gasoline and groceries.
Trump has been under pressure from White House aides since last year to talk more about the economy. Yet as he has done for months, Trump said little about the pain Americans are experiencing from the high cost of living.
Instead, he said concerns about inflation were exaggerated, after a summer in which opponents say he has appeared more focused on renovation and legacy projects in Washington including his White House ballroom.
In his Wednesday night speech Trump again said that the word "affordable" was "fake" and that it was Democrats who caused high prices.
"I'm bringing prices way down," Trump said, a statement that jars with government economic data.
Trump and other speakers did tout his 2025 tax cuts, which led to larger refunds from the tax-collecting Internal Revenue Service this year for many families, and his efforts to reduce drug prices.
'PRETEND THAT I'M ON THE BALLOT'
Trump and many Republicans believe that his MAGA supporters are less likely to vote when he is not on the ballot, as will be the case in November.
"Pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump said to cheers. But Democratic strategists may well have had more reason to celebrate, viewing his determination to put himself at the center of the campaign as advancing their effort to make the election a referendum on an unpopular president.
Trump's strategy is a gambit that risks turning off critical swing voters needed to win congressional races but who have drifted away from Trump and his party over a range of issues, including the economy, the war and immigration raids.
BIG-TICKET PROMISES
Trump used the speech to make several ambitious promises, some of which may be difficult to deliver.
The most extraordinary was a proposal to pay every U.S. adult a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if Republicans win the elections and retain their control of both houses of Congress.
The proposal faces the same obstacle as Trump's previously floated $2,000 tariff rebate, which never won congressional approval: persuading lawmakers to support a measure that could cost more than $1 trillion.
Trump also promised that oil prices would drop "as soon as we win the war with Iran," which he predicted would end "right after Election Day," November 3.
The conflict has shown little sign of ending since the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February, frustrating Trump's efforts to bring it to a close either through military pressure or diplomatic negotiation.
POSSIBLE START OF JD VANCE'S PRESIDENTIAL CAMPAIGN
If Republicans lose one or both chambers of Congress in November, it will likely intensify a simmering debate over who will succeed Trump as the party's presidential candidate in 2028. A central figure in that discussion is Vice President JD Vance.
On Thursday night, Vance delivered a keynote address that offered a glimpse of how he might position himself should he seek the presidency. While embracing Trump's populist politics and combative attacks on Democrats, he devoted far more time to themes of family, faith and children's futures than Trump typically does, casting the election as a fight to preserve what he called Americans' "birthright."
Vance was greeted by chants of "48, 48" – a reference to the idea he could be the 48th U.S. president after Trump, the 47th. "We got to take care of business this November, then we'll worry about what comes next," he said.
A key unknown is whether Trump will eventually anoint a successor, and the president gave no hint of his thinking when he took the stage after Vance. His endorsement could carry enormous weight after a decade in which he reshaped the party and built a fiercely loyal base of supporters.
Trump, speaking to reporters later as he boarded Air Force One to return to Washington, said Vance did "very well" and was a "very talented guy."
"He's been a great vice president, and I think he did a very good job," Trump said. REUTERS

Im Raum stehen drei konkrete Szenarien für eine mögliche Machtablösung. Vom freiwilligen Rücktritt bis zum konstruktiven Misstrauensvotum.
Im 200-Sekunden-Interview stellt sich der CDU-Spitzenkandidat in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Daniel Peters, der drängenden Vertrauensfrage. Er erklärt, warum die Partei trotz drohender Einstelligkeit an ihrem Kurs festhalten will und welche Rolle die Polarisierung durch SPD-Ministerpräsidentin Manuela Schwesig im aktuellen Wahlkampf spielt.
Zudem richtet sich der Blick auf den 25. Jahrestag der Terroranschläge vom 11. September. Aus Washington ordnet Jonathan Martin ein, wie das historische Trauma die amerikanische Gesellschaft bis heute prägt und welche tiefgreifenden Auswirkungen dieses Erbe auf die aktuelle Politik von Donald Trump hat.

The acceleration of persistent inflation components, fuel deficit pressures, the ruble weakening and unpredictability around budget parameters have limited the scope for additional monetary easing, analysts say.
At the previous meeting in July, the CBR cut the key rate for the fifth consecutive time this year, lowering it by 0.25 percentage points to 14%. The regulator said that the accelerated price growth during the summer months was largely attributable to one-off factors, while underlying inflation indicators remained within an annualized range of 4-5%. At the same time, the Bank of Russia raised its 2026 inflation forecast to 6-7% as it highlighted the need for a more gradual monetary easing path.

Researchers eye AI revolution in natural disaster forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
03:20:00 UTC
12:20:00 KST

Researchers eye AI revolution in natural disaster forecasts
- Researchers in Switzerland are using AI and NASA's vast climate data on a supercomputer called Alps to revolutionise natural disaster forecasting.
- AI models can rapidly produce global weather forecasts in minutes and detect early warning signs of disasters like glacier collapses.
- This approach could improve early warning systems, potentially saving many lives by enabling faster and more accurate disaster prevention.
AI generated
LUGANO – A revolution in forecasting natural disasters is under way, say researchers in Switzerland who are training AI models on vast troves of NASA climate data to produce potentially-lifesaving data at lightning speed.
They are feeding the NASA file stash into one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers so artificial intelligence can speed up and expand vital weather and climate forecasting, and spot patterns scientists could not have seen.
AI models are increasingly used in weather and climate forecasting and for early detection of natural hazards.
As well as speed, they carry the promise of spotting previously imperceptible patterns in satellite and other data, potentially making it possible to flag in advance disasters like Nepal’s devastating flood, which in August left thousands dead or missing.
But training such AI models requires vast amounts of high-quality climate and Earth observation data, and significant computing power.
Researchers at Switzerland’s Federal Institute of Technology Zurich (ETH) say they now have both, after copying around 100 petabytes of publicly available NASA data onto servers adjacent to one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, known as Alps.
“This is a huge scientific opportunity,” said Thomas Schulthess, an ETH computational physics professor and head of the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre (CSCS) in the southern city of Lugano.
Standing in front of rows of what look like giant filing cabinets that contain Alps, he told AFP he was excited to have all of NASA’s climate data plugged directly into the machine.
“It’s really enabling scientists to do things we would not even have thought of before,” he said.
Data is ‘everything’
It took approximately a year to copy the roughly six billion NASA files onto servers connected to the supercomputer, said Reto Knutti, a climate physics professor who heads ETH’s Centre for Climate Systems Modeling (C2SM).
That is equivalent to around 20 million feature-length films in terms of data volume, or around a million times the storage on a typical computer, he told AFP.
Now the researchers are using the mass of information to develop AI models that can speed up and expand vital weather and climate forecasting.
“Data is essentially everything,” Knutti said.
“The next step will be making sense of the data.”
That is where the proximity to the massive computing power of Alps comes in, Schulthess said, nodding to the clusters of servers humming loudly just metres from the supercomputer.
“It matters whether you can move the data within a few seconds or whether you have to wait days for the data to come,” he said.
New AI-generated statistical models are far faster than the traditional process of using mathematically equations to simulate the complex processes taking place in the oceans and atmosphere.
There is “a revolution in weather forecasting”, Knutti said, describing the statistical models as “really, really powerful” and “incredibly fast”.
‘Save lives’
Instead of the hours traditionally needed to produce a forecast, a statistical model based on pattern recognition “can run a global weather forecast for multiple days – the whole globe – in a minute or so”, he pointed out.
And while expensive to train, the models are “cheap to run”, he said, meaning “you can do more iterations, maybe every few minutes, to see if some specific weather pattern exists”.
“That allows us to do early warning systems to save lives.”
Not all disasters are foreseeable but those that relate to geology, like landslides and glacier collapses, can often be detected early in the data, if there is capacity to spot the pattern.
Kutti pointed to the case of the Swiss village of Blatten, which was wiped out by a dramatic glacier collapse in May 2025, “that was visible in satellite data more than a year before it actually happened”.
Thanks to close monitoring, Swiss authorities evacuated the village a week before the collapse, avoiding mass casualties.
Closer monitoring could also possibly have sounded the alarm before the devastating Aug 26 glacial collapse on the Nepal-China border.
Nature reported last week satellite image analysis showed some warning signs before the disaster, which, had they been spotted, could have flagged the area “as a hotspot warranting closer attention and monitoring”.
Knutti agreed that this was a good example of how satellite data could potentially be used for “systematic observing systems for disaster prevention that could save hundreds or thousands of lives”. AFP

Defamation lawsuit by former Nickelodeon producer Dan Schneider is thrown out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
03:20:00 UTC
12:20:00 KST

Defamation lawsuit by former Nickelodeon producer Dan Schneider is thrown out
Julia Jacobs
- A California appeals court dismissed Dan Schneider's defamation lawsuit against the creators of "Quiet on Set," which portrayed his workplace behaviour but did not explicitly accuse him of child sexual abuse.
- The court ruled the documentary clearly separated Schneider's misconduct, such as harassment and toxic behaviour, from the child sexual abuse allegations against others.
- Schneider's lawyers expressed disappointment and may appeal, but the court acknowledged that no evidence of Schneider's sexual abuse was presented in the series.
AI generated
NEW YORK – A California appeals court on Sept 10 dismissed a defamation lawsuit filed by the television producer Dan Schneider against the creators of Quiet On Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV, a documentary series that aired accounts of sexual abuse and other inappropriate behaviour on sets at Nickelodeon.
Schneider – who was behind a string of Nickelodeon hits such as All That, The Amanda Show and Drake & Josh – sued in 2024, alleging that the series and its trailer had falsely implied that he had sexually abused children.
The five-episode series had focused partly on Nickelodeon employees who had been convicted of child sex crimes, but the accounts of Schneider’s behaviour did not include allegations of sexual abuse.
In interviews for the series, former employees denounced Schneider as a volatile boss, and objected to sexualised humour in his shows and inappropriate jokes in the writers’ room.
After the series aired in 2024 on what is now HBO Max, Schneider apologised for some of his behaviour on the job, including soliciting massages on set.
But he later filed a defamation suit that accused the series – which he called a “hit job” – of improperly conflating him with those who had been convicted of abusing children.
It pointed in part to the series’ trailer, in which a series of photos and video clips of Schneider are followed by the advertisement of a “true crime event”.
A state court allowed the suit to proceed, finding that a “reasonable viewer” of the series might conclude that it makes “damning implications” about Schneider’s conduct.
In reversing the decision on Sept 10, a three-judge panel with the appellate court determined that the series “clearly distinguishes between the lamentable conduct that its participants attribute to Schneider – gender discrimination, harassment, toxic workplace behaviour and inappropriate sexual innuendo – and the child sexual abuse explicitly attributed to three named individuals”.
Gerry Silver, a lawyer for Schneider, said in a statement in response to the ruling that they were disappointed by the decision and were considering whether to appeal.
“However,” the statement went on, “we are pleased that the court acknowledged that the makers of Quiet On Set presented absolutely no evidence that Dan was sexually abusive towards any of his cast members and agreed that any such allegation is provably false.”
The listed defendants in the case include Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns HBO Max, and Maxine Productions, which produced the series. Representatives for the companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The series included the information that before Schneider and Nickelodeon parted ways in 2018, an investigation into his conduct “did not find any evidence of inappropriate sexual behaviour” or “inappropriate relationships with children”.
The investigation by ViacomCBS, the parent company of Nickelodeon, did find that many people Schneider worked with considered him verbally abusive.
In arguing that viewers had come away from the series with a false impression, Schneider’s lawyers cited online commentary such as a social media post that said: “Dan Schneider needs to be in prison Immediately.”
But the appellate court declined to consider such posts relevant in making its decision.
“Mr Schneider’s attempt to find an alternative meaning than what is expressly stated in the documentary is unavailing,” the appellate ruling said.
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Spanish lawmakers back citizenship for Saharawis

Unknown Publisher

Spanish lawmakers back citizenship for Sahrawis
September 11, 2026
Spanish lawmakers on Thursday voted to grant citizenship to people born in Western Sahara under Spanish colonization — a region now that is now largely controlled by Morocco.
The move could test Madrid's already delicate relations with Rabat, especially after the border crisis in Ceuta.
The lower house approved the bill by:
- In favor: 168
- Against: 31
- Abstentions: 145
The legislation would grant Spanish nationality to Sahrawis born before September 29, 1977, and allow their descendants to obtain citizenship through naturalization.
Estimates of those eligible range from around 70,000 to more than 100,000.
The legislation must now pass the senate to become law.
Morocco claims sovereignty over Western Sahara
Spain's ruling Socialist Party and its left-wing coalition partner Sumar supported the measure, while the conservative People's Party abstained and far-right Vox opposed it.
Sumar lawmaker Tesh Sidi, the first woman of Sahrawi origin to serve in parliament, said the legislation restores the "Spanish national identity card to those Sahrawis who once held and from whom this state took it away."
Spain controlled Western Sahara until 1976. Morocco claims sovereignty over the territory, while an indigenous resistance group, the Polisario Front, seeks independence.
Morocco occupies almost all of the territory. Meanwhile, the Polisario Front across the border in the Algerian town of Tindouf, where tens of thousands of displaced Saharawi people live in refugee camps.
The region remains on the United Nations' list of non-self-governing territories.
How the Ceuta influx raised tensions
The vote comes amid renewed tensions between Madrid and Rabat following a large influx of migrants into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta in July.
Scores of migrants died in their attempt to reach EU territory, most by drowning.
Although most of those who breached Ceuta's borders have returned, thousands remain, many of them unaccompanied minors living in dire conditions.
The incident caused a major rift among EU member states, most publicly between Spain's left-wing government and Italy's far-right leadership.

Eight percent of adult Jewish Israelis have visited the tomb of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov at least once in their lives, according to data collected by the Israel Democracy Institute throughout July and August 2026. The data, summarized in a Wednesday report, is part of a study that will be published by IDI in the coming months and edited by Ariel Finkelstein, Shlomit Ravitsky Tur-Paz, and Ya’ari Padan.
Uman is a pilgrimage site that is visited by thousands of religious Israeli Jews annually, despite the ongoing war between Ukraine and Russia and safety concerns pertaining to travel in the country.
Breslov hasidim traditionally spend Rosh Hashanah at the grave of Rabbi Nahman of Breslov, something that has not changed in the last couple of years since the start of the Russia-Ukraine war.
Rosh Hashanah, or the Jewish New Year, begins at sundown on Friday, September 11.
Tens of thousands of Israelis travel annually to Uman for Rosh Hashana
Israeli pilgrims make up the largest group attending Uman for Rosh Hashanah. Numbers have grown dramatically since the 1990s, with tens of thousands traveling annually. Many travel through organized groups that handle visas, accommodation, and logistics, often coordinating with Ukrainian authorities and local volunteers for safety and support.
Of those who have visited already, nearly half of Israelis polled in the summer of 2026 say they return to Uman once every few years, while another 22.5% say they visit at least once a year.
The report also noted that 13% of Mizrahi Jews have visited Uman compared to only 5% of Ashkenazi Jews and 4% of those with mixed ethnic backgrounds.
Among women who have visited Uman, only 23% have visited the tomb of Rabbi Nachman during Rosh Hashanah, while the remainder have visited at other times of the year, according to the IDI report.
Deleted IDF video instructed haredi draft evaders how to avoid Ben-Gurion checks
An official IDF social media channel in August published a video advising haredi (ultra-Orthodox) draft evaders how to avoid arrest at Ben-Gurion Airport.
The video was later deleted after Army Radio reported it and the station asked the IDF about it.
In practical terms, the video tells haredi men facing a departure restriction to report to the recruitment office before traveling to Uman, allowing them to avoid detention at Ben-Gurion Airport.
It is unclear whether the IDF has a mechanism to prevent someone from reporting for the initial summons, avoiding a departure restriction, traveling to Uman, and then failing to complete the subsequent enlistment process upon returning to Israel.

Antisemitic conspiracy theories blaming Jews and Israel for the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks have resurfaced on social media ahead of the day’s 25th anniversary.
CyberWell, an Israeli non-governmental organization dedicated to fighting antisemitism online, recently identified numerous posts across Meta, Reddit, TikTok, and X/Twitter claiming Jews had planned 9/11, knew the attacks were coming, or secretly had a hand in controlling the terrible events.
Some of the posts used a juice box emoji to subtly refer to the Jewish people in a way that would prevent the post from being flagged by the sites' moderation systems, according to CyberWell.
Others were more direct, pairing images of 9/11 alongside the antisemitic “Happy Merchant” caricature, explained CyberWell, while others still targeted individual Jews directly, calling them antisemitic slurs and accusing them of being involved in the terror attack.
CyberWell noted that some of the posts also recycled the “Dancing Israelis” conspiracy theory, which claims that Israeli men seen near the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001, had advance knowledge of, celebrated, or were involved in the attacks.
Additional posts invoked American billionaire Larry Silverstein, alleging that his absence from the Twin Towers that morning was because he knew of the attacks ahead of time.
Jews account for roughly 10% of 9/11 victims
“September 11th was a horrific terrorist attack on a global scale against the entire free world,” said CyberWell CEO and Founder Tal-Or Cohen Montemayor. “According to US State Department figures, an estimated 200 to 400 Jews died at the World Trade Center, including five Israelis, meaning Jews accounted for roughly 10% of the victims.”
“Those trafficking in conspiratorial hatred online around the 25th anniversary of September 11 undermine the true lessons of this tragic event and tarnish the memory of its victims and the brave first responders who risked their lives to save others.”
“The outrageous and false conspiracy blaming Jews and Israel for the 9/11 attacks continues to spread widely online, amplified by engagement algorithms and, in part, by a lack of effective platform policies to address it,” Cohen Montemayor explained. “CyberWell has recently tracked significant increases in scapegoating of Jews for major world tragedies, yet very few platforms directly address this form of hatred in their Trust & Safety policies.”
She noted that “as AI and LLMs increasingly rely on social media data for training and as a source of knowledge, the risk of antisemitic conspiracies and bias being absorbed and reproduced as fact increases.”
“On the anniversary of 9/11, we must keep national security top of mind,” Cohen Montemayor added. “Foreign state actors are backing and amplifying wild antisemitic conspiracy theories that scapegoat Jews in order to erode social cohesion and security in the West.”
“As major social media platforms increasingly automate content moderation with AI, expert partners who can recognize how antisemitism evolves through coded content and new forms of scapegoating are increasingly vital to effective enforcement against conspiracy theories and disinformation campaigns designed to destabilize societies and sow hatred,” she said.

Editor’s Notes: The Rosh Hashanah accounting of leadership - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
03:08:29 UTC
12:08:29 KST

A newsroom colleague sent me a Facebook page this week. It is called Bulletin Network, it has about 53,000 followers, and it looks like a legitimate news site.
It posts only photographs and short captions about Israeli soldiers and police officers who were killed. Some of the posts are recycled from incidents years ago. Others are made up.
If I knew nothing about Israel, I would probably believe it. In the age of AI, pages like this are cheap to run, and there are countless others. Even harder are the stories that might be true.
Based on a new book by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval, Haaretz this week reported that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed had called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about 10 days before the October 7 massacre and warned him that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major move against Israel.
Within a day, the question had three answers: Netanyahu’s office called the report an “absolute lie.” An Emirati source confirmed it to Hebrew media. The UAE issued a statement that neither confirmed nor denied it.
The job of our newsroom is to tell readers what happened. Going into Rosh Hashanah, I have to admit that on some of the year’s biggest questions, I don’t know.
I don’t know whether that call took place. I don’t know whether Netanyahu wanted the hostages home as badly as he said; some Israelis are certain he did not, and others are just as certain he barely slept until they came back.
I don’t know whether the war with Iran that Israel and the United States launched in February was a victory. The White House declared one, but months later, Iran was still firing at ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
I am sure of one day. On October 13, 2025, the eve of Simchat Torah, the holiday on which Hamas attacked two years earlier, the last 20 living hostages came home. Hamas released them in two groups, two hours apart, in exchange for nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees.
Before the second group left Gaza, Hamas put the hostages on video calls with their families and asked them to send the calls to the Israeli press. The whole country watched, nervous for people most of us had never met.
That morning, US President Donald Trump landed in Israel for his first visit of his second term. He met hostage families and spoke in the Knesset.
He then flew to Sharm el-Sheikh, where more than 20 world leaders gathered for the signing of the Gaza agreement. The day felt surreal. We at The Jerusalem Post were honored to document it as it unfolded.
I judge Trump by what he does rather than what he says, because following what he says will make you dizzy. On October 13, the deal he pushed for brought the hostages home.
That day was the exception. Most of the year was filled with fog, and fog is good for leaders who shout.
Why does the fog help the tough guy?
When nothing can be confirmed, people want someone who sounds sure. The leader who speaks with certainty offers relief, regardless of whether he turns out to be right, and his contempt for opponents can look like conviction.
Next to him, the leader who says a problem is complicated, or who listens before deciding, looks weak.
The fault starts with us. Politicians perform toughness because we reward it. We share the clip in which a minister flattens an interviewer, and we cheer for the communal leader who picks the loudest fight.
Israel needed a strong leader who would not have to take the Knesset, the press, or public opinion into account, 41% of Israelis told the Israel Democracy Institute in 2014. By 2021, 57% said so.
Jews abroad have their own version in the online voices and organizational figures whose followings grow with every enemy they name.
Toughness has looked like strength for a long time. In the First Book of Kings, after Solomon dies, the tribes of Israel gather at Shechem to crown his son Rehoboam and ask him to lighten his father’s heavy yoke.
Solomon’s elders tell him that if he serves the people that day and answers them kindly, they will serve him forever.
The young men he grew up with tell him to promise scorpions where his father used whips. He takes their advice, the northern tribes answer, “To your tents, O Israel,” and the kingdom splits in two for good.
Judged by deeds
In January 1952, some 15,000 people rallied in Jerusalem against Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion’s plan to accept reparations from West Germany, seven years after the Holocaust. Menachem Begin, leader of the opposition Herut party, addressed the crowd, and protesters marched on the Knesset and threw stones through its windows.
Ben-Gurion argued that the murderers should not become the heirs as well, and the Knesset approved negotiations in a 61-50 vote. The money paid for fuel and raw materials the young state needed.
A quarter century later, Begin, by then prime minister, handed back the Sinai for peace with Egypt, settlements included, over the fury of much of his own camp.
Neither man was gentle. Each is remembered for a decision large parts of the country hated, which they each had explained and then lived with.
The elders at Shechem advised listening, and Ben-Gurion and Begin defied a crowd, but both served the people’s interest rather than the leader’s image.
I think leadership is all of it: making the wise decision when it is unpopular, listening to the people you lead, understanding that most problems worth solving are complicated, and leaving people stronger than you found them.
I can’t hand readers a verdict on 5786. Some of the answers may never come. What I can offer is the rule I use for Trump, applied to everyone: Watch what they do.
The Rosh Hashanah prayers are built around kingship. On Saturday and Sunday, Jews will crown one King and ask to be judged, and the remembrance section of the Musaf (additional) service says the record of every creature comes before God, each person’s deeds and his reckoning.
The verdict on this year is not ours to deliver, but what we reward is up to us. The leader who admits what he doesn’t know and makes the hard call away from the cameras should count for more than the one who shouts best.
Before we share the next clip, or the next post from a page we have never heard of, we can ask what the person in it has done.

2026-09-11
03:08:28 UTC
12:08:28 KST

As Rosh Hashanah and the 25th anniversary of 9/11 coincide, Israel enters an election season with every reason to argue and every reason to remember what has endured.
Israel enters 5787 scarred by nearly three years of war and division, yet stronger, more capable, and more deserving of national confidence than our daily politics often allow us to feel.
Rosh Hashanah arrives this year at an unusual junction. Friday marks 25 years since the September 11 terrorist attacks. By sunset, Jews in Israel and around the world will begin the new year.
Americans remember September 11 as a day when complacency was shattered in a few terrible hours. They also remember what followed: strangers helping strangers, political differences briefly shrinking, and a society discovering reserves of courage it had forgotten it possessed. That unity did not last. Few moments of national unity ever do.
Israel learned its own version of that lesson on October 7, 2023. The failures of that day will take years of investigation and accountability to address. Yet the response revealed something equally important.
Israelis who had spent the previous year demonstrating against one another reported for reserve duty together. Communities opened homes to evacuees. Volunteers built supply networks overnight. Jews abroad raised money, came to Israel, and defended it publicly.
Nearly three years later, the emergency that began on October 7 is giving way to a different chapter. The wounds remain. Families mourn. Soldiers are still serving on dangerous fronts. Israel faces enemies that have neither disappeared nor abandoned their ambitions.
First Rosh Hashanah since October 7 attacks with no hostages in Gaza
Still, this Rosh Hashanah carries a fact worth stopping to appreciate: For the first time since the October 7 massacre, no hostage remains in Gaza. The last was brought home in January. The country fulfilled a basic obligation to bring its people back, living and dead.
That gives Israel room to begin asking what comes next. On October 27, Israelis will hold the first national election since the massacre. It will, and should, involve fierce arguments.
There is plenty to fight over: responsibility for October 7, Gaza, Iran, military service, religion and state, the courts, the economy, settlements, relations with the United States, and Israel’s relationship with the Jewish world.
These are real disagreements, and voters should demand real answers. The danger is allowing an election to persuade us that the people voting differently are themselves the problem.
Israel has spent too many years being told that everything depends on defeating the other half of Israel. The Right cannot build a country without the Left and Center. Secular Israelis cannot build it without religious Israelis. Haredim cannot separate their future from the wider Israeli public. Jewish Israelis cannot ignore the Arab citizens with whom they share this state. None of these groups is going anywhere after October 27.
Israeli society continued over past year despite political strife
That is also why this is a year to recover some Zionist confidence. Look at what has survived the past three years:
Children kept being born. Immigrants kept arriving. Hebrew culture kept producing music, books, television, arguments, and jokes. Researchers kept working. Businesses reopened. Communities began rebuilding. Reservists returned from months of service and went back to their families and jobs, often alongside people whose politics they cannot stand.
This is what sovereignty looks like in real life. It is noisy, exhausting, and frequently disappointing. It is also an achievement that generations of Jews could only imagine.
For Jews abroad, the past year has brought antisemitism, hostility toward Israel, and bitter arguments inside Jewish communities. Rosh Hashanah offers a chance to remember that the relationship between Israel and the Diaspora is larger than any Israeli government, American administration, or political dispute. We remain parts of one people, responsible for one another.
Zionism has survived wars, terrorism, diplomatic isolation, economic crises, and bitter internal divisions. It survived October 7. It will survive an election campaign.
5787 will contain an election, arguments, and probably more unpleasant surprises. The test is whether in a year from now, we will still recognize one another as partners in the same extraordinary enterprise: building and defending a Jewish state that remains democratic, confident, decent, and strong.
That is something worth believing in as the shofar sounds and a new year begins. Shana Tova.

Brics summit: What’s on agenda as world leaders gather in Delhi amid global tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
03:08:15 UTC
12:08:15 KST

File Photo: Delhi gears up to host 18th BRICS Summit as global leaders begin arriving
The 18th Brics Leaders’ Summit is scheduled to be held in New Delhi on September 12 and 13, with leaders of the expanded grouping set to discuss global governance, multilateralism, trade, investment, technology, food and energy security, health, disaster resilience and critical supply chains. The summit will also take up major global and regional developments, including geopolitical conflicts and disruptions to global trade and energy routes.The summit is set to begin on Saturday, September 12, with a closed-door meeting of BRICS member countries at 2.35 pm on “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism”. Leaders will then visit the Bharat Innovates Exhibition at 4.25 pm, followed by the official family photograph and a joint tree-planting ceremony at 5.05 pm. Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host a gala dinner for the participating leaders at 7.30 pm.
On Sunday, September 13, leaders of BRICS member countries, partner countries and outreach invitees will begin arriving at 9.55 am. The official group photograph is scheduled for 10.35 am, followed by the main open session at 10.50 am, titled “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth”.
The summit will conclude with the New Delhi Declaration.
Delhi turns into a security fortress
With a large number of foreign leaders and senior dignitaries converging on the capital, Delhi has been placed under a multilayered security grid for the summit.Around 15,000 Delhi Police personnel and 200 companies of paramilitary forces have been deployed, while 500 CCTV cameras have been installed across key locations for round-the-clock surveillance.Security arrangements are particularly tight around the diplomatic enclave and the hotels where visiting leaders will stay. China, Russia and Iran have been allotted separate hotels, with security teams from the respective countries also reaching Delhi ahead of their presidents.The heightened security measures extend beyond the summit venue. The DGCA has restricted certain flying activities across seven northern states, while the use of light and micro-light aircraft, UAVs and similar aerial vehicles has been prohibited within a 300-km radius of Delhi for 52 hours from Friday.Traffic and public movement are also expected to be regulated around key routes and venues during the summit. The New Delhi railway station will see changes to train operations over the summit period, including cancellations, diversions, rescheduling and regulation of services.
The summit is expected to draw a sizable international media contingent, with around 1,200-1,300 journalists expected to cover the event. Delhi has also been decked up for the summit, with Bharat Mandapam at the centre of the two-day diplomatic gathering.
Who arrives when
The following is the arrival schedule provided for media coordination, with ETAs and designated airports:September 10

11.05am: Le Minh Hung, Prime Minister — Vietnam — T3, IGI Airport

4.10pm: Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, President — Kazakhstan — AFS Palam
9.00pm: Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, Minister of Foreign Affairs — Saudi Arabia — AFS Palam
The big arrivals
Putin was the first major head of state to arrive, landing at AFS Palam early morning on September 11. PM Modi is also scheduled to meet the Russian president today. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is arriving at Palam at 2 pm, is scheduled to meet PM Modi in the evening.Xi Jinping arrives at 12.25 pm on September 12, with the Chinese president's visit marking his first trip to India in seven years. PM Modi and Xi are scheduled to hold bilateral talks at 6 pm on Saturday.South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres are among the other prominent arrivals listed in the schedule.

Vance blasts Democrats' 'hate' in fiery Republican convention speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
03:00:03 UTC
12:00:03 KST

US Vice President JD Vance has accused Democrats of running on "hate" and urged voters to send them packing in November, using a prime-time convention speech to rally Republicans ahead of the midterm elections.
Taking the stage on Thursday in Dallas to a huge roar and chants of "JD! JD!", Vance sought to sharpen a convention-long portrayal of Democrats as extremists, saying disagreements within the Republican coalition paled in comparison to those dividing the left.
"This fall, the Democrats are running candidates who will tell your children what they're allowed to say, how they're allowed to live, and, importantly, who they ought to hate," Vance said.
"Because that's what the Democrat Party is about in 2026. It's not about you. It's about foreign fraudsters, and it's about who they hate."
The 42-year-old vice president's appearance also offered Republicans a glimpse of a potential post-Trump future, with Vance widely regarded as an early front-runner for the party's 2028 presidential nomination.
His keynote immediately before President Donald Trump's closing remarks gave him one of the convention's most prominent speaking slots, although Vance has said he will not decide on a White House run until after the midterms.
Republicans enter the November elections under heavy pressure.
US election tracking site Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats will win the House 229-206 and has the Senate on a knife-edge at 50-50. Trump's approval rating has languished in the low-to-mid 30s amid stubborn inflation and an unpopular war with Iran.
High-stakes gamble
The convention has resembled an extended Trump rally more than a traditional party meeting, with no nominations or formal business and more than 50 speakers or presentations each night.
Organisers said 20,000 spectators attended on Wednesday's opening day — close to capacity for the arena, which had conspicuous gaps in the crowd during parts of Trump's speech.
Not all Republicans have embraced the experiment.
Numerous lawmakers in competitive races chose to remain in their districts rather than spend valuable campaign time in Dallas, while both convention nights faced competition from the opening games of the NFL season.
The central Republican gamble remains whether Trump can mobilise voters personally loyal to him even when he is not actually running, without further alienating independents who have soured on his presidency.
Vance's appearance put an additional question before the party: whether one of Trump's potential successors can eventually inherit the political coalition he built.
"I'm not asking you to agree with every policy of our administration," Vance told the crowd.
"I'm asking you to recognise the contrast with the radicals, and the achievements of the last 18 months."

California enacts new curbs on social media for children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

California enacts new curbs on social media for children
- California Governor Gavin Newsom signed laws banning children under 16 from addictive social media features and AI chatbot toys, aiming to protect youth wellbeing.
- The legislation, called "Adam's Law," includes stricter sanctions on AI-generated child sexual abuse content and mandates parental controls on chatbots.
- California joins other states in curbing harmful tech influences on minors amid legal pressures on Big Tech, with Meta agreeing to limit teen usage on Facebook and Instagram.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – California Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law on Sept 10 new tech company restrictions barring children under 16 from exposure to behaviourally addictive features on social media platforms and banning toys containing AI companion chatbots.
The two measures were among 13 Bills Newsom enacted as a package designed to safeguard young people from technology seen as putting them at risk, including greater online privacy protection for minors.
Another measure expanded the scope of criminal sanctions against child sexual abuse material to include any digitally altered or AI-generated content that depicts a person under the age of 18 engaged in sexual conduct.
Still another bans for the next four years the manufacture and sale of toys that incorporate a companion chatbot. A related measure requires parental controls on chatbot programs, along with other safety and risk assessments.
Newsom touted those regulations as the most far-reaching of their kind in the nation. The Bill was dubbed “Adam's Law”, in memory of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old boy who took his own life in April 2025 after he acted, according to his parents, on suicidal thoughts validated in months of discussion with OpenAI’s ChatGPT program.
OpenAI has said it intends to improve ChatGPT safeguards, which the company has acknowledged became “less reliable” as user interactions grow more prolonged.
“We want our children – and every California kid – to grow up in a world where technology supports their wellbeing, rather than exploits their vulnerabilities,” Newsom, a Democrat, said in a statement announcing the measures.
California, home of such leading internet companies as Google, Meta Platforms and Snap, joins a growing list of US states cracking down on business strategies seen as deliberately designed to hook teenagers on social media, despite evidence that extensive use is harmful to their mental health.
While gaining broad bipartisan support, some critics objected to the Bill as an unnecessary restriction on young people’s internet access, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which called the Bill “a massive privacy and free speech nightmare”.
Utah became the first to adopt laws regulating children’s access to social media, followed by others, including Arkansas, Louisiana, Ohio, Texas, Florida and New York, though approaches have varied.
‘Psychologically exploitative’ features targeted
Countries around the world have also moved to curb children’s access to harmful internet content, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16.
California's version, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits children under age 16 from exposure to a number of “psychologically exploitative features intended to maximise engagement that foreseeably lead to compulsive use”.
Those include infinite-scroll feeds, algorithmic autoplay and other features to be defined in future regulations.
Its enactment comes at a time when Big Tech, in the face of mounting legal challenges, has shown greater willingness to accept new restrictions.
Meta agreed three weeks ago to pay as much as US$18 billion (S$22.82 billion) over the next decade and strictly limit how teenagers use its Facebook and Instagram platforms under a deal with nearly all US states to resolve civil claims that the company designed its social media platforms to addict children. REUTERS

Libya's legislative bodies stress political process should follow constitutional declaration
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:54:04 CST
11:54:04 KST

TRIPOLI, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Libya's House of Representatives (HoR) and High Council of State on Thursday stressed that the country's political process should take place within the framework of the Constitutional Declaration and the Political Agreement governing the work of the two councils, with respect for their respective mandates and powers.
The statement was issued following a meeting between HoR President Aguila Saleh and High Council of State President Mohamed Takala, held under the auspices of Türkiye.
The two legislative bodies expressed readiness to host the joint "6+6 Committee" in the coming days to enable it to complete its tasks concerning electoral laws, paving the way for elections.
The "6+6 Committee," jointly formed by the HoR and High Council of State, reached an agreement in June 2023 on laws governing presidential and parliamentary elections. The HoR later adopted amended versions of the electoral laws in October that year.
The High Council of State objected to some of the amendments but backed the version agreed upon by the committee in the Moroccan city of Bouznika, leading to delays in implementing the laws and a halt to the committee's work amid continued disputes over a unified executive authority and the conditions and procedures for holding elections.
In a later development, the "4+4 Committee" signed a final agreement on Aug. 30 under the auspices of the United Nations Support Mission in Libya. The agreement aims to create conditions for holding presidential and parliamentary elections within no more than 24 months under a single executive authority and unified national institutions.
Key outcomes of the agreement include restructuring the board of the High National Elections Commission and addressing several outstanding issues in the electoral laws, notably allowing military personnel to run and vote in presidential elections and allowing dual nationals to run, provided that the winner relinquishes their non-Libyan citizenship before taking the constitutional oath.
The agreement also sets the number of endorsements required for a presidential candidate at 20,000, and stipulates that the elected HoR will handle the drafting of a permanent constitution for the country. ■

Ultimate Championship brings athletics elite together in Budapest
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:53:59 CST
11:53:59 KST

Gabrielle Thomas of the United States attends a red carpet event of World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest, Hungary on Sept. 10, 2026. (Photo by David Balogh/Xinhua)
BUDAPEST, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- The world's leading athletes are set for a three-day showdown in Budapest as the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship opens Friday, bringing together Olympic champions, world champions and Diamond League winners in a new season-ending global event.
A total of 381 athletes from 65 countries and regions will compete across three evening sessions from September 11 to 13 at the National Athletics Center, with 28 titles on offer across 16 track events, 10 field events and two relays.
The championship carries a 10 million U.S. dollars prize purse, with 150,000 dollars awarded to each individual event winner.
At Thursday's pre-event activities, athletes swapped competition kits for suits, evening gowns, sunglasses and high heels as they walked onto the track, showcasing a different side of themselves before the competition begins.
The Ultimate Championship also introduces a compressed competition format. Most individual track events from 100m to 800m begin with semifinals, while the 1,500m, 5,000m, relays and all field events go directly to finals.
Another innovation comes in the 200m semifinals, where athletes will select their preferred heat and lane in seeding order, giving higher-ranked competitors first choice.
World Athletics President Sebastian Coe said at Thursday's pre-event press conference that the championship was designed to bring the world's best athletes together to answer the fundamental question of "who is the best."
"Nobody goes into the sport to sort of figure out who's second best," Coe said.
Coe described the championship as an "incubator for change," saying innovations tested in Budapest could eventually find their way into future World Championships and even the Olympic Games.
Jamaican sprint great Usain Bolt said bringing the world's best athletes together for direct competition was exactly the kind of challenge he enjoyed during his career.
"I've always lived to compete against the best. I live for competition," Bolt said.
Joking that the event had arrived too late for him, Bolt said he would have regarded the Ultimate Championship as being as important as the Olympic Games or World Championships had it existed during his prime.
Friday's opening night will feature several high-profile contests, led by men's pole vault world record holder Armand Duplantis. Titles will also be decided in the women's high jump, men's hammer throw and men's 5,000m, while semifinals in the hurdles, 400m and 800m are also scheduled.
Two Chinese athletes have qualified for the championship, with both competing Saturday.
18-year-old Yan Ziyi will contest the women's javelin after an outstanding season in which she threw 71.74 meters at the Diamond League meeting in Xiamen, setting Asian and world U20 records. She remained unbeaten in five Diamond League appearances before winning the Final in Brussels last weekend.
Zhang Mingkun will compete in the men's long jump final. ■

S. Korea's exports surge 82.6 pct in first 10 days of September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:53:34 CST
11:53:34 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's exports surged in double digits in the first 10 days of September, driven by an exponential growth in semiconductor shipments, customs office data showed Friday.
Outbound shipments totaled 34.97 billion U.S. dollars in the Sept. 1-10 period, up 82.6 percent from the same period last year, according to the Korea Customs Service.
It marked the highest performance for any corresponding 10-day tracking period, topping the previous high of 30 billion dollars set in July.
Daily average exports jumped 82.6 percent to 4.11 billion dollars in the 10-day period.
Semiconductor exports skyrocketed 270.1 percent to 16.48 billion dollars amid expanding global artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investments.
Shipments for computers and peripherals spiked 93.1 percent to 635 million dollars due to strong demand for solid-state drives, fueled by the AI investments.
Exports of oil products, cars, ships and steel products logged a double-digit increase.
The Asian country's imports advanced 20.7 percent from a year earlier to 24.61 billion dollars in the first 10 days of September, sending the trade surplus to 10.36 billion dollars. ■

What Maria Shriver Wants Women to Know About Their Brain Health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
02:52:15 UTC
11:52:15 KST

Only one in five women know that they’re more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease than men, according to a recent survey. Maria Shriver wants that number to climb—and for women to start thinking about their brains decades before symptoms show up.
“When people talk about living longer, you’re seeing a lot about people in the gym,” Shriver said Thursday at the TIME100 Health Leadership Forum in New York. “But what about their brains?”
Shriver founded the Women's Alzheimer's Movement and co-founded the Comprehensive Women's Health and Research Center at Cleveland Clinic. She sat down with TIME deputy editor Kelly Conniff to talk about what women need to understand about brain health, and why the conversation can't wait until later in life.
She became passionate about brain health when her father was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s in 2003. At the time, Shriver said, there wasn’t much information available to help families understand the disease or prepare for how their lives would change. She approached figuring that out as both a journalist and a daughter, while watching family members grapple with the diagnosis in different ways.
Her kids adjusted easily, she recalled, simply accepting the grandfather in front of them as he was. She had a harder time. The man she saw didn't match the father in her memory. Her mother, meanwhile, was losing something else entirely—a spouse, a confidant, a partner.
More than two decades later, scientists know more about how to detect Alzheimer’s early and what may help reduce the risk. Yet a striking disparity remains: Women account for about two-thirds of diagnoses.
One growing area of research focuses on how the brain changes during menopause, and whether interventions during that period could reduce Alzheimer’s risk, Shriver said. It’s unclear whether hormone therapy, for example, could help.
Yet “there’s more to women’s health than menopause,” Shriver added. Brain health, including mental health, is important to talk about throughout every stage of a woman’s life. She pointed to the recent trial of Lindsay Clancy as evidence that women are talking more openly about maternal mental health. She recently had a conversation with six or seven other mothers who discussed the case and began sharing their own emotional and postpartum experiences.
Clancy, a Massachusetts mother, was tried on charges of killing her three young children in 2023. Her attorneys argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, a rare psychiatric emergency distinct from postpartum depression. Prosecutors maintained that she understood her actions were wrong. The trial ended in a mistrial after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
“The fact that we’re talking about postpartum depression, the fact that we’re talking about maternal health,” Shriver said, represents a “huge advancement in my lifetime.”
The open discussion is part of the shift Shriver wants to see across brain health generally—starting with the basics. You shouldn’t have to overhaul your life to take care of yourself. Exercise, sleep, a decent diet, real social connection, and staying mentally engaged all move the needle on brain health. Shriver herself meditates twice daily to manage stress.
Still, she acknowledges these kinds of activities won’t all fit into everyone’s day. They might sound particularly unrealistic to women juggling busy careers or young kids, or taking care of their aging parents. When her four children were young, she said, she would have snapped at any well-intended suggestions to meditate: “You’re out of your mind. Go away. I didn’t even go to the bathroom.”
While it would be ideal if advances arrived even more quickly, Shriver sees the growing attention to women’s health and ongoing research as evidence that change is unfolding in real time. “I’m fully convinced they’ll find a cure for Alzheimer’s,” she said.
The TIME100 Health Leadership Forum was presented by the American Cancer Society, Kite—a Gilead Sciences company, Insulet, Musely, and NMDP.

While they were far from their best, it was a 26th consecutive regular-season win for master coach John Strange's Roosters side, who remain on track to reclaim the premiership they lost to the Broncos last year, with their only loss in round five of 2024.

Just when it looked like the floodgates would open, the Bulldogs worked their way back down the field, and Tagoai powered her way over to bring her side within four points with 10 minutes left in the half.
Seven minutes later, the Dogs' five-eighth Andie Robinson flew high over Baxter to pluck a pinpoint Tayla Preston bomb from the air and touch down.
With Preston's conversion, they were surprise 12-10 leaders at the break, leaving the shortest-priced favourites in NRLW history shell-shocked.
To make matters worse for the Roosters, Baxter left the field at half-time for a head injury assessment and failed to return after the interval.
The Bulldogs stayed on top for the opening 13 minutes of the second stanza, before Tagoai was sin-binned by referee Karra-Lee Nolan for a hip-drop.
Five minutes later, Isabelle Kelly, starting in her 50th game as captain of the Roosters, tore through the middle of the Dogs' defence and found prop Millie Elliott in support for the competition leaders to reclaim the lead.
Taina Naividi was next over the stripe and Canterbury's dream was over.
More tries followed to Pule, Mia Woods, Sergis and Jocelyn Kelleher for a final score that somewhat flattered the minor premiers.
Despite the loss, it was a brave effort from the Bulldogs and coach Brayden Wiliame, in his final game at the helm before Mark O'Meley takes the reins in 2027.

Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are due to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while Chinese President Xi Jinping is also expected to meet Modi on the sidelines of the two-day meeting.

Putin arrived at Palam Air Force Station in New Delhi, where he was greeted by India’s Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia’s Ria Novosti news agency.
Posters of a beaming Modi lined streets across New Delhi to welcome leaders, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
BRICS, which stands for the original members of the grouping – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
It has since expanded, and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – three countries with sharply differing positions on the US-Israel war on Iran launched in February.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit,” Harsh V Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation told the AFP news agency.
“What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of BRICS – today looks like a big constraint on BRICS,” Pant said.
It will be Pezeshkian’s first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda. The Iranian president’s visit marks the first in eight years for the role.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the (expanded) group’s cohesion,” Shilan Shah of Capital Economics told AFP, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the war on Iran in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years, as Moscow’s war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025, but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, where Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.
For China’s Xi, it will be his first visit to India since 2019, and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

Experts Discuss Breakthroughs In Beating Cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
02:39:18 UTC
11:39:18 KST

Leading experts in cancer research reflected on the significant strides made in tackling the disease, along with the work that remains to be done toward finding a cure, at the TIME100 Health Leadership Forum in New York on Thursday.
Resources have been the key toward making important discoveries, said Shane Jacobson, the CEO of both the American Cancer Society, which sponsored the event, and the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network. Philanthropic investments and federal government funding, he continued, have allowed scientists and oncologists to make the progress we see today in cancer prevention and treatment.
Cancer is “omnipresent” Jacobson said. In the U.S., one in three men and women will receive a cancer diagnosis sometime during their lives, according to the American Cancer Society.
“It has been, historically, such a devastating disease,” he said. “We knew so little about it that it has garnered resources—and it takes resources to tackle most of the problems we face in healthcare.”
Developments in tackling cancer—such as the encouraging results of an mRNA cancer vaccine that were announced by Moderna and Merck last month—stem from “decades of progress, decades of new knowledge, decades of even failure, and learning from that failure to bring forth these kinds of results,” Jacobson said.
“It used to be maybe on an annual basis we would celebrate something significant, but the innovation is moving so rapidly that these celebrations, these big moments, are now almost on a monthly basis, and we should expect that speed to continue,” he said. But, he added, just as important as these advances is ensuring that everyone is able to access the drugs and therapies they need—”otherwise,” he said, “the innovation falls short of its potential.”
Vaccines and immunotherapy have emerged as powerful tools to fight cancer, said Dr. Andrea Cercek, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center who was a 2025 TIME100 Health honoree.
“The hope … between vaccines and immunotherapy as well is that they harness the immune system, which is really the most powerful drug we have,” she said. “It can fight anything as long as it’s equipped to do so and it recognizes something is foreign, and so it’s really that combination that needs to happen for therapy to work.”
Cercek herself has been pioneering immunotherapy drugs to treat cancer. In 2024, she and her colleagues released the findings of their study of patients who had a specific type of rectal cancer, revealing that, after six months of being treated with an immunotherapy drug, none of the patients showed detectable tumors, meaning that none of them needed chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery afterwards.
Cercek has expanded her research, and said during the panel that “we’re very close” to seeing this kind of treatment being used successfully for other types of cancer so that patients don’t have to undergo more invasive therapies.
TIME senior health correspondent Alice Park, who moderated the panel, closed the discussion with a big question: Will we cure cancer? And if so, what will that cure look like?
“Absolutely we will,” Cercek replied. “Probably it will be with early detection and prevention—I think that is going to be, ultimately, what cures cancer.”
“Yes,” Jacobson said. “And I think it’s ‘cures,’ plural. It’s not one cure, and we’re seeing that now.”
The TIME100 Health Leadership Forum was presented by the American Cancer Society, Kite—a Gilead Sciences company, Insulet, Musely, and NMDP.

AETC Launches Blueprint with AI Training for All Airmen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
02:36:12 UTC
11:36:12 KST

Strategic guidance from the command in charge of Air Force training lays out a plan to train all Airmen in artificial intelligence and build “Digital Airmen” across the force’s training and education enterprise.
Lt. Gen. Clack J. Quinn, the head of Air Education and Training Command, signed the directive Aug. 17, according to a release from AETC this week. It’s meant to serve as a blueprint for how AETC will integrate AI into all of its training, from pilot education to technical training.
The move follows on Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David R. Wolfe’s announcement in May calling for the service to build a baseline level of “AI literacy” among all of its members, as Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.
The document outlines a force-wide push to equip all Airmen with essential AI skills and transform both instruction and personnel management. The command is now drafting a 90-day implementation plan to put the directive’s changes into effect.
“AETC must master the digital domain to build the mission-ready force our Nation requires. This guidance is the roadmap to transform AETC’s infrastructure and data into a cohesive, AI-driven learning ecosystem,” Quinn said in the release.
The command seeks to drive modernized training approaches across the force.
“AETC will lead the Air Force in demonstrating how a large-scale training enterprise can modernize responsibly, fiscally, and at the speed of relevance,” Quinn said.
Larger AI Efforts
The training and education changes come as the service also announced in April that it plans to “aggressively recruit, train, and retain top-tier artificial intelligence professionals.”
While the Air Force is looking to lean on AI to improve everything from command-and-control and sensor-to-shooter timelines in combat, it also plans to leverage the tools for more administrative purposes too.
AETC’s directive, likely in the works for some time, closely follows the release of a RAND Corporation report in August suggesting the Air Force borrow some tips from civilian technology training for its Airmen, as Air & Space Forces Magazine reported. The report recommended basic AI literacy and other tech tools for Airmen and Guardians as key to the service reaching its long-term goals for both initial training and career-long educational improvement.
The RAND report also recommended the service use a “stackable certificates” model for educating Airmen, breaking up long-form, classroom-based, in-person instruction with mobile and remote options and bite-sized learning opportunities to further an Airman’s education.
The “just-in-time” training model recommended by RAND is common across much of civilian tech education curricula.
AETC’s blueprint appears to implement some of the same ideas, like reduced classroom time, more mobile learning, and better scheduling. Initiatives include:
- Upgraded WiFi and Networks: Modernizing base network infrastructures to deliver fast, reliable, and secure connectivity that supports heavy virtual learning demands.
- Mobile Learning: Expanding secure mobile device access so Airmen can study, train, and complete coursework on the go.
- Cutting Classroom Time: Utilizing personalized, AI-augmented learning pathways to reduce the average time-to-train for technical specialties by 20 percent.
- Smarter Scheduling: Implementing intelligent scheduling algorithms to optimize flightlines, increase pilot production, and eliminate administrative bottlenecks.
To realize these goals, AETC has initiated an “offset-to-modernize” approach, targeting a 25 percent reduction in legacy software sustainment and overhead by “shutting down redundant, slow, and outdated IT systems,” according to the release.
“We will eliminate duplicative and under-performing capabilities to invest in higher-yield ones that deliver a measurable return in instructional capacity, training throughput, or mission resilience,” Quinn said.
By the end of these efforts, AETC expects to produce “Digital Airmen” through its education and training.
“AETC is integrating basic data and AI literacy standards into 100 percent of its core training pipelines—from Basic Military Training through Professional Military Education,” according to the release. “The command is also formalizing digital skills certifications to help Airmen track, develop, and leverage tech talents throughout their careers.”

Hong Kong: Sentencing of Tiananmen activists a ‘triple tragedy’ and affront to history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
02:31:38 UTC
11:31:38 KST

Responding to the sentencing of activists who organized Tiananmen vigils in Hong Kong, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks said:
“During most of the 30 years that Hongkongers commemorated the Tiananmen crackdown with an annual candlelight vigil, it would have been unthinkable that the organizers of the event could be jailed for their peaceful activism. But today’s sentencing illustrates just how much Hong Kong has been transformed in the name of ‘national security’.
“This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history.
“The persecution of the Tiananmen activists exposes the profound fear of dissenting voices that defines Hong Kong’s ‘national security’ regime. But you do not strengthen national security by imprisoning people for peacefully remembering the dead.
“The authorities may believe that punishing prominent figures will deter others, but history shows that demands for truth and accountability do not disappear simply because they are criminalized.
“Today’s sentence is an insult to the victims’ memory and an affront to history. The Hong Kong Alliance activists have committed no internationally recognized crime and should be immediately and unconditionally released. Their right to appeal against these unjust jail sentences must be protected.”
Background
Hong Kong’s High Court today sentenced lawyer Chow Hang-tung to seven years and three months in prison and her fellow Tiananmen activist Lee Cheuk-yan to seven years in prison for “inciting subversion of state power” under the city’s National Security Law. Albert Ho Chun-yan, who previously pleaded guilty to the same charge, was sentenced to five years and two months.
Chow and Lee were among seven members of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China (Hong Kong Alliance) charged with different offences under the Beijing-imposed law in September 2021. Both have been held in pre-trial detention throughout the years since, having been repeatedly denied bail. They have been designated prisoners of conscience by Amnesty International.
Amnesty International has repeatedly raised concerns that the National Security Law, enacted in June 2020, is being used to target civil society groups, journalists, political activists, academics and others for actions that are fully protected under international human rights law.
The Tiananmen vigils commemorated the events of 4 June 1989, when Chinese troops opened fire on students and workers who had been peacefully protesting for political reforms in and around Beijing’s Tiananmen Square. Hundreds – possibly thousands – of people were killed. Tens of thousands more were arrested across China in the suppression that followed.
In the 37 years since the crackdown, all discussion of the incident has been heavily censored in China, and authorities have effectively erased it from their version of history.
From the beginning, commemorating the Tiananmen crackdown was forbidden in mainland China. But in Hong Kong, crowds reaching hundreds of thousands of people would gather annually in centrally located Victoria Park to peacefully remember those killed. The vigil participants regularly called on the Chinese authorities to reveal the truth about what happened and accept accountability for the atrocity; for thirty years, local government did not, in practice, interfere or object.
The last major vigil organized by the Hong Kong Alliance was held in 2019. The Hong Kong vigil was banned in 2020 and 2021, ostensibly on Covid-19 grounds. Since then, the National Security Law has effectively criminalized peaceful protest in the city – including Tiananmen commemorations.

Foreign volunteers most often choose unmanned systems units – Air Assault officer
Major Vladyslav Stadnichenko, a senior officer in the training process organization section of the 199th Training Center of the Air Assault Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Foreign cadets choose various military occupational specialties, but first and foremost, everyone is interested in unmanned systems,” Stadnichenko said.
According to him, foreign volunteers undergo training at the training center alongside Ukrainians. Everyone is trained in Ukrainian. When military units send foreign personnel to undergo BGMT, interpreters accompany them. Some understand Ukrainian, particularly those from Slavic countries. In addition, the instructors have a basic command of English, which also helps with communication.
Stadnichenko noted that many former service members from various countries come to the 199th Training Center for BGMT. In other words, these are people who have already served in the military and, to some extent, find it easier than Ukrainian conscripts who have never served.
“If we compare foreigners serving in the Armed Forces of Ukraine with those fighting on the enemy’s side, people who come to the Russian army from poor countries often have no military experience and do so for financial gain. By contrast, those who join us are people who have already tested themselves, for example, by completing Navy SEAL training (an elite U.S. Navy military unit – ed.). They arrive with basic training already under their belts,” the officer added.
The major also said that the level of training in the Air Assault Forces is quite high because Ukraine is engaged in active combat. The BGMT program is gradually being updated based on battlefield experience, making it more relevant than similar training abroad.
As Ukrinform reported, the Cabinet of Ministers extended the period foreign volunteers may stay in Ukraine to allow them to regularize their legal status.

Texas judge rules TikTok misled users on child safety feature
Sept 10 - A Texas judge ruled on Thursday that TikTok violated the state's consumer protection law by misleading users about how it filtered content for minors and whether its "Restricted Mode" feature shielded children from inappropriate material.
• Texas sued TikTok in January 2025, alleging it marketed its platform as safe for children.
• TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours.
• According to the ruling, Texas said TikTok told users it would remove content that violated its Community Guidelines, but internally classified some of that material as "hard to find" rather than "do not allow," allowing it to remain on the platform. Judge Cory Liu agreed that the practice violated the state's consumer protection law.
• Liu also said Texas had established that TikTok's "Restricted Mode" did not work as advertised and exposed minors to content the company said would be filtered out.
• The office of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said the case will now proceed to trial, where penalties and other remedies would be determined. The trial is expected to be scheduled next month, according to Paxton's office.
• TikTok in August agreed to settle three U.S. lawsuits brought by young people who accuse social media companies of designing their platforms to be addictive and harming their mental health. Separately in August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion to settle U.S. addiction claims. REUTERS
