F-16s That Defended Capital on 9/11 Preserved for History
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
02:18:30 UTC
11:18:30 KST

Three F-16s that flew in defense of Washington, D.C., on Sept. 11, 2001, will be retired and preserved as museum artifacts.
The three planes all flew on 9/11: two were among the first three jets to scramble in defense of the capital and the third escorted Air Force One as it returned to Washington later in the day.
On Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist groups hijacked four U.S. airliners, with two striking the twin World Trade Center towers in New York City and the third slamming into the Pentagon near Washington, D.C. The fourth plane was the one that would eventually crash in Shanksville, Pa.
This week, on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, the National Guard Bureau confirmed that the three planes would be saved:
- Tail number 85-1438, flown by now-Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, will go to the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force in Dayton, Ohio. His plane was the third to scramble on 9/11.
- Tail number 85-1461, flown by now-retired Lt. Gen. Marc Sasseville, will become a static display at Joint Base Andrews. He was the first to scramble, but this was the jet he flew as escort for Air Force One at the end of the day.
- Tail number 86-0255, flown by Heather Penney, now director of research at AFA’s Mitchell Institute of Aerospace Studies, will go to the American Heritage Museum in Hudson, Mass. Penney’s was the second plane to scramble, flying with Sasseville.
Saving the Vipers
Members of the wing began research more than a year ago to figure what had happened to the jets flown on that fateful day, tracking down old paperwork to figure out who signed out which aircraft and then to discover where those tails were today.
Working with the National Guard Association of the United States, a nonprofit association that advocates for the Guard, they reached out to the Air Force, the Air National Guard, the White House, and others, offering ideas for preserving the historic aircraft under the National Museum of the United States Air Force Heritage Program.
Among the D.C. National Guard F-16s flown on 9/11, one remains in regular flying status with the Air National Guard’s 162nd Wing in Tucson, Ariz. That was the plane Caine flew, which will eventually go to the Air Force Museum.
Guard advocates learned three other planes flown on 9/11 had been converted into QF-16 Full-Scale Aerial Target drones. One—the jet Sasseville scrambled in—was destroyed at the end of its flying life in a missile test. The remaining two were headed for a similar fate when the issue of saving the planes was raised with the Air Force and others.
Jon “Ice” Eisberg, vice president at NGAUS, said once the issues were clear, the challenge was getting the attention of the right people.
“This was a team effort,” Eisberg said. “We just reached out to some of our normal contacts. We went to the National Security Council. We went to Office of Public Liaison in the White House. We went to the Pentagon, and we alerted some folks up on Capitol Hill to this issue.”
The challenge in saving the planes was that QF-16s are a limited resource. The conversions are expensive, about $5 million apiece. The last of 127 conversions was delivered to the Air Force by contractor Boeing in April 2025, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine’s 2026 USAF & USSF Almanac.
QF-16 drones are used for targeting, and once their available flying hours are used up, they can be used in destructive live ordnance tests. One program that would benefit from such tests is the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, which the Air Force is developing to extend the range of air-to-air combat capabilities beyond visual range.
Still, saving the planes was a priority, and the Air Force came up with a solution: Run down the clock on the QF-16s available flying time, and when their flying hours were all used up, transfer the planes for preservation.
The 9/11 Mission
In a National Guard Bureau video created for the 25th anniversary, Caine recounted his 9/11 experience. “I was running our flying program” that day, Caine recalled. When he saw the second plane hit the World Trade Center on TV, “it was clear that the United States was at war.”
Caine, a major and the wing’s weapons officer at the time, called for live weapons to be readied on the flightline, but getting weapons ready takes time. Soon after, the White House called, he said, “telling us to get airborne.”
Joining Sasseville, a major and the wing’s operations director, and two junior pilots, Penney and Brandon “Igor” Rasmussen, Caine said the group formulated “a hasty, quickly constructed gameplan.”
The clock was ticking as they waited for official authority to launch, and once they had that, weapons were still not ready. Sasseville, who would eventually rise to become Vice Chief of the National Guard Bureau, told Penney as they headed to their plane that they would have to ram the airliner.
“We had an entire wing of support behind us, getting things moving that day, reacting to that terrible attack,” he said. “The White House communicated with us because we were one of the few units in a position to actually do something. … We took off as soon as we could.”
Penney, a young lieutenant and the daughter of an experienced fighter pilot, has wondered why she got the nod that day. “I like to think it was because I was a good pilot,” she said in a recent conversation. “But I think it was because I was single. It was just me and a dog.”
Everyone was operating on adrenaline, Sassevile said. “No one asked any questions.”
Once on the flightline, they dispensed with the routine pilot’s precheck, climbing directly into their planes, trusting their maintainers to have gotten everything ready. Penney had never scrambled an aircraft before—or even trained to.
They took off without clear rules of engagement—these were arranged once they were airborne—and headed out in search of what would later become known as Flight 93, which crashed in a field in Shanksville, Pa., after the passengers stormed the cockpit to stop the terrorists inside.
In fact, they had already done so when Sasseville and Penney took off, but no one knew that at the time.
“We understood what the threat was,” Penney said, recalling their flight up the Potomac River to the northwest of Andrews. “We were looking for a rogue airliner, flying low. We knew they had turned off their transponders.”
Without missiles or bullets—the F-16 has a gun, but they were loaded only with training rounds—the objective target would have to come down with brute force.
“Our only choice,” Penney said, “was going to be to ram the airliner.”
But first they’d have to find it. Unsure of its location or even what vector it was taking to the capital, they headed up the Potomac, then circled back to defend the city. The plan, Sasseville told Penney, was that he would aim his jet at the cockpit and the terrorists, and Penney would take aim at the tail.
The Federal Aviation Administration had ordered all planes in U.S. airspacer to land, and it gradually became clear that Flight 93 had crashed short of the terrorists’ intended target.
Returning to Andrews, Penney recalled looking down at a base that had come alive, its parking lots full, and a line of cars backed up waiting to get on base. “Guardsman came to their units without needing orders, without waiting for paperwork,” she said. They got planes ready, set up cots in the operations area, brought in food. The Guardsman would fly air combat patrols over Washington for the next 90 days straight, and they were already on duty—before they’d ever received orders or even a call.
“They just told their employers, ‘You know, boss, my nation’s calling,’ and they went.”
Now their planes will endure as a reminder of that day and the clear sense of duty those Airmen displayed when the United States came under attack.

'Fault line'

BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

Brazil’s Supreme Court shuts down early as political chaos mounts

Brazil’s Supreme Court shuts down early as political chaos mounts
Members of the high court have exchanged accusations after one justice was accused of involvement in a bank scandal.
Brazil’s Supreme Court has cancelled a second straight day of deliberations as suspicions of corruption, political bias and police interference loom over several of its members.
Cancellations are rare at the high court. But on Thursday, Chief Justice Luiz Edson Fachin nixed a second consecutive session, calling for the court to reconvene on Tuesday instead.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Brazil orders Discord to suspend livestreams after teen’s death
- list 2 of 3Brazil’s Supreme Court to weigh cases that could weaken Amazon protections
- list 3 of 3Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro names Alfredo Gaspar as running mate
The decision was spurred by an ongoing crisis among the court’s members.
The divisions emerged on September 1, when one justice, Andre Mendonca, unsealed a series of federal police documents that appeared to show a disgraced banker, Daniel Vorcaro, seeking advice from another justice, Alexandre de Moraes.
De Moraes has rocketed to prominence in recent years for his roles in high-profile cases.
He presided over the trial of former President Jair Bolsonaro after prosecutors accused the far-right leader of plotting a coup following his 2022 election defeat. De Moraes also oversaw suspensions of platforms like X and Rumble for failing to abide by court orders, making him a target for Brazil’s right wing.
The document release authorised by Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee, contains roughly 30 text messages sent to a phone number associated with de Moraes, allegedly from Vorcaro.
In response, de Moraes has accused Mendonca of abusing his authority on the court for political gains. He requested a probe into whether Mendonca interviewed Vorcaro without the presence of police or prosecutors.
Tuesday’s session will involve the full Supreme Court bench, and 10 of the justices will discuss whether the 11th member, de Moraes, should be investigated over the text messages.
The tit-for-tat on Brazil’s high court is the latest fallout from the Banco Master corruption scandal.
Vorcaro, the head of the Banco Master financial institution, was arrested in November 2025 on accusations he defrauded investors of billions in lost funds, in one of the biggest banking scandals in the country’s history.
The collapse of Banco Master’s private banking arm left behind more than $7bn in debt.
Lawmakers from across the political spectrum have become embroiled in the unfolding scandal as new details emerge.
The turmoil risks affecting October’s general elections, including a pivotal presidential election.
Left-wing incumbent Lula Inacio Lula da Silva is set to compete for the presidency against Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Both Lula and Senator Bolsonaro have called for investigations into the Supreme Court justices.
The Bolsonaro family itself has been dragged into the Banco Master scandal. In May, the publication Intercept Brasil released a report showing that Senator Bolsonaro petitioned Vorcaro for funds to finance a film about his ex-president father, who is now serving a 27-year prison sentence.
Senator Bolsonaro has denied wrongdoing, claiming he did nothing more than seek private sponsorship for the film, entitled Dark Horse.
But on Thursday, Brazilian police executed dozens of raids related to the Banco Master scandal, including some that targeted two figures involved in the film: Karina Gama, the head of a production company, and Congressman Mario Frias, who served as executive producer.
Senator Bolsonaro has called the probes “attempted political interference” ahead of the elections.

Clinton pointed to media reports saying that Netanyahu got a warning from the United Arab Emirates before October 7, 2023 about Hamas’ plans to carry out a raid across the fence that separates Gaza from Israel.
Netanyahu either did not believe the warning or thought about how he could use the scenario to his advantage so he could "come down hard," which "would enhance his position," she said.
"This was a failure of leadership. This was a failure of protecting the people of Israel," Clinton said about Netanyahu, who is being sought by the International Criminal Court over "war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza."
"I have said repeatedly, I love Israel and I hate Netanyahu's government and his policies,” she said.
"I love America and I hate Trump's government and policies," she added about President Donald Trump, her opponent in the 2016 election, which she lost, setting Trump up for his first term in office.
Clinton, however, did not discuss former President Joe Biden and her Democratic Party’s central role in enabling Israel's genocide in Gaza through massive arms transfers and diplomatic backing. Human rights groups and critics argue that this support made the US government under Biden complicit in mass slaughter of Palestinians and humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
Settler violence in West Bank
Clinton also said it could really make a difference if Netanyahu was no longer premier: "I would hope that a new prime minister would crack down on settler violence in the West Bank. There should be no impunity for that kind of violence."
She warned that letting people having that level of violence in a society is "unfair and wrong" for the Palestinians while also "very dangerous" to Israel.
"Anytime you let people have that level of violence in a society, that you don't stop, that creeps into the whole society," Clinton said.
Clinton’s remarks come amid escalating attacks by the Israeli army and illegal Zionist settlers in the occupied West Bank since the start of the genocide in Gaza in October 2023.
Palestinian authorities have documented killings, abductions, home demolitions, attacks on mosques and vehicles, destruction of agricultural land, restrictions on farmers’ access to their property, and forced displacement.
Palestinians warn that Israeli mass atrocities and settler violence are paving the way for the formal annexation of the occupied West Bank, which would undermine the establishment of a Palestinian state under UN resolutions.

Saudi oil output plunges to lowest since 1990 – Bloomberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
02:00:07 UTC
11:00:07 KST

Saudi oil output plunges to lowest since 1990 – Bloomberg
Saudi Arabia’s crude oil production plunged by nearly 2 million barrels per day in August to its lowest level in over 35 years, as conflicts across the Middle East squeezed the kingdom’s export routes, Bloomberg reported on Thursday.
Riyadh told OPEC that production fell by 1.9 million barrels per day last month to 6.238 million bpd, according to the group’s monthly report obtained by the outlet.
The figure marks a new low since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February, as well as the kingdom’s lowest production level since the beginning of the Gulf War in 1990.
Saudi Arabia has been caught between disruptions on both of its principal maritime export routes. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has been severely restricted amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict, forcing greater reliance on Red Sea routes.
Iranian-aligned Houthi forces in Yemen have also renewed the war against Saudi-backed government forces and declared a maritime blockade against the kingdom.
The Houthis have also directly targeted Saudi energy infrastructure. A missile and drone barrage on Tuesday set oil installations ablaze and forced operations at some facilities to stop, according to the Saudi authorities, although Riyadh has provided few details on the extent of the damage or its impact on production.
The Houthis reportedly seized the strategic port city of Mocha on Thursday, tightening their grip on the approaches to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait – the narrow southern entrance to the Red Sea and a critical route for Saudi oil exports. The group said navigation remains safe for other shipping but not for Saudi vessels.
The pressure is already visible in shipping data, as provisional tanker tracking compiled by Bloomberg shows Saudi crude exports falling by around a third in August.
Riyadh told OPEC that its “supply to market,” which includes crude drawn from storage, stood at 7.122 million bpd, suggesting that the kingdom tapped inventories to compensate for reduced production. OPEC’s separate estimate based on external secondary sources was substantially higher, putting Saudi output at 7.276 million bpd in August.
The mounting threats to both Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb have sent oil prices surging higher. Brent crude settled 6.3% higher at $107.63 a barrel on Thursday, while West Texas Intermediate jumped to $102.48, with both benchmarks reaching their highest levels since May.
The upheaval is already reshaping global energy flows. Russia launched the first shipment from its massive Vostok Oil project in the Arctic this week, opening a new export route via the Northern Sea Route which Rosneft says could eventually supply the equivalent of around 730 million barrels of oil annually.
The US, meanwhile, has secured majority control over more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves under a sweeping investment deal. President Donald Trump portrayed the oil as a “gift” that will help replenish America’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
Those additional supplies could eventually ease pressure on global markets. The immediate shock, however, is already reaching US consumers. The national average diesel price surpassed $6 a gallon for the first time on record on Thursday, according to GasBuddy, after rising nearly 60% since the US and Israel launched the war against Iran in late February.

Everyone wants a line in the State of the European Union speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BRUSSELS — Walk through the EU Quarter of Brussels and you'll see posters plastered on walls and telephone poles asking European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to give animal welfare a starring role in her State of the European Union address.
“Your words matter,” the posters read. “Include animals in your speech.”
As von der Leyen prepares for her big speech on Sept. 16, everyone from the largest lobby groups to cash-strapped NGOs — and even apparently guerrilla campaigners (none of the big animal welfare groups POLITICO spoke to took responsibility for the posters) — are making their pitch for a few precious seconds of the Commission president’s time.
Advertisement
Some are taking the conventional approach. Last month, almost 200 industry associations and national groups signed a letter addressed to von der Leyen demanding she use her speech to commission an expansive, Mario Draghi-style report into the bloc’s appetite for fossil fuels.
Others are a little more in-your-face. Alcohol lobby group SpiritsEurope has set up shop at Place du Luxembourg, where it has organized four days’ worth of events and — naturally — drinks receptions. It also conducted a competitiveness “temperature check” among its members to see how they are feeling, and to hammer home the point that the Commission could be listening more to the demands of an industry that feels somewhat overlooked.
Von der Leyen “can bend the system to her will,” said SpiritsEurope Director General Mark Titterington. “That’s why we take the speech so seriously.”
“It sets the direction, sets the tempo and helps to condition the environment,” he added. “The words that are in there are pored over for meaning.”
Yet it's not just the words in the speech that lobbyists and advocates are interested in — it's the broader message.
“We’re not looking for the president simply to say the word ‘health’,” said Milka Sokolović, director general at EPHA, an EU-wide public health NGO.
Advertisement
She added that despite cuts to the organization — the health NGO has lost 40% of its staff since the Commission slashed its grants last year — it has been making “very concrete asks directly to the Commission, including von der Leyen, on the substance we would expect the speech to reflect.”
That’s in part because the speech acts as a litmus test of what messages have actually cut through.
“When specific asks have already been made through the normal channels, the SOTEU is an opportunity for the president to show whether they have translated into political priorities,” Sokolović said.
Von der Leyen “keeps her cards exceedingly close to her chest in the whole process,” said one former European Commission cabinet member. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
“A mention in that speech is not symbolic; it sends a signal to commissioners, to member states and to the Council that this file matters to the institution's leadership,” said Animal Equality’s Vice-President of Europe Matteo Cupi.
Failure to get a mention in the State of the European Union doesn't mean a topic isn't important — but a line in the speech does show political will to take action.
“Legislation, budgets and implementation create the actual change,” said Sokolović. “But high-level political commitments set the direction. They decide what gets political attention and momentum in the first place. That is why the SOTEU matters."
Advertisement
“A mention is a signal, a specific commitment is politically meaningful, a commitment with a deliverable and timetable is the real outcome.”
But whether lobbyists can even get the access that matters is another question.
The Commission president “keeps her cards exceedingly close to her chest in the whole process,” said one former Commission cabinet member, granted anonymity to speak freely. “In the end, von der Leyen writes the whole thing herself — there are literally four people involved,” the person said, adding that the speech is written only in the few days before it’s presented.
Among the few who do enjoy open access to the Commission’s upper echelons — such as chemicals lobby Cefic — the SOTEU is an “important milestone,” but still only “one step in a broader policy cycle,” said a spokesperson for the group. “What ultimately matters is how political priorities are translated into concrete measures and implemented in practice.”
Tech CEOs have also kept a direct line into von der Leyen. Their main lobby group, DigitalEurope, counted a mention of its AI & Tech Declaration in last year's speech as an “important signal that industry’s voice was being heard,” said Director General Cecilia Bonefeld-Dahl.
She also said the presence of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at this year's event is “a real opportunity to take the EU-Canada partnership to the next level,” with the lobby group keen to act as “a bridge” between Europe and its international partners.
Advertisement
One reason why the speech is so important for lobbyists and NGOs is that there are sometimes surprises within. In 2023’s edition, for example, von der Leyen dropped a bombshell, announcing an anti-subsidy probe into Chinese electric vehicles. European carmakers’ stocks spiked within the hour.
Pauline Bastidon, SpiritsEurope’s director of competitiveness and trade, said one upshot of that announcement was a retaliatory move by China into the EU alcohol sector.
“We are still paying the price for that,” she said. “There can be some very concrete consequences for what is said in the SOTEU speech.”
Additional reporting by Gerardo Fortuna and Max Griera.

Emmanuel Macron speaks with CEO of Dassault Aviation Éric Trappier as they look at a model of a Dassault Vortex space vehicle, at the Grand Palais in Paris on Sept. 9, 2026. | Pool photo by Ludovic Marin via AFP/Getty Images

And what if these visitors from deep space want to invade and have their eye (singular) on Europe? A new path to power for the far right: Don’t moderate. Stay radical.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

For years, Europe’s far right appeared to face a choice: Moderate, or remain on the margins. The Alternative for Germany party’s landslide victory in Saxony-Anhalt suggests there may be a third option — radicalize and win.
The party’s performance in last weekend’s election, where it raked in 44% of the vote, shattered a widely shared illusion among the European mainstream that the far right was somehow destined to mellow on its way to power.
That has broadly been the path taken by Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and France’s Marine Le Pen. The Italian prime minister’s tilt to the mainstream, especially when it comes to the EU and NATO, has given a name to the phenomenon: “Melonization.” Le Pen, for her part, has spent years “de-demonizing” her party, dropping calls to leave the EU and distancing the party from Russia after Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
Advertisement
The AfD has moved in the opposite direction, doubling down on anti-immigration, anti-Islam rhetoric and its pro-Russian stance — and still surging at the ballot box.
With the far right polling strongly ahead of major elections expected this year and next in Sweden, France, Spain, Poland and Italy, the AfD’s breakthrough is reverberating far beyond eastern Germany. It raises a more troubling possibility for Europe’s establishment: that the next wave of populist challengers may see less reason to emulate Meloni or Le Pen — and more incentive to copy the AfD.
The election results in Saxony-Anhalt are proof that “nationalist and identitarian policies” are “exactly the kind of policy we need to win elections and save our countries,” Afonso Gonçalves, the leader of the ultranationalist Portuguese movement Reconquista, said.
The Italian former general Roberto Vannacci, who is challenging Meloni from the far-right flank she used to occupy, also cheered the win. “Now, keep calling us extremists,” he posted on X. “If half the population stands with AfD, the accusations of extremism, by definition, evaporate and vanish.”
Roberto Vannacci gives a press briefing in Rome on June 13, 2026. | Filippo Monteforte/AFP via Getty Images
From across the Atlantic, U.S. President Donald Trump weighed in on his social media platform Truth Social: “Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night. They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations, which have hurt Germany so badly. THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore! MGGA!!!”
Meanwhile, in Italy and France, Le Pen and Meloni have abstained from commenting.
Advertisement
Diverging paths
The schism is not a new one. France’s National Rally broke with the AfD in the lead-up to the 2024 European Parliament election over comments by the German party’s lead candidates minimizing membership in the Nazi SS paramilitary organization.
Following the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a member of Parliament with the National Rally, told French television he was “shocked” that so many “voted for people who downplay Germany’s Nazi past.”
By contrast, the AfD has surged to success in part by empowering some of its most radical figures. Ulrich Siegmund, the party’s leader in Saxony-Anhalt, first came to national attention in 2024 for his participation in a closed-door meeting in Potsdam to discuss plans for the mass deportation of migrants.
The AfD supports what it calls “remigration” — encouraging people of immigrant backgrounds to return to their ethnic countries of origin. The party’s platform in Saxony-Anhalt pitched “financial and non-financial incentives” to push documented migrants to leave the country.
This summer, some of the party’s senior members joined a “remigration summit” headlined by Gregory Bovino, the former commander of the U.S. Border Patrol who championed mass deportation across the Atlantic. They mingled with other far-right politicians and activists from parties such as Spain’s Vox and the U.K.’s Restore Britain, as well as Austrian ethno-nationalist Martin Sellner, who was banned from entering Germany after his participation in the Potsdam event.
In Portugal, Gonçalves is mulling launching a fully fledged political party to compete with the far-right party Chega. A poll commissioned by Reconquista and shared with POLITICO showed the movement could net approximately 5 percent of the vote in general elections.
Advertisement
Reconquista’s potential bid for political power is part of a wider European trend, in which activists are challenging far-right parties by outflanking them on issues like migration. Gonçalves has proposed revoking Portuguese citizenship from immigrants when it was awarded, in his view, “illegally” and “against the values of our nation and our identity.”
In France, rising figures such as Sarah Knafo, a member of the European Parliament whose party is allied with the AfD, have built momentum with campaign strategies similar to those deployed in Saxony-Anhalt, combining far-right stances with strong visual branding.
“There’s a premium on radical rhetoric,” said Jérôme Jamin, a political science professor at Liège University in Belgium who has studied populist movements in Europe and the US. “It pays off, more than it used to.”
Radical rebranding
Whether the AfD’s radicalism will be a winning recipe outside their eastern German strongholds remains an open question. While it fires up the most radical segment of the electorate, it also scares off many voters. That means it can yield significant wins at the local level, but fail at the national level, where candidates need to appeal to a broader segment of the electorate.
Germany’s mainstream parties have also vowed not to cooperate or form a coalition with the AfD. That so-called “firewall” is already making it difficult for the party to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, where it is three seats short of an absolute majority. At the national level, where it is polling at 28%, the possibility looks far out of reach.
In France, far-right firebrand and polemicist Eric Zemmour tried to outflank Marine Le Pen, polling ahead of her in the early stages of the 2022 presidential campaign, only to crash in the actual election.
Advertisement
Eric Zemmour visits an agricultural fair in Chaumont-en-Champagne, France on Sept. 3, 2026. | Sameer AL-Doumy/AFP via Getty Images
Zemmour’s challenge ultimately benefited Le Pen, said a former high-ranking member of his party, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “He made her look less extreme, and in doing so he did her a favor,” the politician said.
Then there’s the problem of governing. Once actually in power, populist platforms have a tendency to crash into reality, be it financial or institutional.
That, in turn, exposes them to the same accusations they have been throwing at centrist parties for years: that they are unable to improve their citizens’ lives in a significant way and should make room for those who can.
In Hungary, Viktor Orbán’s 16-year rule ended in a crushing election defeat earlier this year after the EU’s most autocratic leader failed to deliver on a number of promises. In the U.S., a cost-of-living crisis stoked by the Trump administration’s policies is leaving many Americans behind and has hurt the government’s approval ratings ahead of midterm elections.
Jamin, the political scientist, dismissed the idea that the AfD surge or the rise of online far-right activists is any different in nature from past populist waves in Europe, inflammatory rhetoric included.
“We got Trumpism before the Americans did with [late Italian Prime Minister Silvio] Berlusconi,” Jamin said.
Advertisement
The difference, he said, was the international political environment. Where Washington might have once sought to check Europe’s far-right movements, the Trump administration — with its willingness to blow through legal and constitutional constraints — is instead inspiring them to go further.
“This coming from the White House makes people think, ‘We can do the same, this is the future of politics.’”

Inside Nigel Farage’s battle to get Reform election-ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Nigel Farage reacts as he arrives to address delegates at the Reform UK National Conference in Birmingham, England on Sept. 5, 2026. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images
LONDON — Nigel Farage has always faced a battle to get Reform UK ready for the next general election. Labour’s nascent recovery under Andy Burnham is only increasing the urgency.
The insurgent right-wing force has only about 100 star candidates considered ready to run as MPs — bar a final vet, two people aware of the process told POLITICO. That’s a long way from the 650 needed to contest every Westminster seat.
A nationwide Reform UK roadshow to pluck out more potential candidates begins its second lap of the country next week, with the pressure on to get hundreds more quality representatives before Burnham pulls the election trigger.
Advertisement
Recruiters are also searching for hundreds of prospective peers, which the party believes it might need to prevent the unelected House of Lords from blocking its program for government if Farage does enter Downing Street.
What was always going to be a rush to get battle-ready is taking place under greater urgency amid speculation Andy Burnham, the new Labour prime minister, could trigger an early election, though one is not due until 2029.
Ready or not, here we come
It was late in June that Richard Tice stood on Westminster’s College Green confidently calling for a general election as it became clear that Keir Starmer would be replaced by Burnham.
“Bring it on — the sooner the better,” the deputy Reform leader said, signaling the party was raring to go. That’s not how everyone felt.
“I was sitting there saying no, we’re not,” said one official working on efforts to get election-ready, grimacing and adopting a high-pitched tone to stress just how far from reality this was. They, like others in this piece, were granted anonymity to discuss internal matters.
Those who have participated in the party’s nationwide recruitment tour describe the boot camp-like grillings taking place under a “semi-omerta.”
Advertisement
“It’s like Fight Club,” a senior Reform figure involved in selections joked. “The first rule of parliamentary assessment center is you don’t talk about parliamentary assessment center.”
Reform organizers are all too aware that some of their most careless picks at the last election cost them dear, considering allegations of racism and offensive comments harmed the campaign. To repeat the slapdash approach of old could be fatal to Farage’s chances of ever becoming prime minister.
The party has set up a new vetting process run by Paul Nuttall, the party’s deputy chairman, and candidate testers have already spent nearly 32 days touring the nation. Through Blackpool, Wales, Peterborough and Maidstone, to name but a few stops, old hands have been putting would-be MPs through their paces.
“We’re not here looking to pass you, we’re here looking to fail you,” candidates are told, according to the official quoted above, who has knowledge of the boot camps. “A bad candidate doesn’t just affect themselves — it affects the whole party.”
Senior Reform officials, accompanied by former MPs for rival parties, watch as the wannabes are made to give an impromptu speech, outline a piece of legislation they would introduce as a backbencher and then take part in mock media interviews. All without any forewarning.
“This was significantly more rigorous than the Conservative process,” said one former MP who now acts as a “talent spotter” for Reform. They have watched a string of former Tory colleagues try to win over the judges so they can run for Farage’s party.
Advertisement
“I think there’s a reason for that,” they added. “At the last election there were one or two candidates who attracted a bit of attention because of interesting comments they made.
“Essentially the party was relying on the media to do due diligence for them. This time around there’s nothing of that sort. It is a very impressive procedure.”
The official cited above estimates the reputational damage of having to suspend support for candidates amid allegations of racism shaved off around 4% of Reform’s vote at the 2024 general election.
Farage, who took back day-to-day control of the party while the campaign was at an advanced stage in 2024, had deep concerns himself about some on the party’s last slate.
He privately joked to allies that he was praying for the party not to win in Barnsley North where the candidate had been dropped days before polls opened. The Times reported that candidate said black people should “get off [their] lazy arses” and stop acting “like savages.”
Hence the rigor this time around as Westminster’s favorite game du jour is speculating about the odds of an early election.
Advertisement
Burnham — the theory goes, despite his public protestations — could seek a fresh mandate for his own program of government at a more favorable political moment. Labour has seen a polling bounce since Starmer resigned, and while Reform is still currently neck-and-neck with the party of government they have been trending downwards.
Andy Burnham leaves No. 10 Downing St. in London on Sept. 9, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/ AFP via Getty Images
It makes catching Farage out while his party fights off multiple allegations about dodgy donations a tantalizing prospect for Burnham. Farage himself predicts there will be a general election in the spring.
Yet that prediction doesn’t seem to have sped up the selection process. Reform had hoped to have 100 fully approved candidates ready by last week’s party conference in Birmingham — but with that in the rear-view mirror, they’re not quite there still.
“We’ve got 100, but they’re not all fully, absolutely top-drawer vetted yet,” said one high-ranking Reform figure with knowledge of the numbers. The official, who has knowledge of the boot camps, also cited the 100 figure, adding that they still had another round of assessment in store.
A Reform spokesperson said they didn’t recognize the number and added: “This is an ongoing process that will ensure we are ready for a general election whenever it is called.”
Part of that process is preparing aspiring MPs for the limelight.
Advertisement
“Jeremy Kyle gives them a good working over,” said the talent spotting former MP of the media training would-be candidates have got in store with the Reform-supporting TV presenter.
Plus, the candidates still need to get approved by local branches — though party top brass could impose them in the event of a snap election this year.
Earlier this year, Farage set a deadline of the May local elections for defectors to Reform. But three former Conservatives who lost their seats at the last election are among those being discussed by Reform as potential candidates at the next election. These are Jane Stevenson, Ben Bradley and Jonathan Gullis. Reform declined to comment on individual applications.
During a round of mid-conference interviews, Farage was asked by GB News whether he’d managed to even get half the candidates required for a general election.
“I’m a bit behind the clock, but I think we’ve interviewed about 1,400 so far, so this is cranking up by hundreds every week,” he said, acknowledging the pace must be upped.
Mandate for change
It is not just the selection of Commons candidates that is a pressure point for Reform — significant time is being spent working out how to get its policy platform past an unelected upper chamber that the party believes will be hostile towards the more radical aspects of its agenda.
Advertisement
Peers are officially appointed on the advice of the prime minister of the day meaning much of the 800-strong House of Lords is aligned to previous Conservative and Labour administrations.
That means either Farage stacks the Lords with allies, or convinces the upper house to bow to the will of the elected House of Commons.
A research paper being discussed in Reform circles suggests at least 350 to 450 Reform-aligned peers would be needed to have enough support to drive through most of the party’s government business.
The Salisbury Convention means the House of Lords should not block government bills from passing if they’re mentioned in an election manifesto. And Reform frontbenchers are also drawing up a series of draft bills to be published in the lead-up to an election. It’s hoped the unusual move would allow early scrutiny, and demonstrate the greatest possible mandate for their program.
Danny Kruger, the Reform MP who’s leading the party’s efforts to get ready for government, said: “Depending on the timing of the election, we expect to publish draft bills covering some or all of our mandate priorities.
Farage stands with Danny Kruger, left, at the Reform UK National Conference in Birmingham on Sept. 5, 2026. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images
“These include securing our borders, policing our streets, freeing up energy supply, restoring sovereignty and the rule of law, and fixing government itself.”
Advertisement
Whether they manage to draw up bills to cover “some or all” of Reform’s priorities depends on just how early the election is called.
But how many prospective peers they’ll be able to procure before the election is unclear. Kruger said they will “have a long list of people ready to appoint.”
Two party insiders even believe it’s possible to ram through selections in the period between an election being won and House of Commons business restarting.
Farage’s own comments in his main conference speech indicates a more paced response. He threatened to appoint “hundreds” of new peers only if legislation is not passed, and if that “proves difficult,” the high-profile Brexit campaigner promised a referendum on the make-up of the Lords so they can be “swept away by a British public appalled by them.”
But finding hundreds of would-be peers is no mean feat. The official quoted above suggested Reform could bring back 20 to 25 of the hereditary peers kicked out of the Lords by Labour’s shake-up this year.
They added that some could also come from those who fail tests to become MPs, considering the “different skill set” required in the upper chamber. The Reform spokesperson stressed this is not party policy.
Advertisement
“Some of the people who try and fail to get selected for the House of Commons would actually be fine and right for the Lords,” they said. “Older, wiser, not fighting the fight in the media, it’s doing work in the committees so on and so forth.”
Reform’s media-fighting swashbucklers have been a crucial tool in helping the party cut through with the public, and Farage has left some supporters disappointed that he has not yet appointed anyone to key spokesperson roles, covering topics like health and defense.
As recent scandals underscore, Reform recognizes it must professionalize its operation. But with every layer of bureaucracy added comes a slowing in its processes — and the risk that a snap election catches them short.

Advertisement

Once Trump’s Qatari-donated Air Force One lands at Dublin Airport, he’s expected to be flown by Marine One helicopter into Phoenix Park, a vast urban oasis that was once the hunting grounds for the British ruling elite — and today provides an ideal one-stop shop for diplomacy behind easily secured walls.
But it also sidestepped the U.S. government’s initial wish to have the center of Dublin shut down so Trump could visit the future site of a new American embassy. That had been the hope of Trump’s ambassador to Ireland, a New Jersey property developer and avid golfer named Edward Walsh.

Advertisement

So naturally, while he’s here, President Trump will be guaranteed the full céad míle fáilte,” the Irish official said, using a native phrase proclaiming “a hundred thousand welcomes.”
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to Taoiseach of Ireland Micheál Martin during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House on March 17, 2026. | Alex Wong/Getty Images
Phoenix Park is home to three of the grandest venues for Irish diplomacy: Farmleigh House, a former retreat for the Guinness brewing dynasty and the state’s official guesthouse for visiting dignitaries; U.S. Ambassador Walsh’s Deerfield residence; and Áras an Uachtaráin, the home of Ireland’s ceremonial head of state, President Catherine Connolly. Trump will visit Walsh first, then Connolly at her place, and finally Martin at Farmleigh.
Irish confidence is running high that the ultra-polite Martin can swerve any awkward moments, given how he emerged unscathed from two St. Patrick’s Day visits to the White House. But nails are being bitten over Trump’s encounter with Connolly, a socialist opposition politician who often denounced Trump before her election last year as head of state, a non-government role designed to articulate Irish values, not policy.
For his part, Trump incorrectly presumed, during his only public comments about Connolly, that she was a man.

Likewise, whereas previous U.S. presidents have addressed the joint houses of Ireland’s parliament, an honor most recently bestowed on Biden in 2023, the building will remain closed for Trump’s visit.
“We have the convenient excuse that it’s a weekend,” said the Irish official, who conceded that the parliament has observed exceptional recalls from holiday periods to celebrate Biden and other visiting U.S. presidents. “We never got the impression that this was something President Trump was particularly keen to do anyway.”
Thousands of left-wing protesters, including senior figures from the main opposition party, Sinn Féin, are expected to march through central Dublin while Trump stays in the park. Anti-Trump protesters plan similar demonstrations Sunday in rural County Clare on the final day of the Irish Open, where the national police force and U.S. Secret Service have spent weeks wargaming how best to keep them far from the fairways.
Within the security cordon, Trump seems assured of a warm welcome from Doonbeg’s economically minded locals. They express uniform admiration for a U.S. leader who snapped up the bankrupt local resort at a knock-down price in 2014 and, spearheaded by son Eric, has transformed it into the area’s top employer and a highly profitable venture.
“We are all happy to be here, grateful to be here, and his [Trump’s] presence at the Irish Open makes it a truly international event,” McIlroy told a Doonbeg press conference. “That brings more attention and eyeballs, and that can only be a good thing.”

From Bishkek to New Delhi, Xi advocates Global South cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
09:58:07 CST
10:58:07 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping is heading to New Delhi for this year's BRICS gathering just over a week after he took part in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek.
The two back-to-back multilateral engagements converge on a single, defining theme: galvanizing solidarity and cooperation across the Global South.
EXPANDING FAMILY
The SCO "takes root in the Global South, its heart beats with the Global South, and it is an important pillar of South-South cooperation," Xi said at the Bishkek summit concluded on Tuesday last week, calling on the SCO to "promote the development and rise of the Global South through the SCO Wisdom."
The Chinese leader is expected to put forward further proposals on Global South cooperation at the upcoming BRICS summit, as he has noted that the BRICS is "standing at the forefront of the Global South."
This year marks the 25th founding anniversary of the SCO and the 20th anniversary of the BRICS cooperation mechanism, both milestone occasions.
Riding the wave of the collective rise of the Global South, BRICS and the SCO have over the years expanded their membership and broadened their networks of developing partners. Their members jointly account for more than half of the world's population and about 30 percent of the global economy. This illustrates the fact that the two groupings have evolved into major platforms for Global South cooperation.
Xi has not only joined other leaders of member countries in pushing for their respective expansions, but also put forward new ideas and initiatives like the "BRICS Plus" cooperation approach and the building of an SCO community with a shared future, opening up new vistas for win-win cooperation among Global South countries.
"China has consistently provided a clear vision and momentum for BRICS and the SCO, both conceptually and practically," said Humprey Arnaldo Russel, head of the ASEAN-China Research Center at the University of Indonesia.
"It transformed BRICS from a relatively exclusive grouping into a broader platform for cooperation among developing countries and the wider Global South," he added.
DEVELOPMENT FIRST
At the SCO summit last week, Xi called on countries to "stay committed to putting development first, and open up the prospects for shared prosperity."
Amid a turbulent and rapidly changing international landscape, development still faces severe challenges, and the road to prosperity for the Global South will not be straight.
"The Global South emerges for development and prospers through development. We should make ourselves the main driving force for common development," Xi said during the 2024 BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia.
For Xi, development has always been a priority. He sees it as "the master key to solving all problems," and has consistently called for countries worldwide to jointly pursue development and prosperity.
Xi has stressed repeatedly that no one should be left behind in the fight against poverty in China, and has led a formidable campaign that ended extreme poverty nationwide, which was hailed as "the greatest anti-poverty achievement in history."
His "leaving-no-one-behind" conviction also extends to his efforts to support poverty reduction and spur development across the Global South. "On the path to modernization, no one, and no country, should be left behind," Xi said.
Last week in Bishkek, Xi called for consolidating cooperation in both traditional and emerging fields, from trade, investment, connectivity and energy to artificial intelligence (AI), the digital economy and green industries.
Responding to the Global South's aspirations for common development and modernization, Xi has proposed the Global Development Initiative (GDI), which marks its fifth anniversary this year.
In the last five years, the GDI has mobilized more than 23 billion U.S. dollars, provided support for over 1,800 "small and beautiful" livelihood projects, and sponsored training programs for more than 200,000 people in different professions.
Serik Korzhumbayev, editor-in-chief of the Delovoy Kazakhstan newspaper, said: "Under Xi's leadership, the concept of development has acquired a new international dimension and become part of a broader vision for humanity's shared future."
GREATER VOICE
As the Global South rises, it deserves a bigger say in global affairs.
Last year's SCO Tianjin summit witnessed Xi's proposal of the Global Governance Initiative, a major proposition of China to advance a more just and equitable global governance system.
At the heart of this vision is the conviction that every country has a place and an equal role to play in global governance.
Xi has long argued that international affairs should not be dictated by those with more muscles. "World affairs should be discussed by all, and international norms should be set by all," he said in Bishkek last week. "The domination of international affairs by a few is an injustice left over from history, and global governance dictated by one, a few or a bloc of countries is not true multilateralism."
"As an important part of a multipolar world and a key driving force behind it, the Global South countries ought to have greater representation and voice in international affairs," Xi said.
Over the years, the SCO and BRICS have grown into vital venues for Global South countries to articulate their interests, coordinate their positions and strengthen their collective influence.
Their growing role can be seen in political coordination. The two groupings have issued statements on international and regional hotspot issues. In March this year, for example, SCO member states issued a statement expressing grave concern over developments in the Middle East and the strikes on Iran.
Xi has also pushed for improving global economic and financial governance. In 2014, Xi and other BRICS leaders formally signed an agreement establishing the New Development Bank, creating a new channel for financing infrastructure and sustainable development in emerging markets and developing countries.
At the SCO Bishkek summit, the members reaffirmed the importance of establishing the SCO Development Bank.
Now the push for a greater say is extending into emerging areas that will shape the future. In July this year, Xi announced the creation of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, and called for joint efforts to build a just and equitable system of global AI governance.
"We must carry out extensive international cooperation and help Global South countries with capacity building to bridge the AI and digital divides, promote sustainable development, and prevent creating new historical injustice in AI," Xi said.
Beyond the SCO and BRICS, China has also promoted cooperation and greater representation for the Global South through frameworks such as the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation and the China-ASEAN summit.
Xi has said on many occasions that China has always been a member of the Global South and will always belong to the developing world.
"No matter how the international landscape evolves, we in China will always keep the Global South in our heart, and maintain our roots in the Global South," he once said.■

California enacts new curbs on social media for children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
01:56:01 UTC
10:56:01 KST

California enacts new curbs on social media for children
- California Governor Gavin Newsom signed laws banning children under 16 from addictive social media features and AI chatbot toys, aiming to protect youth wellbeing.
- The legislation, called "Adam's Law," includes stricter sanctions on AI-generated child sexual abuse content and mandates parental controls on chatbots.
- California joins other states in curbing harmful tech influences on minors amid legal pressures on Big Tech, with Meta agreeing to limit teen usage on Facebook and Instagram.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – California Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law on Sept 10 new tech company restrictions barring children under 16 from exposure to behaviourally addictive features on social media platforms and banning toys containing AI companion chatbots.
The two measures were among 13 Bills Newsom enacted as a package designed to safeguard young people from technology seen as putting them at risk, including greater online privacy protection for minors.
Another measure expanded the scope of criminal sanctions against child sexual abuse material to include any digitally altered or AI-generated content that depicts a person under the age of 18 engaged in sexual conduct.
Still another bans for the next four years the manufacture and sale of toys that incorporate a companion chatbot. A related measure requires parental controls on chatbot programs, along with other safety and risk assessments.
Newsom touted those regulations as the most far-reaching of their kind in the nation. The Bill was dubbed “Adam's Law”, in memory of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old boy who took his own life in April 2025 after he acted, according to his parents, on suicidal thoughts validated in months of discussion with OpenAI’s ChatGPT program.
OpenAI has said it intends to improve ChatGPT safeguards, which the company has acknowledged became “less reliable” as user interactions grow more prolonged.
“We want our children – and every California kid – to grow up in a world where technology supports their wellbeing, rather than exploits their vulnerabilities,” Newsom, a Democrat, said in a statement announcing the measures.
California, home of such leading internet companies as Google, Meta Platforms and Snap, joins a growing list of US states cracking down on business strategies seen as deliberately designed to hook teenagers on social media, despite evidence that extensive use is harmful to their mental health.
While gaining broad bipartisan support, some critics objected to the Bill as an unnecessary restriction on young people’s internet access, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which called the Bill “a massive privacy and free speech nightmare”.
Utah became the first to adopt laws regulating children’s access to social media, followed by others, including Arkansas, Louisiana, Ohio, Texas, Florida and New York, though approaches have varied.
‘Psychologically exploitative’ features targeted
Countries around the world have also moved to curb children’s access to harmful internet content, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16.
California's version, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits children under age 16 from exposure to a number of “psychologically exploitative features intended to maximise engagement that foreseeably lead to compulsive use”.
Those include infinite-scroll feeds, algorithmic autoplay and other features to be defined in future regulations.
Its enactment comes at a time when Big Tech, in the face of mounting legal challenges, has shown greater willingness to accept new restrictions.
Meta agreed three weeks ago to pay as much as US$18 billion (S$22.82 billion) over the next decade and strictly limit how teenagers use its Facebook and Instagram platforms under a deal with nearly all US states to resolve civil claims that the company designed its social media platforms to addict children. REUTERS

US Vice President JD Vance reportedly gathered unvarnished assessments of the Iran war behind the scenes that differed from the picture publicly presented by the administration, The New York Times reported.

Vance also reportedly asked for detailed accounts of what remained in commanders' stockpiles and how transferring weapons to the Middle East could affect their ability to deter China, Russia, and North Korea.
The commanders were particularly concerned about depleted stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles, with some warning that supplies of critical munitions were at their lowest levels ever.
Some of Vance's conversations also involved concerns over the administration's overall strategy and the prospects for success.
Different assessment
The report said the private assessments Vance received differed significantly from the picture senior US administration officials, including President Donald Trump, presented publicly.
The report, however, said Vance's calls were made with the knowledge of Trump and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Sean Parnell, a Pentagon spokesman, said in a statement that "to ensure the president's team receives all available data points regarding ongoing operations in the Middle East, the secretary has facilitated direct access to combatant commanders for the vice president and other senior White House leaders."
Vance reportedly told colleagues within days of the war's start that he wanted detailed briefings to inform his views and better advise Trump, seeking military officers' unfiltered opinions to incorporate into his counsel to the president.
Vance tracked the daily details of the conflict, including military operations, the internal dynamics of Iran's political system, and the sourcing of intelligence assessments.
John Ratcliffe, the CIA director, also reportedly gave Vance direct access to agency analysts. Vance called some analysts at their desks to ask about raw intelligence and items included in morning briefings, according to the report.
Pentagon officials also said Hegseth had the Office of Naval Intelligence prepare daily reports for Vance on the Strait of Hormuz, which Trump's other senior aides now receive as well.
The reports described which ships were transiting the strait, their flags, and their cargo.

Hong Kong court sentences Tiananmen vigil activists to between 5 and 7 years in jail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
01:49:17 UTC
10:49:17 KST

Hong Kong court sentences Tiananmen vigil activists to between 5 and 7 years in jail
Three activists who had held annual vigils commemorating the Tiananmen Square crackdown were sentenced to between five and seven years in prison Friday for calling for an "end to one-party dictatorship". Prosecutors had argued that China's constitution enshrines the primacy of the Communist Party.
A Hong Kong court handed three Tiananmen vigil activists jail sentences of between five and seven years on Friday for national security crimes, following a trial that has drawn international condemnation.
Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, Albert Ho, 74 and Chow Hang-tung, 41 have been behind bars since they were charged in 2021. Their sentences are expected to include time already served.
The United Nations, rights groups and foreign governments have condemned their convictions under a national security law that Beijing imposed on Hong Kong following sometimes-violent mass protests that swept the city in 2019.
A court ruled in August that the activists had breached the Chinese constitution by calling for an "end to one-party dictatorship".
Watch more'The world has let this happen': Wu'er Kaixi on Hong Kong's loss of freedoms
Lee and Chow, who pleaded not guilty, were sentenced to seven years and seven years and three months respectively, AFP journalists in court heard.
Ho, a former lawmaker who pleaded guilty in January, got five years and two months.
The verdict read that although the case did not involve violence, and the defendants had not put forward a specific timetable to carry out an "end to one-party dictatorship", their offence was still of "a serious nature".
Prosecutors had argued the primacy of the Communist Party was enshrined in Article 1 of the Chinese constitution. Defence submissions that the defendants genuinely believed they were acting within the law given Hong Kong's freedoms of speech were rejected by the judges.
Chow, a barrister who represented herself, told a hearing last month that she had "nothing to repent for".
She raised both arms and waved at supporters as she was escorted out by officers.
Supporters outside court hugged her mother, Medina Chow Lau Wah-chun, who said her daughter had maintained high spirits during the trial.
"She is not a competent barrister. She is simply an outstanding defendant," her mother said.
Lee crossed himself, smiled and bowed at his wife Elizabeth Tang Yin-ngor and supporters, including high-profile activist Cardinal Joseph Zen, who stood outside gripping each others' hands.
"I'm really sad, and very angry," Tang told reporters, saying Lee would "definitely appeal".
Dozens of police swarmed around the court and set up cordons holding back crowds.
'Afraid of memory'
Hong Kong and Macau were the only places on Chinese soil that permitted public mourning for those killed on June 4, 1989, when Beijing sent troops and tanks to crush protests calling for political reform around the capital's Tiananmen Square.
But public commemoration has been effectively banned in Hong Kong since the Beijing-imposed security law took effect in 2020, following huge pro-democracy protests.
The trio were leaders of the now-defunct Hong Kong Alliance, the group that organised annual vigils in the city's Victoria Park.
National security police chief Steve Li told reporters the sentences are "a stern warning to those who may be contemplating similar acts".
"Do not underestimate our determination to safeguard ... national security," he warned.
The sentences were condemned by officials in Taiwan, which China sees as its own territory, as well as rights groups.
"The pursuit of democracy and human rights is not a crime," Taiwan's top China policy body said, adding that authorities have "fabricated charges and conducted political trials in the name of national security to shield an authoritarian regime".
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said the "harsh sentences" expose "the cruelty and insecurity of a government afraid of memory and the people".
Amnesty International's Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks said the sentencing "illustrates just how much Hong Kong has been transformed in the name of 'national security'".
"This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history," she said.
Watch moreHong Kong, law and order: Inside the rebel city now under Chinese control
Pillar of Shame
The Hong Kong Alliance group also operated a museum dedicated to the crackdown and held events, including a yearly washing of the "Pillar of Shame" – a statue to mourn victims.
The statue was removed from its long-time plinth at the University of Hong Kong in 2021, and other local universities followed suit with similar objects.
Prosecutors argued that evidence in the case, including the statue and archives from the Hong Kong Alliance's museum, should be confiscated.
Judge Alex Lee said Friday the fate of the statue would be decided after a decision was made on its ownership.
Ahead of Friday's sentencing, Chow said "the authorities' true intentions were finally laid bare".
"This prosecution is an attempt to erase memories," she said.
The Danish artist behind "Pillar of Shame", Jens Galschiot, called the outcome of the trial and the statue's potential confiscation "outrageous".
The statue tells the story of Tiananmen, Galschiot told AFP, who has for years sought to reclaim his work.
If it were destroyed, that would also "destroy the story that everybody should know", he said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

Trump absent as New York marks 25 years since 9/11 with first Muslim mayor
New York on Friday marks the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks, with President Donald Trump set to attend a ceremony at the Pentagon while Vice President JD Vance and four former presidents join commemorations at Ground Zero, where victims’ relatives will read the names of those killed.
New York commemorates the 25th anniversary of the devastating September 11, 2001 attacks Friday with a ceremony marked by US President Donald Trump's absence and right-wing outrage at the attendance of the city's first Muslim mayor.
Trump will pay his respects at the Pentagon, not New York, where hijacked planes destroyed the World Trade Center and killed most of the 2,977 total victims on that world-altering day.
Vice President JD Vance and Trump's four living predecessors – Republican George W. Bush, who was in office during the attacks, and Democrats Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton – are all expected at the "Ground Zero" site in lower Manhattan.
No one will give speeches at the ceremony, while bereaved family members will read out the names of all of those killed and a bell rung to mark major moments during the attack.
"Memorials like this and discussions about those events are an important part of keeping it alive and understanding how we prevent tragedies like this from ever happening again," said Robert Kafka, a Chicagoan in his 60s visiting the 9/11 Memorial.

Alongside the former presidents will be Democratic Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the Big Apple's first Muslim mayor, despite a campaign urging him to stay away spearheaded by the right-wing New York Post and former mayor Rudy Giuliani.
A petition, which has gathered more than 100,000 signatures, accuses Mamdani of associating with unspecified individuals who are "dismissive of American institutions or insufficiently critical of extremist ideologies".
"It's concerning to me that the mayor is being treated differently simply because he is Muslim," city council member Shahana Hanif told CNN.
Mamdani won plaudits however for recently revealing thousands of documents showing what city officials knew about toxicity levels of the air in Lower Manhattan following the attacks.
After the initial dust cloud that followed the collapse of the World Trade Center, months of pollution and lingering dust ensued, causing cancers from which thousands of New Yorkers still suffer today.
Read more9/11 then and now: Do September 2001 attacks still shape our world?
'Toxic air'
"People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," Mamdani said Tuesday.
Read moreNew York City releases post-9/11 air toxicity information kept secret for 25 years
Nineteen al Qaeda operatives hijacked four planes on that nearly cloudless day in 2001. Two jets slammed into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers, causing the iconic 110-story buildings to collapse.
A third plane struck the Pentagon, while a fourth crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back.
Beyond those killed on September 11, more than 9,400 other people have died from 9/11-related illnesses, according to the federal program established to provide medical care to those affected.
Some 100 million Americans were not even born or are too young to remember the tragic events.
Logan Miller, 32, lost his uncle during the attacks, and his grandfather to 9/11-related illness in the aftermath.
"I think the next generation just can't fathom what actually transpired and how someone could be impacted by that, and so I actually find them asking more questions," he told AFP.
Huge crowds are expected to gather in Lower Manhattan for the memorial service.
The Secret Service has erected a security ring of steel around the site of the 9/11 Memorial and Museum.
Police commissioner Jessica Tisch said an anti-drone team would be deployed as a precaution, but stressed there was no intelligence of a specific threat to the gathering.
Al Qaeda meanwhile has marked the anniversary by releasing a video showing images of late leader Osama bin Laden and his son Hamza, who Trump said in 2019 had also been killed.
Ahead of the memorial, a drone show with 2,977 lights rose above New York Harbor, one for each person killed in the attacks.

Death of the auction? Sellers move to private sales in softening market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
01:45:53 UTC
10:45:53 KST

in brief
- New data from Domain suggests more property sellers have moved away from auctions to private treaty sales.
- The property platform has also found a rise in listings starting as private treaty.
Property sellers are increasingly moving away from the traditional auction in response to a softening housing market, new data from Domain suggests, with experts arguing that Australia has firmly entered a "buyer's market".
The online property platform has found a sharp rise in listings initially slated for auction being converted to private treaty in capital cities. Across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Canberra, the average proportion sales that are auctions has more than doubled from 29.6 per cent in February to 60.8 per cent in July.
Listings starting as private treaty also increased at the same time, highlighting a substantial move away from reliance on auction-day results as sellers seek the best price for their asset.
Domain's chief of economics and research, Nicola Powell, told SBS News that this shift in seller behaviour reflects the softening market conditions "unravelling across the nation".
"Many sellers are testing the market and realising that there just isn't that buyer depth there anymore," she said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
After major post-pandemic growth and following decades of steady increases, the Australian property market has seen a broad downturn over winter.
Data from property analyst Cotality shows that, while Sydney and Melbourne began to slow at the start of the year, national house price values peaked in March and have declined 3.6 per cent since.
Powell argued spring will likely be slower than usual, with Domain predicting property prices will continue to fall through the rest of the year.
"I think what we're going to see from buyers is they are going to want to get that greater value for money," she said.
The second quarter of 2026 saw the first sustained decline in national housing stock value since 2022, with Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showing a 0.3 per cent drop or $34.1 billion.
Auctions still a good idea
Shannan Whitney, co-founder of prominent Sydney property group BresicWhitney, told SBS News that shying away from auction sales could be the wrong move for sellers.
"Pricing tends to be more in line with where the market needs to be in an auction process than it does in a for sale process," he said.
"I think more vendors will be more comfortable with auction in Sydney over the next three or four months, but it just takes a little bit of time for everyone to work through the cycle."
Whitney expects the property cycle is now through its "first third" after months of price adjustments. It's "natural", he said, for sellers to want to retreat into non-auction sales where they feel safer or more in control during such a period, which he believes is now levelling off in Sydney.
"Vendors genuinely contemplating a sale are now much more aligned and educated about where the market is," he said. "Therefore, we think we expect to see clearance rates probably go up and improve over the next four months."
Sellers who aren't "in line" with the market should consider their position and perhaps pause on a sale for the next 12 months to three years, Whitney advised.
Buyers, on the other hand, are experiencing very favourable conditions. However, Whitney suggested that waiting and expecting prices to continue to drop might not be the best strategy.
Even though the market was soft, trading was better now compared with earlier in the year.
"What we're seeing now is much more engagement from buyers where they see pricing at reasonable, viable levels," he said. "We are seeing properties sell quicker now than we did six months ago."
Rapid corrections
Sustained high borrowing costs and stubborn inflation are some of the key drivers squeezing buyer affordability. At the same time, the surge in listings through autumn and winter forced national average clearance rates down to around 46 per cent.
"Listings have risen, choice is better than it once was, and particularly in markets like Sydney and Melbourne, it is very much a buyer's market," Powell said.
Economists note clearance rates below 60 per cent reduce inflationary pressure on house prices.
Major financial institutions including Commonwealth Bank have forecast a peak-to-trough decline in house prices of 8 to 10 per cent, with the market expected to hit its bottom in early 2027.
Those in the market are already pricing in the changed conditions, Whitney said, noting that the speed of information transfer at present means adjustments and property cycles happen far more quickly than they used to.
The Reserve Bank of Australia is widely expected to raise interest rates for the fourth time this year during its meeting at the end of this month. With an increased cash rate of 4.6 per cent, buyer confidence is expected to take a further hit.
If the RBA does increase rates this month, it is likely to trigger a continued "drag on inventory" as conditions slow even further.
"The cycle for buyers will lengthen and look more favourable," Whitney said.

Foreign carmakers offer steep discounts on petrol-powered cars in cutthroat Chinese market
With more consumers switching to electric vehicles, companies including VW and Toyota are slashing prices on lower-tech offerings
Last month, big international marques including Volkswagen and Toyota offered average discounts of 23.4 per cent on cars powered by internal combustion engines, according to data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). That compared with an average discount of 23.7 per cent in July.
“Because their new cars were priced at a particularly low level, the strong promotional efforts have persisted over the past months, which resulted in a small sales increase,” the association said in a report released this week.
It said that, in comparison, the average discount in 2023 was about 13 per cent.
The accelerating electrification seen on mainland China’s roads over the past decade has eaten into international car brands’ market share in the world’s largest automotive market due to their slow transition to electric vehicles (EVs), according to analysts.
They said the global energy shock arising from the Iran war had exacerbated the foreign carmakers’ bleak sales outlook as more budget-conscious consumers opted for battery-powered vehicles to save fuel costs.
Last month, EVs’ share of vehicle sales on the mainland hit an all-time high of 65.2 per cent, according to CPCA data. However, overall car sales slumped 23.6 per cent year on year.

Ukrainian drones launched an attack on the Russian city of Saratov overnight on Sept. 11, reportedly striking oil and logistics infrastructure, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Independent Russian outlet ASTRA said its OSINT analysis identified a fire at the Rosneft-owned refinery in Saratov. Videos circulating on social media also appeared to show drones and Russian air defenses in operation in the region.
The Saratov Oil Refinery has been repeatedly targeted during Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign against Russia’s energy infrastructure. The facility, which is part of state oil company Rosneft, has an annual processing capacity of roughly 4.8 million metric tons of crude oil.
Saratov Oblast Governor Roman Busargin posted on Telegram around 2 a.m. local time about a threat from unmanned aerial vehicles, claiming that emergency services had been placed on full alert.
Soon after the strike on the refinery, a logistics hub belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Ozon was also reported to be set ablaze in Saratov. Video published by Exilenova+ appeared to show a major fire emanating from the facility shortly after explosions were heard.
Ozon is Russia’s second-largest e-commerce marketplace, behind Wildberries, and operates an extensive network of warehouses, fulfillment centers and delivery infrastructure across the country.
Elsewhere in Russia, explosions were also heard in the port city of Kaspiysk in the Dagestan Republic. No information was immediately known as to the outcome of the reported attack.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports or the extent of any damage. Ukraine’s military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
Saratov is located approximately 460 kilometers (285 miles) east of the Ukrainian border with Russia, near Luhansk Oblast in eastern Ukraine.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have emerged as one of the most economically significant aspects of Kyiv's long-range drone campaign, contributing to fuel shortages and pushing Russian production down sharply over the summer. Russian refinery throughput fell to about 3.8 million barrels per day in August, down from around 5 million barrels per day a year earlier, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing Energy Aspects.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries in an effort to disrupt fuel supplies and reduce energy revenues that help finance Moscow’s war.
