Can Europe recharge its battery industry?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
00:05:47 BST
08:05:47 KST

Can Europe recharge its battery industry?
- Published
Europe has taken some big swings in the battery industry in recent years and has made a couple of high-profile misses.
Both Sweden's Northvolt, external and Norway's Morrow, external filed for bankruptcy and there are fears in Europe that the continent has missed another technology shift.
With more transport and industry switching from fossil fuels to electricity, batteries are likely to be a growth business.
But the length of time required to bring new products to market, coupled with brutal competition, especially from China, means taking a substantial risk.
Could the answer lie at an almost unimaginably small scale? An increasing number of investors and researchers think so.
A single nanometre is one-billionth of a metre, but it's at that level that some of the most consequential work is being done.
"If you can make this work, it touches so many industries [but] it's a risky business," says Christian Rood, chief executive of Dutch tech firm LeydenJar.
Named after a 18th century precursor to electric cells, LeydenJar uses a technique known as plasma deposition to make a lighter, more efficient anode – an essential component of all batteries.
Silicon is a highly effective and cheap material to use in anodes, but pure silicon expands and contracts as the battery operates and is recharged, which causes it to crack.
However, using plasma deposition, LeydenJar can - layer by tiny layer - make an ultra-thin pure silicon foil which resists cracking, allowing a significant increase in battery life, charging speed, and energy density (up to 50%, according to LeydenJar).
"Where normally a pure silicon anode would fall apart, [this] remains stable, so it was a very wonderful invention," says Rood.
"We address the bottleneck in the battery."
Commercial-scale production will start at the end of 2026, but it has taken 10 years to get to this point – the very definition of the time and investment required for so-called Deep Tech innovations.
It's no coincidence that LeydenJar's factory is in the Dutch city of Eindhoven - home to ASML and other important players in the computer chip industry.
"A lot of people talk theoretically about ecosystems; I can tell you this is one of our sources of competitive advantage," Rood says.
"It's really the crossover from semiconductors to batteries that makes us different - once you've demonstrated the principle in the lab, industrialization requires you to work with the semiconductor technology and suppliers.
"That means a lot of risk, but also a lot of opportunity in terms of patenting, in terms of securing your whole intellectual property. And that's much more difficult to do in the US or in China."
Across the Netherlands and Europe more widely there are multiple smaller Deep Tech start-ups looking to develop nanotechnology in the battery market.
One of those is Powall, a start-up in the Dutch city of Delft that is developing commercial-scale equipment for nanocoating the powders that are the raw materials of today's batteries.
Again, the scale is tiny, and once again the technique was born in the semiconductor industry.
Individual powder granules are measured in micrometres, the coatings in nanometres - they are applied using a technique known as atomic layer deposition.
Roderik Colen, CEO of Powall, tells me that the system offers multiple opportunities to adjust and improve the performance of today's batteries.
"Your battery works less well than before after using it thousands of times - that degrading or aging can be slowed down when you're using a nanocoating," Colen explains.
"You can have an exciting new material with a higher capacity or fast charging, all these novel developments. They typically have one element which is very good, but they suffer on the durability side."
And that means they will never be a commercial product.
"That's where we then come in, to give them the protective coating to effectively enable these new materials."
The powders and the coating are carried by gas and brought together in a chemical reaction.
It is, says Colen, a precise but flexible process which can be almost endlessly adapted.
"You have great accuracy in how thick you want to have it. And that makes a difference in performance."
Neither LeydenJar nor Powall are trying to build an entire battery, and both have commercial relationships with customers in Asia.
But Christian Rood of LeydenJar says companies like his can fortify Europe's position in what has become a global contest.
"The easy comparison is with semiconductors, where there's really a race for the best chip technology.
"[Dutch tech giant] ASML is not producing chips; it focuses on a critical step in the production of chips, and in that way, has a seat at the table when it comes to the whole semiconductor battle.
"This is our ambition as well – to have a position where our battery anode is so unique that we have an important position in the supply chain."
So, how do these ambitions play into Europe's goals in the battery industry?
Alexander Brown is a senior analyst at the Berlin-based independent think-tank the Mercator Institute for China Studies (Merics).
"I think having one part of the supply chain based in Europe is great and if that can be a very advanced technological part, which offers the opportunity for high margins, that's fantastic," Brown tells me.
But he cautions that while "there can be collaboration as well as competition at the same time", China in particular will continue to work to reduce its dependence on other regions.
"China is working very hard to develop local alternatives for technologies, including these niche technologies.
"It's no secret that China would love to replace ASML - they're working very hard to do that, and it's not unforeseeable that they will achieve that goal eventually.
"So, I think Europe has traditional strengths in developing very exquisite high-quality products, which can find markets all over the world.
"But I also think it's important for that not to be the only strategy [from the continent's policy makers]."
The challenges of working in such a specialised field are not only technological.
LeydenJar has already reached commercial scale, but Rood says that raising funds within Europe is not always easy.
"There is sufficient financing in Europe, but the risk attitude is quite different than in Asia and in the US," says Rood.
"That means for a company like us that you have to work with different sources of funding at the same time," Rood explains.
He lists government grants, debt financing, help from the European Investment Bank and investors willing to buy a share of the business.
"They set a lot of challenging conditions, and they all want to do their own due diligence. It's hard work," Rood says.
Powall's Colen says Europe, and the Netherlands in particular, is an "innovation powerhouse", and battery technology offers a chance for the continent to make an impact, if the appetite for the risk is there.
"It's a relatively young industry where factories are being built left, right and centre. They're searching for the right tech. So that's where you can play a big role, because the volumes are huge."
Perhaps Europe's place in that business lies not in building huge battery gigafactories, but at the other end of the scale altogether.
As Colen puts it, "small changes make big differences."

From JFK to Biden, Trump joins well-trodden path to the Emerald Isle
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
00:01:55 BST
08:01:55 KST

From JFK to Biden, Trump joins well-trodden path to the Emerald Isle
- Published
When Donald Trump lands in Dublin on Saturday, he will be on a well-trodden international path.
In recent decades, Ireland has become a particularly frequent fixture for US presidential trips.
It stands out among small countries as hosting a high number of visits.
The bond between the two nations was forged by emigration, deepened by economic ties, and cemented by the Northern Ireland peace process – in which Washington played a major role.
Historians generally estimate that around five million people left Ireland for the US in the 19th and early 20th centuries.
Dr Peter McLoughlin, who teaches history and politics at Queen's University Belfast, said that created an "enormous ethnic link".
In 2024, census data found that 32.4 million Americans claimed Irish ancestry – almost one in ten of the population.
That means several presidents have seen political advantage in being seen to explore their heritage.
John F Kennedy was the first president to go to Ireland while in office.
In June 1963, he visited his ancestral homestead in County Wexford, from where his great-grandfather had left during the Irish potato famine in 1848.
In his address to the Irish Parliament, he said: "This has never been a rich or powerful country, and yet, since earliest times, its influence on the world has been rich and powerful."
In the years since, Ireland has become rich by many global measures, with some of the US's biggest firms driving its economic growth.
Tech and pharmaceutical firms - such as Apple, Pfizer and Meta - have key European bases in Ireland.
The rapid expansion of US investment in Ireland in the 1990s coincided with the development of the peace process in Northern Ireland.
Bill Clinton's three visits to the island took in both sides of the border, and he was strongly involved in the Good Friday Agreement in 1998, which largely ended the conflict in Northern Ireland after three decades.
McLoughlin, who has researched America's role, said: "It's one of the examples where you can see US power being used in a successful way to get a peaceful settlement.
"After Clinton, George W Bush was maybe not such a hands-on president as regards Northern Ireland, but his White House was important in making sure the Good Friday Agreement was implemented."
St Patrick's Day in Washington
Politicians, civic leaders and business figures from Belfast and Dublin are hosted in Washington each year on Ireland's national holiday, St Patrick's Day.
The taoiseach (Irish prime minister) traditionally presents the president with a bowl of shamrock, the plant which is a symbol of Ireland.
Dan Mulhall, who was Ireland's Ambassador to Washington from 2017-22, said the yearly access to the White House was "pretty unique".
"I remember some of my European colleagues were kind of puzzled as to how Ireland had pulled this off, given that some of them also have large diaspora communities in the US, but they don't seem to have the same impact or lasting connection with their ancestral homeland as the Irish Americans undoubtedly have."
Barack Obama paid homage to his heritage in 2011, when he visited his great-great-great grandfather's home village of Moneygall in County Offaly.
In a speech in Dublin, he joked: "I've come home to find the apostrophe that we lost somewhere along the way."
Joe Biden described Ireland as "part of his soul" on his trip in 2023, which was the last US presidential visit.
He went to his ancestral counties of Mayo and Louth and marked the 25th anniversary of the Good Friday Agreement.
Donald Trump's visit will be different in content and tone.
He has no known Irish ancestry.
His focus will be on golf rather than genealogy, as he will watch the Irish Open played at his resort in Doonbeg in County Clare.
In Dublin, he will meet the Taoiseach Micheàl Martin and the Irish President Catherine Connolly.
Connolly has a largely ceremonial role as head-of-state, but she has previously been a staunch critic of US foreign policy, particularly in the Middle East.
Earlier this year Trump referred to Connolly as "he" when responding to criticisms she made about the US attack on Iran being "a brutal assault on international law".
"He's lucky I exist," Trump said.
The US Embassy in Dublin criticised a law passed by the Irish Parliament this year to ban the importation of goods from Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory.
The Embassy said the legislation "risked real unintended consequences, particularly for nearly 1000 US companies and the hundreds of thousands of Irish jobs tied to them".
US actions abroad will be the focus of protests in Dublin and County Clare this weekend.
On Thursday a large sand artwork appeared on a beach in Dublin Bay.
The campaign group Uplift carved the words 'No kings - Gaza Iran Ice' into the sand.
Washington's trade policy has been another prominent issue in Ireland, as Trump has expressed unhappiness at the scale of US pharmaceutical manufacturing in the country.
However, tariffs have mostly not been imposed on the sector.
Mullhall, the former Ireland Ambassador to Washington said the economic relationship was "as strong as it's ever been".
He thinks the Irish government will approach Trump's visit with "prudent realism".
"It's not possible to expect that a small country, any country in fact, can deflect Donald Trump from any of his purposes or policies.
"Most countries have adopted the strategy of simply trying to ride out the Trump term and hope for more predictable days ahead.
"So I think the government will play it safe and will be above all else, be wanting to avoid any kind of tension or difficulty between themselves and Donald Trump."
McLoughlin, of Queen's University, sees parallels between Trump's visit and that of Ronald Reagan in 1984, when there was opposition over US foreign policy in Latin America.
The Catholic church was very influential in Ireland at that time and McLoughlin pointed out that senior clergy did not meet Reagan.
"This was a time when many people would have members of the family who were in Latin America as a nun or a priest, and were bringing back first-hand reports of how there were controversial associations with US policy, with right-wing paramilitaries who were engaged in the Cold War struggle."
But he said that amidst the criticism of the visit, the Irish government wanted to "court" Reagan, for "economic reasons, and political reasons involving Northern Ireland".
He added that pictures of Reagan exploring his ancestry, in County Tipperary, helped make the visit "successful" from Dublin and Washington's point of view.
Ireland is more used than most countries to hosting the holder of the most powerful office in the world and the diplomatic delicacies around Trump's visit are another episode in a story dating back many decades.

'NAZA': Guardian-produced film sheds light on Israeli system behind Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
23:00:12 UTC
08:00:12 KST

A new documentary by Oscar-winning Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor has premiered at the Venice International Film Festival, revealing testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders about secret systems used to identify, track and attack Palestinians in besieged Gaza despite expected civilian fatalities.
Titled NAZA, the Guardian-produced film was screened on Thursday in the main competition at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival and is the only documentary competing for the Golden Lion this year.
The film takes its title from NAZA, a Hebrew military acronym for "collateral damage," used by Israeli intelligence to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an attack.
The 80-minute documentary was produced by The Guardian and James Wilson of JW Films, with Jonathan Glazer serving as an executive producer. Wilson and Glazer previously worked together on the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.
NAZA builds on investigations published between 2023 and 2025 by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and The Guardian.
AI systems identify targets for attacks at homes
Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers interviewed for the film describe AI-based systems used to identify large numbers of suspected low-ranking Hamas members as potential targets.
According to their testimony, people identified through the systems were bombed in their homes at night despite knowledge that the strikes would also kill members of their families.
The insiders also describe hacking into the phones of people marked for attack to determine their locations.
Intelligence officers covertly listened to conversations between targets and their wives and children, according to the testimony, sometimes until shortly before attacks on their homes.
Speaking at a news conference in Venice, Abraham said the filmmakers asked the officers to explain their work.
"We just told these officers: 'Please describe to us what you did. How do these systems work? Sketch it out for us.' Sometimes, in just asking the questions, you get the answers," he said.
"Some of them did not express remorse, and some did. Some spoke out of indifference, some out of pride."
Systematic destruction of civilian areas
The testimony also includes first-hand accounts of the destruction of neighbourhoods where the Israeli military estimated that as many as 25 percent of residents were still in their homes.
The interviewees describe the systematic burning of civilian homes and the killing of civilians at a food distribution site.
Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to The Guardian. One of them said the unit's mission was to "thwart peace."
Abraham and Szor said the film focuses on military policies and practices rather than misconduct by individual soldiers.
"Our focus is not on sporadic war crimes committed by rogue soldiers," they said.
Instead, the directors said their focus was on "the orders themselves, the policies, the accepted practices, the language and logic that make those practices possible, and the people who operate within them."
"The system and its cogs," they added.
Abraham described the film as an examination of "systems of mass killing" based on testimony from the 24 insiders.
Gaza genocide
Since the start of the genocide in October 2023, Israel has killed over 73,000 Palestinians, mostly women and children, and wounded over 174,000 others.
Analysts say the estimate is an underestimate, and the actual death toll could be approximately 200,000.
Israel which occupies 60 percent of Gaza has reduced most of the blockaded enclave to ruins and displaced the entire population.
Despite an agreed ceasefire deal in October 2025, Israel continues to violate it daily, killing at least 1,359 Palestinians and wounding 4,571 others.

Hong Kong home prices headed for 15% gain this year, Midland forecast says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
23:00:09 UTC
08:00:09 KST

Hong Kong home prices headed for 15% gain this year, Midland forecast says
As the market digests uncertainties, new property launches are accelerating and buyers are returning to the market, executive says
Hong Kong’s home prices will end the year 15 per cent higher than a year earlier, but still 16 per cent below their high-water mark in 2021, according to local property agency Midland Realty.
Underpinning the positive forecast, the city’s banks were not likely to follow an increase in US interest rates by the Federal Reserve if one occurred this year, executives from the agency said at a press conference on Thursday.
Dave Ma Tai-yeung, CEO of Midland (Residential), said that as the market gradually digested geopolitical and external economic uncertainties, new property launches were accelerating and buyers were returning to the market.
“With the improved market sentiment, developers will accelerate the launch of new projects, and the residential market is expected to further recover,” Ma said.
First-hand residential property transactions, after falling for two consecutive months to just over 800 units in June and July, rebounded to 1,100 units in August, while second-hand residential transactions were also gradually stabilising, according to Midland’s data.
Ma said that first-hand property transactions in the final quarter would increase by 50 per cent quarter on quarter to 5,100 units, while secondary market transactions would rise by 10 per cent to 12,700.
“With residential rents hitting new highs one after another, there is room for property prices to catch up,” Ma said.

25 Years After 9/11: Whatever Happened to Mass-Effect Terrorism?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

25 Years After 9/11: Whatever Happened to Mass-Effect Terrorism?
One mystery about 9/11 is why no attack of comparable scale has followed. With new motivations, enhanced delivery and AI-devised weapons, there should be no complacency.
9/11 changed everything. It led to two decades when the US and much of Europe became fixated on Islamism. Western strategists became fluent in half-absorbed subjects such as Wahhabism, Pashtun tribal customs, Frontier Crimes Regulations and the Anbar Awakening while giving insufficient attention to Chinese economic dominance and Russian military rearmament. Who knows what that diversion of strategic and intellectual resources (and the chaos it left behind in the region) has cost the West?
9/11 also bookends that remarkable period from the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1989/90 when peace and reconciliation seemed to break out everywhere. The Oslo Accords of 1993 appeared to chart a trajectory towards a two-state solution in Israel/Palestine. One year later the peaceful multiparty elections in South Africa were nothing short of a miracle. For years Afrikaners had insisted they would fight black rule until the last drop of white blood. This was the brief ‘unipolar moment’ under the then-still largely benign supervision of Washington.
‘Both Triumphant and Disastrous’
9/11 ushered in a new world – one with which Thomas Hobbes would be all too familiar. ‘Covenants, without the sword, are but words and of no strength to secure a man at all.’ ‘Force and fraud are in war the two cardinal virtues.’ Almost every quote from Leviathan is applicable.
Of course, first and foremost, 9/11 was a tragedy for the victims and their families. It was an act of appalling savagery. It was not only the largest terrorist attack in history by a country-mile, but it also introduced a new concept of mass-effect terrorism.
From the terrorists’ point of view, it was also an attack of breath-taking scale and ambition. Osama bin Laden had the imagination to view an aircraft full of fuel and passengers as a terror weapon by knitting together two of Al-Qaeda’s (AQ) previous failures: the truck-bomb attack on the World Trade Center in 1993 and the 1995 Operation Bojinka in the Philippines. Both attacks had been planned by Ramzi Yousef, whose uncle, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, was the chief planner for 9/11.
Contrary to widespread opinion, the concept of mass-effect terrorism had been exercising minds in Washington and Whitehall long before 9/11
It was also, from an AQ viewpoint, both triumphant and disastrous. Its success was that a superpower overreacted for two decades and allowed 9/11 to shape the whole of Western foreign policy as a Global War on Terror. Its failure was due to Washington’s largely successful determination to destroy AQ, a success which was only imperilled when President Trump approved the feckless Doha Accords with the Taliban in 2020, opening the way to the return of AQ to Afghanistan the following year. The latest UN report on terrorism confirms that AQ continues to re-establish itself.
‘Terrorist Ambitions Remained High’
As early as 1998, the British government had warned Washington that it was the likely next target in an operation which would involve hijacked aircraft. This story was told in detail by RUSI for the 20th anniversary of 9/11. The intelligence was briefed to both Presidents Clinton and Bush (junior). Contrary to widespread opinion, the concept of mass-effect terrorism had been exercising minds in Washington and Whitehall long before 9/11. If they had not made the intellectual leap of imagining airliners as weapons, they had nonetheless been thinking a great deal about mass-casualty attacks. This was prompted by three convergent factors.
First, in 1995 a doomsday cult known as Aum Shinrikyo released sarin on the Tokyo metro in an attack which (had it been carried out more effectively) could have killed thousands. This led to much discussion of how to react to a similar attack on the London Underground. There was also concern about chemical and biological substances being brought into the country inside the diplomatic mail bags of state sponsors of terrorism (the bags being protected from scrutiny by the Vienna Convention of 1961).
Second, there were fears about AQ getting its hands on nuclear material and producing a dirty bomb (not a nuclear explosion). At the time, it was believed that fissile material was being sold by former employees of the Soviet nuclear programme and finding its way through Central Asia to Pakistan. Most of it was a scam called ‘red mercury’ which was thoroughly investigated at the time, but there were enough more credible reports to create uncertainty.
Finally, it was known that AQ had two scientists working on chemical, biological and nuclear (CBN) experiments out of Derunta camp near the Afghanistan–Pakistan border. Not all the fine detail was available, but one of the scientists, Dr Sultan Bashiruddin Mahmood, had previously worked on Pakistan’s own sovereign nuclear programme. This story was well told a decade later by the veteran journalist Peter Bergen.
‘Herein Lies the Real Mystery’
Thus began a decade-long US fixation with the danger of terrorists obtaining access to Pakistan’s nuclear weapons. President Obama insisted that ‘The single biggest threat to U.S. security, both short term, medium term and long term, would be the possibility of a terrorist organization obtaining a nuclear weapon.’
Once 9/11 had happened, the assumption was that there would be numerous copycat attacks. In London, much focus was devoted to the towers at Canary Wharf, which housed some of the world’s premier financial institutions and which were also close to the flight paths of both Heathrow and London City airports.
In the years immediately after 9/11, terrorist ambitions remained high, including the Bali bombings in 2002 (202 killed), the Madrid train bombings in 2004 (193) and London 2005 (52). There were two dangerous plots foiled in the UK, Crevice in 2003 and Rhyme in 2004 but the only one on the scale of 9/11 was Operation Overt in 2006, AQ’s plan to bring down seven airliners in mid-Atlantic. Fortunately, it was thwarted by MI5.
And herein lies the real mystery. There have been numerous nasty and costly terrorist attacks since, but none on the 9/11 scale. There is a danger of sounding callous when observing that none of Mumbai in 2008 (166 killed), Paris in 2015 (130) and Sri Lanka in 2019 (269) come even close to 9/11 (2,977).
‘There the Comparison Ends’
Two types of terrorism have emerged since Overt in 2006.
The first was ‘urban siege’, ‘swarm’ or ‘rampaging’ terrorism which we first saw at Mumbai in 2008 and the Westgate shopping mall in Nairobi in 2013 (which killed 71). This is an effective form of terrorism because it captures press attention for hours (62 hours in the case of Mumbai) and makes prompt armed response extremely difficult. However, it is also costly for the terrorists, who are nearly always killed or captured, and their supporting organisations and states identified. The Indians were relentless in following up the Mumbai attack although Lashkar-e-Tayyiba still exists and represents a significant threat to regional peace.
The second (and now the most common) is ‘lone wolf’ terrorism usually committed by lone (and lonely) young men who have become self-radicalised online in their bedrooms and take the family car or a kitchen knife and seek to kill as many people as possible. The problem with this second type is that it is almost indistinguishable from wider mental health problems brought about by social isolation. It risks a substantial drain on the precious resources of security services, which need to be focusing on strategic threats (such as those posed by Russia, Iran and China as well as terrorist groups).
In terms of mass casualties, only one is comparable with 9/11: the brutal Hamas incursion into southern Israel on 7 October 2023. As a proportion of Israel’s population, it is probably the most lethal terrorist attack in history. But there the comparison ends. The attack involved guns, knives and grenades – a far cry from the use of aircraft as a weapon against a ground-based target.
'Still Too Early to Say'
Aircraft and their passengers have often been targets before, notably Pan Am Flight 103 at Lockerbie in 1988 (270 deaths), UTA Flight 772 the following year over Niger (170) and the often-forgotten Air India Flight 182 off the Irish coast in 1985 (329). But in each case the aircraft and passengers were the target rather than the means of delivery against an objective on the ground. 25 years after 9/11, one would have expected to see several similar attacks using aircraft against buildings or (even worse) against stadiums full of spectators.
Why has this not happened?
Advances in drone technology in Ukraine since 2022 could provide terrorists with an effective means of delivery at a time when countermeasures are still in their infancy
Precautions taken by airlines should take some credit. Cockpit doors have been strengthened, and protocols have been largely enforced, although there are signs of laxness creeping back in.
Security services have used bulk data to identify suspicious trends and plots early. AI will help here. It is now much harder for terrorists to operate as groups.
And the US military, its intelligence services and allies wreaked considerable damage on both AQ and Islamic State from 2001 through until 2019.
So, was 9/11 a one-off rather than, as was feared, the start of a new trend? It is still too early to say. Motivation for terrorism remains strong (especially following the destruction of Gaza since October 2023). Advances in drone technology in Ukraine since 2022 could provide terrorists with an effective means of delivery at a time when countermeasures are still in their infancy. And AI could enable terrorists to research and develop lethal payloads.
As we remember 9/11, it is still too early to welcome the absence of successful repeat during that costly quarter-century.

Retro looks, current jibes: Netas give '80s a new spin

NEW DELHI: "The 80s called, I answered," quipped agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan as he posted on X a picture of him from that era. Congress Kerala posted an invented Gujarat street scene; BJP Telangana replied with a fabricated bar scene tagged "Lusiana, Italy", apparently alluding to Sonia Gandhi's birthplace.The '80s came calling, and India's politicians answered with aviators, old albums and a little swagger. Then party accounts joined the nostalgia trip, remembering to pack a few jibes for the other side.Union commerce minister Piyush Goyal shared an AI portrait of himself in a suit and aviators, saying: "Vibing to the 80s trend". Union ports, shipping and waterways minister Sarbananda Sonowal wrote: "80s vibes: Styles fade, but the appeal is forever!" A line fit for a campaign, vintage or otherwise.Assam CM Himanta Biswa Sarma chimed in: "Back to the 80s eh!" Telangana CM Revanth Reddy appeared beside a motorbike in his post. For a while, the competition seemed to be over who wore the decade best.Others let their albums do the talking. Congress neta Renuka Chowdhury offered a reality check: "Me? I've got receipts." She shared what she de-scribed as an '80s Savvy magazine cover featuring herself.Union minister Kiren Rijiju followed his AI makeover with a throwback he said needed neither AI nor ChatGPT.
Congress MP Shashi Tharoor posted pictures with his sons, Ishaan and Kanishk. "I thought I'd join the trend the old-fashioned way," he wrote, a real photograph a boast of its own amid the trend built on imagining the past.BJP's Tamilisai Soundararajan shared wedding footage featuring then chief minister MGR and opposition leader M Karunanidhi. Rival camps on one guest list.
The party accounts added their own gloss. BJP Tamil Nadu's montage of PM Narendra Modi mixed AI styling with archival photographs, ending with "karmayogi". Congress Sevadal posted AI images of Rahul Gandhi.Then came the knowing captions. Congress Kerala's AI image showed a bald man in an Omni van: "A Gujarat street in the 80s." A roadside sign said in Hindi: "Please smile, you are in Delhi." BJP Telangana's bar scene was dated "Circa-1970's". Neither named its target.The clothes belonged to another decade. The urge to have the last word was entirely up to date.

Israel says it destroyed strategic Hezbollah stronghold in southern Lebanon
Unknown

Children of 9/11 to finally get a major health study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
22:57:00 UTC
07:57:00 KST

Children of 9/11 to finally get a major health study
- Around 25,000 children were exposed to toxic dust from the 9/11 attacks, but few were included in early health studies tracking long-term illnesses.
- The US Congress and CDC will fund a major study starting in 2027 to track health impacts on children exposed during or before 9/11.
- Experts stress community support is vital for recruitment, and findings may guide prevention for children exposed to similar disasters worldwide.
AI generated
When hijacked planes brought down the World Trade Center’s twin towers on Sept 11, 2001, roughly 25,000 children were living or attending school nearby in Lower Manhattan and thousands more were in surrounding neighbourhoods. Some were infants and toddlers, while others were still in the womb.
Even though they were exposed to the massive toxic cloud and settling dust containing pulverised concrete, glass fibres, asbestos and other pollutants in the days and weeks after the towers fell, very few of these children were enrolled in the government-funded follow-up health studies of 9/11 survivors. Those were mainly for first responders and other adults.
As a result, there were no means of tracking chronic illnesses, including cancers, cardiovascular diseases and reproductive health outcomes, that may only now be emerging as those children reach their 30s and early 40s, scientists say.
Major questions remain about whether exposure to the toxins and the trauma on 9/11 and afterwards increased their long-term health risks, according to scientists.
To address these gaps, the US Congress announced in 2022 that it would fund a study of these individuals to be conducted with oversight by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
In August, the CDC said it will be seeking applications from researchers to set up the World Trade Center Youth Research Coordinating Center and to identify and track a Youth Research Cohort.
The agency has specified that study participants must have been 21 years old or younger, or in utero, and living below 14th Street in Manhattan or anywhere in Brooklyn on and after 9/11.
A cohort of similarly aged but unexposed individuals will be recruited for comparison.
It is not clear how many participants the CDC hopes to recruit, but an agency spokesperson said it expects to spend up to US$50 million (S$63.4 million) in total programme funding. The estimated start date for the project is July 1, 2027, the spokesperson said.
Members of the public can sign up online for updates and register to be notified when enrolment opens to those who are qualified.
The CDC’s World Trade Center Health Program and the New York City Department of Health’s World Trade Center Health Registry both offered services for children in the early years after the attacks.
But most affected youngsters sought care from their own paediatricians, whereas many adult survivors were uninsured and needed the programmes’ services, recalled lung specialist Joan Reibman of NYU Langone Medical Center.
In adult survivors and first responders, dozens of types of cancers and other health issues related to their exposure have been identified. But data on the effects of childhood exposure has so far come only from small studies.
Reibman, founder of the World Trade Center Environmental Health Center, said gathering participants will require a great deal of community support.
“These people are spread across the United States right now. They’re all older. They may not necessarily want to go back to that period of time,” she said. “There’s going to have to be a lot of work with community groups to try to recruit them.”
Reibman and Leigh Wilson, the current medical director of the World Trade Center Environmental Health Center, both acknowledged that children in war zones today may face some of the same long-term consequences as the children of 9/11.
“I would love to prevent every and any adverse effect on these children,” Wilson said.
Studying the children of 9/11 may shed light on preventive and mitigating measures and resources that could be put in place, Wilson added.
“You have to identify and start studying all exposed populations immediately, whether they’re adults or children,” Reibman said, and “unfortunately we haven’t learnt it from the World Trade Center disaster”. REUTERS

I went into France's prehistoric caves. The world hasn't looked the same since
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
22:55:32 UTC
07:55:32 KST

One Saturday in mid-May, five of us stood inside a cave in the Ariège Valley in southern France, in complete silence and absolute darkness. We were two archaeologists, a Jungian analyst, a painter and me. I opened my eyes wide and saw nothing. I heard someone's stomach rumble, heard my companions breathing, felt them beside me. Water dripped, each drop echoing. Was this what our prehistoric ancestors heard?
Homo sapiens first entered this cave between 14,000 and 17,000 years ago. They ventured into its depths carrying torches and oil lamps to paint animals on its walls. More than 500 human footprints have been discovered here, including those of three small children.
I closed my eyes. I found myself looking into myself and into the eternity before I was born. I had never felt anything like it. Uncontrollable sobs rose from somewhere deep inside me and filled the cave. I stood there and wept, longing for everything we humans had been before we became estranged from the world, and for everything I, too, had been tens of thousands of years ago.
We spent three hours inside Niaux Cave, but had no sense of how much time had passed between entering and leaving. Time inside a cave is different from time outside. We were deeply moved.
Dr. Ella Assaf Shpayer, 39, a researcher and lecturer in the Department of Archaeology at Tel Aviv University, was very quiet inside the cave and remained so after we emerged.
"What did you feel in there?" I asked her.
"A year ago, I dreamed I was swimming inside myself," she replied. "I was consciously searching for quiet. I knew I had to go deeper and deeper to find it. When I reached my diaphragm, I found a long, spiraling seashell. I felt it inside me, along with the quiet I'd been looking for. I knew I'd come to the right place.
"Prehistoric humans had a thing for seashells. In Europe, Neanderthals collected them, painted them red, wore them and buried their loved ones with them. Sometimes they even risked their lives diving deep to find them. The shells must have been more than ornaments. Surely they wouldn't have risked their lives just for decoration. In the cave, I felt I was swimming inside myself, and I felt the quiet I'd experienced in the dream. Standing in that darkness, I felt a profound peace. The darkness was powerful, but also enveloping, soft and deep. It even felt familiar. An ancient familiarity, something the body and soul remember from long ago."
"It made me think of the Ten Plagues of Egypt," added Dr. Guy Perel, 58, a Jungian analyst and poet. "The plague of darkness is described as a tangible darkness, something you can feel with your hands, touch. The darkness in the cave is dense, but not frightening at all. It holds you up. It's amazing, and cold. You feel as though you're flying."
Niaux was the first stop on our journey through seven caves where prehistoric paintings have been discovered. We had come to experience these places together and better understand how creativity, belief, consciousness and human ability had converged here, finding expression in paintings tens of thousands of years old.
We wanted to enter these ancient wombs, the places where prehistoric humans had experienced an expansion of consciousness. We hoped ours might expand, too.
We set out just days after the cease-fire was announced in the 2026 Iran war. We came from the painful reality of our lives, a reality devoid of reason, compassion and love. Perhaps the instinct that had drawn prehistoric humans into the depths of caves had brought us here, too.
But first, the story of how this journey began.
About 10 years ago, Perel came across "Return to Chauvet Cave: Excavating the Birthplace of Art," by the French prehistorian Jean Clottes. Through it, he encountered the 36,000-year-old paintings discovered in Chauvet Cave in 1994.
The cave contained hundreds of paintings of animals: bison, woolly rhinoceroses, mammoths, deer, cave lions, horses, one particularly famous owl and many others. Yet there was only one painting of a human being. Known as "Venus and the Sorcerer," it depicts a woman's lower body with a mysterious figure above her. Many researchers believe the figure combines human characteristics with those of a bison or an aurochs.
Perel was astonished. He had never imagined cave paintings could be "so beautiful, profound and complete." They stirred powerful feelings in him, and he began studying the subject.
"At some point, insights started coming to me," he says.
"They weren't intellectual. They came through experience and a spiritual connection. I felt I was stepping into the shoes of the prehistoric artist."
That was how he began writing the long poem "A Cave," which took him three years to complete.
"I would sit down to write, and the questions and answers would emerge through the poetry. 'Why did you go in? What happened to you there?' I asked the prehistoric artist. Writing was like entering a cave. I felt I'd managed to enter an altered state of consciousness without actually going inside one."
A year after "A Cave" was published, Perel was contacted by Prof. Ran Barkai, 58, a prehistoric archaeologist, researcher and senior lecturer in the Department of Archaeology and Ancient Near Eastern Cultures at Tel Aviv University. For 17 years, Barkai directed excavations at Qesem Cave, an archaeological site near present-day Rosh Ha'ayin. His research focuses on the Paleolithic and Neolithic cultures that existed in our region. His particular interests include stone tools; prehistoric humans' relationships with animals, the world and caves; and the altered states of consciousness experienced by prehistoric artists.
Barkai walks everywhere, whenever he can. He is almost never cold, but he enjoys gathering wood for the fireplace at his home in Pardes Hanna and sitting by the fire in winter, "just like Neanderthals and their predecessors, because gathering wood was a central task throughout the human past," he explains.
"I started playing with ideas about what caves and their paintings meant for human consciousness," Barkai says. "I was looking for things to read outside the mainstream, and that's how I came across Guy's poem. It blew me away."
The two began meeting beneath the royal poinciana tree at the entrance to Tel Aviv University. Their long conversations led to a book they wrote together with the mysterious title "Why Do They Have No Faces?" (in Hebrew, Idra Press, 2025).
In it, they ask why, some 40,000 years ago, our forefathers and foremothers began painting deep inside caves they did not live in. Why did they so rarely depict themselves? And when they did, why did they leave the human figures faceless? Both authors were also preoccupied by how these questions might relate to the disappearance of large animals from the face of the Earth at that very same time.
In their view, cave art served a shamanic rather than an aesthetic purpose: it was a ritual intended to repair a disruption in the world by appealing to what anthropology now calls "the spirit world." Drawing on their respective fields, they offer a complex explanation. They believe the paintings were an attempt to mend a deepening fracture in the world by recreating the animals on cave walls.
Shortly after its publication, the book found its way into the hands of the painter Gideon Rubin. Rubin, 53, who has lived in London for 25 years, is known for paintings in which every human figure is faceless.
The grandson of the painter Reuven Rubin, he did not always paint this way. On September 11, 2001, he stood on a rooftop in New York and watched the Twin Towers burn. He says he will never forget the taste of dust that lingered in his mouth for four days after the disaster. He has not painted a person with a face since.
"Sometimes you come across a work that feels as though it was made just for you. That's how I felt about this book," says Rubin, who became friends with Perel and Barkai after reading it. "I understood not only why I paint without faces, but so many other things, too. It was as though someone had lit little candles along the path I'm walking."
"Ran and Guy's book looks at how human beings cope with crisis," says Dr. Assaf Shpayer, the fourth member of our group. As a child, she was intrigued when her father told her that other human species had once existed and become extinct. When she began studying archaeology at Tel Aviv University, she realized she wanted to investigate these mysterious people. Her research has since focused on two subjects: prehistoric children and the significance of horses to prehistoric humans.
"Children in prehistory have barely been studied," she says. "I'm very interested in how people understood childhood, and how prehistoric humans saw children and their place in the world."
It was the children, and the traces she believes they left in the caves, that drew her to the journey.
My work as a journalist brought Perel and me together, and we became friends. A year and a half ago, I read his and Barkai's book between ayahuasca ceremonies in the Peruvian jungle. It affected me profoundly. In one vision, I was an old woman dying in a cave. A fire burned beside me, and a prehistoric woman sang me a farewell song. I felt a peace I had never known. I was happy.
When the two invited me to join them on a journey through the caves, I agreed immediately. The five of us set out.
Almost all the paintings we saw were made by people researchers now call the Magdalenians, who lived in Western Europe between 20,000 and 13,000 years ago. They take their name from Abri de la Madeleine, an archaeological site in the Dordogne region of southwestern France discovered in the 19th century.
The Magdalenians were hunter-gatherers who lived in small groups, probably of 15 to 30 people. They moved fairly often, depending on the seasons, their neighbors and the availability of food. They were skilled hunters whose main prey were deer, horses, bison and ibex.
"What was life like for the Magdalenians?" I asked Barkai.
"Life was one long picnic. They got up in the morning, hunted, lit a fire, ate, gathered food, chatted, danced, sang and painted, until circumstances told them it was time to move on. They followed a familiar circuit, returning to the same places again and again. At certain times, they gathered with other groups to celebrate, exchange gifts and exchange genes."
How do we know this?
"Objects from distant regions have been found at some archaeological sites, which suggests these encounters took place. Modern hunter-gatherers live this way, so we assume prehistoric humans did, too. We also assume their creative expression went far beyond the evidence that survives, because much of it involved perishable materials or decorations on their bodies."
What happened to them when they entered a cave?
"Entering a deep, dark cave changes the way the senses work. Sight, our dominant sense outside, is completely neutralized, so the other senses sharpen. Consciousness is a sensory response to the world, so it takes on a different character inside a cave. You also need light to find your way through deep, dark caves and paint inside them. There's abundant evidence that prehistoric humans used torches and stone lamps fueled by fat.
"The air in these caves contains about 21 percent oxygen, and fire brings that down to as little as 13 percent, causing oxygen deprivation. This increases dopamine release in the brain, heightening feelings of contentment and euphoria. So that, too, necessarily alters consciousness. We assume people knew fire had this effect and experienced it from an early age. It gave them the expansion of consciousness they were seeking in a space they saw as a portal between worlds."
My heart skipped a beat when the entrance to Niaux Cave came into view. Everything around it was in bloom, and enormous white clouds sailed across the blue sky. I could feel its depths and coolness waiting for me.
"It looks as though it created the whole valley," Perel said.
"Not created it. It's swallowing it," Barkai said.
The cave is two kilometers long. Soon after entering, you encounter graffiti that visitors have been leaving here since the early 17th century. Martin, for example, was here in 1652, and Louise came 34 years later.
The cave is damp, with a constant temperature of 12 degrees Celsius, or 53.6 degrees Fahrenheit. This is one reason the magnificent paintings in its depths have survived so well. In places, the ceiling rises dozens of meters overhead; elsewhere, visitors have to stoop to avoid hitting their heads. Stalactites hang above still pools of water. The cave is vast, spacious, beautiful and regal.
After walking 400 meters, we passed through a narrow passage, and the first paintings appeared: red and black dots, short lines, dashes and stripes, and a line with a loop at one end that resembled a club or a pregnant woman. These symbols also appear in many other caves in the region and in neighboring Spain. Some were painted with tools, others with fingers. A few are so well preserved that fingerprints are still visible.
Sometimes the paintings face one another or appear on either side of a prominent crack in the wall. Perhaps they are waymarkers, a tribal language or even musical notation. Perhaps they prepare visitors to enter a sacred space. There are many interpretations, all conjecture.
The spot where we stood is not part of the regular tour because of an especially fragile work etched into the clay and sand of a small passage: a rare depiction of a fish. A salmon or a trout, rendered in a few precise lines, it has been swimming in place for some 15,000 years.
"Why was this fish etched in that little passage, in that hidden place?" I later asked Barkai.
"I think they chose animals that embodied the ability to pass between worlds and reach places humans cannot," he said. "Deep water is one such world, one that has always had a place in mythology. Just as birds mediate between humans and the heavens, fish may mediate between humans and the depths. There is clay where the fish was etched, and water certainly flowed here. That supports the hypothesis, but it's still only a hypothesis."
We hadn't realized it, but our encounter with the fish and our silence in the darkness had taken place at the entrance to the Salon Noir, the cave's holy of holies. This cathedral of rock, some 20 meters high, contains six panels with dozens of animal paintings, together considered one of the pinnacles of prehistoric art. All the animals are drawn in charcoal, hence the name Salon Noir, or Black Chamber.
Before entering, visitors are asked to turn off their flashlights. For a moment, they stand in darkness while the guide fits a filter that allows her to illuminate the paintings without damaging them. The pause is brief, but the effect is dramatic: when the flashlight comes on, the animals emerge from the darkness. There are dozens of bison, horses, ibex and deer, including one deer particularly celebrated for its elegance.
For decades, researchers thought a single artist had painted them all. The styles are remarkably similar, and the arrangement suggests a carefully planned composition. The cave's curves, protrusions and hollows give the animals volume and life. They seem to spring from the walls. When the guide moved her flashlight to mimic a flickering torch, they actually galloped.
But in the early 1990s, radiocarbon dating revealed that the animals were not the work of one person. Magdalenian artists, men and women, had visited the cave over hundreds of years, each adding a contribution.
For decades, many researchers believed the paintings were a form of hunting magic intended to ensure a successful hunt. The problem is that they contain almost no hunting scenes, and depictions of wounded animals are also rare. Today, most researchers believe we will never know why the paintings were made and are unwilling to endorse any particular theory. Many disagree with Barkai and Perel's interpretation of the art as a shamanic attempt to repair a disruption in the world by recreating the animals' spirits on cave walls.
What does seem clear is that the artists must have spent a great deal of time observing the animals and knew them well. The creatures are majestic, sometimes enormous. Standing before them, you feel awe.
"People sometimes think they painted what they dreamed or imagined," Perel says. "But we argue that they weren't painting imaginary animals. They were bringing the animals' spirits into being on the rock to repair something in the spiritual, archetypal world. The cave is a portal to that world. In the Jungian approach, what emerges from the unconscious isn't considered imaginary or less real than everyday reality. A dream is a way of encountering another layer of reality, one that is usually hidden from us.
"In the encounter with the rock and the painting on it, something from that hidden world took on a body and became visible. By entering a particular psychological and creative state, the person allowed the 'animal spirit' to materialize on the stone. In that sense, the painting doesn't represent another reality. It is that reality appearing within our own."
It was already evening when we sat by the river in the town of Foix, watching swallows fly above the water. We talked and fell silent, laughed and fell silent. We were human beings and we were animals flickering on the cave walls, drawing closer to ourselves and to one another.
That night, I dreamed of my mother.
Months later, each of the caves we visited still returns to me, especially at night, when my consciousness hovers between waking and sleep. The Gargas cave complex left a particularly deep impression. At the foot of the Pyrenees, near the village of Aventignan, it is known for its hand stencils: 231 in all, in different sizes and colors, some belonging to children.
The stencils were made by placing a hand against the rock and spraying pigment from the mouth. Gargas also contains animal paintings, engravings, some 100 square meters of finger tracings on the ceiling, feminine symbols and numerous depictions of what some researchers interpret as female genitalia. Animal bones, placed there by prehistoric humans, are wedged into cracks in the walls.
We had the caves to ourselves with our guide, Nicolas Ferrer, who is in his 50s and lives in Aventignan. His grandmother sold tickets here, his parents were guides, and he has worked here since he was 14. His love for the place, and his wonder at it, come through in every word.
Local people have known of the cave complex since at least the 16th century, and a graffito dated 1587 survives on its walls. No one then understood the significance of the art around them. Its discovery and study began only in the late 19th century. As in many other caves, new finds still come to light from time to time. The art is attributed to the Gravettian culture, which existed between 30,000 and 20,000 years ago, but remains of the Mousterian culture, created by Neanderthals, have also been found.
We entered through a steel door almost concealed by vegetation and moss. The upper cave is small and narrow, vertical and winding. Bats once lived here, and their droppings damaged the paintings. They were not the only ones to cause harm. Scientists once marked and highlighted engravings in ways that would be unthinkable today. People from National Geographic, for example, used a red pen.
"Maybe in 50 years, researchers will look at what we're doing here and lose their minds," Ferrer says.
The temperature inside is about 11 degrees Celsius. Over the past decade, it has risen by half a degree, and the cave has become drier. Seventy sensors collect data every 15 minutes, but global warming is unlikely to be kind to the art within.
Ferrer showed us the hands scattered through the space, tucked into recesses and spread across the walls: black, red, yellow and white. Only 17 show all five fingers. The others are sometimes missing one, two or even three. Ferrer told us that people once thought the stencils had been made by people who had lost fingers, but it later became clear that this was not the case. Those who made them most likely folded their fingers before spraying the pigment. The stencils are thought to represent some kind of code.
"I met a group of deaf people, and when they stood in front of the hands, they cried," Ferrer told us. "They knew nothing about the new hypotheses, but to them it was clearly sign language. The positions of the hands meant something, and so did the colors."
In their book, Perel and Barkai discuss the many hand stencils found in caves. Were these the first selfies in human history? they ask playfully. They then offer a complex explanation: the point of contact with the cave wall expresses an abstract aspect of the self that extends beyond the physical body.
Later, we stood before a panel bearing children's hand stencils.
"Children have something we adults don't, and prehistoric humans recognized it," Assaf Shpayer said. "It's no coincidence they brought them here. They weren't just teaching them or making them part of the community. They also valued their qualities, their flexibility of thought. Children are closer to the other worlds because they haven't been here long, so they were seen as intermediaries between this world and the other."
Very different from how Western societies view children today.
"It couldn't be more different. Today, children are seen as sponges to fill with information. We teach them and turn them into adults like us. I thought about this a lot when I had children. I'm not a hunter-gatherer, and my children go to kindergarten and school, but I try to let them experience things for themselves without constantly telling them what to do or how best to do it. I don't always manage it."
"This is where I realized that what makes caves addictive is going in and coming out," Rubin added. "Your age disappears inside the cave. Once you've been in, you experience the world outside differently. The volume goes up. You take everything in, hear everything. I lie on the grass, listen to the birds, feel the curvature of the Earth. I lie with my eyes closed and see. I open them and see a horse in the clouds. Maybe 30,000 years ago, someone lay there just as I do, saw a horse in the clouds and then went and created it?
"It's an experience of altered consciousness that brings you back to something that was always there, but that you'd lost touch with. I think I'll keep returning to caves all my life. They're where I understand my place in the world better."
"Gargas is another world," Barkai says. "I think people came here looking for answers, performing rituals to solve problems. I think that, for them, caves were places to send messages, to reach wherever they wanted to go."
Reach where?
"Whatever lies beyond the cave, beyond its walls."
Why do you think they put animal bones into cracks in the walls?
"I think they saw the cracks as a connection between the cave and whatever lay beyond its walls, like the cracks between the stones of the Western Wall, where people leave notes with their requests. And what they wanted was animals. The animals were disappearing, and people wanted to send the message that they depended on them."
Two or three days later, we arrived at Rouffignac Cave. This immense cave, situated between two streams, had been known to local people for centuries. The earliest account of its existence appears in the early 17th-century writings of Jean Tarde, a vicar, astronomer, geographer and friend of Galileo Galilei.
In 1929, the industrialist Charles Plassard bought the estate containing the cave. He and his son Louis were curious nature lovers, and on one of their explorations they noticed figures on the ceiling. They invited researchers from the University of Toulouse, who discovered the first engravings: two mammoths facing each other. The cave turned out to contain more than 250 animal figures, including some 160 mammoths, as well as four human figures.
The discovery immediately sparked a heated controversy. Several researchers claimed they had seen some of the paintings as early as the late 1940s and had even reported them, only to be told they were modern scribbles. Others claimed the paintings were forgeries. Defending their authenticity was Abbé Henri Breuil, one of the world's foremost scholars of cave art, known as the "Pope of Prehistory." Breuil examined the paintings and declared them genuine.
We arrived at midday on a very hot day. Waiting at the entrance was Frédéric Plassard, a fourth-generation member of the family with a doctorate specializing in Paleolithic art. His wife is also an archaeologist, as was his father. In 2020, with visitors kept away by the COVID lockdowns, the couple explored the cave and discovered 12 new engravings, including a figure that may represent a woman.
"I'm more of a caveman than prehistoric people were," he says, "because I've spent far more time in here than they did."
The cave extends for more than eight kilometers, roughly five miles. It was the coldest cave we visited and the only one with an electric train, which carries visitors along the first kilometer. Visitors are not allowed to get off at most points along the route, but that rule did not apply to us.
We boarded and headed inside, following the route the prehistoric artist had taken 13,000 years earlier. The ride seemed endless, the outside world receding behind us. Along the way, we saw the beds dug by cave bears that had hibernated here for tens of thousands of years before prehistoric humans arrived. The bears had scratched the walls, and people had extended those marks with their fingers. Plassard believes they were continuing the bears' work in the hope of acquiring their great strength.
Seven hundred meters into the cave, Plassard invited us to get off the train. Before us was the first mammoth. A simple drawing, just an outline and tusks, yet it looked almost alive. It seemed to be looking at something. There was a young mammoth, too, with two short tusks.
"I'm sure whoever drew it had studied a real, living mammoth," Plassard said. "They probably studied carcasses, too, and knew the animals' anatomy well."
One hundred meters farther on, two groups of mammoths faced each other. We asked Plassard whether such an encounter could have happened in real life. Mammoths disappeared long ago, he explained, but we might learn something about them from their living relatives, African elephants.
"An encounter like this between two groups is unusual," he said. "We also have reason to think these mammoths are males, not females, and groups of males like this don't exist."
How do we know they're males?
"Because of the marks near their temples, which may represent secretions from the male's temporal gland during periods of sexual arousal and high testosterone levels. But males don't gather like this, so this isn't a scene from nature. It's a symbolic expression. Even looking at the animals they chose to paint, it's hard to draw a simple connection between the art and the local environment. For some 20,000 years, across different parts of Europe and in different environments, they kept choosing the same small selection of large herbivores."
What do you mean?
"If there were still mammoths in the Dordogne 16,000 years ago, they were probably very rare. The artists may have studied their anatomy and behavior somewhere else, perhaps 300 or 400 kilometers away, then painted them here months later. So it's hard to see this art as a straightforward depiction of the natural world around them."
We ventured deeper and reached a chamber with a low ceiling covered in drawings of 26 mammoths, 12 bison, 11 horses, 12 ibex and three rhinoceroses. Some even seemed to be smiling.
We said goodbye to Plassard and drove to our next destination. A rabbit and an ibex crossed the road, and we saw a statue of the Buddha in the forest. Out of habit, I glanced at my phone and read about the world we had sought to escape: a plane crash, people killed, war with Iran looming once again. The suffering of modern humans, inflicted by modern humans.
I asked my companions whether they thought there had been wicked people and narcissists among prehistoric humans, too. Had there been troubled psyches and personality disorders? They thought so, but fewer. People then, they believed, had experienced themselves as part of a greater whole rather than as separate individuals. Ego was not what drove someone to paint in the darkness. They hadn't gone there to win admiration for their talent, where no one could see their work. Freedom from the ego is the greatest happiness one can know. There is nothing like it.
By then, we all understood: the shift in consciousness that takes place deep inside a cave is the realization that we are part of the universe. It has the power to make us better human beings, humbler, more whole.
On our last day, we sat on a cliff at sunset, looking out over the forest and the river flowing far below. We listened to the birdsong and said nothing. For those few minutes, we were human beings without nationality, without culture, without history. We were blank pages flying through space.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
Yemen’s Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday as their offensive against Saudi-backed government forces intensified. Saudi Arabia launched dozens of airstrikes over the past 24 hours, the Houthis said, after the Iran-backed group carried out attacks on Saudi territory that wounded dozens of people.
Yemen's Houthis seized control of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday, with witnesses telling AFP of fighters marching on the area chanting "death to America, death to Israel".
Saudi Arabia meanwhile launched dozens of airstrikes in the last 24 hours, according to the military spokesman for the Houthis, who control large parts of northwest Yemen and launched a large-scale offensive last week against Riyadh-backed Yemeni government forces.
The Houthis launched attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens of people wounded, in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
A Yemeni military source told AFP on Thursday that the Iran-backed Houthis were advancing towards the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait "after having taken control of Mocha".
The waterway, which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal, has gained importance as a transit route since the start of the wider Middle East war, which saw Iran blockade the Strait of Hormuz.
The regional war has disrupted maritime traffic in the Gulf, causing oil prices to soar.
On Thursday, the US oil contract WTI surpassed $100, after Brent North Sea crude -- the main international benchmark -- already did so on Wednesday.
After Mocha's capture, the leader of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, said the protection of the country's coasts and restoring state control of them was an "Arab and international interest".
The military source said the Houthis also seized Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea, "after rocket attacks and a ground assault carried out using boats transporting fighters".
In a statement, Tarek Saleh, who heads the Yemeni National Resistance Forces that controlled Mocha, said he moved his command centre "to a safe location" to regroup.
Government forces have paid "a heavy price in recent days in the face of a Houthi offensive that was planned and supported by Iran", he added.

'Maritime coercion'
Before the offensive, the Houthis already controlled a large part of Yemen's north, including the capital Sanaa, as well as the major port city of Hodeidah on the Red Sea.
But they did not yet hold any areas directly overlooking Bab al-Mandab.
With their drones and missiles, the Houthis have been able to disrupt traffic in the Red Sea.
But "controlling the coast would strengthen Houthi maritime coercion", said Andreas Krieg, a security expert at King's College London.
The advance of the Houthis in Mocha, as well as in the nearby areas of Khokha and Hays, has driven many people to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
Mohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an "apocalyptic" atmosphere in the port city.
Mujahid Tahami, who also set off for Aden, said some families had fallen victim to "looting by gangs as they tried to flee".

Hundreds dead
Yemen relapsed into war in July after years of relative calm punctured by sporadic violence and deepening poverty.
Since last week, the fighting in Yemen has left more than 500 dead, mostly combatants, according to an AFP tally compiled from several sources.
It has also forced nearly 20,000 people to flee their homes, the International Organization for Migration said on Tuesday.
On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition battling the Houthis said the group fired ballistic missiles and drones at several cities in southern Saudi Arabia.
On Thursday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Saudi Arabia had launched 64 strikes on Yemenover the previous 24 hours.
Their Al-Masirah TV channel reported 10 strikes on Taiz province in western Yemen.
The United Nations Security Council met Thursday to discuss the conflict with its Yemen envoy, Hans Grundberg, who called for "the active investment of every member of this body to contain what could be the precipice for a far more dangerous conflict".
The emergency meeting was brought together by the United Kingdom, which called on the Security Council to "send a clear and consistent message: the Houthis must de-escalate, cease their attacks, and return to a path towards peace".
The hostilities kicked off in July when the Houthis let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
The government retaliated by striking Sanaa airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia.
The ongoing exchanges risk returning Yemen to a conflict that left hundreds of thousands of people dead and sparked one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Yemen's capital and forcing out the government, fought the Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

Trump administration proposes axing grace period for H-1B visa holders after job loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
22:46:00 UTC
07:46:00 KST

Trump administration proposes axing grace period for H-1B visa holders after job loss
- The Trump administration proposes ending the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders to stay and find new jobs after losing employment, requiring immediate departure instead.
- This change targets skilled workers including H-1B, E-1, E-2, L-1, O-1, TN, H-1B1, and E-3 visa holders, potentially disrupting tech companies reliant on foreign talent.
- The Department of Homeland Security expects companies to hire US workers or reapply for visas, while critics warn the rule would harm immigrant workers and businesses.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration has proposed eliminating a 60-day grace period that allows certain immigrants, including skilled workers on H-1B visas, to stay in the United States and find a new sponsor after losing their job, according to a government notice posted online on Sept 10.
Under the planned rule change, published in the Federal Register by the US Department of Homeland Security, those with H-1B and certain other temporary work visas would have to leave the country as soon as their employment ends – a potential blow to top American tech companies that rely heavily on foreign workers.
It is the latest step by US President Donald Trump to limit legal immigration since returning to office in January 2025. His administration has also introduced higher visa fees for skilled workers and recently paused immigrant visa appointments at US missions globally while it implements a new training programme.
Companies affected by the change could see some disruption, DHS wrote in its proposal, but it said the jobs could go to American workers instead. In some situations, immigrant workers who leave could potentially reapply if their employer petitions for them, it added.
“DHS presumes that they will either offer the same jobs to equally qualified US workers or go through the I-129 petition process depending on their workforce requirement,” the notice said.
The 60-day grace period, in place since 2017, allows foreign workers time to find another US job or get their affairs in order – whether selling a home or pulling children out of school – before leaving the country.
“Many H-1B workers have been here for years, and they and their families have established themselves in their communities,” said Gabriel Chin, a professor at the UC Davis School of Law. “I see no legitimate reason to force them to leave because they are changing jobs.”
Visas critical for tech companies
H-1B visas, established by Congress in 1990, are especially critical for tech companies seeking talent from India and China, allowing them to fill roles where there is sometimes a lack of qualified US workers.
Consultancy companies such as Deloitte, PwC and Ernst & Young as well as outsourcing firms such as Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, HCL Tech and LTIMindtree are top H-1B sponsors.
Lawyers for Berardi Immigration Law, which specialises in business-related immigration issues, said the move would “sharply compress the timeline HR teams have to manage layoffs and offboarding for foreign national employees”.
“It seems like every week this administration announces a new step to make life more difficult for immigrants in the US and the companies and communities that rely on them,” said Todd Schulte, president of FWD.us, an immigration advocacy group.
If implemented, the change would also apply to E-1 international trader visa holders; E-2 commercial vehicle operator visa holders; L-1 short-term work for executives or managers with international companies; O-1 visas for people “with an extraordinary ability” in science, sports or the arts; and TN professional workers.
It would also affect H-1B1 skilled worker visa holders from Singapore and Chile and E-3 specialty worker visa holders from Australia.
The rule is subject to a two-month public comment period before it can be finalised. REUTERS

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 11, 2026
Houthis advance in Yemen, threaten Saudi oil exports
Iran-aligned Houthis seized control of Yemen’s port city of Mocha on Sept 10 and advanced down the Red Sea coast to strategic islands, military sources said, hours after President Donald Trump said he expected the Iran war to end after the US midterm elections.
Yemeni government military sources said the Houthis had gained further leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern outlet of the Red Sea and one of the world’s most important shipping routes, and had reached the islands of Hanish.
If the Houthis were to gain control of the waterway on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, it could give their backer Iran a critical advantage in the war with the United States, reducing supplies through a second major transit corridor and sending oil prices surging.
It could also make it harder for Trump to find an exit from a war that has hurt his Republican Party’s electoral prospects ahead of the November midterms.
Anthropic disrupts Russian, Chinese AI campaigns
Anthropic on Sept 10 said it had disrupted several alleged malicious uses of its Claude models over the past eight months, including a suspected Russia-linked cyber espionage campaign and efforts by Chinese AI firms it accused of trying to extract and replicate Claude’s capabilities.
Cybercriminals and state-backed hackers were increasingly using AI not just to assist with tasks but to orchestrate and execute large portions of cyberattacks, Anthropic said in its latest Threat Intelligence report, adding that humans were often overseers rather than hands-on operators in the campaigns.
Anthropic said it had disrupted what it described as attacks from seven China-based laboratories during that period. Among the labs Anthropic named were tech giant Alibaba, Moonshot, DeepSeek and Xiaomi.
At least five killed in strike on Ukrainian shopping centre
At least five people were killed and nearly 70 others wounded on Sept 10 when a Russian strike hit a shopping centre in Pavlohrad, central Ukraine, the authorities announced.
The attack came as both sides step up long-range barrages on each other hundreds of kilometres behind the front lines, increasingly targeting civilian sites alongside factories, refineries, warehouses and ports.
According to statistics verified by the United Nations, civilian deaths in Ukraine are running at their highest rate since the first months after Russia invaded in February 2022.
Several killed in bus crash near Swiss Alpine village
A number of people were killed and several others injured after a bus carrying a Dutch tour party flipped over in a remote Alpine region of eastern Switzerland, police said on Sept 10.
Police in the canton of Graubuenden said the accident occurred near to the village of Susch, and images of the scene published online showed the vehicle lying on its side next to the road, surrounded by police and emergency service personnel.
A spokeswoman for the General Dutch Association of Travel Companies (ANVR), acting as spokesperson for tour operator OAD, said a serious accident had taken place involving an OAD bus and that 48 passengers were on board, all Dutch nationals.
Bayeux Tapestry ‘mania’ sweeps UK as exhibition opens
London’s Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opened on Sept 10 to a British public gripped by “mania” over the medieval artwork depicting the Norman conquest of England, on display outside France for the first time.
Excited visitors who had tickets for the first day of the sold-out exhibition queued outside the British Museum ahead of the opening, where some staff had donned period costumes.
“It is back here for the first time in 950 years!” 46-year-old Catherine Pitt told AFP in the queue outside the museum entrance.
