Multiple job holders? One reason is fewer hours per job
We already knew the concerning data that more Australians than ever hold multiple jobs.
It's the highest in both number (1 million people) and percentage: 6.9%
Among younger people aged 20–24, it's even higher: 11.2%.
So an interesting addition to the data comes from anonymised and aggregated workforce data across healthcare, hospitality, retail and services from scheduling tool Deputy.
Its data suggests that changes in shift-work patterns provide context to the numbers:
- Across all sectors, total hours worked fell 7.7% month on month — the steepest decrease of 2026 — but employers locked in shifts an average of 8.3 days ahead (up 24.1% from July) to give workers more certainty.
- Healthcare drove the strongest changes, scheduling 13.5 days ahead to help scarce care workers balance second jobs. Specifically, in-home care lifted its average notice period by 102% (to 12.1 days) and NDIS providers by 51% (to 10.2 days).
- Retail and Services both added workers while reducing hours per employee, a sign that work is being spread across more people rather than concentrated in fewer roles.
- Hospitality was part of a universal cooldown in shift volume, contributing to the first month in 2026 where all four major sectors declined in hours worked. However, like other sectors, hospitality venues rostered further ahead than they did in July to offer workers more stability.
There is obviously a little guff in information from a scheduling software business about the importance of scheduling, but Ciaran Hale, chief technology officer at Deputy, makes a good point about the reality facing people working multiple jobs:
"The 8.3-day rostering figure is the most important number in this month's (data)," he said in a statement.
"It shows employers are starting to treat certainty as part of the employment offer. For many hourly workers, a second or third role is no longer unusual. When one roster does not fill a week, people need enough notice to coordinate another job, caring responsibilities or study. Predictability is what makes those working arrangements viable. Employers appear to understand that. They are absorbing higher award rates by planning more deliberately, not simply by cutting people loose.
In what is reality, but I can't help but be a bit deflated by: employers that lean into helping their staff work multiple jobs are more likely to retain them.
"The businesses that give their teams a roster they can build a life around will be the ones best placed to retain them."
In other interesting notes, "terminations fell 21.4%, the lowest monthly total of 2026, while new hires were effectively flat".
The report said retail and services "both added workers while reducing hours per employee, a sign that work is being spread across more people rather than concentrated in fewer roles".
Copper 3‑month rolling futures tumble from record highs: analyst
Copper 3‑month rolling futures reached a record high of $US14,853 per tonne in intraday trading on Thursday, the highest price year‑to‑date, according to Vivek Dhar, head of Commodities and Sustainability Research at Commonwealth Bank.
However, prices tumbled by around 4.5% overnight to $US14,183/t, the CommBank noted.
"We expect that the upward trajectory in copper prices was clipped by a combination of macroeconomic factors, namely the spike in Brent crude to about $109/bbl, but also due to speculation around copper prices' steady uplift being a 'speculative bubble' rather than related to supply‑demand fundamentals," said Mr Dhar.
He said the key drivers supporting prices had been predominantly supply‑related.
"The International Copper Study Group (ICSG) estimates that in the first half of 2026 global mined copper production decreased by 1.1% y/y, with concentrate production in Chile, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Indonesia falling by 8% y/y, 34% y/y and 32% y/y respectively."
Another key driver supporting prices currently was the movement in global stocks of refined copper, Mr Dhar said.
"Over the last 24 months total exchange stocks, which include those in the COMEX, LME and SHFE exchanges have lifted from about 575kt to 1.06Mt in the two years to 10 September 2026," he said.
"The rise in volume is almost entirely due to the rise in COMEX stocks in the US, where inventory levels at the end of August 2026, have now exceeded the last peak in August 2003."
He said this occurred due to "the expectation that the Trump administration will place a 15% import tariff on all refined copper products from the start of 2027" after previously placing Section 232 tariffs on semi‑finished and derivative copper products last August.
Mr Dhar added that despite the overnight fall in prices, copper remained at record historical highs,
"According to Shanghai Metals Market (SMM), China's imports of copper scrap, as well as its domestic scrap production have increased month on month since June.
"This, along with increased concentrate and refined supply over the remainder of the year and into 2027 is likely to alleviate tight supply conditions, which in turn will support lower copper prices."
BOJ set to lift rates next week but offer few clues on terminal
The Bank of Japan (BOJ) is set to raise interest rates next week, most likely by 25 basis points, and may signal faster future tightening if price pressures heighten risks of an inflation overshoot, according to four sources familiar with its thinking.
A hike to 1.25% would bring the BOJ's policy rate to levels unseen in 31 years. A rate hike just three months after its last one in June also suggests a faster pace of tightening, especially if the bank raises rates again this year.
Many in the central bank saw conditions falling into place for another rate hike with the economy on course for a moderate recovery and price pressure building, sources said.
The BOJ also expected financial conditions to remain loose even if it raises interest rates to 1.25%, the sources added.
While the yen's recent rebound could ease pressure on prices by moderating import-cost increases, the currency's past declines and a renewed surge in fuel prices would keep the BOJ on guard over inflation risks, they said.
"With underlying inflation so close to 2%, the BOJ needs to be extra mindful of upside price risks," said one of the sources, a view echoed by three more sources.
The BOJ raised interest rates to 1% in June and pledged to push borrowing costs higher if economic and price developments align with its baseline projections.
While it kept rates steady in July, the BOJ signalled a strong chance of a near-term hike by warning of the risk of an inflation overshoot due to price pressures from the Middle East conflict, a weak yen and brisk AI-related demand.
Analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to hike rates to 1.25% at the September 17-18 meeting, 1.5% by end-March next year and then to 1.75% in the second quarter of 2027.
Most saw the terminal rate at least at 1.75%.
With markets having fully priced in a September hike, some market players had bet the BOJ could spring a surprise by going with a bigger-than-expected 50-basis-point hike.
With no immediate risk of an abrupt jump in wage and price growth, however, the BOJ would likely opt for the usual 25-point hike next week and wait for more data to gauge whether another near-term increase would be necessary, the sources said.
"Underlying inflation is about to reach 2%, but we don't see it sharply overshooting that level," BOJ board member Kazuyuki Masu said on Thursday, suggesting that he saw no imminent signs of a spike in inflation that warranted a big hike next week.

LG defends smart-TV features amid audio surveillance allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:33:28 UTC
06:33:28 KST

LG defends smart-TV features amid audio surveillance allegations
Recent allegations into LG’s smart TVs have raised new questions about the nonconsensual data it harvests.
South Korean consumer-electronics company LG has denied allegations that its smart televisions record ambient conversations, listen while on standby and store recordings for later transmission.
On Wednesday, the company told Al Jazeera that voice data is only recorded when a user presses and holds the voice button on the TV remote or activates its “Hi LG” wake word, after the user has activated the Far-Field voice recognition feature.
“Other than these instances, the TVs do not collect or record ambient conversations,” LG said, adding that voice data is only processed via explicit user commands.
“The audio is immediately deleted if the wake word is not recognised,” the company said.
The statement comes after a 135-minute investigative report released on Monday by a popular tech media outlet and YouTube channel, Gamers Nexus, with Level1Techs and independent security researchers. The investigation examined LG televisions’ data collection and security systems, raising questions about how the devices handle users’ private information.
By analysing network traffic and software, the researchers purport to have discovered that these televisions actively track users and harvest a glut of local network data, including audio transcripts.
Inside LG’s controversial tracking system
Gamers Nexus said its researchers were able to record audio through an LG television while it was in a state of hibernation, meaning that even if the microphone switch on the TV is turned off, other microphones exposed to the TV might not be, such as the remote.
The result, Gamers Nexus says, is “216,000,000 Spy TVs” in the US alone.
On its website, LG says it has 49 million smarts TVs in the US and 216 million globally.
Recorded background noise in the room, including as far as 12 metres (40 feet) away from the TV, was also being archived, they said.
Yash Vekaria, a computer science researcher at the University of California, Davis, says that because TVs stay in homes for years, often past their update support, “prompt patching from LG matters”.
“This vulnerability can allow sniffing [of] much more critical conversations … Imagine government officials discussing national security in their hotel room [next to an] LG TV”, Vekaria said.
The researchers further alleged that unmatched wake-word interactions or unclear sounds could remain stored locally, transcribed and preserved on the device as plain text in case the local network is disconnected and uploaded later to LG servers.
Copies can stay in temporary storage spaces, known as buffers, without the user knowing, Vekaria said.
Privacy risks generally stem from poor design and selective disclosure. The more disconcerting threat lies in a compromised device, Vekaria added, which could be made to execute any command its hardware allows.
The researchers also said they found text transcripts derived from audio captured by the television, even after 10-15 seconds of silence after invoking “Hi LG”.
The claims have not been independently verified by Al Jazeera.
“It raises a question of purpose,” says Vekaria, “a voice command is only useful in real time, so audio queued for later upload is presumably being kept for something else, such as logging, analytics or model training. LG should explain what”.
Vekaria says he is not aware of any concrete evidence that ambient audio or transcripts feed into LG’s advertising or profiling systems.
“What we do know is that LG runs an advertising business built on household data, including the Automatic Content Recognition [ACR] tracking documented in our research, and that its voice pipeline appears to capture and retain more than users would expect.”
Still, there may be simpler explanations, he says, “such as diagnostics or improving speech recognition … but even those involve keeping recordings from people’s homes without meaningful consent”.
The smart home is listening
The researchers also said that the televisions scanned home networks for other devices and collected information including internal IP addresses, nearby Wi-Fi networks and location data.
LG said scanning for nearby devices is a “standard” smart-TV function.
Device discovery can serve “legitimate functions” such as screen casting, media sharing and connecting smart-home products, like Amazon’s Alexa, said Anna Maria Mandalari, a lecturer in communications and networking at University College London.
LG stated that ACR, voice recognition and interest-based advertising are all “separate features”, each requiring “explicit user opt-in consent” and each of which can be disabled through the TV’s settings.
Depending on how device discovery is implemented, Mandalari said, a television may “obtain the names, addresses, manufacturers and types of other devices on a household network” – information that can reveal the composition of a home and help “create a broader profile of its occupants”.
LG’s advertising arm, LG Ad Solutions, has openly marketed the breadth of information it can derive from connected households. Corporate videos featured in the Gamers Nexus investigation show LG representatives saying: “We know who is in the LG household,” and, “We know which devices are there.”
LG told Al Jazeera that it was “committed to providing transparency” and that it rejected “deceptive practices”.

Opals knocked out of Basketball World Cup as Magbegor's torn ACL confirmed
The Opals have been knocked out in the quarterfinals of the Women's Basketball World Cup in a 23-point loss to Spain just hours after receiving more devastating injury news about captain Ezi Magbegor.
Half an hour before the tip-off in what turned out to be a comprehensive 89-66 loss to Spain, Magbegor's WNBA team, the Seattle Storm, revealed the star forward had torn her ACL.
Magbegor, who only returned to the court in early July after partially tearing her Achilles in March, went down early after taking a knock to her right knee in Australia's qualification final win over Italy.
"It makes me emotional when I see anyone go down," Opals coach Sandy Brondello said after the loss to Spain.
"But Ezi's come back from an injury and it's just another injury. [It's] just really unfortunate. She's a key part of what we want to do. It sucks, but that's sport isn't it?
"She's got to have a great recovery and she'll get back, I don't have a doubt about that. Just disappointed for Ezi that she's going through another rehabilitation."
Magbegor joined fellow stars Alanna Smith (leg injury) and Jade Melbourne (illness) on the sidelines, while veteran Sami Whitcomb was ruled out before the tournament with injury and Cayla George did not play due to pregnancy.
Smith suffered a lower-leg injury in the opening game of the tournament, while Melbourne played only three minutes against Italy and could not take the floor in the quarterfinal.
The Opals made a great escape after surrendering a 20-point three-quarter-time lead against the Azzurre thanks largely to a 30-point explosion by 21-year-old Izzy Borlase, but the missing players were too much to overcome in the final-eight showdown.
Ally Wilson was Australia's top scorer with 13 points as the team shot just 40 per cent from the field and had 23 turnovers.

Brondello said the difficult World Cup would be valuable experience for the team, which boasted seven players in their first major international tournament, with the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics looming large on the horizon.

Peru joins US-led ‘Shield of the Americas’ security alliance
The Fujimori administration is the latest right-wing government to join the alliance, which promises a more aggressive approach against crime in the Americas.
Peru will join the “Shield of the Americas”, a regional security alliance led by the United States that shares intelligence and cooperates in military operations against drug cartels.
Keiko Fujimori, Peru’s recently elected right-wing leader, announced the move on Thursday after talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US forces sink vessel ‘linked to Ecuador criminal gang’
- list 2 of 3Marco Rubio says US seeks more economic and security ties in Latin America
- list 3 of 3US announces $45m in security funding, additional naval vessels for Ecuador
“We appreciate this opportunity [to join the initiative], because for us, having previously had to tackle terrorism, [we] know how difficult it is to confront criminality today,” Fujimori said.
Her government also awarded Rubio the Order of the Sun, one of the country’s highest civilian honours.
Rubio’s visit to the Peruvian capital, Lima, caps his three-day, three-country tour of South America to shore up ties between US President Donald Trump and conservative allies in the region.
The diplomat praised Fujimori’s decision to join the Shield of the Americas, also known as the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC), which has advocated for greater military involvement in the fight against crime.
“It is a shield against these threats to the sovereignty of these independent nations,” Rubio explained.
“It is a shield against these transnational criminal groups that, in many cases, have more money and better military equipment than the state. That is unacceptable, and the only way to defeat it is to confront it forcefully.”
Fujimori, a former first lady and the daughter of former President Alberto Fujimori, was sworn into office in July after campaigning heavily on security-related issues.
Peru is the world’s second-largest producer of cocaine, behind Colombia, and reports of crimes like extortion have spiked in recent years.
But Washington’s involvement in the region remains a controversial prospect, given its history of past interventions and its support of right-wing leaders accused of human rights abuses.
Al Jazeera correspondent Teresa Bo explained that the closer cooperation has also raised concerns about the prospect of eroding Latin American sovereignty.
“This has generated lots of fear among many people in this part of the world of what a greater influence of the United States, of what a military influence of the United States, could bring about,” she said.
Rubio attempted to tamp down those concerns during his visit, saying the US would only intervene with the permission of local authorities.
“We’re not going to do anything that our partners don’t ask us to do,” Rubio said. “We don’t want to do less than what you ask of us, but we’re not going to do more than what you ask of us.”
Nevertheless, in Lima, protesters gathered outside the government house where Fujimori’s meeting with Rubio was taking place. Some carried signs that read, “Marco Rubio out of Peru, no to Shield of the Americas.”
“We have said that Peru is nobody’s colony, and it is not the back garden of any country in the world,” Soledad Lozano, one of the protesters, said.
The Trump administration has also indicated that it would like countries like Peru distance themselves from China, which overtook the US as Peru’s primary trading partner.
In February, for instance, the Trump administration criticised Peru for allowing China to construct a mega-port in Chancay, warning that “cheap Chinese money costs sovereignty”.
“China has major investments in Peru right now,” Bo explained. “It controls a port that is 80km away from Lima, and what the US is trying to do is increase its presence in the Western Hemisphere and to try to cut a bit of economic dependency that many countries in Latin America have with China.”
Peru is critical not only to US security strategy in Latin America, but also to its economic interests. It is an important source of mineral resources, as the world’s third-largest producer of copper.
In January, Washington designated Peru a major non-NATO ally, and the US State Department approved a possible $1.5bn foreign military sale for work at Callao Naval Base, Peru’s main naval hub near Lima.

Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski meets with a United States Senate delegation
10.09.2026

The talks focused on European and transatlantic security, Russia's aggression against Ukraine, and the further development of Polish-American bilateral relations.

The talks also covered key aspects of Polish-American relations, particularly cooperation in the fields of security and defense. Minister Sikorski emphasized the strategic importance of the partnership between Poland and the United States and the role of dialogue with the US Congress in further strengthening bilateral ties.
The members of the delegation serve on US Senate committees whose work is particularly relevant to security, foreign policy and economic cooperation. Senator Thom Tillis is Co-Chair of the Senate NATO Observer Group, which supports dialogue between the US Senate, the US Administration and the North Atlantic Alliance.

The Global South cannot afford to let its maritime border disputes fester
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:30:05 UTC
06:30:05 KST

Makane Moïse Mbengue is professor of international law at the Faculty of Law of the University of Geneva and director of the Department of International Law and International Organisation.
The ocean looks like peace from afar and truth up close, they say. But beneath the waves, the map of the world’s oceans is far less settled than it looks. Today, dozens of sea borders remain unresolved. Like so many conflicts, they owe their origins to complicated questions of where one country’s territory ends, and another’s begins.
Many involve overlapping claims to areas rich in resources; and a disproportionate number concern the waters of the Global South. Africa’s coastline is a stark example. The continent has the highest number of unsettled sea boundaries. These disputes are liabilities, and at the worst possible time.
The conflict in the Middle East has shaken energy markets around the world but nowhere has been more exposed than the Global South. This vulnerability is why governments in these regions can no longer afford to leave these borders unsettled. As future chokepoints preventing much-needed resource development, they also risk confrontation and create grey zones ripe for illegal fishing.
Global conflicts are not just disrupting energy markets, but the legal order that maritime security, and much else, depends on. The need for governments to engage with these disputes has rarely been more urgent, and there is no better time for the Global South to show how international law can and should provide solutions.
Lessons can be drawn from recent developments in the Gulf of Thailand. In May, Thailand withdrew from a 25-year-old memorandum of understanding with Cambodia to resolve their maritime boundary and peacefully develop undersea energy resources valued at over US$300 billion. Rather than escalate, Cambodia initiated compulsory conciliation proceedings under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).
Thailand accepted the offer in June, and a commission of international legal experts has now formed to hear the dispute and peacefully work towards a resolution. Cambodia, the smaller nation of the two and in open conflict with Thailand months ago, has secured a hearing on a dispute it could never have won by force.

Kazakhstan was not admitted to Eurovision 2027, despite applying for full membership in the EBU
Kyiv • UNN
Kazakhstan will not make its debut at the Eurovision Song Contest 2027 because its broadcaster does not meet the requirements for full EBU membership. Khabar remains an associate member.
Kazakhstan will not be able to make its debut at the adult Eurovision Song Contest in 2027 after its public broadcaster "Khabar" failed to meet the requirements for full membership in the European Broadcasting Union. Politico reports, as UNN writes.
Details
The EBU explained that Kazakhstan is not part of the European Broadcasting Area, is not a member of the Council of Europe, and does not have official observer status in the organization.
Thus, the "Khabar" agency currently does not meet the requirements for full membership
Canada made it, Kazakhstan did not
"Khabar" remains an EBU associate member. Kazakhstan has already participated in the Junior Eurovision Song Contest five times—from 2018 to 2022—coming second twice. However, associate membership does not automatically grant the right to compete in the adult contest.
Kazakhstan has introduced paid entry permits for Russians06.09.26, 07:15 • 10915 views
At the same time, geographic location is not a determining criterion. Australia participates in Eurovision by special invitation, while Canada became a full EBU member after the rules were changed and is due to make its debut in the contest in 2027. Canada meets the requirements, in particular thanks to its observer status in the Council of Europe.
Thus, Kazakhstan remains outside the main Eurovision for now, while its broadcaster retains only the status of an EBU associate member. The union did not specify whether the country might be given the opportunity to join the contest in the future.

Unknown Publisher

06:29:41 KST

Ukraine says its forces struck Russia’s Makhachkala port on the Caspian Sea and confirmed damage to three Russian warships in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in a series of long-range attacks.
Ukraine’s General Staff said the Makhachkala Sea Commercial Port in Russia’s Dagestan was hit overnight on 10 September, with a fire recorded at the site. The extent of the damage is still being assessed.
The Special Operations Forces (SSO) said Ukrainian units struck oil infrastructure at the port in a joint operation with other Defense Forces. The port’s oil terminal handles tankers with a capacity of up to 10,000 tonnes, while an oil depot is located nearby, according to the SSO.
Makhachkala is Russia’s only ice-free deepwater port on the Caspian Sea and operates year-round. The General Staff said it is an important link in the Russia-Iran logistics corridor, which Moscow uses to bypass Western sanctions.
According to the General Staff, the route is used to transport military-related cargo in both directions, including components and Shahed-type attack drones from Iran to Russia, and explosives, drone components, and ammunition from Russia to Iran. A base of Russia’s Caspian Flotilla is also located near the port.
The SSO said damaging the port’s oil infrastructure could reduce Russia’s ability to use the Caspian Sea to transport and transship energy resources.
Fire Point, a Ukrainian drone manufacturer, said Ukrainian forces used its FP-1 drones in the attack. The company said Makhachkala had been used as a transit point for Iranian attack drones delivered to Russia by sea before being moved onward for use against Ukraine.
Fire Point also said the port handled more than 2.9 million tonnes of cargo in the first eight months of 2026, including more than 2.08 million tonnes of oil.
Three Russian warships hit in Novorossiysk
Ukraine’s General Staff also said further analysis of data confirmed damage inflicted on three Russian warships in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk on 9 September, along with fuel-oil storage facilities at the port.
The General Staff identified the vessels as the small sea minesweeper Zheleznyakov, the frigate Admiral Essen, and the Project 11711 landing ship Pyotr Morgunov.
Visual analysis published by Exilenova+ reported strikes on another Russian warship, the Buyan-M-class corvette, as well as confirming strikes on the frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov. The outlet said the Essen was hit in its superstructure and caught fire.
The Buyan-M class is capable of carrying Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. Russia has used such ships to launch strikes against Ukraine.
The Ukrainian General Staff said operations against key Russian military targets are continuing.

If the Houthis gain full control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, it could give their backer Iran a critical advantage in the war with the US, reducing supplies through a second major transit corridor and sending oil prices surging.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, has relied on the Red Sea route since the Iran conflict effectively closed Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil used to flow.
Global oil prices were on track to end the week above US$100 a barrel for the first time since mid-May, though they were slightly lower on Sept 11 after the Financial Times reported that foreign ministers in the Middle East were trying to work out a temporary deal to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

They announced they would deploy weapons and aircraft to eliminate any movement of the “terrorist” Houthi militias in strategic areas, including the road leading to the coastal city of Mocha, which the militant group captured on Sept 10 along with the Red Sea islands of Hanish.
Military spokesman Colonel Majed al-Nazili called on civilians to avoid using the route between the city of Taiz and Mocha and steer clear of equipment belonging to the Houthis, mountain fighters who withstood years of devastating Saudi air strikes during Yemen’s civil war.
Fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government forces has intensified in recent days, with the Iran-aligned group shifting its focus to control over Yemen’s long coastline instead of just the north and the country’s most populous areas.
Reuters reported on Sept 10 that the dramatic Houthi advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in Iran’s war with the US, according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources.
Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close US ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.
While Iran describes the Houthis as an ally, it publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are “not a proxy”.
Trump rejects Saudi calls to bomb Houthis, Axios reports
Saudi Arabia has been bombing Houthi targets in Yemen but not the strategic areas the group has seized this week. This has raised questions about why Riyadh is not stepping in more forcefully to help its Yemeni government allies as Iranian arms and advice helped the Houthis make significant gains.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called US President Donald Trump twice on Sept 10 and urged him to launch strikes against the Houthis, Axios reported, citing two US officials.
Trump rejected the request, and US officials said the administration does not intend to take direct military action against the Houthis at this time, the report said.

EU urging Kiev to mobilize women – Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:24:36 UTC
06:24:36 KST

EU urging Kiev to mobilize women – Moscow
The EU is encouraging Ukraine to start mobilizing women amid chronic manpower shortages and has demanded that Kiev immediately make “a political decision” on the matter, the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) has said.
Kiev launched its mobilization campaign soon after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022. Amid mounting frontline losses and desertions, the mobilization drive has grown increasingly violent. Recruitment officers have repeatedly been filmed chasing, beating, and forcibly detaining reluctant conscripts before bundling them into vehicles in what in Ukraine has become known as ‘busification’.
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, described the idea of expanding the campaign to include women as “a step in the right direction” at a recent informal EU foreign ministers’ meeting, the SVR said on Thursday, citing information it had obtained. She allegedly warned that Kiev could soon run out of manpower due to a growing shortage of men fit for military service and said that Ukraine should use Israel as a “model to follow.”
The mobilization of women has long been a subject of debate in Ukraine. MP Mariana Bezuglaya argued as early as 2024 that it was time Kiev started targeting women to meet its conscription quota. Last year, the Ukrainian presidential administration’s deputy head, Brigadier General Pavel Palisa, also voiced support for mandatory conscription of women.
According to the SVR, Brussels demanded that Kiev immediately “move from words to action” and make a formal decision to start mobilizing women.
Under current Ukrainian law, men aged 25 to 60 are subject to mobilization, while those aged 23 to 60 are generally barred from leaving the country. Women can serve voluntarily.
Kiev’s brutal mobilization campaign has encountered large-scale draft-dodging and desertion. According to Euronews, around 1.15 million fighting-age Ukrainian men had ended up in the EU as of summer 2026, despite the ban on travelling abroad. According to the SVR, up to 5.6 million Ukrainians are currently residing in other European nations, with women accounting for 43.4% of them.
Many men have proven ready to risk their lives to flee the country illegally through forests, rivers, and mountainous terrain. In February, the head of the Ukrainian border agency, Andrey Demchenko, reported that over 70 apparent draft dodgers had died since 2022, most while trying to cross the Tisza River along Ukraine’s border with Hungary and Romania.
Brussels has reportedly urged EU governments to devise legal mechanisms for sending back Ukrainian refugees residing in the bloc, the Russian intelligence service said, adding that the European Commission sees them as a reason behind the “rise of far-right sentiment” in countries such as Germany or Poland.
Some Western officials have also voiced support for the mobilization of Ukrainian women.
Last year, former UK Defense Secretary Ben Wallace said Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky should have launched a truly mass mobilization.
“Zelensky took a view that he was going to preserve the 18 to 28-year-olds, so it’s not a mass conscription,” Wallace said at the time, adding that the Ukrainian leader should have mobilized everyone and “asked Europe to train them because that is not a hard ask.”
Ben Hodges, a former top commander of US forces in Europe, argued earlier that Kiev should consider both drafting women and lowering the mobilization age to 18. “I also think that there is enough work for women in the army,” he said.
Moscow has slammed Ukraine’s NATO backers as pushing the nation into a war “to the last Ukrainian,” describing the conflict as a Western proxy war against Russia fought through Ukraine.

Military hospitals in the Russian Federation are overcrowded, and wounded soldiers from the front are being transferred en masse to civilian hospitals
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
00:20:01 EEST
06:20:01 KST

Military hospitals in the Russian Federation are overcrowded, and wounded soldiers from the front are being transferred en masse to civilian hospitals
Kyiv • UNN
Military hospitals in the Russian Federation cannot accommodate all the wounded, so they are being placed in civilian hospitals. This complicates civilians' access to scheduled medical care.
Russian military hospitals are unable to cope with the number of wounded arriving from the front, which is why entire wards in ordinary civilian hospitals are increasingly being converted for them. The Moscow Times reports this, citing an investigation by Vot Tak, UNN writes.
Details
According to the publication, restricted wards for Russian military personnel operate, in particular, in St. Petersburg, Yaroslavl Oblast, and Siberia. They function under a special regime, and in some cases staff members sign nondisclosure agreements.
As early as 2023, the Russian authorities planned to transfer nearly 5,000 beds in 27 civilian hospitals across 11 regions to the Ministry of Defense. The list of these medical facilities was not officially released.
There are not enough places in the wards
According to medical workers, the situation is particularly difficult at the Kirov Military Medical Academy in St. Petersburg. One of its wards is designed for 40 patients, but up to 86 people may be there at the same time. Additional beds are installed in the corridors, while mattresses are used in the wards.
According to estimates by Vot Tak, Russian military medical institutions currently have at least 58,300 beds, through which around 1 million wounded people may pass over the course of a year. Despite this, medical workers report a shortage of places.
The transfer of military personnel to civilian hospitals also affects other patients. Wounded participants in the war against Ukraine are admitted as a priority, while the number of doctors has not increased, making it more difficult for civilians to receive scheduled medical care.
According to an assessment by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), as of June, the total losses of the Russian army in the war against Ukraine had reached approximately 1.4 million military personnel, including those killed, wounded, and missing.

====================================================================================================

Earth cooked to its hottest month on record in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:17:00 UTC
06:17:00 KST

August was the hottest month ever recorded around the world, blowing far past a key climate threshold, due to the dangerous double whammy of human-caused climate change and a supersized El Nino, the European climate service Copernicus said Thursday.
August's sizzle also helped push the globe and the United States to swelter through the hottest Northern Hemisphere summer scientists have measured.
Last month, the world averaged 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit (16.96 degrees Celsius), which technically was one-hundredth of a degree Celsius more than the all-time global mark set in July 2023, but because that's also the uncertainty level, it's considered a tie, said Samantha Burgess, strategic climate lead for Copernicus.
"It is now time to stop acting surprised that our warming planet keeps getting warmer. This is occurring exactly as forecast by scientists literally decades ago," Texas A&M University climate scientist Andrew Dessler said in an email.
"The interesting question is not whether we will keep breaking heat records (we will), but whether we're going to do anything about it or just stand there while the climate train runs us over."
Globally, August was 1.65 degrees Celsius (nearly 3 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, far exceeding the longer-term 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold set by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. The eight hottest months on record have all been from July 2023 on, according to Copernicus data.
"Our climate system is really operating well outside the range we would have expected just a decade ago," Burgess said Wednesday from the United Kingdom that has been beset with heat waves.
"We've transitioned from climate being very abstract and perhaps impacting the global South or far away places to climate impacting and disrupting our daily lives with schools closing, hospitals being overwhelmed, roads melting, train lines buckling. And the reality is we will get more of these conditions that we've seen this summer."
Global monthly ocean temperatures in August tied a March 2024 all-time for warmest month recorded, while Aug. 22 set a record for hottest day recorded in the world's seas, according to Copernicus.
"This summer has really been exceptional. We've seen records that existed for close to 100 years be broken, in the U.S. in particular," Burgess said.
The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration announced Wednesday that for the first time, summer in the Lower 48 states was hotter than during the peak of the devastating Dust Bowl in 1936.
June through August of 2026 in the contiguous United States averaged 74.37 degrees (23.54 degrees Celsius), nearly four tenths of a degree warmer than the mark set 90 years earlier.
Globally, this past summer also tied, with 2024, for the hottest on record, according to Copernicus.
In the U.S., August smashed heat records by more than half a degree Fahrenheit, averaging 75.58 degrees (24.21 degrees Celsius) and the average daytime high was a blistering 88.56 degrees (31.42 degrees Celsius), also a record. July was similarly record-hot in the U.S., erasing another long-standing Dust Bowl mark.
That records are regularly getting broken, and that August and not July, which is traditionally warmer, set an all-time record, are signs that human-caused climate change is accelerating, Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather said.
Copernicus data goes back to 1940. NOAA data for the United States goes back to 1895 and global data, which generally matches Copernicus data but takes longer to calculate, dates back to 1880.
Several scientists said that while El Nino is a factor, this natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps and warms weather globally is nowhere as big a cause as the heat-trapping gases emitted as humans burn coal, oil and natural gas.
"While El Nino is starting to ramp up the heat, the underlying driver remains our relentless burning of fossil fuels. Climate change makes every El Nino hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil, and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming," said Friederike Otto, a climate scientist at Imperial College London.
Burgess said El Nino generally adds only one or two tenths of a degree Celsius (two to four tenths Fahrenheit) to the global temperature, with the overwhelming rest of the heat coming from the burning of fossil fuels.
This El Nino is forecast, however, to break records for strength in the coming months. And as temperatures continue to rise, heat waves, storms, floods and wildfires will get more frequent and more dangerous, said Texas Tech climate scientist Katharine Hayhoe.
According to Hausfather, "it is increasingly likely that 2026 ends up beating 2024 as the warmest year on record, and almost certain that 2027 beats both, potentially reaching as high as 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels on the back of an unprecedentedly strong El Nino event."
Some days may hit an even higher climate threshold, 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above mid 1800s, Burgess said.
"Until humanity stops burning colossal amount of coal, oil and gas, the pollution this causes will keep baking our planet, and extreme heat will keep smashing all-time records, killing millions and costing trillions, hitting transport and health systems, and pushing up prices for household basics like food," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said.
"This is the spiraling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling."

According to U.S. estimates, hundreds of officers from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps are in Yemen, where they are cooperating with the Houthis. One U.S. official suggested that the ultimate goal of Tehran and the Houthis may be to block the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
How the U.S. is helping Saudi Arabia
According to CNN, Washington has helped Riyadh use a system that enables real-time monitoring of the battlefield situation. The U.S. is also providing geospatial data to help select targets during Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Houthis seize Mokha, global energy flows under threat - Reuters10.09.26, 17:25 • 9092 views
At the same time, U.S. military personnel are not directly participating in the strikes. The U.S. exchanges intelligence with Saudi Arabia, but does not refuel Saudi fighter jets or provide other operational support that Washington supplied during previous military operations against the Houthis.
According to CNN sources, current U.S. assistance is focused primarily on coordinating Saudi Arabia’s operations and improving their effectiveness.

New drug that slows progression of type of MND to be listed on PBS
A new drug that slows the progression of a type of Motor Neurone Disease will be listed on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.
Health Minister Mark Butler says from October 1, Tofersen (Qalsody®) will be listed for the first time for the treatment of MND patients with a form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
The medication works by reducing the production of SOD1 protein which helps slow the progression of MND and allows people to maintain function for longer.
It's believed the medication, which normally costs $28,600 per script, will benefit 70 Australians.
"It will provide significant relief to the we think 70 or so patients every year who will be able to access it. They have a particular genetic mutation, a particular subtype of ALS," Butler says.
ASIO chief says agency has foiled 16 terror threats since Bondi attack
ASIO Director-General Mike Burgess has warned terrorism remains an "enduring, evolving" threat, while marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 terror attacks.
In a statement published online, Burgess described the domestic spy agency's work in the aftermath, and how the "horrors of that day resonated deeply in ASIO".
He also used the opportunity to warn of the ongoing terror threat in Australia, including revealing that 16 terror threats have been foiled since the Bondi terror attack nine months ago.
And he described one recent case involving an individual who wanted to "blow up a school", motivated by a mix of ideological and extreme Christian beliefs.
"Spikes in grievance, intolerance and polarisation are degrading our security environment and making politically motivated violence more likely," he said.
"The conflict in the Middle East contributed to this, fuelling frustration and anger, as did social media algorithms that amplified and accelerated grievance narratives.
"Whether online or in the real world, when intolerance is tolerated, when violent rhetoric and violent acts are left unchecked, they become normalised, creating a permissive environment for further violence."
Nationals leader dismisses warning from SA premier on migration
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has dismissed a warning from the South Australian premier to avoid a "political race to the bottom" with One Nation on immigration.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has released a statement remembering 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

"We all remember where we were, and how we received the shocking news," Taylor says.

Rudd says Australia's 'she'll be right mate' attitude doesn't work in security environment
Former prime minister Kevin Rudd says Australia has, over time, become "complacent" about securing Australia's national security.
The former PM says all sides of politics need to talk about securing Australia's national security in an increasingly dangerous environment.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast earlier, Rudd says that extends to the economy and the rise of artificial intelligence.
He says Australia's "she'll be right mate attitude" won't work in the future.
"We need to face also very difficult and hardline economic decisions for the future through industry policy in ensuring that we've got growth sectors for the future of the economy," Rudd says.

John Howard reflects on visit to US during 9/11 terrorist attacks
Former prime minister John Howard says he thinks Australia did the right thing by signing up Australia to the war on terror following the 9/11 terrorist attacks.
Howard was on a visit to the United States in Washington DC to address the US Congress when the terrorist attacks happened.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Howard says he visited the Pentagon the day before a plane deliberately crashed into the headquarters of the US defence department.
"I just knew that it meant a lot to the whole world, and it certainly meant that I quickly came to realise just how important our association with the Americans was," Howard says.
Howard says his foreign minister, Alexander Downer, suggested invoking the ANZUS treaty, which was intended to protect Australia.
"This was clearly an attack on the metropolitan power of the United States. So we decided that what we should do is take advantage of that opportunity and we invoked it."

Labor's 20 per cent gas reserve ceiling will prevent too much LNG supply, Bowen says
Chris Bowen says the 20 per cent ceiling for Labor's proposed gas reservation policy will prevent Australia from reserving too much gas.
The federal government yesterday unveiled its plans for an east coast gas reservation policy.
Initial plans involved requiring gas exporters to reserve at least 20 per cent of their exports. But the draft released yesterday makes that a ceiling, not a fixed requirement.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Bowen says the plan released yesterday will ensure Australia achieves "modest oversupply".
He says that will be calculated by the Australian Energy Regulator every five years.
"What we've landed on is the model we announced yesterday, which is reservation up to 20 per cent of exports, but with the Australian Energy Regulator assessing demand each year on a five-yearly rolling basis," Bowen says.
"That really gives us the opportunity to genuinely provide that modest oversupply each year. So, cater for all the gaps, all the shortages that are always forecast in just a little bit extra, but not reserving gas that Australians don't use or don't need."
Deputy PM pushes back on SA premier's migration comments
Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles has pressed the case for reducing Australia's migration despite warnings from SA's premier.
SA Labor Premier Peter Malinauskas used a speech to the Sydney Institute to warn the major parties of a "political race to the bottom" with One Nation on immigration.
Speaking to Channel Nine, Marles says while he agrees migration shouldn't be a political football, the migration rate should match the country's infrastructure and services.
Asked when the federal government will announce its immigration policy, Marles says Labor is working on a set of policies to bring migration down.
"This shouldn't be a political football. Skilled migration does play a really important part of the economy ... but equally we need to have a migration rate which matches the infrastructure, the services we have in the country and that's why we need to be bringing it down," Marles says.
One Nation senator says party has nothing to apologise for over Hastie 'traitor' carton

Butler says PM, Taylor will have 'productive discussions' over migration
Health Minister Mark Butler says he hopes the PM and opposition leader will have "productive discussions" over immigration.

NEW DELHI: For the first time in 8 years, an Iranian president will visit India with Masoud Pezeshkian set to arrive in New Delhi for the 18th BRICS summit on Friday, amid escalating West Asia tensions that have cast a shadow over the summit. Shortly after his arrival, Pezeshkian will participate in the BRICS Business Forum meeting along with PM Narendra Modi, Russian President Vladimir Putin and other leaders before joining Modi for a bilateral in the evening.The last Iranian president to visit India was Hassan Rouhani in 2018. While Iran has confirmed participation by the president in the BRICS summit, Saudi Arabia and the UAE - both parties to the West Asia conflict along with Tehran - will be represented by foreign minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud and Abu Dhabi crown prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan respectively.
Pezeshkian is likely to reiterate his message before Modi for India to help end the war and suitably address Tehran's concerns related to the current situation, including through a strong condemnation of "illegal aggression" against Iran, in the proposed BRICS declaration. In his meetings with both Putin and Pezeshkian on Friday, Modi is expected to stress the need for new members to subscribe to consensus in the grouping on critical issues and work together for a unified joint declaration.
India agreed to the recent SCO Bishkek Declaration that condemned attacks on Iran. The declaration did not name the US or Israel though to prevent any resistance from members that have also cultivated ties with Washington.However, with the presence of UAE in BRICS, balancing the interests of both sides has not been easy for India’s BRICS chairship. It’s unlikely that the UAE will agree to an SCO-like formulation without seeking an explicit condemnation of Iranian attacks.
Gulf states like the UAE and Saudi Arabia are only dialogue partners in SCO.India will prioritise the UN Charter, dialogue and diplomacy, freedom of navigation and civilian protection in the declaration. If the deadlock persists, the government will look to insulate economic agreements from the West Asia discord by acknowledging respective national positions.The BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting earlier this year ended without a consensual statement, with Tehran adamant on a condemnation of the alleged violation of international law by the US and Israel and accusing the UAE of being directly involved in aggression against Iran.

NEW YORK, September 10. /TASS/. More than 100 American military advisers are working in Saudi Arabia, providing Riyadh with intelligence and targeting support amid the escalation of the conflict with the Yemeni rebel movement Ansar Allah (the Houthis), CNN reported.
According to its information, this cooperation is being carried out within the framework of a joint command formed several weeks ago to counter the Houthis. According to an unnamed US administration official, a total of about 200 American military personnel are deployed in Saudi Arabia.
It is noted that American troops do not directly participate in strikes and do not assist in refueling Saudi military aircraft.
The armed confrontation between the Saudi-backed government forces and Houthi rebels has been ongoing in Yemen since August 2014. The situation deteriorated dramatically in early September, when the rebel Yemeni movement launched an offensive in the country’s southwest. Simultaneously with their ground offensive, the Houthis started to deliver drone and missile strikes on coastal areas in the Red Sea and the outskirts of the southwestern Yemeni city of Taiz in an attempt to cut supply routes to the Red Sea coastal city of Mocha and advance toward areas near the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Secret US-Cuba energy deal reportedly collapsed over political demands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:00:35 UTC
06:00:35 KST

The Trump administration secretly explored an energy deal with Cuba earlier this year that would have provided US oil and investment to the island in exchange for major economic and political changes, according to media reports.
But Cuban resistance and political pressure in Miami prevented the agreement, US media reported on Thursday.
The proposal would have provided Cuba with US oil if Havana agreed to privatise its state-owned energy company, CUPET.
Washington also wanted US investors to gain control of the company, which operates refineries, storage facilities and fuel distribution through CIMEX, part of the military conglomerate GAESA.
"The deal with Cuba, while much smaller in its scale would have sent shockwaves throughout the Cuban government establishment, as it was also tied to a demand that the country's handpicked president, Miguel Diaz-Canel, seen as an incompetent figurehead by Trump administration officials, leave power," Miami Herald reported.
"It would have given the United States significant sway over the country as Cuba’s main oil provider, aligning with President Donald Trump's 'Donroe' Doctrine of US influence in the Western Hemisphere," it reported, citing sources.
The proposal came after Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro was abducted and ousted by US forces Januray 3, ending oil supplies Caracas provided to Havana.
No negotiations
Cuba produces only about 40 percent of the oil it consumes, while its aging power grid and Soviet-era plants have suffered repeated breakdowns.
The Trump administration later declared a national emergency related to Cuba and threatened tariffs against countries supplying the island with oil.
In February, Washington authorised the sale of US oil to private Cuban entities, signaling its interest in Cuba's energy sector.
"The Cuban people deserve freedom, not another deal to keep the same regime in power," US Republican Representative Maria Elvira Salazar said at a congressional hearing in April.
US officials met Raul Guillermo Rodriguez Castro, the grandson of former leader Raul Castro, in Saint Kitts and Nevis in February, according to the Miami Herald.
Rodriguez Castro reportedly said Cuba could accept economic reforms, but Washington could not dictate how the country was governed.
US lawmakers Carlos Gimenez and Mario Diaz-Balart questioned reports of negotiations with the Castro family, while Salazar opposed any agreement that could preserve the existing government.
The Trump administration later shifted toward sanctions, targeting GAESA in May and CUPET in June.
Cuba's foreign minister said on Monday that communication channels with Washington remained open but that there had been "no progress" and no negotiations were currently taking place.

Zelenskyy expects progress in energy talks after meeting Trump

Zelenskyy expects progress in energy talks after meeting Trump
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he expects to meet with a US delegation at the end of September, when Ukraine will raise issues related to energy and food security.
Source: European Pravda, citing Zelenskyy's comments to journalists after his meeting with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney
Details: Zelenskyy said he does not expect serious negotiations with Russia during the pre-election period in Russia but hopes for results from a meeting with the US side at the end of September on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
He added that Kyiv remains in daily contact with the US delegation, with energy and food security among the key issues.
"We speak about what outcome we can have, how to prepare for the trilateral meeting, and what outcome can be after the trilateral meeting. Yes, all the partners in the world raise the topic of grain and agricultural products, which Russia began to block in the Black Sea. We responded, and we did the same. But we have to respond. Otherwise, Russia will never stop this war," he said.
Zelenskyy expects results from a possible meeting with US President Donald Trump in New York. However, he noted that Russia could intensify its attacks on Ukraine during this period.
"But knowing Russia, when they hear that we have somewhere negotiations with Europeans, with Canadians, with Americans, when they hear, they try to intensify attacks on us. So just to break any kind of negotiations, just to break any kind of dialogue. But we believe in peace, and we will move in such a direction. There's only one way to stop the war, no other way," the Ukrainian president said.
He specified that he expects the first results of the talks with the US at the end of September.
Background: US President Donald Trump said that he had had a "great" conversation with Russian leader Vladimir Putin at the beginning of the week and that Putin wants to make a deal to end the war in Ukraine.

Europe unable to finance all of Kiev’s requests this year — WSJ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:58:23 UTC
05:58:23 KST

NEW YORK, September 10. /TASS/. Europe is unable to provide additional multibillion financing to Ukraine as the Kiev government wants, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) wrote.
Vladimir Zelensky’s multibillion-dollar requests "couldn’t come at a worse time for European governments," the newspaper wrote. European officials warn in private conversations "they might not be able to foot the bill for everything Ukraine wants."
The growing popularity of the Alternative for Germany party (AfD) in Germany and Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, who oppose financial support to Ukraine, prompts European leaders to decline new financial commitments to Kiev.
At this point, the EU "is trying to avoid reopening discussions over new money, knowing the political blowback that could generate."
Earlier this week, The New York Times (NYT) reported that Zelensky’s announcement about an unexpectedly large defense budget shortfall surprised and unsettled many European officials and raised questions about how efficiently these funds were used.
Late last month, Zelensky complained that the defense ministry’s budget shortfall stands at $27 billion, including $8-10 billion needed for arms procurements and almost $20 billion - for salaries.
Ukraine has drawn up budgets with record deficits for several years. Kiev acknowledges that the country has completely exhausted its own resources and that finding funds is becoming increasingly difficult. On August 20, Zelensky admitted that the shortage of funds had become a major challenge, with the defense budget alone facing a $27-billion shortfall. Former Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmitry Kuleba said that no one in Kiev understands how to fill the budget gap.
On August 18, Kuleba stated that Kiev had "reached the ceiling" of international support and would not receive more from the West than what is currently provided. He warned that Kiev must be extremely cautious when calculating what it can rely on from external sources. Nevertheless, the government aims to secure an even larger sum of $52 billion from its partners in 2027.

Checks on e-commerce platforms from October: FSSAI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:54:13 UTC
05:54:13 KST

New Delhi: Having secured nearly 2,000 convictions in food safety cases across the country, Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is now stepping up enforcement, including holding e-commerce platforms responsible for products sold through them and proposing stricter action against high-fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) foods near schools, its CEO Rajit Punhani said Thursday.FSSAI will begin checks on e-commerce platforms from next month. Platforms will have to carry out due diligence and ensure that products listed on them comply with food safety regulations."We are holding e-commerce platforms responsible. They cannot take this plea that they are just aggregators, they are just platforms. It is your responsibility, your due diligence," Punhani said.FSSAI has already held consultations with e-commerce companies. Punhani identified e-commerce and labelling as two major consumer-focused reforms expected over the next year.
The regulator has also proposed restricting the sale of HFSS food within 50 metres of schools to protect children from unhealthy food. Punhani said the earlier challenge was the absence of a clear definition of HFSS food. The Indian Council of Medical Research-National Institute of Nutrition, a govt nutrition research institute, has now provided criteria that FSSAI plans to use.
On enforcement, Punhani said FSSAI had suspended licences, closed establishments and launched prosecutions. Around 600 people had been arrested in criminal cases involving unsafe food in the previous six months, he said. He cited around 1,900 convictions and 33,000 notices issued across India for food safety violations, including adulteration, mislabelling and substandard food.
FSSAI is also tightening rules on food claims and marketing. It does not allow "100%" claims except in cases under litigation, while "pure" and "natural" can be used only for single-ingredient products, provided nothing has been added. The regulator has also written to Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade and the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks over the use of "healthy" as a trademark.Punhani said the term "energy drink" would not be allowed on labels as it could mislead consumers, with such products classified as caffeinated beverages, while the proposed red warning system would also cover aerated, carbonated and caffeinated beverages. The regulator has issued notices to six celebrities over misleading food-related endorsements, with three having responded.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Zelensky: First FREYJA anti-ballistic system expected to be ready by year-end
The Ukrainian President said this while speaking to media representatives in Canada, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“We are working on FREYJA, and we are very pleased that today we had an opportunity to discuss it with the Prime Minister, and Canada will join this program. This will be our new anti-ballistic system. The companies told us that they need 20–30 years for a new ballistic missile system. I said that we do not want such a long war. Absolutely not. No, that belongs to a different world, to the 20th century. Today, there are new technologies and a new Ukraine, and we can do all of this faster. And we expect to have the first system by the end of this year,” Zelensky said.
He noted that the FREYJA anti-ballistic program was discussed in Norway and in Canada today.
“And we also expect that in New York we will have a clearer understanding of the timeline for all our steps, because this is about defense,” the Ukrainian President said.
As reported earlier, FREYJA is a prospective pan-European project for an integrated air and missile defense system focused on intercepting ballistic missiles. Ukraine is developing it jointly with European countries, with the participation of Fire Point, as a cheaper and mass-produced alternative to the U.S. Patriot air defense systems.

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk attends a press conference after a meeting of the Visegrád Group leaders in Bratislava, on Sept. 10, 2026. | Tomas Benedikovic/AFP via Getty Images
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a ‘direct threat’ was averted at a border crossing with Ukraine on Wednesday night and warned of further incidents linked to Russia in the near future.
His comments came just one day after a Russian drone hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, killing two people and wounding several others.
“Last night, thanks to cooperation between our services and their Ukrainian counterparts, a direct threat to a border crossing was averted,” Tusk said in a press conference after a meeting of the Visegrád Group leaders in Bratislava Thursday.
Advertisement
Tusk did not provide any further details about the nature of the threat or which of the 18 border crossings between Poland and Ukraine was affected.
The prime minister added that the incident was just a taste of what is to come and noted he had received a “fairly precise report” from the CIA regarding possible events in the coming months.
“We must anticipate various scenarios; both Poland and all of Europe need to be prepared for different possibilities concerning the situation not only on the Russian-Ukrainian front but also along the EU’s eastern flank.”
The incident at the border crossing between Moldova and Ukraine’s Odesa region left two people dead, causing President Maia Sandu to call for further European air defense support for Ukraine.
Russia also struck a Moldova-Ukraine border crossing in August.
“As you know, Russia has already resorted to provocative attacks on border crossings—for instance, in Moldova. We expect similar actions targeting border crossings with Ukraine in other countries, including Poland,” said Tusk.
Advertisement
In August, after a briefing with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, he warned that “escalation from Russia’s side is progressing,” and called for more air support for Ukraine as it is “crucial for our security.”
He said the next six months would be decisive and made it clear that provocations against NATO members should not be ruled out.
The CIA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ford announces $1 billion investment at Kentucky plant following DOT criticism on China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:48:14 UTC
05:48:14 KST

DETROIT — Ford Motor on Thursday announced a $1 billion investment to build a new paint shop at its crucial Kentucky Truck Plant.
The facility, which Ford has called its most important and profitable plant globally, produces the automaker's large F-250 to F-550 Super Duty trucks as well as the Ford Expedition and Lincoln Navigator SUVs.
The announcement comes two days after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expressed "profound concern" about the automaker's U.S. "manufacturing integrity" and ties to Chinese companies that the Trump administration believed could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and U.S. automotive industry.
Ford, which regularly touts its position as the top-producing automaker in the U.S., called the comments a "wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines."
Paint shops are a critical and costly part of a vehicle assembly plant. The new facility for Ford is expected to replace the plant's "existing paint shop and further [modernize] one of Ford's most important manufacturing operations," the company said in a press release Thursday.
The Detroit automaker said it would break ground on the facility later this year. A Ford spokesperson declined to disclose when the company expects to complete the new paint shop.
Ford noted the investment is the latest following roughly $4 billion in announcements for its Kentucky facilities in recent years.
"These investments demonstrate our confidence in Kentucky's workforce, our commitment to American manufacturing, and our belief that the future of mobility and energy will be built right here in the United States," Ford CEO Jim Farley said in the release.
Duffy's criticism was addressed to Farley in a letter released by the Trump administration Tuesday. Following a lengthy response from Ford, the White House's Rapid Response account on X released a positive statement Wednesday, calling Ford "a GREAT American company."

Morocco denies involvement in migrant surge into Spain’s Ceuta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:46:16 UTC
05:46:16 KST

Morocco denies involvement in migrant surge into Spain’s Ceuta
Foreign Ministry says ‘no facts’ proving Rabat’s involvement after 70,000 migrants surged into Spanish enclave in July.
Morocco’s Foreign Ministry says there is no evidence of Rabat’s involvement in the mass migrant crossing into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta in July.
More than 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta from nearby Morocco on July 30 and 31 in an unprecedented surge that left scores dead and sparked European Union infighting over migration.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Thousands protest in Spain as Ceuta’s migration crisis festers a month on
- list 2 of 3Spain’s Sanchez says Russia, Israel spread disinformation on Ceuta crisis
- list 3 of 3Spain asks EU for help to process 5,000 Ceuta migrants amid local unrest
While most have since returned, more than 100 people died, according to local officials and civil organisations.
Local authorities say thousands – including unaccompanied minors – remain in the enclave where they are living in makeshift camps or on the streets and beaches. Their presence has fuelled near-daily protests by residents angry at the Spanish government’s handling of the crisis.
Spain’s opposition parties have since targeted the government’s relationship with Morocco and accused Rabat of facilitating or orchestrating the crossing.
“Why continue to level accusations against Morocco when no evidence, facts, or reports establish any involvement on the part of Moroccan authorities?” the ministry said in a statement on Thursday.
“Why are illegal migrants not being returned, even though the Moroccan government has officially committed to readmitting them? Why are unaccompanied minors being kept away from their families, when Morocco has urgently requested their return?” it added.
The ministry asserted that Morocco refuses to be used as a “pre-election political pawn”, nor does it accept being made the “scapegoat in political score-settling”. Spain will hold national elections by mid-2027.
The Moroccan Foreign Ministry highlighted the close security, migration and economic ties between Rabat and Madrid since Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez backed Morocco’s autonomy plan for Western Sahara in 2022.
On Wednesday, Spain declassified intelligence reports that had warned of potential “mass entries” by migrants into Ceuta just before the incident occurred.
A declassified military intelligence document from July 30 stated that it is “highly likely that the Moroccan authorities are not actively encouraging the migratory wave, but have so far acted in a negligent and passive manner”.
Morocco does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta or Melilla, the other autonomous Spanish enclave bordering Morocco.

At least 26 children died in a fire at two schools in Congo
Kyiv • UNN
In Bukavu, 19 girls and 7 boys died in a fire at two schools. Dozens of children were injured, and the death toll may rise.
At least 26 students were killed and dozens more injured in a fire that engulfed two neighboring schools in the city of Bukavu in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Associated Press reports this, citing the authorities of South Kivu province, UNN writes.
Details
Among those killed were 19 girls and 7 boys. Authorities warn that the death toll may rise.
According to preliminary data, the fire broke out in a residential building, after which the flames spread to the nearby schools. Local administrator Moise Lubala told AP that some students were trapped inside the building.
Some children suffocated at the school
According to Lubala, several students were unable to escape from the Furaha secondary school, and some of them suffocated.
Lawrence Kanyuka, a spokesperson for the M23 group, which controls Bukavu, had earlier reported that 24 students had been killed and 29 people taken to local medical facilities.
Nurse Siza Jean-Baptiste told AP that boys and girls of various ages from the Furaha and Ujamaa schools were brought to the BDOM Nyamlagira medical center. The children were wearing school uniforms when they were admitted.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell says league could rework TV packages in next media deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:44:33 UTC
05:44:33 KST

MELBOURNE, Australia — NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he will consider reworking game packages when the league inks its next media rights deal to adjust for modern TV consumption habits and the shift to streaming.
"One of the things we're doing as a league is talking to our partners, talking to future partners, potential partners ... and evaluating, should we repackage our current packages? Should we think differently about where we go with those things?" Goodell said in an exclusive interview with CNBC ahead of the Week 1 game between the San Francisco 49ers and the Los Angeles Rams, the league's first regular-season matchup in Australia. The game will take place Thursday night at 8:35 p.m. ET.
The NFL currently sells two Sunday afternoon game packages, a Sunday Night Football slate, a Monday Night Football package, and Thursday Night Football games. Fox and Paramount Skydance-owned CBS have the Sunday afternoon game rights, while NBC has Sunday Night Football, Disney's ESPN and ABC own Monday Night Football and Amazon has Thursday Night Football.
Netflix also bought the rights to five additional NFL games this season.
The NFL has an opt-out clause that it can trigger at the end of the 2029-30 season to redo and resell its existing packages. Goodell wouldn't say if the league plans to take advantage of that option.
"We don't have to make that decision today. That's the reason you have an option," Goodell said. "[What] we said all along is that the option would be incredibly valuable to the NFL — to be able to evaluate what's happening in the media landscape, to be able to look at the things that are happening out there and make the best decision for our fans and for our clubs and how we make sure we present our game in the best possible way and do it with the proper value."
Several of the NFL's current media partners are undergoing significant transformations this year.
Paramount is attempting to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery for $110 billion in a deal that's been delayed amid an antitrust challenge. Fox has agreed to buy Roku for $22 billion. Comcast said earlier this year it plans to spin off NBCUniversal.
The shifting media landscape is likely to factor in when the NFL renegotiates its packages.
Goodell also noted that reaching fans globally is a new priority for the league, which will play games in countries including Spain, France and Brazil this season. Netflix owns the global broadcast rights to the 49ers-Rams game.
Still, most NFL game rights are U.S.-only.
"The world is changing for our partners. It's changing for us. It's changing for fans. Our fans are moving to other platforms," said Goodell. "I think one of the challenges for us is to look at the changes, evaluate what's working, what's not, what we think is going to work beyond those option dates and the partners that can bring the greatest opportunity to reach those fans on a global basis. ... We've never looked at it that way until recently."
Goodell said broadcast TV will continue to play a major role in the league's media rights strategy to ensure that local markets have free, over-the-air access to games. Local broadcast stations simulcast games on streaming services such as Netflix and Amazon Prime Video so regional fans can watch.
"One hundred percent of our games are available on broadcast television. I see that continuing," said Goodell.

Xi Jinping and Putin Won’t Hold Bilateral Talks While Moscow and Beijing Clash Over Gas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:38:03 UTC

- Category
