Xi Jinping and Putin Won’t Hold Bilateral Talks While Moscow and Beijing Clash Over Gas
Chinese President Xi Jinping will not hold a separate bilateral meeting with Russian leader Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi.
Russian aide Yuri Ushakov confirmed that no formal two-way contact between Putin and Xi is planned for the gathering, though he suggested the two leaders might still speak briefly in the corridors for a informal conversation, according to The Moscow Times on September 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The decision follows their previous encounter on August 31 in Bishkek during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, which failed to achieve progress on the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline project intended to deliver up to 50 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually to China.
Sources familiar with the negotiations indicate the two sides remain unable to agree on pricing. Beijing seeks a rate of around $50 per thousand cubic meters, matching domestic Russian prices, or $120 to $130, matching prices for Russian industrial consumers.
In contrast, Moscow proposes pricing based on the Power of Siberia 1 pipeline, which stands at roughly $250 to $260 per thousand cubic meters.
This proposed rate is approximately 40% lower than Gazprom’s prices for non-CIS international buyers, which hover around $420 per thousand cubic meters.
While public economic negotiations face bottlenecks, covert military-technical cooperation between Moscow and Beijing reportedly continues to deepen behind closed doors.
Bilateral documents from clandestine forums have previously exposed a reported joint strategic plan to disable the Starlink satellite network alongside a high-tech partnership to co-develop hypersonic missile defenses and autonomous AI-driven drones.
This illustrates a highly transactional exchange of Russian frontline combat data for advanced Chinese electronics.

Need social media firewalls, safeguards for minors: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:37:12 UTC
05:37:12 KST

NEW DELHI: With minors' access to social media platforms banned in many countries, Supreme Court Thursday took the first step in this regard by seeking govt's response to a PIL that said opening a social media account is akin to signing a contract - which is impermissible for a person below 18 years of age under Indian law.The plea by senior advocate H S Phoolka, on behalf of NGO Just Rights for Children Association, found resonance with a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, which said there was a need for safeguards and firewalls to protect minors.Phoolka said children were at present permitted to independently create and maintain accounts on social media platforms and access digital platforms "notwithstanding their statutory incapacity to enter into a contract under Section 11 of Indian Contract Act, 1872", and said such contracts are void ab initio.The NGO said the absence of an effective and uniform mechanism giving practical effect to such statutory incapacity in the digital environment exposed children to "foreseeable risks, including online grooming, sexual exploitation, trafficking, behavioural profiling, misuse of personal data, cyberbullying, exposure to age-inappropriate content and other harms affecting their safety, dignity, development and well-being".
It requested the court to direct govt to ensure that persons below 18 years of age are not permitted to enter into contracts with digital platforms, including social media, online gaming, content-sharing, live-streaming and other user generated content platforms. It said minors could be permitted to access lawful, educational and age-appropriate digital content through accounts maintained and controlled by their parents or guardians, subject to an appropriate regulatory framework.Phoolka said social media platforms applied US law in India, not Indian law. In US, a person above 13 years can lawfully enter into a contract. CJI Kant said, "We need some safeguards in India." Justice Bagchi said, "There should be some firewalls."
The NGO said opening of accounts includes acceptance of contractual terms and conditions, user agreements, privacy policy, etc, which govern the relationship between the platform and the user.Referring to provisions of Digital Personal Data Protection Act, the NGO said Section 9 required verifiable parental or guardian consent for processing a child's personal data. The Act also imposes restrictions concerning detrimental processing, tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising, it said.However, the existing statutory framework does not expressly prohibit a person below 18 from independently creating an account on a digital platform nor does it prescribe a uniform mechanism for preventing such independent opening of accounts, it said.

building a life in virtual worlds: the places we inhabit and lose
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:35:23 UTC
05:35:23 KST

building a home in the virtual world
Before exploring a virtual world, players start by building a house. In Minecraft, the first night can mean quickly putting together a shelter from whatever is nearby, while in Animal Crossing: New Horizons, players arrive on an empty island and slowly fill it with houses, gardens, paths, and furniture. In The Sims, building and arranging a home has always been part of the game. Different games, same habit: make a place, then come back to it. As games have become larger and more social, those places have taken on a life of their own. Players spend hours decorating houses, meeting friends, hosting events, or simply hanging around. In some VR worlds, people even sleep there. At a certain point, it becomes difficult to describe these spaces as just part of a game. There is a catch, though. The house might be yours in every practical sense, since you built it, furnished it, and spent time there, but the world around it belongs to someone else. And that can disappear.
image courtesy of Andyisyoda
from navigation to dwelling
Players move through game worlds to complete objectives, collect resources, encounter other characters, and trigger narrative events, but dwelling begins when that relationship with the environment changes and the world stops being somewhere the player simply passes through. A bed becomes a place to return to, a chest gives possessions an order, furniture is moved around, crops are planted outside, and a familiar room gradually turns into a meeting place for friends. None of these actions necessarily advances the central objective of the game, yet their repetition gives the environment a different meaning: through everyday routines and small acts of maintenance, an abstract digital landscape begins to acquire familiarity, memory, and a sense of place.
Martin Heidegger’s writing on dwelling and Gaston Bachelard’s reflections on the domestic interior offer one way of thinking about this shift. For both writers, inhabitation is also a way of establishing a relationship with one’s surroundings and finding orientation within them. Digital environments bring that idea into a different context. An open world may appear to offer unlimited freedom, but its scale can also make it difficult to establish any sense of familiarity. Without fixed points, routines, or places to return to, a seemingly limitless landscape can remain anonymous. Building a home changes that relationship by creating a point of reference within the larger world, somewhere the player can leave and return to, alter over time, and gradually make familiar.
The Sims | image courtesy of Electronic Arts
the house as interface
Since its first release in 2000, The Sims has allowed players to construct houses and then watch their inhabitants negotiate the spaces they have created. The arrangement of a floor plan affects movement, access to objects, daily routines, and the small interactions that take place between characters, so that building a house is inseparable from observing what happens inside it.
This approach grew out of The Sims creator Will Wright’s long-standing interest in systems and simulation, as well as in the ways people interact with their environments. Architectural ideas, including those associated with Christopher Alexander’s A Pattern Language, formed part of the wider thinking behind the game and its attempt to translate spatial relationships into an interactive model. This life simulation game gave players a system they could test and modify, often discovering the consequences of their decisions only after the inhabitants began using the spaces. A poorly arranged room might interrupt circulation, while inaccessible objects or awkward layouts can interfere with the routines that structure everyday life inside the house. Players learn about space through trial and error, adjusting walls, furniture, and rooms in response to the behavior of the characters they are trying to accommodate.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, when movement restrictions confined many people to their homes and forced the domestic interior to accommodate an expanding range of activities, the relationship between domestic life and digital space became particularly visible. Released in March 2020, Animal Crossing: New Horizons became one of the defining cultural environments of that period. Players arrived on an undeveloped island and gradually transformed it through construction, landscaping, collecting, and decoration. Players could redirect rivers, reshape the terrain, lay paths, and fill the island with gardens and outdoor spaces. Over time, many built cafés, markets, libraries, laundromats, and parks, using the same tools they used inside their houses to shape the rest of the island.
The game also runs on the same clock as the player’s everyday life. Shops open and close at certain hours, fruit grows back, flowers need attention, and seasonal events arrive throughout the year. During the pandemic, when days often felt repetitive and disconnected from their usual routines, this gave people small reasons to return to the game.
image courtesy of Nintendo
from the bedroom to the city
The idea of making oneself at home in a virtual environment can take surprisingly literal forms. In VRChat, some users sleep while wearing a headset, spending the night in digital bedrooms, apartments, or landscapes alongside people who may be physically thousands of miles away. Michael Yin and Robert Xiao examined this practice in their 2023 CHI study, Drifting Off in Paradise: Why People Sleep in Virtual Reality, finding that the boundary between the physical room and the virtual one does not simply disappear. Users often try to make the two correspond, using blankets, fans, and other objects in their physical surroundings to make what they see and hear in the headset feel more real.
Unlike a game session built around movement or achievement, sleep requires the user to give up control and remain in one place. The virtual environment becomes a place to be with another person, even while the body remains elsewhere. That same capacity to inhabit a digital space has also been used at a very different scale. Since 2012, UN-Habitat’s Block by Block initiative has brought Minecraft into participatory planning workshops, where residents can work together on models of streets, parks, and public spaces. The workshops give residents blocks to move, buildings to alter, and spaces to discuss directly inside a shared model of their neighborhood. Minecraft has also been used to make architecture do something more political. The Uncensored Library, created with Reporters Without Borders, takes the form of a monumental virtual library containing journalism that has been censored in different countries.
Built inside a game known for its open-ended worlds and amateur construction, the project turns a familiar architectural type into a way of circulating information across national borders.
architecture after the physical constraint
Architects and designers have also approached game environments as spaces that deserve architectural analysis in their own right. You+Pea, the practice founded by Luke Caspar Pearson and Sandra Youkhana, studies video games through plans, sections, axonometric drawings, and other architectural forms of representation, treating interactive worlds as spatial systems with circulation networks, boundaries, visual relationships, and urban structures. A player experiences a virtual world through movement, while architectural drawing can reveal relationships that remain difficult to perceive during play. A section or axonometric can expose the organization of an entire environment at once.
Space Popular has similarly investigated the relationship between physical and virtual architecture. The work of the studio considers how domestic space changes when conventional boundaries between physical and digital environments become less distinct. Projects such as The Venn Room ask what happens when separate physical interiors overlap through shared virtual environments. A living room can remain physically private while simultaneously functioning as an entry point into a shared digital space. Who has access? Where does privacy begin? What happens when distinct spaces overlap? Virtual architecture does not eliminate these concerns but gives them new conditions.
London Developers Toolkit | image by You+Pea
THE TENANT IN THE VIRTUAL HOUSE
Virtual housing becomes particularly strange when there is not enough of it to go around. In Final Fantasy XIV, housing plots occupy specific locations within residential districts, where houses sit alongside one another and players compete for a limited number of available properties. A home can therefore become attached to a particular place: a street, a neighborhood, and a group of nearby players. Its location matters, and so does the possibility of losing it. The housing system is designed to return unused plots to the market, meaning that a player’s relationship to their home is never entirely secure. Keeping a house also depends on conditions outside the game itself. Players need access to the game, an internet connection, and enough time to log in and maintain their property. When real-world emergencies disrupt those conditions, the consequences can extend into the game, which is why Square Enix has suspended housing demolition during certain crises. It is an odd version of homeownership. Players can spend months furnishing a house and shaping it around their habits, while knowing that the land beneath it belongs to the game and that the rules governing it can change without their involvement. The house may feel personal, but the terms of staying there are set elsewhere.
PlayStation Home offers a different version of the same problem. Sony’s social virtual world, which operated from 2008 to 2015, gave users apartments and shared spaces where they could decorate interiors, collect objects, and meet other players. Like many online worlds, it encouraged people to spend time and money building environments that were meant to become familiar. Then the service closed. With the shutdown came the loss of access to the spaces that depended on it. Apartments, interiors, and social hubs could no longer be entered in the way they had during the operation of the platform, leaving behind screenshots, videos, files, and memories of spaces that had once been part of people’s everyday online lives. When an online world shuts down, its spaces can become inaccessible. Fan communities have tried to preserve some of these lost worlds by collecting files, screenshots, and recordings. What remains is often only fragments of places that people once built, visited, and called their own.
Final Fantasy XIV housing neighborhood
can a corporate server be a home?
Across these worlds, a different way of thinking about architecture starts to take shape. In The Sims, a floor plan affects how characters move through and use a house. In Minecraft, the same building tools can produce a temporary shelter, an elaborate home, or a model of a public square. Animal Crossing turns an empty island into a place shaped by routines, collecting, decoration, and social life, while social VR brings the physical body into an even closer relationship with digital space.
Taken together, these examples show how many different forms dwelling can take in a digital environment. It can involve building a shelter before nightfall, arranging a room around everyday routines, competing for a place in a virtual neighborhood, or adapting a physical bedroom to sleep alongside someone who is elsewhere. The spaces and technologies differ, but each example complicates the idea that a virtual world is simply somewhere to visit.

Israeli-made film about Gaza gets 25-minute ovation in Venice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:35:12 UTC

Breadcrumb
Israeli-made film about Gaza gets 25-minute ovation at Venice premiere
A chilling new documentary about Israel's AI-powered mass killing of civilians in Gaza from two Oscar-winning Israeli filmmakers received a 25-minute ovation at its premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Thursday.
The audience clapped continuously for Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor after the screening, an AFP reporter witnessed, setting what is thought to be a new record in Venice after a 23-minute ovation for another film about Gaza last year.
In their film "NAZA", Abraham and Szor used conversations with 24 different Israeli military or intelligence whistleblowers who spoke on condition that their identities be protected.
"We are letting the soldiers and the officers speak about what they did," Abraham told AFP.
"The goal was very simple: we wanted to hear in as much detail as possible, how the systems of killing in Gaza looked like, how they operated."
The 80-minute film left many audience members stunned, with interviewees describing how they felt like they worked in a killing "factory" or a lethal video game.
"NAZA" draws its name from a euphemism used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that are expected to be killed in an airstrike.
It was described as an "urgent, gut-punch" by film magazine Screen, while The Hollywood Reporter said it inspired "outrage...indignity as well. Most certainly disgust, on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime".
Israel's bombardment of Gaza has killed more than 73,600 Palestinians and wounded over 174,500 others since October 2023, according to Gaza's health ministry, whose figures the United Nations deems reliable.
First-person testimony
The men and women featured in "NAZA", with their voices and faces digitally altered, detail an AI-powered system known as "Lavender" that was used to identify people for assassination.
"It was done on a mass scale, like a factory," one says, filmed like all of them at night on a roof terrace with an eerily quiet Tel Aviv as the background.
"Lavender" uses data from the mass surveillance of Gaza, where the entire telecommunications network is monitored by Israel, to identify targets based on their phone calls, movements and interactions.
"The systems parameters are so complex, it's hard to understand," one interviewee, who said he worked on the system, told the filmmakers.
Others describe the systematic destruction of civilian homes, the disregard for war and humanitarian laws, and a "general atmosphere" of "hatred" towards Palestinians.
"It's like a video game because everything is done remotely," one interviewee involved in identifying targets says at one point.
Another describes it as "insanely fun".
Gaza films
The result of a nearly three-year investigation, "NAZA" is the only documentary in competition at this year's Venice Film Festival, which wraps up on Saturday.
Along with Palestinian peers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, Abraham and Szor won an Oscar in 2025 for their film "No Other Land" about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
Their latest movie has been produced by Britain's Jim Wilson with help from Jonathan Glazer -- the team behind Auschwitz-set Oscar winner "The Zone of Interest" -- as well as Britain's Guardian newspaper.
The war in Gaza retains broad Israeli public support, but Abraham and Szor said they hoped it would encourage Western nations to drop their backing for Israel and apply pressure through sanctions.
"Those of us inside Israel and Palestine trying to fight for change, need it," Abraham told AFP. "You are weakening the people inside who are supporting human rights and a political solution by refusing to act."
Israel denies deliberately targeting civilians in Gaza, accusing Hamas of hiding among the population of the densely packed and besieged enclave where around two million people lived before the war. The Palestinian group rejects these claims.
Last year, "The Voice of Hind Rajab", a docu-drama about the killing of a five-year-old Palestinian girl by Israeli forces, picked up second prize at the festival after receiving a 23-minute standing ovation at its premiere.
Increasing numbers of top entertainment figures are openly criticising the far-right Israeli government, as part of a shift in public opinion in Western countries against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies.
Foreign journalists have been prevented from reporting from Gaza since the start of the conflict, except under tightly controlled conditions with the Israeli military.

Russia calls on West to abandon intent to renew sanctions against Iran — envoy to UN

UNITED NATIONS, September 10. /TASS/. Russia will continue to uphold the need for the UN Security Council to comply with decisions terminating resolutions on Iranian sanctions, and calls on the West to abandon attempts to renew them, Russia's Permanent Representative to the UN, Vasily Nebenzya, has stated.
"Russia will continue to uphold the integrity and the need for strict compliance with previously adopted Security Council decisions on the termination of resolutions on the Iranian issue. We call on our Western colleagues to abandon their unlawful intention to achieve their restoration and to stop hindering the normal functioning of the Council, primarily within the framework of its legitimate subsidiary bodies," the diplomat said at a UN Security Council meeting.
The permanent representative noted that Russia "will continue to obstruct attempts to revive Committee 1737" on sanctions regarding Iran's nuclear program.
Russia, together with China, opposed holding the meeting and put the issue to a vote. Eleven members of the Security Council voted in favor of holding it, Russia and China voted against, and Pakistan and Somalia abstained. Voting in the Security Council on the agenda is procedural and does not provide for the right of veto of permanent members. Given the voting results, the agenda was approved.

Germany expels more than 150 Russian diplomats and their family members following sabotage in Leipzig
Kyiv • UNN
After a drone attack at Leipzig Airport, Berlin is closing Russian institutions and expelling more than 150 diplomats and their family members. Moscow denies the allegations.
More than 150 employees of Russian missions and members of their families must leave Germany after Berlin held Russia responsible for the drone incident at Leipzig Airport. This was stated by the Embassy of the Russian Federation in Germany, The Moscow Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
The decision is related to the closure of Russia's Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. The Russian Embassy expressed outrage at the actions of the German authorities and said that more than 150 employees of Russian missions and members of their families must leave the country within a short period of time.
No evidence, no arguments, only the usual "highly likely" reasoning and an unprecedentedly inadequate reaction
Sabotage at Leipzig Airport
At the beginning of August, several drones carrying explosives were discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport. One of them was located near a Ukrainian military transport aircraft, while another was found not far from the airport.
Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt later stated that those behind the "hybrid attack" had acted on the orders of Russian state structures. After this, Berlin decided to close the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in the capital.
In response, Moscow announced the closure of the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg by September 18. The branches of the Goethe-Institut in Russia are also to cease operations.

Anthropic disrupts Russian, Chinese AI campaigns targeting its Claude models
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:26:03 UTC
05:26:03 KST

Anthropic disrupts Russian, Chinese AI campaigns targeting its Claude models
- Anthropic disrupted multiple AI-driven cyberattacks over eight months, including a Russia-linked espionage campaign and Chinese firms trying to copy its Claude model's capabilities.
- Chinese companies like Alibaba, Moonshot, DeepSeek, and Xiaomi were accused of extracting Claude’s AI through massive fraudulent activities and using AI to train their own models.
- A Russian hacking group, Midnight Blizzard, used AI extensively in phishing and malware evasion against Ukrainian targets, showing AI's growing role in complex cyberattacks.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Anthropic on Sept 10 said it had disrupted several alleged malicious uses of its Claude models over the past eight months, including a suspected Russia-linked cyber espionage campaign and efforts by Chinese AI firms it accused of trying to extract and replicate Claude’s capabilities.
Cybercriminals and state-backed hackers were increasingly using AI not just to assist with tasks but to orchestrate and execute large portions of cyberattacks, Anthropic said in its latest Threat Intelligence report, adding that humans were often overseers rather than hands-on operators in the campaigns.
“A majority of the operations... were enabled by AI via direct execution or orchestration. The use of AI went beyond simple questions and responses from a chatbot but rather involved the use of multi-agent frameworks executing” tasks, Anthropic said.
Anthropic said it had disrupted what it described as attacks from seven China-based laboratories during that period.
Among the labs Anthropic named were tech giant Alibaba, Moonshot, DeepSeek and Xiaomi.
Operators it linked to Alibaba ran what Anthropic called the largest “illicit distillation” attack, allegedly aimed at extracting capabilities of Claude models and using them to improve the Chinese tech firm’s Qwen models, the company said.
Anthropic said it observed more than 151 million exchanges it attributed to Alibaba between May and July 2026, peaking at nearly three million a day from more than 3,500 accounts it described as fraudulent.
Distillation refers to the process of training smaller AI models using output from larger, more expensive models in a bid to lower the costs of training a new AI tool.
Rather than running bulk queries, Kimi chatbot creator Moonshot and DeepSeek allegedly routed live customer conversations, which sometimes included sensitive information, through Claude and used its responses as training data, Anthropic alleged.
A hacking group whose tradecraft was consistent with Russia-based threat actor Midnight Blizzard allegedly ran phishing, hotel Wi-Fi hijacking and WhatsApp-takeover operations against Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic targets, using AI at nearly every stage, Anthropic said.
The group allegedly used AI to build a system that automatically detected when its malware was flagged by security defences and rewrote the code until it evaded detection again.
Anthropic also identified what it called “new categories of threat actors” misusing Claude, including those using the platform to “develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs, and other munitions, as well as the targeting and control systems that operate them.”
The report detailed incidents of operators using Claude to develop software for weapons design and development, or to support intelligence gathering and procurement related to weapons programs, in China, Russia, and Yemen.
The company said that it detected and disrupted activity linked to affiliates of the ShinyHunters cybercrime collective, one of the most prolific cybercrime enterprises in recent months linked to attacks on major corporations around the world.
Jacob Klein, head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, said in an interview that models have become more capable over the last year, raising new risks.
“A year ago, let’s say you wanted to optimize a drone or optimize the software on a missile, the models just wouldn’t be as good at that task as they are now,” he said. REUTERS

Israel says it destroyed Hezbollah underground complex at Lebanon's Ali al-Taher
Unknown

Israel says it destroyed Hezbollah underground complex at Lebanon's Ali al-Taher
Sept 10 - The Israeli military destroyed Hezbollah underground infrastructure at the Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Thursday, adding that the operation completed the consolidation of a security zone in the area.
Israeli forces would remain in the area to prevent the Iran-aligned Hezbollah militant group from re-establishing its presence and rebuilding its capabilities, the two officials said in a joint statement.
The Ali al-Taher ridge, about 15 km (10 miles) from the Israeli border, has become one of the most contested areas of the war between Israel and Hezbollah. Hezbollah is believed to have built an underground command centre and weapons stores there, according to Lebanese security sources who spoke to Reuters in July.
Lebanon's state news agency NNA said the Israeli military carried out a powerful blast at the ridge, with tremors and the sound of the explosion felt across Nabatieh and surrounding areas.
The Israeli military said its forces had established "operational control" over the ridge, both above and below ground, before dismantling the infrastructure. The network extended for more than 2 km (1.24 miles) and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and drones, as well as anti-tank missiles, mines and explosive devices, it said.
The military said a central command complex belonging to Hezbollah's Badr unit was located within the underground infrastructure. The complex contained command centres, weapons storage rooms and living quarters that allowed fighters to remain underground for extended periods, it said.
Israel has pushed into southern Lebanon and seized several strategic positions since the conflict erupted on March 2.
The ridge has been one of Israel's main operational focuses and lies within an expanded, self-declared Israeli buffer zone in southern Lebanon.
A U.S.-brokered framework agreed after a June ceasefire called for Israeli forces to gradually withdraw from southern Lebanon while Lebanese troops disarm Hezbollah. The process has stalled, however, with Hezbollah refusing to give up its weapons and Israel saying it will not withdraw until the group disarms. REUTERS

Report: More than 100 US military personnel operating in Saudi Arabia, helping select Houthi targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:25:41 UTC
05:25:41 KST

More than 100 US military personnel are operating in Saudi Arabia, helping its military to select Houthi targets. 
They are part of a joint command center established in recent weeks, to  provide intelligence and real-time information, but they do not participate directly in strikes, CNN reported, citing five sources familiar with the operations. The U.S. forces also are not providing the kind of operational assistance they did in the past.
The US has helped Saudi Arabia use a targeting tool allowing  military officers to see in real-time what is happening on the battlefield, one US official told CNN.
The joint command was established after U.S. intelligence indicated that there are currently hundreds of Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps officers in Yemen, working alongside the Houthis with goal of ultimately shutting down the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, a key global chokepoint between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea in the Horn of Africa.
The Houthis on Thursday seized Perim Island, a tiny but potentially crucial position at the narrowest point of the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait. Houthi forces also have reached several other strategically important islands nearby, according to reports.
Bab al-Mandab links the Indian Ocean and Asia to the Red Sea, Suez Canal and Europe, making it a critical artery for global trade. Its importance has increased further since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz after its war with the United States began in late February.
The Houthi activity comes days after the Iran-backed group launched a major missile and drone attack against oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia. Riyadh reported at least 73 people wounded and several energy facilities damaged and temporarily knocked out of operation.
Saudi Arabia has responded with extensive airstrikes across Yemen in support of government forces. Houthi officials claimed Riyadh carried out around 40 strikes on Thursday morning alone in areas including Taiz, Hodeidah, Al-Jawf and Marib.
The escalation has effectively ended a four-year period of relative calm between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.

August 2026 Was the Hottest Month Ever Recorded: Copernicus Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:20:23 UTC
05:20:23 KST

August was the planet’s hottest month ever recorded, capping a remarkably grim summer of heat records. With El Niño strengthening—and climate change continuing to heat things up—more records are likely in store well into next year.
Data from Copernicus, the European Union’s climate agency, shows that last month tied with July 2023 for Earth’s hottest month. (July is also usually the hottest month of the year.) This July also tied with July 2024 for the second-hottest July on record, while June 2026 was the second-hottest June ever recorded. The news comes on the heels of a separate announcement on Wednesday from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which declared this was the hottest summer for the US, beating a previous record set during the Dust Bowl.
The sweltering summer is a grim sign of how burning fossil fuels is pushing temperatures up around the globe while unleashing more intense and longer heat waves.
“August 2026 was a remarkable month in the global climate record,” Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, said in a statement. “Combined with record global sea surface temperatures and the warmest summer on record for Western Europe, these observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans. The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies, and ecosystems across the world.”
The global average temperature for August was 1.65 degrees Celsius (3 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial average, according to Copernicus. While it was hot globally this summer, the impacts played out with dangerous and sometimes deadly results locally.
Researchers estimate that as many as 35,000 people died during heat waves in Germany, France, and Spain this summer. Record-breaking fires also raged across parts of Europe, unleashing the first documented fire cloud in France and threatening a key NASA observatory in Spain. In North America, wildfires in Canada and northern parts of the US filled areas across the Northeast with smoke.
Climate change has boosted background temperatures, but the El Niño roiling the eastern Pacific Ocean has piled on more heat. El Niños usually coincide with a temporary uptick in global temperature from 0.1 to 0.2 degrees Celsius. This year’s El Niño is forecast to reach record strength and upend weather around the globe. But the full impact on the planet’s temperature won’t be felt until next year, meaning that next summer may be even hotter than the one we just lived through.
Climate scientists have warned that the world needs to prevent long-term average warming from breaching 1.5 degrees Celsius to avoid the worst impacts of climate change. While temperatures above the threshold for a single month don’t represent a permanent breach of this temperature, they’re a sign that the world is getting closer to this benchmark.
Earlier this month, the UN warned in a report that the world is likely to cross the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold in a few years. To slow and eventually reverse the rise in global temperatures, the world needs to stop burning fossil fuels and lower carbon emissions.
“This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires, and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead,” UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres said in a statement. “We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition.”

AI Should Be a Wake-Up Call For Universities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:17:31 UTC
05:17:31 KST

The debate over how AI will impact higher education has narrowed into a single and well-worn groove: in a world where machines can think, how do we make sure students still learn to think?
This is an important question, but this debate is based on a faulty assumption that the only purpose of college is to develop intelligence. Missing from the debate are the unique human qualities that really do define us, such as curiosity, the search for meaning, and inner growth. These aren’t extracurriculars—they’re a core part of what true education is about.
Universities are now forced to ask what should define higher education: information or formation?
The word “education” descends from the Latin educare—to nourish, to bring out. Education, at its root, was never only about filling a mind with information. It was about drawing out and nourishing all the unique qualities that define us.
From their medieval origins, universities understood their mission as being the formation of the whole person, what 13th-century theologian Thomas Aquinas called capax universi. But over the years, the ambition of the university has been narrowed, and the most essential questions about the meaning of life have been expelled from the classroom.
Some see AI as a threat to be managed. I would counter that it is precipitating a pivotal opportunity to reinvent higher education and embrace the broader scope it once had.
Curiosity
When we have a technology that can give instant answers to any question, the questions take on more importance. We’re born naturally curious. As Aristotle put it, “all men by nature desire to know.” One study found that pre-school children ask about 100 questions a day. But that plummets as they get older, roughly disappearing by middle school.
Even though curiosity is one of our defining qualities—and one that AI can’t replicate—it’s an aptitude that grows the more we use it. The point isn’t just in seeking answers, but in seeking growth and expansion. Curiosity is the precursor to both questions and the wisdom that follows.
With AI, the danger is not just outsourcing the task of finding answers but in generating the questions altogether. The friction of sitting with mystery, puzzling through ambiguity and complexity, can be waved away with a prompt. Offloading cognition can lead to offloading the appetite for wonder.
In the age of AI, the capacity not just to ask questions but to want to ask questions is a core skill to teach. So how could a university do that? One way: make question-asking, instead of answer-giving, the explicit goal of a course. It could be a first-year seminar built entirely around inquiry. The students could be graded on the quality of the questions they learn to pose—not the answers.
Another: a "follow the question" requirement, which is the converse of a thesis. Here, students could choose a question when they arrive at campus and pursue it across all their time at the university. These should be big, open-ended questions. Why is there suffering? What is beauty? What makes for a good life? Students could examine the question through the different lenses of their different courses: through science, art, literature, etc. There’s no final answer, but rather an accounting of how the question deepened, or changed, or impacted the student’s thinking and growth.
Meaning and purpose
To help students find the meaning and purpose they’re seeking as they come into university life, it is essential that schools support students' desire to define meaning.
This is the opportunity AI presents universities with: to meet the longing of students who arrive on campus hungry for meaning, purpose, and something larger than themselves—and at the very moment in their lives when it matters most.
One way to do this is to build meaning and purpose into the vocational core. In a study by Stanford’s William Damon, he found that over half of the students were in college to find purpose, not just to be trained to make a living. And yet he also found that most colleges weren’t providing resources to help students find their purpose. So career advising could be reframed around purpose and calling—not just credentials and salary. Damon recommends hands-on learning, often through volunteering that connects students’ passions to the real world, and providing mentors or “spark coaches.”
Inner growth
Meanwhile, AI is increasingly capable of recursive self-improvement. But what about nurturing that same impulse in humans, and instilling in students the skill of continuous self-improvement and inner growth?
To do this, universities could add a “capstone of the self” alongside a thesis. In addition to a traditional capstone project, schools should give seniors a chance to produce a reflective synthesis of who they’ve become and who they want to be—an examined-life portfolio. It recognizes inner development as an essential outcome of a degree and gives students the opportunity to make sense of their years of growth and to have more clarity about what really matters.
Reclaiming the mission of the university isn’t about going back to the past—it’s about connecting to what’s always been there in order to go forward. To educate has always been about nourishing the whole person, not just the intellect.

US slaps new sanctions on networks 'aiding Iran's proxies in Middle East'
The U.S. government announced new sanctions on Thursday against firms and individuals that it says are aiding Hezbollah and other Iranian proxies in the Middle East as it intensified its campaign to isolate Iran economically.
The latest sanctions are part of the Treasury Department's "Operation Economic Outcast," first announced 24 August, which aim to cut off the revenues that Tehran is using to fund the war, build missiles, conduct cyberattacks and support the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
Thursday's actions by Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control hit entities and individuals in Iraq, Lebanon and Turkey that Washington said supported Kataeb Hezbollah, an Iraqi Shia paramilitary group under the command of the IRGC, and Hezbollah, a Lebanese Shia party, the Treasury said in a statement.
The Treasury also announced a settlement with a U.S. citizen who agreed to pay $1.43 million to settle their potential civil liability for 39 apparent violations of sanctions on Iran, and issued a broad whistleblower appeal for tips on any sanctions evasion or money laundering by Iran.
OFAC also issued a bulletin making clear that it would deny most Iran-related licensing requests, except in exceptional circumstances, and said its licensing division had immediately begun denying "the vast majority" of outstanding Iran-related specific license requests.
"OFAC will maintain this licensing policy until Iran changes its behaviour, including obstructing the Strait of Hormuz, attacking U.S. personnel and partners in the Gulf, and pursuing nuclear and conventional weapons," Treasury said.
“Operation Economic Outcast is targeting those who continue to stand with the failing Iranian regime,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Whether they finance terror, launder money, or help Iran evade sanctions, we will find them, cut them off from the U.S. financial system, and dismantle the networks keeping the regime afloat.”

Details
Joining would give Ukraine access to the European Union’s secure satellite communications, intended primarily for governmental and security needs. In the future, this would also enable Ukrainian and European military personnel to use a joint secure communications system.
Ukraine may be connected to IRIS²

The start of the negotiations opens the way for Ukraine’s integration into the European infrastructure of secure satellite communications. The parties still have to agree on the final terms and timeline for joining.

Meta tests out putting fact-checking in users’ hands across Latin America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:11:31 UTC
05:11:31 KST

Meta tests out putting fact-checking in users’ hands across Latin America
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
Meta is expanding its shift away from professional fact-checking. The tech giant announced it's trialling it's crowdsourced "Community Notes" system across 16 countries in Latin America. Meta says the system will only fully roll out once it is confident it works, but critics warn that with misinformation, manipulated images and AI-generated content spreading rapidly, crowdsourced checks may come too late to prevent false claims from reaching millions. Vedika Bahl explains the risks.
The list covers Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay and Venezuela.
The move is part of Meta’s wider effort to replace its network of professional fact-checking partners with a system that puts more responsibility for identifying misleading content in the hands of its users.
The company began recruiting contributors in the region on Wednesday. But during the initial testing phase, Community Notes will not be visible to the wider public.
Meta has not given a timeline for a full rollout, saying it will expand the system once it is confident it works effectively.
So, what are Community Notes?
It's inspired by the model first introduced by Elon Musk on X, formerly Twitter.
Instead of professional fact-checkers reviewing posts and adding corrections, Community Notes allows participating users to suggest notes that provide additional context or challenge potentially misleading information.
Other contributors then rate those notes. They are designed to appear only when there is broad agreement among contributors with different viewpoints.
Meta says the approach is intended to provide context without allowing a small group of professional fact-checkers to decide which posts should be flagged or what a correction should say.
Mark Zuckerberg announced the end of Meta’s US professional fact-checking programme in January 2025, replacing it with Community Notes. The decision came just days before Donald Trump returned to the White House and was presented by Zuckerberg as a move towards greater free speech.
But can Community Notes reallu replace professional fact-checking?
The sheer volume of false claims and misleading images posted every day make this difficult for Community Notes to be enough. There are millions or billions of posts per day and there’s nowhere near enough contributors to review all this content.
Community Notes also take time to contribute, which is less likely from day-to-day users rather than professional fact-checkers. Notes rely on users volunteering their time to identify problematic content, write corrections and then assess notes submitted by others, and corrections often only appear after misleading content has already been widely viewed and shared.
The International Fact-Checking Network has criticised Meta’s decision, arguing that Community Notes alone cannot do enough to tackle harmful misinformation at the scale of Meta’s platforms.
The timing of the Latin American rollout has also raised concerns.
The region has experienced a string of closely contested elections in recent years, while politicians have increasingly relied on social media to reach voters. Some have also been accused of deploying coordinated disinformation networks to create the appearance of support.
Meta’s own Oversight Board, the semi-independent body that reviews some of the company’s content-moderation decisions, has urged Meta not to treat Community Notes as a direct replacement for professional fact-checking.

The US Supreme Court is currently weighing a similar request.
At issue are a set of finalised rules released by the US Postal Service (USPS) in late August that would place new requirements on mail-in balloting.
The rules direct states to redesign mail-in ballots to include unique barcodes that can be scanned, so that the federal government may track them.
States would also be required to submit a list of voters slated to receive ballots by mail. The Postal Service would retain the right to “not transmit mail-in or absentee ballots” if the mail-outs do not comply with the new standards or if the voters in question do not appear on the submitted lists.
The case heard on Thursday involved a coalition of voting rights advocacy groups, including the League of Women Voters.
They argued that the new rules, championed by Trump, a Republican, would effectively disenfranchise certain voters who rely on mail-in ballots.
But the Trump administration has argued that the rules are necessary to ensure election security.
In asking the appeals court to lift the injunction, the US Department of Justice argued that the plaintiffs’ case appeared to be based on an unfounded premise that Postal Service intends to seize control of election administration.
It emphasised that state election officials would retain full control over who is permitted to vote by mail and that the Postal Service’s role would be limited to ensuring that envelopes for the mail-in ballots comply with the “modest” new design requirements.
The appeals court, however, denied the Trump administration’s motion to dismiss the injunction, citing the potential for confusion ahead of the midterm vote.
It also affirmed parts of the lower-court ruling, issued by US District Judge Indira Talwani, an appointee of Democratic President Barack Obama.
“The district court made detailed findings about the chaos and widespread disenfranchisement that would occur between now and November 3 should the Final Rule take immediate effect,” the appeals court said in Thursday’s decision.
It cited issues including that “it would be impossible for some States to reprint compliant envelopes” and that the Postal Service would face the “herculean task” of scanning “tens of millions of ballot envelopes” using a digital portal that is not yet functional.
“There is no countervailing record evidence disputing the district court’s findings on these points,” the appeals court added.
Under the US Constitution, election administration falls to the states. But Trump has pushed for greater voting restrictions ahead of the pivotal midterms, in an effort to combat alleged election fraud.
Critics, however, have framed his actions as an effort to sway the outcome. Currently, Trump’s Republican Party holds majorities in both chambers of Congress. But with Trump facing drooping poll numbers, Democrats are seeking to flip Congress to their control.
All 50 US states allow for some form of mail-in voting. Twenty-nine states allow voters to ask to cast ballots by mail without providing a reason, and eight conduct their elections entirely by mail.
The legal battle over the mail-in ballots has stretched on for weeks, creating uncertainty ahead of the vote.
In addition to the voting advocacy groups challenging the new rules, a group of 24 states, plus the District of Columbia, have also filed a lawsuit.
Last month, the US Supreme Court lifted an earlier injunction issued by Judge Talwani blocking the rules from taking effect.
The Trump administration last week once again made an emergency petition to the high court to intervene and pause Talwani’s ruling.
The new rules came after Trump issued an executive order in March calling for tighter rules to govern voting by mail.
Trump has also repeatedly pushed the false claim that his defeat in the 2020 presidential election was the result of widespread voter fraud.
An anonymous whistleblower statement released on September 1 by Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal alleged that the Postal Service had rushed to implement the new rules, but that the result was a faulty system that risks disrupting the delivery of mail-in ballots.

Man jailed after threatening to kill son's teacher in French village
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
21:10:51 BST

Man jailed after threatening to behead son's teacher in French village
- Published
A man has been given a six-month jail term in France after he threatened to behead a female primary school teacher who had disciplined his son at a village primary school.
The 47-year-old was sentenced after a fast-track hearing on Thursday, six days after the events unfolded in Le Fauga, a village with a population of about 2,600 just outside the southwestern city of Toulouse.
The teacher has been granted official protection and has gone on sick leave.
French Education Minister Edouard Geffray said: "No teacher should be afraid to do their job. Attacking one of them is attacking the entire institution."
Over the summer, Geffray steered through a law aimed at protecting staff from a "significant risk" to their safety or health from a member of a student's family.
The minister said this case would trigger one of the first uses of the decree.
The case revives terrible memories in France of the beheading of a teacher in the Paris suburb of Conflans-Sainte-Honorine six years ago. Samuel Paty was murdered in a jihadist attack outside his school by an 18-year-old Chechen refugee.
In Le Fauga, the teacher's colleagues did not go into work on Monday because of what had happened the previous Friday.
The threat was made after the man had been called in for a chat with the school, according to Toulouse education chief Karim Benmiloud.
Le Fauga Mayor Jean-Marie Puig told BFMTV that the man's son had been disruptive in class and he had been sent to another class to calm down.
The child continued to misbehave in the second classroom and the teacher later told him off for acting up.
The teacher was later threatened by the father, who according to the mayor had waited for her "outside the school and apparently threatened to cut off her head if she'd been a man".
The parent subsequently apologised, however a judicial complaint was made and he went before a judge in Toulouse on Thursday afternoon.
According to French reports from the court in Toulouse, the judge told the man that such remarks were disturbing, particularly in light of the Samuel Paty case, "which remains fresh in the minds of all French people".
The Toulouse prosecutor had asked for a period of six months' house arrest, however the judge said the man should serve the time in jail because of the seriousness of his actions.
"I'm really not proud of myself," the man said, according to the prosecutor's team.
The sentence also requires him to undergo a citizenship course and avoid contacting the victim or approaching the school.
The decree passed in July allows for a student to be transferred to another school in a case involving significant risk to staff, and where education authorities have intervened.
It is thought the boy and a younger sister may now be moved to another school outside Le Fauga.
The teacher involved, who is in her 50s, is said to be very shocked by the threat.

Morocco says not involved in Ceuta migrant influx
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:05:16 UTC
05:05:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Morocco says not involved in Ceuta migrant influx
Morocco said on Thursday there were "no facts" establishing its involvement in the massive migrant rush into Spain's North African exclave of Ceuta in July.
More than 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta from Morocco on 30 and 31 July in an unprecedented, chaotic surge that left scores dead and sparked European Union infighting over the touchy issue of migration.
The Moroccan foreign ministry said there were "no facts or reports proving any involvement by the Moroccan authorities".
The ministry added that Rabat refused to become the "scapegoat for political score-settling" in Spain.
The statement marked the kingdom's first official reaction to a Spanish police report accusing Morocco's security forces of "total permissiveness" when the mass crossing took place.
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has consistently avoided blaming Morocco, noting that there was no "solid proof" that the North African country orchestrated the migrant rush.
On Wednesday, Spain declassified intelligence reports that had warned of potential "mass entries" by migrants into Ceuta just before the incident happened.
A declassified military intelligence document on 30 July states that it is "highly likely that the Moroccan authorities are not actively encouraging the migratory wave, but have so far acted in a negligent and passive manner".
But Sanchez on Wednesday said on X that with the information available "no one could have foreseen the migration crisis that unfolded".
Morocco's foreign ministry instead questioned Spain's handling of the crisis.
"Why are illegal migrants not being turned back when the Moroccan government has officially agreed to readmit them?" the statement said.
"Why are unaccompanied minors being kept away from their families when Morocco has urgently requested their return?"
"The answer to these questions is not to be found in Morocco, but rather with the relevant Spanish stakeholders," the ministry said.
Still, Rabat called the crisis "regrettable" and said the events warranted "a thorough examination" to establish their circumstances and "ensure that they do not happen again".
The ministry also stressed the importance of ties with Madrid, saying Morocco had chosen to pursue relations based on "good neighbourliness, political understanding, economic partnership, and security cooperation".
Morocco also noted that Spain was its leading economic partner.
Most of the migrants who entered Ceuta have returned to Morocco, but thousands have remained in often dire living conditions, increasing tensions in the small city and causing a political storm for the government.
The EU on Wednesday said it was granting Spain 115 million euros ($130 million) in emergency aid to help bolster border security and assist returns.

====================================================================================================

Researchers tracked 43,000 women for 14 years. Here’s what happened to their political views as gender equality improved.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:00:13 UTC
05:00:13 KST

People who champion social equality are often the loudest critics of the political status quo. A new study finds that as nations actually achieve greater gender parity, these egalitarian individuals become much more likely to defend the very political systems they once criticized. The research, published in the journal Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, shows how shifting social realities can alter deep-seated psychological motives.
After World War II, democratic societies began adopting formal legal frameworks designed to guarantee gender equality. These structural changes eventually sparked a slow but steady cultural shift toward more egalitarian attitudes across the globe. Psychologists define system justification as the human tendency to defend and rationalize the existing social or political order. Historically, researchers linked this tendency to anti-egalitarian beliefs.
People who preferred strict social hierarchies generally defended the political establishment to maintain their dominant position in society. In contrast, people with egalitarian views typically criticized the establishment in hopes of dismantling those hierarchies. Social dominance theory has guided psychological research on prejudice for decades. It proposes that human societies naturally form group-based hierarchies, but individuals vary in how much they support this structure.
Researchers have documented how a preference for hierarchy predicts prejudice against minority groups and opposition to affirmative action. Conversely, individuals who favor equality actively scan their environments for signs of unfairness and work to dismantle power imbalances. For a long time, researchers viewed these egalitarian individuals as permanent critics of the status quo. Psychologists assumed that the drive to achieve equality inherently required a person to challenge the institutions around them.
Yet, recent studies show that egalitarian people are highly accurate at detecting when inequality is actually absent. This raised a new question for psychologists. If a society successfully implements equal rights, egalitarians might logically shift from criticizing the system to defending it. Sarah Buhl, a psychologist at Chemnitz University of Technology in Germany, led a research team to test this idea in a real-world setting.
Buhl and her colleagues focused on New Zealand. Over the past decade and a half, the country has achieved high levels of gender equality, including reaching gender parity in its parliament. The researchers wanted to see if this measurable increase in societal fairness altered how women viewed the political establishment.
The researchers analyzed fourteen years of survey responses from 43,924 women who participated in the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study between 2009 and 2023. The surveys asked participants to rate their agreement with statements supporting group-based hierarchies, which measured their level of egalitarianism. The surveys also asked participants how much they believed the national political system operated as it should, providing a measure of system justification.
To track objective changes in societal fairness, the team paired these survey responses with the country’s annual score on the Global Gender Gap Index. This index measures national parity in areas like economic participation, political empowerment, health, and education. By tracking the same women over time using a statistical technique called multi-level modeling, the researchers could observe how individual beliefs shifted in tandem with national progress.
In the earlier years of the study, when gender inequality was relatively high, the results aligned with traditional psychological expectations. Women who held anti-egalitarian views strongly defended the political system. Meanwhile, women with egalitarian views were highly critical of the establishment.
As New Zealand became more gender-equal over the fourteen-year period, this dynamic shifted. The overall population became more egalitarian. At the same time, the most egalitarian women grew less critical of the political status quo.
Because the establishment was increasingly reflecting their own values, these women began to legitimize the socio-political system. The research team used specialized statistical tests to ensure the timeline of these changes made sense. They confirmed that shifts in national gender equality preceded the changes in how women justified the system.
The research team also broke the data down by demographic groups to see if the benefits of gender equality were felt universally. They compared the responses of women from majoritized backgrounds, defined in this study as white and heterosexual, to women from minoritized backgrounds. Minoritized groups included ethnic minorities and non-heterosexual women.
The shift in system defense was driven entirely by majoritized women. As national gender equality rose, egalitarian women from majority groups became more supportive of the political system. They experienced the direct benefits of these societal changes and adjusted their political views accordingly.
For minoritized women, the rise in national gender equality did not change the relationship between their personal beliefs and their view of the establishment. Egalitarian women from minority groups remained highly critical of the political system regardless of the country’s rising score on the Global Gender Gap Index. These groups often continue to face compounded disadvantages that broad gender parity metrics do not fully capture.
When the researchers analyzed data from male participants in the same national survey, they found a different pattern. The rise in national gender equality did not lead egalitarian men to increasingly defend the system. The research team suspects this is because rising gender equality creates a psychological conflict for men, who traditionally benefit from patriarchal structures. Because men’s group interests do not directly align with dismantling male advantages, their responses to an increasingly equal status quo were more ambiguous.
Because New Zealand is already one of the most socially progressive countries in the world, the actual variation in gender equality over the study period was relatively small. The changes in survey responses, while mathematically robust, were similarly subtle. Testing these ideas in countries undergoing more dramatic social transformations could reveal even stronger shifts in public attitudes.
The Global Gender Gap Index also functions as a broad proxy for fairness. It heavily weighs representation in corporate leadership and national politics, which might not reflect the daily realities of domestic life or unpaid labor. Future studies could explore how the division of household chores or local community dynamics influences a person’s willingness to defend the political system.
Because the data relies on observing natural changes over time, it cannot prove that the rising equality scores directly caused the psychological shifts. Experimental research where participants are exposed to different levels of social progress could help confirm the exact mechanisms at play. Understanding these changes will help psychologists map how human behavior adapts to an increasingly equal world.
The study, “Rebels With(Out) a Cause: The Influence of Gender Inequality on the Relationship Between Egalitarianism and System Justification,” was authored by Sarah Buhl, Danny Osborne, Chris G. Sibley, and Frank Asbrock.
