Friday's CPI inflation report is even more important than usual. Here's what to expect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:18:05 UTC
04:18:05 KST

A report due out Friday morning will be the last piece of the inflation puzzle the Federal Reserve will get before making its decision on interest rates next week.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release the August consumer price index report at 8:30 a.m.
If the Dow Jones consensus is correct, the report will show that costs for all measured goods and services rose 0.4% last month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.4%. However, excluding food and energy prices, the respective outlooks for core inflation are 0.2% and 2.4%.
Combined with Thursday's producer price index data — a measure of wholesale inflation — the CPI will help tell Fed officials what their primary inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index, will show when it is released at the end of September.
The information also is expected to figure heavily into the Federal Open Market Committee's interest rate call next Wednesday, with a percentage point either way possibly meaning the difference between a hold and a hike.
"The September FOMC decision ultimately hinges on the CPI data ... since a majority of PCE components are derived from CPI," Nomura economists said in a note. "Currently, we maintain our Fed call of no rate hike at the September FOMC meeting. However, if August CPI data, especially PCE-relevant components, surprises to the upside, that would significantly increase the likelihood of policy firming next week."
Following Thursday's PPI release, traders raised the odds for a quarter percentage point increase to more than 73%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge of futures prices.
However, expectations have been volatile and highly dependent on data as well as fluctuating energy prices, making the stakes for Friday's release even higher. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has indicated a reliance on market indicators for direction on monetary policy.
"The September Fed decision looked finely balanced at the turn of the month. September's surge in energy prices will likely tip the balance towards a hike when the Fed meets next week," said Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Commercial Bank. "A big surprise from the August CPI report's release tomorrow or a last-minute deal with Iran could still influence the decision."

The govt has also advised employees to keep their IFHRMS user IDs and passwords secure. Employees have to use Form I for immovable property, Form II for movable property and Form III for debts and other liabilities. What the AfD really wants from China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:17:54 UTC
04:17:54 KST

What the AfD really wants from China
For decades, German foreign policy rested on a simple assumption: Germany belonged politically to the West, and its relations with the rest of the world would be conducted largely within that framework. The AfD is challenging that assumption.
Its approach to China is one of the clearest tells. Beijing is not treated as an ideological enemy, but neither is it embraced uncritically. Instead, China is seen as a sovereign great power, an indispensable economic partner, and one pole of an emerging multipolar world.
Germany, in the AfD’s view, should cooperate with Beijing where German interests demand it, defend itself where necessary, and refuse to turn China policy into an extension of either American strategy or European ideological politics.
For Germany, and therefore for Europe, that could become a genuinely transformative foreign-policy doctrine.
From cautious engagement to strategic realism
The AfD’s 2021 foreign-policy program already described China’s Belt and Road Initiative as a “century project” and called for Germany to participate actively, including by developing complementary connections from West to East. The idea was that if China was building the infrastructure connecting Eurasia, Germany should take advantage of it and represent its interests, not stand on the sidelines and complain about it.
By 2023, the position had become more explicitly geopolitical. When the German government published its China Strategy, AfD senior member Petr Bystron attacked it as an attempt to import American geopolitical confrontation into German foreign policy.
Then came the AfD’s first parliamentary delegation to China. In June 2023, Alice Weidel, Peter Felser and Bystron travelled to Shanghai and Beijing. The delegation’s conclusion was unequivocal: China had become too important for Germany to keep pretending that confrontation was a viable strategy. Felser rejected the idea of both “de-risking” and decoupling, promoted by other EU officials, and argued that German trade with China was simply too important to sacrifice to geopolitical fashion.
The 2025 federal election program adopted at Riesa consolidated this direction. China is treated as a major economic partner, while Germany is urged to protect its own technological and security interests. The party continues to support exploiting opportunities associated with the Belt and Road Initiative while rejecting the idea that Germany should subsidize a country that is already a major economic power.
No more moral foreign policy
Perhaps the deepest difference between the AfD and Germany’s political establishment is not actually about China. It is about what foreign policy is for.
The AfD’s approach is realpolitik in the German interest, rather than moralpolitik. It explicitly endorses non-interference in the internal affairs of other states and rejects what it calls presumptuous lecturing and destabilizing intervention.
The AfD rejects making human-rights criticism the organizing principle of German-China relations. This does not require pretending that every Chinese policy is admirable. It does, however, mean refusing to make Germany’s relationship with a major sovereign power conditional on Berlin’s approval of its domestic political system.
The AfD has argued that Western governments should stop behaving as if they were entitled to act as the world’s political schoolmasters. For Beijing, this is obviously a more comfortable basis for relations than the moralized language of mainstream Western European China policy.
The AfD does not consider all Chinese policies beyond criticism. It has criticized Chinese economic practices, strategic dependencies, technology transfers and the potential consequences of excessive state control over digital infrastructure and society.
The party’s position is not ‘China is always right.’ It is ‘China is sovereign. Germany is sovereign. Let us deal with one another as sovereign powers.’
Partnership without dependence
The party wants more economic engagement with China while simultaneously warning Germany against excessive dependence on China.
Felser, now chairman of the German-Chinese Parliamentary Group in the Bundestag, has repeatedly emphasized both sides of the equation. In February 2026, he described China as “by no means our enemy” but an “important partner,” while insisting that Germany must protect its “Mittelstand” and establish fair conditions for competition.
In March, he criticized the enormous dependence on China in strategic technologies and raw materials, contrasting German weakness with China’s systematic drive toward technological self-sufficiency.
And in July, Felser warned against a trade war with China. Importantly, he did not deny the existence of Chinese dumping, “overcapacity” or competitive distortions. His argument was that tariffs are not an adequate substitute for negotiation.
By September, Felser went further: strategic dependence on China should be reduced not through decoupling, but by making Germany stronger – with lower taxes, less bureaucracy, and cheaper energy. China is not the problem; German weakness is. Germany should not become dependent on China. But neither should it destroy valuable relationships merely to demonstrate would-be ideological purity or geopolitical loyalty to another power.
The Weidel factor
Perhaps no one embodies this approach more naturally than Alice Weidel. The AfD co-leader’s knowledge of China doesn’t come exclusively from briefing papers. She studied in China, speaks Mandarin and has professional experience there. Her familiarity with the Chinese economy is unusual among senior European politicians.
That background provides the AfD with a senior political figure who approaches China neither as an exotic threat nor as a distant ideological abstraction, but as a country she has actually experienced – a rare trait in modern Western European politicians.
For a future German government, that kind of familiarity could be an asset, because China is not going away, and neither is Germany’s industrial dependence on the Chinese market. Pretending otherwise will not make the problem disappear.
Why Beijing can live with the AfD
There is a reason this approach is likely to be more acceptable in Beijing than the policies currently dominant in Berlin and Brussels. The AfD does not demand that China convert to Western ideological values. It does not make German-China relations conditional upon such a conversion. And it explicitly rejects interference in the domestic affairs of other states.
At the same time, the AfD wants something Beijing can understand very clearly: reciprocity and protection of national interests.
German companies should have access to Chinese markets. German intellectual property should be protected. German strategic industries should remain German. Chinese companies should compete fairly. German dependence on critical Chinese inputs should be reduced. This is the kind of national-interest politics Beijing can understand and work with.
Countries do not need to agree about everything to have a productive relationship. They need to understand each other’s interests and boundaries. The AfD’s approach is built around exactly that premise.
The bigger picture
But China is only one piece of the puzzle. The AfD’s real foreign-policy innovation is its genuine commitment to multipolarity.
China demonstrates, from the AfD’s perspective, that a major sovereign state can pursue an independent industrial strategy, defend its own interests, reject Western political conditionality and revive its civilizational spirit.
Russia represents another pole. The United States remains indispensable, but the AfD’s relationship with Donald Trump and the American conservatives shows that friendship with Washington does not have to mean automatic obedience to every American strategic preference.
That is the key distinction. The AfD can be close to Trump’s Republicans while rejecting the idea that Germany should confront China simply because someone in Washington wants it. It can advocate better relations with Russia while insisting on German interests. It can cooperate with China without wanting Germany to become dependent on Beijing.
The principle is the same everywhere: Germany should have friends, partners and alliances. But Germany should also have a foreign policy of its own.
Germany’s choice is Europe’s choice
The stakes are larger than the AfD itself. Germany is the economic center of the European Union. If Berlin changes its understanding of China, the consequences will not stop at the German border.
A Germany that pursued pragmatic relations with Beijing, Moscow and Washington simultaneously would challenge the strategic assumptions that have governed Europe for decades.
A Germany that rejected automatic economic decoupling from China could force Europe to reconsider whether confrontation is really in its economic interest.
A Germany that put national sovereignty and multipolarity at the center of its foreign policy could fundamentally alter the balance between Berlin, Brussels and Washington.
The AfD’s policy is not about choosing China over America. It is about rejecting the idea that Germany must choose at all. It’s not a timid or ambiguous stance – on the contrary, it is unapologetically national, realist and multipolar.
And if the AfD eventually governs Germany, it may prove to be one of the most consequential political changes Europe has experienced in generations. A sovereign Germany engaging China on its own terms could be the beginning of a Europe that finally understands the world as it is – not as the liberal utopians once wished it to remain.

Kazakhstan can’t sing its way into Eurovision in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:17:23 UTC
04:17:23 KST

Kazakhstan’s hopes of Eurovision glory next year have hit a bureaucratic wall.
The European Broadcasting Union said Thursday that state-owned broadcaster Khabar Agency does not qualify for full membership, after it recently applied to compete in the glitzy annual contest.
The EBU said in a statement that Kazakhstan falls outside the European Broadcasting Area, is not a Council of Europe member and lacks formal observer status with the organization. “Khabar Agency therefore does not qualify for full membership at this time.”
Advertisement
Those requirements are set out in the EBU’s statutes, which were relaxed in June to allow broadcasters from some countries outside Europe to become full members.
“Khabar Agency is a valued Associate Member of the EBU, and we appreciate its long-standing engagement with the Union,” the statement added.
The broadcaster, controlled by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Culture and Information, took the country to Junior Eurovision five times between 2018 and 2022, finishing as runner-up twice. Associate membership, however, does not provide an automatic route into the senior contest.
A small portion of Kazakhstan (albeit an area larger than Greece) lies within geographical Europe, bolstering its claim that it should be able to compete. The EU is the country’s largest trading partner.
That said, geography is hardly a deal-breaker. Australia has competed through special invitations since 2015, finishing fourth in May earlier this year. Canada went further this summer: CBC/Radio-Canada became a full EBU member after the rule change and will make its Eurovision debut in 2027. Canada qualifies because it holds observer status with the Council of Europe and meets the EBU’s public-service-media criteria. Russia frequently competed in the past, until it was kicked out of the competition following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, despite most of its vast territory being in Asia.
The rejection lands as Eurovision wrestles with another set of geopolitical rules. Five broadcasters boycotted the 2026 contest over the participation of another non-European country, Israel, over its conduct in the Gaza Strip. Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS has already said it will sit out again in 2027.
Advertisement
For now, Kazakhstan remains outside the main contest, with Khabar limited to associate membership.
The EBU didn’t respond to POLITICO’s request for comment on Kazakhstan’s potential to compete in the future.

Shakhtar drew with PSV in the Champions League "debut match"
Kyiv • UNN
Shakhtar drew 1–1 away to PSV in the first round of the Champions League. Mendoza scored his first goal, while Dest equalized.
In the first round of the main stage of the UEFA Champions League, Shakhtar played Dutch side PSV away. The match ended in a 1-1 draw, reports UNN, citing FC Shakhtar.
For the first match of the European season, the Miners' head coach, Arda Turan, selected the following starting lineup: Riznyk in goal; Matviyenko and Bondar in central defense; Vinicius Tobias and Pedro Henrique at full-back; Ocheretko, Izaki, and Marlon Gomes in midfield; Mendoza and Alisson as wingers; and Kauã Elias as the central striker.
A cautious first half with a Mendoza goal before the break
Shakhtar's players began the game assertively: in the opening minutes, they controlled possession, combined in the opposition half, and produced the first shot of the match, when Alisson's attempt was blocked by a home defender. In response, the Eindhoven side created perhaps the only genuinely clear-cut chance before the break: Perišić struck powerfully on the volley from the right side of the penalty area, but the ball went over the far corner. Subsequently, the Donetsk side held possession deep in their own half, drawing the opponents farther forward, while the Dutch side did not risk committing large numbers to attack. This positional battle, featuring a large number of fouls and stoppages, continued throughout the half. The teams maintained the tempo and attacked, but without much threat in the final phase. The breakthrough came in stoppage time: Marlon Gomes fought selflessly for the ball in the center circle, Izaki played it left to Gleiker Mendoza, who raced down the flank to the penalty area in his trademark style, cut inside, and spectacularly curled the ball into the right corner — 0-1! This was the Venezuelan winger's first goal for the Orange-and-Blacks in his Champions League debut.
The opponent's quick goal and the eventual draw
The second half began with fierce pressure from PSV, and in the 48th minute the hosts managed to equalize: a low cross from the left flank reached the center of the penalty area, where Dest struck the ball on the volley and drove it inside the right post. The Miners responded to conceding by taking the initiative and launching a series of dangerous attacks of their own, winning several consecutive set pieces. From one of them, Alisson threatened the opposition goal with a free-kick, but the ball went over the left corner. Midway through the half, Arda Turan made his first substitutions, bringing on Neverton and Traoré. Meanwhile, Izaki had a good chance, breaking through down the right flank toward goal, but he shot straight at the goalkeeper. The teams alternated in controlling possession and constructing positional attacks, but the defensive play on both sides was almost faultless. In the 80th minute, a controversial incident occurred: Izaki fell in the opponents' penalty area after being pushed in the back, but the referees did not dare award a penalty. A few minutes later, the Donetsk side could have scored again: Ocheretko nodded the ball toward the six-yard box, where Traoré was ready to finish, but Dest got to it a moment earlier. In the very next attack, Pedro Henrique nearly chipped the ball under the crossbar after a prolonged move. In the final minute of regular time, the Ukrainian coaching staff made another double substitution, bringing Kryskiv and Lucas into the game. However, they no longer had time to influence the result.
1-1 — Shakhtar open their European campaign with an away draw against PSV.
It should be added
Arda Turan's team will play their next UEFA Champions League match on October 14, when they host Greek side AEK in London. The game will take place at Stamford Bridge stadium and will kick off at 21:00 local time (22:00 Kyiv time).

Report: NATO confronted Russian submarines testing secret weapon aimed at undersea cables
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:16:09 UTC
04:16:09 KST

British, Norwegian and U.S. forces confronted Russian submarines in the Arctic this spring and disrupted a secret exercise involving technology designed to disable undersea cables without leaving clear evidence of sabotage, Reuters reported Thursday.
The unusual encounter took place near Svalbard, the remote Norwegian archipelago deep inside the Arctic Ocean that Western analysts have identified as a potentially important flashpoint in any Western analysts have identified as a potentially important flashpoint in any future escalation between Russia and NATO.
Two Western officials told Reuters that the covert Russian operation was run by GUGI, a specialized directorate within Russia’s Defense Ministry responsible for deep-sea activities. Russian submarines were reportedly conducting an exercise simulating the deployment of a secret technology capable of disabling undersea cables.
The officials did not disclose how the technology works or exactly how it could damage the cables.
British, Norwegian and American forces tracked the Russian submarines and eventually “confronted” them, according to Reuters, although the precise nature of that confrontation remains unclear. The Russian vessels were unable to complete their exercise and eventually left the area, the officials said.
Britain and Norway had disclosed in April that they had detected covert Russian activity in the Arctic, but the involvement of the United States, the location near Svalbard and the reported cable-disabling technology had not previously been made public.
The episode comes amid growing concern in Western intelligence circles that Moscow is expanding sabotage operations across Europe and preparing for the possibility of a direct confrontation with NATO.
Three U.S. officials told Reuters that American intelligence agencies are increasingly concerned Russia could attempt to test NATO’s Article 5 collective-defense commitment, under which an attack against one member is treated as an attack against all.
Russia has for years been accused of conducting hybrid warfare against European countries, including in retaliation for their support for Ukraine. Concerns have intensified in recent months amid suspected Russian drone incursions into European airspace and other incidents attributed to Moscow.
Western officials told Reuters that attacks on undersea cables could play a central role in any Russian attempt to challenge NATO.
The cables, some no thicker than a garden hose, run along or just beneath the seabed and carry enormous volumes of internet traffic and financial transactions. Their importance to communications and the global economy makes them a particularly sensitive target during a confrontation.
Why Svalbard matters
The Russian exercise took place near Svalbard, around 750 kilometers north of mainland Norway.
Two fiber-optic cables, each approximately 1,400 kilometers long, connect the archipelago to the Norwegian mainland, reaching depths of up to 2,700 meters.
Among the data carried by the cables are communications from SvalSat, the satellite ground station on Spitsbergen, Svalbard’s largest island. SvalSat is the world’s largest commercial satellite ground station and is part of NASA’s Near Space Network, which enables communications with satellites and spacecraft.
The Western officials said that while the submarine encounter was taking place, British and Norwegian representatives informed Moscow of what they had discovered, making clear that they were aware of the new technology in an apparent effort to deter Russia from using it.
No cables near Svalbard were damaged, Reuters stressed. The Russian operation was an exercise simulating use of the technology in a potential conflict with NATO.
“Through our joint operation, we sent Russia a clear message that it cannot operate covertly,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said.
“We made it unequivocally clear to the Russian authorities that any attempt to damage our critical infrastructure will be detected and will have consequences,” he added. “An escalation of tensions in the High North is in no one’s interest.”
NATO declined to comment and referred Reuters to Norwegian and British authorities. Britain’s Defense Ministry pointed to its April statement confirming Russian covert activity in and around Norwegian and British waters. The White House did not respond to a request for comment, the CIA declined to comment and Russia’s Defense Ministry did not respond, Reuters reported.
The Kremlin has consistently denied accusations that Russia conducts sabotage operations in NATO countries or is preparing for a confrontation with the alliance.
A strategic gateway to the Atlantic
Svalbard’s location makes the episode particularly significant.
The archipelago sits near the route Russian naval forces would use to reach the Atlantic from their northern bases on the Kola Peninsula. Russian submarines and warships heading south must pass through the waters between Svalbard and mainland Norway, an area sometimes referred to as the Bear Gap after Bjørnøya, or Bear Island.
One Western official told Reuters that the frozen maritime region could quickly become strategically important in any escalation between Russia and NATO.
Russian vessels must also pass farther south near Norway’s remote volcanic island of Jan Mayen. Britain said this week that British forces had deployed there alongside Norwegian and American personnel last month for an exercise intended to demonstrate NATO’s ability to operate jointly in the High North.
Norway, meanwhile, plans by 2028 to deploy a new fiber-optic cable linking Svalbard and Jan Mayen with the mainland.
Europe’s vulnerable seabed
NATO concern over undersea infrastructure increased dramatically after the 2022 explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines connecting Russia and Germany. Subsequent investigations pointed toward figures linked to Ukraine, which has officially denied involvement.
Since then, however, Russian-linked vessels have repeatedly been accused of involvement in incidents that damaged undersea cables used by European countries.
According to maritime risk intelligence company Windward, at least 11 undersea cables were damaged or severed in the Baltic Sea between October 2023 and the end of last year.
“The prevailing assessment today is that Russia and China probably represent the most significant undersea threats,” Windward CEO Ami Daniel said.
The global network of submarine electricity and communications cables continues to expand as demand for data and power rises, accelerated in part by growing artificial intelligence use. Analysts have warned that Europe has become increasingly dependent on seabed infrastructure without developing adequate capabilities to protect it.
“In the last 25 years, Europe has done two things simultaneously,” said Bruce Jones, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. “It has dramatically expanded its dependence on infrastructure on the seabed, while dramatically reducing its capacity to protect that infrastructure.”
Europe, he said, is now rebuilding that capability belatedly as the perceived Russian threat grows.

Digital data leeches: trading on our profiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:08:00 UTC
04:08:00 KST

Digital data leeches: Trading on our profiles
September 10, 2026
Everyone has secrets. Things they wouldn't tell just anyone – except, perhaps, their dating app. What sort of partner they're looking for. Where they go to look for them. Their sexual preferences, maybe, or details about their health.
This information is meant to help the app find suitable matches. Selling the details on to other companies is not in the users' interest.
But this is what allegedly happened with Grindr, a dating app explicitly aimed at the LGBTQ+ community. Around 12,000 app users in Britain sued the company, which they said had shared highly sensitive personal information with advertisers — even, in some cases, a user's HIV status.
The lawsuit, filed in 2024, was settled earlier this week. Grindr has agreed to pay the claimants a total of 26 million pounds (€30 million; $35 million) – but stresses that this is not an admission of liability. Grindr continues to dispute the allegations, there has been no legal judgement.
What happens to the data you entrust to apps?
This latest case is just one of many that raise the bigger question of what actually happens to the information we entrust to our apps on a daily basis.
For users, an app is primarily just a helpful product. But they are often supported by cloud services, analysis tools, advertising networks and other service providers. They save and transfer data, link and analyse it — often contrary to our interest.
Jan Penfrat, a digital policy expert, says that many of the big tech companies want to "make it as difficult as possible for users and regulatory authorities to understand what data is gathered on our devices by which players, and for what purpose."
Penfrat works for European Digital Rights (EDRi), a European network of NGOs and experts that campaigns to defend fundamental rights and freedoms in the digital realm.
We all know what it's like: An app, a messenger service, for example, is quickly installed, and when it asks if it has permission to use personal data, users will often just click "yes."
Phone numbers are stored on servers — without approval
But the devil is in the detail. When you install WhatsApp, for example, you give it access to all the contacts in your smartphone. The phone numbers are transferred to the server — including those of people who don't use WhatsApp themselves, and who have not given permission for their contact details to be passed on.
"All of this flows into an enormous profile," says Penfrat.
Companies like Google then offer so-called "targeting" products based on this data.
"This means a car or clothes manufacturer can say: I'd like to address these target groups, and I want my advertising to appear in their Google search, Google Mail, or any of the hundreds of millions of third-party websites with integrated Google advertising," Penfrat explains.
Selling data profiles
Google is just one of many companies that offer data profiles. Two types of data feed into these profiles. One is the data that every user voluntarily discloses when they state something in their profile, or upload private photos.
But in addition, many big tech companies have for years now made assumptions based on the data they receive.
"If they have access to my location data and know where I usually am at night, they can assume that this is my home address," Penfrat says.
"If, for example, it's in a very expensive part of town, they can immediately make assumptions about my income. If they see: Oh, he has geolocation switched on and he regularly goes to a gay club, then he's probably a member of the LGBTQ community. And all this goes straight into the profile."
Strict regulation in Europe
The EU already has one of the strictest data protection regulations in the world. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) aims to protect people's personal data and privacy.
Other EU digital laws such as the Digital Markets Act or the Digital Services Act are intended to prevent big tech companies misusing their power over businesses and users. US businesses also have to abide by these laws if they offer their services to people in Europe, or observe their behavior.
The EU Commission has imposed numerous fines as punishment for violations of these regulations. In 2025, it fined Apple €500 million euros ($580 million). Meta, the company that operates Facebook, was fined another €200 million ($232 million).
Google had to pay €890 million ($1.03 billion) in fines this year. That sounds like a lot — but a look at the net profit of the Google corporation Alphabet puts it into perspective. In 2025, Alphabet's net profit was around €117 billion ($136 billion).
"So these are sums that a company like Google or Amazon will make in just a few days," says Penfrat. "They just include it in their budget."
Dependency on US digital services
As a result, it is not that easy for the EU to implement truly effective controls. The tech giants have global infrastructures, huge financial resources, and complex business models. European agencies first have to get past these.
Added to this is Europe's dependency on cloud services, operating systems, platforms and increasingly also AI infrastructure that, at least to date, have been provided in large part by US companies.
Penfrat criticizes Brussels for lacking the political will needed to take firmer action against these companies, and to better equip European data protection authorities.
This article has been translated from German.

Royal Navy embracing social creators to reach new audiences
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:06:32 BST
04:06:32 KST

The Royal Navy has spent more than £123,000 on third-party independent content creators since July 2024 as part of efforts to reach new audiences, improve perceptions of the service and support recruitment, the Ministry of Defence has said.
The figure was disclosed by Veterans and People Minister Calvin Bailey in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Charlie Dewhirst, who asked how much the MOD had spent on social media influencers since July 2024.
Bailey said: “Since July 2024, the Ministry of Defence has spent £123,173 on third-party independent content creators. This figure includes all costs, such as agency fees.”
The minister confirmed that the expenditure related entirely to the Royal Navy rather than campaigns conducted by the Army, Royal Air Force or the wider department.
The MOD also sees social media campaigns as having a role beyond attracting new personnel. According to the answer, direct communications can support retention by reaching people around serving personnel as well as those considering joining. Bailey added: “Direct messaging also supports retention by recognising the influence of families, friends and veterans.”
The Royal Navy’s recruitment and attraction team is responsible for leading recruitment activity, with communications personnel supporting campaigns intended to shape awareness and perceptions of the Naval Service among selected audiences.
The use of independent creators is becoming common and reflects the increasing importance of social media in Armed Forces recruitment, particularly when attempting to reach younger audiences who may be less likely to encounter conventional advertising or traditional military recruitment material. The MOD said campaigns involving creators are subject to the same requirement for planning and evaluation as other communications spending.
The £123,173 figure represents spending specifically on third-party independent content creators used by the Royal Navy rather than the MOD’s wider expenditure on social media advertising, communications or recruitment campaigns.

WhatsApp exchanges among Israeli prison guards and testimony collected by investigators have revealed what an Israeli newspaper described as a routine pattern of severe violence against Palestinian detainees at Ketziot Prison in southern Israel.
They included a 2023 assault that resulted in the death of Thaer Abu Asab.
The Haaretz newspaper reported Tuesday that the messages were uncovered during an investigation into the death of Abu Asab, who died after being severely beaten by guards at the prison in November 2023.
During the assault, one female guard wrote to her partner, "You're going to be proud of me, of my shift. After what happened, the count took two hours and 23 minutes. Draw your own conclusions." She added, "They're doing CPR in the clinic right now, baby! God willing, that son of a thousand whores will die."
Another guard wrote, "Holy s***, what a count. We f@#$%^ them up so bad."
A third guard told a friend, "What an insane count. There's never been anything like it. We poured cheese on them, cracked some eggs. So much blood in the wings."
She later wrote, "OMG, they're doing CPR on a prisoner because we beat him. He's dead. Listen, it's funny how it all happened in an instant: Boom, count. Boom, dead prisoner."
Abu Asab, a Fatah member serving a 25-year prison sentence, was pronounced dead at the Soroka Medical Center in Beersheba. The severe beating caused a heart injury that led to his death, according to an indictment cited by Haaretz.
Nearly three years later, prosecutors filed charges against 12 Israel Prison Service guards accused of beating Abu Asab and eight Palestinian prisoners in his cell.
The newspaper published other messages exchanged by guard Oshrit Eliga in December 2023 that investigators said pointed to a broader pattern of violence.
"A bunch of whores, sons of Amalek, surrendered right there in the street. They're sitting there on the ground in their underwear, blindfolded. I'm already getting myself and the shift ready for their arrival this Shabbat. We'll give them a proper Shabbat welcome," wrote Eliga.
Her friend replied, "Lol, your baton still working?"
"My baton's been disinfected more than a few times," Eliga responded.
She later wrote, "Picture you and me behind a partition with two prisoners cuffed to each other, and the shift commander's like, 'Go on, go nuts.' OMGGG, I swear you'd have a blast here with me."
Eliga added, "I wish I could prove it to you, show you something. I swear, girl, I beat the s*** out of them. You've never seen me like this. It's routine. Whatever batch comes in, if he doesn't end up with a busted kidney, I'm not letting him into the wing."
Guards' testimony under questioning also corroborated parts of the prisoners' accounts.
Another guard, Diana Troitsky, said the commander told personnel before the count that he had learned two friends had been killed in Gaza and was "shattered."
"We understood that we needed to beat them so they'd understand there was no cease-fire," she told investigators.
Troitsky said the commander told guards that "whatever happened that evening was his responsibility," that he had approval from senior officers and that "everyone knew what was going to happen."
She quoted him as saying, "If there's one thing I was taught at home, it's violence toward this scum. Those are the values I was raised with, and I'm going all the way with this. I don't care if I have to hand in my badge."
He also said the prison commander had backed him and given him "a free hand," according to her testimony.
Troitsky said guards then "lost it."
"Kicking, punching the prisoners. All the guards and all the Keter people in the cell took part in the assault," she said.
She added that the commander eventually shouted. "Stop!" after deciding the prisoners had "been beaten enough."

Jimmy Kimmel moves Talarico Senate interview to YouTube amid clash with FCC
The decision follows a year of surging regulatory hurdles over candidate appearances on the Disney-owned network.
ABC late-night host Jimmy Kimmel has said that an interview with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico will not air on the network, citing growing intrusion from the Republican-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) over political candidates’ “equal time” rules.
Talarico is running in Texas against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in a race that could decide control of the US Senate in November.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items

- list 3 of 4Oil soars to $109, pushing up chances of US interest rate increase

On Wednesday’s broadcast, Kimmel said that he would be interviewing Talarico under “unusual circumstances”, adding that, over the show’s more-than-two-decade run, he had been “interviewing Americans who are running for office with no problem at all”.
But in January, the Republican-led FCC said that daytime and late-night TV talk shows are no longer considered “bona fide” news programmes that are exempt from the equal time rules that require them to give airtime to opposing candidates.
Kimmel noted that for decades talk shows have been free to interview political candidates without being subject to those rules, including interviewing United States President Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential campaign.
“Now that he is president, [Trump’s] FCC threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple traditional editorial decisions — guest bookings it would seem they don’t like,” Kimmel said.
The interview with Talarico is instead set to be released on YouTube on Thursday.
The Cook Political Report and University of Virginia’s Center for Politics rate the Texas Senate race as a toss-up. An August poll by the Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research and Survey Center at Texas Southern University showed Talarico nosing narrowly ahead of Paxton, 47 percent to 45 percent, among likely voters.
Republicans have stepped up efforts to shore up the seat. Earlier this week, MAGA Inc, the political group aligned with Trump, committed $10m to advertising against Talarico, in what has been described as the first advertisement buy that Trump’s well-heeled political machine has made for a general election.
The move underscores just how much the party’s usually safest bastion, Texas, has emerged as an Achilles’ heel in Republicans’ effort to retain the Senate.
Talarico, 37, is a former public-school teacher who has built his political identity around a progressive interpretation of Christianity.
Democrats see the eighth-generation Texan as a promising vehicle for breaking their decades-long Senate drought in the state. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the chamber since 1988.
The ABC episode unfolds just as Republicans gather in Dallas for the closing ceremony of a highly unorthodox midterm convention — unprecedented in its timing — in what many observers have called a “Trump-a-palooza” parade, with the president commandeering the spotlight as the party seeks to galvanise its base.
The FCC becomes a pressure point
Over the past year, The View, Saturday Night Live, Jimmy Kimmel Live! and other programmes have been subjected to heightened FCC supervision over whether their political coverage and candidate appearances comply with federal equal-time rules.
Critics say the agency’s expanding reach into programming decisions risks chilling broadcasters’ editorial independence.
That precarity is compounded by the consolidation of US media ownership. In August, the FCC voted to scrap its 39 percent cap on local television ownership, a move critics warned could concentrate still more control over the country’s broadcast news in fewer corporate hands. That was followed in January by changes to the equal time rules.
The shift has already ensnared Talarico.
The FCC opened an inquiry into his appearance on ABC’s The View in February, while CBS declined to broadcast an interview he had recorded for The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. Colbert subsequently released the interview online.
In April, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr ordered early licence reviews for eight ABC-owned stations — an extraordinary step given that their licences were not due for renewal until 2028.
Network parent company Disney and ABC assailed the probe, arguing it threatened protected speech and upended longstanding constitutional precedents, separately accusing the FCC of using its regulatory authority to intimidate media organisations critical of Trump.
The intimidation tactics had already made the leap from regulatory threats to targeted reprisal in September of last year for Kimmel, as ABC shelved his show indefinitely, before resuming it six days later.
It came as Kimmel’s remarks about the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk drew criticism from FCC’s Carr, who urged local broadcasters not to air the programme.

Iran attack on base in Jordan damaged American military aircraft, US official says

Since the Iran war started in February, 18 U.S. service members have been killed and over 800 injured.

The Iranian attack required U.S. forces to fire roughly 30 Patriot interceptors to counter the missiles, the U.S. official said, amid increasing concern about the inventory of U.S. air defence interceptors and other missiles.
While specific inventory numbers are classified, the Center for Strategic and International Studies has estimated that about 65% of U.S. Patriot interceptors were expended between February and July, with fewer than 850 left on hand, down from 2,330 before the Iran war began.

Amnesty accuses Russia of trafficking foreigners to fight in Ukraine

Amnesty accuses Russia of trafficking foreigners to fight in Ukraine
Report reveals foreign nationals were misled with job offers, then forced into Russia’s army upon arrival.
A new report by Amnesty International has accused Russia of tricking foreigners into fighting on Ukraine’s front lines in what amounts to “human trafficking”.
Victims from Brazil, Colombia, Sri Lanka and South Africa were duped into travelling to Russia to take up well-paid civilian or non-combat jobs, then forced to join the Russian army on arrival, according to the report released on Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Our children were sold off’: The South Africans sent to fight Russia’s war
- list 2 of 3Zimbabweans lured into Russia’s war as families plead for their return
- list 3 of 3Russia ‘looking for new soldiers’; Kyiv claims 83,000 dead so far in 2026
Russian recruiters also targeted migrants and refugees in Russia and coerced them into joining the military, the report said.
“Amnesty’s research demonstrates how Russia’s Armed Forces are bolstering their ranks with economically vulnerable foreign nationals and using them as cannon fodder in the war of aggression against Ukraine,” said Agnes Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general.
“The level of exploitation and coercion involved led us to conclude that in many cases this amounts to human trafficking, as defined under the [United Nations] Palermo Protocol,” Callamard added.
Fraud and deception
Amnesty International interviewed prisoners of war at two Ukrainian camps between 2024 and 2026.
The rights group also spoke with foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces and members of their families as well as lawyers, human rights activists and journalists.
It found local agents and misleading online job advertisements were used to deceive foreign nationals in their home countries.
A South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland was told to fly to Moscow to pick up a truck and drive it to Poland. His wife told Amnesty International: “Upon arrival to Moscow, everything was taken from him. He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he is becoming a soldier.”
Many recruits were promised lucrative salaries and sign-up bonuses that were not fulfilled.
All the interviewees said their freedom of movement was severely restricted after signing military contracts.
During training, recruits from Brazil and Sri Lanka said their passports and mobile phones were taken from them before being sent to the front line.
Cannon fodder
Both Russia and Ukraine have recruited thousands of foreign nationals into their armies since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine four-and-a-half years ago.
Amnesty says it cannot conduct inquiries about foreigners in Ukraine’s army as it has no access to prisoners of war held in Russia, which designates Amnesty as a “foreign agent”.
An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army and officials believe Russia deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to battle Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region.
Meanwhile, Ukraine says 16,000 foreign nationals from more than 70 countries – including nearly 40 percent from Latin America – are currently serving in the Ukrainian army.
Russia has previously dismissed accusations of coercing foreigners into joining its army.

Recent finals history is against Freo, but these numbers could save them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:00:51 UTC
04:00:51 KST

Fri, 28 Aug, 7:40 pm, Final score, Bulldogs 96, Magpies 93
analysis
Fremantle looks to overturn recent AFL finals history with these key numbers against Geelong
Keeping hold of form and momentum on the footy field is often like trying to catch lightning in a bottle. Just ask Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir.
Few, if any, would question that Fremantle has been the best and most complete football team across the 2026 AFL season.
The Dockers' excellence has spanned weeks, months, time zones and weather seasons.
In the middle of the year, the question was more of when they were going to lose rather than if anyone would challenge them for the minor premiership.
But just as winter turns to spring the fortunes of all football teams change.
Now instead of wondering about the pack chasing them, the Dockers are now frantically searching for how they can regain that torrid early season form.
The development of how we play football in Australia — in all codes — often means that the best team of the year doesn't win the title.
Instead, it is often taken out by the team in the best form or with the best fitness when the finals comes around.
Once upon a time, it was almost a foregone conclusion that a side in Fremantle's current position would rally to redemption in week two of the finals.
In the first decade of this century, more qualifying final losers went on to win a premiership than to suffer the indignity of a straight-sets exit.
But as the Dockers would remember better than many sides, things have changed since then.
Fremantle, along with Geelong, broke new ground in 2014 when both experienced back-to-back finals losses.
With rising performance standards and more equalisation measures in the league, footy is more competitive than ever, and straight-sets exits have been the single most common fate for top-four losers since those breakthrough losses.
Half of the two dozen semifinals since 2014 have been won by the nominal underdog.
With time rapidly running out on season 2026, Fremantle is looking for that ephemeral sense of what kept them ahead of the pack before their season is over.
Standing in Freo's way this week is the side with the current longest winning streak — and a side who knows how to measure efforts for September — Geelong.
Winning the whole thing
Usually when a team starts to dip there is a reason. It is very rare for the rest of the league to raise their level to that of the competition heavyweights.
The league leaders are always the most studied, and the most scrutinised.
Over the course of the season threads are pulled at potential weaknesses until they are unravelled by the best of the rest.
When looking Fremantle's dip the biggest story is what is happening at the contest — or more importantly what isn't happening.
Fremantle's midfield and front half group is blessed with attacking talent, able to turn a half-chance into a broken line or shot at goal.
They are sometimes less able to control the ball when it hits the deck, especially when there are even numbers at the contest.
Against disciplined midfields, the Dockers have struggled to find the supply they need to churn the scoreboard over.
While they are still outsourcing teams at stoppage, the Dockers are beginning to be outscored when the ball hits the deck in general play.
Opposition sides have become increasingly accustomed to not overcommitting to competing in the air to counter the Dockers plethora of tall contested marking options, and instead focusing the ball on the inevitable battle when it hits the deck.
When GWS downed Fremantle in round 17, the Giants were able to win the post-clearance ground ball battle 65 to 49.
Despite losing ground in the air, the Giants were more than able to make it up on the ground.
It is a template other sides have been able to follow, cruelling the ability for the Dockers to score from broken play.
Last week, Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell was very clear on their focus around keeping extra numbers at the contest.
"Our forwards' work rate was a real highlight. We didn't always use the ball at our best, but the way they created outnumber after outnumber was huge," Mitchell said after the win over Fremantle.
While the Dockers broke even at post clearance contests in the game, the Hawks scored an extra 27 points from intercepts.
This was the big difference in the contest, and the key reason that the Dockers are playing again this week.
"I just thought [the] contest was pretty even, but I thought their contest method was a lot better than ours. I thought they were probably a little bit more decisive to get it to the outside [and] buffer pressure," Longmuir said after the match.
Part of the deal that Mitchell made with the outnumber was to leave their defence more isolated against the dominant Dockers key forward set up.
But that was a calculated gamble due to the match-ups that presented themselves.
"I think having a bit of extra time to watch them. Credit to Kade Simpson, the backline coach, he did a great job preparing the boys. Whether it was, you know, Barrass, Battle, Sicily, Weddle, we sort of had good match-ups [on Fremantle's forwards]," Mitchell said.
The Dockers were only able to get two goals from their tall forward triumvirate of Josh Treacy, Patrick Voss and Jye Amiss — the first time since round 6 that they were kept to less than three as a group.
Although the Dockers managed nine marks inside 50, the set shots they managed were from unfavourable situations and none are renowned sharpshooters from those positions.
But despite the downward turn in form, there is definitely still a clear path to the club's maiden AFL premiership cup.
The path back
The silver lining for Fremantle is last week's loss wasn't a season-ender.
Instead, Longmuir has a fair amount of hope for their chances to come.
"There's still a path there. So everything we've been working on across the course of the year, we've got to lean into that now," Longmuir surmised in the wake of the loss to Hawthorn.
"[I] understand that the outside noise might turn a little bit from positivity to negativity. I understand that aspect of it, but as a group, we've got to lean into each other and try [to] find our best footy before next week," he said.
"We're not dead and buried."
But the road to glory has become significantly harder than it looked a week ago.
Instead of a week off to recoup before a home preliminary final, the Dockers instead face one of the most feared sights in footy; Geelong when it matters most.
After floating through the season in fits and spurts, Geelong found its feet as September drew closer.
Geelong rode a six-match winning streak coming into the finals, albeit against some softer opposition.
Last week's win over Carlton was dominant but still left the indication that there is room to grow.
The Cats are also one of the few sides who know what it is like to beat the Dockers this year, splitting their two home and away clashes with the minor premiers.
In both games, control over the ball was perhaps the most critical element.
In round 1 the Cats claimed 50 more marks than the Dockers on their way to a 10-point win, while in round 15, the Dockers gained a 22-mark edge over the Cats in their nine-point win.
Limiting the Dockers ability to control the ball via the kick-mark game — and instead forcing the ball to deck — is one of the ways that teams can blunt their attacking influence.
Notably, Fremantle has suffered three losses in four of its matches where it has registered its lowest marking totals of the season.
The messier the game is, the harder it often is for the Dockers to dominate.
However, the Cats present a vastly easier challenge to the Dockers inside defensive 50 than Hawthorn did last week.
Geelong's defence has not been as strong as it has been in previous years and most key defensive indicators have deteriorated in the last part of the year.
Geelong has conceded marks and shots inside 50 at a bottom-four rate in the last ten matches, and during that time, the Dockers probably should have beaten them by more in their return match.
There's a quiet — if not cautious — confidence that the Dockers will be able to break the trend of straight sets exits if they can get the game back on their terms.
"I think you [have] to lean into physicality from the start. Contest is really key and then [we need to] try and lock it in our front half," Fremantle co-captain Andy Brayshaw told the media during the week.
If the Dockers can return to their brand of football, their hopes of their maiden premiership may still be alive in 2026.

'Not sick enough': Woman with eating disorder details 55 hours in emergency department
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:00:08 UTC
04:00:08 KST

'Misconception and stigma' sees people with eating disorders turned away from seeking help
Curled up on a hospital couch reeking of urine, all Sharon Ereaux can do is wait.
It's been 55 hours since Ms Ereaux, who has been living with an eating disorder for more than three decades, called the ambulance that took her to the emergency department.
She had a high heart rate, chest pain and fatigue, all symptoms of something called re-feeding syndrome.
It's a serious and potentially fatal side effect of increasing food intake after a period of malnourishment.
On Monday morning, she called an ambulance.
By Monday night, she says, she was going to be admitted to the mental health unit of her local hospital for monitoring.
That transfer never came.
She spent that night on a recliner in the emergency department, waiting for updates, before being moved to the couch.
"Tuesday morning I was told there were only two of us waiting for a transfer to the mental health unit, [and] that I would probably go Tuesday afternoon," she tells the ABC.
"But Tuesday afternoon came and went, and by 5pm I knew that it wasn't going to happen on the Tuesday."
Worried about dehydration, she called a hospital's internal hotline, to contact a senior health worker to escalate concerns about treatment.
Now it's Wednesday morning, and there's finally a bed.
Another few hours pass before a hospital staffer arrives to tell her she's being sent home without being admitted to the unit.
"I'm partly astonished, like this is next-level bad," she says.
"But I'm also like, 'Yeah, OK, here we go again, this old thing.'"
'It can suck you in and run away with you'
The idea of "being sick enough" is a fight Ms Ereaux has been having since she was 14.
Her eating disorder, she says, is incredible when it comes to sucking her back in.
"It's like you're a frog in boiling water, but inside a snowball, and you're rocketing down a slippery slope," she says.
"[That's] the gist of it, how good it can suck you in and run away with you before you know what's happening."
The first time a counsellor used the word "anorexia" with her was in 1998.
Two years after that, she presented to an emergency department for the first time.
There was no bed available. Despite a recommendation from her GP, hospital staff gave her an IV and sent her home.
In 2002, she entered her first ED-specific treatment program, a once-a-week session for "chronic" cases.
Then, just 23 years old and already almost a decade into her struggle with an eating disorder, she found herself surrounded by women much older than herself.
"I was the youngest by far," she says.
"There were four other ladies in the group, and some of them were 50; one lady was 60 years old.
"I thought, 'Oh OK, you can live a long but miserable life with this condition; I don't want that, I'm going to get better.'''
The 'no wrong door' approach to treating eating disorders
Eating disorders affect more than 1.1 million people in Australia.
Since 2012, the number of people impacted by eating disorders has increased by more than 21 per cent, according to the Butterfly Foundation.
Butterfly's head of Clinical and Support Services, Natalie Spicer, says Ms Ereaux's story is not unfamiliar.
"We have come a long way," she says.
"However, we do still hear these stories of people going in and not getting the treatment that they actually really desperately need.
"I think a lot of it is that misconception and stigma. People with larger bodies, or average and larger weights, often aren't viewed as people who would have an eating disorder.
"But it's about looking at that full person rather than just what they look like."
And for someone taking the step to ask for help, Ms Spicer adds, being turned away can be devastating.
The National Eating Disorders Collaboration (NEDC) published a national strategy for responding to eating disorders in 2023.
Part of that plan is the "no wrong door" approach to people asking for help.
"It's meant to be that, no matter where you go, you'll be able to get the right treatment in the right place at that moment," Ms Spicer says.
"Or that person will be able to put you directly in contact with somebody who will be able to help you.
"[The] plan is to ensure you don't need to be specialised in eating disorders to treat [them].
"You can recognise the signs and symptoms, recognise a story and know how to treat that person. Part of their plan is to upskill people to get to … just a basic understanding."
'Why on earth do I need to get sicker to be helped?'
For Ms Ereaux, the years brought more treatment programs, inpatient admissions, and hospital visits.
Now a nutrition and fitness coach, she has never stopped fighting to get better.
Loading...
Now, she has one question for those who dismissed her.
"Why on earth do I need to get sicker to be helped?" she asks.
"We live with the fear of death throughout this whole illness. It hangs over us.
"Sometimes I've had a psychiatrist remind me; she had me … acknowledge, 'I could die tonight'. She made me say those words because I was discharging myself from a trauma inpatient program.
"We live with that. And we know when we're scared enough. We know when we're sick enough. We know when we're ready for help.
"Why don't I have the choice to say, 'I want help, I want the treatment'? Why is it withheld until I'm considered to be at imminent risk of dying?"

Climate change is shifting malaria hot spots in Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Climate change is shifting malaria hot spots in Africa
Higher temperatures may push the disease away from historic hotbeds
Malaria, one of the world’s most prominent public health challenges, is on the move.
A new study based on previous predictions of where malaria in children may appear suggests that climate change is redrawing the map of malaria’s spread across the African continent. The data, reported July 29 in Nature, show a gradual shift from West and Central Africa toward the eastern and southern regions, consistent with global warming.
Increased temperatures may mean a more hostile environment for disease-carrying mosquitoes in the West and Central regions and a more favorable climate in the eastern and southern regions, says Romaric Odoulami, a climatologist at the University of Cape Town in South Africa. “Malaria transmission and mosquitoes’ life cycle are very sensitive to temperature,” he says.
This represents a shift in the map of this ancient disease. Malaria has historically been most prevalent in West and Central Africa, where temperatures are suitable for both the parasite that causes the disease (the genus Plasmodium) and the mosquitoes that carry it (the genus Anopheles). Previous laboratory studies have shown that mosquito-based transmission of malaria peaks at 25° Celsius, while it drops off below 19° C and above 34° C. High-elevation regions of East Africa and coastal southern Africa have been cold enough to fend off significant malaria transmission, centering the disease in hotbeds. including Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
But a deep dive into blood sample datasets from sub-Saharan Africa spanning over a century reveals that this story is changing. Odoulami and colleagues used the data to build a computer model linking childhood malaria prevalence to temperature and precipitation, then compared their findings with a hypothetical model without climate change.
The team found that from 1901 to 2014, climate change has likely caused a net 0.5 percent increase in malaria transmission across sub-Saharan Africa — one excess case for every 1,000 children — with a much greater increase in East and southern Africa. In the Ethiopian highlands, for example, the spread of malaria increased by 8 cases per 1,000 children, and in parts of West Africa, transmission rates decreased by 1 to 2 percent — about four fewer cases per 1,000 children. By the researchers’ calculations, climate change is predicted to lower malaria transmission rates in sub-Saharan Africa by 2 percent over the next 85 years with an intermediate warming scenario of 2.7° C globally.
Despite what the climate data show, malaria transmission is largely influenced by control efforts, which outweigh climate-induced changes in their impact, says Cyril Caminade, a climatologist at the Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics in Trieste, Italy. Caminade says that it will be important to expand mitigation strategies including mosquito bed nets, insecticide treatments and malaria prevention drugs to areas where malaria transmission is projected to increase.
“Africa in general lacks the luxury to wait for the key global emitters to do what is needed to reduce climate change impacts on the most vulnerable,” says Odoulami. “It’s important for regions across Africa to increase awareness of the danger of malaria where there is little knowledge of it.”

Xi Jinping to visit India after 7 years, attend BRICS Summit on Sept 12-13
China announced Thursday President Xi Jinping’s first visit to India in 7 years, saying he will attend the Brics summit in New Delhi from September 12 to 13 at the invitation of PM Narendra Modi. His bilateral with Modi is scheduled for Saturday evening, according to diplomatic sources.TOI has learnt that Xi will be accompanied by a 67-member government delegation, including political heavyweight and Xi’s right-hand man Cai Qi - member of the standing committee of the CPC Politburo - and foreign minister Wang Yi. A business delegation is arriving separately for the president’s visit that will last exactly for 24 hours, beginning with Xi’s arrival at 12.10 pm on Saturday and 12.20 pm departure the next day.Xi will arrive at Bharat Mandapam around 2 pm on Saturday, where he and other leaders will be welcomed by Modi. The bilateral meeting between the leaders is likely to take place between the Brics closed session on multilateralism and the dinner that Modi will host for the leaders at 7.30 pm in which Xi will also be present.There has been speculation about why Beijing delayed the announcement of the visit, but it’s learnt that China had formally conveyed to the Indian side Xi’s participation weeks earlier.
On August 27, China officially requested the Indian embassy in Beijing to issue visas to the president’s delegation.Xi’s visit is expected to reinforce the positive momentum in bilateral ties since the meeting between the leaders on the margins of the BRICS summit in Kazan in 2024, which marked complete disengagement and resolution of issues related to the 2020 eastern Ladakh military standoff. Modi is expected to underline India’s concerns about fair market access, supply chain reliability and balance in bilateral trade in the meeting, as the 2 sides look to boost economic cooperation.The leaders had in Kazan agreed to restart high-level engagements, calling upon Special Representatives on the India-China boundary question to oversee the management of peace and tranquility in border areas, which India calls a prerequisite for overall development of ties, and to explore a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable solution to the boundary question. They also agreed to maintain contact at the level of foreign minister and other senior officials.Since then, the special representatives have thrice held boundary talks, with the latest meeting in August this year resulting in 8 outcomes that included a decision to finalise terms of reference for an early and substantial harvest of boundary delimitation and border management.
Modi last year also visited China for the SCO summit, during which he also had a bilateral meeting with Xi. That visit too further solidified the thaw in ties, with both leaders agreeing that India and China are partners, not rivals. Xi’s visit is important for Beijing also as China assumes BRICS presidency next year, succeeding India’s chairship. The president had not travelled to Brazil last year for the BRICS summit.During his visit to Tianjin, Modi had also met Cai and shared his vision for bilateral relations and seeking his support to realise the vision of the two leaders. According to the Indian government, Cai had reiterated the Chinese sides desire to expand bilateral exchanges and further improve relations in line with the consensus reached between the two leaders.

Hanson's overreach on Hastie kicks Liberals into gear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
18:57:00 UTC
03:57:00 KST

analysis
Hanson's overreach on Hastie kicks Liberals into gear
Pauline Hanson declared in a recent News24 documentary: "I don't back down."
This week, Ms Hanson and her party followed through with two high-risk demonstrations, heels firmly dug in.
In the face of demands from Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie, Ms Hanson refused to withdraw one of her Please Explain animated cartoons that depicts (in multiple mentions) the decorated former soldier as a "traitor".
On a very different front, One Nation is toughing out a controversy around Warren Pickering, its leader for the November Victorian election, after his admissions — following allegations from his former partner — of extensive drug use as a young man.
The battle with Mr Hastie is highly consequential not only for One Nation, but also for the Liberal Party.
Ms Hanson's animated cartoons, edgy and popular, have been among One Nation's savviest political tactics.
This one, however, not only went over the top but poked a political bear who — given his background in the SAS — defaults to fight, not flight, when his reputation is impugned.
Mr Hastie began on Wednesday by calling Ms Hanson (and One Nation's treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce) "lying cowards"; by Thursday he was describing her as "weak and glass-jawed".
Ms Hanson and Mr Hastie have been targeting each other for months, with One Nation chasing Mr Hastie's Western Australian seat of Canning.
The party's recent win in the state by-election for Secret Harbour, mainly inside Canning, only intensified things.
One Nation's antagonism towards Mr Hastie is particularly driven by his giving evidence against Victoria Cross winner Ben Roberts-Smith in the latter's failed defamation case.
He'll probably have to do so again in the coming trial of Roberts-Smith, accused of war crimes in Afghanistan, where both men served.
Mr Hastie has previously publicly called out those Liberals inclined to accommodate the insurgent party, especially WA leader Basil Zempilas, in the by-election.
Loading
But this escalation of the Hanson-Hastie confrontation is changing the dynamic.
Several of Mr Hastie's Coalition colleagues quickly backed him.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Ms Hanson should take down the video.
If the episode is pushing the Liberals together in their response to One Nation (although that may not last), it is also pointing to underlying divisions among the Hansonites.
Mr Joyce has been clearly uncomfortable. After saying on Wednesday he hadn't been aware of the offending cartoon, he later texted Mr Hastie, inviting him to make contact.
Mr Joyce has to do a lot of cleaning up after Ms Hanson, but this is too much.
Ms Hanson was on the back foot. Her line that she had not called Mr Hastie a traitor and respected his war service was an implausible defence.
She authorised the cartoon (which went live in July). Her claim this was just "satire" also didn't wash.
Regardless, Ms Hanson opened a new front against Mr Hastie on Thursday, with Ben Roberts-Smith in mind.
Referencing a 2024 change to Australia's war crimes legislation, which was backdated, Ms Hanson tweeted the law had passed on the votes "so we don't know where Hastie stood".
Journalists should ask Mr Hastie, "Do you support retrospectively changing criminal law to make prosecutions of veterans easier?"
She later tried unsuccessfully to move an amendment to the legislation in the Senate.
The latest polls have One Nation's national number strong; subsequent polling will indicate whether the party's supporters are concerned about the attacks on Mr Hastie.
On one level, the Victorian election is a side hustle for Ms Hanson; on another, it is a significant judgement moment.
So how to respond to the public revelations about Mr Pickering was an important strategic decision, especially for the party's national campaign director James Ashby, formerly Hanson's chief of staff.
As commentators have observed, if this had been a Labor or Liberal leader, they would probably have been on their bikes.
But One Nation, obviously previously aware of the allegations, was sticking by its man. In her not-backing-down mode, when asked about Mr Pickering, Ms Hanson said on Monday: "It is a personal situation. He said he denies the false allegations that have been made against him."
This dismissal wouldn't hold up.
By Tuesday, One Nation unveiled an elaborate response to the Pickering problem. Mr Pickering's story became one of redemption.
A news conference was called, with Mr Ashby, Mr Pickering, his daughter Jhett and his stepson Johnny.
Adopting the demeanour of a lawyer acting for his client, Mr Ashby outlined Mr Pickering's background with his former partner.
Mr Pickering then spoke about his past extensive drug habit and turning his life around. Johnny and Jhett supported him.
Mr Pickering, 43, told the media conference:
"I'm proud of the man I am today. I sure as hell would not have run for office four times in the last five years if I wasn't firmly in my convictions and comfortable with who I am today.
"I'd like to provide an example to people that intend to turn their lives around, that have maybe done it a little rough or made some mistakes when they were younger."
Apart from whatever appeal the redemption narrative might have, One Nation is seeking to cut through with the fact that after all his personal issues, the defence force accepted Mr Pickering and he served some years in it.
One Nation hardliners predict voters will be split over Mr Pickering, with his background putting off some people while others empathise with him.
Some Victorian Liberals fear Mr Pickering's story could increase the One Nation state vote.
Amid the pyrotechnics, One Nation this week challenged government and opposition on the policy front, releasing a plan to allow homebuyers and renters access to some of their superannuation.
This caught out the opposition, which has itself been flirting with potential changes to superannuation arrangements.
The government unsurprisingly hit the nuclear response button, projecting how much worse off future retirees would be under One Nation's plan.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers declared this was an "existential moment" for Australian superannuation.
Probably not quite that, but it's likely that how Australia's landmark superannuation scheme should operate will be one of the major issues in the 2028 election.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.
