‘Tyrant Lizard Queen’ offers a nuanced look at T. rex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Tyrant Lizard Queen offers a nuanced look at T. rex
The book fleshes out the life of this fearsome predator
Tyrant Lizard Queen
Riley Black
St. Martin’s Press, $29.00
Tyrannosaurus rex is the ultimate villain. Hollywood writers have pitted the ferocious dinosaur against King Kong or tasked it with terrorizing children in an SUV. And museum curators prop up casts of T. rex skeletons to show them mercilessly downing prey, thrilling millions of visitors around the world each year.
It’s easy to see why. This 12-meter-long, eight-metric-ton carnivore needed to down nearly 150 kilograms of meat a day, often pulverizing and swallowing bones in the process. But in Tyrant Lizard Queen, paleontologist and science writer Riley Black asks readers to “consider the animal behind the kaiju-like façade.”
Black enlists Snag, a fictional T. rex trying to survive in a forest set in prehistoric Utah. When we meet our heroine, she’s newly hatched and already under constant threat. A pterosaur picks off four of her siblings and long-necked Alamosaurus threatens to trample her remaining kin.
Tyrant Lizard Queen follows Snag through the pit stops typical in many coming-of-age stories: peer rivalries and first loves. Enter Sweet, a fellow female T. rex. Their rivals-to-lovers arc sees the teen tyrants face off over food and later attempt mating, a clumsy encounter as awkward as any first kiss. When the eventual father of Snag’s brood turns on her in an attempt at cannibalism, the two team up to dispatch him.
But it’s not just Snag’s relationship status that’s complicated. The research behind how exactly a T. rex like Snag played, slept, fought and mated can be spotty, at best. After all, behaviors are difficult to capture in the fossil record.
To fill these gaps, Black draws inspiration from modern animals, including crocodilians and flightless birds such as emus. She outlines this process in the appendix, offering a behind-the-scenes look at how one brings the most feared yet beloved dinosaur to life. “No two visions of the same dinosaur are the same,” Black writes. “Plonk two paleontologists down in front of the same Tyrannosaurus skeleton and … they will imagine two different tyrannosaurs.”
Black’s T. rex is less diva and more underdog. The killer queen we meet was 80 million years in the making, Black points out. The evolutionary journey from a pipsqueak skirting the edge of the food web to a dino monarch wasn’t easy. “The number of things that had to go strangely right for a tyrannosaur to end up getting the rock-star billing in a museum hall is astounding,” Black writes.
And like a misunderstood starlet who has finally made it big, Snag has depth. She both shaped and was shaped by her environment. Tyrannosaur hunting habits “nudged other dinosaurs to develop speed, armor and the ability to hide,” Black writes. Meanwhile, the actions of prey dinosaurs engineered the very habitat that a T. rex like Snag needed to thrive. Seed-riddled herbivore dung helped provide plant cover for T. rex on the prowl and rainwater-filled sauropod footprints served as T. rex watering holes. “Habitat changes the hunt,” Black writes. “And the hunt changes the habitat.”
Tyrant Lizard Queen brings Earth’s greatest carnivore to life in a way that defies the stereotype of T. rex as a mere flesh ripper. Still, the unanswered questions surrounding this iconic beast stalk Snag through the pages. But Black embraces the uncertainty, arguing that such riddles have fueled our century-long investigation into this terrible lizard.
“The core of paleontology is imagination,” Black writes. “Dinosaurs thrive in the gaps our questions create.”

Supreme Court, arrest, emigration.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:59:12 UTC
01:59:12 KST

Daria Bunkova and Nabi Balabekov. Photo: personal archive
In early September, Moscow activists Daria Bunkova and Nabi Balabekov fled Russia after being arrested over an “unauthorized rally.” On August 10, they had gone to the Supreme Court, which was hearing a government lawsuit to strike the anti-war Yabloko party from the upcoming September election ballot, and handed out leaflets in support of the party.
Mediazona recorded Daria and Nabi’s story of how a routine action in support of a legal political party ended in detention, torture and emigration from Russia.
Daria Bunkova: I’m 23 years old. I went to my first rallies [in support of imprisoned opposition leader Alexei Navalny] in 2021, which is also when I experienced my first arrests. I was 17 at the time. Later, as a volunteer, I participated in the election campaign for Boris Nadezhdin, as well as campaigns for the Moscow City Duma. I even ran as a Yabloko party candidate in the municipal elections in Podolsk [near Moscow]. We also worked on restoring the memorial plaque for [murdered Novaya Gazeta journalist] Anna Politkovskaya. I worked briefly as a journalist for RusNews [, an independent outlet]. Sadly, I’ve had to cut my studies short, I was a third-year political science student at the State Academic University for the Humanities (GAUGN).
Nabi Balabekov: I’m 21. For me, it all started with Yekaterina Duntsova’s initiative group in 2023. From there, it was a “slippery slope”: Boris Nadezhdin’s campaign, the Moscow City Duma campaign. I put up Last Address memorial plaques [a civic initiative commemorating victims of Soviet political repression] several times, and sang anti-war songs on the streets—last year, I sang Pornofilmy’s “This Will Pass” on Nikolskaya Street in central Moscow, and I plastered homemade leaflets around. I was studying advertising and public relations at the Institute of Modern Education and Information Technologies (ISOiIT).
Daria: Nabi and I met during the Nadezhdin campaign. We got married in May of this year.
Nabi: [At the rally supporting the Yabloko party outside the Supreme Court in Moscow], law enforcement didn’t pay any specific attention to us. [Riot police] OMON were photographing people’s passports, forcing some to take out their phones and delete photos of the officers. At most, a Centre E [the anti-extremism police] operative snapped a few photos of us, but he was photographing everyone.
Daria: I think that Centre E guy was new, he was acting like a total idiot.
Nabi: He took a picture of us, walked away, then decided to take another one.
Daria: I was brushing Dasha Kozyreva’s hair at the time, and he photographed that several times. Basically, yeah, we figured he wasn’t very experienced.
Nabi: And when the police started clearing everyone out, he was on his phone saying, “Mom, I’ll call you back, mom!”
Centre E officers detained the activists a week after the Supreme Court formally struck Yabloko from the ballot. Daria Bunkova was detained on the evening of August 17 in the stairwell of her apartment building. Nabi Balabekov was taken to the police station by plainclothes officers after he went there to find out why his wife had been detained. Both were brought to the Tsaritsyno district police station in Moscow.
Nabi: At the station, we went up to the second floor, and the Centre E guys said, “We need a private room for a talk.” A female police officer gathered her things and left her office. The door was locked with a key. They showed me my phone and said, “Unlock it.” I said, “No,” and they immediately started beating the shit out of me. Slaps to the face, then they threw me face-down on the floor. They tried to handcuff me, attaching my hand to my leg, but they couldn’t manage it because the handcuffs were the wrong size. They kept telling me, “There’s nothing manly about you!” I don’t know what that was about—how can you even say that while beating up a guy who had just spent the last four days in bed with a fever?
Then they threatened to start drowning me. They said something about Dasha, implying I was going to end up disabled. They threatened to shoot me, one operative said to another, “Give me a gun, I’ll fucking shoot him right now.”
This was not the first time security forces had beaten Balabekov. On February 17, 2024, the day after Alexei Navalny died in prison, Nabi was detained at the Wall of Grief memorial in Moscow. The young man had staged a solo picket, holding a sign that read, “All that is needed for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing.” Eight police officers dragged Balabekov off a snowbank and began beating him—a scene partially captured on video by Sota.vision.
Nabi: There were two of them [in the room] at first, then four. Police officers kept coming in and out—they didn’t physically assault me themselves; they just stood nearby, laughing, and chiming in with their own bullshit. I decided to unlock my phone: it wasn’t worth the risk. I didn’t know when a lawyer would arrive or if they’d even be allowed in. It was my fourth day with a fever nearing 39°C, and I was completely drained.
I unlocked it, and they started digging through my phone, asking questions: What do you do? Where do you work? How long have you been married? You’re from Dagestan—how are your relatives? They asked about everything. I lied, made things up, and when I refused to answer, they’d step in close and raise a fist at me. They told me I wouldn’t be allowed to see a lawyer because “it’s not required for administrative cases.”
Daria: They told me the same thing. We were on different floors. I was in this holding cell—just a small corner with a table and a bench. I was sitting there with a few men, and the Centre E operatives would come by, try to talk to me, and leave. They didn’t explain anything or tell me what charges I was being charged with. They tried to threaten me. One of them said, “Is your little group of like-minded friends more important to you than your life and your husband’s life?”
They kept swearing and screaming: “You’re an extremist, you’re a Navalny lover!” Sometimes they played ‘good cop’: “Look, let’s talk off the record, just heart-to-heart, as people, come on.” They tried to convince me that Nabi was cooperating and had told and showed them everything. They asked for my phone password countless times.
Nabi: They asked me for it, too.
Daria: Did they ask you for my password?
Nabi: Yes.
Daria: But I was simply confident that they wouldn’t beat me because I’m a woman. It’s not a guarantee, but this time it turned out that way. <...> Some of the men in the cell were also asking me: “What are you in for?” Blah, blah, blah, asking about politics. And to this day, I’m not sure if they were asked to do that, or if they had just been sitting there a long time.
Nabi: They repeatedly offered me “confidential cooperation.” They said, “Look, you can keep going to whatever rallies you want, but you work for us.” Like, some police officer would be detaining you, and you just tell him our number, and they'll let you go immediately. They asked, “Why don’t you want to? Are we lepers or something?”
Lawyers were finally allowed to see the detainees several hours later. The activists spent the night at the police station. On August 18, Moscow’s Nagatinsky District Court sentenced Bunkova to 10 days in jail and Balabekov to 15 days on charges of “violating the rules of holding a public event.” Both served their sentences in separate blocks of the notorious Sakharovo special detention center outside Moscow.
Nabi: The windows of their block faced the exercise yard, and Dasha and I were able to shout to each other through two sets of bars. We passed each other cigarettes and tea. They were like mini-dates. One time, Dasha made a bird gesture with her hands: we are flying away [from Russia]. I nodded.
Daria: I said, “I’ve decided for myself that yes.” And Nabi said, “I’ve decided for myself that yes, too.” I think the red line for me was the fact that Nabi was tortured.
Nabi: I just felt it in my gut... the closer it got to the end of my sentence, the more anxious I became. I thought they were going to put me on the “carousel” [a tactic where Russian security forces rearrest activists immediately upon release on new fabricated charges while quietly deliberating a criminal charge]. The fact that those Centre E guys went through my phone, what happened at the station... In total, they had our phones for about four hours. I didn’t even know what they could have done with them. I felt like if I got detained one more time, it would be my last time. And I felt it—this was the limit.
Dasha got out of the detention center on August 27, quickly wrapped up all our affairs while I was still locked up, and bought tickets to Georgia. I was released on September 1, and by the 3rd, we flew out.
Daria: So far, the realization [of leaving Russia] hasn’t fully set in. It feels like the time people normally spend on vacation—a week or two. Once that time passes and we don’t go back, that’s when the realization will hit harder. Right now, we’re just riding the euphoria: new places, we’re walking around, and I feel like I can breathe more freely. But I think all the missing-our-homeland stuff is still ahead of us.

Zelensky’s visit to Canada could bring new defense and energy deals – analyst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:58:00 UTC
01:58:00 KST

Zelensky’s visit to Canada could bring new defense and energy deals – analyst
The assessment was made by diplomat and international analyst Ihor Dolhov, according to Ukrinform.
According to him, Ukraine’s key priorities at present are protecting its airspace and ensuring the continued operation of its energy system amid possible Russian attacks.
“These visits, like every foreign trip by a head of state, are important. They are probably particularly important now. On Sunday, the U.S. President envoys visited Ukraine. There were lengthy talks and some optimistic signals, but the main conclusion is that the war will not end tomorrow, and it will not end this year, so we need to prepare for a difficult winter,” the diplomat said.
He recalled that these issues were also among the key topics discussed at the Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting in the Ramstein format.
“Therefore, these two themes – what to use to protect Ukrainian skies, how to defend ourselves, and how to get through the winter under constant Russian attacks, particularly against our energy infrastructure – are the main issues right now,” Dolhov explained.
Before traveling to Canada, Zelensky visited Norway. According to Dolhov, despite the visit being prompted by a mourning event, it also provided an opportunity to hold talks on further support for Ukraine.
Norway is one of Ukraine’s key partners in military and financial assistance. In particular, the country is involved in procuring missiles for the U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems.
“Norway is one of Ukraine’s main partners when it comes to military and financial assistance. In particular, when we talk about Ramstein and the procurement of Patriot missiles, Norway is a leader. Norway is constantly allocating funds to purchase Patriot missiles from the United States, and at the latest Ramstein meeting it also announced another contribution of $200 million,” the diplomat noted.
He also highlighted the importance of cooperation between the Ukrainian and Norwegian defense industries.
Dolhov described the partnership with Canada as strategic for Ukraine. Zelensky’s current visit is the first state visit by the Ukrainian President to the country.
“This is also an important event because the strategic partnership with Canada is important to us from various perspectives. In terms of cooperation during the war, in terms of support for Ukraine from Canadian businesses and companies, and, of course, it is worth noting that Canada has one of the largest Ukrainian diasporas, which is also actively involved in projects to support Ukraine,” Dolhov said.
Energy could become a separate area of cooperation. According to the expert, Canada has significant oil and gas reserves and produces equipment that could be useful in supporting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
“So, I hope there will be new agreements and concrete results both for defense and for ensuring the operation of our energy system throughout the winter,” the international analyst concluded.
As Ukrinform reported, following his visits to Norway and Iceland, the Ukrainian President arrived in Canada, where he plans to hold a series of meetings with representatives of the Canadian government and defense industry.

'Until safer times' — Kyiv’s cultural life pauses as the city adjusts to new drone threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:55:39 UTC
01:55:39 KST

'Until safer times' — Kyiv’s cultural life pauses as the city adjusts to new drone threats
People gather at an overlook near the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra as smoke rises from a Russian drone strike in Boryspil district, in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Aug. 27, 2026. (Diego Fedele / Getty Images)
In a post on Instagram, Alyona Gudkova sits with her head in her hands.
The founder of Kurazh, a popular Kyiv festival combining a flea market, food, music, dancing, and fundraising, had just announced that the project would suspend operations "until safer times."
Another post on Instagram showed a crowd dancing at Kurazh, with Light Dark Light Again by Angie McMahon as the soundtrack — capturing the rhythm of Kyiv in the fifth year of full-scale war, moving between moments of normality and sudden danger.
Together, the posts drew thousands of likes and hundreds of comments, many filled with broken-heart and hugging emojis. They came at the end of another summer Kyiv had managed to live through. But by its final weeks, that sense of normality was slipping, raising a harder question: had adaptation itself reached a limit?
Kurazh had paused before — during the COVID pandemic, and again after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. But each time, it came back. Since 2023, the project has held 20 events, including three this year.
This time, Gudkova does not know when Kurazh will return, saying it could possibly be not until spring. And the pause will also be costly: it means freezing an operation that employs 14 people, brings together more than 200 businesses at each event, and normally generates around Hr 7 million (about $157,000) in revenue per event.
She estimates the shutdown alone will cost around Hr 4 million (about $90,000) through March 2027, not including lost revenue.
"The hardest times are now," she told the Kyiv Independent.
It was not one problem, she said, but the accumulation of many: worsening security, falling spending, exhaustion, and uncertainty over what comes next. People are saving money for winter and basic needs rather than spending it on entertainment, she added.
For much of the full-scale war, Russian aerial attacks on Kyiv came mostly at night in the form of mass missile and drone strikes, allowing residents to recover some sense of normality during the day. Packed concerts, festivals, restaurants, and bars became symbols of a city determined to keep living despite the war. Rare daytime attacks could disrupt plans, but they rarely disrupted the rhythm of the whole city.
In recent weeks, the pattern has changed, and Russia now sends a steady stream of its newer jet-powered attack drones around the clock, giving the capital a constant soundtrack of air raid sirens, air defense fire, and explosions.
"Now Russia is terrorizing cities every day, both day and night. People are getting used to the alerts," Gudkova said. "There is a certain fatalism — life has to go on anyway. But as an organizer, what scares me is that people may lose their vigilance."
read also
Other organizers followed suit. The Book Country festival was postponed until spring. GogolFest, returning to Kyiv after a nine-year break, moved part of its program to spring. In Zhytomyr Oblast, the Deruny festival — a famous celebration of the traditional potato pancake — was canceled as well. Several smaller events were also called off or postponed.
Kyiv authorities later announced new restrictions on mass events, temporarily banning outdoor entertainment and sports events at venues without shelters.
New rules
On Aug. 27, Kyiv recorded 13 air raid alerts in a single day, the highest number since the start of the full-scale invasion. The grim records continued into autumn, with the capital spending around 17 hours under alerts on Sept. 8.
By late August and early September, repeated Russian drone attacks were stretching across both night and day, paralyzing life across the city. A brief lull during a visit by U.S. envoys for peace talks on Sept. 6 ended the following day, after they left Kyiv.
The city is now looking for new ways to live with the threat.
"To pretend that we are unbreakable and holding on — Ukrainians are sick of those words."
Authorities introduced different levels of air raid alerts, allowing businesses to keep operating during lower-level drone threats while requiring them to stop during more serious attacks.
Kyiv also shortened its curfew and extended public transport hours to keep the city functioning as the threat became more constant.
For Gudkova, however, continuing at any cost no longer felt like resilience.
"To pretend that we are unbreakable and holding on — Ukrainians are sick of those words," she said. "I don't see the point in carrying that further. There is no point in lying."
"Sometimes you have to take one step back to take two steps forward," she added, trying to stay optimistic.
Reading the room
Not everyone is stopping. Founded in 2024, the ethno-techno project CMYK was built during the full-scale war and has known little but adaptation.
Liliya Chernenko, CMYK's PR manager, says every season has brought a different challenge. For the team, simply continuing to develop the project and hold events in Kyiv in the fifth year of the war already means a lot.
"Especially because CMYK is meant to reconnect audiences with traditional Ukrainian music, a link disrupted by Russian and Soviet policies," she told the Kyiv Independent.
When the Deruny festival in Zhytomyr Oblast was canceled over security concerns, CMYK, which was in charge of the music program, and local authorities found a way to move forward: they kept the concert program, scaled down the event, and shared the exact location only with those planning to attend.
"You constantly have to read the room. You can spend several months planning an event, and then suddenly have to ask whether it is appropriate to hold it that day at all — for example, if the city declares a day of mourning after a Russian attack," Chernenko said.
They have done this before. In January, amid extreme cold, mass blackouts, and heating disruptions, CMYK still held its Malanka (a Ukrainian winter carnival celebration). "We see these circumstances as part of reality," Chernenko said, "and remember that it can always get worse."
Now, the team expects large events in Kyiv to become smaller and move to venues with shelters or underground spaces.
"We will probably have to learn from front-line cities and develop our own solutions," she said.

The likelihood of a Fed interest rate hike next week just got a lot higher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:55:17 UTC
01:55:17 KST

A swell of unfriendly factors for inflation likely will push the Federal Reserve to an interest rate hike next week and there's possibly another before the end of the year, judging by market pricing Thursday.
Traders pushed chances for a rate increase to 70% in morning action, following a report showing increasing wholesale prices in August and a coincidental jump in U.S. crude oil prices past $100 a barrel, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge.
They also nudged chances of another increase in December to close to 60% as inflation dynamics are proving stubborn and more likely to generate a central bank reaction.
"As the conflict with Iran drags on longer than many expected, inflation pressures are becoming increasingly entrenched, leaving investors in search of a catalyst strong enough to change the inflation narrative," wrote Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial. "At this rate, a hike in rates next week appears likely."
The producer price index, a measure of wholesale and pipeline cost pressures, rose 0.4% in August. Though that was in line with forecasts, it followed an upwardly revised 0.1% increase in July, together pushing the annual PPI level to 5.4%, slightly higher than forecast.
At the same time, intensified hostilities in the Middle East spooked commodities traders, sending U.S. crude up 4% to just over the $100 barrier.
Finally, the European Central Bank announced a quarter percentage point hike and raised its inflation forecast on worries that the Iran war would have deeper economic impacts and inflict a longer-term hit on consumer prices.
"More pressure is coming because crude and refined products have kept rising since the August data was collected," said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation. "The ongoing spike in oil, combined with low jobless claims, make it hard for the Fed to not hike next week."
One more report
Central bank policymakers will get their final look at inflation data Friday when the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases its consumer price index.
The Dow Jones consensus is for a headline annual reading of 3.4%, though the core excluding food and energy is forecast at 2.4%.
The Fed, though, focuses on the Commerce Department's personal consumption expenditures price index, which showed core at 3.3% in July and headline at 3.7%. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh reemphasized recently that the PCE price index is the central bank's official yardstick for inflation.
Bank of America senior U.S. economist Stephen Juneau estimated that, accounting for the August PPI reading, core PCE is tracking at a 0.26% monthly rate, which would get rounded up to 0.3%.
"This could move significantly tomorrow after CPI, but if we are correct, it should greenlight a hike at next week's Fed meeting," Juneau said in a note.
BofA has one of the most hawkish Fed forecasts on Wall Street, expecting three increases at upcoming meetings.
While that's out of consensus with current futures pricing, recent developments point to a more aggressive Fed when it comes to inflation fighting.
Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners, said that even a soft CPI reading might just indicate that companies are having a harder time passing through higher prices to consumers.
"Those who just look at consumer prices for their inflation information and interest rate predictions are not looking at the complete picture, and today's PPI is evidence still of an inflation problem throughout the supply chain," Boockvar said.

State-owned QatarEnergy is considering supplies from both operating and under-construction US export projects, the report said, citing people familiar with the private negotiations.
The potential agreements would mark the first indication since the war began that Qatar is looking beyond the Middle East to expand its LNG portfolio and secure alternative supplies for its customers.
Qatar previously accounted for around one-fifth of global LNG supplies, but its shipments have almost entirely stopped because of the risks associated with moving gas tankers through the Strait of Hormuz.

Before the conflict erupted in late February, Qatar had been advancing plans to nearly double production from its Ras Laffan LNG export complex by 2030.
However, the facility -- described as the world’s largest LNG plant -- was damaged in an Iranian strike during the early weeks of the conflict. Full repairs could take between three and five years, according to earlier reports.
With no clear end to the war in sight, the prospect of a prolonged conflict is reportedly pushing Qatar to strengthen its LNG trading activities and find supplies outside the Gulf.
Qatar already has access to some US LNG through its ownership stake in the Golden Pass LNG terminal in Texas. The facility began exports in April and has since been gradually increasing production.
QatarEnergy Trading, the company’s trading arm, has also expanded its capacity to market and ship US-produced LNG, mainly through shorter-term transactions.

75 per cent chance of ‘historic’ El Nino this year: US agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:54:50 UTC
01:54:50 KST

75 per cent chance of ‘historic’ El Nino this year: US agency
- The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration reports a 75% chance of a historic El Nino event in late 2026, surpassing previous events since 1950.
- El Nino is causing record-high Pacific sea temperatures, disrupting global weather patterns and increasing the risk of droughts, shifting rainfall, and extreme conditions worldwide.
- This strong El Nino will likely boost global temperatures, possibly making 2026 or 2027 the hottest years on record, compounding long-term climate change effects.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The US weather agency said on Sept 10 that the El Nino pattern in the Pacific was strengthening and there was a 75 per cent chance it would reach “historic” intensity this year.
Forecasters have been tracking an exceptional El Nino this year as the climate phenomenon has gained pace, driving tropical Pacific sea temperatures to record highs.
Scientists are increasingly confident this “super” El Nino could exceed any in the modern era, with potentially damaging knock-on impacts around the globe.
In its latest El Nino assessment, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said the odds of a history-making event had increased since its last report a month ago.
“During the October-December 2026 season, there is a 75 per cent chance of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Nino events dating back to 1950,” it said.
In August, confidence was 69 per cent.
El Nino is the warm phase of a natural climate cycle that occurs every two to seven years and is characterised by above average ocean temperatures across the Pacific.
Sea surface temperatures have reached record highs in the tropical Pacific in recent months and NOAA said some areas of deeper water were more than 10 deg C above average.
El Nino episodes alter winds, air pressure and cloud patterns, reshaping weather and raising the odds of extreme conditions thousands of miles away.
Major El Nino events often produce drought across parts of the Amazon, Indonesia and Australia, a disrupted Indian monsoon and shifting rainfall in the tropics.
“With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Nino are larger, though not guaranteed,” NOAA said.
The EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service said on Sept 10 its latest El Nino forecast “favours further strengthening, in oceanic indices, until the end of the calendar year, after which uncertainty in prediction increases.”
The Copernicus outlook combines El Nino predictions from nine of the world’s leading meteorological centres into a single forecast.
El Nino also temporarily boosts global temperatures, compounding the long-term warming caused by climate change and increasing the risk of extreme weather.
Scientists interviewed by AFP say 2027 is almost certain to set a global temperature record but 2026 is fast becoming a serious contender as El Nino strengthens. AFP

Report: Iran resumes ballistic missile production at underground sites despite heavy wartime damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:54:09 UTC
01:54:09 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday evening that Iran is again attempting to rebuild its nuclear capabilities, vowing that Tehran would not obtain a nuclear weapon as long as he remains in office.
“President Trump announced this evening that Iran is trying to arm itself again with nuclear weapons. That is true,” Netanyahu said during remarks at the Western Wall ahead of Rosh Hashanah. “After we destroyed its immediate ability to produce nuclear bombs, both in Operation Rising Lion and Operation Roaring Lion, they are trying again.”
“I promise you here, at the Western Wall, ahead of Rosh Hashanah: As long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons,” he said.
Netanyahu added that Israel was continuing to strike what he described as the Iranian axis. “At the same time, we are striking the Iranian axis, not only very hard in the Gaza Strip, but also in Lebanon. We destroyed the Beaufort Ridge and are now dealing with the Ali Taher Ridge. More will follow.”
His comments came as The Wall Street Journal reported that Iran has resumed producing ballistic missiles at underground facilities, assembling new weapons from components stockpiled before the war despite extensive damage inflicted by U.S. and Israeli strikes.
According to the report, Tehran is assembling both liquid-propellant missiles, which must be fueled shortly before launch, and solid-propellant missiles that can be stored ready to fire. Intelligence has detected activity at several underground facilities, including the Khojir military complex in southeastern Iran, while Iran is also trying to establish new underground assembly sites to make future production harder to target.
Production is still believed to be considerably lower than before the war. U.S. and Israeli strikes damaged factories and other industrial facilities required to manufacture missiles and their components, while the U.S. naval blockade has complicated Iran’s ability to import parts and materials used to produce solid rocket fuel.
Still, the renewed activity illustrates the difficulty of permanently dismantling Tehran’s missile program and chips away at what Washington and Jerusalem had presented as one of the war’s major military achievements. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in April that Iran’s missile program had been “functionally destroyed” and that Tehran had “no ability to replenish” the weapons it was firing.
The Pentagon told the Journal that U.S. forces had destroyed as much as 90% of Iran’s drone, ballistic missile and naval industrial base and had significantly degraded its ability to launch missiles and drones. A White House official did not directly address whether missile production had restarted, but said Iran’s military had been severely weakened.
A U.S. official said Iran likely resumed low-rate production after reaching a preliminary agreement with Trump in mid-June to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin negotiations aimed at winding down the war.
Before the fighting, Iran had accumulated stocks of finished warheads, airframes, guidance systems and other components, allowing it to assemble missiles without immediately restoring its entire manufacturing network.
Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst specializing in Iran’s military, told the Journal that the number of missiles Tehran could assemble depends on the size of those stockpiles and how many underground facilities remain operational.
“We could be talking about hundreds of missiles or possibly thousands of missiles,” he said.
Iran depleted much of its stockpile of completed missiles during the war, forcing it to reduce the size of its barrages, but analysts believe it still possesses thousands of ballistic missiles. Tehran has continued firing missiles at U.S. military positions across the Middle East and has also launched several attacks on U.S. warships in recent days, though none was hit.
Satellite imagery reviewed by the Journal indicates Iran has been rapidly repairing military infrastructure, including roads, production sites and entrances to underground missile bases damaged in earlier strikes. Israeli military assessments cited in the report suggest weapons stored deep inside the tunnels may have survived largely intact.
Iran nevertheless faces substantial obstacles to restoring production to prewar levels, including damage to chemical facilities used to make liquid propellants and industrial mixers needed to manufacture solid fuel.
Experts said Iran deliberately dispersed and buried much of its missile infrastructure because it expected the program to face repeated attacks. The renewed production could help Tehran sustain a prolonged war of attrition, particularly as Iran’s missile stocks are pitted against increasingly strained U.S. and Gulf inventories of air-defense interceptors.

Shabana Mahmood has urged police to curb the activities of far-right, anti-migrant groups which have “obvious malign intent” after a weekend of chaos caused by balaclava-wearing vigilantes.
In a meeting on Thursday, the home secretary told senior officers to make “full use” of their powers, including bans on face coverings, after police were assaulted and ports were disrupted in Kent and Hampshire.
She signalled the need for “strong deterrence” and improved intelligence in light of new tactics being deployed by groups such as Patriot Platform, led by the convicted kidnapper Daniel Thomas, which helped to organise the protests.
Mahmood told the officers: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents. This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.”
The Home Office and police were criticised in the aftermath of the weekend for failing to take a hard line on the far right. Environmental campaigners and civil liberties groups have complained that there appears to be a “two-tier” approach, with peaceful climate protesters prosecuted more aggressively than far-right agitators.
Police in Dover on Saturday and then Portsmouth on Sunday were taken by surprise when hundreds of protesters wearing black clothes and face masks massed to oppose what they say is illegal immigration via small boats.
Both protests are believed by police to have been far-right inspired, with evidence emerging that those behind them were determined to avoid detection.
Thursday’s online meeting was held ahead of this weekend, when further disruption is predicted to take place.
Mahmood told senior officers to make better use of intelligence to ensure they have the correct resources and expertise in place, and made clear the government’s expectation that police should make full use of the powers at their disposal to ensure anyone who is committing a criminal offence is dealt with “robustly”.
The home secretary urged police to make full use of digital evidence, including body-worn video, facial recognition technology, CCTV, ANPR and other intelligence products to identify offenders.
The move raises the possibility that Hampshire police will insist that protesters due to meet in Portsmouth at 12.30pm on Saturday will be ordered to take off any face coverings.
Forces have planned an “enhanced and coordinated approach to intelligence gathering and operational planning” ahead of the weekend – laying the groundwork for a more proactive response.
Labour’s Crime and Policing Act, which took effect in April, gave police powers to create mask-free zones at protests, backed by fines of up to £1,000 or one month’s imprisonment, or both.
The power only applies to people who are trying to conceal their identity, rather than those covering their face for reasons of religion, health or work, and officers must take reasonable steps to notify the public of the restriction.
Saturday’s protests in Dover, which Thomas claimed to have organised, blocked the town’s roads for several hours, disrupting traffic heading to and from the port.
Kent police initially claimed that they had no warning of the Dover protest. That claim fell apart when the force admitted there were warning calls to police on Friday evening which were not acted upon.
After a dinghy carrying 120 asylum seekers was rescued on Sunday near the Solent, about 200 black-clad men gathered at Eastney Marina. Protesters blocked roads, leading to alleged assaults on several officers. No one was arrested at either demonstration.
Patriot Platform has attempted to bring together disparate local “patriot” groups rather than construct a single hierarchical organisation.
In a further development, RNLI volunteers and staff have been warned not to wear the charity’s branding because of the “unacceptable abuse” they have faced from anti-migrant protesters.
The charity has issued security advice since the protests in Dover and Portsmouth, which saw its workers targeted for bringing some small boat migrants ashore.
This week, footage posted on social media showed volunteers being labelled as “traitors” after helping to look after people who had arrived in a dinghy in Portsmouth. Protests have been held at RNLI sites, including on Wednesday, when a small anti-migrant gathering was held at the RNLI College in Poole, Dorset.
Commenting after the meeting, the deputy chief constable Andy Mariner, the NPCC lead for public order, said: “Policing is continually assessing and preparing for protests and any potential impact on public safety. This includes working closely with local forces, specialist teams, communities and partners, monitoring publicly available information, and ensuring the right resources are available where needed.
“We have stepped up this activity this week at a national level, supporting local forces to ensure we have the right information, support and operational capacity in place to respond should we need to.
“This includes ensuring commanders are ready to use every power at our disposal, from arrests and dispersal orders to more recent powers which can help police manage protests, where it is proportionate and necessary to do so.”

Cyberattack in Berlin: 1.4 million files on the Dark Web
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:51:00 UTC
01:51:00 KST

Cyberattack in Berlin: 1.4 million files on the dark web
September 10, 2026
It was a story that almost went unnoticed amid all the clamor surrounding the closely watched state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. This highly alarming story is one of many recent reports that have detailed attacks on infrastructure or drone attacks on airports carried out by hostile foreign powers. Incidents like this one in the German capital highlight just how vulnerable Germany's data networks are.
So what exactly happened? Since early September, employee files, official correspondence, pay stubs and even scanned ID documents have been appearing on the dark web. The hacker group Rhysida stole the data and then tried to extort the Berlin city government. They demanded a ransom of 30 bitcoins, which is equivalent to about €2 million ($2.3 million), or else they would publish the sensitive data.
But last Friday, Berlin's Governing Mayor Kai Wegner stated: "The State of Berlin will not give in to blackmail."
The data was subsequently published on the dark web, the part of the internet accessible only to tech-savvy users, where a lot of illegal activity takes place. In total, the data set consists of approximately 1.4 million records.
An employee unknowingly opened a phishing email
Two departments of the city government serving approximately four million residents have been compromised: the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transportation. This time, the attack wasn't carried out by foreign intelligence agencies, but by criminals.
The hackers initially gained access to protected data between August 7 and 14 without being detected. Rhysida, a cybercrime group believed to originate from eastern Europe, has been attacking public institutions around the world since 2023, claiming responsibility for nearly 280 attacks, primarily in the US.
The hackers were able to gain access when a Berlin Transportation Authority employee replied to a phishing email, a message disguised to appear genuine and benign. Opening one of the attachments inadvertently grants the attackers access to the victim's network.
In Berlin, the state government's secure fiber-optic network connects approximately 600 locations, ranging from municipal offices to senate departments.
Data disclosure could have serious consequences
The list of sectors that experts believe could be compromised illustrates the real gravity of the data breach. In addition to the personal data of employees and citizens, this includes information on combi-heat and power plants, fuel storage facilities, emergency power supply systems as well as prisons and water treatment plants.
In an interview with the Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper, Jochim Selzer of the Chaos Computer Club said that the publication could have serious consequences for the people affected — even if the data only appeared on the hard-to-access dark web: "The more you know about a person, the better you can impersonate them and the better you can figure out what you need to know about them in order to, say, place an order on their behalf."
Is changing passwords enough?
And what about the political authorities responsible? The Berlin state government has instructed its employees to change their passwords. That, however, sparked outrage from Thorsten Schleheider, the vice-chairman of Berlin's police union.
He said that Berlin's data has been inadequately protected for years and that many employees have not received sufficient training: "It is unthinkable that highly sensitive data was compromised for days, and the only action taken appears to be instructing employees to change their passwords."
To address the data breach, the Berlin Senate has set up a coordination office involving all Berlin administrative agencies. It has also established contact with federal agencies such as the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), based in Bonn.
Mayor Kai Wegner said, "We will inform, advise and support those employees and Berliners who were affected as quickly as possible."
Berlin state elections on September 20 remain safe
The Berlin authorities were, however, able to provide reassurance regarding at least one issue of concern. They announced that the September 20 election for the Berlin State Parliament is not at risk.
State Election Commissioner Stephan Bröchler told the Bild tabloid: "As things stand, all systems and processes necessary for the election remain unaffected — including election preparations, the actual election day itself and the steps leading up to the release of the preliminary results."
Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) was at least indirectly affected by the data theft. The stolen information also includes details about the controversial expansion of the Chancellery in the heart of Berlin.

Morocco election campaign begins as 27 parties vie for power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:48:28 UTC
01:48:28 KST

Breadcrumb
Morocco election campaign begins as 27 parties vie for power
Morocco's official election campaign kicked off on Thursday, with 27 political parties competing for 395 seats in the House of Representatives ahead of a nationwide vote later this month.
The campaign, which began on 10 September, will run until midnight on 22 September, with Moroccans heading to the polls the following day to elect members of the lower house of parliament.
The election comes five years after the 2021 vote dramatically reshaped Morocco's political landscape, propelling the National Rally of Independents (RNI) into first place and dealing a crushing defeat to the Justice and Development Party (PJD), which had led the government for a decade.
The RNI went on to form a governing coalition with the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) and the Istiqlal Party.
Those three parties are once again among the major forces competing in the election, alongside the Socialist Union of Popular Forces (USFP), the Popular Movement, the Party of Progress and Socialism (PPS), the Constitutional Union and the PJD.
The campaign is expected to focus heavily on domestic concerns, including employment, education, healthcare and purchasing power, as parties seek to win over voters amid economic and social pressures.
Authorities have introduced regulations governing campaigning, including rules on electoral spending, advertising, the use of public spaces and equal opportunities between candidates.
The 2026 election rules also address campaigning on social media and digital platforms, including the use of artificial intelligence and the dissemination of misleading or manipulated AI-generated content.
How does Morocco's election work?
Morocco has a bicameral parliament made up of the House of Representatives and the House of Councillors, but the September election concerns only the 395-seat House of Representatives.
Of those seats, 305 are contested through local electoral constituencies, while the remaining 90 are allocated through regional lists.
Under changes introduced for the 2026 election, the regional lists are exclusively made up of female candidates, strengthening women's representation in the lower house.
Moroccans do not directly elect their prime minister, officially known as the head of government.
Instead, voters elect members of parliament through a proportional representation system based on party lists.
A party would need 198 of the House's 395 seats to secure an outright majority, something that is difficult under Morocco's fragmented multi-party electoral system.
Under Article 47 of Morocco's constitution, King Mohammed VI appoints the head of government from the political party that finishes first in elections to the House of Representatives.
If the winning party falls short of the 198 seats needed for a majority, it must negotiate with other parties to form a governing coalition capable of securing parliamentary support.
The proposed government must then present its programme to parliament and win the confidence of an absolute majority of the House of Representatives, or at least 198 votes.
Following the 2021 election, the RNI emerged as the largest party with 102 seats and subsequently formed a coalition with PAM and Istiqlal.
Calls for election boycott
The election campaign has also been accompanied by calls for a boycott from Al-Adl wal-Ihsan, one of Morocco's largest Islamist movements.
The group has urged Moroccans not to participate in the election, arguing that the country's current electoral system does not provide the conditions necessary for genuine democracy, freedom and justice.
Al-Adl wal-Ihsan said elected institutions lack real political decision-making power and raised concerns about restrictions on political participation and what it views as an absence of genuinely free competition.
The movement stressed that its boycott did not amount to withdrawing from public life, but was instead a rejection of what it described as an ineffective political process.
It called for a new political horizon capable of bringing about meaningful democratic change in the country.

2026-09-10

01:45:23 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Finland's government has proposed tighter residence permit rules Thursday for international students, including a one-year waiting period before their family members can apply to join them and new language proficiency requirements, according to a media report.
The Yle public broadcaster reported that Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government submitted the proposed legislative changes to parliament, seeking to address financial difficulties faced by some foreign students.
Under the proposal, family members would be able to apply for residence permits only after the student has lived in Finland for at least one year. Currently, they can submit applications at the same time.
The government also wants to set specific financial requirements in euros for international students and review the required amount every three years to reflect inflation and living costs.
A new language proficiency requirement would allow authorities to reject residence permit applications from students who lack sufficient skills in the language of instruction.
Government reports have found that some students arrive without adequate language skills, while others use student permits primarily as a route into the Finnish or wider EU labor market, according to Yle.
“Students coming to Finland must have a genuine ability to pursue their studies, to get by with their own financial resources and to build their future here,” said Employment Minister Matias Marttinen.
The family reunification waiting period is scheduled to take effect April 5, 2027, with other changes from October 2027.

Gaza amputees tell TNA of life after devastating limb loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:44:41 UTC
01:44:41 KST

Breadcrumb
'Everything is difficult': Gaza amputees tell TNA of life without limbs and vital support
For Adli Obeid, even travelling a short distance through Gaza has become an exhausting ordeal.
The 40-year-old father of four from Shujaiya in eastern Gaza City lost his right leg during Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave and now relies on crutches to navigate streets filled with rubble and destruction.
He is among more than 5,000 Palestinians who have undergone amputations since the war began in October 2023, according to new figures from Gaza's health ministry. Obeid and other amputees told The New Arab that a severe shortage of prosthetic limbs, mobility aids and rehabilitation services has compounded the difficulties of living with their injuries.
"Everything has become difficult since I lost my leg. Before, I could walk wherever I wanted, take care of my children and go to work without thinking about whether the road was suitable for me. Now, even going a short distance can be exhausting because there are no proper roads and so much rubble and destruction everywhere," Obeid told The New Arab.
"The injury did not only take away my leg. It took away a part of my independence. I sometimes feel that I am a burden on my family because there are things I used to do myself that I now need help with. Mentally, it has been very hard. I have four children, and I want to be strong for them, but there are moments when I feel frustrated, angry, and helpless," he continued.
Obeid said he is constantly reminded of his disability, particularly because of a shortage of wheelchairs, crutches and medicine in Gaza amid Israeli restrictions on aid entering the Strip.
Gaza's health ministry said on Tuesday that it had documented at least 5,000 amputations since the start of the war, including around 980 children and 555 women.
The ministry's breakdown also included 595 men and more than 2,870 other cases.
Israel's war on Gaza has been determined to be a genocide by leading rights groups.
Another amputee, Mansour al-Qerem, a 42-year-old father of three from Gaza City, said one of the most difficult changes since losing his leg has been his inability to move freely and play with his children.
"You feel that your role as a father has changed because you cannot always do what you used to do. The psychological impact is very heavy. At first, I could not accept what had happened. You look at yourself and realize that your body has changed forever," he told The New Arab.
"There is no opportunity to recover mentally because the war is still affecting every part of our lives. You are not only dealing with the loss of your leg. You are also dealing with destruction, displacement, the loss of people you know and the fear of what comes next," he added.
Al-Qerem said that while a small number of organisations provide support for amputees in Gaza, the scale of need far exceeds the assistance and number of prosthetics available.
"An amputee needs more than a crutch. We need rehabilitation, prosthetic limbs, physiotherapy, medical treatment, and psychological support. I believe international disability organisations can do much more. The world has seen the number of people who have lost limbs in Gaza, but the needs of these people do not end when their wounds heal. An amputee may need years of rehabilitation and support to regain independence," he said.
Low-quality prosthetic limbs
A spokesperson for Islamic Relief, an international aid organisation, told The New Arab that even the prosthetic limbs that are available are low quality.
"Child amputees face particular challenges as their bodies are still growing so their prosthetic limbs need regular replacement, but there are few available," the spokesperson said.
Islamic Relief also noted that medical staff have faced the brunt of the Israeli offensive, with medics exhausted and traumatised.
"Most hospitals and primary health centres are shut down and those that are open face a constant struggle due to lack of fuel and supplies," the spokesperson added.
"Nowhere near enough aid is getting into Gaza. The Israeli blockade continues to restrict the movement of people and supplies in and out of Gaza – limiting vital supplies and preventing critically ill civilians from leaving for treatment. Gaza has been starved of supplies for almost three years".
The organisation said that despite aid trickling into the enclave, much more needs to enter, and the world needs to increase its pressure and political action on Israel to protect civilians and respect international law.
Double amputations
The health ministry said the overall figure also includes people with double amputations and other complex injuries requiring urgent medical intervention to save remaining limbs.
Israel's offensive on Gaza, which is continuing despite an October ceasefire, has also left more than 10,000 people needing intensive and long-term rehabilitation programmes because of the nature of their injuries, the ministry said.
In a statement, the ministry described physical therapy and rehabilitation services in Gaza as a "crucial lifeline".
New data also shows that around 300 people have neurological and spinal cord injuries requiring specialised care and rehabilitation, while most medical centres and healthcare facilities have been targeted or severely damaged, according to the ministry.
Activists and human rights groups have warned that conditions in Gaza are putting sick and injured people at risk of serious health complications, particularly amid severe shortages of medical supplies, prosthetic devices and artificial limbs.
According to the World Health Organization, around 43,000 of 172,000 wounded people have suffered life-altering injuries.
Gaza's health ministry has called on international organisations and UN agencies to urgently facilitate the entry of vital rehabilitation supplies and equipment into the enclave.
It also reiterated calls for land crossings to be fully opened, particularly for critical cases requiring urgent treatment outside Gaza or care that is unavailable in the enclave.
Despite the shortage of medical equipment, doctors and specialists have continued working in difficult conditions, at times treating people in displacement tents because patients are unable to reach healthcare facilities.
UN agency UNRWA has said Gaza now has the largest group of child amputees in modern history.

US Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed congressional map in Missouri
Rejection comes as Republican official in Missouri faces contempt charges for ignoring a lower court ruling.
The United States Supreme Court has again rejected a request from the administration of President Donald Trump to use electoral district maps that would favour his Republican party in the state of Missouri.
The court issued the latest order on Thursday, without noting any dissents to the decision, apparently clearing the way for Missouri to use the old map in mid-term elections this November that could determine which party controls the House of Representatives.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Alabama pushes US Supreme Court to approve congressional map for midterms
- list 2 of 3Missouri Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed map from November’s midterms

Earlier in the week, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump -appointee, rejected another request from the administration to put the new Republican-backed map into effect, without referring the case to the full nine-member court, or offering an explanation for his decision. Kavanaugh handles emergency matters from Missouri.
Contempt charges for Republican official
Missouri’s battle over its congressional districts has spanned more than a year and spawned confusion over which districts will be in place for voters.
The rejection on Thursday came hours after a federal judge allowed Missouri’s top court to proceed with a contempt hearing against Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins.
The state’s top court previously ordered Hoskins not to use a Trump-backed map in the general election and instead to use districts passed after the last census.
At the same time, US District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump -appointee, on Tuesday barred Hoskins from using anything other than the new map Trump supports.
The state Supreme Court then ordered Hoskins to appear for a contempt hearing on Thursday for not following its orders and instructing local election authorities to use the Trump-backed districts.
State attorneys representing Hoskins had asked Clark to halt the contempt hearing – but he declined.
Redistricting plans
Missouri was the second Republican-led state, after Texas, to enact new districts after Trump urged Republicans last year to redraw House districts to their advantage ahead of the midterm elections.
The revised Missouri districts target a Kansas City-based seat held by Democratic Representative Emanuel Cleaver by shedding parts into neighbouring districts and stretching the remainder into rural Republican areas. The goal is to help Republicans win seven of the state’s eight House seats in the midterm elections — a gain of one seat.
Redistricting opponents collected hundreds of thousands of petition signatures seeking to force a statewide vote on the new districts. They submitted the signatures in December. But Hoskins waited until August — on the same day as Missouri’s primary — to reject the petition. Hoskins asserted that a referendum petition could not be used for congressional redistricting.
The delay allowed Missouri to use the new districts in its August primary. Republican state officials have argued it would violate voters’ federal rights to switch districts before the general election.
But the Missouri Supreme Court last week ordered Hoskins to put the redistricting referendum on the November ballot, which he did. It also ruled that the new districts never became law and instead were suspended retroactively to the December petition submission.
The state then appealed to the US Supreme Court to block the state court’s findings. Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected their request.
The court barred Hoskins from using the new map and said the old map — passed by Republican legislators in 2022 after the last census — must be used in the November election. The US Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to hear an appeal of that decision. But Clark issued his conflicting order moments later.

01:43:34 KST

Trump’s Iran war now has a midterm election problem
Trump has tied the end of his war on Iran to the midterm elections. But with Iran holding firm, the political cost is mounting.
United States President Donald Trump has claimed that the seven-month-long war with Iran will end “immediately after” the US midterm elections in November, framing the ongoing conflict as an attempt by Tehran to influence the vote.
“They’re desperate to try and affect the election,” he told reporters on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump vows to be at centre of US midterms: Republican convention takeaways
- list 2 of 4Benjamin Netanyahu has overseen a genocide: In his telling, he’s a victim
- list 3 of 4IAEA accuses Iran of ‘noncompliance’
- list 4 of 4Trump promises $5,000 payouts if GOP wins midterms: Can the US afford it?
Trump’s latest claims of Iranian capitulation are not new. Tehran has thus far withstood sustained strikes by the US and Israel intended to eradicate its military capacity, as well as a naval blockade of Iran’s ports intended to choke the country’s economy. In late August, the US ratcheted up the economic pressure even further, threatening secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners.
“It was a statement that was more likely meant for an internal [domestic] audience,” Ali Alavi, an Iran lecturer at SOAS University of London, said of Trump’s predictions of Iran’s post-election collapse. ”It was Trump’s method of communicating that the only reason it seemed as though he was failing in his Iran policy before the midterms is because Iran wanted it to be perceived that way.”
The cost of war
The cost of Iran’s failure to capitulate is being felt across the United States ahead of the midterms, which could see Trump’s Republican Party lose one or both houses of Congress.
Petrol prices – a key measure of the cost of living in the world’s largest economy – have climbed to a national average of $4.27 a gallon according to the American Automobile Association, up nearly 30 percent from a year ago.
Trump’s approval rating has also plunged from the high-40s when he returned to office in January 2025 to the low-to-mid 30s today.
The US electorate’s pain extends beyond the pump. A 2026 LendingTree survey found that 29 percent of buy-now-pay-later users had used the loans to buy groceries, while 47 percent said they had paid late on a buy-now-pay-later loan at least once in the past year.
Separately, economists at the University of Michigan have found that rising fuel costs and inflation linked to the war on Iran are weighing on consumer confidence and purchasing power.
“Iran has prepared for a long war,” Sanam Vakil, director of Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa programme, said. ”It may be that part of that was a secondary plan to hold out long enough to destabilise the US midterm elections once it realised that negotiations with the current administration were not going anywhere.”
Top Democrats, including the party’s Senate leader, Chuck Schumer, have been explicit in their calls for Trump to end the war on Iran.
Given Republican difficulties over the Iran war and other issues, Center for American Progress international policy analyst H.A. Hellyer described the situation ahead of the November 3 congressional midterms as one where the Democrats aren’t as much poised to win as the Republicans are positioned to lose.
“The question really is one of [voter] turnout,” he explained. “It’s not that many members of the Republican base will suddenly switch to supporting the Democrats, as much as they’ll stay home and not vote.”
Foreign policy, Hellyer said, rarely influenced voters, but “economics matter”.
“The price of things, like the petrol they get from the pump, matter – and it’s this that might swing [the election],” he added.
Irrespective of their claims of military success, both the US and Israel face a reckoning with an electorate that their leaders had promised easy victory: the US and Trump in November’s midterms and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu in a crucial general election in October. Iran, ruled by an unelected Supreme Leader and with no legislative elections scheduled until 2028, faces no such countdown.
“For Iran, victory is about surviving long enough to extract a serious diplomatic undertaking from its opponents that it won’t be attacked,” said Vakil of London-based Chatham House. “Victory is about demonstrating leverage, but negative leverage, in proving that it can still disrupt the world’s economy, no matter what the state of its military.”
“For some in the government, that includes retaining control over the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. “For others, that’s just a potential bargaining chip in negotiations, but for all: victory is survival and finding a way to convert it to stability. It’s a tall task.”

Somaliland offers 2,000 troops for Gaza stabilisation force

Israel ally Somaliland offers 2,000 troops for Gaza stabilisation force
Somaliland is willing to deploy 2,000 troops for a planned US-led force in Gaza, President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi on Wednesday, adding that he is waiting for Washington or Israel to formally request its participation.
Speaking on the sidelines of the MEAD conference in Washington, which focuses on developments in the Middle East, Abdullahi stressed that the breakaway region of Somalia was not volunteering for the mission.
“If they ask, we can provide,” he said, adding that, if requested, his forces are "ready", with an army of approximately 25,000 soldiers and a coast guard of around 1,500 personnel.
As part of the Gaza peace plan envisioned by US President Donald Trump's self-styled "Board of Peace", an International Stabilisation Force (ISF) would be deployed to Gaza to secure areas following the withdrawal of Israeli forces. The force would also train new Palestinian police forces and support the delivery of humanitarian aid.
Abdullahi's comments come after Uganda approved the deployment of army troops to the ISF last month, becoming the first African state to declare its participation in the stabilisation force.
However, the prospect of Ugandan troops joining the mission has prompted debate in the country.
Opposition lawmakers were probing further details about the nature of the deployment, while raising questions over Kampala's approval and whether it has wider African backing.
Politicians in the country were particularly skeptical regarding whether Uganda acted without consulting its partners in the African Union (AU), as the bloc has consistently expressed support for the Palestinian cause and backed the implementation of a two-state solution.
Meanwhile, Israel has spent decades developing relations with several African countries, signified recently in Tel Aviv's official recognition of Somaliland as an independent state -- a position rejected by Somalia and most countries.
Somaliland subsequently opened an embassy in Jerusalem in June during Abdullahi's first official visit to Israel.

Starting September 10, the buses will operate during curfew hours, from 1:00 a.m. to 5:00 a.m.

Belgium should not hold everyone hostage over frozen Russian assets - MEP Auštrevičius
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:40:00 UTC
01:40:00 KST

Belgium should not hold everyone hostage over frozen Russian assets - MEP Auštrevičius
That’s according to the Lithuanian Member of the European Parliament, Petras Auštrevičius, who spoke in an exclusive comment for Ukrinform, following a new initiative by a group of MEPs to reopen the debate on Russian assets.
Commenting on the stance of Belgium, where the Euroclear depository holds the bulk of immobilized Russian assets, the politician called for preventing a single country from halting decisions that are crucial for the entire Europe: “One objection country as Belgium shouldn't keep everybody else as a hostage,” the MEP stated.
He pointed out that the scale of Ukraine's financial needs far exceeds current temporary instruments, making a comprehensive solution crucial.
“I think we have much more on the plate in order to discuss and find certain solutions. So that's why, even knowing how difficult it might be, it doesn’t stop us, and so we came with this letter in order to try to open the doors for discussions and finally, hopefully, find a certain way forward,” Auštrevičius added. “Ukraine will need much more than 90 billion loan money for its existential survival.”
In their joint letter to EU institutions, MEPs suggested establishing a technical vehicle or a new European instrument to manage the assets, which could decouple the process from national clearinghouses and mitigate legal pressure on Brussels.
“I guess that vehicle is something which might be useful, because not this kind of clearinghouse, but definitely a new institution might be in charge, and kind of a bit disconnected from Belgium,” Auštrevičius explained. “We have to be very practical, even suggesting some technical solutions.”
The Lithuanian politician noted that treating immobilized funds as untouchable is a fundamental mistake, as the aggressor must bear full financial accountability for destruction in Ukraine.
“We make a mistake, first of all, keeping those immobilized, frozen Russian assets as something holy, not touched by us,” the MEP declared. “It would be a very strong message to Russians that they are responsible and they have to pay, and we will use their money to the final penny.”
Addressing whether the EU political elite is ready to revisit the issue, the MEP admitted that while there may be hesitations, waiting is simply not an option.
“Well, I think the European Union is never ready for such a radical decision, but is there any better time? Do we have time just to sit back and do nothing?” Auštrevičius questioned.
He noted that despite the lack of immediate enthusiasm among some officials, the evolving circumstances are the reason while the issue must be pushed onto the agenda.
“The situation didn't improve, and we need more and more financial means and support for Ukraine. So that's why, even knowing that there will be no big political appetite to take this issue, we have to push it for an uneasy, but undeniably needed discussion once again to renew this debate about frozen assets,” he stressed.
Concluding his comment, Petras Auštrevičius rejected scenarios in which European taxpayers are forced to absorb the costs of rebuilding Ukraine while Russian funds remain intact.
“I don't see, even with the final peace solution on today's situation, that will we not use Russian money” Auštrevičius asked. “Who will pay for reconstruction of Ukraine? Not Russia? So then who, Belgium? I don't think so.”
As reported, the initiative by the group of MEPs aims to reactivate political consultations among the European Commission, the Council of the EU, and member states to establish a viable mechanism for utilizing Russian assets to secure long-term support for Ukraine.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:39:25 UTC
01:39:25 KST

Several Arab countries have condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s illegal entry into Syria’s Mount Hermon and urged the UN Security Council to take action to halt attacks on the sovereignty of the Arab country.
Netanyahu entered the occupied Syrian area of Mount Hermon on Wednesday accompanied by Defence Minister Israel Katz, in a move that observers viewed as part of his campaign ahead of Knesset elections scheduled for October 27.
In a statement on Thursday, the Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry strongly condemned Netanyahu’s “illegal entry” into Syrian territory, describing it as a “flagrant violation” of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a “blatant breach” of international law.
It said continued Israeli incursions and attacks inside Syrian territory represented an “escalation that undermined security and stability in the region.”
It also demanded that the UN Security Council fulfil its responsibilities by stopping the attacks and ensuring Israel’s compliance with relevant international resolutions, stressing the need to respect the 1974 Agreement on Disengagement of Forces between Syria and Israel.
Similarly, Qatar strongly condemned Netanyahu’s “illegal entry” into Syrian territory and crossing of international borders.
The foreign ministry said it constituted a “blatant violation” of the sovereignty of the Syrian Arab Republic and a “flagrant breach” of international law.
The ministry urged the international community to take urgent action to compel Israel to comply with international resolutions, particularly the 1974 Agreement on Disengagement of Forces, and to halt its repeated attacks on Syrian territory.
Saudi Arabia also condemned in the strongest terms the “illegal entry” as a “flagrant violation” of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and a blatant breach of international law.
In a statement, the Saudi foreign ministry stressed the need for Israel to “halt its violations and actions against Syrian territory and to comply with the 1974 Agreement on Disengagement of Forces to preserve regional security and stability.”
‘Provocative’
Separately, Egypt condemned the “repeated Israeli incursions” into Syrian territory.
In a statement, the foreign ministry rejected all Israeli violations and incursions, warning that “continued escalation could fuel tensions and undermine regional security and stability.”
It reaffirmed Egypt’s full solidarity with Syria and support for its sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity.
The Syrian foreign ministry on Wednesday also condemned Netanyahu’s “illegal entry” as a “provocative” move and a violation of its sovereignty, territorial integrity and international law.
Jordan’s foreign ministry called the “flagrant violation” of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity a “blatant breach” of international law.
In a video filmed during his visit, Netanyahu, wearing a bulletproof vest, said he was standing at the summit of Mount Hermon on the eve of the Jewish New Year, pointing to Damascus, Lebanon and the Syrian Golan Heights.
Netanyahu claimed Israel had established unprecedented “absolute control” over the area stretching from Mount Hermon towards the Yarmouk River.
He said Israel would not allow “terrorist forces” to establish a presence near its borders.
Katz, meanwhile, signaled that Israel intended to maintain its occupation of the area. “We are here on Mount Hermon, and we will not move from here,” he said in a separate video.
Israel has occupied Syria’s Golan Heights since 1967 and unilaterally annexed the territory in 1981, a move not recognized by the international community.
