My mother-in-law buys overly girly clothes for my daughter. I try to be gracious but it kills me – do I tell her to stop?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:00:41 UTC
00:00:41 KST

I am the mother of a six-year-old girl, and I have relatively progressive views about gender. Among other things, I try to give my daughter a choice of clothes that are practical – T-shirts, leggings – and that tend to be unisex in colour scheme. There are no overly fussy and frilly skirts and dresses in pink and sparkles in her wardrobe. As much as possible, I try to buy non-sweatshop brands. These choices are part of a world system of values I want to show my daughter – that being a “girl” is so much more than just wearing a frilly dress; that we can have well-made things without contributing to the suffering of others.
My mother-in-law, on the other hand, loves buying these sorts of clothes for her granddaughter. She is a kind and caring woman, and this is one of her love languages. These clothes are often gauche, overly feminine, expensive and poorly made.
I try my best to be gracious in accepting these things but it kills me to pass them to my daughter to wear. I feel as though she is enforcing these specific views on gender, through fashion, on my daughter, that don’t align with how I want to raise her. As a result, my mother-in-law becomes hurt that I’m not dressing my daughter in these ugly froufrou clothes; and I feel guilty about wasting her time and money.
Should I be upfront with her about what clothes I do and don’t want her to buy for my daughter? Or am I overthinking it and should let this slide?
Eleanor says: For what it’s worth, to be defined by rejecting something is still to be defined by it. “Overly feminine”, “ugly froufrou”; these are still judgments about how to be a girl well.
I completely share your taste here, so I point this out from right next to you in the trenches of thinking about femininity and pink and frills for young girls. It took me so long to work out that just as the firm belief that women must be “girly” is freighted with all kinds of sexism, the firm belief that we mustn’t is freighted with other generalisations, too – some no less sexist. For instance, “if feminine, vapid”. (Why, when I need to seem serious at work, do I dress more like a man?)
This isn’t to say your careful selection of your daughter’s wardrobe is wrong. It’s a wonderful counterbalance to all the nonsense that the world will expect her to love. But there’s a slight risk that in trying to get our girls away from “you must love frilly skirts and pink”, we swing all the way to a different kind of enforcement: “you mustn’t love frilly skirts and pink”. And that’s the seeds of a complex: the clues that clothing is somehow grave, contains rules, is something you can get wrong.
I think the bigger issue is that your mother-in-law is treading on a parenting preference of yours. She’s either not noticing or not minding the gulf between your tastes in things to buy your daughter. Neither is very thoughtful of the fact that this is your child.
Perhaps she feels your rejection of her taste is judgmental. But presumably she doesn’t like some things you like, and she wouldn’t want you to infer that, as a result, she thinks you’re bad or wrong. So it needn’t mean that when you don’t share her taste, either. That may be a useful way of framing things: we’re just different. No need to fear that. Your taste just isn’t hers, and you’re the parent.
Could you perhaps redirect some of this impulse to buy things? If it’s a love language, could it be more exciting for her to buy stuff your daughter is actually interested in – equipment for a hobby, toys, stationery? Or objects that can express a bit of your mother-in-law’s taste but that your daughter doesn’t have to wear, and that are more likely to be made ethically – like a kind of food, a local treat, a decoration? Could you nudge her towards at least buying costumes for playing make-believe – so they don’t seem to say that this is how girls should dress, all the time?
This strategy is a bit cheekier, but you could also say you’re trying to not let your daughter get too used to expensive things and lots of presents. That way it’s not about what your mother-in-law gives: you could ask her to focus instead on teaching her things, or making things together. That may make her feel less rejected while still meaning you don’t have to come home with a bag full of taffeta.
I so understand trying to teach your daughter important values through her clothes and consumer choices. Perhaps one lesson you can model is that Mum and Grandma have different ideas about important things, and that’s OK.

====================================================================================================

‘Things sort of get mushy’: inside the cryonics facility where ‘patients’ pay to be frozen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:00:40 UTC
00:00:40 KST

I’m standing atop a very tall ladder, peering down through a haze of liquid nitrogen vapour into a giant stainless steel flask containing three smaller containers.
Inside the smaller wedges – which are labelled 005, 006, 007 – are three of Peter Tsolakides’ “patients”. The frozen bodies belong to people who, before their death, paid handsomely to be cryogenically frozen in the hope of one day being brought back to life.
The ladder is inside a normal-looking shed in an industrial estate in Holbrook in regional New South Wales. Next to the shed is a grassy block strewn with several wrecked Hondas. Across the road is the local fire brigade.
Since it opened in 2023, the shed has housed the southern hemisphere’s only cryonics facility. Inside, seven patients are “suspended” head-down in liquid nitrogen at -196C. Four to a flask – a dewar, as they’re known in the business.
Tsolakides’ company, Southern Cryonics, is selling people “a chance of life extension”.
The gamble costs more than $200,000. Experts say there’s no way it will work.
Cryonics, they explain, remains a “dream”. Any attempted resurrection would be akin to taking a defrosted, and decidedly mushy strawberry, and believing it could be made firm and vibrant again.
But proponents say cryonics offers adventure. And a glimmer of hope of a longer or potentially limitless life.
Tsolakides, the chair of Southern Cryonics, makes no promises. “Basically, you need to have conquered death, cured all diseases and then be able to bring people back from the dead,” he says.
He puts the likelihood of his patients being brought back to life in 250 years’ time at about 10%. That’s more than nothing, he says.
But as with any risky venture, it pays to read the fine print.
A shed and a submarine
Holbrook is small town off the Hume Highway halfway between Melbourne and Sydney. It’s home to the decommissioned submarine HMAS Otway, stranded in a park 250km from the ocean.
Southern Cryonics is one of six such facilities in the world, according to its operators. There are two in the US and one each in Switzerland, China and Russia.
It’s thought there are about 1,000 people cryogenically frozen worldwide. Tsolakides describes the community as “tight knit”.
“Almost nobody’s interested in cryonics,” he tells Guardian Australia. “The people who we get joining us are people who’ve had a sort of life interest … but never knew it was available” in Australia.
Southern Cryonics chose Holbrook for its storage facility because of its proximity to Sydney and Melbourne and the fact it’s unlikely to be hit by earthquakes or floods.
The cryonicists need somewhere relatively safe given that patients are frozen indefinitely. They’re in the dewar until humanity develops the technology capable of “reviving” them; or, as their contract stipulates, the company goes bust. In that case, their body may be “disposed of”.
Conveniently, Holbrook was already home to a cattle-breeding association, and hence a delivery destination for the liquid nitrogen needed to freeze bull semen and embryos.
Southern Cryonics has two dewars so far. They’re basically big Thermos bottles.
Inside one are the first four of Tsolakides’ patients to be frozen. In May 2024, a man who died in his 80s was the first to be loaded upside down in his Trivial Pursuit-style quarter-cylinder wedge.
The second dewar has room for one more patient. Being in the shed, looking down into that space, I feel an immense loneliness.
Tsolakides says women are less likely than men to be interested in being frozen. That’s because, he suggests, women don’t like the idea of waking up in a future without family or friends.
‘A very strict protocol’
I am the first journalist allowed into the shed since the initial suspension in May 2024.
The shed is unremarkable apart from the two towering dewars – and a crash-test dummy, fully dressed and lying on the floor. It was used to test the winching mechanism for depositing bodies into the dewars.
Jim Davis, from Parkes Liquid Nitrogen, is there to top up the dewars. The metal flasks release plumes of vapour when they’re refilled. They were initially topped up once a month but that’s been increased to fortnightly at the request of two early clients who were worried about supplies running low after their mothers died and were suspended.
Davis also delivers the icy liquefied gas to police dog and cattle breeders, hospitals, engineers and human IVF clinics. “If they’re freezing it, I’m doing it,” he says.
Demand is increasing all the time, and supplies must be replenished regularly, Davis says.
You can’t seal liquid nitrogen in a vessel without the container blowing up, meaning it slowly escapes. “If I sealed one of these tanks, mate, the building wouldn’t be here,” he says.
To give patients the best chance of avoiding cellular destruction, their body undergoes an eight-hour “vitrification” process as soon as possible after death, Southern Cryonics says.
Another of Tsolakides’ companies, CryoPath, arranges a third-party medical perfusionist company to carry out the vitrification.
After someone dies, their body is cooled as quickly as possible – including by placing ice packs around their head. The corpse is then pumped with antifreeze-like embalming chemicals that turn it into a “glass-like state”, Tsolakides says, hopefully protecting it from the extreme temperatures inside the dewar.
“It’s a slow process,” he explains. “You have to follow a very strict protocol.”
After a body has been “stabilised” – usually at a funeral home – it’s transported to Holbrook and stored upside down. But not every patient in the shed has undergone this procedure. Some underwent a “straight freeze”.
In the Southern Cryonics contract, clients are asked to acknowledge that any known cryonic suspension method will probably result in physical damage to their body, which may be irreversible. The contract notes there will be another fee, yet to be determined, for any future revival.
Science v ‘mysticism’
Associate Prof Saffron Bryant, a cryopreservation expert at RMIT University in Melbourne, says current science “does not support our ability to quite preserve a whole body at this time”.
Bryant says cells, embryos and blood products can be successfully “cryopreserved” through vitrification. She says it’s “sort of like antifreeze you might put in a car” to prevent ice forming and protect cells from damage.
But it is not possible to deliver a cryoprotectant to everywhere in the body or even, at this stage, to a single organ.
“If you’re trying to cool a whole body down at the same rate, you’re going to have the outside, like the skin, cooling down faster than the inside,” she says. “We [use] that strawberry analogy – where things sort of get mushy.”
Bryant says even if it were possible to deliver cryoprotectant to the whole body and cool it at the correct rate, the underlying cause of death would remain.
The “heart attack or the Alzheimer’s or whatever it was that killed them” happened and no amount of freezing could reverse that, the academic says.
As to whether it’s possible to revive someone’s consciousness along with their physical body, Bryant considers this question to be more in the “realms of mysticism” than science.
Asked if she thinks Southern Cryonics is a scam, Bryant replies: “I’m not allowed to answer that.”
The initial stabilisation process costs an estimated $60,000. Clients then have to pay a further $150,000 to Southern Cryonics for their indefinite storage and a $350 annual “membership fee”.
The company “demands payment upfront” and Southern Cryonics recommends people take out a $210,000 life insurance policy.
Tsolakides says it costs about $5,500 a year to keep a patient suspended. Most of that goes towards liquid nitrogen and staff costs.
He plans to invest $100,000 from each client in “blue-chip” funds which he says could result in a collective pool of billions of dollars over the 250 years he estimates it will take for revival to become feasible.
On its website, Southern Cryonics says most suspensions are funded through life insurance and it can help people obtain a policy through a broker.
But Tsolakides acknowledges only one Australian customer’s insurer has agreed to pay so far and it was reluctant. He knows of “two or three” major insurers that will pay for cryonics but he won’t name them.
The Council of Australian Life Insurers says it can’t verify or endorse claims made by Southern Cryonics, CryoPath or any broker about using life insurance to fund cryonic suspension.
Its chief executive, Christine Cupitt, says nominating a cryonics provider as the beneficiary of a life insurance policy is a “significant decision” that people should consider carefully.
‘It is a dream’
Dr Kate Falconer, an Australian legal academic who specialises in death law and teaches at University College Cork in Ireland, says the cryonics community is made up of a small number of “diehard true believers”.
“Look, I think they probably do believe it,” she says. “But at the end of the day, it is a dream. There’s nothing concrete there.”
Falcolner nevertheless shows her students a New York Times video from 2015 where a young woman with terminal cancer talks about having her brain frozen after death.
“It’s incredibly moving [and] it really does hit home that there are some people who are choosing it because it is their only hope of any kind of long life.”
The latest suspension at the Holbrook facility occurred in June after a man in his 90s died. Southern Cryonics’ youngest patient is a woman who died in her 40s and whose premature death devastated her family.
The facility manager, Philip Rhoades, says he once preserved the brain tissue of a 15-year-old boy who took his own life. That was at the request of the teenager’s parents.
The preservation was done by Rhoades’ earlier venture, the Neural Archives Foundation, a registered charity which claims to preserves brain tissue as a “historical archive”.
Rhoades says the organisation makes use of “normal biomedical storage” across Australia. His own parents’ brains are preserved along with 12 other human brains and three dog brains.
Rhoades is a left-leaning vegetarian with a big family but no children of his own. He was planning to open a “life extension village” near his home in Cowra, in NSW’s central west, but says that was foiled by red tape.
“There was too much bureaucratic stuff,” he says. Instead, he’s thinking of turning the block into a GP clinic adjoined by a “biomedical research facility” for “radical life extension treatments”.
When he dies, Rhoades would love to be “uploaded to a supercomputer as soon as possible”. But as he doesn’t think that will be possible given that he’s in his 70s, he plans to be frozen and stored in the Holbrook shed.
Future generations will want to revive their great-great-great grandparents, Rhoades says.
“If the technology is possible at all … I think it will become very popular to talk to revivees.”
He thinks patients could be revived by 2080 and that someone who had a “good preservation” has more than a 50% chance of making it. But he knows there are no guarantees.
“If you get woken up in the future, you’ve hit the jackpot, really.”

It’s a remote, roofless ruin in a Tasmanian ghost town – and it just sold sight unseen for $300,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:00:39 UTC
00:00:39 KST

On the edge of the main highway winding from Hobart to Tasmania’s west coast, the concrete shell of the Royal Hotel stands like a spacecraft lingering on otherworldly terrain.
One of the few official ruins in Tasmania, the old building is roofless, weathered by the elements – and has just sold for $300,000.
Located in the ghost town of Linda, near Gormanston, the historic property was snapped up sight unseen by a Perth chef, Naiche, and his partner. They plan to explore opening an eatery in the adjacent (functional) building.
Set on a stretch of road where the town’s welcome and goodbye signs sit barely a kilometre apart, the property comprises the abandoned hotel and adjacent building equipped with a commercial kitchen, living room, bathroom and bedrooms.
From a bird’s eye view, the roofless concrete walls expose the ruin’s layout like a dollhouse. Its smooth, human-made edges stand out against surrounding mountainous landscape, laden with jagged boulders and low-hanging clouds.
When the sun hits the muted greys of the country, the colours turn into warm hues of brown, orange and green.
Originally constructed from timber in 1901, the hotel was destroyed by fire nine years later before being rebuilt in reinforced concrete. It catered to prospectors drawn by gold at the nearby North Lyell mine, where a 1912 fire claimed 42 lives. Over subsequent decades, the hotel serviced local copper miners and earned a reputation for brawls – including a fatal stabbing in 1925 – before the mines emptied and the pub was abandoned in 1952.
In recent years, the dark grey shell has served as a pit stop for road trippers seeking ghost-town photo opportunities. It has also been used as a backdrop for light projections during the Unconformity arts festival.
The adjacent building was previously operated by Zara Trihey as Linda Cafe – catering to visitors that included hikers, cyclists and rafters heading towards the Franklin River and Strahan.
‘Buying a wreck’
Dominic Romeo, a historic property agent who handled the sale, says the listing attracted interest across Australia, the UK and US.
Romeo, who has spent 40 years restoring historic country houses, described the Royal Hotel as a “huge historic shell”.
“Buying a wreck, sight unseen, is another level,” he says.
“I love these types of buyers, they have a sense of adventure and purpose. The purchasers are from Perth, WA. They did not inspect the property, but what makes it even more interesting is that they have never been to Tasmania.”
According to the West Coast council mayor, Shane Pitt, the region’s scenery is unique to the rest of Tasmania, with dense natural growth rainforests, rolling peaks and freshwater lakes filled with rainbow, brown and brook trout.
“We class the whole west coast as remote,” he says, estimating the hotel to be 15 minutes’ drive from the major town of Queenstown, two hours from Burnie and three and a half hours from Hobart.
The region surrounding Queenstown, Gormanston and the Linda Valley has a distinctive “lunar landscape” from a legacy of historic mining and timber harvesting, that has “started to be overtaken by floral growth”.
‘Visitors want to know the history’
The chief executive of the Tourism Industry Council Tasmania, Amy Hills, says sites like the Royal Hotel spark curiosity among travellers.
“There is a rawness to the west coast that draws visitors in,” Hills says. “Buildings like this help tell those stories and connect visitors to the history of the community. The new owners have the potential to give visitors a reason to stop and engage with the hotel’s story.
“Visitors want to know the history – what was it like before it closed in the early 1950s? Who spent time there, and what did its presence bring to the area at that time?,” she says. “There is something exciting about discovering an unexpected place on a road trip.”
Hills says tourism is vital to the state’s economy, particularly in regional areas.
“The industry directly and indirectly supports approximately one in six jobs across the state,” she says. “In regional communities that flow-on impact can be particularly significant.”
Pitt says a there has been a surge in adventure tourism on the west coast, driven by wilderness cruises, heritage railways and the nearby Mount Owen mountain bike trails, some of which end in the Linda valley.
“Those riders may be attracted to the eatery,” he says – if it offers something distinct from nearby Queenstown.
The local community “is one that is willing to support those having a crack”, Pitt says.
“It would be good to see the old Royal Hotel renovated back to its former glory, but this will take a lot of time, money and hard work. Telling the story of the building would certainly be a great start.”

Russia sanctions bill faces make-or-break moment before US midterms, Ukraine says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:00:20 KST

Russia sanctions bill faces make-or-break moment before US midterms, Ukraine says
It remains unclear whether the U.S. House of Representatives will vote next week on sweeping legislation that would impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk told reporters on Sept. 10.
The bill faces a narrow window for consideration before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The House's final pre-election session begins Sept. 14 and will last only four days. If lawmakers do not take up the legislation next week, its consideration would effectively have to start over after the elections.
"That was the main message I conveyed to the members of Congress," Vlasiuk said after returning from Washington, where he advocated for the bill.
"Is there a possibility that this bill will be passed by the House next week? Yes, there is. Are the chances of that happening high? It's hard to say at this point."
House Speaker Mike Johnson has cast doubt on whether the legislation will reach the floor before the election, adding uncertainty to a bill that has been stalled since April 2025.
The legislation gained significant momentum in the Senate on Aug. 7, when lawmakers overwhelmingly backed it in an 86-11 vote. The bill, authored by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, a longtime supporter of Ukraine, now faces a more difficult path in the House.
Pressure on Russia
The bill would give U.S. President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, as well as five countries helping Moscow evade energy sanctions.
China, India, and Turkey are among the largest buyers of Russian oil, while the European Union, China, and Turkey are major importers of Russian natural gas.
The list of targeted countries would be reviewed every 180 days.
Countries importing less than 15% of Russia's total natural gas exports and actively reducing those imports would be exempt.
The legislation would also impose sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, major Russian financial institutions, including the Central Bank, Sberbank, and Gazprombank, and Russian state-owned companies.
It would further target foreign entities supporting Russia's defense-industrial base, major Russian energy projects, and Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia continue exporting oil despite Western sanctions.
The bill also includes measures targeting China's support for Russia's defense industry.
Supporters in Congress have presented the legislation as a way to increase pressure on Moscow and demonstrate continued U.S. support for Ukraine.
The Senate vote reflected broad support for tougher measures against Russia. It also came shortly after Graham's death in July, following his return from a visit to Ukraine.
Trump's position
Despite the Senate's overwhelming vote, the legislation faces several obstacles in the House, including concerns among Democrats about the powers it would grant Trump.
Some House Democrats fear the bill could provide the president with a new legal basis for imposing broad tariffs at a time when his existing tariff authority is facing legal challenges, according to a person familiar with the matter.
It also remains unclear whether Trump would use the authority against Russian energy buyers, particularly China, given trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.
Vlasiuk expressed similar doubts about whether the White House would ultimately implement the legislation if it were to become law.
"There is broad support within American society and the political establishment for increasing pressure on Russia and achieving peace," he said. "Does this mean the White House is immediately ready to take specific actions? I don't know."
"It does mean the relevant departments would be technically ready to propose appropriate solutions."
For Kyiv, however, the immediate focus is on getting the bill through the House before lawmakers leave Washington for the election campaign.
"We do not delve into the intricacies of U.S. domestic politics," Vlasiuk said. "We are the Ukrainian people, who need the support of the American people."
"The U.S. Congress could provide that support to the Ukrainian people."

Skater Kamila Valieva Loses Neutral Status

Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva, who returned to competition in January after a long doping ban, has once again been barred from competing in international events after losing her status as a neutral athlete, the International Skating Union (ISU) said Thursday.
Valieva, who was at the center of a doping scandal that rocked the 2022 Winter Olympics in Beijing, is among 234 Russian and Belarusian athletes who applied for neutral athlete status, the sport's global governing body said in a statement.
Russian and Belarusian skaters were banned from international competition following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, although they were authorized to take part in events in the 2026/2027 season on the condition that they compete under a neutral flag.
To be granted this neutral status, athletes must meet three criteria: they must not be members of the army or security services of Russia or Belarus, must not have taken part in the war waged in Ukraine, and must never have publicly supported the war against Ukraine.
Mark Kondratiuk, the 2022 European individual champion, also had his neutral status revoked.
The ISU said two other Russian skaters, Alexandra Stepanova and Ivan Bukin, do not meet the neutral status requirements. It did not specify which criteria Valieva had failed to meet, but the skater's social media pages contain posts supportive of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev said Thursday that the four skaters will challenge the decision at the Court of Arbitration for Sport in Lausanne.
"The Figure Skating Federation of Russia and our skaters, who have been unfairly deprived of the right to compete in international events under the auspices of the International Skating Union, will soon file a claim against the ISU with the CAS," Degtyarev said.
Valieva returned to competition in January, four years after the Olympic doping scandal that led to her lengthy suspension. She was a 15-year-old prodigy and became the first skater in history to land a quadruple jump at the Olympics, winning gold in the team event.
However, it later emerged during the Beijing Games that she had tested positive for the banned heart medication trimetazidine following the Russian championships in December 2021. Valieva claimed it was the result of accidental contamination.
After multiple appeals, she was suspended for four years dating back to December 25, 2021.

Bulgarian financier and reformer Krasimir Angarski dies aged 73
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:59:09 UTC
23:59:09 KST

News
OBITUARY
Bulgarian financier and reformer Krasimir Angarski dies aged 73
Thursday 10 September 2026 16:51
Thursday, 10 September 2026, 16:51
PHOTO BNR
Font size
Prominent Bulgarian financier Krasimir Angarski has died at the age of 73 after a brief illness, his family said, as reported by BNT.
Angarski was one of the architects of Bulgaria’s tax reforms in the early years of the democratic transition and later played a key role in the introduction of the currency board.
Born in Sofia on January 28, 1953, Angarski graduated from the University of National and World Economy. He joined the Ministry of Finance in 1980 and went on to head the tax administration for Sofia and Sofia Region. He was among the authors of Bulgaria’s tax-administration legislation.
In 1997, Angarski served as Minister without Portfolio in Stefan Sofiyanski’s caretaker government, where he headed the group drafting the legislation for the introduction of the currency board. Introduced that year following a severe financial and banking crisis and a period of hyperinflation, the system fixed the lev to the German mark, and later to the euro, while placing strict limits on the central bank’s ability to issue money.
He subsequently became Secretary for Economic Affairs to President Petar Stoyanov. He also taught at the University of National and World Economy and, from 2001 to 2004, served as Executive Director of DSK Bank.
Krasimir Angarski leaves behind a lasting contribution to the institutions and financial reforms that shaped Bulgaria’s economic transition.

NATO allies disrupt Russian exercise involving secret weapon targeting subsea cables, Reuters reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:58:27 UTC
23:58:27 KST

NATO allies disrupt Russian exercise involving secret weapon targeting subsea cables, Reuters reports
NATO allies disrupted a covert Russian naval exercise near Norway's Svalbard archipelago involving technology designed to disable critical subsea cables without leaving a trace, Reuters reported on Sept. 10, citing Western officials.
The operation was carried out by Russia's Main Directorate for Deep Sea Research (GUGI), which used deep-sea submersibles to simulate deploying the technology, according to two Western officials who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Britain, Norway, and the United States tracked and confronted the Russian vessels at sea, preventing them from completing the exercise before they eventually left the area, the officials said.
No subsea cables were damaged during the operation. The exercise focused on simulating how the technology could be used in the event of a conflict with NATO, while officials declined to explain how the system works.
"Through our joint operation, we sent a clear message to Russia that they cannot operate covertly," Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said in a statement to Reuters.
"We have made it unequivocally clear to Russian authorities that any attempt to target our critical infrastructure will be detected and met with consequences," he added.
The operation took place near Svalbard, where two roughly 1,400-kilometer-long (870 miles) fiber-optic cables connect the Arctic archipelago with mainland Norway. The cables carry satellite data from the SvalSat ground station, which is part of NASA's Near Space Network.
Undersea sabotage has climbed up the political agenda across Europe with instances of damage to subsea cables and Russian vessels lurking near critical underwater infrastructure on an increasingly frequent basis since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In April 2026, the U.K. said it had intercepted a Russian operation near critical underwater infrastructure in British waters. A Russian attack submarine entered U.K. waters while other vessels linked to GUGI were detected conducting what the British government described as "nefarious activity" over critical undersea infrastructure.
Between 2024 and 2026, more than 20 subsea cables in the Baltic and Arctic regions were damaged, though many of the incidents have not been formally attributed to Russia.
NATO has since stepped up patrols and monitoring around critical underwater infrastructure, including through missions in the Baltic and High North.
Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to Reuters' request for comment on the Svalbard operation.

James Tasamba

The Democratic Republic of Congo has allocated $120 million in reparations to the victims of Uganda's illegal occupation of parts of the country in the early 2000s, according to a statement on Thursday.
In the first phase, the government intends to spend $30 million to fund community infrastructure projects in each of the affected communities in four provinces: Tshopo, Ituri, Bas-Uele and Haut-Uele, said the statement by the Justice Ministry.
To be funded are health, education, water and socio-economic development projects.
“These funds will be used to support community projects aimed at honoring the memory of the victims and strengthening social cohesion,” it said.
Justice State Minister Guillaume Ngefa promised transparent management of the funds and consultation with the target communities.
“Reparation is a duty of justice and a responsibility of the State,” he said.
On individual compensation, the ministry said it would be considered in the second phase of the implementation, which will begin as soon as the audit and validation of the lists of eligible victims are finalized.
The development is in implementation of a 2022 judgment by the International Court of Justice, which ordered Uganda to pay $325 million in reparations to Congo for its role in the conflict in the eastern part of the country between 1998 and 2003.
The court ruled that Uganda had violated international law when its troops occupied parts of eastern Congo and supported other armed groups in the country.
The court ordered Uganda to pay the sum in five yearly installments of $65 million starting in September 2022.
A total of $260 million has already been paid by Uganda, according to the Congolese Justice Ministry.

AI in malicious hands poses greater threat than losing control, says Anadolu CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:56:49 UTC
23:56:49 KST

Artificial intelligence (AI) getting out of control is problematic, but its falling under the control of bad, immoral and genocidal people is a much bigger problem, Anadolu CEO Serdar Karagoz said on Thursday.
Karagoz attended GITEX AI Türkiye, held at Istanbul Expo Center and hosted by the Presidential Finance and Investment Office with the strategic support of the Industry and Technology Ministry, where Anadolu acts as the global communications partner.
Speaking at the panel titled "Creative Industries Rewired — What Happens When AI Enters the Studio?" moderated by Gokhan Yucel, the head of the Communications Department of Türkiye's Finance and Investment Office, Karagoz said AI will greatly change media and journalism activities, just as it does every area of life.
Explaining that AI will change the consumption process of media content along with the production process, Karagoz defined AI as a greater change than all previous changes.
Noting that AI will also completely change journalism, Karagoz said unmanned journalism, journalism with fewer people and faster journalism will be possible.
Emphasizing that Anadolu assigns some tasks to AI in its operations, Karagoz stated that AI achieved success in fulfilling these tasks.
Giving an example from Anadolu's news monitoring module, Karagoz said reporters used to get the first news from a police radio or personal witnessing, but now a defined module in the social media system triggers an alarm when a user uploads a photo of an accident at the 67th kilometer of the Northern Marmara Motorway, allowing the agency to evaluate it as a tip and quickly send a reporter to the scene.
Underlining that AI is also useful in perfectly applying spelling rules, Karagoz noted that they previously employed copy editors for this purpose but will no longer hire in this field.  
'AI cannot take responsibility'
Pointing out that AI does not play a role in the decision-making phase, Karagoz added that a decision-making AI module might be emerging while this panel is being held.
Karagoz mentioned that an AI module deciding which is good and which is bad might be under development right now, but such an agent does not exist at the moment.
He stated that humans decide what it should be directed to because humans hold the will, conscience and responsibility.
Stressing that the final consumer has started to care about who wrote the news and who will take responsibility for it, Karagoz said an AI engine cannot say it wrote the news and holds the responsibility.
Karagoz highlighted that humans possess the final decision, will, responsibility and the ability to distinguish between good and bad.
Raising the critical question of whether AI makes news agencies less or more important, he said the importance of news agencies increases in an environment where everyone has the ability to produce news thanks to AI.
He added that people will want to get news from a corporate structure that inspires trust, has a sense of responsibility and stands behind its news.
Karagoz stated that while they are speeding up in terms of production, they are also reaching a more reliable and important point in terms of news consumption thanks to AI.
Stating that the daily AI usage rate of news producers reached 75%, Karagoz noted that journalists will eventually reach a position where they are faster and make fewer mistakes. 
'A good journalist uses AI instruments well'
Emphasizing that journalists will gradually move from routine news production to a decision-making position, Karagoz said a good journalist will be one who makes good decisions and uses AI instruments well.
Karagoz predicted that journalists will demonstrate more value-centered decision-making actions in the coming days, weeks and months, which will increase the importance of journalism.
He added that there will be a journalism where costs are reduced and time is used efficiently on one hand, while its importance increases on the other.
Karagoz said the values of corporate structures like news agencies will increase over time.
Pointing out that Anadolu discusses being a journalist in an AI-powered world as a vision, Karagoz reminded that there used to be a single newspaper, then regional newspapers emerged, and later newspapers started providing sports and automobile supplements to customize for the consumer.
Karagoz stated that media organizations will now customize more specifically and this will happen thanks to AI.
He added that journalists will use all these AI tools during the decision-making phase to create personalized news that the consumer desires. 
'AI cannot put forward a new scientific theory'
Mentioning that the greatest changes in the world started with the invention of the printing press, Karagoz said the printing press facilitated the spread of knowledge but it could not write a Shakespeare piece or Ibn Tufail's Hayy ibn Yaqdhan.
Karagoz said AI also cannot put forward a new scientific theory while discovering the codes of DNA.
Drawing attention to the fact that AI cannot dream, Karagoz said AI can produce an illusion or hallucinate, but it cannot dream.
Karagoz stated that this is the biggest problem and when it is solved, humanity might face what the people who resigned in fear from big AI companies predicted.
Touching upon the consequences of AI getting out of control, Karagoz said AI getting out of control is a problem but its falling under the control of bad, immoral and genocidal people is a much bigger problem.

North Korea spends war windfall on arms, infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:56:00 UTC
23:56:00 KST

North Korea spends war windfall on arms, infrastructure
September 10, 2026
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un is spending the money that his troops have earned fighting in Ukraine to fund a long wish list of projects that were previously beyond his financial reach.
South Korea's National Intelligence Service estimated in May that Pyongyang received at least $7.7 billion (€6.6 billion) in financial aid and economic value from Russia in the preceding three years for committing men and materiel to Moscow's war against Ukraine — and potentially as much as $14 billion.
That is a significant amount given that the North's GDP for 2024 stood at $26.6 billion.
Kim's support for Russia has been lucrative, and a slew of reports are now identifying where that money is being spent.
A portion of the funds is being put aside for the Regional Development 20x10 Policy, unveiled in January 2024 and which aims to construct modern industrial facilities in 20 regional cities per year for the next 10 years to improve living standards outside Pyongyang.
Benefiting from Russian money
More civil programs are being designed, observers say, although most appear to be earmarked for the "elites" who reside in Pyongyang.
"Before the alliance with Russia, the general infrastructure was poor due to a mixture of economic mismanagement and sanctions," said Martyn Williams, senior fellow for the Korea program at the Stimson Center in Washington, DC.
"With the breakdown in consensus on the United Nations Security Council and renewed trade with China and Russia, things are starting to move along now," he told DW.
"There are several large programs to build factories and hospitals across the country, [Kim] has ordered the development of entire new districts of Pyongyang and there's a rural housing project building tens of thousands of rural homes," he said, along with investment in "the modernization of several sectors of the economy."
However, he said, structural problems still need to be overcome.
"There is investment going into building, but the large new hospital in central Pyongyang was built some time ago and sat unused for a while, until medicines and equipment could be procured," he said. "North Korea is great at building, but keeping it running is the key — so we look to see if that will happen."
IAEA warns of new nuclear facility
More of the financial windfall is clearly being put into the military. On Wednesday, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it had identified a new uranium enrichment facility at the Yongbyon Nuclear Complex with an estimated 28 cascades of centrifuges.
The IAEA estimated that the facility would permit the regime to produce 85 kilograms of weapons-grade highly enriched uranium a year, enough for four nuclear warheads.
Satellite images also show that the North is enlarging and upgrading the west coast port of Nampo and Chongjin, on the east coast of the peninsula, to accommodate a new generation of warships.
On Monday, Kim attended the commissioning ceremony in Wonsan of the 5,000-ton destroyer Kang Kon, with the North Korean leader claiming the vessel was capable of launching nuclear weapons and would be able to "deal a deadly retaliatory blow at the enemies."
The third area of heavy investment has been in major improvements in roads, ports and bridges. This infrastructure stagnated during years of isolation under international sanctions but is now needed to facilitate the deployment of more troops to Russia and the arrival of advanced military technology, energy and consumer goods in return.
On Tuesday, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River, with customs posts and warehousing facilities under construction on both sides of the waterway. The bridge underlines the rapidly expanding ties since Kim and President Vladimir Putin announced a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2024.
The route will permit greater truck-borne exchanges, reduce costs and potentially be used for the transit of North Korean men, weapons and ammunition to Russia. It also further reduces the leverage of sanctions on North Korea.
"A lot of these projects, such as improving trans-border rail and road connections, building customs facilities and so on, were started before the pandemic and have followed an on-again-off-again pattern ever since," said Marcus Noland, executive vice president at the Peterson Institute for International Economics in Washington.
"After difficult times during the pandemic, which was accompanied by border closure, the North Korean economy appears to have grown for the last several years on the back of Ukraine war revenues and cybercrime."
Hinterland 'stagnating'
Noland said he has the impression that Pyongyang is faring relatively well economically, along with a number of cities on the China border thanks to renewed trade, "but the hinterland continues to stagnate."
While the Ukraine conflict and Pyongyang's alliance with Moscow have been an economic boon to North Korea, analysts say, it's not clear what will happen when the war inevitably comes to an end.
"The North Korean regime could be in a difficult spot if peace were to break out in Ukraine," said Noland. "If the war-related revenues were to dry up, the country could experience an economic decline and associated discontent after a period of rising expectations," he stressed.
"I am not saying that it would be enough to destabilize the system, but I do think that a transition to peace in Ukraine could present challenges that would have to be navigated by the regime."

Rising prices at the pump are squeezing US households and businesses weeks ahead of key midterm elections, pressuring President Donald Trump’s administration, as average diesel costs hit new highs.

Energy costs jumped by 4.2 per cent over the month, notably boosted by the cost of diesel fuel, which surged 24.1 per cent, the Labor Department report said.
The costs of regular petrol and diesel in the United States have risen since US-Israeli strikes targeting Iran in late February prompted Tehran to choke off the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation.

The Federal Reserve’s rate-setting committee is due to meet next week and high inflation could push policymakers towards raising rates.

Houthis capture Yemeni town of Mocha: Why it’s important
The seizure of the historic port city threatens global energy supplies, cuts vital supply lines, and triggers mass displacement.
Houthi forces grabbed control of the Yemeni port city of Mocha on Thursday, in a major offensive that comes amid escalated fighting between the Iran-aligned movement and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government.
Hundreds of women and children left Mocha, seeking shelter in the Saudi-backed government-controlled provinces of Lahij and Aden, as the growing violence also threatened to exacerbate an already devastating humanitarian crisis across the Taiz and al-Hodeidah provinces, where more than 20,000 people have been displaced due to clashes over the past two weeks.
Al Jazeera’s Yemeni affairs editor, Ahmed al-Shalafi, highlighted the immediate civilian toll of the military shift. “Areas south of Hodeidah and Mocha witnessed waves of displacement towards Dhubab and Aden,” he said.
Sudden withdrawal
The fall of Mocha is the culmination of a massive Houthi offensive that exposed vulnerabilities within government-aligned defences. According to al-Shalafi, the Houthis applied pressure from three distinct axes starting on September 3: western Taiz, southern Hodeidah, and Mocha city itself.
The combat was intense on the outskirts of Mocha.
A key factor that helped the Houthis take control of the city was the withdrawal of the National Resistance Forces from the fighting, said al-Shalafi and Al Jazeera correspondent Maha Ali, who was reporting from Taiz.
The National Resistance, led by Tareq Saleh — nephew of Yemen’s former President Ali Abdullah Saleh, who was killed by the Houthis after initially allying with them — has been a central part of the Saudi-backed alliance, and the internationally recognised government it leads.
The Houthis took control of Mocha “following the withdrawal of the National Resistance Forces from them at dawn today and their movement towards Mocha”, al-Shalafi said. He added that it is unclear whether the National Resistance Forces withdrew “to arrange their ranks, or for a military reason, or due to their inability to withstand the intense military formations”.
According to Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, Saleh ordered forces to execute “a tactical withdrawal and repositioning in exchange for the Houthis’ advance in the al-Waziyah and Mawza fronts”, and instructed them to establish an alternative command centre.
Expanding fronts
The conflict is rapidly spilling over into maritime and distant terrestrial domains. Reuters quoted four unnamed sources as telling it that the Houthis “were launching attacks on the strategic Red Sea islands of Hanish”.
Simultaneously, Ali reported that “the military media of the National Resistance announced that the air aviation [of pro-government forces] targeted Houthi positions in Al-Tuhayta, Al-Salif, and Kamaran Island in Hodeidah governorate, while the Houthis launched two ballistic missiles towards the strategic Zuqar Island”.
Clashes also intensified inland. In Marib, “warplanes targeted Houthi reinforcements coming from Sanaa in Fardhat Nihm and others heading to north and south of Marib”, Ali reported.
Global chokepoint
Mocha’s geography makes its capture a global concern. The city sits approximately 75km (47 miles) north of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Known as the Gate of Tears, this narrow passage is a critical artery for crude oil and fuel travelling from the Gulf to the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, as well as for Asian commodities and Russian oil.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry explained that controlling Mocha could give the Houthis a “stranglehold along the Bab al-Mandeb”.
Furthermore, it severs critical anti-Houthi supply lines, including “the road linking Mocha with Taiz” running south from Mocha, and supply lines through Mocha’s port.
“This is a turning point right now in the war,” defence policy analyst Wolfgang Pusztai told Al Jazeera. “This might lead to a breakdown of the government forces in the southern part of Yemen.”
“The port of Mocha was the last harbour fully under control of the internationally recognised government,” Pusztai said.
The international community is reacting with alarm.
A spokesperson for the United Kingdom’s Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office declared that “the Houthis bear full responsibility for this crisis”, and urged them to “cease their attacks and escalation immediately”.
Coffee origins
Long before it became the focal point of a geopolitical crisis, Mocha was the Arabian Peninsula’s premier commercial hub and the birthplace of the global coffee trade. Mocha coffee gets its name from the city.
Mentioned in ancient Himyarite texts as “Makhn”, the city was first seized by Abyssinians in 517 AD before they were expelled by the Himyarite King Dhu Nuwas.
The Ottoman Empire overtook the city in 1536-1538 AD, transforming it into a military base to launch raids against the Portuguese.
Ironically, it was the Portuguese who became the first Europeans to taste Yemeni coffee when the Sheikh of Mocha hosted them and offered a “black drink that refreshes the body and relaxes the mind”.
According to historians, the Sufi scholar Ali bin Omar al-Shadhili first brought coffee to Mocha from Abyssinia.
The Ottomans initiated the first export operations through the port in 1536, sending beans via the Red Sea to Suez and Alexandria, where they were sold to Europeans. The Dutch secured their first commercial coffee deal in 1628, eventually smuggling live seeds to cultivate in Java and the Americas.
Mocha’s golden age extended through the 17th and 18th centuries. However, the city’s prominence faded in the late 19th century due to conflicts between the Ottomans and the British, and the rapid rise of rival ports in Aden and Hodeidah.
This economic decline devastated the local demographics: Mocha’s population plummeted from approximately 20,000 in the 19th century to just 1,000 in the 1930s, before a slow recovery brought the numbers back up to over 10,000 by 2004.

23:52:58 KST

The Ukrainian Defense Forces targeted a gas treatment unit used for deethanization at the Novy Urengoy Condensate Processing Plant (ZPKT) on September 9.
The OSINT project CyberBoroshno published information about the damaged facility.
The unit processes gases released during the deethanization of unstable gas condensate. These gases contain ethane, an important feedstock for producing ethylene and polyethylene.
The processed gases are intended for the Novy Urengoy Gas Chemical Facility, which has a design capacity of up to 400,000 metric tons of low-density polyethylene per year. Damage to the plant could disrupt raw material supply and affect operations in this production chain.
The Novy Urengoy Gas Processing Facility is owned by Gazprom Processing and is one of the region’s key gas condensate infrastructure facilities. The facility’s total design capacity is approximately 19.5 million metric tons of raw materials per year.
This strike was the farthest from Ukraine’s state border since the start of the full-scale invasion. The previous record was set in July 2026, when a modernized FP-1 struck the Omsk Oil Refinery at a distance of about 2,500 km.
The Ukrainian company Fire Point reported its involvement in the attack. It is believed the company’s FP-1 long-range strike drone was used to strike the facility.

European Central Bank chief warns inflation to remain well above target for extended period
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:51:12 UTC
23:51:12 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde warned Thursday that the war in the Middle East and recent developments in Russia’s war against Ukraine would keep headline inflation well above the bank’s 2% target for an extended period.
Lagarde spoke to reporters in Berlin after the ECB Governing Council raised its three key interest rates by 25 basis points.
“The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period,” she said.
Lagarde noted that short-term inflation expectations remained elevated but said the ECB continued to foresee stabilization in the medium term.
She stressed that the bank remained committed to setting monetary policy to ensure inflation stabilizes at its 2% target.
The Governing Council adopted the rate decision unanimously, she said, adding that the outlook remained highly uncertain, with risks tilted upward for inflation and downward for growth.
Lagarde said the Governing Council did not discuss possible future moves and that looking too far ahead would have little value because economic conditions were changing rapidly.
The ECB would remain focused on incoming data, with its next move impossible to predict, she added.   
Economy, inflation surprise ECB
Lagarde acknowledged that the resilience of the eurozone economy and recent inflation figures had surprised the Governing Council.
The ECB had anticipated stronger pressure from food prices, while headline inflation was now expected to remain elevated for longer than initially projected. The developments were incorporated into its updated forecasts. 
Bond markets closely monitored
Addressing rising global bond yields, Lagarde said changes in the balance between supply and demand were among the main drivers.
Growing corporate funding needs and artificial intelligence investment were contributing to increased activity in global bond markets, while the size of the US market was also playing a role.
“At the ECB, we are monitoring developments in the bond market very closely, particularly with regard to long-term interest rates,” she said.
Lagarde also stressed the importance of the digital euro, saying digital central bank money had become necessary and would reduce Europe’s dependence on non-eurozone actors.
Responding to reports that she could step down before her term expires next fall, Lagarde said, “If there were any developments regarding my personal future, they would be announced immediately. At this point, there is nothing to announce.”

Poland unveils a new jet-powered strike drone

2026-09-10
14:49:32 UTC
23:49:32 KST

- WB Group unveiled Gladius 2, also called Warmate 30, a turbojet-powered loitering munition with a reduced radar and heat signature and a 30 kg warhead.
- The Polish company has not disclosed the weapon's range, speed, cost or production timeline, or whether it is covered by Poland's existing Gladius contracts.
Polish defense manufacturer WB Group has unveiled Gladius 2, a new loitering munition built for a reduced radar and heat signature and powered by a turbojet engine for a fast run into the target area.
The company also refers to the weapon as Warmate 30, tying it to WB Group’s existing Warmate family of strike drones.
The munition carries an interchangeable 30 kg (66 lb) warhead and can be fired from a shipping container or from a dedicated launcher vehicle. WB Group designed Gladius 2 to work with its broader Gladius reconnaissance-strike system, which pairs the FT-5 Łoś reconnaissance drone with strike effectors under a battle-management system called Topaz, letting an operator spot a target with one aircraft and destroy it with another.
Gladius 2 builds on the original Gladius system, which WB Group has offered with a range of more than 100 km (62 miles) using earlier, electrically powered Warmate variants. Development work on the newer version began in September 2022 and has drawn on lessons from the war in Ukraine, according to the company. WB Group first showed early visuals of the Gladius 2 effector at industry events earlier in 2026 and has said it plans to give the system its first full public unveiling at MSPO, Poland’s main defense trade show in Kielce.
WB Group names its Warmate variants for their warhead weight. The company has previously said it was developing Warmate 5, Warmate 20 and Warmate 50 models alongside the lighter Warmate 3, which carries a smaller warhead out to 70 km (43 miles). Warmate 30 places the new design between those weight classes, with a 30 kg warhead matching the payload of what WB Group has also called Warmate 2 in past product literature.
The Polish military has already committed billions of złoty to expanding its Gladius and Warmate inventories. In May 2026, Poland’s Armaments Agency signed contracts with WB Group for more than 400 Warmate loitering munition systems, nearly 200 FlyEye reconnaissance drones and 12 battery-level fire modules for the Gladius system, financed in part through the European Union’s SAFE defense-loan program. WB Group has not said whether Gladius 2 or Warmate 30 is included in that order or represents a separate future offering.

Ukraine&apos;s partners in the Freyja anti-ballistic program are working on its implementation 24/7 — Fire Point CEO
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:49:29 EEST
23:49:29 KST

Ukraine's partners in the Freyja anti-ballistic program are working on its implementation 24/7 — Fire Point CEO
Kyiv • UNN
The Freyja anti-ballistic system will have an open architecture and at least two versions of each critical subsystem.
Most European companies involved in implementing the Freyja antiballistic program are working on the project according to Ukrainian timeframes — 24/7. CEO of leading Ukrainian defense company Fire Point Iryna Terekh said this during a panel discussion at the MSPO International Defence Industry Exhibition in Poland, as reported by UNN correspondent.
Iryna Terekh said that she had returned from Oslo the previous day, where a meeting of the steering committee was held with the companies participating in the Freyja project. Such meetings are held regularly to coordinate work at a high level.
"It is a kind of information update at a very high level. And what I particularly like is that most of the participants in the Freyja project are European companies. They work according to Ukrainian timeframes. So, to answer the technical question, 24/7 — they are very committed to this work," she said.
According to her, Freyja is a priority project, since intercepting ballistic missiles is one of the greatest challenges in the defense industry. Iryna Terekh emphasized that the project's level of ambition is extremely high, but that its implementation is possible.
"Is it easy? No. But is it possible to do? Absolutely, yes. Because we have the best people on the ground to create an independent European antiballistic shield," the Fire Point CEO said.
Iryna Terekh also recalled that Freyja would operate according to somewhat different principles compared with a conventional air defense system. In particular, the system will not have a kill switch, that is, a remote shutdown capability; it is to be interoperable and not dependent on a single supplier. According to her, Freyja is being built on a "Lego" principle, which will allow different manufacturers to join the project and integrate their components.
"This requires an open architecture, a common protocol, and the sharing of intellectual property so that none of the participants has the ability to shut down the program. We also do not want to depend on one particular supplier. And we also expect to have at least two options for each critically important subsystem to ensure its compatibility and replaceability," she added.
To add
Earlier, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy together with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a meeting with the heads of defense companies from partner countries dedicated to implementing the Freyja antiballistic program. The meeting was attended by the heads of the defense companies FirePoint, Kongsberg, Weibel, Saab, Diehl Defence, Hensoldt, Thales, Safran, Sener, and Leonardo. The parties agreed on what exactly leaders and government officials should do at their level, while manufacturers and developers should do at theirs.
What is Freyja
Freyja is a Ukraine-initiated project for a joint European antiballistic system, the first track of the Antiballistic Coalition, which comprises 10 countries and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to ensure the interception of Russian ballistic missiles.
The project is being built around the Ukrainian FP-7.x interceptor missile developed by Fire Point, while other components are supplied by European manufacturers. As Fire Point General and Technical Director Iryna Terekh told UNN, development has reached the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem — radars, the launcher, the data transmission channel, and the command center — while tests are being conducted up to twice a week. The system's first interception of a ballistic target is scheduled for 2027.

Apple makes biggest change to iPhone release cadence in 7 years in Ternus' first showcase as CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:45:52 UTC
23:45:52 KST

In John Ternus' debut showcase as CEO, Apple unveiled a swarm of new products, including its first foldable phone called the iPhone Duo, as well as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max with a larger screen.
But the biggest news for investors from Wednesday's event may be the absence of an iPhone 18 without the Pro moniker.
Analysts in recent months have largely expected this shift in Apple's annual cadence, and foresee Apple releasing its mainline iPhone at an event in the spring, when the company has previously announced new low-cost models, including the iPhone SE and iPhone 16e.
The least expensive new iPhone announced on Wednesday was the iPhone 18 Pro, which starts at $1,199 in the U.S., representing a $100 price increase. Prior to the event, the iPhone 17 cost $799, but was listed at $899 afterwards. Apple raised prices of Macs and iPads in June in response to a global shortage in memory and other components that former CEO Tim Cook called "unsustainable" in an interview with the Wall Street Journal.
Ternus replaced Cook at the helm on Sept. 1, becoming just the second Apple CEO since Steve Jobs resigned in 2011 shortly before his death. Cook has warned that supply constraints will persist, and the company noted during its earnings call in July that it would become an even bigger issue for the company during the September quarter.
Holding the mainstream iPhones until the spring is a new tactic for Apple. Industry analysts said on Wednesday that the company has been looking to smooth out its revenue from quarter to quarter, and could potentially achieve that with the split-launch strategy.
Historically, Apple's biggest quarter has been its first fiscal quarter, which is the first full quarter of iPhone sales and also includes Christmas. The two quarters that follow are typically much slower.
A big iPhone launch in March or April with a lower-priced device would do a lot to smooth out Apple's sales during its slower season, analysts said .
"When Apple puts all the focus on the last quarter of the year, of course that generates quite strong revenues, but they were missing when the second quarter comes along with with much lower sales," said Francisco Jeronimo, a vice president at market researcher IDC, in an interview. "I think this will give them some stability in terms of balancing the revenues throughout the year."
Last decade, Apple split its iPhone lineup into two broad parts when it released the iPhone 11 and a more expensive Pro version with its best displays and cameras. Since then, Apple has announced its Pro and standard phones at the same fall event with identical release dates.
Apple's average selling prices (ASPs) have been going up in recent years, as its Pro phones sell better than the mainline options. The new approach plays into that trend, but has potential downsides, according to Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan.
"In our view, the split launch could support mix and ASPs," Mohan wrote in a note this week. But, he added, it "creates some risk that price-sensitive consumers defer upgrades until the lower-priced models arrive."
In the first half of 2026, Apple's iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max represented 54% of iPhone sales, according to IDC estimates. The regular iPhone 17 represented 26% of iPhone sales.
"That's how Apple has been playing the game as as the market started to slow down in terms of of smartphone adoption and upgrades," Jeronimo said.
There's also a supply chain play at work. Releasing only two new models instead of four could significantly simplify what Apple has to secure from its supply chain, said Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research. 
"High memory pricing is not helping Apple launch multiple iPhones at the same time," Shah said. 
At the close of Wednesday's event, the company introduced the foldable iPhone Duo, which will start at $1,999, in line with competitive offerings from companies like Huawei.
Craig Federighi, senior vice president of software engineering, said Apple had redesigned much of its iOS software to take advantage of the two screens, moving buttons and other controls. Users can multitask with two apps at the same time and can use Apple's stylus called Pencil.
"For a device that plays such a central role in your life, a larger display would open up entirely new possibilities," Ternus said at the launch. "We think the best way to achieve that is with a foldable design."
The phone will be powered by the new C2 modem, the second-generation modem Apple has made in-house and a move that further reduces reliance on Qualcomm. Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer, said in the keynote video that C2 is 50% faster than its predecessor and runs at 15% lower energy.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
- Rate increase comes at ‘inopportune time for Germany,’ says ifo President Clemens Fuest
- Harm of inaction to ECB’s credibility would have been greater, says ING economist Carsten Brzeski
Economists described the European Central Bank’s (ECB) decision Thursday to raise its key interest rates by 25 basis points as an inevitable “insurance” move against inflationary pressures.
The ECB Governing Council raised the deposit facility rate, its key monetary policy benchmark, from 2.25% to 2.50%.
The rates on the main refinancing operations and marginal lending facility were also increased to 2.65% and 2.90%, respectively. The new rates will take effect Sept. 16.
Economists said the move was necessary for the eurozone, but warned of the potential effect on Germany’s already weak economy.   
Rate hike comes at inopportune time for Germany
Clemens Fuest, president of the Munich-based ifo Institute, said the interest rate hike was unavoidable, noting that eurozone inflation is above 3%.
“In Germany, inflation is somewhat lower. Given an economy that, despite some bright spots, remains quite weak, the interest rate hike comes at an inopportune time for Germany,” said Fuest. “However, the ECB has a mandate to conduct monetary policy for the entire eurozone.”
Fuest said the ECB had to act as core inflation also remained significantly above its 2% target. 
Move aimed at staying ahead of curve
Carsten Brzeski, ING’s global head of macro research and chief economist for Germany, described the increase in the deposit rate to 2.50% as an “insurance” rate hike.
He said the move demonstrated that the ECB remained highly vigilant and sought to stay ahead of the curve by preventing higher energy prices from spreading through the broader economy.
The recent escalation in the Middle East and the surge in oil prices had strengthened the case for an increase, he said, although indicators, including core and services inflation, continued to show limited second-round effects from higher energy costs.
Brzeski noted that lifting the policy rate to the upper end of what the ECB considers its neutral range did not carry a significant risk of making monetary policy excessively restrictive.
“The harm of doing nothing, at least for the ECB’s credibility, is clearly larger,” he said.
Brzeski, however, warned that additional rate increases would be more complicated, stressing that there was a significant difference between a resilient economy and an overheating economy requiring restrictive monetary policy.
With public finances under pressure and bond yields rising rapidly, the ECB would be unlikely to intensify the strain, he said.

BERLIN, September 10. /TASS/. The decision to close the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg and Goethe-Institut branches in Russia came as a tit-for-tat response to Berlin’s unfriendly steps to undermine Russian-German relations, the Russian Embassy in Germany said in a statement.
"Laments by certain German officials, politicians, public figures and the media about the upcoming closure of the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg and Goethe-Institut branches in Russia are met with surprise. Being fully aware that Russia’s actions are nothing but a mirror response to Berlin’s unprecedented, unprovoked measures aimed at dismantling Russian-German relations, they still continue to describe the situation as 'glaring injustice,'" the embassy said.
The embassy recalled that "the closures of Russia’s Consulate General in Bonn, the country’s largest consular mission abroad, and of the Russian House of Science and Culture in Berlin, the world’s largest Russian House, were triggered by allegations of Russian involvement in the incident involving a malfunctioning drone that was discovered at Leipzig on the night of August 5, 2026."
"There has been no evidence and no arguments, only the familiar ‘highly likely’ rhetoric and an unprecedentedly disproportionate reaction, which other EU countries obediently joined at Berlin’s signal," the statement reads.
At the same time, Russian diplomats called it notable that "the German side describes its actions as a 'measured and proportionate' response to Russia’s 'hybrid threats.'"
The Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Monday that, in response to Germany's unfriendly actions, Russia would close the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg and Goethe cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk.
In accordance with the decision, Russia is revoking its consent to the operation of the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg, so it must cease operations no later than September 18, and all its employees must leave Russia. Furthermore, Russia is closing the German Goethe Cultural Center, and its employees have been ordered to leave the country by September 13.
On September 1, the German government officially placed responsibility for the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August on Russia and announced the cessation of the Russian House, the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, and other measures. Russian President Vladimir Putin pointed out that Germany's new anti-Russian decisions, taken under the pretext of the drone incident at Leipzig Airport, are yet another grave mistake by the German authorities, contrary to the interests of their people. In his opinion, these decisions are linked to the domestic political situation in that country and, in particular, the difficult situation of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Spanish spies warned Madrid day before Ceuta migrant invasion

Spanish spies warned Madrid day before Ceuta migrant invasion
Spanish intelligence warned of plans for migrants to breach Ceuta’s border by land and sea just a day before tens of thousands of people poured into the enclave from Morocco, newly declassified documents show.
The revelations have fueled accusations that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government failed to give the full story about what it knew before the crisis.
The small Spanish territory on the North African coast has faced severe pressure since more than 70,000 people crossed from Morocco in late July. Most have since returned or been sent back, but thousands remain, straining local services and fueling criticism of Madrid’s handling of the crisis.
Ceuta Mayor-President Juan Jesus Vivas warned that the enclave is “on the brink of collapse” and accused Morocco of pursuing a “policy of harassment.” Speaking in Brussels on Tuesday, he urged the EU to take a tougher stance toward Rabat and accused Sanchez’s government of failing to respond adequately before, during, and after the crisis.
The Spanish government released 40 declassified documents on Wednesday, including intelligence reports, alerts, and communications from security agencies. In a July 29 note to Moroccan intelligence, Spain’s National Intelligence Center (CNI) said it had identified Facebook and WhatsApp groups promoting an attempt by migrants to enter Ceuta the following day “both swimming and via the [border] fence,” potentially taking advantage of Morocco’s Throne Day celebrations.
The CNI also alerted Madrid’s representative in Ceuta to calls for “an assault on the fence and by sea” at 8 PM the following day and sent similar warnings to Spain’s Civil Guard. “There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers. Just to give you an idea of the scale,” the agency wrote about the online mobilization.
Once thousands began crossing, a Spanish Defense Ministry intelligence report described Moroccan forces as passive and negligent in stopping them. “It cannot be ruled out that Morocco may attempt to exploit the situation that has arisen in Ceuta to further its strategic interests,” the assessment said.
Sanchez has maintained that Madrid had no warning capable of predicting what happened. He told lawmakers last week that intelligence had not anticipated the “scale or probability” of the influx, while insisting that Moroccan police had “allowed the border to be crossed.” He had previously told parliament there was “no information” indicating the magnitude of the crisis Spain would face in the final days of July.
The crisis has triggered a political backlash in Spain and put Ceuta’s services under severe strain. Protests have demanded faster deportations and targeted Sanchez’s government, with demonstrators reportedly chanting “Sanchez, traitor, resign.”
Vivas has warned that the situation is “untenable,” telling Brussels this week: “If Ceuta falls, Europe falls.”
