In an interview with FRANCE 24, former football star and current president of the Cameroonian Football Federation Samuel Eto'o spoke about the recent backlash towards FIFA president Gianni Infantino and confirmed he will support him for re-election because of "everything he has brought to African football", adding that the African federations will defend what seems "right to us given the challenges that we face in our own federations".
Gianni Infantino, the president of the International Federation of Association Football (FIFA) is still in hot water because of his plan to sell stakes of the World Cup to private investors which has sparked a massive outcry. Despite the project being abandoned, the European, Asian and North American confederations have called for his departure. The African Confederation of Football (CAF) which has unanimously sided with him, however.
"We don't face the same challenges as those in Europe or South America for some cases. Our budgets are limited yet we are expected to perform just as well as those major footballing nations. So, I think for that reason alone, and I'm sure you'll agree with me, that we can't broach this issue from the same point of view", says Eto'o.
And while the European Football Federation (UEFA) is preparing a complaint against Gianni Infantino, Samuel Eto'o explains that "UEFA will defend its own interests. And it's perfectly normal for them to do so, just as it is normal for Africans to defend their own interests". Asked about the African continent’s support for Infantino, he added: "We are trying to come together to defend what seems right to us, given the challenges that we face in our own federations".
"I will vote for Gianni Infantino"
The president of the Cameroonian Football Federation also spoke about his relationship with the FIFA president, saying "in my heart, president Gianni has become, well beyond the world of football, a brother, a big brother, a friend, someone we watched to come to the fore, someone we've supported, with whom we have built things together that serves football".
Gianni Infantino is officially running for re-election at a congress scheduled in a few weeks. He needs a simple majority of the 211 federations and the 54 members of CAF for another mandate as president. "If I remain president of the Cameroonian Football Federation, I will vote for him for everything he has brought to African football" confirms Eto'o. "But, in addition to that, I will campaign among my fellow presidents so that for once all 54 presidents of the Confederation of African Football will vote in favour of Gianni. I believe President Gianni is the one who has brought the most to Africa."
On the other side, Constant Omari, a former president of the Congolese Football Federation, has called for Infantino to resign. He claims that African football leaders are morally corrupt, and he believes Gianni Infantino holds compromising information on the continent's federations. "On this particular question though, and I made this clear to president Constant, I am fully aligned behind president Infantino and I will campaign for president Infantino to win once again", Eto'o underlined.
"Since I have been at FIFA, I'm sorry to say, but I haven't yet heard a single exchange that was given under some form of threat. In my own confederation, however, and I always made this very clear with President Motsepe, I haven't always agreed with his administration and I haven't always agreed with those who were in place", he added.
"I'm very happy at the Cameroonian Football Federation"
Patrice Motsepe, the president of Confederation of African Football, has announced a few weeks ago that he will not run for another term in 2029. Asked about his own ambitions on the continental scene, Eto'o assured that today he is "very happy at the Cameroonian Football Federation" and "we still have many challenges to overcome, and we will keep working to ensure that victories keep coming our way".

Germany sets its sights on Russia's shadow fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:31:00 UTC
23:31:00 KST

Germany sets its sights on Russia's shadow fleet
September 11, 2026
On September 1, when the German government publicly blamed Russia for the failed drone attack on Leipzig Airport, it announced a series of retaliatory measures.
Among them was a tougher crackdown on the so-called Russian shadow fleet. The term refers to often aging, poorly maintained and inadequately insured vessels, mostly oil tankers, with opaque ownership structures, which Russia uses in an attempt to circumvent sanctions.
But detaining such vessels is far from straightforward, Julian Pawlak, a maritime security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, told DW. International maritime law, he noted, is fundamentally designed to protect the freedom of commercial shipping.
"The transport of these goods on the high seas is not, in itself, illegal," Pawlak explains. "What complicates matters is that parts of this shadow fleet are linked to so-called hybrid activities, including acts of sabotage, espionage and possibly drone operations and related disruptions."
Germany has not done enough to address the issue so far, argues Sara Nanni, a security policy spokesperson for the Green Party.
In a recent interview with DW, she complained, "Russia is financing both its war against Ukraine and its aggressive behavior toward Europe through its shadow fleet."
Action must be taken against it, she said. "That is the only thing that could persuade Russia to return to the negotiating table."
She accuses the German government of failing to take action. "Other countries are doing it in the Baltic Sea, but Germany isn't. I keep hearing the interior minister say that it is technically or legally difficult. But I believe the decision not to do it is a political one. And I think it is wrong."
Finland shows another way to tackle the shadow fleet
By "other countries," she is referring, for example, to Finland. In late 2024, the tanker "Eagle S" damaged the Estlink 2 power cable in the Gulf of Finland by dragging an anchor across the seabed. Finnish border guards subsequently detained the vessel.
Although a court later dismissed charges of aggravated criminal damage, Sönke Marahrens, a security expert at Kiel University, praised the Finnish response in an interview with DW: "They sent a clear message to the other side: We know what you're doing, and we're stopping you. And you could see that after this clear warning, the other side got the message and changed its behavior."
In addition to Finland, the United Kingdom, France and Sweden have also adopted a tougher approach toward suspicious vessels. Within its territorial waters, the Swedish Coast Guard specifically targets tankers and cargo ships suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet for inspection. Vessels are routinely detained if they are found to be carrying forged documents, lack adequate insurance, pose a risk to maritime safety or violate environmental regulations.
Russia's threats: just a bluff?
It is easy to assume that the German government's restraint aims to avoid escalation with Russia. That impression is reinforced by the fact that the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is considered right-wing extremist in parts, won the state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on a platform that, despite the war in Ukraine, advocates closer relations between Germany and Russia. According to opinion polls, concerns about the prospect of war in Europe were also a decisive factor for many voters. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, even described Germany's accusations against Moscow as "the beginning of a real war."
Johannes Peters of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, however, believes such fears are unfounded.
"Other European countries have taken a more robust approach, and despite those concerns, and indeed despite Russian rhetoric, very little has actually happened," Peters said.
"Russia has not escalated the situation. Instead, it has largely avoided confrontation. In particular, we have seen that laden tankers, which are extremely valuable, are now avoiding Swedish waters because Sweden has stepped up efforts to stop and inspect vessels."
After the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, "The federal government will make those responsible for hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for it."
Peters believes: "If you use strong rhetoric, sooner or later you have to back it up with action. The chancellor has put the government under pressure to follow through."
Armed Russian crews on board
Security expert Pawlak, however, cautions that inspecting suspicious Russian vessels is not without risk.
"Of course, any such operation has to take into account the possibility that Russian warships may be escorting these vessels or, as has increasingly been the case, that armed crews with ties to Russian mercenary groups may be on board," Pawlak said. "Those are risks that must be factored into the equation."
Estonia experienced those risks firsthand in the case of the oil tanker "Jaguar." In May 2025, the vessel's captain ignored instructions from the Estonian authorities while passing through the country's coastal waters. Estonian officials attempted to stop and inspect the suspicious tanker. Russia responded by scrambling a fighter jet, prompting Estonia to stand down and allow the vessel to continue on its way.
"It is important to consider the region in which these activities are taking place," Pawlak says. "In the Baltic Sea, Russia is naturally much closer geographically and therefore has other options at its disposal, including the deployment of military units in support." Farther afield, however, for example in the English Channel between the United Kingdom and France, that becomes more difficult: "Russia cannot escort or protect every shadow fleet vessel."
Inspections would raise costs for Russia
While maritime security specialist Johannes Peters firmly supports taking action against shadow-fleet vessels where justified, he cautions against harboring illusions.
"We are not going to be able to shut down this shadow-fleet system through inspections alone," he said. "Rather, the aim is to saddle Russia's shadow fleet with risks and uncertainties and to increase the costs of operating it."
He offers a simple example: "If only one ship a day can make the journey instead of three, that translates into losses of hundreds of millions of euros a day. If a voyage takes not x days but x plus four, that, too, cuts into Russia's earnings. And revenue from oil exports is vital to Russia's war economy."

What Germany's move to officially blame Russia for the suspected hybrid attack at Leipzig airport means for Germany and NATO was the topic of discussion in DW's weekly Berlin Briefing podcast.

Kremlin calls energy sector Ukraine's 'Achilles' heel' as it dismisses aerial truce
The Kremlin on Sept. 10 rebuffed U.S.-backed proposals for a mutual pause in aerial strikes between Ukraine and Russia, signaling that Moscow would continue striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Kyiv is not offering a "permanent settlement that would fully align with (Russian) interests" and merely seeks a truce in an area that is Ukraine's "Achilles' heel."
The comments come as a rejection of the latest U.S.-Ukraine proposal for an aerial truce, which was put forward during the visit of U.S. peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv last weekend.
Kyiv has repeatedly called for a full ceasefire along the current front lines as the first step toward peace talks, a proposal that the Kremlin has rejected as it continues to press its territorial demands.
Peskov alleged that Ukraine opened "Pandora's box" by carrying out strikes against economically important targets in Russia, noting that the Russian "military is carrying out large-scale, systematic, and planned attacks on the corresponding targets in Ukraine."
Russia has been systematically targeting Ukraine's energy grid since the first year of the full-scale war, inflicting heavy damage on the country's infrastructure and causing regular blackouts.
Ukraine, in turn, has been striking Russian oil refineries, depots, and other strategic targets to undercut Moscow's budget revenues and increase economic pressure on the Kremlin to end the war.
The Kremlin spokesperson reiterated that Russia's peace conditions have not changed.
Moscow has called for Ukraine to cede the entire Donbas region — a partially occupied and strategically important region in Ukraine's east — and relinquish its NATO membership ambitions.
Peskov's comments signal that the latest U.S. peace efforts have made little headway as Ukraine braces for a new wave of Russian strikes against its energy grid.

Survey: Swiss voters doubt politicians' abilities in global crises

Survey: Swiss voters doubt politicians’ abilities in global crises
A majority of Swiss voters doubt the country’s political system’s ability to take effective action. At the same time, they are in favour of closer international cooperation and greater government investment in the future.
These are the findings of a representative survey, as announced by the Swiss Society for Social Welfare (SGG) on Wednesday. The survey was carried out on behalf of the SGG by its think tank, Pro Futuris, and the University of Bern.
According to the survey, fewer than a third of respondents believe that Swiss politicians are capable of responding to global crises at an appropriate pace. A relative majority assessed Switzerland as poorly prepared for geopolitical and security challenges.
More
Swiss public backs development aid even as politicians cut budgets
In response, three-quarters of participants favour closer cooperation with other democracies. Around 60% prefer security cooperation with partners such as the European Union or NATO to extensive autonomy. Opinions were mixed regarding closer ties with the EU.
Domestically, respondents see the greatest challenges in healthcare costs, immigration and housing costs. Around 73% are in favour of the state investing more in areas such as research, education and infrastructure.
At the same time, a relative majority of 40% would like to see fewer economic regulations. However, just under 80% of respondents believe that businesses should take on more responsibility for the country’s economic standing. A majority also expects government action on the issue of artificial intelligence.
With this survey, the SGG has launched “Mission Suisse”. This “non-partisan and cross-sectoral initiative” aims to strengthen the capacity of Swiss democracy to take action.

‘I’m spending my savings just to survive’: Iran’s economic crisis fuels new protests
Despite severe security risks and an ongoing war, retirees, nurses, workers, teachers and students have held sit-ins and protests across Iran since this summer, most often over economic hardship. With prices going up every few hours, salaries and pensions going unpaid for months, and unemployment increasing, our Observers say life is becoming “impossible”.
Every week, the regime hands down severe sentences to arrested protesters, including death sentences. It also relentlessly arrests journalists, artists, activists and athletes for the slightest public expression of anti-regime views or for failing to observe restrictive Sharia rules on social media.
Over the past eight months, the Islamic regime in Tehran has executed at least 54 prisoners for political reasons, including 31 protesters who took part in the mass anti-regime protests in January, according to the Iran Human Rights Group based in Norway.
But many Iranians continue to protest despite the risks.

Since the US-Israeli war against Iran began on February 28, the country's already devastated economy has deteriorated further, creating unprecedented hardship. The situation has worsened since the Trump administration imposed a naval blockade on Iran in the Persian Gulf on April 13. Iran can now import very little through the country's main ports in the Persian Gulf and, more importantly, can export very little oil, a major source of government revenue. On August 29, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that the US naval blockade had caused Iran to lose 35 percent of its imports and exports.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
FRANCE 24 spoke to several Iranians who described their experiences of an economy in free fall amid an ongoing war and after decades of sanctions, mismanagement and corruption.
'Prices change hour by hour'
“Sirvan” is the CEO of a small startup or used to be. Since the war began, he has had to fire all of his employees and now runs the business alone. [We are concealing his identity for security reasons.]
 I can only describe the situation as “free fall”. A few months ago, I had to fire all 12 of my employees. I know many other employers who had to do the same.
Prices used to increase month by month or week by week. Now they change hour by hour, and I’m not exaggerating.
One day, I had an order and checked the price of a machine a client needed to replace. In the morning, it was around 180 million toman [€660, based on the exchange rate on September 9, 2026]. By noon, when I wanted to buy it, the price had risen to 220 million toman [€814]. I informed the client, and he changed his mind. He is trying to continue with the defective machinery he already has.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
A cellphone seller explained in a video posted on social media on September 7 how rapidly changing prices have made it increasingly difficult to run a business in Iran:
‘Doing business in Iran is a joke now. This morning, an online customer wanted to buy this cellphone. Its wholesale price for us was 70.8 million toman [€262, based on the exchange rate on September 9, 2026]. I told him the price was 72.8 million toman [€269]. He bought it and transferred the money.
Fifteen minutes later, when I wanted to send the cellphone to his address, the price in our system was updated. By then, I had to buy the phone myself for 71.8 million toman [€266].
Just a few minutes later, before we had even sent it to the customer, our online pricing system was updated again, and the price for us had increased to 72.8 million toman [€269]. So I had to send it to the customer without making any profit.
It doesn’t matter. I’m recording this video six hours after I sold the cellphone, and the wholesale price for us to buy the same phone is now 76.5 million toman [€283].’
'Importing has become a game of chess'
“Sirvan” continues:
 ‘It’s impossible to run a business in this situation. If I sell something now, I cannot replace it in my stock for the same price at which I sold it.
Part of the problem is the nonstop rise in the toman-dollar exchange rate. But this new situation has another cause. Since Trump imposed the naval blockade on Iran and the UAE refused Iranian ships access to its ports, importing anything has become a game of chess and an extremely costly process for any product we need to bring into the country.
All imports now come through overland routes, either by lorry or rail. It is complicated, slow and very expensive. We first have to send the goods from the exporting country to a neighbouring country, which adds another fee. Then we have to store them there, which adds another cost. After that, we have to bring them into Iran by rail or lorry, adding another exorbitant expense.
And once you finally have the product after paying all those costs, you still do not know how much you need to sell it for in order to have enough capital to buy it again through the same complicated system. So, in practice, almost no one can really do business.’
At least 40 percent of the Iranian population has fallen below the absolute poverty line, compared with 34 percent before the war, while another 40 percent is at risk of doing so, according to several estimates.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
'I sold my car, I have to sell my house too'
Amir is a 75-year-old retiree living in Tehran.
 After decades of hard work and earning what I would describe as an upper-middle-class living, I have now had to start working again. My pension does not even cover the first week of the month, and I’m one of the lucky ones: I receive my pension every month. There are millions of retired people who have not received theirs for months.
I work as a driver for Snap [editor’s note: Snap is the Iranian equivalent of Uber].
Before that, I had to sell my car and buy a cheaper one, using the remaining money to pay for my wife’s medicines and medical bills. I could no longer afford them. Some medicines are difficult to find, and they are expensive.
We now want to sell our house and buy two apartments in a cheaper neighbourhood. We would live in one, and my daughter would live in the other. She can no longer afford her monthly rent despite working full time.
According to the director of the Iranian retirement syndicate, as of September 7, the Iranian government had not paid pensions for five months.
'I literally have four jobs'
Nilou is a young graphic artist. While the minimum wage in Iran is around 17 million toman [€63, based on the exchange rate on September 9, 2026], Nilou says she recently paid almost €30 for a small amount of chicken and meat.
 I’m tired. I’m depressed. I see no future ahead of me. I literally have four jobs. I work for three companies as a graphic designer, and I also work in a shop as a salesperson. But over the past couple of months, I have no longer been able to keep up with the rising prices.
For years, I managed to build up a small amount of savings. I had bought gold ingots and dollars as savings, but now I’m selling them little by little just to pay the bills and survive. I live alone; I don’t eat much. But just a few days ago, I had to pay 1.5 million toman for some fruit [5.50 €, calculation based on exchange rate on Sept 9, 2026]. For a little chicken and meat, I paid around 8 million toman [29.70 €], and that will last only two weeks. Some shampoos and conditioners cost 6 million toman. [22 €]
In a few months, when I have spent all my savings, I will no longer be able to afford this life. I think I will have to move into my parents’ apartment. What we have is not a life. I’m sure that if the situation continues like this, people will organise another huge protest, despite the massacre we endured just a few months ago.
Estimates suggest that Iran’s annual inflation rate reached as high as 80 percent in August 2026, rising to around 130 percent for food.

Swiss firms fear exclusion from EU innovation procurement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

Swiss firms fear exclusion from EU innovation procurement
The European Commission intends to reform the European Union's public procurement market. This could prevent innovative Swiss firms from bidding for funds.
The EU aims to promote innovation within member states. Public funds are also to be channelled into these initiatives. New rules may soon be introduced that govern how these funds are allocated.
This is an important decision for Switzerland, a centre for research and development that is closely intertwined with Europe. However, according to the EC’s proposal, Swiss companies will, in principle, not be allowed to bid for the public procurement funds.
The funding is aimed at new experimental technologies – solutions that local authorities or public enterprises want to procure but which are not yet available on the market.
Examples include robots for hospitals or artificial intelligence (AI) software for rubbish collection.
The EC wants to simplify this area of public procurement. This is because, out of every €100 (CHF94) spent on public procurement in Europe, only 60 cents is currently invested in innovative projects. The equivalent figure in the United States is 50 cents for every €7, according to the EC.
More
The Swiss-EU bilateral treaty updates, explained
The EU wants to catch up and thereby strengthen innovative sectors in Europe. According to EU Commissioner Ekaterina Zareva, this should be done on a cross-border basis.
Key technologies
Very often, key technologies are too expensive to develop within a single member state. Like other procurement regulations, the new law provides for a European preference.
Some 50% of the funding is to remain within the EU or in countries with relevant agreements. These include the European Economic Area (EEA) states and countries in the Balkans. Switzerland does not have such an agreement.
As a non-member, it cannot benefit from its status as a major centre for research and innovation. The exclusion, however, is not directed against Switzerland, the EU Commissioner said.
Once Switzerland ratifies the Bilateral III accords, which would clarify its relationship with the EU, Swiss companies could also benefit, according to sources in Brussels.
More
Cantonal majority: an obstacle that could scupper the Swiss-EU deal
Swiss concerns
The fact that the EU gives preference to its own market is not entirely new. But representatives of the Swiss business community are concerned.
Stefan Brubacher, director of Swissmem, the association representing the mechanical engineering, electrical and metalworking industries, expressed disappointment. “This naturally harms Switzerland, but above all it harms the EU,” he said.
“Swiss companies and universities are among the best and most important partners, including our research infrastructure. Our companies have a great deal to contribute in this area,” said Brubacher.
This leaves Switzerland in the position of having to convince the EU to include it in the new rules governing innovation procurement.

A judge in Moscow has sentenced Andrei Kushanryov, a former senior executive at the state nanotechnology corporation Rosnano, to nine years in prison after finding him guilty of embezzling billions of rubles meant for the development of a high-tech memory chip.
State prosecutors had accused Kushnaryov of conspiring with former Rosnano deputy board chairman Yury Udaltsov and others to misappropriate public funds between 2013 and 2021, when he served as investment managing director at the state corporation and CEO of its subsidiary Crocus Nanoeletronics.
Udaltsov reportedly fled from Russia to Germany in 2015 and remains wanted.
Prosecutors said the funds were allocated to launch Russian production of MRAM chips in partnership with France’s Crocus Technology. Investigators had alleged that more than 7.5 billion rubles ($89.2 million) went missing from a total budget of nearly 12 billion rubles.
“Kushnaryov and the others never intended to develop new nanotechnology projects and knew full well that the project would never actually be carried out,” Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office said in a statement.
Kushnaryov, who pleaded not guilty, was ordered to pay a fine of 76 million rubles ($904,000) and barred from holding senior corporate roles for two and a half years.
A judge at the Gagarinsky District Court also granted Rosnano’s lawsuit against Kushnaryov for 7.5 billion rubles in damages.
The ruling is the latest in a legal crackdown against former executives of Rosnano, which former Kremlin adviser and veteran reformer Anatoly Chubais headed for over a decade.

artist gerhard richter designs hexagonal doha pavilion from his strip paintings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:29:21 UTC
23:29:21 KST

A Gerhard Richter painting can begin with a photograph and end as something far more experimental. In Doha, one of those studies is becoming a building. The German artist has designed a permanent hexagonal gallery pavilion for MIA Park that takes the visual system behind his Strip paintings and expands it into a space visitors can walk inside. Realized with Selldorf Architects, Doha Pavilion: Gerhard Richter will open on November 20th, 2026, beside the Museum of Islamic Art.
Its six exterior walls are wrapped in repeating printed patterns derived from Richter’s 2011 artist’s book Patterns. The source goes back another year, when Richter digitally divided an image of his Abstract Painting (724-4) fromdes 1990 into two vertical strips, then kept subdividing the image until it reached 8,192. Each strip was mirrored and repeated into a horizontal symmetrical pattern. What began as a way of taking a painting apart now covers the surface of the building.
gerhard richter’s images multiply along the interior
Three large-scale Strip paintings line the interior walls of the Gerhard Richter pavilion in Qatar, which push the same process almost to the limit of what the eye can register. Each horizontal band corresponds to a slice of the original photograph only 0.08 millimeters wide. At the center, the artist places Strip Tower, a freestanding sculpture designed specifically for the pavilion, lifting the bands away from the wall and into the room.
Two floor-to-ceiling Mirrors occupy the narrower walls between the paintings. Richter has worked with mirrors since the 1980s, and here they make the pavilion behave differently as people move through it. Paintings repeat across their surfaces, visitors enter the image, and the compact interior seems to stretch far beyond its actual footprint. The room becomes part gallery and part optical device.
architectural model of Doha Pavilion Gerhard Richter | image courtesy of Selldorf Architects
an idea that began with a visit to doha
Richter traces the pavilion back to a trip to Doha in 2013, two years after he began developing the Strip paintings. He recalls the city’s architecture and history giving him the idea for a structure that could bring several threads of the work together. ‘The Pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the Patterns that first led me to the Strips,‘ he explains. ‘Doha is the right place and the only place for my Pavilion.‘
The repeated symmetry across the facade also draws a connection to the geometries of Islamic art, where patterns can continue far beyond the visible edge of a surface. Here, that logic passes through Richter’s digital process and comes back at architectural scale. A stone sculpture titled Brunnen (Well) sits directly outside, extending the work into MIA Park.
architectural model of Doha Pavilion Gerhard Richter | image courtesy of Selldorf Architects
opening with the first Rubaiya Qatar
The pavilion will be inaugurated on November 20th, one day before the opening of the first Rubaiya Qatar, a new international visual arts quadrennial running through April 30, 2027. More than 50 regional and international artists will participate across museums and public sites in Doha, with Richter’s pavilion joining the city as a permanent work after the inaugural edition closes.
There is something pleasingly circular about where Richter’s process has ended up. One painting was photographed, divided again and again, mirrored across thousands of slivers, and eventually translated into the walls of a building. Inside, those fragments return as paintings and sculpture while the mirrors pull whoever enters into the composition. A digital experiment from more than a decade ago has gained a fixed address in Doha.
commissioned by:Qatar Museums | @qatar_museums location: MIA Park, Museum of Islamic Art, Doha, Qatar opening: November 20th, 2026 works inside: three Strip paintings, two floor-to-ceiling Mirrors, Strip Tower exterior work: Brunnen (Well)

US producer inflation tops expectations as energy costs jump amid Iran war
The Producer Price Index was up 5.4 per cent year-on-year last month, a significant acceleration from the 4.8 per cent rise in July
US wholesale inflation picked up more than expected in August, government data showed Thursday, driven by higher energy costs in the month – particularly for diesel – as the US war with Iran continued.
Rising prices at the pump are squeezing US households and businesses weeks ahead of key midterm elections, pressuring President Donald Trump’s administration, as average diesel costs hit new highs.
The Producer Price Index (PPI) was up 5.4 per cent year-on-year last month, the Department of Labour said. This was a significant acceleration from the 4.8 per cent rise in July and above the 5.3 per cent that economists expected in a consensus forecast published by MarketWatch.
On a month-on-month basis, PPI rose by 0.4 per cent, in line with analysts’ expectations published by MarketWatch.
Energy costs jumped by 4.2 per cent over the month, notably boosted by the cost of diesel fuel, which surged 24.1 per cent, the Labour Department report said.

How a new tool in Lithuania helps people read letters from their Jewish ancestors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:28:32 UTC
23:28:32 KST

At a family reunion in California in 2013, Felicita Trueblood discovered a portal to the past: a binder full of letters from her great-grandfather, a rabbi in Ukraine, from before World War II.
As exciting as the discovery was, the letters were illegible to her - until now, thanks to an artificial intelligence tool developed by Sergii Gurbych, a researcher in Lithuania who hungered for information about his own Jewish past. They unveiled a world of grief but also brought Trueblood solace, uncovering the truth about her great-grandfather’s death.
The letters, about 50 pages in total, had sat untouched for decades in her cousin’s house in Palm Springs. They were penned in Yiddish by Pavel Malisoff, Trueblood’s great-grandfather in Konotop, Ukraine - then in the Soviet Union - to his son, Trueblood’s great-uncle Solomon, who immigrated to the United States and changed his last name to Malis.
Between 1927 and 1934, the letters bridged two worlds - on one side, a father in Ukraine witnessing a community on the brink of destruction, and on the other, a son journeying from New York to California under the weight of the Great Depression. Malis died in 1985. For nearly a century, no one else read those pages.
At the 2013 reunion, none of the living family members could decipher their ancestor’s Yiddish letters, written in Hebrew script. Trueblood, who is now 75, felt compelled to take charge of the treasure trove. She grew up in San Diego with few traces of her Jewish past. Her mother, Malisoff’s granddaughter, became a Christian Scientist before marrying her father, a non-Jewish descendant of colonial Americans. Trueblood wanted to know who her great-grandfather was and the life he inhabited, long cut off from her family memory.
“I was raised outside the Jewish community, with no day-to-day connection,” Trueblood told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. “But I was always fascinated.”
Trueblood soon ran into obstacles. She found only a handful of translators who could help decipher the handwritten letters, and the cost of hiring them to work through the whole stack was prohibitively high.
VILNISH turns handwritten Hebrew, Yiddish letters into digital text
But 13 years after inheriting the letters, she saw a Facebook post about VILNISH, a new project in Lithuania that aims to turn handwritten and historical printed texts in Yiddish and Hebrew into digital texts that can be easily searched and translated.
Gurbych, a researcher at Vilnius University’s Center for the Study of East European Jewish History, built the AI model behind VILNISH, which launched late last year. Born in Ukraine, Gurbych studied Hebrew and Yiddish alongside electrical engineering. At Vilnius University, he focuses on developing digital approaches to analyzing archival Jewish texts.
Gurbych is particularly interested in texts written between World War I and World War II, when Jewish cultural and intellectual life flourished in Vilnius. In 1925, Vilnius became the first headquarters of the Yiddish Scientific Institute, or YIVO, which continues to preserve the Yiddish language and Eastern European Jewish heritage in New York City.
Gurbych turned to a wealth of diaries, memoirs, and other documents written by Jews in the interwar period and stored in the National Library of Lithuania. They provided the perfect material to teach a language model to recognize handwritten texts from the period. As he trains VILNISH on more and more handwriting types, it becomes a more universal tool.
Soon after Gurbych publicized the service, he began to hear from people like Trueblood, who sought to read letters left behind by their relatives.
Their urge to connect with the past was familiar to Gurbych. His own grandfather was a Jew born in 1915 in the Polish city of Łódź. During the Holocaust, he escaped the Łódź Ghetto days before its liquidation by the Nazis, when most of the 67,000 Jews who lived there were killed. Gurbych’s grandfather settled in present-day Ukraine, then part of the Soviet Union.
Gurbych is drawn to pieces of writing that evoke the atmosphere, the tastes and smells of life for Jews in Poland before their communities were destroyed.
“I want to know more about the world where my grandfather lived,” said Gurbych. “He died in 2001, and I just feel that I didn’t speak with him about this time enough. He was a person who lived in the Soviet Union, so he was just closed, and didn’t very much like to talk about his Jewish background and about life in interwar Poland.”
Trueblood contacted Gurbych in May. Within a month, he sent her translations of all her great-grandfather’s letters. She was stunned by the vivid images of Malisoff’s life in Konotop, marked by poverty and separation. All of his 11 children were forced to relocate across the Soviet Union or immigrate to Canada and the United States.
Konotop was racked by famine during Stalin’s rapid forced collectivization of agriculture. Malisoff described “people walking half naked, hungry, with only a few coins in their pockets, without a piece of bread, without proper clothing, silently, without work and without money.” The “spiritual condition” was destroyed, he wrote, as the Sabbath, the holidays, kosher food, circumcisions and religious teaching disappeared - “as though they had never existed.”
It wasn’t just an AI language model that supplied her these windows to the past, said Trueblood. Gurbych had the knowledge of Jewish history and religious tradition to explain the terms her great-grandfather, a rabbi, used and to point her toward the stories and texts he referenced.
“What I got back was just beautiful, because he understands the context, the history, the biblical references,” she said.
Trueblood discovers through VILNISH how her great-grandfather died
She also made a discovery that shifted her understanding of how her great-grandfather died. Trueblood and her other living relatives knew that Malisoff had been tortured by Stalin’s regime for receiving small packages of money from family members in California. They always believed that was how he died.
But after the letters from Malisoff stopped abruptly in 1934, other letters from his wife and children revealed the truth: Malisoff had died not from torture, but from a heart attack at 74. A letter from one of his children in the Soviet Union gave Trueblood the unexpected gift of her great-grandfather’s dignified death and memorial service.
“Our old father of blessed memory has passed away, but his good and beautiful name has not died,” the letter said. “It lives on, and will continue to live for many years. The town paid him the highest honors. The entire town, old and young alike, accompanied him on his final journey, and he was given the place of highest honor in accordance with his good deeds.”
Gurbych hopes that VILNISH will retrieve such memories for many more people like Trueblood, while also helping academic researchers who face huge sets of archival documents in Yiddish and Hebrew that few people can read.
The tool also has the potential to support the descendants of Jews who were persecuted during the Holocaust as they prepare materials to confirm their eligibility for repatriation or citizenship, such as synagogue records, internal rolls of Jewish communities, and other historical documents.
Trueblood was struck by how many others have yet to access threads to their past, as stacks of paper like hers sit untouched in attics and libraries.
“These letters are all over the world,” she said. “There are thousands of them out there that haven’t been translated.”

UK man charged with aiding Russian intelligence, planning drone factory sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:28:27 UTC
23:28:27 KST

A British man appeared in a London court on Thursday accused of providing information about factories that manufacture drones and offering to sabotage them on behalf of Russian intelligence.
Joshua Cammidge, 31, has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparing an act of sabotage after contact with the GRU Volunteer Corps, which prosecutors said was controlled by Russia's GRU military intelligence agency.
Appearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court, prosecutor Warren Stanier said Cammidge was accused of providing details of four drone factories near his home in Swindon, west England, and volunteering to commit an act of sabotage.
Prosecutors say he also conducted research about a Wi-Fi jamming device and undertook reconnaissance.
Cammidge did not enter a plea, but Stanier said that in a police interview he had strenuously denied the charges and said he had had no intention of carrying out any sabotage.
Russia's embassy in London has not commented on the case.
Stanier told the court that Cammidge, who was arrested in Swindon last week by counterterrorism officers, had been communicating between August 28 and September 3 with a British national who had gone to Russia to fight against Ukraine.
"The essence of those conversations was the location of factories in the UK which manufacture drones and the sabotage of those factories," Stanier said.
Stanier said other conversations Cammidge had had with an ex-partner and a trusted work colleague showed he was being requested to do so by the Russian intelligence services.
Cammidge was remanded in custody and will appear at London's Old Bailey court on September 25.
UK's deteriorating relations with Russia
Relations between Britain and Russia have deteriorated sharply since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with British authorities increasingly warning about possible Russian espionage, sabotage and other hostile state activity.
Russia warned last month it could strike British military targets in response to Ukrainian attacks that use British-supplied long-range missiles.
"Russia is constantly probing us and testing us," British defense minister Wes Streeting told lawmakers on Thursday.
Two years ago, the UK's domestic spy chief said the GRU was seeking to cause "mayhem" across Europe, and there have been warnings from other European countries in recent weeks that Russia was stepping up a 'hybrid' war against allies of Ukraine.
Germany has blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle airport last month, though Moscow's embassy in Berlin said the Leipzig incident was just another example of unsubstantiated accusations.
"I know people will be concerned about recent incidents across Europe, intended to sow fear, create disruption and undermine support for Ukraine. They will not succeed," British security minister Dan Jarvis said on Wednesday.
In a separate case, Russia's FSB internal security agency said on Thursday that it had detained a former guard at the British Embassy in Moscow who it said had collected personal data on British diplomats on behalf of Ukrainian intelligence.

====================================================================================================

The Diaspora mirror: How global Jewish warmth is healing Israel’s war-weary youth - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:27:52 UTC
23:27:52 KST

Every year before Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish world turns inward for heshbon nefesh, an accounting of the soul. We examine our roots, our heritage, and the complicated cords that bind us as a people.
For decades, the relationship between Israel and the Diaspora has too often settled into a familiar pattern: Israel as the military and cultural center, the Diaspora as its financial supporter.
Israelis went abroad as emissaries and educators; Jewish communities abroad sent money and support home.
There is another way to understand this relationship, and one of the best places to discover it is a Jewish summer camp.
For Jewish communities abroad, camp is often the defining Jewish experience of the year: an immersive world where Jewish identity, Zionism, friendship, and leadership are lived rather than simply taught.
As Israel struggles with the trauma left by the October 7 massacre and the war that followed, there is something profound to learn from that culture of warmth, belonging, and peer-to-peer leadership.
This summer, at Hadassah Youth Neurim Village in Beit Yanai, that lesson came alive at Hallelujah Summer Camp, a flagship initiative of Netaim, the organization carrying forward the vision of the late Ofir Libstein alongside Shiri Madar, Netaim’s CEO.
The program works with what Libstein and Madar called the “periphery of the Diaspora”: more than 150 Jewish communities around the world with fewer than 2,000 members.
Ami Magen, manager of the youth village, puts the purpose simply: “For me, the key is helping our youth rewrite their story, changing their narrative from victim to hero, from survivor to leader.
“When a teenager realizes that even from the lowest point they have experienced, they still have something of value to give to someone else, that is the ultimate empowerment.”
At Hallelujah, Israeli teenagers – many from the war-torn Gaza border communities – encountered young Jewish leaders from Brazil, Argentina, Australia, Uruguay, Romania, and Bulgaria.
They arrived not as donors or rescuers, but as counselors, friends, and role models.
Camp director Tomer Revivo and project initiator Doron Moshe deliberately built Hallelujah around a different leadership culture.
Moshe had spent years as a Habonim Dror emissary in South Africa, where he encountered a looser, warmer approach to youth leadership.
“I would prefer a thousand times that the campers are 10 minutes late, or that a scheduled activity falls apart entirely,” Revivo said, “as long as we do things with warmth, coloring, and genuine human connection. We wanted to build an organizational culture of smiling and unconditional embrace.”
That philosophy was tested almost immediately.
One camper from the Gaza border communities, grieving relatives murdered on October 7, began isolating himself and lashing out. His Argentinian counselors asked Revivo to let them keep him rather than send him home.
They took personal responsibility for him, walking with him and listening. By the end of the summer, he returned home with a notebook filled with handwritten messages of love from counselors who had refused to give up on him.
Lior Avril, an Israeli coordinator from Ashdod, watched foreign counselors give up their own breaks to sit with campers at lunch, sometimes communicating in limited Hebrew.
During an ecology lesson, counselors from Brazil, Argentina, and Australia painted themselves blue and turned the subject into a Smurfs-themed sing-along.
Then came a harder moment. An Israeli camper directed a racial slur at a Black Brazilian counselor. Rather than demand punishment, the counselor sat with the boy for two and a half hours, discussing racism and the weight of words.
By that night’s talent show, the two were dancing together on stage.
Opening up the Israel-Diaspora relationship
Hallelujah's phone-free week created another unexpected transformation.
“On the first day, you see children who are completely lost, sitting in corners, unsettled because they can’t take photos or check social media,” Avril said.
“But by the second and third day, something beautiful happens. They open up. They start talking to the person next to them at the table. They start singing, laughing, and spontaneously dancing.”
For Moshe, this represents something larger than a successful camp. It reverses the traditional direction of the Israel-Diaspora relationship.
“Historically, major communities like Geneva or Glasgow were used to a very specific, patron-recipient relationship,” he explained.
“They expected us to bring traumatized delegations from the Gaza border communities so they could fundraise for them, put them in hotels, and give them a respite park as their contribution to Israel’s rehabilitation. We flipped that script entirely.”
Instead, Netaim told those communities: “Our youth are coming to volunteer, they are coming to work, and they are coming to contribute to you.”
The exchange continues after camp. Israeli graduates can go on to volunteer in Jewish communities such as Geneva, Barcelona, and Glasgow, bringing their own energy and connection to Israel back to communities that have given so much to Israel.
The mirror works in both directions.
Boris, 19, from Curitiba, Brazil, said Israel taught him something about his own Jewish identity. “In the Diaspora, we have to actively be Jewish,” he said. “We have to actively practice and celebrate so we don’t forget, so we keep connected.”
Israeli teenagers, meanwhile, heard what antisemitism looks like when it is not a chapter in a history book.
Lali, from Perth, described hiding her Star of David necklace and locking her community center’s doors during hostile protests. Pedro, from Rio de Janeiro, recalled a Jewish friend who opened his lunchbox at school to find a swastika drawn in ketchup.
Then there is Dora, 18, from Bulgaria. She first came to Hallelujah as a shy 14-year-old camper. This summer she returned as a counselor. Her mother told her she had come home transformed.
Her school in Sofia later nominated her to represent Bulgarian youth at the World Zionist Congress, and she now runs social media campaigns against online antisemitism.
“The Jewish world cannot survive without Israel at its center, but Israel also needs the strength of the Diaspora,” Dora said. “Hallelujah showed me that we are one family, and we must protect Western values together.”
As we dip apples in honey this Rosh Hashanah, Hallelujah offers a powerful lesson about the Jewish people: our strength is held across borders, generations, and cultures.
“The rope of the Jewish people is held from both ends,” Moshe said. “They help us when we need it, and we must help and strengthen them.”
Perhaps that is the mirror Israel needs now. To heal its young people, it may need to look outward and rediscover what Jewish communities abroad have been practicing all along: the power of belonging, warmth, chosen identity, and one another.
Shana Tova.
The writer is a travel photojournalist, explorer, and Israeli storyteller who has led NGOs on the frontlines and brought Israel’s most pressing stories to international audiences.

Israeli polls split on 2026 Knesset election possibilities, as Yashar, Likud vie for primacy - poll

Less than 24 hours after the closing of the Knesset 2026 party lists, five polls published Wednesday night presented a highly fragmented political picture.
In four of them, Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party is the largest party, while in an i24NEWS poll, the Likud surged into first place by a significant margin.
Ofer Winter’s party crosses the electoral threshold in all five polls, while Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha’s party crosses only in the KAN News poll.
The bloc map also remains unclear: Two polls show a tie, while in the others the Zionist opposition bloc maintains an advantage, except for the i24NEWS poll, in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc strengthens significantly.
i24NEWS: Likud leads with 27 seats
The most notable poll of the evening was conducted by i24NEWS and Direct Polls. Unlike all the other surveys, the Likud led by Netanyahu was in first place with 27 seats, while Eisenkot’s Yashar received only 22. Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad fell to 10 seats, the Democrats received 9, United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit received 8 each, and the Joint List, Yisrael Beytenu, and Shas received 7 seats each. Religious Zionism and Zehut received 6 seats, Ra’am received 5, and Ofer Winter’s People of Israel received 4. The Reservists and Economic party of Hendel and Zelekha was far below the threshold with 1.4%, while Blue and White received 1.1%.
Based on the seat distribution, Netanyahu’s bloc together with Winter would receive 60 seats, the Zionist opposition bloc would receive 48, and the Arab parties would receive 12.
Channel 13: Netanyahu, Zionist opposition tie at 53 seats
The Channel 13 News poll presented a completely different picture: Eisenkot received 22 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud fell to 19. Bennett received 13 seats, Shas 7, and Winter 4. Hendel and Zelekha received 3.2% and remained below the electoral threshold. Benny Gantz’s Blue and White and the Haredi Public party also failed to enter the Knesset.
The bloc map showed a complete tie: 53 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc and 53 for the Zionist opposition bloc, with the Arab parties holding the remaining 14 seats.
KAN News: No clear winner, Hendel and Zelekha cross threshold
The first KAN News poll following the closing of the party lists also showed no clear winner between the blocs. Yashar strengthened by one seat and reached 24, while the Likud rose to 21. Bennett’s B’Yachad received 12, the Democrats 9, United Torah Judaism 8, and Otzma Yehudit, Yisrael Beytenu, and Shas received 7 each.
Religious Zionism and Zehut received 5 seats, Winter’s People of Israel received 4, and here came the significant difference compared with most of the other polls: Hendel and Zelekha’s Reservists and Economic list crossed the threshold and received 4 seats.
The Joint List received 7 seats, and Ra’am received 5. Blue and White, the Haredi Public party, and Noam remained outside the Knesset. The bloc map: 52 seats for Eisenkot’s bloc, 52 for Netanyahu’s bloc, 12 for the Arab parties, and 4 for Hendel and Zelekha.
Channel 12: Eisenkot's Yashar leads with 25 seats
In the Channel 12 poll, Yashar maintained first place with 25 seats, while the Likud received 21. Bennett received 13, the Democrats 10, and Yisrael Beytenu 9.
United Torah Judaism received 8 seats, the Joint List and Shas received 7 each, Religious Zionism and Zehut received 5 each, and Winter’s People of Israel strengthened to 5 seats. Ra’am closed the list with 4 seats.
Hendel and Zelekha remained below the threshold with 2.9%, Blue and White received 1.4%, and the Haredi Public party received 1%.
In the bloc map, the current coalition together with Winter received 52 seats, the Zionist opposition bloc received 57, and the Arab parties received 11.
Walla: Netanyahu bloc, with Winter, at 51 seats
The Walla poll by Lazar Research also placed Eisenkot in first place with 25 seats. The Likud received 21, Bennett’s B’Yachad 14, and Yisrael Beytenu and the Democrats 9 each. Otzma Yehudit, United Torah Judaism, the Joint List, and Shas received 7 seats each. Religious Zionism and Zehut received 5 each, Ra’am received 5, and Winter’s People of Israel received 4.
Hendel and Zelekha received 2.8% and did not cross the threshold, while Blue and White fell to 0.9%. As a result, Netanyahu’s bloc together with Winter stood at 51 seats, the Zionist opposition bloc at 57, and the Arab parties at 12. The poll was conducted the morning after the closing of the lists among 506 respondents, out of 3,603 people contacted, with a maximum sampling error of 4.4%.
Yashar leads poll average, ahead of Likud by nearly two seats
When averaging the five polls published Wednesday night, Eisenkot’s Yashar leads with an average of 23.6 seats, ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud with 21.8. In third place is Bennett’s B’Yachad with 12.4 seats, followed by the Democrats with 9.4 and Yisrael Beytenu with 8. United Torah Judaism receives an average of 7.8 seats, Otzma Yehudit 7.4, the Joint List 7.2, and Shas 7. At the bottom of the list are Religious Zionism and Zehut with 5.4 each, Ra’am with 5, and Winter’s People of Israel with 4.2 seats.
A clear picture also emerges among parties below the threshold: Hendel and Zelekha’s Reservists and the Economic party stand at an average of about 2.7% across the five polls, although it crosses the threshold in the KAN News poll and receives 4 seats. Gantz’s Blue and White remains far behind with an average of about 1.1%. The Haredi Public party receives an average of about 0.8%, and Noam for Israel is around 0.2%.
The bloc averages also show no clear outcome: Netanyahu’s bloc, including Winter, stands at 53.6 seats, compared with 53.4 for the Zionist opposition bloc. The Arab parties receive an average of 12.2 seats, leaving a gap of only two-tenths of a seat between the two main blocs.

Who is funding UK's far right? Danny Tommo's US, Israel links
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:26:16 UTC
23:26:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Who is funding Britain's far right? Danny Tommo's US, Israel links
A new far-right group behind violent anti-migrant protests in southern England is being led by an activist who previously received tens of thousands of dollars from a US-based pro-Israel organisation with a history of supporting Britain's anti-Muslim right.
Hundreds of far-right protesters descended on the UK's south coast over the weekend for two anti-immigration demonstrations. Dressed in black and wearing balaclavas, protesters blocked roads in Dover, while clashes broke out with police in Portsmouth as the group sought to prevent migrants from entering the country.
The group, calling itself Patriot Platform, was set up in June by Daniel Thomas, a close confidant of far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as "Tommy Robinson".
Thomas, who goes by the name "Danny Tommo", has emerged as a prominent figure in Britain's extremist anti-migrant movement. But his rise also highlights the links between sections of the British far right and wealthy conservative and pro-Israel networks in the United States.
Thomas previously received $32,000 from the Middle East Forum (MEF), a US-based anti-Islam and staunchly pro-Israel think tank that has also supported Yaxley-Lennon's activism.
The funding helped Thomas organise a major "Free Tommy" rally in London in 2018, despite him having only recently been released from prison and having no previous experience organising protests.
Now, eight years later, Thomas is attempting to build a nationwide network of masked activists that he has described as a "patriotic army".
From convicted criminal to far-right organiser
Originally from Hayling Island near Portsmouth, the 37-year-old father of four is thought to have served as a tank driver with the King's Royal Hussars before being discharged early on medical grounds.
In 2016, he was sentenced to two years in prison after being convicted over a drug-related attempted kidnapping. Portsmouth Crown Court heard that Thomas and two other men stormed into a man's house armed with knives and tried to drag him into the street, mistakenly believing he had stolen £10,000 worth of drugs from them.
After his release, Thomas styled himself as a born-again Christian and claims to have begun attending church every week.
It was around this period that he befriended Yaxley-Lennon and began making a name for himself as a far-right agitator. His first major involvement came when he helped organise the 2018 London demonstration supporting Yaxley-Lennon, who was then serving a 13-month jail sentence for contempt of court.
Since then, Thomas has established himself as a leading figure in Britain's far right, broadcasting anti-migrant videos to hundreds of thousands of followers online.
He has also worked with the far-right Raise the Colours movement, whose members hang British flags from lampposts and engage in anti-migrant activism.
Thomas has spoken of plans to deploy vessels in the English Channel to intercept migrant boats and lock down the port of Dover.
US pro-Israel funding
Thomas's emergence within the British far-right was aided by financial support from the Middle East Forum, a US-based think tank known for its strongly pro-Israel and anti-Islam positions.
US court documents show that the organisation gave Thomas a $32,000 grant in 2018 to fund the "Free Tommy" rally.
The funding places Thomas within a broader transatlantic network that has provided financial and political support to Yaxley-Lennon and other anti-Muslim activists in Britain.
The relationship between Thomas and the MEF appears to have broken down soon afterwards, however, with the organisation accusing him of misappropriating at least $7,000 of the grant for personal use.
Details of the relationship emerged six years ago when the think tank sued its then-communications chief, Lisa Barbounis.
In its unsuccessful lawsuit, the MEF alleged that Barbounis had begun a drug-fuelled affair with Thomas after the rally, leaked confidential information and failed to disclose his alleged misuse of grant money.
The dispute provided a rare glimpse into the financial networks that helped bankroll figures emerging from Britain's anti-Muslim street movement.
Building a 'patriotic army'
In June, Thomas launched Patriot Platform, which describes itself as an organisation for the "sons and daughters of this island" who want to "take our country back".
Its website says it wants to get "boots on the ground" to "organise, mobilise and act with purpose".
Thomas aims to establish cells of paramilitary-style protesters across the country that can be mobilised around anti-migrant campaigns.
Before setting up the group, Thomas said he had been "inspired" by an anti-migrant pogrom in Belfast earlier this year.
"We are going to produce a patriotic army of thousands and thousands of English and British men that are done with protesting, done with walking down roads, and want to make a difference," he said after visiting the city.
The Dover protest marked the group's first major public appearance. Footage posted on social media showed black-clad men jumping from the back of a truck before marching to block the road to the ferry terminal while chanting "Christ is King".
Thomas has claimed the movement is non-violent and operates within the law.
But in Portsmouth, hundreds of masked protesters clashed with police and vehicles were damaged. Hampshire Police said a small number of officers were injured.
Thomas subsequently blamed the violence on "lefties trying to make us look bad".
Several days later, he mobilised another group of black-clad supporters in central London, where they gathered outside the offices of the Daily Mail, which Thomas has accused of doxxing his mother.

The pharaohs were black: How one scholar reclaimed Africa’s past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:25:24 UTC
23:25:24 KST

‘The first civilizations in the world’: He shattered the myth of European supremacy
“One can no longer see ‘darkest Africa’ set against a ‘deep dark past’,” wrote Senegalese historian and philosopher Cheikh Anta Diop (1923-1986), one of the key figures in Pan-Africanism. His words resonate like a manifesto that proclaims: Africa was a center of civilizational development long before the arrival of Europeans. Diop believed that the narrative of an”underdeveloped continent” was just a political construct, and dedicated his life to debunking this myth.
Under French rule
Cheikh Anta Diop was born on December 29, 1923, in the village of Thieytou, Senegal. By that time, the territory had been under French control for several decades. The French conquest of Senegal spanned two and a half centuries, beginning with the establishment of the first trading post in Saint-Louis in 1659.
By the end of the 19th century, the entire territory of modern Senegal was under colonial rule. In 1895, it became part of French West Africa, an administrative entity stretching from the Atlantic coast to Lake Chad.
The French administration implemented a policy of ‘assimilation’, aiming to transform local elites into conduits of the metropole’s cultural expansion. The ‘white man’s mission’ revolved around introducing the ‘savages’ to French culture – however, not as ‘citizens’ with equal rights, but merely as ‘subjects’ benefiting from the ‘benevolent’ influence of culture. Only those who adopted the metropole’s culture were labeled ‘developed’ and granted access to civil society. Diop would later rise against this cultural imposition.
The region where Diop was born boasted rich intellectual traditions. From the 11th to 15th centuries, the territory of present-day Senegal was a major crossroads of interaction between the West African empires of Ghana, Mali, and Songhai, as well as the states of the Wolof, Serer, and Toucouleur peoples. The region thrived thanks to trans-Saharan trade, agriculture, and pastoralism. Mosques were built, and intellectual centers sprang up around them.
Spiritual roots of the brotherhood
Diop was named after his uncle, Cheikh Anta M’Bake. His family belonged to the Mouride brotherhood, which Diop regarded as the only independent Muslim brotherhood in Africa.
Tariqa (from Arabic tarīqa, meaning ‘path’) is a Sufi spiritual tradition that unites murids (disciples) around the marabout (their spiritual guide). Resistance to European colonization catalyzed the formation of new tariqas (Sufi orders) in Africa, including the Mouride brotherhood. It was founded in 1883 by Amadou Bamba Mbacké – a relative of Diop. Amadou Bamba was born in the village of Mbacké into a family of a marabout from the Qadiri order, the oldest order in Senegal.
The French colonial authorities viewed Amadou Bamba and the Mourides as a threat. The influence of his persona and the brotherhood was so significant that colonial administrators feared a potential jihad. As a result, he was arrested and exiled – first to Gabon, then to Mauritania, and later placed under house arrest in Senegal until 1912. Diop’s uncle faced a similar fate, being expelled from Senegal to Gabon.
The Mourides managed to overcome repression and form a union that was influential both in the religious and economic aspects. A love for work was among the brotherhood’s ideological foundations, and it also shaped Diop’s views.
Clash with the metropole
Diop first studied at a Quranic school, then graduated from the University of Dakar, and later from the Sorbonne. In 1946, at the age of 23, he left for Paris. He studied not only the humanities but also developed an interest in mathematics, physics, and chemistry. Diop combined his studies at the Department of Higher Mathematics with the study of Egyptology and Linguistics at the Department of Philosophy.
Diop’s teachers included the leading thinkers of the era: historian Henri Lhote, ethnologist Marcel Griaule, and physicist Jean Frédéric Joliot-Curie. The wave of decolonization had already begun, but had not yet gained full force. The ideas that had driven colonization still dominated Parisian educational institutions at the time – for example, the ‘Essay on the Inequality of the Human Races’ (1853-1855) by Arthur de Gobineau, who laid the foundations of racial theory.
In the late 1940s, Diop co-founded the journal Présence Africaine – a publication that provided African scholars with a platform for public debate denied to them by academic journals.
It was in this journal that Diop first published his essay ‘A Linguistic Study of the Ouolove: The Origin of the Language and Race of the Valaf’, dedicated to the history and culture of his native people. The journal became a space for testing Diop’s ideas about the ‘African origins of civilization’ and the significance of Ancient Egypt. He first spoke about the need to use and develop African languages in his article ‘When Can We Talk About an African Renaissance?’
What is Afrocentrism?
Diop chose to return and work in Senegal to construct African history from the perspective of Africans themselves, rather than through imposed Eurocentrism. Thus, armed with knowledge derived from various academic disciplines, he fought colonialism not only in its external manifestations but also sought to liberate minds.
Afrocentrism is an intellectual and political concept that affirms the primacy of an African cultural and historical perspective in the study of humanity’s past.
Diop’s reflections on the history of Egypt and its connection to Western Sudan (based on archaeological, linguistic, historical, and geological data), his rejection of demeaning ideas about the ‘primitive’ cultures of sub-Saharan Africa, and his assertion of the independence and primacy of African civilizations, their fundamental significance, and their influence on human development formed the foundations of Afrocentrism.
In 1954, Diop published his first book, ‘Nations Nègres et Culture’. The historian postulated the primacy of African cultures, especially ancient Egyptian culture, in shaping humanity’s cultural heritage. According to his position, civilizations arose on the African continent. “These first Black civilizations were the first civilizations in the world, the development of Europe having been held back by the last Ice Age, a matter of a hundred thousand years.” It followed from this that Europe’s civilizing mission and its ‘imposition’ of education were conceptually untenable.
“All the classes of Egyptian society belonged to the same Black race”
Diop advanced the thesis that the civilization of Ancient Egypt was founded by black people. Drawing on linguistics and anthropology, the historian argued that the population of Egypt in the predynastic period was Negroid.
“The typically Negroid features of the pharaohs Narmer, 1st dynasty, the founder of the line of pharaohs, Djoser, 3rd dynasty (with him all the technological elements of Egyptian civilisation were already in place), Cheops, the builder of the Great Pyramid (of Cameroonian type), show that all the classes of Egyptian society belonged to the same Black race,” he wrote. According to Diop, social structures that later spread to other African cultures were first developed in the Nile Valley.
Among his major works, which shed light on the history of the development of African state formations, are ‘Precolonial Black Africa: A Comparative Study of the Political and Social Systems of Europe and Black Africa, from Antiquity to the Formation of Modern State’, and ‘Civilization or Barbarism: an Authentic Anthropology’.
Diop sought to restore the true role of Africa and its peoples in human history and wanted others to recognize Africa’s contribution to world culture. The works of Russian scholars also aided Diop in his scientific research and in confirming his hypotheses. For example, in one of his works, Diop cites Soviet Arabist Vasily Struve.
He wrote, “Since V. V. Struve published the ‘Papyrus of Moscow’, the international scientific community knows with certainty that two thousand years before Archimedes, the Egyptians had already established the rigorous formulae of the area of the sphere: S = 4xR2… Struve writes: ‘Also, we must admit that in mechanics the Egyptians had more knowledge than we wanted to believe.’”
“The history of Black Africa has been written with dates as dry as laundry lists”
Without the liberation of consciousness, the liberation from colonial shackles remains a formality. European colonial systems deliberately alienated the African peoples from their culture and artificially constructed a ‘colonial identity’. They cultivated the idea that the culture of the metropole was Africa’s culture, and denied the existence of a local cultural and intellectual heritage.
Behind this approach, Diop saw the deep mechanism of colonialism. Restoring historical memory was for him part of the national liberation struggle. He wrote, “Until now (1960), the history of Black Africa has always been written with dates as dry as laundry lists, and no one has almost ever tried to find the key that unlocks the door to the intelligence, the understanding of African society.”
Defending the idea of cultural continuity among Africans, Diop advocated for a single federal state of Black Africa. The idea for this project was revealed in the 1974 work ‘Black Africa: The Economic and Cultural Basis for a Federated State’.
The political goal became the main driver of his historical research. Diop pursued three interrelated goals: to dispel colonial prejudices about Africa and restore historical pride to its peoples; to identify common cultural traits that could become the foundation of pan-African unity; and to draw lessons from early political and economic models that would help build a future state.
Diop turned to the experience of the USSR as an example of self-reliant development and of building national identity while preserving local cultures. “It will be possible appropriately to choose one of the major African tongues and promote it to the level of sole governmental and cultural language for the entire continent. It will cover all territorial languages in the same way that Russian is overlaid on the language of each Socialist Republic within the Soviet Union,” he wrote.
Diop vs Senghor
Diop came from an environment that the colonial authorities tried to declare non-existent. A Muslim scholar from a Sufi brotherhood with a centuries-old intellectual tradition, he was able to increase his knowledge and substantiate the untruthfulness of the colonial position.
Long before French administrators declared Africa a ‘dark continent without a past’, strong mechanisms of knowledge transmission based on religious teachings existed throughout Africa and in Western Sudan.
Diop combined scientific and political activities. He founded the opposition Bloc of the Senegalese Masses and became its secretary general. In 1962, the scientist was imprisoned for opposing the pro-French course of then President Leopold Senghor. His party, The National Democratic Rally, was officially recognized only in 1981, after Senghor left office.
The relationship between the two thinkers was difficult. Diop rejected the doctrine of Negritude developed in part by Senghor. Instead, he advocated an African renaissance based on the development of African languages.
To this day, Diop’s works remain the subject of heated debate and give a powerful impetus to the development of science in Africa. The Fundamental Institute of Black Africa (Institut Fondamental d’Afrique Noire, IFAN), created by the colonial administration, was renamed Université Cheikh Anta Diop (UCAD) in 1987 in honor of the scientist.

EU weighs expanded Frontex powers in migration policy overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:25:00 UTC
23:25:00 KST

The European Commission is reportedly preparing a major overhaul of Frontex rules that could significantly broaden the EU border agency’s powers as the bloc moves to tighten migration controls.
Euractiv reported Wednesday that the Commission is expected to propose the review in October, with plans likely to give Frontex a stronger mandate to cooperate with non-EU countries, a greater role in return operations and expanded powers to tackle cross-border crime and hybrid threats.
The proposal is also expected to include plans to triple the agency's standing corps to 30,000 officers.
Elements of the overhaul are expected to be outlined by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen during her State of the European Union address next Wednesday, according to EU officials cited by Euractiv.
The changes could also allow Frontex to carry out returns from one non-European territory to other countries outside the EU, a role not provided for under its current legal framework, and which would require a new legal basis.
The agency could additionally gain greater flexibility to deploy in non-EU countries without requiring a full status agreement.
The review follows a major migration surge in Ceuta, Spain's enclave on Morocco's northern coast, where tens of thousands of migrants crossed into the territory in July, reigniting debate about management of the EU's external borders.

Houthis seize Mokha, global energy flows under threat - Reuters

Houthis seize Mokha, global energy flows under threat - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
The Houthis seized the port city of Mokha in Yemen and strengthened their influence over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. This happened some time after Donald Trump’s statement on the situation in the region.
On Thursday, September 10, Houthi militants seized control of the port city of Mokha in Yemen. This threatens global energy flows, Reuters reports, as reported by UNN.
Details
This happened several hours after President Donald Trump said he expected the war to end after the midterm elections.
Four Yemeni government military sources said that the Houthis had strengthened their influence over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the southern outlet from the Red Sea and one of the world's most important maritime routes — and had begun launching strikes on the strategic Hanish Islands.
At the same time, official Tehran denies its ties to the Houthis, saying that it "has nothing to do with them."
Additionally
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, or the "Gate of Tears" (so named because of the dangerous shipping conditions), is located between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast. As Reuters notes, this makes the strait an important prize for the Houthis, who control Yemen's most densely populated areas and a significant part of the country's north.
It is one of the world's most important routes for transporting crude oil and fuel from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean Sea through the Suez Canal on Egypt's Red Sea coast, as well as for goods bound for Asia, including Russian oil.
Recall
The port of Mokha on Yemen's Red Sea coast suspended commercial and maritime activity after a series of Houthi missile attacks.
