Ministry seeks return ambassadors to help Ukrainians come home
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
17:08:48 EEST
23:08:48 KST

The Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity of Ukraine is working on a return ambassador initiative involving volunteers who will help Ukrainians abroad get more information about life and opportunities in specific communities in Ukraine, the ministry said on its website on Thursday.
The initiative is primarily focused on Ukrainians who do not have the opportunity to return to their previous place of residence.
The ambassador operating model was developed on September 7-10 in Vinnytsia during a workshop titled "Return Ambassadors in Communities: From Idea to Implementation."
In particular, representatives of non-governmental organizations and 20 communities from various regions of Ukraine participated in the workshop.
"Our task is to ensure that Ukrainians abroad have as much information as possible to make their personal decision to return to Ukraine: what support programs are available in the state, which community to choose for life, what documents to process, and so on," Deputy Minister of Social Policy, Family and Unity for European Integration Ilona Havronska said.
According to her, it is also important that Ukrainians abroad can feel that they are expected not only at the state level, but also at the level of people. The return ambassador initiative should facilitate the introduction of potential returnees to a specific community and help them establish local contacts.
At the same time, the ambassadors will not replace professional return consultants. The ambassadors will help people learn more about life in a specific community from a resident's perspective and establish local contacts, while consultants will provide professional information about available state and local programs, services, and tools.
Such consultants will work in Unity Centers and partner organizations of the Unity Network.

Sofia Municipality will seek up to €367 million in loans to modernise public transport and upgrade key streets and boulevards, following a decision by the Sofia Municipal Council today.

Severe storms caused widespread flooding across parts of Italy on Thursday, leaving one woman dead after her car became trapped in a flooded underpass in the northeastern Friuli Venezia Giulia region, Italian broadcaster Rai News reported.
The 83-year-old woman drowned in Latisana, in the province of Udine, after water flooded the underpass and trapped her car.
Flooding was reported across several northern and central regions, with roads and underpasses submerged, rivers and streams overflowing, and emergency crews carrying out rescues and evacuations.
In Tuscany, more than 63,000 lightning strikes were recorded over 12 hours, while 115 millimetres of rain fell in the Grosseto area.
More than 200 operations were carried out by the regional Civil Protection system and firefighters, including rescues from flooded underpasses.
In Lombardy, 45 people were evacuated after a major landslide in Val Masino, in the province of Sondrio, while flooding also affected parts of the Spedali Civili hospital in Brescia.
Water entered the hospital's cardiac intensive care unit, prompting the precautionary relocation of two patients.
Minor flooding was also reported in other areas before the situation was brought under control.
In Milan, the Lambro River overflowed its banks overnight, temporarily flooding streets in the city.
Several cars were also trapped in an underpass in nearby Vimodrone, with firefighters responding to assist those inside.
Flooding and heavy rain also disrupted rail services in Friuli Venezia Giulia, where underpasses in Latisana, San Giorgio di Nogaro and Torviscosa were submerged.
Delays of up to an hour were reported, while replacement buses were deployed on some routes.
In Liguria, the Lavagna River overflowed in several places in Calvari, near Genoa, while flooding and fallen trees were reported in parts of Tuscany, Marche and Piedmont.
An orange weather alert is in effect in four regions, Veneto, Emilia-Romagna, Tuscany and Marche, as an Atlantic low-pressure system brings further heavy rain and thunderstorms across central and northern Italy.
Authorities have warned of further flooding, landslides and rapid rises in smaller waterways in areas affected by the rainfall.

German foreign minister urges voters to back Ukraine, NATO as far right surges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:03:24 UTC
23:03:24 KST

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul addresses a press conference at the Franz Liszt University of Music Weimar in Weimar on Sept. 3, 2026. | Jens Schlüter/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — German officials must do more to convince voters of continued support for Ukraine and the country’s commitments to NATO, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Thursday.
NATO is undergoing a “political stress test” both from the external threat posed by Russia and from skepticism at home that had become “visible and tangible” in recent state elections, he said at the conference of German ambassadors in Berlin.
He made a similar appeal over Ukraine, saying Germany would continue to stand by Kyiv and arguing that its support was not only for Ukraine but “for the benefit of our security in Europe.”
Advertisement
The call comes after the AfD won 43.8% in the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its 2021 result and leaving Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats a distant second at 17.2 %.
Wadephul argued Thursday that the way forward was not to retreat from Germany’s commitments, but to do a better job of explaining why they matter.
He cast the challenge in stark historical terms, invoking the collapse of Germany’s democracy between the two World Wars. “Germany knows from the Weimar Republic what could happen if Democrats are not ready to defend their system,” he said. “We have to show that we have learned our lesson.”
The Weimar Republic, Germany’s first parliamentary democracy, was progressively hollowed out amid economic crisis, political paralysis and growing support for anti-democratic forces before Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor in 1933.
As for the results of Sunday's vote, they were not only the AfD’s strongest-ever showing, but the highest vote share won by any party in the state since German reunification.
During the campaign, AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund repeatedly presented spending abroad as money missing at home. He told regional broadcaster MDR that Germany was “giving away money all over the world” and pointed specifically to support for Kyiv: “Every minute, €20,000 goes to Ukraine. That is all money we are missing.”
Advertisement
That message is feeding into an increasingly uncomfortable guns-versus-butter debate in Berlin, just as Merz’s coalition negotiates the 2027 budget. Germany is set to spend roughly €140 billion on defense next year while facing mounting pressure over pensions, health care and other public services.
The scale of the shift is stark: Defense spending next year will almost match the roughly €145 billion federal contribution to the pension system, according to Kiel Institute calculations. In 2022, Germany spent about €50 billion on defense compared with €115 billion on pensions.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte backed Wadephul’s broader message, telling the ambassadors that Germany’s choices had consequences far beyond its borders.
“I count on every one of you in this room to carry that message with you: that a stronger Germany makes Europe stronger, that a stronger Europe makes NATO stronger,” he said, speaking at the same conference.
Rutte also played down the risk that electoral gains by far-right parties could weaken the alliance. NATO would work with “whoever is elected,” he said, adding that he had “no doubt that the alliance will stay very strong.”

Shyness makes facial expressions seem more intense, but only in certain cultures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:00:47 UTC
23:00:47 KST

People with higher levels of shyness tend to perceive other people’s facial expressions as more intense, but this effect appears to depend heavily on their cultural background. A recent study found that shyness heightens the perceived intensity of emotions among young adults in Mainland China, but the same pattern does not appear in Canadian populations. The research, published in Psychological Reports, suggests that cultural rules about how we display our feelings play a major role in how personality shapes our perception of others.
Emotions are a universal human experience, but the way we display and interpret them depends on where we grow up. In Western societies, expressing emotions openly and directly is generally encouraged. In contrast, many East Asian societies place a higher value on social harmony, which often translates to more subdued emotional displays. This idea is supported by a variety of prior studies. For example, a 2016 review noted that people in Western cultures tend to experience and value high-energy emotions, while people in Eastern cultures tend to prefer and experience calmer, lower-energy emotional states.
Because emotional displays are more restrained in collectivist cultures, individuals in these environments might learn to pay closer attention to subtle changes in facial expressions. This cultural tuning can even be seen at the neural level. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that simply hearing an emotion word changed how the brains of Chinese immigrants processed facial expressions, while having no such effect on the brains of White American participants.
Beyond cultural background, individual personality traits also influence how we read faces. Shyness is a personality trait characterized by feeling nervous, timid, or self-conscious in social situations. People with high levels of shyness often experience a strong fear of being judged by others, which can cause them to become highly vigilant when navigating social interactions. Prior research hints that shy individuals might overestimate the intensity of negative emotions, seeing them as more threatening than they actually are.
Until now, it was unknown how a person’s shyness and their broader cultural environment might combine to shape how they judge emotional intensity. Emotional intensity refers to the physical strength or energy of a feeling displayed on someone’s face. A slight smile represents a low-intensity emotion, while a wide grin represents a high-intensity emotion. To address this gap, researchers led by Xiaoxue (Sonia) Kong, an assistant professor at the University of Northern British Columbia, and Gabriel (Naiqi) Xiao, an associate professor at McMaster University, set out to see if the link between shyness and emotion perception changes across different cultural contexts.
“Previous research has shown that both cultural background and individual personality traits can influence how people perceive facial emotions, but very few studies have examined these two factors together,” Kong and Xiao told PsyPost.
“We were particularly interested in shyness because shy individuals may be more sensitive to social and emotional cues and shyness is also a personality trait whose expression and implications can be shaped by culture. So we wanted to bring these two areas together.”
The researchers recruited 160 young adults for their experiment. This included 47 participants living in Mainland China, alongside 59 White participants and 54 East Asian participants living in Canada. The East Asian Canadian group primarily consisted of individuals originally from regions like Mainland China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan who had been living in Canada for four to ten years.
To measure shyness, the participants completed a widely used questionnaire that asked them to rate how strongly they agreed with statements about feeling nervous or tense in social settings. Next, the participants completed a computer-based emotion perception task.
During this task, participants looked at photographs of faces expressing happiness, sadness, anger, fear, or a neutral state. To prevent the participants from struggling to read the faces of people from unfamiliar backgrounds, the researchers only showed faces that matched the participant’s own racial group. The researchers used specialized software to blend emotional faces with neutral faces, creating five specific levels of emotional intensity: zero percent, 25 percent, 50 percent, 75 percent, and 100 percent. Each face appeared on the screen for a brief moment, and the participants then used a sliding scale from zero to 100 to rate how intense the emotion looked.
When analyzing the results, the researchers found that participants across all three groups were generally accurate at tracking emotional intensity. As the physical intensity of the facial expression increased in the photographs, the participants’ intensity ratings reliably increased as well.
However, the participants’ level of shyness had a distinct impact on these ratings depending on their cultural group. Among the participants living in Mainland China, shyness acted as a strong amplifier. The higher a Chinese participant scored on the shyness scale, the more intense they perceived all the facial expressions to be. This heightened sensitivity applied across the board, whether the face was showing a positive emotion like happiness or a negative one like fear.
“One finding that surprised us was that the effect of shyness was not limited to negative emotions,” the researchers explained.
“Previous research has often linked shyness to heightened sensitivity to socially threatening or negative emotional cues, but in our study, shyness was associated with greater perceived emotional intensity more broadly among the Mainland Chinese participants.”
This amplifying effect of shyness was completely absent in both the White Canadian and East Asian Canadian groups. For the participants living in Canada, being highly shy did not change how intensely they rated the facial expressions.
“We included both White Canadian and East Asian Canadian participants, in addition to participants living in Mainland China,” the researchers noted. “The fact that the two Canadian groups showed similar patterns, while the Mainland Chinese group differed, suggests that where people live and the cultural environment they experience may be important alongside ethnic background when we think about personality and emotion perception.”
“The way personality influences our perception of other people’s emotions may depend on the cultural context in which we live,” they added. “This suggests that shyness does not necessarily operate in the same way across cultures.”
The researchers suggest that in Chinese culture, where emotional restraint is the norm, shy individuals might develop an intense sensitivity to subtle facial changes to avoid social missteps. Because they are less exposed to loud or exaggerated emotional displays, they might react more strongly when reading expressions. Their heightened vigilance makes any emotional display register as stronger. In contrast, Western cultures encourage more direct emotional communication, which might reduce the need for shy individuals to be on such high alert. The social costs of misreading a facial expression might simply be lower in a Western environment.
The fact that East Asian Canadians did not show the same pattern as Mainland Chinese participants suggests that they may have adapted to Western communication styles. It is also possible that the varied backgrounds within this immigrant group diluted the cultural effect observed in the Mainland Chinese sample.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. First, the study relied on static photographs of facial expressions. In real-world social interactions, people express emotions dynamically through moving facial muscles, body language, and tone of voice. A photograph might not fully capture how a shy person reads a shifting emotional situation in everyday life.
The study also focused on three specific groups, which means the results cannot automatically be applied to people from other ethnic or cultural backgrounds. Different societies have their own unique rules about emotional expression, and incorporating a wider variety of global populations could provide a more complete picture of how personality and culture interact.
Additionally, while the study included East Asian Canadians, the researchers did not measure exactly how much these individuals had adopted Canadian cultural norms. Tracking how immigrant populations adapt their social perception over time could offer deeper insights into the way cultural shifts alter emotional processing.
“Our findings should not be interpreted as suggesting that all shy Chinese individuals perceive emotions in a particular way, or that culture alone causes these differences,” the researchers clarified. “Our sample consisted of young adults from three specific groups, and we used static facial expressions in a laboratory setting.”
“Future research with more culturally diverse samples and more naturalistic emotional interactions will be important for determining how broadly these findings generalize,” they concluded.
The study, “Shyness and Facial Emotion Perception: A Cross-Cultural Study,” was authored by Xiaoxue Kong, Wei Fang, Skade Fernando, Naiqi G. Xiao, and Louis A. Schmidt.

The Eleventh Hour by Salman Rushdie audiobook review – stories with levity and laughter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:00:38 UTC
23:00:38 KST

Five short stories and five readers make up Salman Rushdie’s collection, The Eleventh Hour, his first work of fiction since the near-fatal attack in 2022 where he sustained life-changing injuries. These tales find the author exploring legacy, mortality, loneliness and the ageing process. In these potentially bleak themes, Rushdie finds levity and laughter, as well as profundity.
Late, read by the actor Naveen Andrews, is a ghost story set in King’s College, Cambridge, where an honorary fellow, SM Arthur, wakes up dead in his college room and wonders if he will be trapped there for eternity. He meets a lonely but very much alive Indian student, Rosa, who is stuck at college for the holidays. Sid Sagar reads The Old Man in the Piazza, an allegory about free speech and how “we have become bar room moralists. Does the thumb point upward. Does it turn down? … We are all now gladiators in the Colosseum of the Thumb.”
The best of the stories, In the South, is narrated by Neil Shah who gives characterful voice to two elderly neighbours in Chennai, India, who spend their days bickering with each other on their porches. They are known as Senior and Junior because one is 17 days older than the other. Despite their cantankerousness, the two draw comfort from one another’s presence. When Junior dies on the street after being toppled by a passing Vespa – on the same day that a tsunami hits the south of the country – Senior comes to understand how “death and life [are] just adjacent verandas”.

What Is Russia’s Secret Undersea Cable Weapon and Why Does NATO Fear It?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:00:26 UTC
23:00:26 KST

- Category
- World
What Is Russia’s Secret Undersea Cable Weapon and Why Does NATO Fear It?
An unknown Russian undersea weapon has reportedly been caught operating near critical seabed cables—but what is this system, how does it attack infrastructure on the ocean floor, and why has it put NATO on alert?
NATO allies confronted Russian submarines training to deploy a previously unknown weapon built to sever undersea cables in Arctic waters near Svalbard this spring, Reuters reported on September 10. The weapon was designed to disable the cables without leaving any traceable fingerprints.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The operation's precise location and the United States' involvement had not been disclosed until now. Britain and Norway acknowledged in April that they had uncovered covert Russian activity in Arctic waters, but the new technology, the site of the exercise and Washington's role emerged only with the latest reporting.
The clandestine operation was carried out by GUGI, Moscow's Main Directorate of Deep-Sea Research, which used deep-sea submersibles to simulate deploying the technology, the officials stated. A joint effort involving Britain, Norway and the US tracked and confronted the Russian vessels at sea. The submarines were prevented from completing their exercise and eventually left the area.
"Through our joint operation, we sent a clear message to Russia that they cannot operate covertly," Norway's Defense Minister Tore Sandvik declared in a statement. "We have made it unequivocally clear to Russian authorities that any attempt to target our critical infrastructure will be detected and met with consequences," he added.
OSINT project WarMonitor, citing Reuters, added that British, Norwegian, and US forces disrupted the exercise this spring, forcing the Russian vessels to withdraw.
Russia damaged no cables, and the drill focused on rehearsing deployment in the event of a conflict with NATO, the officials noted. British and Norwegian representatives took their findings to Moscow to signal their awareness of the technology, hoping the disclosure might make the Kremlin hesitate to use it.
The cables at the center of the operation are no thicker than a garden hose yet underpin global internet connectivity and financial transactions, Reuters reported. Two 1,400-kilometer fiber-optic lines link Svalbard to mainland Norway, lying as deep as 2,700 meters below the surface.
They carry vast volumes of data downloaded at the SvalSat ground station, described as the world's largest and part of NASA's Near Space Network. Norway plans to complete a new fiber-optic cable connecting Svalbard and Jan Mayen to the mainland by 2028.
The face-off underscored the strategic value of the Bear Gap, one Western official indicated. The 400-mile-wide stretch between southern Svalbard and mainland Norway is a corridor that Russian nuclear submarines from the Kola Peninsula must cross to reach the Atlantic. Britain deployed forces to the volcanic island of Jan Mayen in August alongside Norwegian and US allies to demonstrate NATO's ability to operate jointly in the High North.
The confrontation comes as some Western intelligence officials fear the Kremlin is intensifying sabotage across Europe and preparing for a possible clash with NATO, Reuters reported. Three US officials indicated that analysts are increasingly concerned Moscow may test the alliance's mutual-defense pact, Article 5, with subsea cables a likely target of any such effort.
In August, CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited intelligence counterparts in Moscow, in part to warn against escalating sabotage operations in Europe, according to two people familiar with the matter.
Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to a request for comment, and the Kremlin consistently denies conducting sabotage in NATO countries or plotting any confrontation.
Earlier this year, GUGI's activity had already surfaced in foreign waters. In April 2026, Britain disclosed a covert Russian submarine operation near UK waters that threatened energy pipelines and data cables, involving an Akula-class submarine and two deep-sea submarines tied to the same directorate.
Undersea cables carry roughly 99% of the UK's international telecommunications and data traffic, and London subsequently committed an additional $136 million for P-8 submarine-hunting aircraft as suspicious Russian vessel activity increased.

US Navy plans compact Silent Anvil torpedo as China’s submarine fleet surges

US Navy plans compact Silent Anvil torpedo as China’s submarine fleet surges
The weapon is expected to be air-launched and suitable for use across a range of platforms
The US Naval Air Systems Command issued a request for information – a step towards development – to industry in late August for the Silent Anvil Air-Launched Torpedo (SAA-LT).
While air-launching a torpedo from stand-off range is not new – the US Navy already has the High Altitude Anti-Submarine Warfare Weapon Capability (HAAWC) – the SAA-LT would be much smaller.
HAAWC adds a glide kit to a Mark 54 lightweight torpedo and can be launched by P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft from altitudes of up to 30,000 feet (9,140 metres).
According to the request for information, the navy wants the new weapon to weigh up to 268lbs (122kg) while measuring up to 70 inches (178cm) long and 7.5 inches (19cm) in diameter – dimensions intended to broaden the range of aircraft that could carry it.
The requirements also envisage that Silent Anvil would be compatible with aircraft carrier storage and handling systems, potentially allowing carrier-based platforms to field the weapon.

Munich: The massacre the world must never forget - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

A day the world watched
September 5, 1972, should have been a day celebrating the Olympic ideal. Instead, it became one of the darkest days in the history of international sports and one of the most infamous terrorist attacks against Israelis.
Members of the Palestinian terrorist organization Black September infiltrated the Olympic Village, attacked the Israeli delegation, and took eleven Israelis hostage. All eleven were ultimately murdered. They were athletes, coaches, and officials who had traveled to Germany to compete, never imagining that they would become targets of terrorism.
The attack was carefully planned to exploit the global spotlight of the Olympics. The terrorists understood that an attack on Israel's delegation would command the attention of millions around the world. They were right. The world watched the hostage crisis unfold, watched the failed rescue attempt at Fürstenfeldbruck airfield, and watched as 11 Israelis lost their lives.
But behind the headlines were 11 human beings.
They were not just names
Moshe Weinberg, Yossef Romano, Yossef Gutfreund, Ze'ev Friedman, David Berger, Eliezer Halfin, Amitzur Shapira, Kehat Shor, Mark Slavin, Andrei Spitzer, and Yaakov Springer were not political abstractions. They were husbands, fathers, sons, coaches, and athletes with families and futures ahead of them.
They went to Munich representing Israel and returned home in coffins. Their families did not get to watch them compete or welcome them home. Instead, they had to bury the people they loved.
That is what terrorism does. It turns human beings into targets and families into casualties.
The man I met in Beirut
My connection to Munich became personal years later in Beirut.
In December 1978, I met a striking, almost playboy-looking man at the Hilton Hotel. I had been told to go to the bar and ask for "the Red Prince." I had no idea who I was about to meet.
During our conversation, he told me that the United States would eventually secure "land for peace." When I asked whose land, he answered, "Israel's." He also told me he had received numerous warnings from the CIA about attempts by Mossad to assassinate him.
At the time, I did not understand the significance of the man sitting across from me. It was only later that I realized who he was: Ali Hassan Salameh, the man known as the Red Prince.
Salameh was a senior Palestinian operative, intelligence chief to Yasser Arafat, and a central figure in the Black September organization. Israeli intelligence accused him of helping plan the Munich massacre. The meeting had been arranged by my friend Saad Haddad, the Lebanese military officer who founded and commanded the South Lebanon Army during the Lebanese Civil War.
The long shadow of Munich
Salameh remained a powerful figure within the Palestinian movement and maintained close ties to Arafat and the Palestine Liberation Organization. Israel continued to regard him as a major terrorist target.
On January 22, 1979, just weeks after our meeting, Salameh was killed in Beirut when a car bomb exploded as his convoy passed through the city. The assassination was widely attributed to Mossad and was part of Israel's campaign against those it held responsible for the Munich massacre.
His death could not bring the eleven Israelis home. But Munich had already changed the world. Terrorists had discovered that they could turn innocent lives into political leverage and use television and the international media as a global megaphone.
The Olympics were supposed to bring nations together in peace. Instead, they became the stage for an act of calculated murder.
The lesson we must remember
More than five decades later, the greatest danger may be forgetting what Munich taught us.
The language of terrorism changes. Organizations change. Weapons change. But the ideology that dehumanizes innocent people remains. We can debate governments, borders, negotiations, and political solutions. We can disagree passionately about policy. But there can never be a legitimate political justification for murdering innocent civilians.
Munich was not simply an attack against Israel. It was an attack against the principle that innocent people should be protected from political violence.
And the world has seen that lesson repeated many times since.
Remember the 11
I remember the 11 Israelis who went to Munich to compete and never came home. I remember their families, whose lives were permanently changed by their murders. And I remember sitting across from Ali Hassan Salameh at the Hilton Hotel in Beirut.
That encounter taught me something I have never forgotten: history is ultimately about choices. The men who planned Munich made choices. The men who carried out the massacre made choices. And the nations that watched had to decide how they would respond.
More than 50 years later, we are still living with the consequences.
Munich remain a warning about what happens when hatred becomes an ideology, terrorism becomes a political weapon, and the murder of innocent people is rationalized in the name of a cause.
We must remember the eleven because their lives mattered, their families mattered, and their memory still matters.
When terrorism is tolerated, it never remains confined to its first victims. Eventually, it threatens everyone.
Dr. Mike Evans has written 120 books and is a #1 New York Times bestselling author. He is the founder of the Friends of Zion Museum in Jerusalem, the Ten Boom Museum in Holland, and Churches United with Israel, one of the largest Christian Zionist networks in America, with more than 30 million followers.

Four people with long Covid euthanised in NL last year
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Four people died by euthanasia last year after suffering with long Covid, according to the Dutch regional euthanasia review committee.
The youngest patient was 51-years-old, the other three were over 65. In another six cases, long Covid played a role in the decision to end their lives but was not the primary factor.
An estimated 400,000 people in the Netherlands currently suffer from long Covid, many of them have severe symptoms that stop them working or being able to enjoy basic everyday activities.
The Dutch Health Council this year urged the government to give more clarity around the situation with long Covid and do more to help treat those suffering from it.
Last month, a national research and investigation centre was launched by the Long-Covid Foundation, to help prolong work into treating the illness.
Government funding of €40 million dried up, so the foundation raised €500,000 to give to seven scientists to keep researching possible treatments.

Swiss intelligence publishes dossier on Nazi doctor Mengele
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:59:02 UTC
22:59:02 KST

Swiss intelligence publishes dossier on Nazi doctor Mengele
The Swiss Federal Intelligence Service (FIS) has published online the dossier held at the Federal Archives on Josef Mengele, the concentration camp doctor known as the "Angel of Death of Auschwitz". This followed a legal dispute over access to the dossier, which had initially been refused.
The intelligence service had wrongly refused access to the dossierExternal link, as the FIS announced on Thursday. It stated that it had assumed the protection period, which had been extended under archiving law, would run until the end of 2071. It was only after a complaint was lodged against the most recent refusal of access, which took place in February 2026, that it became clear the FIS was in the wrong.
More
The Swiss return of Nazi ‘Angel of Death’ Josef Mengele
In 2001, when the then police service of the Office of the Attorney General handed the 217-page dossier over to the Federal Archives, the government had in fact adopted a liberal access policy. The Independent Commission of Experts on Switzerland and the Second World War, known as the “Bergier Commission”, had already examined the dossier for its report. However, it is stated that it was not apparent to the FIS that the Mengele dossier had, in effect, already been declassified.
The dossier contains numerous newspaper reports, most of which focused on the suspicion that Mengele had stayed in Switzerland on several occasions – even while he was still the subject of an international arrest warrant.
It also contains police reports, parts of which have been redacted. These include entry bans and arrest warrants against Mengele, as well as police reports on investigations into suspects who may have provided Mengele with a hiding place.
Very few redactions
The FIS states that it has carried out “as few redactions as possible”. Personal data of federal administration employees with links to the FIS and its predecessor organisations, information subject to statutory source protection, and data relating to third parties – with the exception of public figures – are protected.
The FIS also states that it will carry out a general review of its access policy regarding archived documents. The historian Gérard Wettstein, who had lodged the complaint, expressed his delight back in May in a report on Swiss Public Television SRF’s Tagesschau news programme at this “important step”, which would make it possible to dispel myths about Mengele’s stays in Switzerland.
The doctor Josef Mengele (1911–1979) was responsible for cruel and often fatal medical experiments at the Auschwitz concentration camp. He was known as the “Angel of Death of Auschwitz”. After the war ended, he fled to South America. In 1979, he drowned in a swimming accident.

‘Support is conditional’: Europe’s defense ambitions collide with economic squeeze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:58:03 UTC
22:58:03 KST

Europeans increasingly accept the need to spend more on defense as the continent faces new security threats and growing doubts over US protection. But when it comes to paying for it, support has clear limits.
Polling of nearly 19,500 people across 15 European countries by the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) found growing support for higher defense spending compared with 2025, alongside declining confidence that the US would come to Europe's defense.
Yet just 39% of the poll's respondents supported some reductions in public spending to fund national defense investment, while 45% opposed such a trade-off and 17% were undecided.
"There is a real window at the moment that is supportive of efforts to increase European defense spending and defense investment," Jana Kobzova, co-director of ECFR's European Security Programme, told Anadolu.
"But it's also very clear from the survey that this support is conditional."
While voters increasingly recognize that the security situation around Europe has changed, Kobzova said economic pressures remain their most urgent concern.
They are effectively telling governments that they understand the case for investing more in defense, she said.
"We understand why you're doing this. We understand that the security situation around Europe has changed. We understand that the transatlantic relationship has changed. We know we need to invest more. We support it," she said, summarizing the public mood.
But voters have another message for their governments.
"You also need to look after our most important priority at the moment, which is the economic squeeze," she added.
Support for reducing public expenditure to fund defense varied sharply across Europe.
It was strongest in Estonia, where 55% backed the proposal and 34% opposed it. The Netherlands followed with 54% support and 32% opposition.
In Poland, 49% supported the trade-off, compared with 30% who opposed it, while 21% remained undecided. Portugal recorded 47% support and 36% opposition.
In both France and the UK, 43% supported cuts in other areas of public spending to fund defense, while 40% opposed them.
Elsewhere, opposition exceeded support.
In Sweden, 38% backed the proposal and 43% rejected it. Denmark recorded 37% support and 51% opposition, while in Switzerland the figures were 37% and 50%, respectively.
Resistance was more pronounced in southern and central Europe.
In Spain, 32% supported reductions in public expenditure for defense, while 54% opposed them. Around 30% of Germans supported the trade-off, compared with 56% who rejected it. In Austria, support stood at 28% and opposition at 59%.
Italy registered the strongest opposition among the countries surveyed, with only around one-fifth of respondents backing the proposal and 63% opposed.
Kobzova said the national differences could not be explained by geography alone. Historical experience, political culture, confidence in government, fiscal pressures and perceptions of immediate military threats all shape public attitudes.
“I think it’s all of the above,” she said when asked whether the variations were primarily driven by threat perception, trust or national political traditions.
Northern and eastern European countries generally have stronger traditions of military preparedness and tend to perceive Russia as a more immediate threat, she said.
"They've been used to investing in their own armies," Kobzova said of the Scandinavian countries, pointing to a tradition of greater self-reliance in meeting national security needs.
By contrast, military preparedness became less of a priority in parts of Europe after the Cold War.
The survey, published this summer, also exposed a growing divide between Europeans' confidence in their neighbors and their faith in the US as a security partner.
When respondents were asked whether other European countries would help defend them in the event of an attack, confidence was positive across almost the entire sample, with Denmark, the Netherlands and Sweden recording particularly strong levels.
“Even among the voters of very Eurosceptic parties, they still believe that their European neighbors would come and help them,” Kobzova said.
By contrast, net confidence that the US would intervene was negative in every country shown in the survey.
The findings point to a growing belief that Europe must take greater responsibility for its own security, even as many Europeans remain reluctant to write off the transatlantic relationship altogether.
“A lot of them think this is a break, not a breakup,” she said.
Many Europeans appear to believe relations with Washington could recover after a future change in US political leadership.
European governments, however, cannot build long-term defense plans around the most optimistic assumptions about future US policy, she argued.
“It’s the responsibility of our political leaders not to plan for best-case scenarios but to plan for worst-case scenarios,” she said.
Trust between Europe and the US has been significantly damaged since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, Kobzova said, with European leaders increasingly expecting that the initial response to a security crisis would have to come from Europe.
"The lessons the European leaders are learning are that any response is not going to start in Washington," she said. "It's going to start with European determination to address the challenges that they might face."
The US could still play an important role, she argued, but may be slower, more selective and more demanding of its allies.
"The US is not going to be the first responder, but they may still be a responder," she said. "They might come a bit later."
Europeans are more receptive to defense spending when the money is linked to building the continent's own industrial capacity.
The survey found broad backing for purchasing weapons from European manufacturers rather than suppliers outside the continent. Net support was positive in almost every country surveyed, with Denmark recording the strongest result.
The pattern was largely reversed when respondents were asked about buying more weapons from the US. Net support was negative across nearly the entire sample, with Poland the main exception.
The findings suggest voters are not opposed to defense investment in principle. Many are more receptive when spending strengthens European companies, expands industrial capacity and reduces dependence on outside suppliers.
“What matters is not just how much is spent, but how it is spent,” Kobzova said.
Voters expect "competent governments making good decisions," she added, suggesting that sustained public support will depend on whether defense programs deliver credible military capabilities and visible economic benefits.
“Some of the strategic capabilities are for now only with the US,” she said, adding that replacing them “is not going to take a year.”
Europe's investment decisions will also have to reflect the changing character of warfare demonstrated in Ukraine, including the large-scale use of drones, missiles and integrated air-defense systems.
Germany illustrates both the scale and the political difficulty of that transition. As Europe's largest economy, its ability to turn higher spending into lasting military capacity will be critical to the continent's broader push to take greater responsibility for its own defense.
Berlin has committed itself to a major expansion of its armed forces, but German voters remain deeply divided over the financial implications. Around 30% supported cuts in other areas of public spending for defense, while 56% opposed them.
Kobzova said Germany's hesitation must be understood in the context of its post-war political history.
"Germany's history of the past 80 years shows that the country is, sometimes for all the right reasons historically, afraid of its own power," she said.
Europe's post-war security system was built partly around the assumption that Germany would not need to develop overwhelming military strength because it could rely on NATO, the US and its European partners.
But that caution is increasingly colliding with demands for Germany to assume a greater security role.
“There is a recognition that that change is needed,” Kobzova said.
But recognition alone will not guarantee political consent.
“It takes time, it needs political stability, and it needs sustained leadership and attention,” she said.
The challenge facing Germany reflects a broader dilemma across Europe: How far can governments increase defense spending if voters see it coming at the expense of public services or living standards?
Kobzova compared that shift to paying more to insure a home as the risks around it increase.
For decades, many European states felt relatively secure, allowing governments to keep defense budgets limited while relying heavily on the US for protection.
“If your house was in a safe place, your insurance was quite low,” she said.
But as the risks facing Europe have grown, so has the cost of security.
“Our insurance premium in Europe has gone up,” Kobzova said.

Much of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:57:56 UTC
22:57:56 KST

A nightly tourist tax may be unfamiliar territory in the UK, but countries in continental Europe have been cashing in on these kinds of levies for decades.
Tourists usually need to pay the tax on the day they check out of a hotel or holiday let, and are often surprised by an extra fee on top of their accommodation costs.
Among the earliest introductions of a tourist tax was in Austria in 1842, specifically targeting those who stayed in spa and wellness retreats.
Similar measures were later implemented in France, Italy, Germany and Switzerland as a way to prevent the inhabitants of towns hosting such high-end resorts from paying for costs incurred by wealthy visitors.
Italy’s tourist tax structure has gone through various changes. During Benito Mussolini’s fascist regime, it was broadened to include any town or city classified as a tourist destination.
The tax was then completely abolished for the World Cup in 1990 as Italy embraced more visitors, only to be brought back in nationally in 2011, with Rome becoming the first city to reintroduce the levy.
Depending on the destination, and sometimes the hotel type, the nightly fee typically ranges from between €1 (£0.86) and €10 per person, although guests of five-star hotels in Milan pay €12.
Venice has also had an entrance fee in place since 2024, although that is only targeted at day-trippers.
The overnight levy is a serious earner for popular Italian destinations. In 2024, Rome made €222.4m, followed by Milan (€109.3m), Florence (€82.9m) and Venice (€38.9m), according to data from Siope, the finance ministry’s tracker of public money flows.
The revenues are supposed to be spent on local services, especially in towns and cities buckling under the pressure of overtourism, or on maintaining monuments. However, the reality is that cash-strapped municipalities use it for other expenses.
“All municipalities want the fee because they need the money,” said Gianluca De Gaetano, the manager of the Rome unit for Federalberghi, the hotels’ association.
Tourists mostly just absorb the payment, even if begrudgingly. “They tend to complain when they find that the services in a city are not up to par, especially if they’ve already paid a lot for their accommodation,” said De Gaetano.

US pushing NATO allies to undo ICC, pull out of founding treaty: report

2026-09-10

22:57:55 KST

The US has launched a diplomatic push pressing its NATO allies to help dismantle the International Criminal Court (ICC) and withdraw from its founding Rome Statute, Politico reported.
At a closed-door meeting in Brussels in mid-July, US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker urged member states to abandon the tribunal and immediately halt all material assistance.
"The United States will systematically dismantle the capabilities of the ICC; we firmly request that you immediately take steps to withdraw," the US Mission to NATO wrote in a diplomatic paper.
"Let us end the charade of the ICC once and for all."
Whitaker warned allied nations that Washington "will be watching closely who stands with America," while American envoys simultaneously raised the matter during bilateral discussions with European counterparts.
The diplomatic paper urged partners to "examine the threat" posed by the court and "publicly condemn" its "overreach".
Most NATO countries, except the US and Türkiye, are signatories to the Rome Statute.
Sanctions on ICC
The French delegation emphasised "France's unwavering support for the ICC", and Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen affirmed that the Netherlands "fully" supports the institution.
An ICC spokesperson said the tribunal "remains focused on carrying out its mandate impartially, independently and in accordance with the Rome Statute," remaining "steadfast and resilient" despite attempts to impede its operations.
The campaign follows mounting US measures against the tribunal under a February 2025 executive order declaring a national emergency over ICC actions concerning the US and Israel.
Washington sanctioned several court personnel, including ICC President Tomoko Akane in August and nine of the court’s 18 judges.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant have been wanted by the ICC since 2024 for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The White House, the US State Department, and the US Mission to NATO have not commented on the report yet.

Record China-US gap in bond yields unlikely to trigger capital flight: Marsh Investment
Executives say dollar dominance remains intact as borrowers diversify funding and use offshore yuan bonds to help manage elevated US financing costs
The widening yield spread between Chinese and American government bonds is unlikely to trigger catastrophic capital flight from China, according to investment executives at Marsh Investment, who attribute the record spread to the United States’ fiscal pressures and global macro trends rather than a structural retreat for Chinese assets.
The spread between benchmark 10-year US Treasury bonds and equivalent Chinese sovereign bonds hit a record 3.17 percentage points this week. Yields on US Treasury bonds rose to 4.85 per cent – their highest level since 2023 – while China’s 10-year yield held at 1.68 per cent.
While the expanding gap has raised fears that higher US returns could siphon capital away from Chinese assets and weigh on the yuan, executives at Marsh Investments – formerly known as Mercer – downplayed the risk during a media briefing on Thursday.
“In the pantheon of things driving broader moves in the dollar and US rates, we do not see [capital flight] as a major impact compared with other forces at play,” said Niall O’Sullivan, global chief investment officer at Marsh.
O’Sullivan attributed elevated long-term US yields to global supply-demand imbalances, expanding US national debt and heavy corporate borrowing – particularly across the tech and artificial intelligence sectors.
The unusually wide yield gap has also fed broader debate about whether the combination of high US borrowing costs and mounting government debt could eventually weaken the dollar’s dominance in global finance.

The relevant committee has recommended for the third time that the Verkhovna Rada abolish the duty-free allowance for parcels worth up to 150 euros
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:54:30 EEST
22:54:30 KST

The relevant committee has recommended for the third time that the Verkhovna Rada abolish the duty-free allowance for parcels worth up to 150 euros
Kyiv • UNN
The Verkhovna Rada committee recommended adopting bills on VAT for parcels worth up to 150 euros starting from the first euro. The new rules may come into effect no earlier than July 2027.
The Verkhovna Rada Committee on Finance, Tax and Customs Policy has for the third time recommended that Parliament adopt two related draft laws on the taxation of small postal and express shipments worth up to €150 ordered through marketplaces. The documents provide for the abolition of the tax exemption for parcels worth up to €150. UNN reports this, citing a committee meeting.
Details
The committee recommended that the Verkhovna Rada adopt draft law No. 15460, "On Amendments to the Customs Code of Ukraine Regarding the Specifics of Customs Formalities for Goods Moved (Sent) Across the Customs Border of Ukraine in International Postal and Express Shipments," as well as draft law No. 16051-1, "On Amendments to the Tax Code of Ukraine Regarding the Specifics of Value Added Taxation of Transactions Involving the Distance Sale of Goods Moved (Sent) Across the Customs Border of Ukraine in International Postal and Express Shipments," as a basis and in their entirety.
Additional information
On Tuesday, September 1, the Verkhovna Rada once again failed to pass the draft laws abolishing the tax exemption for parcels worth up to €150. The two draft laws in question are Nos. 15460 and 15112-d.
Draft law No. 15460 introduced amendments to the Customs Code of Ukraine (which regulates customs procedures, border-clearance rules and the €150 threshold for import duty).
Under the draft law, VAT on imported goods purchased through marketplaces was to be introduced starting from €0.
Currently, international shipments worth up to €150 are not subject to import VAT or import duty. Under the proposed rules, the threshold itself would remain, but its effect would change: goods worth up to €150 would be exempt from duty only. Thus, VAT at the standard rate of 20% would be charged starting from the first euro of the value of the goods.
For shipments worth more than €150, the basis for calculating the duty would change. It would be charged at a rate of 10% of the parcel’s entire invoice value, rather than only on the amount exceeding €150.
At the same time, private unsolicited gifts worth up to €45 were also expected to remain exempt from taxation. The new rules would not apply to the distance sale of alcohol and tobacco.
Requirements were to be introduced for the record-keeping of marketplaces and their representatives in Ukraine (for non-resident marketplaces), as well as a special guarantee for the use of the distance-sale scheme.
A transitional period is предусмотрено for postal operators, express carriers and marketplaces to adapt. During the first year, administrative liability would not apply for unintentional errors related to the incomplete or late payment of VAT on parcels worth up to €150, provided that the tax itself is paid in full.
Draft law No. 15112-d, "On Amendments to the Tax Code of Ukraine Regarding the Taxation of E-Commerce Transactions with Value Added Tax," was intended to amend the Tax Code of Ukraine (which establishes the rules for assessing and paying VAT on e-commerce and parcels).
The revised draft law No. 15460 underwent almost no changes. On September 7, the government approved draft law No. 16051, which was approved by the government instead of No. 15112-d. In addition to the provisions set out in draft law No. 15112-d, the document provides for bringing the rules concerning politically exposed persons (PEPs) into line with the wording agreed upon with the EU.
Thus, according to the draft law, if a politically exposed person ceases to perform prominent public functions, banks must continue to take into account the person’s ongoing risks for at least twelve months from the day following the day on which that person ceased to perform prominent public functions.
At the same time, the entity conducting primary financial monitoring must take into account the risks that remain inherent to the politically exposed person, including:
-  the level of influence the person may still have;  
-  the scope of powers with which the person was vested;  
-  the connection between past and current powers, etc.  
After at least twelve months have elapsed since the date on which a person ceased performing prominent public functions, the subject of primary financial monitoring must continue taking measures until it establishes that business relations with such a person do not pose the risks inherent to politically exposed persons.
The proposed effective dates have also been changed: the provisions of the Tax Code and the Customs Code are to take effect no earlier than July 2027. Previously, it was envisaged that they would take effect on January 1, 2027.
It should be noted that on June 9, the Verkhovna Rada adopted as a whole draft law No. 15111-d on the taxation of digital platforms. On June 11, it was signed by Verkhovna Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk, and on June 12, it was sent to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for signature, after which the document has been "stuck" with the head of state.
The fact is that during the second reading, a provision was submitted to the document envisaging changes to the financial monitoring system for politically exposed persons. It was included in the draft by the relevant committee and subsequently supported by the parliamentary chamber.
PEPs include current and former top officials: from members of parliament, ministers, and the president to heads of law enforcement agencies, members of the NBU Board, and ambassadors.
Draft Law No. 16051 provides for removing heads of structural divisions of the central office of the National Bank of Ukraine and employees responsible for conducting financial monitoring of a bank in which more than 50 percent of the shares in the authorized capital are owned by the state from the list of public figures.
Under the law, banks and other financial companies are required to conduct enhanced financial monitoring of PEPs, their close relatives, and business partners.
PEP status is lifelong. At the same time, enhanced financial monitoring applies throughout a person's tenure in a top position and for 12 months after their dismissal. However, banks and other financial institutions may continue to conduct enhanced checks on a PEP if they believe that the person remains high-risk.
The amendments to the draft law introduce penalties for banks that decide to continue enhanced monitoring of a PEP's transactions after 12 months have elapsed since the person's dismissal from a top position.
According to some members of parliament, it is precisely because of this amendment that Zelenskyy has still not signed the aforementioned draft law. Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko stated that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has still not signed the law on taxing income from digital platforms, adopted back in June, because during its consideration, lawmakers introduced an amendment concerning changes to the financial monitoring of politically exposed persons.
At the same time, an alternative draft law No. 16051-1 was submitted yesterday to government draft law No. 16051; it repeals the provisions concerning PEPs.
As already noted, it was this draft law that the committee recommended. It should be noted that the alternative document also provides that taxes on parcels will be credited to the special fund of the State Budget of Ukraine and directed toward meeting the needs of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

Coal demand to rise 1.2% to 8.94 bln metric tons in 2026 amid conflict — IEA

Unknown Publisher

13:53:25 UTC
22:53:25 KST

PARIS, September 10. /TASS/. A sharp rise in natural gas prices resulting from the Middle East conflict and the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz is driving up global demand for coal, according to a report on the coal sector by the International Energy Agency (IEA).
Global demand for the combustible solid fuel, which had been expected to decline slightly year on year, is now forecast to rise by 1.2% in 2026, reaching a record 8.94 bln metric tons.
The situation could change again in 2027, according to experts' forecasts. Much will depend on whether shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which carries a significant share of liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments, resumes. However, if this waterway remains largely closed to LNG shipments, coal demand could rise further.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, on the night of July 8, the United States resumed large-scale strikes on Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached regarding the Strait of Hormuz. Around 25% of global oil trade and about 20% of LNG trade passes through the strait. The US administration subsequently effectively signaled an end to the use of large-scale military force against Iran and a shift toward attempting to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

The planet Mercury is shrinking far faster than we thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:52:30 UTC
22:52:30 KST

Everyone gets wrinkles eventually—even planets. On Mercury, these signs of aging look like hills and ridges, called shortening structures, across its surface. As the planet shrinks and contracts over time, more of these ridges rise up. And according to a new analysis, there are far more of them than scientists had realized.
Scientists have long known that Mercury’s interior was shrinking: for the past 4.5 billion years, the planet has contracted as it cooled from its fiery origins. But the new research, published in Geophysical Research Letters on Thursday, shows that it’s actually shrunk a lot more than previously estimated, providing new insight into the planet’s evolution and makeup.
Mercury is particularly mysterious because it is so close to the sun: It is difficult to send spacecraft there (just one has ever entered orbit, although another mission is about to attempt that feat). And the light from our home star is so bright that it is hard to observe Mercury from Earth. We’ve certainly never been able to land a craft that could peek beneath its surface. That means planetary scientists must rely on data from remote satellites to paint a picture of the planet’s history and inner layers.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The new analysis focused on the planet’s surface roughness, such as craters or debris, and found that particularly rough areas have made the wrinkles harder to see. Accounting for that obstruction, the researchers estimate that Mercury has likely shrank 10 to 30 percent more than previously thought.
“In this work, the authors have thought about an additional angle to figuring out Mercury’s geological history from afar, which is the effect of surface roughness from billions of years of impact bombardment,” says Paul Byrne, a planetary scientist at Washington University in St. Louis, who was not involved in the study. “If their results hold, and I’m confident they will, then we’ll have taken a step further in investigating planets we can’t yet visit in person.”
Byrne presented findings at a 2013 conference that indicated that Mercury had shrunk by about 11 kilometers; the new study suggests it instead may have done so by up to 23 kilometers, or about 14 miles. Even that might be an underestimate, the new study’s authors write, because existing surface data may be incomplete.
Retracing the history of Mercury enables scientists to better understand what’s going on underneath its rocky surface, says Gaku Nishiyama, lead author of the study and a planetary scientist at the German Aerospace Center.
“The new estimates on Mercury’s radial contraction would tell a different scenario of Mercury’s thermal evolution,” Nishiyama says. “So what would be the implication on Mercury’s evolution when this new estimate is used? This is the next question that we have to tackle.”
The implications could stretch galaxy-wide, Byrne adds. He is “positive” that other celestial bodies such as the moon and Mars may show similar shrinkage.
“Do those worlds next!” he says.
