Finland tightening rules for foreign students
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
16:37:31 EEST
22:37:31 KST

Finland's government has proposed further measures to address financial challenges facing international students.
Petteri Orpo's (NCP) right-wing government has proposed to roll out a one-year waiting period for foreign students' family reunifications, "to clarify the amount of required financial resources", as well as add an education-related language skill requirement for student resident permit applicants, a press release said on Thursday.
The government submitted the proposal to Parliament on Thursday.
According to the government, supervision data suggests that most international students in Finland thrive academically and can reside in the country without significant hardship — though some face income difficulties.
"Students coming to Finland must have a genuine ability to pursue their studies, to get by with their own financial resources and to build their future here. Through these legislative amendments, we will ensure that international students have the necessary prerequisites to do so," Minister of Employment Matias Marttinen (NCP).
Misleading recruiters
According to a report from the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment, students' financial struggles often stem from two sources: foreign recruitment agencies that falsely advertise Finland's job market, and excessive agency fees that leave students in debt.
The government has also proposed that international students' family members should only be able to apply for residence permits after the student has been in the country for at least a year.
"In this way, the student would have a reasonable idea of the financial resources required for a family to live in Finland. Currently, the student’s family members can apply for a residence permit at the same time as the student," the release explained.
Financial requirements
The government has also proposed clarifying the financial requirements for international students by establishing specific income amounts in euros through legislation and government decree.
It said that at the moment, current requirements are unclear, so this change would ensure students understand the actual cost of living in Finland before arriving.
According to the government, that would also provide authorities with clear, standardised criteria when evaluating whether applicants have sufficient funds during the residence permit application process. To keep pace with inflation and changing living costs, the required income amount would be formally reviewed and updated every three years, the government release explained.
Language requirements
The government proposed introducing a language proficiency requirement for student residence permits. This would allow authorities to deny permits to applicants lacking necessary language skills, while avoiding extra administrative work for educational institutions or additional steps for students who already meet the language standards.
Ministry reports have identified two key problems:
First, some students arrive with insufficient English (or other language of instruction) skills, making it impossible for them to successfully complete their degree programs.
Second, some individuals are exploiting student permits not to study, but simply as a pathway to enter the Finnish or broader EU job market without genuine academic intentions, according to the release.
"The act and amendments are scheduled to enter into force on 5 April 2027. The application of the one-year waiting period for family reunification would begin at that time. Other amendments would become applicable in October 2027," the release read.

Israel has cut off water to 47 Palestinian families in the northern West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:36:00 UTC
22:36:00 KST

In the northern Jordan Valley, 47 Palestinian families have gone without water for over a month after Israeli forces bulldozed the roads to their herding community and cut the pipelines that once fed it.
Lutfi Bani Odeh has lived on this land for 45 years. Through them all, the nearby towns of Atouf and Tammoun were where his children went to school, where his family sought healthcare, where they bought what they needed, and sold what they produced. Since early August, all of that has been cut off.
“The Israeli army bulldozed the road to our area, and we have no way to Tammoun except through the hills, which we are forced to walk on foot,” Bani Odeh said, adding that he now spends hours walking seven kilometers on foot, a commute that previously took minutes by car. “The army bulldozed the road I could drive on,” he explained. “I walk seven kilometers just to bring food, medicine, diapers, and other needs, and soon our children will have to walk the same distance when the school year begins in a few weeks.”
But the road is not the worst of it. “We can endure isolation and the lack of some basic needs for a time,” Bani Odeh said. “But we can’t live without water.”
Bani Odeh is one of approximately 300 Palestinians — nearly half of them children — facing imminent displacement in Ras al-Ahmar, Ath-Tha’la, and eastern Atouf in the northern Jordan Valley, after Israeli forces severed the last water pipelines supplying the communities. The water cutoff is part of the construction of a 22-kilometer Israeli military barrier, known as the “Crimson Thread”, running from Ein Shibli to the Tayasir military roadblock, which passes through Palestinian-owned agricultural land and has been described by Israeli rights organization B’Tselem as a deliberate strategy of expulsion.
As of June 30, 2026, B’Tselem documented that Israeli military attacks and settler violence had forcibly displaced 64 Palestinian communities in the West Bank, affecting more than 4,328 people.
In the northern Jordan Valley, the 47 families who have been cut off from water, are farmers and livestock herders living in Ras al-Ahmar, a small rural community east of the village of Atouf, in the Tubas governorate of the northeastern West Bank. Their main activity is raising livestock, and together, they own approximately 15,000 sheep and goats.
Abdallah Bisharat, mayor of Atouf, told Mondoweiss that the Israeli military’s construction work has cut off water pipes and blocked the road to the area, leaving the families isolated. “We in the Atouf village council have been trying to send livestock feed and potable water tanks, but most of the time the Israeli army has been sending us back,” Bisharat said.
The Israeli military is permitting the restoration of an irrigation water line but not the line that feeds the homes, and is blocking the movement of materials needed for livestock work into the area. Families are allowed to leave and return on foot, but vehicles are not permitted to pass.
The barrier’s construction, which began in March 2026, has already caused extensive damage to the area. According to B’Tselem, it has resulted in the uprooting of more than 300 olive and grape trees, the destruction of crops and greenhouses, the demolition of kilometers of water and irrigation pipelines, and damage to approximately 45,000 dunams (4,500 hectares) of agricultural land. The barrier’s full route, once complete, is expected to isolate residents from their land and enable the seizure of around 50,000 dunams (5,000 hectares).
Families have been collecting whatever they can in tanks hauled by tractors through the hills. “We have little water that we have been able to get in tanks carried by tractors, through the hills, but we need to ration them,” Bani Odeh said. “We are limiting our hygiene, our drinking, our cooking, and we have given up on irrigating our vegetables, which have all dried out and died.”
The sheep and goats can go longer without water than humans can, which leaves families with a narrow margin. But Bani Odeh makes clear that the margin is closing. “We can’t live like this for long, nor can our livestock, and we need the water restored.”
Moving out is not a viable option for most families. “We have around 15,000 sheep and goats, which we have no room for except on our land,” Bani Odeh said. “If we move out, we will be forced to sell most of our livestock, which are our main source of income.”
Bisharat says the choice the families face is stark. “These families live from their livestock, and they don’t have any space in the town to graze and keep them,” he said. “Their choice is to sell their livestock and leave, or try to hold on and stay for as long as they can.”
Last week, the Jerusalem Post quoted Israeli army sources saying that some of the families have their homes built without permits in Area C — the approximately 60 percent of the West Bank under full Israeli civil and military control under the Oslo Accords, where Israel’s civil administration bans Palestinian construction. The army said each family’s case was being examined separately through the legal system, and that the barrier project “may be affecting” the water supply in the area.
Bani Odeh’s response is simple. “These are our lands, and we have always lived here,” he said. “And whatever the reason is, who cuts water off from dozens of families? What can justify this?”
The Wall and Colonization Resistance Commission documented 2,256 attacks against Palestinians and their property in July 2026 alone — 1,458 by Israeli forces and 798 by settlers — describing the pattern as coordinated settler violence backed by military protection. These attacks have targeted communities, farmland, and infrastructure across the West Bank, and Ras al-Ahmar is one node in that pattern.
The families there are, in Bani Odeh’s words, “holding to their last bit of capacity to endure.”

Rethinking Humanitarianism | Will aid-for-hire become the new normal?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:35:34 UTC
22:35:34 KST

Share & more
Editor’s note: This episode was made in collaboration with Start Network as part of a series that explores what really drives change in the humanitarian system, and what it tells us about future efforts to transform the system for the better.
In the previous collaborative episode between Rethinking Humanitarianism and Start Network, Fogbow CEO Brook Jerue questioned why the aid sector was so “infatuated” and critical of his company – a small private American firm delivering aid in high‑conflict contexts like South Sudan and Gaza.
In this follow‑up episode, host Tammam Aloudat speaks with Beatrice Lindstrom – co‑author of a recent policy brief on the rise of privatised, militarised, and politicised aid actors – to situate Fogbow within the larger context of these emerging operators, and to examine why their growing "subsumption" of professional humanitarian roles deserves closer scrutiny.
Lindstrom, who is also a human rights lawyer and a senior clinical instructor at Harvard Law’s International Human Rights Clinic, warns that we may be sliding towards a future where “aid-for-profit” becomes normalised at the risk of harming affected communities.
She draws distinctions between firms like Fogbow and entities such as the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, whose US‑Israeli‑backed activities were linked to Israel’s killing of thousands of aid seekers. Yet, she argues, they share structural features that matter: corporate structures and incentives, close relationships with states that are parties to conflict, and approaches that risk turning aid into an instrument of military and political strategy.
A central concern for Lindstrom is the ambiguous nature of these companies, which “seem to be asking to be held to corporate transparency standards rather than humanitarian ones”. That mix, she says, creates “a grey zone of accountability” in which people in crisis – and the public funding much of the response – lack clear information on who is calling the shots, whose interests are being served, and what safeguards exist when those interests clash.
Lindstrom links this shift to “massive defunding” of professional aid organisations and a deliberate policy turn by major donors like the United States. This is embracing “a philosophy around aid that is entirely instrumentalised to serve American interests, and where private actors are named as core actors to carry out that plan”.
While private actors have long been in the humanitarian space, Lindstrom says the sector is “on the cusp of a broader trend” where aid-for-profit models risk becoming increasingly accepted and entrenched, “and I think that that's exactly why it's so critical that we scrutinise these actors adequately right now, before they are legitimised”.
Lindstrom says traditional NGOs also fall short, especially on accountability to affected people, but insists that this cannot be a reason to abandon core principles.
“I don't think we're disproportionately focused on for-profit companies here, but rather that this conversation now needs to be applied to these new actors in the same way that it's been applied to nonprofit organisations,” she says. “We all share a responsibility to fight for a model of aid grounded in needs and rights, and kept at arm’s length from politics.”

Beatrice, private companies have been involved in humanitarian response for years and in different forms, but your report suggests something different is happening now. What changed? And where do organisations like Fogbow, for example, fit in in that evolution?
Beatrice Lindstrom
Yeah, I think it's true that private companies, including private military companies, have a long history of work in the humanitarian sector. But what caught our eye is that I think the moment that we're finding ourselves in right now is that these actors seem to be taking on a distinct role that was previously carried out by professional humanitarian organisations of a nonprofit nature, which is the actual coordination and delivery of aid. There are humanitarian safeguards in place. But I think what we're seeing now with companies like Fogbow is a lot of questions. Tammam Aloudat
So let me try to unpack a bit of what you said. One of it is, you repeatedly said “professional humanitarian,” and this is one of the things that came in the discussion with the CEO of Fogbow, is that what even is professional? Anybody can deliver aid.
Brook Jerue
“Anybody can be involved in a humanitarian effort. Just because certain people call themselves humanitarian doesn't mean they have, like, a monopoly of, like, ‘I can only deliver aid. I'm the only person who can deliver aid.’”
Tammam Aloudat
And I want you to just frame what when you say insistently “professional humanitarian.” The second part is he also insisted that they follow the exact same ethos as all humanitarian actors or aid actors, even though at the same time we can't see their accounts or donors or so on, because, as he said, they are a private company and they don't have to show us anything.
Beatrice Lindstrom
Yeah, let me take those in in parts. The humanitarian field has long been governed by pretty specific standards, by laws, and the actors that have been carrying out humanitarian assistance over time have historically been of a nonprofit nature, right? And I think what matters there is that when an entity is structured as for-profit, as a corporation, they have a fiduciary duty to their shareholders to maximise profit. And one of the big questions that's raised by these companies is what happens when those profit-making motives come into tension with the interests of aid beneficiaries. That is one key distinction I think between these actors. Another piece that we're seeing that is different is also the militarisation of aid. And so these new companies are largely led and staffed by people with military and intelligence backgrounds, and I think that that matters. Those backgrounds may bring a lot of expertise in logistics and operations in insecure environments that can be valuable, but they also come with distinct risks. I think past experience and studies show that when there is a militarised ethos in aid delivery, that it creates a different kind of relationship with beneficiaries and a securitisation of aid that can actually lead to harm for the beneficiaries themselves. And finally, a key distinction that I would draw here is also the relationship between these entities and governments. So they often carry out operations at the behest of governments that are actually parties to the conflicts that they are operating in, and this, of course, is a significant departure from traditional humanitarians that ground their operations in impartiality and independence and in neutrality. And in turn, those principles are so crucial for ensuring that the delivery of aid is not only taking kind of a myopic view of how many bags of aid is delivered, but actually what is the impact of that aid on civilians in conflict, and on the conflict as a whole, and the crisis as a whole.
Tammam Aloudat
So, Brook Jerue, the CEO of Fogbow, in the interview we had with him, seemed genuinely stumped at why so much attention is being paid to them when all they want to do is deliver aid as well as they can.
Brook Jerue
“Honestly, we get a lot of flack because we're an outsider coming in. I'm more happy to come work with everybody, and help. I don't understand why we get this blowback for helping people, you know, that are on the cusp of starving to death.”
Tammam Aloudat
And there were a couple of streams that you've just mentioned. Beatrice Lindstrom
Yeah, I mean, I think that there's a central concern here that there's just a lot of ambiguity around these actors. So on the one hand, they are corporations that, by their legal structure, creates this duty to shareholders, regardless of whether any one individual project may be returning a large profit or not. And they seem to be asking to be held to corporate transparency standards rather than humanitarian ones, and that the funding sources are largely not disclosed. And I think if profit is not the motive here, then it's reasonable to ask: Why this legal form with these incentives, rather than operating as a nonprofit or other structure that is more clearly aligned with humanitarian purposes? And I think ultimately my concern here is that this combination can create a sort of a grey zone of accountability, because they can present themselves as mission-driven when it's convenient, but also as a commercial actor when it's advantageous, without being fully transparent about, again the funding sources, the contractual obligations, and who ultimately has decision-making power. And in a humanitarian context, that ambiguity matters because people in crisis and the public that is funding much of this work, they deserve clarity about whose interests are being served, and what safeguards exist when those interests conflict.
Tammam Aloudat
I've asked him several times about transparency, because he kept saying there's no difference in ethos, there's no difference in sources of information, and he even insisted that there's no difference in relationship with governments, or…and I said there is a significant difference. Your books are not open. And he insists, ‘Oh, that's because we are a private company, not an NGO’, and it, it went in circles. He said there is accountability to donors, which is by its nature on the particular project that those donors have funded. So there's no full accountability or open books as, let's say, MSF does. He used an example of contractors by the humanitarian sector. He said, they kept insisting on Maersk, which is a shipping company. Said WFP uses Maersk. What's the difference? In your view, is there an argument there? And what's the issue with transparency that [is] getting stuck in my throat all the time that I can't get over.
Beatrice Lindstrom
Yeah, I mean I think that there are a couple of concerns here. One is that I would also ask about: Beyond transparency to donors, what about transparencies to the affected communities, to the beneficiaries of aid? What access to information do they have about where this aid is coming from, and who is calling the shots as to what populations are being targeted here? One of the concerns that we have with these actors is that there's a strong emphasis on the value add being about access, that part of what these organisations bring is that they're able to enter areas where other actors, for security reasons or other logistical reasons, haven't been able to enter. And of course, there's a lot to be said for short-term relief. I think there's no question that getting food or medicine to people in desperate situations can absolutely save lives and be of critical importance. But I think if we're serious about impact, we have to zoom out and look at the bigger picture, and emergency access, I think, is only one piece of the puzzle, and it can sometimes come at real cost. Decades of humanitarian work have shown that access isn't just about getting trucks or planes into the right places, but it's about politics, it's about power, it's about how aid is used once it's there. And in places like South Sudan, where Fogbow has operated, you know, I think we've seen time and again well-intentioned aid get instrumentalised in ways that can actually fuel conflict or deepen divisions. And so the questions aren't just, you know, can you get in or are others willing to go, but they also have to include things like how is access being negotiated? With whom? Does limited access in certain instances actually end up helping a government over the long term that might be starving its population and help it escape accountability? Does it effectively support counterinsurgency? If you target one group and not another, does that inflame ethnic tensions? And these are just some of the dilemmas that I think experienced and principled humanitarian organisations have spent years learning how to navigate. They don't always get it right, but they have safeguards, and standards, and a long historical memory of what's gone wrong before that they build on. And so, I think transparency is not only about funding sources, but it's also about a broader view into how these entities are approaching these kinds of problems, and I think so far we haven't really seen assurances that these are considerations that are being taken into account. And if I may just loop back to your earlier question around the insistence on humanitarian principles, you know, I think it's certainly positive that entities like Fogbow are stating a commitment to humanitarian principles. They themselves use the tagline of being “the next generation of aid”, and so in that context, adherence to humanitarian principles is of crucial importance. But I think the difficulty is that independent reporting, including reporting by The New Humanitarian, raises real questions about how that's actually played out in practice. And so, if we take South Sudan for example, Fogbow carried out airdrops that were reportedly concentrated in government-controlled pockets inside opposition territory, which raises concern that there's a blurring of aid and counterinsurgency. They at times reportedly targeted areas that were largely held by government forces where civilians had left, meaning that the military forces that remained were the beneficiaries of the aid and delivered aid in bags that was marked with the South Sudanese flag, which, from the perspective of a beneficiary, signals an alignment with the South Sudanese government, and I think in turn calls into real question the commitment to impartiality and independence in practice. And so along with the broader governance issues that we pointed to, like transparency around funding sources, I think the way that the approach to aid in practice raises real questions about the actual adherence to humanitarian principles.

Beatrice Lindstrom
I've spent the last 15 years of my career working with communities that have been harmed in the name of aid and in the course of aid. I have worked with communities that were impacted by the cholera epidemic in Haiti that was brought by UN peacekeepers, by survivors of sexual exploitation and abuse, and the list goes on. And so, I'm no stranger to critiques of humanitarian aid when it's not done right. But I think that if I were to boil down the core concern that I've had over the course of that work, so many of those concerns seem to not fully register in this moment. And so, is there a legitimate concern around needing more efficiency? Yes. But the answer to that, I think, cannot be that we situate aid outside of a framework that's grounded in rights and duties and protocols that exist for the very reason of protecting beneficiaries who are some of, by definition, some of the most vulnerable marginalised people in the world. I think the answer can't be a move away from needs-based, rights-based aid that has been such a core principle of the humanitarian system for decades. And so, I don't see the critiques of these companies as one that is exclusive to for-profit companies. I think that they pick up on a conversation that has been had within the humanitarian sector and outside of the sector for a very long time. I don't think that it's that we're disproportionately focused on for-profit companies here, but rather that this conversation now needs to be applied to these new actors in the same way that it's been applied to nonprofit organisations. And I think it's concerning that rather than taking these critiques as a starting point that need to be grappled with, that there seems to be a suggestion that these new actors should essentially be exempt from some of those critiques, and I think it's not enough to say we have good intentions, we're able to access a particular crisis in a particular way, and that therefore this is now the new model that others should follow.
Tammam Aloudat
To go back to one of the points you mentioned. When I asked Mr. Jerue about accountability to affected people, he seemed a little surprised with that question. His answer was consistently that they don't deliver anything themselves. They use properly scrutinised local NGOs that are approved by others, like WFP. But that's the extent of where he addressed anything like accountability to affected people. And not to appear to, you know, give a blank check to anyone else in terms of accountability to people who are, you know, served by a aid, but is that enough? Is there another layer of consideration when it comes to corporations and accountability to people?
Beatrice Lindstrom
No, I think it's clearly not enough, and it's not enough on several different levels. So first and foremost, I think we would need to know a lot more about what those relationships look like, about who is making the decisions, about what expertise and perspective companies like Fogbow are bringing to this to ensure that they also have a view into how the aid is ultimately being delivered. I think it's absolutely a positive step to be working with local NGOs. I mean, of course, localisation has been a big focus of the aid industry for some time. And I do find it alarming that there isn't a deeper grappling with some of those questions, not just around the role of local NGOs, but also the role of people themselves; the ultimate beneficiaries of the aid and what role they get to have in access to information, in participation, in decision making, and ultimately what avenues exist in practice if harms were to occur. Where does a displaced person in South Sudan go to seek accountability if they have been harmed by an airdrop? Those are the questions that I think we would need clear answers to in order to feel assured that accountability is a part of the picture.
Tammam Aloudat
We hope that existing frameworks, standards, principles, legal instruments are binding or an actual concern to humanitarian actors as they behave. Is there sufficient guardrails in those tools to govern the work of private institutions or private corporations like Fogbow and others?
Beatrice Lindstrom
I think that there's a bit of a tension around the extent to which aid historically has been grounded in rules and responsibilities. So on the one hand, international humanitarian law is quite clear about the guardrails about aid needing to be impartial, and independent, and grounded in humanity and neutrality. There are limitations on aid actors, you know, when their involvement with certain parties to the conflict become so involved that they themselves become parties to that conflict. And so, on the one hand, I think international law, especially in conflict settings, does provide some real guardrails. International criminal law also ensures that when conducts like we saw from the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, when people are killed in the course of aid delivery, that that at times can amount to real violations for which there should be real accountability. And yet at the same time, a lot of the standards that come into play on a day-to-day basis in the, in humanitarian operations are largely voluntary. And I think from where I sit, one of the biggest gaps that we've seen is ultimately whether these standards translate into accountability for people themselves. And there, I think that we've always had a big gap, and that gap is only threatens to become wider in this context of introducing new actors who are not even operating within some of those voluntary standards. And I think the other added complication here is the opacity that comes with corporate structures around, you know, where are they headquartered. Again, who is funding them? Who is ultimately responsible for calling the shots? And all of those things matter from the perspective of whether accountability and justice will actually be delivered in a situation where there is harm. And so I think that there is a lot of work that needs to be done to reclaim a rules-based ethos around humanitarian assistance. I think that that is a challenge for, sort of, traditional professional humanitarian actors themselves. But it's also a challenge for states who are funding humanitarian assistance in this moment and who are choosing where to invest critical funds. And it's a challenge for all of us who care about the future of humanitarian assistance. I think that we have a real moment here where the question shouldn't just be about the survival of aid, but also about what shape, what approaches aid takes into the future. And those questions only become more urgent in the context of increasing disastrous conflicts around the world.
Tammam Aloudat
You mentioned [the] Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, and that was really annoying to the CEO of Fogbow because, in his mind, he sees himself as closer to WFP than he is to GHF. Their singular argument is we don't carry weapons, so we're not a militarised aid [organisation], and everything else doesn't matter. And obviously, part of what we're discussing doesn't only…like Fogbow is not the singular actor. There are a range of them with a range of funding mechanisms and harms and benefits and so on. Is he right in saying that they are closer to WFP than to GHF?
Beatrice Lindstrom
I think that there are clear distinctions between companies like Fogbow and entities like the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, but also that there are some key traits that they have in common that are really important for understanding the broader moment that we're in, and the emergence of a potentially new trend towards corporatisation, militarisation, and politicisation of aid. And so, I think what they have in common is that they're corporatised or profit-driven entities that have taken on core humanitarian functions. And even in the context of the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, which is a foundation by name, but operates through corporate actors, that that description I think still holds. And similarly, Fogbow got its start with the involvement of a foundation that was meant to channel funding to the corporate entity. So there's this kind of blurring of corporate and for-profit and nonprofit entities that we see as a constant here. I think whether the staff themselves carry guns or not is maybe not the exact question to be focused on here. I wouldn't be surprised if the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation took the same position that, you know, they were operating in an environment where most likely the vast majority of the deaths that occurred near GHF sites were carried out by IDF soldiers and not by GHF staff themselves. But I think the problem is a broader positioning, sort of an enabling environment that is created by the approach that's taken to aid. So their… I do think it's relevant to the nature of the staffing and leadership and the backgrounds that the leadership of these organisations come to the work from. And then I think there's also this question of the relationships to states that are parties to the conflict themselves, and whether that's through direct contracts, or subcontracts, or funding, or a broader kind of political support that these entities seem to be enjoying. And from all of this, I think we see distinct human rights risks flow. So, I guess the key thing that I would point to here is that these entities, I think, operate within a different logic where humanitarian assistance is instrumentalised by states that have clear political aims in the context where they're providing funding or support for these entities. And I think this sort of aid-for-hire approach, it can create conditions for both direct and indirect harms. And so while we see the scale of the harms being vastly different in Gaza versus in contexts where Fogbow has operated, I think we have to grapple with those risks, and those risks I think stem from some of the structural setups of these entities.
Tammam Aloudat
When I brought up the issue of collaboration with states, two things came to me from the answer he gave. One is: What's wrong, who doesn't deal with states? And obviously it's a long conversation. Like there are limitations to dealing with states, and there are choices that can be made if dealing with states proves harmful, but what was fascinating to me was [that] he seemed really puzzled at me finding being close to the United States government problematic. That, you know, why wouldn't we be in line with the U.S. government?
Beatrice Lindstrom
Yeah, I mean, I think this goes back to our earlier, the earlier part of our conversation where we talked about, sort of, the disconnect from the broader critiques of aid that have been a part of the conversation in humanitarian assistance for decades. Of course, the politicisation of aid is not something new. It's something that actors have had to grapple with for a long time. And as you note, there are decisions to be made. And I think that it's, it's not a coincidence that some of the most effective humanitarian organisations in the world decline to accept money from the United States government because the U.S. government has had a history of using aid to further political aims. And I find it deeply troubling that the conversation is not about the details of the when and the how, but that the conversation seems to stop at the question of whether this is even a legitimate conversation to be had. Because I think what that does is it misses the last decades of learning, of lessons that have been hard learned in the humanitarian sector, and where we still don't always get the answers right, but at least we're most often asking the right questions. And if we're not even asking the right questions, that raises deep concern for me that it's a matter of time before affected communities bear the harms of this kind of approach to aid.

Tammam Aloudat
How likely is [it] that this model of privatised, militarised corporate aid will become seen as fully legitimate? I mean, it's obviously more convenient to some governments because there's less annoying humanitarians asking questions, but is it actually possible that this would become the funded or the prominent one? And what would humanitarianism look like if this happens?
Beatrice Lindstrom
My sense is that where we're finding ourselves today is at the beginning of a potential trend, but that there are real reasons to be concerned that this might be a broader trend. And I would point to a couple of things. I think one is that, of course, this is happening in the context of massive defunding of professional aid organisations. And the pivot, especially from the United States government, also involves an express embrace of a philosophy around aid that is one that is entirely instrumentalised to serve American interests, and where private actors are named as, kind of, core actors to carry out that plan. We can point to a few examples where this is starting to happen more and more, but it's happening against the background of a real policy shift and a prioritisation of investment in American companies, and I think that that is one of the reasons why we should be concerned that we're at the cusp of a broader trend. I think the second reason I would point to is that if you look at the history of the involvement of private military contractors in the humanitarian sector, we see a cycle of mandate expansion. So they started out in pretty limited roles where there was a clear delineation of responsibility, but over time they've sought out new roles and new responsibilities. And then the second step of that cycle has been a legitimisation of companies in those roles that happens through contracting, that happens through a general embrace of these actors as legitimate in this place. And then finally a subsumption of those roles, where companies take the place of nonprofit actors in carrying out those functions. And I think that where we're finding ourselves right now is somewhere between a mandate expansion into the delivery of humanitarian assistance and a real question about where we are in terms of legitimisation. So on the one hand, we have the world's largest funder of humanitarian assistance really embrace these actors, but still a lot of pushback from professional humanitarians and from people who understand the field. And I think that that's exactly why it's so critical that we scrutinise these actors adequately right now, before they are legitimised, and before we kind of enter the next phase of mandate expansion. I think that there is real concern that we could end up in a place where aid-for-profit becomes more and more of a new normal.
Tammam Aloudat
What would it take for private companies to be useful or to participate in that landscape without, or with the least harm possible? What's the role of humanitarians? And I ask that question in a time where, as you know, under the severe budget cuts, humanitarians are willing to accept anything that doesn't annoy donors. So there is a pressure on accepting that, or on not opposing it, or not exposing the donors wanting more political leverage. So, what should we as humanitarians do for that trend to be the least harmful possible?
Beatrice Lindstrom
I don't think we can overstate the difficult situation that many humanitarian organisations find themselves in in this moment. And for many organisations, this is existential, right? But I think as long as our focus is on survival of any one programme, on any one organisation, that we risk losing the forest for the trees. I think we need to be really cautious about what we're willing to give up in that process. I think that there was a real moment of clarity when the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation entered Gaza, where the humanitarian sector really took the lead in pushing back against this and in standing up and naming this for what it was, and by and large, you know, declaring it unacceptable. And I think it's that kind of moral clarity that is needed in this moment. I think, even beyond the humanitarian sector, we all have a shared responsibility to fight for a model of aid that is grounded in needs and rights, and is separate from politics. I think that there's a lot that's being asked of all of us in this moment, but also that there's a real opportunity here to find clarity in what is the most fundamental aspects of aid that we need to preserve into the future.

Beatrice, thank you very much for your time. This is really useful and helpful in understanding this trend. I hope we can continue the conversation.
Beatrice Lindstrom
Absolutely, thank you so much for having me. I really appreciate your focus on these really tough questions. I’m grateful to have the opportunity to contribute to the conversation.

Parents as “customers” fuelling school disputes, council says
Unknown

22:31:53 KST

Parents as “customers” fuelling school disputes, council says
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Parents are falling out with schools and turning to dispute committees to settle grievances, according to the the government’s independent education council. This is happening partly because parents are being turned into “customers” of the education system, where they can publicly compare and select schools.
The council was asked to look into the problem by the former education minister and sent its findings on Thursday.
Tension between parents and schools is usually blamed on social media, polarisation and a more individualistic society, it said, but that explanation leaves out the part played by law and policy in setting the two sides against each other.
Policy changes, such as the 2014 passend onderwijs reform, which leaves parents and schools to agree between themselves when a child qualifies for additional support, have raised tensions. Previously, an outside committee would make these decisions.
Websites allowing parents to compare schools on performance data, such as exam pass rates and the share of pupils recommended for pre-university education, have also created a customer and provider dynamic, the report said.
Disputes taken to the national dispute committees for schools rose steadily until 2024, with a slight dip last year. The number of secondary teachers who say dealing with parents is giving them stress is rising, and in primary schools a third of all teachers say the same.
The council’s two main recommendations are that ministers should consider what a policy will do to the relationship between parents and schools before introducing it, and that parents should be given more say collectively rather than only as individuals with a complaint.

Iran’s gamble: Tehran attacks US warships as blockade squeezes its economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:30:17 UTC
22:30:17 KST

Iran is taking increasingly dangerous risks against the U.S. Navy as it tries to break a costly stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz, where an American blockade and new sanctions are placing growing pressure on Tehran’s already battered economy.
In at least three incidents over the past week, Iranian forces fired missiles at U.S. warships, including an aircraft carrier, attacks not seen since the war began in February. Senior officials cited by The Wall Street Journal said Iran used maneuverable warheads in the strikes, marking a significant escalation. U.S. Central Command said the vessels successfully evaded the attacks.
The incidents have nevertheless raised concerns among U.S. officials that Iran may be improving its ability, potentially with Chinese or Russian assistance, to threaten American naval forces around Hormuz. A successful strike on a U.S. warship could almost certainly trigger a major American response and push the conflict into a far broader and more destructive phase.
Yet Tehran appears increasingly willing to accept that risk. Nineteen U.S. Navy ships are enforcing a blockade that has effectively halted Iranian oil exports, while fresh American sanctions have disrupted Iran’s financial system and accelerated the rial’s decline.
“Iran is escalating because it sees no other options,” said Mark Sievers, a former U.S. ambassador to Oman, across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran. “It is under immense pressure because of the blockade and the new sanctions.”
The calculation, analysts say, is not to match American military power but to make maintaining the status quo increasingly expensive for Washington. Iranian missile attacks and threats to commercial shipping force the United States to devote ships, air defenses and increasingly scarce missile interceptors to protecting its forces and keeping maritime traffic moving.
“Iran may see value in the risks that would accompany a successful strike on a U.S. warship,” said Alice Gower, a partner at a London-based political risk consultancy. Such an attack could shake global markets and Gulf states while forcing President Donald Trump to choose between an expensive military response and appearing weak ahead of the midterm elections. “Either way, Iran sees an advantage,” she said.
Oil pressure drives the escalation
The latest fighting began in late August, when U.S. forces struck targets in Iran after Tehran attempted to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran responded by attacking U.S. forces and oil tankers, ending roughly a month of relative calm and driving oil prices sharply higher.
The attacks on U.S. naval forces have continued even after Washington struck Iranian tankers in retaliation. They also represent a sharper approach than Tehran had taken in recent weeks against U.S. military assets in Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan, where reports said nine fighter jets were hit at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base.
But former officials and analysts say attacks on American ships are unlikely to break the blockade itself. Retired Vice Adm. John Miller, a former commander of U.S. naval forces in the Middle East, said American vessels can move farther from Iranian territory while continuing to enforce it.
“Defending the ships is certainly a major consideration,” Miller said. “We can move our ships farther away if we think they are in any danger and still continue to enforce the blockade.”
The economic consequences for Iran are already severe. Ship-tracking firm Kpler says no Iranian crude has crossed the blockade since the U.S. Navy reinstated it in mid-July, while stockpiles intended for China are rapidly being depleted.
The loss of oil revenue is depriving Tehran of its main source of foreign currency. The rial has plunged, annual inflation has risen above 80%, and the International Monetary Fund forecasts a 5.4% contraction in Iran’s economy this year, its steepest decline since the 1980s.
Other Gulf producers, meanwhile, have largely managed to keep their oil moving. The United States is escorting convoys through Hormuz, while Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are sending more crude through pipelines that bypass the strait.
Tehran’s ‘crown jewel’
That leaves Hormuz as one of Iran’s most important remaining sources of leverage. If Tehran loses its ability to threaten shipping through the strategic waterway, it also loses one of the few tools it has left to impose economic and military costs on the United States and its regional partners.
Maintaining that threat, even at the risk of a direct hit on an American warship, therefore remains central both to Iran’s military strategy and to its bargaining position in any future negotiations.
“Hormuz is the immediate concern and the main battlefield, but it is also Tehran’s greatest source of leverage,” Gower said. “It will not give it up easily. It is the crown jewel.”
The gamble carries dangers far beyond Iran and the United States. As Washington intensifies pressure on Iranian energy exports, Tehran has a growing incentive to make Gulf states and global markets share the cost of the confrontation.
“The more Washington attacks Iranian energy exports, the greater Iran’s incentive to make sure the price of the conflict is felt beyond its borders,” Gower said.

AI bottleneck-breaker: China’s Huawei touts high-speed optical module
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:30:08 UTC
22:30:08 KST

AI bottleneck-breaker: China’s Huawei touts high-speed optical module
Company claims it has the industry’s first 7.2-terabit-per-second NPO module, as firms race to set next-generation AI infrastructure standards
The Shenzhen-based tech giant showcased what it called the industry’s first 7.2-terabit-per-second (Tbps) near-packaged optics (NPO) product at the China International Optoelectronic Exposition (CIOE) in Shenzhen this week.
The technology replaces traditional copper wiring with light-based signals to shuttle vast amounts of data between AI processors at higher speeds and lower power consumption than current systems.
As AI clusters grow to include thousands of interlinked processors, conventional copper connections are hitting physical limits in bandwidth, transmission distance and power efficiency. NPO aims to solve this by bringing optical components closer to network switching chips, shortening electrical connections and reducing signal loss and power consumption.
Huawei’s module combined 36 channels operating at 200 gigabits per second each, giving it an aggregate bandwidth of 7.2Tbps, according to Man Jiangwei, director of Huawei’s advanced optoelectronics laboratory.
The capacity puts the module among a new generation of high-density optical interconnect products emerging for AI systems, alongside 6.4Tbps optical engines developed for co-packaged optics by US chipmaker Broadcom.
“We have already fully entered the product development stage,” Man said in an interview with the South China Morning Post on Thursday. “Once the whole supply chain and manufacturing system is in place, I believe it won’t be long before we can move quickly into volume production.”

Ukrainian defense startup Swarmer, which went public on Nasdaq (ticker: SWMR) in March this year, has announced a deal to acquire Ukrainian ground robotic complex (UGV) and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) manufacturer Ratel Robotics, in a deal that could be worth $224 million.
According to Swarmer's release, the agreement provides for payment in cash and stock, contingent on the achievement of all performance targets (earn-out).
Completion of the deal depends on the fulfillment of the relevant conditions, as well as obtaining the necessary approvals from regulators and shareholders and compliance with applicable legal requirements.
"Combining a combat-proven launch platform with our autonomy software, which has also proven its effectiveness in combat, is the key to creating universal and interoperable solutions," Swarmer co-founder Alex Fink was quoted as saying in the release.
The release said Ratel Robotics has signed contracts worth a total of $86 million this year and is in talks with a number of NATO countries as part of the "Build With Ukraine" initiative.
Among Ratel Robotics' key products are modular unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) platforms used for battlefield logistics, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance, drone launches and demining.
Among other things, the company is also developing two variants of UAVs, mobile workshops, and solar-powered trailers.
Ratel Robotics currently employs more than 300 people. These employees are expected to join Swarmer once the deal closes, bringing the combined company's total headcount to nearly 500.
Swarmer stressed that Ratel Robotics founder and head Taras Ostapchuk will continue in his role at the company and will report directly to Fink.
"Together with Swarmer, we plan to combine ground and aerial capabilities while delivering an increasingly higher level of autonomy. This is the next stage in the evolution of modern warfare: minimizing the threat to people and shifting risk onto unmanned systems," Ostapchuk said.
Ratel Robotics is a Ukrainian manufacturer of unmanned systems that has been developing solutions to support Ukraine's Defense Forces on the battlefield since 2023.
According to the release, Swarmer's core areas of activity include autonomous swarm coordination, multi-domain unmanned systems integration, AI-based collaborative autonomy, and command-and-control software for distributed robotic operations. In addition, the company's clients include drone manufacturers that license Swarmer's software to integrate with their hardware platforms.
As previously reported, Swarmer posted a net loss of $4.5 million in January-March 2026, compared with $0.7 million in the same period of 2025. Revenue fell to $20,300 from $110,700, while operating expenses rose to $4.5 million from $0.8 million.
The company was founded by Serhiy Kuprienko and Alex Fink in May 2023. Its stated headquarters and marketing and sales office are in Austin, Texas, while engineering teams are split between offices in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Warsaw, Poland. The company's holding structure includes subsidiaries in Ukraine, Poland and Estonia.
It later emerged that Kuprienko announced on July 26 his decision to step down as global chief executive officer (CEO); following his departure, the duties of the company's chief officer have been carried out by the CEO of Swarmer's U.S. office and co-founder, Fink.
Swarmer's net loss widened to $7.3 million in the second quarter of 2026, from $1.6 million in the same period of 2025, while revenue rose to $216,000 from $138,200.
Swarmer's revenue fell to $0.31 million in 2025 from $0.33 million a year earlier, while its net loss widened to $8.53 million from $2.07 million.

How to Treat Age Spots Without Damaging Your Skin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:29:29 UTC
22:29:29 KST

If your face, arms, or hands have started accumulating age spots, you may be wondering whether you can safely fade—or completely remove—them.
The answer is probably yes. But before you start trying to erase anything, see a dermatologist. What people casually call an “age spot” could be one of several different skin changes, some of which require medical attention rather than a brightening serum.
“The most important point is not to treat the words ‘age spot’ as a diagnosis,” says Dr. Erum Ilyas, a board-certified dermatologist in King of Prussia, Pa. “Before focusing on how to fade or remove a spot, first make sure you know what you’re treating.”
Here’s how dermatologists recommend identifying age spots, treating them, and preventing more from appearing.
First, make sure it’s actually an age spot
A true age spot, also known as a solar lentigo, is a harmless patch of excess pigment often caused by cumulative exposure. It’s usually flat, evenly tan or brown, and has a smooth, well-defined border, says Dr. Rebecca Dufner, a board-certified dermatologist in Plano, Texas. It also tends to “sit there quietly year after year.”
But people often use “age spot” to describe all sorts of marks that become more common over time. These can include seborrheic keratoses, which are benign growths that may look raised, waxy, or “stuck on,” as well as actinic keratoses, precancerous growths that are often rough or scaly. More concerningly, certain skin cancers—including melanoma—can resemble an ordinary brown spot.
That’s why it’s important to have a dermatologist examine your spots before cosmetically treating them, particularly if you’ve never had them checked.
Pay close attention to a spot that appears suddenly; changes in size, shape, or color; becomes raised; or starts itching, bleeding, crusting, or refusing to heal. Dufner also recommends using the “ugly duckling” rule: If one spot simply looks different from all of its neighbors, it deserves professional attention.
“If your eye keeps being drawn to a spot because something about it seems different or unfamiliar, it’s worth having it examined,” Ilyas says. Dermatologists can inspect it with a dermatoscope, which reveals patterns and features that aren’t visible to the naked eye. If necessary, they can biopsy it.
How to fade age spots at home
Once a dermatologist has confirmed you’re dealing with harmless age spots, you can try fading them at home. Just prepare to be patient: Topical treatments are “a slow game—think months, not days,” Dufner says.
Prescription retinoids and azelaic acid are among the strongest topical options, she says. Over-the-counter products containing vitamin C, niacinamide, kojic acid, arbutin, glycolic acid, tranexamic acid, or thiamidol may also gradually lighten the spots. Hydroquinone can be effective, but it’s best used under a dermatologist’s supervision; prolonged overuse can cause a difficult-to-treat blue-black discoloration called exogenous ochronosis.
Start with one active ingredient rather than assembling an elaborate—and potentially irritating—skin-care chemistry experiment. Because older skin tends to be thinner, drier, and more fragile, Dufner recommends beginning slowly, moisturizing regularly, and scaling back if your skin becomes irritated.
Skip the DIY concoctions
Your kitchen isn’t a dermatology clinic. Dufner advises skipping lemon juice, apple-cider vinegar, and hydrogen peroxide, which “can irritate or even burn the skin” and potentially leave behind more discoloration. Baking soda and aggressive at-home peels can also damage the skin and trigger post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
Don’t pick, scrape, burn, or attempt to freeze a growth at home, either. These approaches can cause “chemical burns, infection, scarring, or permanent pigment changes,” Murphy-Rose says. Plus, you could inadvertently remove a lesion that should have been biopsied.
Dufner also recommends avoiding high-strength, unregulated “skin-bleaching” creams sold online. If a product promises to erase years of sun damage almost instantly, consider that a reason to be suspicious.
Which in-office treatments work best?
In-office procedures generally work faster than topical products. For true age spots, “the heavy hitters are lasers and light-based treatments,” Dufner says. These procedures target excess pigment and can clear spots more quickly and completely than creams. Depending on your skin and the extent of the discoloration, a dermatologist might use a laser to treat a few defined spots or a light-based treatment to address more widespread, freckle-like sun damage. Other options include cryotherapy, which freezes individual spots with liquid nitrogen, and chemical peels.
Seborrheic keratoses require a different approach because they’re “benign skin growths rather than simply excess pigment,” Murphy-Rose says. Once a dermatologist has confirmed the diagnosis, they can simply be left alone. If a growth becomes irritated, catches on clothing, or bothers you cosmetically, a dermatologist might remove it using cryotherapy or a shave procedure. The best method depends on the spot’s thickness, size, and location, as well as the patient’s skin type.
None of these procedures is automatically the best choice for everyone. An overly aggressive treatment—or a laser used at the wrong setting—can cause irritation, scarring, or unwanted dark or light patches.
Skin tone is especially important. People with more melanin-rich skin have a greater risk of developing post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation or hypopigmentation after certain procedures, particularly cryotherapy, Murphy-Rose says. Look for a board-certified dermatologist who has experience performing the proposed treatment on people with your skin tone.
Age matters, too. Mature skin may bruise or tear more easily and take longer to heal. “Gentler is smarter,” Dufner says. A dermatologist might use lower laser settings, introduce topical ingredients more gradually, or allow additional healing time between treatments.
Can you keep age spots from returning?
Even after successful treatment, age spots can return—and new ones may continue appearing. That’s partly because “many of the spots we see today reflect sun exposure that occurred years or even decades ago,” Ilyas says. “We can’t undo that past exposure,” so additional spots may become visible even after existing ones have been treated.
Consistent sun protection can, however, reduce additional UV damage and help keep existing pigmentation from becoming darker. Murphy-Rose recommends applying a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30 every day, as well as wearing hats and sun-protective clothing. Even after an age spot has been removed, she says, new ones “can develop if the skin continues to receive significant UV exposure.”
Sunscreen also gives topical treatments a better chance to work. Without it, Dufner says, “you’re trying to fade the spots while UV exposure is telling the skin to make more pigment at the same time.”
Her advice is simple: “Treat the spot, then protect your skin from the sun so you don’t keep making new ones.”

National polls have Sunday’s election on a knife-edge, with the centre-left opposition bloc led by the Social Democrats just a few percentage points ahead of the right-wing group – a gap that has tightened over the past month.
In the middle of the row, representatives of the Left Party and the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), bitter rivals from opposite ends of the political spectrum, campaign a metre apart.
Migration is a key election issue. Multicultural Malmo, with more than a third of the city’s 368,000 residents born outside Sweden, has become the centre of the debate.
For the right, the city represents failures of integration, a cautionary tale it says of what happens when immigration goes unchecked. Beyond Sweden, Malmo draws disproportionate interest.
In 2017, the populist English politician Nigel Farage branded it the “rape capital of Europe”, a claim a leading Swedish criminologist dismissed as nonsense, while Germany’s far-right AfD has used it in its narratives about the dangers of immigration.
Strength in diversity
In the city’s town hall, a grand building with a Dutch Renaissance-style facade, Anfal Mahdi, an opposition councillor in Malmo for the Left Party, sits amid the splendour of green velvet chairs, historical oil paintings and royal portraits.
Right-wing politicians ignore the socioeconomic challenges of living in the areas built under Sweden’s “Million Programme”, she said, referring to an ambitious scheme to build one million new homes between 1965 and 1974.
It began as a social housing initiative for working-class Swedish families. In later decades, as many of those families moved out, the apartments were allocated to migrant and refugee newcomers.
Observers say what began as a utopian welfare project gradually became the physical framework of today’s segregated suburbs.
Mahdi, whose family fled Iraq after the Gulf War, grew up in one of these areas during cuts to the welfare state that had defined modern Sweden, as public spending tightened after its early-1990s economic crisis.
But what they lacked in welfare, they made up for in diversity, she said.
“I had friends from Bosnia, Palestine, Somalia and when we grew up we did not have much, but we leant on each other,” she said.
The city’s most famous son, Zlatan Ibrahimovic, grew up in Rosengard, a Million Programme estate on Malmo’s eastern side that police still classify as a “particularly vulnerable area”. The famous footballer regularly credits the area for shaping the skill and confidence that defined his career.
“It’s often in these neighbourhoods that people can shine; there is a sense of community that doesn’t exist elsewhere,” said Adam*, a 20-year-old florist who also grew up in one of the areas Sweden officially labels “vulnerable”.
He rejects the stereotypes associated with Malmo, saying young people here are far more concerned with the cost of living, finding work and the everyday pressures of getting by.
Mahdi shared this sentiment, saying “wallet politics”, relating to healthcare and unemployment, are central issues for all sections of society.
Healthcare tops voters’ concerns nationally, while unemployment in Malmo, at around 11 percent, is among the highest of any Swedish municipality.
But not everyone sees it that way.
Lena, a 78-year-old campaigner for the Moderate Party, which leads the right-wing bloc, believes integration along with schooling are taking centre stage. At the last election cycle, it was care for the elderly, she said.
Jacob, a 19-year-old resident who was speaking to representatives of various parties, said a taboo has been broken with more young people turning right, including towards the SD, now polling as Sweden’s second-largest party.
The far-right party with neo-Nazi roots could enter government for the first time if the right-wing bloc wins: Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has promised cabinet posts, including the migration portfolio.
‘Divisive politics’
Sara, a woman in her twenties of Palestinian heritage, said “divisive politics” are normal now. The rhetoric around immigration and Islam in particular has left her feeling some “don’t want integration or even assimilation, they just want you to leave”.
Under the current right-wing government, many teenagers who grew up in Sweden with their families were ordered to leave on turning 18 while their parents were allowed to stay. The government paused the separation in March after a public outcry and moved to reform in June.
In February, the Swedish Migration Agency ordered an eight-month-old boy born in the country, Emanuel, to be deported alone to Iran while the rest of his family kept their permits.
The system concerns Binto Drammeh, whose father is of Gambian heritage.
“Our uncle was made to leave as he didn’t meet the income threshold,” she told Al Jazeera.
The government has repeatedly raised the salary threshold for work permits, most recently in June, when it increased from 80 to 90 percent of the Swedish median wage.
Failing to meet it could ultimately lead to a deportation order.
Criminal networks
Crime is another main election issue.
With a population of 10.6 million, Sweden has one of Europe’s highest rates of deadly gun violence, even though lethal violence fell last year to its lowest level since 2012.
Among the challenges, criminal networks are recruiting children as young as 12 to transport weapons, sell drugs and carry out contract killings. In 2024, Danish gangs were found to be hiring Swedish teenagers to carry out shootings and bombings.
How to tackle the problem divides the parties.
The right prioritises punishment and deterrence, while the left and centre-left emphasise tackling root socioeconomic causes, rehabilitation and preventive social work. The lines are not always clean, however: the Social Democrats backed lowering the age of criminal responsibility, while the Left, Green and Centre parties voted against it.
TikTok politics
Young voters appear more engaged than at the last election.
Lena of the Moderate Party said: “I haven’t met one person who said they won’t vote,” while Mahdi said the Palestine issue has had a galvanising effect.
“Right now, all the posts on my TikTok page are from party accounts; they got a lot of likes and views and many videos are trending,” said Jacob, the 19-year-old resident.
Yet some are undecided about whom to vote for, partly because of Sweden’s unusual bloc system. Built on the idea of consensus, it means a vote for one party’s policies may be diluted in coalition, or are hard to push through.
“I will be honest, I have not voted yet,” Adam said, as he looked out at the array of campaign booths next to his flower stand. “Young people are interested in politics, but many of us think that no matter who comes, nothing will really change.”

Burak Bir

Britain on Thursday condemned renewed Houthi attacks in Yemen and against Saudi Arabia, warning that the escalation threatens regional stability and Red Sea shipping.
The Foreign Office called on the Houthis to halt the attacks, including those targeting civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.
"We offer our condolences to those injured and affected and stand with Saudi Arabia, the internationally recognised Government of Yemen, and our regional partners," the statement added.
It said the Houthis bear “full responsibility for this crisis,” adding that the renewed conflict puts vulnerable Yemenis at risk and has deepened humanitarian suffering.
The Foreign Office also pointed to the international dimension of the conflict.
“Houthi attacks endanger wider regional stability, and freedom of navigation and vital trade routes through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb,” it warned.
It said Saudi Arabia and Yemen have the right to defend their security and sovereignty in accordance with international law.
The statement comes amid Yemen’s broadest escalation since 2022, when a UN-sponsored truce was initiated before the peace process stalled and military confrontations resumed in July.
Yemen's conflict began after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Ryazan oil refinery shuts down after drone attack, Reuters reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:26:00 UTC
22:26:00 KST

Ryazan oil refinery shuts down after drone attack, Reuters reports
According to Ukrinform, Reuters reported this, citing two industry sources.
According to the agency’s sources, the Ryazan refinery’s main unit, AVT-6, as well as another major unit, AVT-4, were shut down following the attack.
It is noted that AVT-6, which, according to the sources, caught fire during the attack, is capable of refining 8 million metric tons of crude oil per year (about 160,000 barrels per day), which accounts for nearly half of the refinery’s capacity.
According to the publication, the AVT-4 unit can process 4 million metric tons of crude oil per year.
The plant’s other main unit, AVT-3, has been undergoing maintenance since mid-May.
Sources reported that repairs to the damaged units could take up to several weeks.
Rosneft did not respond to a request from Reuters for comment on the attack on the refinery.
According to industry sources, the Ryazan Refinery processed 13.1 million metric tons of crude oil in 2024, accounting for about 4.9% of Russia’s total refining volume.
This year, the facility produced 2.2 million metric tons of gasoline, as well as 3.4 million metric tons of diesel fuel and 4.3 million metric tons of fuel oil.
It is noted that the Ryazan refinery, which supplies fuel to Moscow, came under drone attack on May 15 and July 29. After the first attack, repair work at the plant lasted until about mid-July, and after the second, for about two to three weeks, sources said.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Defense Forces struck oil refineries in three regions of Russia, as well as a storage facility and launch sites for attack drones in the Kursk region.

MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. The "imaginary threat" posed by a drone to Vladimir Zelensky’s plane at the Chisinau airport, Ukrainian provocations, and strikes on ships in the Black Sea were the main topics of Thursday’s briefing by Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
TASS has compiled the Russian presidential press secretary’s key statements.
On Ukrainian provocations
- The Ukrainians "have tried, are trying, and, by all appearances, will continue to try to stage provocations" in order to "draw their Western backers deeper and more closely into the war."
- The Kiev regime’s provocations are a matter of heightened attention for Russian intelligence agencies: "This is a matter of heightened attention for our intelligence agencies. They are doing their job."
- As for the detention of a former UK embassy security guard in Moscow, who turned out to be a Ukrainian Security Service (SBU) agent gathering information on British diplomats, the loss of control over Kiev’s actions should be a cause for concern in Europe: "In theory, this should be a cause for serious concern in European capitals."
On alleged threat to Zelensky’s plane from drone
- The "threat" posed by a drone to Vladimir Zelensky’s plane at the Chisinau airport was imaginary, and the Ukrainians themselves have acknowledged this: "This imaginary 'threat' to the plane never existed, and the Ukrainians have already acknowledged this."
On Kiev’s terrorism
- Russian President Vladimir Putin discusses issues related to the special military operation with servicemen on a daily basis, including measures to protect Russian facilities from Ukrainian attacks: "All of these issues and others related to the special military operation are discussed daily by the president with defense officials, and appropriate measures are being taken."
- Having failed to turn the tide in the special military operation zone, the Ukrainian authorities are resorting to terrorist activities: "Unable to reverse the clear dynamics on the front lines, the Ukrainians are resorting to such terrorist activities."
On strikes against ships
- "A huge number of commercial ships" in the Black Sea are being used to transport weapons for the Ukrainian military; they "are being destroyed and will continue to be destroyed."
- Strikes against ships in the Black Sea cannot negatively affect relations between Russia and Turkey: "No, they cannot."
- Russia did not initiate the strikes on ships in the Black Sea; Kiev opened this "Pandora’s box": "Russia did not initiate this. I want to remind you of a statement by President [Vladimir] Putin, who said that we did not carry out any strikes. It was only after the Ukrainians began striking our civilian infrastructure and economic facilities that they opened Pandora’s box."
On Latvia’s intentions
- Latvia stands to lose a great deal due to the introduction of tariffs on grain from Russia and Belarus: "Because these export items were also beneficial to the Latvians themselves."
- Trade wars continue, and Latvia appears to be inspired by "overseas methods of dealing with customs duties."
- "Global markets are much richer than Latvia alone, and there are always alternative markets."
On BRICS summit
- Many BRICS countries face illegal restrictions and are seeking ways to ensure mutual settlements: "Many countries within BRICS face pressure and illegal restrictions imposed by third countries. Naturally, these countries seek ways to facilitate mutual settlements as they engage in economic cooperation, such as creating joint investment platforms, and so on."
- These issues will be on the agenda of the upcoming summit.
