Economic Watch: China's green industries bring solutions, cooperation opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:52:31 CST
21:52:31 KST

XIAMEN, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- When 121 electric buses rolled into Copiapó, Chile, last year, they helped turn the city into the first in Latin America to operate a fully electric public bus system.
Made by Chinese bus manufacturer King Long and shipped thousands of miles from Xiamen, east China's Fujian Province, the buses are a great example of how Chinese companies offer the world green solutions and help other countries shift to cleaner energy.
"Equipped with high-power motors, these buses can cope with steep slopes across Chile," said Yu Danyao, chief brand officer of Xiamen King Long United Automotive Industry Co., Ltd.
King Long entered the Chilean market in 2007 and has since sold more than 1,500 buses in the country, Yu said. The company develops pure-electric, hybrid and hydrogen-fueled vehicles and adapts them to local conditions.
In Saudi Arabia, it has developed a battery thermal-management system designed to withstand high temperatures and dusty conditions. In Europe, it has introduced buses designed to reduce energy consumption and meet stringent environmental standards.
King Long's green vehicles have been sold to more than 150 countries and regions, with cumulative sales exceeding 160,000 units, according to the company.
Apart from King Long buses, exhibitors at the 26th China International Fair for Investment and Trade in Xiamen are also showcasing a range of green technologies, including smart energy-storage systems, water reclamation technology, and new power systems.
Tackling the climate crisis calls for joint global efforts and China boasts highly advanced green solutions, making bilateral cooperation in this field essential, said Janna Laine, counselor for public diplomacy and communication at the Embassy of Finland in Beijing. Finland is a guest country of honor at the fair this year.
The Finnish trade and economic delegation, comprising over 40 enterprises and institutions, pays particular attention to sectors including the circular economy, resource recycling, advanced manufacturing, industrial digitalization and healthcare, according to Sakari Puisto, minister of economic affairs of Finland.
"We look forward to concluding multiple business cooperation deals during this visit," said Puisto.
The fair, which runs from Tuesday to Friday, attracted delegations from 129 countries and regions, with 60 setting up exhibition areas. Its exhibition space expanded to 200,000 square meters from 120,000 square meters last year, according to the Xiamen Municipal Bureau of Commerce. The figures offer tangible signs of growing international interest in China as a partner in trade, investment and supply chain cooperation.
The energy storage sector is no exception. The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence data centers is generating huge demand for electricity and energy storage systems.
"For 24-hour high-load scenarios such as data centers, short-duration energy storage solutions cannot meet requirements. Long-duration energy storage has become standard for new-energy infrastructure," said Ding Changfu, senior product strategy manager with Xiamen Hithium Energy Storage Technology Co., Ltd.
The company is investing 400 million euros in a battery and energy-storage production base in Spain, which is scheduled to begin operations next year.
By 2025, Hithium had sold its products in more than 40 countries and regions, while its order book extends into 2027, said Wang Pengcheng, the company's co-founder and president.
"Green and sustainable development represents an unprecedented global consensus and a profound industrial revolution," Wang said.
"As Chinese enterprises speed up global expansion, green investment has become a new highlight of external investment," said Zhou Xiaoyan, executive vice president and secretary-general of the China Council for International Investment Promotion.
From photovoltaic and wind-power equipment to lithium-ion batteries and new-energy vehicles, China is bringing its green development solutions to the world, Zhou said. ■

AU marks 24th anniversary amid call for continental unity, global influence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:52:18 CST
21:52:18 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Marking the African Union (AU) Day, Chairperson of the African Union Commission (AUC) Mahmoud Ali Youssouf has called for a renewed commitment to the ideals of Pan-Africanism, solidarity, and continental unity.
Celebrated every year on Sept. 9, this year's 24th anniversary commemorated the historic Sirte Declaration of 1999, in Libya, in which African leaders took the decision to establish the African Union to accelerate integration and strengthen Africa's voice globally.
The annual African Union Day serves as an avenue to celebrate some landmark achievements of the union, and an opportunity to reflect on the major challenges faced by the continent and the successes of the continental bloc.
In a press statement issued late Wednesday, the AUC chief emphasized that the priorities of the AU are heavily centered around accelerating economic integration, advancing peace and security, and reinforcing Africa's global voice.
Youssouf also highlighted that this year's commemoration arrives shortly after the United Nations General Assembly endorsed a significant African-led initiative, adopting a non-binding resolution that encourages the use of the Equal Earth cartographic projection in maps worldwide to replace the Mercator projection.
"A map may change how the world sees Africa, but Africa's destiny will ultimately be shaped by how Africans see themselves. The time has come to see Africa in its true size, its true strength and its true potential," he said. "Africa is not seeking a larger place in the world; Africa is reclaiming its rightful place in the world. Our task is to translate this renewed confidence into unity, prosperity, peace and influence."
The chairperson underscored that Africa's remarkable progress must also be measured by the tangible quality of life enjoyed by its people, pointing directly to the AU's 2026 focus on sustainable water availability and safe sanitation for citizens.
He called upon member states, regional economic communities, private sector actors, civil society organizations, women, and the youth to persistently collaborate toward building an integrated, self-confident African continent fully capable of independently shaping its own future destiny.
Though the historic declaration was formally signed in 1999, the Pan-African bloc was officially launched during the Durban Summit in 2002 in South Africa. It succeeded the Organization of African Unity (OAU) to boost economic cooperation, continental unity, and peace across the entire African region. ■

Kenyan researchers leverage AI to enhance malaria surveillance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:52:01 CST
21:52:01 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Kenyan researchers are set to deploy artificial intelligence (AI) in tracking and surveilling mosquito populations, marking a major technological advancement in the fight against malaria.
Eric Ochomo, a lead entomologist at the Kenya Medical Research Institute's Center for Global Health Research, stated on Wednesday that the AI-powered technology, known as VectorCam, is being integrated into ongoing malaria vector research to augment conventional surveillance techniques.
The VectorCam system combines standard smartphones with specialized light boxes and artificial intelligence algorithms to quickly identify mosquito species and analyze population characteristics, enabling researchers to collect high-precision field data more efficiently.
"The technology is helping to tell the mosquito species, feeding status and the sex. The mosquito collected is then placed on the AI device to allow collection of the data," Ochomo said in comments published by a local daily newspaper.
Ochomo noted that malaria remains a major public health challenge across Sub-Saharan Africa, and in Kenya specifically, continuing to drive high rates of morbidity and mortality despite decades of intensive control interventions.
Sunny Patel, co-founder of VectorCam, who was also quoted by the newspaper, explained that field operations will leverage local networks, with Community Health Promoters utilizing smartphone-based tools during routine community engagements.
He added that artificial intelligence holds transformative potential for national malaria control programs by strengthening vector surveillance, forecasting localized outbreaks, refining diagnostics, optimizing treatment strategies, and guiding targeted resource allocation.
The two researchers noted that AI-powered mosquito surveillance will be carried out in part by Community Health Promoters across malaria-endemic regions.
This technological integration complements core vector control interventions, including Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets, Indoor Residual Spraying, and larval source management, which have been instrumental in reducing malaria transmission across Kenya. ■

====================================================================================================

Whispers of Chinese characters on ceramic glaze: A ceramic micro-calligraphy inheritor's story
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:52:01 CST
21:52:01 KST

Liu Dachuan creates a ceramic micro-calligraphy artwork at his studio in Jingdezhen, east China's Jiangxi Province, Aug. 14, 2026.
There goes an old Chinese saying that "the scenery changes with each step." This saying can be true when you look at a ceramic micro-calligraphy artwork, on which Chinese characters are written in tiny little sizes so that you can not even notice them from a distance.
Micro-calligraphy, or weishu, is an age-old Chinese art that wields the traditional Chinese writing brush to produce Chinese characters of astonishing minuteness with naked vision. This art form has deep roots in antiquity, with its earliest traces found in the oracle bone inscriptions from the Western Zhou Dynasty (1046 BC-771 BC).
Ceramic micro-calligraphy, which combines the delicate art with polychrome ceramic, demands high in its making as the ceramic needs to go through high-temperature firing in kiln after the writing. To create a piece, the craftsman, relying solely on his naked eyes, uses a custom fashioned brush, with ultra-fine hairs and high-temperature-resistant pigments, to paint delicate motifs directly onto the ceramic's surface, no errors or corrections allowed. When the ceramic goes through repeated firings in the kiln, even the slightest deviation in temperature control can make all previous labors in vain. Upon completion, the artwork is seen with tiny little Chinese characters interlaced with paintings, complementing each other beautifully.
The art has become a treasure of traditional Chinese crafts with irreplaceable artistic values, and was inscribed as one of China's national-level intangible cultural heritages in 2014.
Liu Dachuan, a 47-year-old senior craftsman from south China's Guangdong Province, has dedicated himself to the art of ceramic micro-calligraphy for decades. He can inscribe up to 163 Chinese characters on a single square centimeter of porcelain, all perfectly distinguishable under a magnifying glass. Liu has formed a modern artistic style while carrying on the traditions, and his works have won multiple widely recognized awards.
"Writing micro-calligraphy with the naked eye tests not only your eyesight, but also your very soul," Liu said, adding that a machine might replicate the shapes of characters, but it could never depict the flowing spirit unique to the tip of a brush.
To bring ceramic micro-calligraphy to a wider audience, Liu held solo thematic exhibitions, and further established a studio in Jingdezhen, where he formally accepts apprentices and guides them step by step in the art. He also hosts public welfare open classes and intangible cultural heritage experiencing salons, where he offers lectures on the history of micro-calligraphy to local ceramics artisans and tourists on study tours.
Regarded as premium collectible art pieces, ceramic micro-calligraphy artworks have won great favor from cultural institutions and museums, collectors and art lovers across the country. Meanwhile, as craftworks embodying the charm of oriental beauty, they have also appeared in exhibitions of many foreign countries, often being selected as gifts for culture exchanges, and being collected by overseas museums. In a way, they have become artistic carriers to promote the traditional Chinese culture and the exchanges between China and the world. (Xinhua)

Namibia's inflation hits 30-month high as fuel prices surge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
20:51:51 CST
21:51:51 KST

WINDHOEK, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Namibia's annual inflation rate climbed to 5 percent in August, its highest level since February 2024, as surging fuel prices drove up transport costs, the Namibia Statistics Agency (NSA) said Thursday.
The rate rose from 4.4 percent in July and 3.2 percent in August last year, according to the agency's latest Consumer Price Index bulletin. Monthly inflation accelerated to 0.6 percent from 0.1 percent in July.
Petrol and diesel prices increased 25.1 percent year on year, driving a 17.1-percent rise in the cost of operating personal transport equipment. Higher vehicle licence and registration fees also contributed to the increase, the bulletin showed.
Overall transport prices rose 13.2 percent, the largest annual increase among the main expenditure categories, compared with a decline of 1 percent a year earlier. Transport contributed 2.0 percentage points to headline inflation, making it the biggest contributor.
Public transportation service prices increased 14.9 percent, with higher fares recorded across taxi, rail, air and bus services.
Meanwhile, annual inflation for food and non-alcoholic beverages eased to 4 percent from 5.2 percent in August last year.
Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels recorded annual inflation of 4.3 percent, up from 3.4 percent a year earlier, contributing 1 percentage point to the overall rate.
Core inflation, which excludes selected volatile food and energy items, stood at 3.8 percent in August, the NSA said. ■

BRICS 2026: Who’s coming and what’s on the agenda?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:50:17 UTC
21:50:17 KST

BRICS 2026: Who’s coming and what’s on the agenda?
The BRICS summit comes to New Delhi this weekend, bringing leaders from the expanded group of major emerging economies together for two days of talks. 
India will host the September 12-13 meeting at Bharat Mandapam, the convention center that hosted the Group of 20 (G20) summit in 2023. Russian President Vladimir Putin is expected to arrive in India this weekend for the summit, along with other heads of state and government of the group of emerging economies. 
The agenda is broad but straightforward: trade and development, technology, energy and food security, reform of global institutions, and closer cooperation among BRICS members. The leaders will also exchange views on major global and regional issues. 
India has framed its 2026 chairmanship around ‘Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability’, under a broader ‘Humanity First’ approach. 
This is India’s fourth time chairing BRICS, after 2012, 2016, and 2021. It also comes as the group marks 20 years since its establishment. 
Which countries are in BRICS now? 
The BRICS grouping has grown considerably from its original five members: Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. It now also includes Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Indonesia. BRICS has emerged as a major grouping because of its economic weight and population size.
 Together, they now account for nearly half of the world’s population, around 40% of global GDP, and 26% of international trade, according to Indian government data.
The group’s growth comes at a time when the ability of groupings such as the G7 and G20 to influence the world economy is waning amid narrow geopolitical agendas and attempts at economic coercion.
Who is attending the BRICS summit in India? 
The gathering is expected to bring together leaders of the Global South who also have the ability to set the direction of the global economy – individually and collectively.
Host country India has recorded strong economic growth this year, the fastest among major economies, reflecting well on Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Russian President Vladimir Putin is attending, the Kremlin has confirmed. Modi and Putin are also slated to hold talks in New Delhi on the sidelines of the summit, with bilateral ties and international issues expected to feature prominently in the discussions.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is attending, the Chinese Foreign Ministry confirmed on Thursday. The ministry said it “sets great store by BRICS cooperation” and supports India in hosting a successful summit. Some reports suggest that Xi will arrive with a 400-member delegation.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has confirmed that he will attend. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto are among the other leaders expected in New Delhi, with Modi and Pezeshkian also scheduled to meet.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will not travel to New Delhi and is expected to be represented by a senior government official. Bangladesh, which was invited by New Delhi, has said it will not send a representative.
Leaders and representatives from other BRICS members, partner countries, and outreach invitees will also take part.
What will BRICS leaders discuss in New Delhi? 
India has divided its presidential agenda into four broad areas.
‘Resilience’ covers issues that directly affect economies and households – health, agriculture, food and energy security, disaster preparedness, and supply chains.
‘Innovation’ covers startups, small businesses, science and technology, digital public infrastructure, and AI. ‘Cooperation’ includes development and reform of global governance institutions.
‘Sustainability’ covers renewable energy, climate action, and adaptation.
Trade, investment, and financial cooperation will also feature, along with efforts to give developing and emerging economies a greater voice in international institutions. 
Current global developments will form part of the discussions as well. The Indian Foreign Ministry said the leaders will share perspectives on “global and regional matters of mutual importance.” 
A packed schedule focused on inclusive global growth
Saturday is primarily for the group’s full members. Leaders will first meet behind closed doors for a session on ‘Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism’. 
They will later visit the ‘Bharat Innovates’ exhibition, followed by a group photo, tree-planting ceremony, and a dinner hosted by Modi. The table gets wider on Sunday, when leaders from BRICS partner countries and outreach invitees join the summit. 
The main session will focus on ‘Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth’. The summit is expected to conclude with the adoption of the New Delhi Declaration, setting out the positions and priorities agreed on by the group.

Polish Lubawa Unveils Net Screen Against FPVs and Grenade Launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:50:07 UTC
21:50:07 KST

Polish company Lubawa S.A. has developed the lightweight “Lekka osłona siatkowa” net screen to protect vehicles from shaped-charge munitions and FPV drone strikes.
Militarnyi’s correspondent reported on this from the MSPO 2026 international defense exhibition in Poland.
The system is designed to protect military vehicles and other assets from shaped-charge anti-tank munitions such as the PG-7V and PG-7VM.
Its modular design allows its dimensions to be adapted to a specific vehicle.
The screen is built around a frame made of composite material or an aluminum alloy.
The frame includes cables made of tear-resistant material. The manufacturer also applied a special coating to protect the structure from weather conditions.
The cables are tensioned using fabric straps placed along the edges of the frame. Once tensioned, the straps are secured with Velcro fasteners. Metal parts are installed at cable intersection points to prevent shifting.
Individual screen sections can be connected to one another using rigid ball joints or Velcro straps.
The system is attached to the vehicle’s hull using adjustable brackets. These allow the required distance between the net screen and the vehicle’s surface to be set.
During the exhibition, this anti-drone protection system was demonstrated on a Bobr 3 armored reconnaissance vehicle.
In August 2026, Poland also held a parade marking Polish Armed Forces Day and the 106th anniversary of the 1920 Battle of Warsaw.
During the event, in addition to the aforementioned Bobr 3, South Korean KLTV armored vehicles fitted with these net screens were also displayed.

Germany misappropriates over a third of additional defense debt in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:47:42 UTC
21:47:42 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The German government misappropriated more than a third of the new debt intended for defense spending in 2025 to finance other areas of the federal budget, an economic report revealed on Thursday.  
The ifo Institute's report detailed how Germany utilized its 2025 defense debt exemption; Emilie Hoeslinger, the author of the study, stated that the state took on €28.6 billion ($33.2 billion) in additional debt under the exemption.
Hoeslinger found that €11 billion of these funds failed to generate additional defense spending, resulting in a 38.5% diversion rate.
The researcher explained that this mechanism created financial leeway in the tax-financed core budget for other nonmilitary purposes.
The institute revealed that the government allocated €900 million from this defense exemption to the federal highway company Autobahn GmbH.
The report noted that the largest legitimate defense spending increase went toward ammunition procurement, with a surge of €2.32 billion.
Hoeslinger highlighted that spending on military research and development remained low at €883.8 million, making up only 1.2% of the total exemption expenses.
The author warned that this concentration on conventional equipment ignored future-oriented capabilities like unmanned systems and cyber defense.

Hundreds of thousands lack adequate shelter at Sudan’s Tawila camp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:47:35 UTC
21:47:35 KST

Over 665,000 displaced people face shelter crisis in Sudan’s Tawila
Insufficient aid and shelter increase hardship for displaced in Tawila, as malnutrition and disease spread rapidly.
Blue tents stand in tight rows at the Daba Naira camp in Tawila, 68 kilometres west of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur in Sudan, racked by war.
The tents were set up by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), with support from the Turkish Disaster and Emergency Management Authority.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Mass grave with 25 bodies found in Sudan’s Kurmuk after army retakes town
- list 2 of 3Is Sudan’s battlefield shaping the terms of its next political phase?
- list 3 of 3Where water conflicts pose the biggest threat in 2026
Relief teams have erected 3,000 new tents in recent months, but the number is negligible compared with the needs of more than 665,000 displaced people, the IOM said in a statement.
The most pressing question remains: how can this number of tents possibly be enough for hundreds of thousands of displaced people, especially when rainfall threatens to turn the low‑lying ground into swamps?
Promises of aid
Abdelbagi Mohamed Hamid, the minister of social welfare and humanitarian affairs coordinator in the Darfur region, told Al Jazeera Arabic that the regional government appealed to donors, including the Turkish ambassador, to provide tents for the displaced.
As a result, Turkiye allocated 30,000 tents to be distributed in Darfur and Kordofan through the IOM. Abdelbagi said 3,000 of 6,000 expected tents were erected in the Daba Naira camp in Tawila. Another 2,450 were delivered to the Salam, al‑Wihda and al‑Nakheel camps in Shaeria locality in South and East Darfur.
The minister said the Malha locality had the greatest need for humanitarian assistance in Darfur, followed by Tina, Karnoy and Um Baru areas. The Tina border crossing should be opened to allow the delivery of aid to these isolated areas, which suffer from acute shortages of food, medicine and fuel, while the war has deepened their isolation and worsened their humanitarian situation, he said.
Abdelbagi warned that providing shelter alone is not enough to confront the crisis, given the looming danger of famine, which could prove deadlier than the war itself, as humanitarian organisations struggle to reach many affected regions.
Worn‑out tents
The arrival of the new tents coincided with the beginning of the rainy season and an outbreak of fires sweeping through displacement camps, increasing the suffering of displaced people living under tattered canopies without protection from wind and rain, amid acute shortages of food, clean water and healthcare.
The IOM warned of persistent and worsening humanitarian needs in Tawila, as services deteriorate and diseases like cholera spread amid a lack of clean drinking water, resulting in watery diarrhoea and skin infections. The camps are overcrowded and lack basic sanitation.
The organisation, while continuing to expand the number of shelters in the Daba Naira camp, cannot keep up with the rapid pace of displacement.
‘Dropping like flies’
Ahmed Mousa, a displaced man from el-Fasher who is staying in the Daba Naira camp, told Al Jazeera that the new tents do not cover even a tenth of the camp’s needs, with people sleeping in the rain in the open and children falling ill without adequate care.
Fatima Ibrahim, a displaced woman in the same camp, said people fled el-Fasher in search of safety – only to find themselves exposed to the elements, hunger and disease.
“We see the new tents from afar, but they are not enough. We are dropping like flies from hunger and disease. Our children fall ill before our eyes, and we don’t even have medicine,” she said, adding that many families slept on bare ground without protection from the cold of night and the heat of day.
Famine ‘may be more dangerous than war’
The Minister of Agriculture in the Government of Darfur region, Al‑Sadiq Barango, told Al Jazeera in a statement that the famine may be more dangerous than the war, amid declining seasonal rains and the drying of agricultural lands and livestock pastures.
He says the war has driven farmers to abandon their land, while cultivated areas, particularly fruit farms and cash‑crop plantations, have been attacked and destroyed by armed groups.
Barango described the situation as “ominous signs of a looming catastrophe,” and called for urgent humanitarian intervention, as starvation threatens thousands of people across Sudan, with Darfur the most affected due to years of conflict and the collapse of agricultural infrastructure.
‘Tawila is not just numbers’
Tawila hosts about 665,000 displaced people, most of whom fled el-Fasher and its surroundings, according to the IOM’s statement. Their number had more than doubled between March and September 2025, from 238,000 to more than 652,000.
More than 70 percent of households in Tawila lack healthcare, while half of families have been unable to obtain treatment, according to the organisation’s estimates. Children under the age of five and pregnant women are the most affected, with rising rates of malnutrition and infectious diseases.
Adam Rijal, spokesperson for the Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugees, told Al Jazeera that “Tawila is not just numbers,” noting that needs exceed capacities dozens of times over, and warning of more deaths, especially among children and the elderly, due to hunger, disease and the absence of basic services.
Relief challenges
Humanitarian organisations face major difficulties reaching displaced people because of rough terrain and the spread of checkpoints belonging to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which is at war with the Sudanese government and controls vital routes in the area.
Local activists say that aid trucks are sometimes subjected to looting and extortion, which raises the cost of relief and delays its arrival to those who need it. Many displaced people – according to field reports – have been forced to walk long distances to obtain limited food rations, while others go weeks without assistance.
In Tawila, where hundreds of thousands live in worn‑out tents amid disease outbreaks and the hazards of the rainy season, the need for shelter, food and care is growing, while 3,000 tents are nowhere near enough to confront a humanitarian catastrophe that is worsening by the day.

Poland says it has lost about €113.5bn due to war in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:45:00 EEST
21:45:00 KST

Poland says it has lost about €113.5bn due to war in Ukraine
Poland's Statistics Office has reported that the country has incurred losses of more than PLN 490 billion (about €113.5 billion) in connection with the war in Ukraine.
Source: Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Analysts from Poland's Statistics Office calculated that the household sector suffered the greatest losses as a result of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Its losses amounted to PLN 292.1 billion (€67 billion). The business sector, meanwhile, lost PLN 126 billion (€29 billion), while the government and local government sector lost PLN 72 billion (€16.5 billion).
The calculations cover the four years of the war in Ukraine from 2022 to 2025. Total losses over this period were estimated at PLN 490.1 billion. This amounts to about 3.5% of Poland's combined GDP for 2022-2025.
The Statistics Office took into account, among other things, the scale of aid provided to Ukraine and Ukrainians, the situation on the labour market, and changes in the economy and demographics. It also analysed Poles' attitudes and the impact of the war and the influx of refugees into Poland on households and businesses.
As Statistics Office head Marek Cierpiał-Wolan explained, the calculations also included the loss of households' purchasing power due to slower wage growth following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, opportunity costs related to the defence budget, and the decline in gross value added in Polish industry.
Regarding the latter, statisticians highlighted the significant impact of the war in Ukraine on Poland's construction sector. The decline in gross value added in this part of the economy was estimated at PLN 120.9 billion (€27.9 billion).
The start of the war also led to higher material prices, with non-ferrous metals, crushed stone, glass, cement, asphalt, steel and plastics becoming more expensive.
Background:
- Recently, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said there are signs that Russia is seriously preparing for an escalation and that the next seven to eight months could be critical for the security of Ukraine, Poland and the entire region.
- Earlier, Polish President Karol Nawrocki said that he believes support for Kyiv in its fight against Russian aggression should continue because Ukraine's success is in Poland's strategic interests.

Durrani urged Pakistan to reverse the decision and allow the students to complete their medical degrees before returning to Afghanistan.

The human rights organization pointed out that students had spent years studying medicine and could now see their education abruptly ended, with little prospect of resuming their studies elsewhere.

What Kazakhstan’s New Unicameral Parliament Means for Its Foreign Policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:43:00 UTC
21:43:00 KST

In early June, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed enabling laws, putting into effect the new constitution passed via referendum in March 2026. Among the most significant changes was the abolishment of the bicameral parliament and its replacement with a new unicameral body, the Kurultai, whose 145 deputies were subsequently elected through party lists on August 23.
While the domestic consequences of the changes to the legislature have been debated widely, the question of how they will affect Kazakhstan’s foreign policymaking remains underexamined.
With the abolishment of the bicameral parliament – comprising an upper house, the Senate, and a lower house, the Mazhilis – the number of committees under the new legislature was reduced to eight, down from 13 (seven in the former Mazhilis and six in the Senate).
Under Article 61 of the prior constitution, the dual-committee structure provided checks and balances within the legislative branch. The Mazhilis’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defense, and Security served as the primary chamber for drafting, amending, and holding preliminary readings for security and international agreements, while the Senate’s Committee on International Relations, Defense, and Security acted as a second layer of technical and diplomatic vetting. Treaties and defense pacts moved sequentially through both chambers and both committees. The Senate could approve, return for revisions, or reject a bill passed by the Mazhilis.
Another structural change lies in how deputies are selected. In the previous bicameral parliament, the president could appoint a certain number of deputies, and often appointed seasoned diplomats such as former ambassadors, ex-ministers, and career officials. The most prominent example is the current president, Tokayev, who was twice appointed as Senate speaker. Under the previous constitution, the Senate speaker was designated to become acting president if a sitting president stepped down or could not perform their duties – that’s what happened in 2019 when Nursultan Nazarbayev resigned. When Nazarbayev resigned, that arrangement delivered the presidency to an experienced diplomat, an outcome read at the time as a signal that Nazarbayev considered foreign policy the greatest challenge of the transition.
Although the previous Senate could reject the Mazhilis’ bills, it rarely rejected one outright. A strong presidency in Kazakhstan mostly sets direction of foreign policy, and the upper and lower chambers were typically aligned with the president’s objectives and policies. There was a case in 2011 when the Senate rejected a Mazhilis bill on the planned deployment of military personnel to Afghanistan. Most of the time, however, the two chambers did not come into conflict, and international agreements and treaties passed smoothly.
Under the new Kurultai, all foreign policy affairs fall to the Committee on International Relations, now chaired by Marat Kozhayev. The committee will be responsible for legislative review and preliminary scrutiny of international treaties, security pacts, and bilateral agreements. Given how much further the presidency has been consolidated under the new constitution, the Kurultai’s foreign policy outlook is likely to align closely with Tokayev’s. And with all deputies now elected through party lists, the Kurultai may lack experience in international law and negotiation that the previous Senate held via presidential appointments, as mentioned above.
Tokayev has framed these constitutional and structural reforms as a modernization, an answer to the turbulence in world politics. The changes are supposed to push the agenda of creating an “effective, transparent and responsive” system. Ambitious as it is, this path poses several risks to foreign policy. First, with no second layer of review, the risk of ratifying rushed or flawed agreements increases.
Second, the new system further consolidates executive power. The president holds the right to dissolve the Kurultai if it repeatedly rejects the presidentially nominated parliamentary chairman, further weakening the legislature. Moreover, according to Article 42 of the new constitution, the president, as the head of state, holds the authority to determine the primary directions of foreign policy, as well as negotiate and sign treaties. A newly created advisory institution, the People’s Council (Halyk Kenesi), will also “possess the right of legislative initiative and will be empowered to introduce bills to parliament,” as well as “the power to prepare legislation for the Kurultai and, on the same basis as parliament, to propose nationwide referendums.” Notably, the People’s Council consists of 126 members drawn from three categories – ethnocultural organizations, local governments (Maslikhats), and civil society – but all approved by the president.
To minimize the risks to Kazakhstan’s foreign policy now that the Senate, its chamber of sober second thought, has been abolished, the country should consider introducing minimum review windows to avoid rushed decisions, empowering the Kurultai’s Committee on International Relations, and ensuring that the newly created People’s Council remains strictly an advisory, consultative forum.

Iran nuclear file is back at the UN Security Council. What now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:41:41 UTC
21:41:41 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran's nuclear file is back at the UN Security Council. What will happen next?
The International Atomic Energy Agency's Board of Governors has referred Iran to the UN Security Council over its alleged failure to comply with nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first such referral in 20 years.
The 35-member board adopted the resolution on Wednesday by 23 votes in favour, with Russia, China and Niger voting against and eight countries abstaining.
Submitted by the United States, Britain, France and Germany, the resolution follows an earlier decision in June 2025 that found Iran to be in "non-compliance" with its obligations.
The latest move represents a significant diplomatic escalation between Tehran and Western powers, but with Russia and China holding veto power at the Security Council, it remains unclear whether it will result in any concrete action against Iran.
So why has Iran been referred, what could happen next, and what does it mean for Tehran's nuclear programme?
Why has Iran been referred to the Security Council?
The referral stems from the IAEA's previous finding that Iran had failed to comply with its nuclear non-proliferation obligations.
The agency's concerns predate the latest US-Iran war and centre partly on Tehran's failure to provide satisfactory explanations for traces of uranium found at undeclared Iranian sites that the IAEA had spent years investigating.
The Board of Governors ruled in June 2025 that Iran was in "non-compliance", but referring the matter to the Security Council on that basis required a separate resolution.
Wednesday's resolution also builds on a more recent decision calling on Iran to declare its remaining enriched uranium stockpile and allow IAEA inspectors to verify it.
What exactly does the new resolution do?
The resolution asks IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi to report on the latest decision and previous resolutions to all IAEA members, as well as to the UN Security Council and General Assembly.
Unlike a consensus decision, the resolution was put to a vote. Twenty-three countries backed it; Russia, China and Niger opposed it; and eight abstained.
It was submitted by four Western states: the US, Britain, France and Germany.
The referral itself does not impose new sanctions or other penalties on Iran. Instead, it formally brings the issue before the Security Council and increases diplomatic pressure on Tehran.
Why is the decision significant?
It is the first time Iran's nuclear file has been referred to the Security Council on non-compliance grounds in two decades.
It also comes during a vastly different political and military environment.
The June 2025 non-compliance finding was adopted just one day before Israel began bombing Iranian nuclear facilities, with the United States subsequently joining the attacks.
Iranian nuclear sites have also been targeted during the latest US-Israel war with Iran, while the IAEA has been unable to regain access to key facilities that were struck.
That has left the agency facing significant gaps in its knowledge about Iran's nuclear activities, including the fate of its highly enriched uranium.
How has Iran responded?
Iran has rejected the resolution as politically motivated.
Its mission to the IAEA said that "once again, a political resolution on Iran was adopted without consensus" by the agency's Board of Governors.
Tehran blamed the current situation entirely on what it described as the "criminal acts of aggression" committed by the United States and Israel, adding that Washington's objective of forcing Iran to surrender "will never be achieved".
Iran had warned before the vote that it would respond if the resolution was adopted, although its initial reaction did not specify what measures it might take.
Could the UN Security Council impose new measures on Iran?
In theory, bringing the issue before the Security Council opens another arena for international action against Tehran.
In practice, however, significant measures are considered unlikely.
Russia and China, both allies of Iran, are permanent members of the Security Council and possess veto power.
Both countries voted against Wednesday's IAEA resolution, meaning they could block attempts to impose measures against Tehran at the UN.
The immediate significance of the referral is therefore largely diplomatic: it further escalates the confrontation between Iran and Western powers and places the nuclear dispute formally before the Security Council.
What happened to Iran's enriched uranium?
This remains one of the biggest unanswered questions surrounding Iran's nuclear programme.
Iran has not allowed IAEA inspectors to return to bombed nuclear facilities, including the country's three uranium enrichment sites, which were destroyed or severely damaged in US-Israeli attacks.
Tehran has also not provided an account of its enriched uranium stockpile.
Before the strikes, the IAEA estimated that Iran possessed 440.9kg of uranium enriched to as much as 60 percent purity.
That is significantly above the levels normally associated with civilian nuclear energy and relatively close to the roughly 90 percent enrichment associated with weapons-grade material.
According to the IAEA's benchmark, the stockpile would have been sufficient, if further enriched, for around 10 nuclear weapons.
The agency believes more than 200kg of the stockpile remains at one site, although it is unclear how much survived the attacks undamaged.
Grossi has described the uncertainty surrounding the material as a "serious proliferation concern" and called for the situation to be addressed urgently.
Does this mean Iran is building a nuclear weapon?
No. The IAEA's non-compliance finding and the referral to the Security Council do not in themselves establish that Iran is building a nuclear weapon.
The dispute concerns Iran's compliance with its safeguards and reporting obligations, unanswered questions surrounding nuclear material and the IAEA's inability to verify the status of its enriched uranium stockpile.
Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes.
The immediate question is therefore not whether the Security Council will determine that Iran has decided to build a bomb, but whether the referral can increase pressure on Tehran to restore cooperation with inspectors and account for its nuclear material.
With Russia and China likely to oppose punitive Security Council action, the referral may ultimately have greater diplomatic significance than immediate practical consequences.

RN 'breach': Amid 'severe' differences with 'bright, young' Bardella, Le Pen 'dictates party line'

François Picard is pleased to welcome Victor Mallet, Financial Times Senior Editor at the World News Desk. He interprets the emerging tensions between Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella as more than a clash of personalities. They reveal a deeper struggle over the political future of France's far-right National Rally is becoming as they find themselves in prime position in their hunt to capture the French presidency. Bardella is formally president of the party and has developed his own political constituency, particularly among younger voters and parts of the business community. Yet Mallet argues that Le Pen continues to exercise the decisive ideological and strategic authority.
The controversy over Bardella’s migration agreement with Nigel Farage therefore matters less, in his reading, for the substance of the agreement than for the autonomy Bardella appeared to claim by making policy internationally sans Le Pen’s approval. As Mallet puts it, The party line falls very clearly on Marine Le Pen’s shoulders.
The disagreement also exposes competing visions of the RN’s political future. On pensions and economic policy, Bardella appears more willing to acknowledge fiscal constraints and entertain reform, while Le Pen remains attached to the party’s socially protective economic platform. Strategically, Bardella seeks to broaden the RN into a coalition encompassing the center-right as well as the nationalist right; Le Pen, in Mallet’s account, remains more protective of the party’s established identity and policies. Their constituencies are complementary as well: Bardella brings youth, social-media appeal and business support, while Le Pen possesses experience, working-class identification and a more practiced popular touch.
This is why Mallet ultimately sees reconciliation as the only rational outcome. Neither figure is necessarily strong enough to discard the other without cost. The Le Pen-Bardella partnership is therefore both an electoral asset and a source of instability. With the RN in a commanding position, Mallet crystallizes the stakes in one striking formulation: “It’s the RN’s election to lose.”

The ECB raised interest rates for the second time due to rising oil prices
Kyiv • UNN
The ECB raised the deposit rate to 2.5% amid inflation of over 3% due to higher energy prices. The regulator forecasts 3% inflation in 2026.
The European Central Bank (ECB) raised interest rates for the second time this year — a move expected by the market, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The publication notes that the regulator is seeking to curb rising inflation caused exclusively by higher energy prices due to the war involving Iran.
The sharp rise in oil and natural gas prices caused inflation in the eurozone (which comprises 21 countries) to significantly exceed 3% last month, deviating substantially from the ECB's target of 2%.
The recent escalation of the conflict points to further price pressures, which could eventually affect wage levels as well.
"The outlook remains highly uncertain: there are risks of both higher inflation and slower economic growth," the ECB said in a statement.
The ECB also raised its forecast for economic growth in 2026 to 0.9% (from the June figure of 0.8%) and now expects average inflation to stand at 3.0% this year and 2.5% in 2027.
Following Thursday's increase, the ECB's benchmark deposit rate reached 2.5% — the upper end of the "neutral" range, which officials believe neither restrains nor stimulates economic growth.
Although financial investors expect further rate hikes later this year and in 2027, the ECB is unlikely to rush into its next steps given the ambiguous economic outlook.
Recall
In June the European Central Bank raised its key interest rates for the first time in nearly three years. The reason was accelerating inflation in the eurozone amid rising energy prices due to the war surrounding Iran.

Israeli whistleblowers detail Gaza civilian toll in Venice film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:37:30 UTC
21:37:30 KST

Israeli whistleblowers detail Gaza civilian toll in Venice film
VENICE, Sept 10 - Mass civilian deaths were routinely built into Israeli military targeting decisions in Gaza, according to a Venice Film Festival documentary unveiled on Thursday that challenges official accounts of the war.
"NAZA", directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, takes its title from an Israeli military term for the expected number of "collateral casualties" in air strikes and draws on testimony from intelligence officers and soldiers.
There was "mass killing on an industrial scale", one of the officers says in a series of anonymous interviews.
The film received a 25-minute standing ovation at its premiere, by far the longest of the festival so far this year.
AI SYSTEMS GUIDING THE ATTACKS
Gaza health authorities say more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military campaign, which was triggered by an attack on Israel by Hamas militants in October 2023 that killed around 1,200 people.
Israel says it has gone to great lengths to avoid civilian casualties and that Hamas uses Gaza's civilians as human shields in densely populated areas - a claim Hamas denies.
The film tells a different story.
"We show in our film a targeting system that is, by design, targeting people in civilian spaces, in their family homes," Abraham told Reuters. "Sometimes it can be 500 NAZA ... destroying entire villages or entire neighbourhoods."
Intelligence officers described an AI-assisted system that identified targets using data gathered from thousands of hacked mobile phones. They said the phrase "daddy's home" picked up on a child's phone would be enough to trigger an airstrike.
The officers also described the killing of civilians in Israeli-designated no-go zones, including near aid distribution centres. The location of the zones was not disclosed to residents, one officer said: "They have to learn with blood."
The United Nations said last year that more than 400 Palestinians were killed while seeking aid. Israel acknowledged civilians had been harmed at distribution centres and said it had amended its rules of engagement.
LOOKING BACK TO THE HOLOCAUST
Several of the officers interviewed compare what they witnessed to historical patterns of dehumanisation and discuss parallels with Israel's actions and the Nazi Holocaust.
"It's a link that comes from the soldiers," Abraham said.
"In a situation where so often you see how the memory of the Holocaust is used as a means to justify Israel's actions in Gaza, it's very important to draw a more universal conclusion."
The Israel Defense Forces did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment about the documentary.
All the interviews are filmed on rooftops in Tel Aviv at night, with scenes of destruction from Gaza only shown briefly at the end. The directors said they wanted to highlight the contrast between daily life in Israel's commercial capital and the devastation unfolding roughly 60 km (37 miles) away.
"We wanted to show how life in Tel Aviv goes on," said Szor, who won an Oscar with Abraham last year for their documentary "No Other Land", about Israeli demolitions in the West Bank.
She added that many Israelis feel no empathy for Palestinian civilians. "There is a big part of Israeli society who are saying out loud that there are no innocent people in Gaza."
Many officers in the film came from elite units and do not fit the stereotype of ideological hardliners. "They sometimes describe themselves as left-wing," she said. "And they perhaps are the people who are responsible for the most killing."
Abraham doubted that Israel would bring anyone to justice for the civilian deaths without outside pressure.
"I hope there will be justice and accountability for the crimes. ... It depends on holding people to account and on the political will of the United States and the EU," he said.
"NAZA" is one of 21 films competing for Venice's Golden Lion award, which will be presented on Saturday. REUTERS

The tight monetary policy stance, which will be maintained until price stability is achieved, will strengthen the disinflation process through demand, exchange rate and expectation channels, the bank said in a statement, accompanying its rate decision on Sept. 10.
The committee will determine the policy rate by taking into account realized and expected inflation and its underlying trend in a way to ensure the tightness required by the projected disinflation path in line with the interim targets, it added.
Monetary policy decisions are made prudently on a meeting-by-meeting basis with a focus on the inflation outlook, it said.
In case of a significant and persistent deterioration in the inflation outlook, monetary policy stance will be tightened, according to the statement.
The committee reiterated that it remains highly attentive to upside risks on inflation.
Despite monthly fluctuations, recent inflation figures and leading indicators suggest that the underlying trend of inflation is decelerating, said the bank.
Data on economic activity as well as the limited pass-through of supply shocks to domestic prices confirm the weakness in domestic demand, it added.
“On the other hand, elevated energy prices amid geopolitical developments pose an upward risk to the inflation outlook. The impact of geopolitical developments on the inflation outlook through the cost channel, economic activity and expectations is closely monitored,” said the bank.
Under the new Medium-Term Program (OVP) targets, released on Sept. 6 covering 2027-2029, annual consumer inflation is projected to reach 28.4 percent by the end of 2026, before declining to 21 percent in 2027, 13.5 percent in 2028 and 9 percent by the end of 2029, returning to single-digit levels.
The next MPC meetings are scheduled for Oct. 22 and Dec. 10.

Is Finland to blame for the world's falling Pisa scores? Some think so
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:35:51 EEST
21:35:51 KST

This week, Pisa results showed Finnish teenagers are scoring lower in reading, math and science. But Finland is far from the only country where dropping results on the triennial international study have caused a major stir.
The Pisa comparison of wealthy OECD countries shows that 15-year-olds' skills have declined sharply since the early 2000s in most developed countries.
UK news outlet The Economist examines why this might be happening.
The Covid-19 pandemic at the beginning of the decade disrupted learning, and those effects are now showing up in the latest results. Another factor the newspaper highlights is the impact of smartphones on children's ability to concentrate and read.
Fooled by Finland?
The Economist recalls that when the first Pisa tests were conducted in 2000, Finland's exceptionally strong performance attracted international attention.
Education policymakers from around the world rushed to Helsinki to find out what Finland had done right.
Many were surprised to hear that Finnish schools had relatively few tests and that, especially for younger children, education was described as being "play-based," The Economist writes.
In Finland, there was also an emphasis on teachers spending less time lecturing at the front of the class and more time helping pupils learn things for themselves.
According to The Economist, that was the message Finland quickly exported to countries around the world.
It points out, however, that few countries have seen their Pisa scores fall as dramatically as Finland.
Critics of Finland's education model, the newspaper says, argue that the country's strong results in the early 2000s were actually more likely the result of a more traditional school system that had remained in place into the 1990s, rather than the "progressive" teaching methods that Finland became famous for.
If that is the case, this mistake may have sent dozens of school systems down the wrong path, the paper writes.
It notes that the UK took its education system in a different direction during the 2000s. Their schools have placed greater emphasis on factual knowledge rather than more vaguely defined skills. Exams have also remained relatively rigorous, according to The Economist.

Three suspects have been arrested on suspicion of passing off sport horses as horses for slaughter during raids in Sint-Gillis-Waas and Kruisem (East Flanders) and Zaventem (Flemish Brabant) East Flanders Federal Judicial Police have confirmed. By forging passports and constantly moving the horses trained for equestrian competitive disciplines around both at home and abroad, they were able to sell sport horses as slaughter horses. This earned the suspects considerably more money.
International intelligence revealed that Belgians too were involved in malpractices in the international horse sector. Horses were being traded from Ireland to the European mainland, with some of them ending up in slaughterhouses here.
A horse dealer from East Flanders was found to have played a key role in this, according to the Federal Judicial Police of East Flanders. The horse dealer also collaborated with others from the Netherlands, France and Ireland.
The gang sold sport horses that had been given all sorts of medication as slaughter horses, because this yielded the trader and the others much more money. Sport horses of little value could fetch up to 1,500 euros as slaughter horses.
24 searches at home and abroad
A total of 24 premises were raided in Belgium, the Netherlands, France and Ireland: 4 in Belgium, 7 in the Netherlands, 7 in France and 6 in Ireland. More than 200 investigators were deployed, both at home and abroad.
In Belgium, the raids took place in Sint-Gillis-Waas, Kruisem and Zaventem. “Three Belgian suspects were arrested during these searches,” East Flanders Federal Judicial Police say.
The identity, origin and welfare of more than 1,000 horses was also checked. “A significant number were seized under administrative and judicial orders. Further investigations are underway to determine where other horses involved have been taken”.
In addition to the seizure of horses, registers, invoices and communication devices were also seized. Furthermore, more than 100,000 euros in cash was found and seized.
Two suspects remanded in custody, third released on bail
Three suspects appeared before an investigating judge on Wednesday. Two of them were remanded in custody, whilst the third suspect was released on bail.

Why Is China Less Active in the 2026 Ebola Epidemic?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:34:00 UTC
21:34:00 KST

The Ebola epidemic spreading through the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) could become the largest Ebola outbreak on record if infections continue at their current pace. More than 6,700 people had been infected and more than 3,200 had died by September 2026. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a form of Ebola for which there is currently no licensed vaccine or approved treatment.
The crisis is unfolding at a remarkable moment for global health. The United States is retreating from the global health system it once led. Beijing is the world’s second-largest economy and holds substantial interests in the DRC’s copper and cobalt industries. That matters not because Beijing has an obligation to replace Washington. Rather, the outbreak offers a test of whether, as the United States pulls back from global institutions, China will step forward.
During the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak, which caused approximately 11,325 deaths and more than 28,600 cases, China emerged as an unexpectedly prominent donor. By late 2014, Beijing had provided assistance valued at 750 million yuan, including laboratories, food aid, and health personnel. What was particularly striking, however, was the speed with which China’s aid arrived. Ebola was first detected in Guinea in March 2014, and by April, China had sent 4 million yuan worth of assistance. This was quickly followed by several firsts for Beijing, including the use of chartered flights to deliver humanitarian relief and the deployment of its first overseas infectious-disease field hospital.
Western countries, on the other hand, were slower to react. It was not until the outbreak had expanded dramatically during the summer of 2014 that the United States, Britain, and other major donors mounted large-scale responses. By then, China had already been providing assistance for months. Although Western countries would ultimately contribute more money, the significance of China’s early response went beyond its dollar value. It demonstrated Beijing’s growing willingness to assume a visible role in international affairs, foreshadowing a decade of intensifying geopolitical competition.
Humanitarian concerns were not the only interests at stake. Officially, Chinese authorities talked about South-South cooperation, multilateralism and subtle criticism of Western indecisiveness. Western analysts, however, saw additional strategic interests, such as reducing the risk that Ebola would reach China and testing Beijing’s capacity for overseas power projection.
The response offered scientific benefits as well. The crisis gave Chinese scientists rare access to outbreak data and field specimens. Chinese teams gained valuable experience establishing and operating mobile biosafety laboratories, capabilities that would later become increasingly important as China expanded its role in infectious-disease preparedness.
China today is wealthier, more diplomatically influential, and far more technically capable than it was a decade ago. Yet as of late August 2026, Beijing had provided $4.5 million – around 30.2 million yuan – in direct support to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and sent a few teams of medical experts. All assistance is valuable. But the level of support from China remains far smaller than many would have expected.
On the American side, despite the Trump administration’s broader retreat from foreign aid and its “America First” approach to global health, the United States has committed more than $512 million directly to Ebola response. Furthermore, the administration has requested more than $1.4 billion in additional funding from Congress. This suggests something more complicated than a simple transfer of global health leadership from Washington to Beijing.
One explanation is that China simply faces less pressure to prove itself. In 2014, China was still establishing its identity as a major global actor. Ebola offered an unusually visible opportunity to demonstrate that Beijing could provide international aid at a moment when Western governments appeared hesitant. Today, China’s global status is no longer in question. It finances infrastructure across much of the developing world, sits at the center of global manufacturing, and has built deep diplomatic relationships throughout Africa.
A second explanation is that the scientific incentives have changed. During the 2014-2016 outbreak, China could pair humanitarian assistance with an expanding research agenda, such as developing a vaccine against the Zaire Ebolavirus that was ravaging Western Africa. The current scientific landscape is different. Many of the vaccine and therapeutic candidates prioritized by the WHO are being developed outside China. With less obvious scientific ownership, Beijing may have fewer incentives to pair humanitarian assistance with a high-profile research agenda.
A third explanation may be the differing geopolitical environment. China in 2026 is operating amid slower economic growth and a more difficult geopolitical environment. Chinese citizens may want to see resources focused on issues at home. Further, an expansive intervention in eastern DRC would also carry operational and security risks. Lastly, Ebola competes for attention with wars, economic instability, and other international crises that are defining 2026.
China’s own rhetoric creates an important test. Its June 2026 white paper on global governance argued that major countries should assume greater responsibility and that international cooperation should produce concrete results. Ebola provides an opportunity to put those principles into practice.
The current Ebola crisis also presents areas where China could make distinctive contributions. Its strong manufacturing and logistical capacities could make it an important surge supplier of diagnostics, protective equipment, and other medical goods. On the diplomatic front, China can mobilize its strong relationships with African partner countries to become a multiplier of African and WHO capacities, assisting with the continent-wide response.
Greater transparency could help. More detailed public reporting on the scale, timing, and purpose of Chinese assistance would make Beijing’s contribution easier to assess. Western governments, for their part, should avoid treating Chinese participation reflexively as a geopolitical threat. Both sides should look for areas where cooperation is possible.
The larger lesson extends beyond Ebola. The decline of American leadership does not necessarily mean that another power will automatically fill the void. China may have the resources to do so, but whether – and where – it chooses to deploy them is a different question.
For the people confronting Ebola on the frontlines, however, geopolitics is secondary. The immediate objective is simpler: preventing as much suffering as possible. The test for Washington and Beijing is not which country replaces the other, but whether both can use their considerable capabilities to bring the outbreak under control.

South Africa protests US Mandela auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:32:02 UTC
21:32:02 KST

South Africa protests US Mandela auction
South Africa has asked its highest court to prevent 29 objects linked to anti-apartheid leader and former President Nelson Mandela from being sold in the US, arguing that their export without authorization threatens the country’s cultural heritage.
The South African Heritage Resources Agency (SAHRA), Robben Island Museum, and the Department of Sport, Arts and Culture brought the case before the Constitutional Court on Tuesday. Judgment was reserved following the hearing.
The disputed collection includes Mandela’s identity document, iconic shirts, writings, glasses and gifts from former US presidents. In its court filing, SAHRA warned that the objects were “at risk of being lost to the national estate.”
The objects are under the control of Mandela’s eldest daughter, Makaziwe, and Christo Brand, a former Robben Island prison warder who became his friend. In late 2021, Makaziwe consigned the objects to New York-based Guernsey’s auction house for a sale intended to finance a memorial garden near her father’s grave.
The legal battle centers on whether the objects are protected under South Africa’s heritage laws. SAHRA says their association with the former president means they cannot be exported without its approval. Makaziwe argues that the agency has not demonstrated the historical significance of each item and has questioned its claim to be acting in her father’s interests.
The collection also includes a broken, handmade key from Robben Island. Brand says he found it in a prison desk and did not use it to open Mandela’s cell. During the hearing, his lawyer reportedly acknowledged that the object had been misrepresented in marketing material linking it directly to Mandela.
The auction was initially announced in 2021 but suspended after SAHRA intervened. The Pretoria High Court later ruled against the agency, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court of Appeal in January after finding that SAHRA had not shown why each item qualified as protected heritage.
The dispute comes amid wider efforts by African governments to prevent historically significant objects from being sold abroad. Ethiopia obtained the withdrawal of artefacts looted from Maqdala from a British auction in 2021 and halted the sale of a ceremonial shield in 2024. Benin also secured the suspension of a Paris auction in December 2024 involving a royal scepter attributed to King Behanzin, which it considers to have been looted by French colonial forces.
Mandela spent 27 years in prison for opposing South Africa’s white-minority government before leading the transition to multiracial democracy and becoming the country’s first black president in 1994. He served until 1999 and died in 2013 at the age of 95. Mandela received the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize jointly with then-President F.W. de Klerk for helping negotiate an end to apartheid.

Chinese-built tank explodes during live-fire exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:31:26 UTC
21:31:26 KST

- A tank explosion during a live-fire drill at Bangladesh's Hathazari Field Firing Range killed two soldiers and seriously injured an officer on September 9, 2026.
- Video and local reporting identify the tank as a Chinese-built Type 59, though the Bangladesh Army has not officially confirmed the model.
Two Bangladesh Army soldiers were killed and an officer was seriously injured on September 9, 2026, when a tank exploded during a live-fire exercise at the Hathazari Field Firing Range in Chattogram.
The Bangladesh Army’s Inter-Services Public Relations Directorate, known as ISPR, confirmed the accident.
ISPR said the blast happened while the crew was firing the tank’s main gun during a field exercise, killing both soldiers inside and seriously wounding the officer. The wounded officer was airlifted to the Combined Military Hospital in Dhaka for treatment. The directorate said it has opened an inquiry and has not yet determined what caused the explosion.
The Bangladesh Army has not officially named the tank involved, but video from the range and multiple local media reports identify it as a Chinese-origin Type 59 main battle tank. The Type 59 is built by Norinco, China’s state-owned defense manufacturer, and is a Chinese-licensed derivative of the Soviet T-54 that entered service with China’s People’s Liberation Army in the late 1950s.
Bangladesh has kept its Type 59 fleet in service for decades rather than retiring it, running many of the older hulls through local upgrade programs. Some have been rebuilt to a higher standard known as the Type 59G Durjoy, which adds modernized fire control, improved protection and updated combat systems. It remains unconfirmed whether the tank involved in Wednesday’s explosion was an older baseline Type 59 or an upgraded Durjoy variant.
Investigators will need to determine whether the blast stemmed from a mechanical failure in the aging vehicle, a problem with the ammunition, or another factor tied to the live-fire exercise. The Bangladesh Army has not said whether firing was suspended at Hathazari following the accident or released the identities of the two soldiers killed.

It would be cynical if, at the same time, Russia were able to export its own grain through our ports. We will not help Russia mitigate the consequences of its own war.”
Estonia will continue working with Latvia and Lithuania to find a regional or common European Union solution to halt the transit of Russian grain and prevent the export of grain stolen from the occupied territories of Ukraine.
“If pressure emerges to start transporting Russian grain through Estonia, we are prepared to impose our own sanctions to prohibit it,” Tsahkna said.

Amid Iran war, Italy's exports to Arab markets fall dramatically
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:27:41 UTC

Breadcrumb
Amid Iran war, sharp decline hits Italian trade with Arab countries
The US-Israeli war on Iran that erupted in the Gulf in recent months has cast a shadow over trade relations between Italy and Arab countries, at a time when companies were already facing a highly volatile economic environment due to rising energy costs, disrupted supply chains and growing geopolitical risks.
The Arab region is particularly important to the Italian economy, given its close trade and investment ties and the diversity of sectors that rely on its markets.
Amid continued uncertainty over the course of the Iran war, concerns have emerged that regional unrest could put additional pressure on Italian companies, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, and their ability to maintain a presence in foreign markets.
During the first four months of the war, Italian exports to the United Arab Emirates recorded their largest decline, falling by 879 million euros, or 27.3%.
Kuwait ranked second, with a decline of 649 million euros (-73.6%), followed by Qatar, where exports fell by 345 million euros (-52.2%).
Italian exports to Iraq also fell by 129 million euros (-40.7%), to Iran by 70 million euros (-52.6%), and to Bahrain by 55 million euros (-51.2%), according to data from the Italian Confederation of Craft Trades and Small and Medium-sized Enterprises.
Francesco Angeloni, scientific coordinator of the Mediterranean Observatory at the Saint Pius V Institute for Political Studies in Rome, said that "the decline in Italian exports to Middle Eastern countries is not an isolated phenomenon but falls within a context of tension for the macroeconomy".
"The Italian National Institute of Statistics documented an increase in the inflation rate in August to 3.3% year on year, the highest level since September 2023, driven by rising energy prices, as the Gulf war, which is causing exports to erode, is pushing up fuel and other prices," Angeloni told The New Arab.
He described what is happening as "a double blow to exporting companies that are losing export revenues from Middle Eastern markets while experiencing inflation in production and shipping costs".
"The repercussions that could affect small and micro manufacturing companies could translate into job cuts or business closures, particularly in the fashion, furniture and industrial machinery sectors," he noted.
He explained that "the national labour market in Italy remains relatively resilient so far, with the unemployment rate falling to 5.8% in July".
However, he added that "we are dealing with a figure that portrays the situation before the latest effects of the war, which are fully affecting production".
"If the decline in exports becomes entrenched, the impact on employment in areas known for craft and artisanal industries may take some time to emerge, as is usually the case in crises linked to external demand," he said.
Angeloni further pointed out that "the government's approach in this context is based on two pillars, extending the reduction in fuel duties, a measure that the Italian Confederation of Craft Trades and Small and Medium-sized Enterprises considers insufficient".
"The second move involves discussions with the Italian Trade Agency ICE, the financial and marketing services agency for international trade SIMEST, and the Italian Export Credit Agency SACE to strengthen the financial resources and international marketing of exporting companies," he said. "These measures are moving in the right direction, but it is difficult for them alone to be enough to offset the repercussions of a geopolitical shock of this magnitude".
"These data confirm for us, from a geopolitical perspective, a familiar lesson: instability in the Gulf will not remain confined to the region but will spread through value chains to reach local Italian economies, often faster than trade policy can respond to it," he added.
"The evidence shows that we need a structural strategy to diversify markets, for example, by strengthening the presence in entities such as the Mercosur bloc (the Southern Common Market), which is growing during the same period, rather than relying only on emergency interventions on the energy front," the prominent Italian expert concluded.
The Italian Confederation of Craft Trades and Small and Medium-sized Enterprises said in an analysis issued last week that Italian companies are paying the highest price for the Gulf war, with their exports to the Middle East recording a sharp decline during the first four months of the war, between March and June 2026.
According to the analysis, the value of Italian exports to the Middle East reached 26.4 billion euros but fell by 2.2 billion euros during the war, a year-on-year decline of 22.7%.
This is the largest decline among all European countries, with Italy alone accounting for 46.1% of the total decline in European Union exports to Middle Eastern countries.

Kinneret takes hit as water level drops amidst Israel's desalination plant shutdowns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
12:27:35 UTC
21:27:35 KST

The algal bloom crisis that shut down desalination plants in southern Israel for nearly two weeks has taken a toll on the Kinneret (Sea of Galilee). Within ten days, the lake lost roughly 870 million gallons (3.3 million cubic meters) of water as pumping surged to maintain a steady water supply for domestic and agricultural use across the country.
Since the crisis began early this month, water authorities decided to step up pumping from the Sea of Galilee alongside increased extraction from underground aquifers. The move is designed to offset the drop in supply caused by the offline desalination facilities.
Over the last ten days, the water level of the Sea of Galilee dropped by 4 inches (10 centimeters) - from 699.8 feet (213.40 meters) below sea level to 700.1 feet (213.50 meters) below sea level. This marks the lowest water level recorded on September 9 since 2018.
By comparison, eight years ago on the exact same date, the lake stood roughly 34 inches (87 centimeters) lower than it does today. That means despite the current drop, the Sea of Galilee's overall condition remains significantly better than it was during the same period in 2018.
However, increased pumping isn't the only factor driving the decline. At this time of year, natural evaporation causes the lake level to drop by about a third of an inch (1 centimeter) per day. Pumping required by the algal crisis accounts for an additional 0.8 inches (2 centimeters) of loss since the start of the month.
Kinneret steps back into its former role
Drawing water from the Sea of Galilee for Israel's national supply was once standard practice, but since the rollout of the nation's major desalination plants, relying on the lake for drinking water had virtually stopped.
In recent years, the strategy had even reversed: rather than extracting water from the Sea of Galilee, Israel launched the "Reverse National Water Carrier" project to channel desalinated water back into the lake to reinforce the national reservoir. That system became operational in the past year, with desalinated water actively routed into the lake via the Tzalmon Stream.
With desalination plants sidelined, the Sea of Galilee was once again forced to supply the national water network.
All plants have resumed operation this week for the first time since outages began in August. However, only the Hadera facility is operating at full capacity. According to YNet, the remaining plants (there are six in total) are running at around 50% capacity.
Once the desalination facilities return to full capacity, pumping from the lake is expected to taper off, allowing the Sea of Galilee to gradually return to its modern role - a strategic reservoir that receives desalinated water rather than a primary source of drinking water.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.
The Environment and Climate Change portal is produced in cooperation with the Goldman Sonnenfeldt School of Sustainability and Climate Change at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. The Jerusalem Post maintains all editorial decisions related to the content.
