Questions swirl over Trump's pledge to give $5,000 payouts if GOP wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:31:19 UTC
20:31:19 KST

Questions swirl over Trump’s pledge to give $5,000 payouts if GOP wins
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- President Trump vowed to send every U.S. adult a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” if Republicans keep control of Congress, a stunning midterm gambit that would cost more than $1 trillion and need lawmakers’ approval.
- Economists balked at the proposal, questioning whether any future Congress — regardless of party control — would pass a plan that would balloon the national debt and annual deficit.
WASHINGTON — President Trump’s pledge to give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of Congress in November is drawing scrutiny over its legality, the price tag and whether he truly intends to follow through on such a spectacular promise.
Speaking at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday night, Trump told the crowd that if the GOP wins, Americans will “win with us” and get paid. He added: “It will be called the Trump Dividend.”
But the proposal — which would need congressional approval — raised immediate questions about whether the president can legally promise voters a payout contingent on his party’s success at the polls and drew criticism from both sides of the aisle, including some GOP donors, who saw the idea as a potential bribe.
“I am hugely in favor of winning the midterms, and love much about this admin, but am strongly against bread and circus bribes,” Joe Lonsdale, co-founder of technology firm Palantir and a Republican donor, said on X.
Legal experts, meanwhile, say the pledge — however unusual — is unlikely to run afoul of federal bribery and vote-buying statutes. It is almost certainly protected by the 1st Amendment, said UCLA law professor Rick Hasen.
The president, who won reelection based on a promise to turn the economy around, now faces a reckoning in midterms centered largely on his economic record.
“I believe they are constitutionally protected,” Hasen wrote Thursday on his Election Law Blog. “How is this different from a candidate pledging if elected to secure ‘medicare for all’ or to cut everyone’s taxes?”
Trump told CBS News after his speech on Wednesday that he doesn’t think the payouts would need congressional approval. “I think they will do it if we needed it,” Trump said, “but I think not.”
The White House did not respond when asked if the president had received a legal opinion on the proposal or who had signed off on it. But in a statement, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle dismissed the criticism, saying it was fueled by “the doomers and naysayers” who have consistently doubted Trump’s ability to deliver on his campaign promises.
“President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong, drawing a clear contrast with the Democrats’ record of historic inflation, unfettered illegal immigration, skyrocketing crime, and weakness on the world stage,” Ingle said. “With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results.”
Trump offered the proposal as his standing with voters has been sliding for months, and as a growing number of Americans have expressed disapproval with his heavy-handed tariff policies, crackdowns on immigrant labor, persistent inflation and ongoing war in Iran that has increased fuel prices.
Hours before Trump promised the payments, he told reporters that he believes the war with Iran will be over “immediately” after the midterm elections, and that as a result, gas prices will go down. Trump did not offer a clear timeline as to when after the midterms it would end.
“They’re going to be tumbling down, and we’ll get them down. I think for gasoline, we’ll get them below $2 a gallon,” the president predicted. He claimed Iranian leaders “can’t hold out any longer,” but are trying to affect the outcome of the election so that Democrats win and “leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon.”
Despite the economic pressures, Trump said the $5,000 payments would be possible due to the United States’ “tremendous strength and success economically.” They would cost more than $1 trillion, add significantly to the country’s nearly $1.8-trillion annual budget deficit and exacerbate concerns about inflation. Last month, the national debt topped $40 trillion for the first time.
Economists balked at the proposal, questioning whether any future Congress, regardless of party control, would pass a plan that would balloon the national debt and annual deficit.
The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimated it would cost $1.2 trillion, or 3.5% of the GDP, a move that “would nearly double the deficit during a time when we’re at full employment, inflation is running ahead of target, and bond yields appear to signal more inflation in the future,” said Eric Zwick, a professor of economics and finance at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business.
“I find it hard to imagine any Congress would be willing to do this at this scale,” Zwick said, noting that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — the signature legislation of Trump’s second term — cost less than a third as much as Trump’s newest proposal per year, and barely passed with party-line support.
Valerie Ramey, a senior fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford and a research associate of the National Bureau of Economic Research, said Trump’s policy proposal would likely lead to even higher inflation and interest rates.
“Distributing $1.3 trillion in dividends to Americans when federal debt is already at 100% of [gross domestic product] would be a highly irresponsible policy,” Ramey said. “It might even lead to a U.S. debt crisis.”
Some Republican candidates, however, endorsed the idea.
“I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) wrote on X late Wednesday. “Because Republicans (and America) will win!”
Vice President JD Vance appeared to try to walk back Trump’s proposal — at least in part — by suggesting the dividend payments would not go to the wealthy. Vance suggested it could be paid for by U.S. tariff revenues, though the suggested payment dwarfs what the U.S. has taken in through the protectionist measures.
Trump has made similar promises. Last year, he promised to use tariff revenue to give middle- and low-income Americans a $2,000 dividend. That proposal has not materialized.
David Becker, the executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, said Trump’s proposal appeared to be a “desperate” attempt to sow doubt ahead of the midterm elections.
“Ultimately, it is going to be up to voters whether or not they trust this man to deliver on his promises,” Becker said. “If I were a voter, I would be asking myself, why are you promising to do this in 2027? You control both houses now. Why not deliver on this promise now?”
Asked in an interview with Fox News on Wednesday why he was not giving the money now, Trump blamed Democrats, who are in the minority.
“Because the Democrats can’t do it,” he said. “Because with them it is negative growth, with us it is so positive.”
This article includes reporting by the Associated Press.

Empty shelves, shattered warehouses: Ukraine's Jews prepare for fifth Rosh Hashanah at war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:30:26 UTC
20:30:26 KST

To supply sweet holiday kits to tens of thousands of Jews in the embattled country, Chabad Ukraine said it is "working under complex hardships” to give hope that “the sweet tradition of Rosh Hashanah won't stop."
Amid intensifying shelling in Ukraine's cities, Ukraine's Jewish communities remain on high alert ahead of the High Holy Days.
Kyiv's Jewish communities have weathered repeated attacks on the capital. On August 29, Reuters reported that at least 37 people were killed after a Russian drone attack on a Kyiv-area ammunition depot sparked a detonation. Moscow's air attacks on Kyiv and surrounding regions dragged into a third straight day, killing residents, damaging homes, and derailing daily life.
This follows an unfortunate pattern, as a Russian strike on July 2 launched 74 missiles and 496 drones overnight, killing at least 20 people and wounding more than 90, according to Ukrainian authorities, sending Jewish families back into shelters just a day after they'd returned from a respite camp run by the Jewish Relief Network Ukraine (JRNU) in the Carpathian Mountains.
However, as fighting in the country becomes routine, with the sounds of explosions having become part of daily life, community rabbis are working around the clock to produce mass amounts of kosher honey, essential to the unique culture of Rosh Hashanah.
Essential food products to be unloaded at foot of Jewish centers in various cities
The main phase of the operation has officially commenced: a fleet of massive aid trucks set out from supply centers toward dozens of Jewish communities scattered throughout the country.
Huge pallets of essential food products were unloaded at the foot of Jewish centers in various cities, then transported directly to community members' homes through an internal, organized, and dignified distribution system.
The diverse list of food items included poultry, fresh meat, locally produced jars of honey, dairy products, canned goods, various spreads, honey cakes specially airlifted in from Israel, and festive honey pastries imported from Zaporizhzhia.
To add extra value to the package, informational pamphlets were included. Beautifully designed and adapted into the local language, they explain the meaning of the High Holy Days and include a unique, rich calendar combining Jewish content with images from community life.
'Situation has become extreme'
Jewish communities in Ukraine are reportedly expecting record participation this year in synagogues and various holiday activities. As such, Jewish resilience continues to thrive. "We are preparing for an unprecedented number of worshippers who will come to Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur prayers," says Rabbi Simcha Levenharts, a Chabad emissary in Kyiv who is coordinating the distribution effort.
"The situation has become extreme in recent days," Levenharts said. "Warehouses in the area have been destroyed, and the shelves in stores are simply empty. People can barely go shopping because the chains are closed for many hours because of the alarms."
JRNU said some Rosh Hashanah supplies were brought by air from Israel, including honey cakes and other holiday goods. Communities are also distributing chicken, meat, and jars of honey.
Despite the worsening security situation, Jewish leaders say they are preparing for unusually high synagogue attendance over Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
"We are preparing for an unprecedented number of people to come to Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur prayers," Levenharts said.
"After such a long and exhausting period of war and uncertainty, people are looking more than ever for togetherness and tradition, so they don't break and can remain strong."
Chabad organizing massive logistical efforts to ensure holidays marked with greatest possible dignity
The JRNU, which is behind the distribution of aid packages to the country's Jews, made a strategic decision: to produce most of the basic food and holiday products on Ukrainian soil itself, at special local factories prepared in advance for this purpose.
The Kyiv area is surrounded by logistics hubs and giant warehouses that have absorbed serious hits and daily bombardments in recent weeks, but by some miracle, the factory chosen for producing the pure honey has remained standing.
While these logistics hubs are absorbing heavy bombardment and shelling, Chabad is organizing massive logistical efforts to ensure the holidays are marked with the greatest possible dignity and to strengthen communal solidarity despite the dangers on the ground.
As the noise of the machines mixes with air-raid sirens, the production workers continue working there under constant alertness. In addition to the honey factory, which was certified kosher by Rabbi Yehoshua Vishetzki of the "Ukrkosher" kashrut system, special meat and poultry slaughter operations have also been certified kosher under strict standards, amid the chaos of war.
JRNU has spent the war years building local production and distribution infrastructure – including factories, kosher slaughter operations, and a delivery network – to sustain religious life for Ukraine's Jewish population without relying on imports that wartime logistics make unreliable.
The honey factory near Kyiv is ostensibly one facet in that system, illustrating both the scale of the effort and the risks involved in running it inside an active war zone.
In the Jewish community of Kyiv, connecting to tradition by “manufacturing kosher food in Ukraine not only instills local pride but aids the country’s struggling economy as well”, says Chabad.org.
Drones fall near Kremenchuk rabbi's home
The security threat has reached Jewish community leaders directly.
Rabbi Shlomo Salamon, chief rabbi of Kremenchuk, said two drones fell close to his home this week.
"Just today, a few hours ago, two UAVs fell right near our home and immediately brought us back to the difficult atmosphere of the war," Salamon said.
"In days like these, when food warehouses are being bombed, and you can feel the shortages and uncertainty in the stores, the joy of receiving these substantial and festive food packages is enormous," he said.
In Poltava, Chief Rabbi Yosef Segal said residents were also encountering shortages.
"Many stores are dealing with empty shelves, and there is a shortage of basic food products," Segal said, adding that holiday food packages were providing both practical help and emotional support.
In Cherkasy, Rabbi Dov Axelrod said preparations for Rosh Hashanah were continuing despite the deteriorating security situation.
"The preparations for the holiday fill the synagogue and the community with a feeling of togetherness, family, and hope for a better and sweeter year," he said.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Yair Golan files NIS 2.55 million defamation lawsuit against Sara Netanyahu over October 7 remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:30:24 UTC
20:30:24 KST

Democrats faction head Yair Golan filed a NIS 2.55 million lawsuit against Sara Netanyahu on Thursday, accusing the prime minister’s wife of defaming him and endangering his life by implying that he knew in advance about the October 7 Hamas attack.
The suit, filed in the Central District Court in Lod, asks the court to order Netanyahu to pay damages and publish a correction and clarification.
The dispute stems from an August 31 interview with Channel 14, in which Netanyahu questioned how Golan, a former IDF deputy chief of staff, reached southern Israel on the morning of the attack.
“When you are a military officer of such a high rank and claim that you fought on October 7, you were already there early in the morning, already dressed and prepared,” she said. “At a very, very early hour, when others did not know, such as the prime minister.”
Golan argues that an ordinary viewer would understand those remarks as suggesting that he knew the attack was coming before it began, failed to warn anyone, and may even have been involved in a betrayal of the country.
Court will have to decide how a reasonable viewer would understand comments
The lawsuit also argues that Netanyahu cast doubt on Golan’s documented rescue efforts by saying that he “claims” to have fought that day.
Netanyahu has rejected that interpretation. Responding to a warning letter sent by Golan on September 1, she said her remarks had been distorted and were directed sarcastically at those who, she argued, failed to alert the prime minister promptly after the attack began.
Later in the interview, when asked about theories alleging betrayal on October 7, Netanyahu said she was “not part of any theories.” Likud said following Golan’s warning that she had not alleged a conspiracy and had, in fact, said the opposite. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later said that “there was no betrayal on October 7; there was a failure.”
The court will ultimately have to decide how a reasonable viewer would have understood the interview as a whole, not merely how either side now describes it.
Golan’s actions on October 7 have been widely documented. After the attack began, he left his home, collected military equipment and drove south. Oz Davidian, who took part in rescue operations alongside him, has said Golan arrived in the Nova music festival area at around 11:30 a.m. Golan helped rescue six people who had fled the festival, according to the lawsuit and previous reporting.
The lawsuit says the interview was followed by concrete threats against Golan, including threatening letters and warnings relayed by intelligence officials. It says he consequently expanded his private security arrangements, adding substantial costs as he campaigns ahead of the October 27 election.
Alongside the defamation claim, Golan is attempting a less conventional civil argument. He claims Netanyahu’s remarks violated a legal provision barring publications that create a real possibility of encouraging violence, and that the alleged violation therefore entitles him to damages under civil law.
That does not amount to a criminal charge or prosecution; Golan is asking a civil court to find that the alleged incitement breached a legal duty intended to protect people from violence.
Golan seeks double compensation
Golan is also seeking double compensation without proof of specific financial damage for what he describes as multiple intentional publications, up to the total NIS 2.55m. claimed.
To support his allegation that the remarks were aired deliberately, the complaint says the interview was prerecorded and that Prime Minister’s Office and Likud adviser Topaz Luk acknowledged viewing it before broadcast. Golan argues that Netanyahu or those accompanying her therefore had an opportunity to remove the passage.
The lawsuit comes seven weeks before the election, in which Golan is leading the Democrats against Netanyahu’s Likud. Golan alleges that the timing was intended to damage him politically.
Two other men, Amir Sade and Eyal Giler, have both sent Netanyahu pre-suit warning letters over separate remarks she made about protest-related criminal cases during the interview.
“We are putting an end to this,” Golan said after filing the case, accusing the Netanyahu family of branding political opponents as traitors to escape responsibility for October 7.
Netanyahu will now have an opportunity to file a defense.

IAEA exposes North Korea's secret nuclear enrichment facility, expansion of weapon infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:29:47 UTC
20:29:47 KST

North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex that could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, and started operating an expanded annex at its Kangson enrichment site, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said.
The Vienna-based nuclear watchdog said in a report that the findings pointed to a steady expansion of North Korea's nuclear infrastructure at multiple locations.
In the report, dated August 28, the IAEA said it relied on satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by North Korean state media, to track Pyongyang's nuclear activities. The agency has had no inspectors in North Korea since 2009.
It identified a new two-story building at Yongbyon as the site's second uranium enrichment facility by comparing state media photographs of a June visit by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un with satellite images taken during the building's construction.
Photographs from the visit indicate gas centrifuge cascades are installed on both the upper and lower floors of the main building, the report said, adding the building could accommodate up to 28 of the cascades shown in the photographs.
Expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material
The report also said there were indications that operations began in January at a uranium enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, within an annex that had been constructed in 2024.
The IAEA said the developments in North Korea's nuclear program violated UN Security Council resolutions.
"The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of the DPRK’s production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern," IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said in a statement to the board of governors on Monday, referring to the North's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
The report accompanied Grossi's statement.
Pyongyang has repeatedly rejected the agency's authority. North Korea's mission to the United Nations in Vienna said last September that North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state had become irreversible and the IAEA had "no legal right… to interfere in the internal affairs of a nuclear weapons state which exists outside the NPT," referring to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

Asylum applications fall to lowest level in EU since 2021
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:28:52 UTC
20:28:52 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The number of asylum applications lodged in EU+ countries fell to its lowest first-half level since 2021, the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) said Thursday.
EU+ countries received around 332,000 applications for international protection in the first six months of 2026, a 17% decline from the same period last year.
The EU+ comprises the 27 EU member states as well as Norway and Switzerland.
The agency said the decline, which has continued since late 2024, reflected a change in the nationalities seeking asylum amid Syria’s “fragile but ongoing political transition,” as well as EU cooperation with countries of origin and transit.
It added that the escalation of hostilities in the Middle East had not resulted in an increase in asylum applications in the EU+.
Afghans submitted the highest number of applications at 39,000, down 7% year-on-year. Applications from Venezuelans fell by nearly one-third to 33,000, with 93% lodged in Spain.
Applications from Bangladeshis, meanwhile, rose 13% to 20,000.
France received the largest number of applications at 69,000, accounting for about one-fifth of the EU+ total. It was followed by Italy with 66,000 and Spain and Germany with 55,000 each.
Together, the four countries received around three-quarters of all applications.
Greece recorded the highest number relative to its population, receiving 23,000 applications, roughly one for every 400 residents.
The EU+ recognition rate stood at 31%, meaning fewer than one-third of first-instance decisions resulted in applicants being granted international protection.
Around 56% of applications came from nationalities that may be subject to border or accelerated procedures under the EU’s new asylum rules because of low recognition rates or designation as safe countries of origin.

From Gaza to Lebanon: The Same Media Playbook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:27:41 UTC
20:27:41 KST

Breadcrumb
How Gaza's media playbook reached Lebanon
What we're seeing in the Western media coverage of Lebanon very much mirrors what we saw and what we continue to see in terms of the coverage of the Gaza genocide.
But what we saw in Gaza was not new. It reflected a longer pattern of dehumanisation directed at Palestinians and, more broadly, the Arab world. That framework has translated easily into coverage of Lebanon.
The same patterns reappear: omissions that obscure Israeli responsibility, the misuse of language such as "ceasefire", chronic underreporting, and the assumption that almost any Israeli action can be justified in the name of destroying Hezbollah, just as similar arguments were used to justify actions against Hamas in Gaza.
In Lebanon, this often takes the form of headlines that describe destruction without clearly identifying who is carrying it out. The deliberate nature of the destruction is frequently absent from reporting, even when Israeli officials have been open about plans that involve the displacement of Shia communities and the clearing of Shia villages. Instead, media coverage often relies on sanitised language such as "evacuation", masking the coercive reality on the ground.
The result is systematic underreporting.
When organisations such as Amnesty International conclude that Israel is committing the war crime of unlawful transfer, those findings often receive little attention in mainstream Western media. More broadly, statements and reports from NGOs documenting abuses frequently struggle to gain significant coverage.
Yet the underlying logic remains the same. The idea that an entire village can be destroyed in the pursuit of Hezbollah echoes the rationale used in Gaza, where vast destruction was justified through the stated objective of eliminating Hamas.
If those tactics were normalised in Gaza, it is hardly surprising to see them reproduced in Lebanon.
What much of the media adopted was essentially the language of the Gaza playbook, and that same framework was then applied to Lebanon.
But that is precisely the problem. Gaza is not a playbook. It is a genocide, involving some of the gravest crimes of our time.
And yet, through that framing, what emerges is a whitewashing of the genocide itself, alongside the normalisation of similar tactics in Lebanon and, increasingly, in territories occupied by Israel in Syria.
At the heart of all this is a failure to contextualise Israel as an expansionist state. Without that broader context, these actions are presented as isolated security measures rather than as part of a larger political and territorial project.

EU must assume political leadership in space policy: French president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:26:33 UTC
20:26:33 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron called on the EU Thursday to assume stronger political leadership over its space policy, warning that Europe remains “fragile” in a sector increasingly linked to sovereignty, security and economic competitiveness.
“The European Union must fully assume political leadership over an ambitious, clear and demanding space policy,” Macron told the first International Space Summit at the Grand Palais in Paris.
Macron said the bloc should pursue “genuine technological independence” and retain the ability to choose its partners for critical capabilities.
“Europe must rank among the world’s leading players, particularly in communications and artificial intelligence,” he said.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen echoed Macron's call for greater cooperation, warning that Europe's current strengths do not guarantee its future position.
“To remain at the forefront, Europe must act together, invest at scale, and turn our market into a competitive advantage,” she said.
The global space economy is expected to nearly triple from around $630 billion today to $1.8 trillion by 2035, von der Leyen added.
She said the Commission had proposed €131 billion ($152 billion) for defense, security and space under the EU's next long-term budget, five times the funding currently available.
Macron stressed the need for large-scale, affordable access to space, saying Europe should be capable of launching several hundred metric tons into orbit annually at competitive costs.
“Europe cannot invest billions in these rockets and then purchase launches only sporadically,” he said.
Von der Leyen said the Commission and the European Space Agency were committed to developing a new European vision for access to space by pooling demand and acting as an anchor customer for European launches.
“This is how we keep a competitive space transport industry in Europe, and keep our independent access to space,” she said.
Macron announced that France would invest €20 billion through 2030 in the space sector, along with an additional €40 million through the French space agency CNES for an observation program.
Von der Leyen also highlighted the growing security dimension of space, citing threats including signal jamming, spoofing and cyberattacks on satellite networks.
“Our security on Earth increasingly depends on our security in space,” she said, adding that the EU is developing a European Space Shield to strengthen defenses and address critical capability gaps.
Macron also warned that “space is no longer a sanctuary,” calling for stronger international governance.

Fact check: Why is Russia claiming Western 'interference' in Duma elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:26:03 UTC
20:26:03 KST

Fact check: Why is Russia claiming Western 'interference' in Duma elections?
As the Russian legislative elections near, the Moscow propaganda is accusing the West of plotting to disrupt the vote — the same charge Western governments have repeatedly leveled against the Kremlin.
Russia's upcoming elections for the State Duma, the lower house of the parliament, between Sept. 18 and 20 are seen by democracy watchdogs as little more than a rubber stamp for the regime's grip on power.
Yet in recent months, Russian officials and media have stepped up claims that Europe plans to tamper with the process.
Russia's foreign intelligence alleged on Aug. 31 that the EU plans "provocations" at polling stations in Russia and abroad and, together with Ukraine, plots cyberattacks against Russia's election infrastructure.
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, in comments reported on Sept. 8, claimed the EU is training "secret" monitors to watch the Duma vote.
And Vasily Piskaryov, head of the State Duma commission "investigating foreign interference," alleged that "extremist" groups plan to conduct "fake exit polls" at Russian embassies.
Piskaryov also accused "European NGOs," designated as "undesirable organizations," of recruiting Russian-speaking citizens to pose as fake electoral experts and spread disinformation amid the election campaign.
Russian officials have not provided evidence of their claims — which were widely reported by Russian state and pro-state media — and the EU has dismissed the accusations in comments to the Kyiv Independent.
"It is not the first time that Russian authorities accuse Western states of interfering in Russian elections without any compelling evidence," Julia Smirnova, a disinformation researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), a Germany-based monitoring agency, told the Kyiv Independent.
Smirnova listed three main goals of the narrative: discrediting any criticism by the exiled Russian opposition, casting Russia as a country besieged by foreign powers, and distracting from its own interference abroad.
Siege mentality
Democracy watchdogs regard Russian elections as neither free nor fair, citing vote-buying, coercion, and a crackdown on the opposition, according to the U.S.-based NGO Freedom House.
While the ruling United Russia party is all but certain to win, certain Kremlin-aligned parties are allowed to run as "systemic opposition" to create the appearance of democratic competition.
Parties diverting from the Kremlin line — like the "pro-peace" Yabloko party — are not allowed to run. "Non-systemic" opposition politicians have been imprisoned, branded extremists, forced into exile, or killed.
Russian authorities have also been systematically dismantling any independent monitoring infrastructure.
Golos, Russia's only independent election watchdog, was designated a "foreign agent" in 2013 and later dissolved.
Only state-sanctioned actors are permitted to monitor Russian elections, with independent NGOs and international organizations, such as the OSCE's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, being shut out.
In violation of international law, Russia is also planning to hold parliamentary elections in the occupied Ukrainian territories, which it regards as its "new" regions.
Expecting widespread criticism of the elections' legitimacy, the Kremlin is preemptively dismissing such criticism as outside meddling.
"The recent accusations are aimed, firstly, at discrediting any criticism of the Russian regime by exile media or politicians as foreign interference," Smirnova told the Kyiv Independent.
They are also meant to reinforce the image "of Russia being under attack by foreign powers."
As the expert notes, the Kremlin has similarly denounced Western support for Russian civil society during the Russian elections in 2011 and 2012, or their coverage by Western media, as "interference."
And the Kremlin propaganda launched a similar campaign ahead of the previous State Duma elections in 2021, accusing the West at the time of trying to discredit the process, and Western media of "spreading fakes" about the election.
Distraction and 'whatabaoutsim'
Yet another goal of Russia's unfounded accusations, Smirnova says, is the Kremlin's attempt to distract from its own election interference.
When Lavrov accused Europe of plotting to send "secret monitors" to the Duma elections, he also lashed out at the EU over alleged tampering in the Romanian presidential election.
Romania's constitutional court in December 2024 annulled the results of a presidential vote and ordered a rerun after Romanian intelligence identified a Russian-backed social media campaign to prop up the fringe far-right presidential candidate Calin Georgescu.
German authorities reported a Russian-linked disinformation campaign before the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt — won by the far-right, Kremlin-friendly AfD party — and France is investigating possible Russian interference ahead of its own 2027 presidential vote.
"By accusing the EU of what Russia is currently doing itself in European countries, Russian intelligence agencies are using the tactics of 'whataboutism' and hollowing out the notion of election interference," Smirnova commented.
Editor's note: This article was published as part of the Fighting Against Conspiracy and Trolls (FACT) project, an independent, non-partisan hub launched in mid-2025 under the umbrella of the EU Digital Media Observatory (EDMO). Click here to follow the latest stories from our hub on disinformation.

GA-ASI’s Uncrewed Combat Aviation Portfolio Answers Call for High-End Warfare Capability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:19:00 UTC
19:19:00 KST

General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI), the company that introduced the world to unmanned warfare, has systematically transformed its aircraft lineup to address the defining requirements of modern high-technology warfare: range, persistence, payload, survivability, and scale against advanced adversaries.
The portfolio now spans from the company’s enhanced MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian platforms capable of long-range maritime strike, to the expeditionary Mojave STOL, to the Air Force’s newly selected FQ-42A Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) — its first uncrewed fighter — and, most recently, to the Wildfire Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA), a theater-range platform engineered for affordable, attrition-tolerant combat mass.
According to GA-ASI President David Alexander, the United States has entered an era where winning demands large, capable Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS) that can operate from friendly airspace into contested environments affordably, without risking aircrews.
“We’ve never been a company that rested on its laurels,” said Alexander. “The conversation around uncrewed systems has changed, and frankly, it should. The battlefield has evolved, threats have evolved, and so have we.
“We’re keeping ahead of the game, and, in the case of our FQ-42A and Wildfire aircraft, we’ve designed them from the start to overmatch threats today and into the future.”
Physics Demands Large Airframes
Losses in contested environments have prompted some observers to suggest moving away from large UAS platforms. Alexander sees those same operations as validation for continued investment in evolved large UAS.
“Yes, we’ve seen combat losses,” he said. “We’ve also heard Pentagon leaders call our Reaper the ‘MVP’ of the campaign. That tells you something important. When a system consistently delivers decisive effects, you modernize it and build on it. And I believe that’s where the Department of War is headed.”
Alexander emphasized that Reaper was purpose-built to provide persistent surveillance, long endurance, and precision strike. MQ-9A delivers these capabilities at scale and at a fraction of the cost of manned platforms that put pilots’ lives at risk, he added.
The proliferation of small drones — quadcopters, gliders, and short-range rockets — doesn’t change fundamental operational requirements, he said.
Despite the hype, smaller platforms “can’t change physics,” Alexander noted.
“Long-range, high-payload, high-endurance missions require large, hefty airframes with significant wingspan, fuel capacity, and payload volume,” he continued. “If we are serious about surveilling and targeting across wide ocean areas, tracking mobile missile units, and holding adversary assets at risk from standoff distances, large UAS modernized for contested environments are the decisive advantage.”
Wildfire: Delivering Attritable Mass at Theater Range
Wildfire represents GA-ASI’s answer to a critical requirement: affordable combat mass that can sustain losses while maintaining operational pressure across contested theaters.
This theater-range, high-production UAS is designed specifically for high-threat environments:
Combat payload and range: Wildfire can carry two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles (LRASM) or four Joint Strike Missiles (JSM) for meaningful combat distances and has a ferry range that exceeds 8,000 nautical miles. This enables delivery of weapons, sensors, electronic warfare capabilities, or communications relay deep into contested battlespace.
Modular architecture: Open interfaces and modular payload hard points enable modularity to support rapid mission reconfiguration, allowing commanders to adapt as threats and priorities shift during operations.
Volume production: Leveraging more than 5 million square feet of manufacturing capacity and advanced production processes, Wildfire is engineered to be built and fielded in numbers sufficient to absorb attrition while maintaining persistent theater-wide pressure.
Combined with Gambit Series capabilities, Wildfire delivers what defense leaders call “attritable mass”— large numbers of capable systems whose loss does not constitute strategic setback because they are affordable, uncrewed, and replaceable.
Gambit Series: Autonomous Combat Jets for Peer Threats
The Gambit Series represents GA-ASI’s family of autonomous jets for high-end contested operations. Built around a common core comprising roughly 70 percent of key components, the platform’s modular architecture drives down costs while simplifying production, logistics, and sustainment.
Recently selected by the U.S. Air Force for its CCA program, the FQ-42A — designed to fly alongside fighters like the F-22 — is a variant of GA-ASI’s Gambit 2.
Across six missionized Gambit variants, the architecture supports:
- Long-endurance ISR in contested airspace
- Air-to-air combat
- Adversary training for advanced threat replication
- Stealth reconnaissance in denied areas
- Carrier-based naval operations
- Penetrating air-to-ground strike and suppression of enemy air defenses
All Gambit aircraft are designed for human-machine teaming with advanced fighters and other UAS, extending sensors, adding weapons capacity, and imposing complex targeting dilemmas on adversary defenses — precisely the type of effects envisioned in modern Air Force operational concepts.
Mojave STOL: Airpower, Hold the Tarmac
Built on GA-ASI’s other pioneering aircraft, Mojave STOL addresses a critical vulnerability in modern combat: dependence on large runways.
Short Takeoff and Landing (STOL) capability: Mojave STOL operates from austere, unprepared locations — open fields, dry riverbeds, even amphibious assault ship decks — generating uncrewed combat airpower from sites adversaries cannot easily target or predict.
Advanced sensor integration: Controllable via human-portable, laptop-based ground control systems, Mojave STOL carries cutting-edge radar, electro-optical/infrared, and signals intelligence payloads, providing a comprehensive operational picture for precise targeting and situational awareness to support dispersed forces.
In a combat environment where large runways are vulnerable to adversary strikes, Mojave STOL establishes airfields without airports. Its rugged construction enables persistent ISR and strike capability sourced from improvised mobile launch and recovery sites.
MQ-9B: Evolved Flagship Platform for Standoff Operations
MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian remain GA-ASI’s flagship multi-mission ISR platforms, now upgraded for long-range contested operations and integration into distributed kill chains.
Long-range weapons integration: New pylons with 30-inch lug spacing accommodate larger standoff munitions, including LRASM and JSM. Combined with MQ-9B’s advanced ISR suite, this transforms the aircraft into a long-range strike and maritime interdiction platform capable of engaging far outside adversary standoff ranges.
Resilient communications: Integration with proliferated Low Earth Orbit (pLEO) satellite constellations provides low-latency, high-bandwidth, jam-resistant connectivity. In combination with DoD-standard cybersecurity, MQ-9B maintains secure command-and-control and sensor links globally, even under electronic attack.
For Air Force and joint planners, MQ-9B has evolved beyond counterinsurgency roots into a standoff sensor-shooter that functions as a resilient node in distributed operations.
Urgency Driven by Evolving Threats
Alexander noted that changing battlefield conditions have continually driven the company to advance its technology and operational concepts.
“When you look at the threats we’re seeing in Ukraine and Iran, we already knew our aircraft would need to evolve, and we’ve been pushing ahead there for years now,” he said. “But it seems like every morning the news puts fresh urgency behind delivering that vital combat capability while finding ways to strip out some of what drives up costs.”
That urgency is backed by unmatched operational experience. To date, GA-ASI has accumulated nearly 10 million flight hours, the vast majority in combat operations.
Taken as a whole, Alexander said, the aircraft portfolio shows that GA-ASI is serious about retaining its position as the leading provider of UAS to the United States and its allies.
“We know, to our core, what it takes to deliver relevant systems,” he said. “We have the people, infrastructure, and capacity in place, today, to do it at scale.
“GA-ASI is ready to answer the call.”

EU gives final green light to 6 billion euros in defense aid for Ukraine, Patriot missiles purchase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:10:21 UTC
19:10:21 KST

EU gives final green light to 6 billion euros in defense aid for Ukraine, Patriot missiles purchase
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The European Commission approved a 6.1 billion euros ($7.1 billion) tranche of defense aid for Ukraine on Sept. 11, along with several requests for Ukraine to source weapons from outside the bloc, namely Patriot missiles.
The approval allows Ukraine to use funds from the EU's 90-billion-euro ($104-billion) support loan to purchase U.S.-made PAC-3 Patriot interceptors, one of the few weapons capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
This, however, does not mean an immediate delivery of the missiles. There is a global shortage of Patriot interceptors, while Ukraine is bracing for a new wave of Russian strikes against its energy grid in winter.
EU member states voiced support for the new defense tranche and the Patriot purchase earlier this week, but the steps still needed final approval from the European Commission.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius confirmed at a press conference in Brussels on Sept. 11 that the EU's executive arm has signed off on the measures.
With the latest package, the EU has approved all of the 28.3 billion euros ($32.9 billion) earmarked for Ukraine's defense under the support loan this year.
So far, 8.4 billion euros ($9.7 billion) of that defense money has been disbursed, a process that can only occur once Ukraine provides receipts for cross-checking. Kubilius said another 4.7 billion euros ($5.5 billion) is now being processed.
In April, EU countries approved the 90 billion euro support loan for Ukraine, intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv's defense and budgetary needs in 2026 and 2027, to be delivered in tranches.
The loan also includes requirements to buy weapons from the EU and Ukraine. Any item where more than 35% of the value of its components comes from third countries requires explicit approval.
Kubilius mentioned that five such derogations had been granted: three for Ukrainian companies to source drone components, and two for U.S components, including the PAC-3 missile interceptors.
Justifying the decision to grant the exemptions, Kubilius said: "Ukraine's military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical products in the required quantities and within very short time frames."
The commissioner did not explain which countries would benefit from the exemption for drone components, but an earlier such exemption, made in April, allowed Kyiv to source components from China.

Former Western Special Forces Allegedly Trained Russians in Europe After Full-Scale Invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:25:49 UTC
20:25:49 KST

- Category
- World
Former Western Special Forces Allegedly Trained Russians in Europe After Full-Scale Invasion
Former members of Western special forces, including personnel reportedly linked to Britain’s elite Special Air Service, may have trained Russian citizens and even active-duty military personnel at private combat centers in Europe after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to an intelligence assessment obtained by The Telegraph on September 9.
The assessment reportedly reaches that conclusion with a “high degree of confidence” and is now being examined by Australia’s intelligence service.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The memo was prepared for the Australian Secret Intelligence Service based on interviews with two former Australian special forces members and a serving reservist.
Those interviewed said they had been approached about instructor positions at private training facilities in Bulgaria and Serbia where Russian clients were allegedly receiving military instruction.
One of the facilities named in the assessment is Alfa-Metal, a private training center in Bulgaria offering special forces-style courses and advanced sniper instruction.
Courses cost roughly €4,000 per participant and are marketed toward clients including private military contractors, bodyguards, and corporate security personnel.
According to the intelligence memo, European private training centers continued accepting Russian citizens even after the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, including for advanced close-quarters combat courses.
The people interviewed for the assessment said employees at the center indicated Russian nationals were still receiving training there as recently as 2025.
The allegations raise particularly serious questions because Alfa-Metal publicly presented itself as having access to instructors with extensive Western military experience.
The company’s website displayed an image of the SAS emblem, while Alfa-Metal also advertised for a British instructor with a special forces background. In addition, it included instructors with the Australian Commando Regiment, US police forces, and the US Navy SEALs background.
An instructor profile on the company’s website additionally featured a man who claimed 12 years of service within US Army Special Operations Command, listing experience in counterterrorism, Ranger training, airborne operations, jungle warfare and long-range surveillance.
According to The Telegraph, Alfa-Metal has strongly denied the central allegations. The company said it had not trained Russian citizens since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion and denied ever employing former SAS personnel.
The training center initially also rejected allegations of links to Alfa Region, a Russian private security company.
After The Telegraph questioned Alfa-Metal about material on its own website, however, the company acknowledged that the two businesses had maintained “historical professional contacts.”
The relationship is significant because Alfa Region has promoted the Bulgarian training center and advertised courses involving instructors said to have experience in special forces and police units from several countries.
The intelligence findings have not been independently verified by The Telegraph.
Sources connected to the SAS have also questioned whether former members of the unit were actually involved in training Russians, arguing that such activity would run directly against the culture and values associated with Britain’s special forces community.
The Australian Secret Intelligence Service is now examining the allegations contained in the memo. Findings from that investigation could ultimately be shared with Britain, the United States and other members of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance, The Telegraph noted.
The UK Defense Ministry declined to comment on matters involving British special operations forces or intelligence.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia has bypassed Western sanctions to acquire advanced 3D-printing equipment comparable to technology used in Rolls-Royce manufacturing, helping Moscow cut the cost of its jet-powered drones roughly in half as it rapidly expands production.

‘Hoping draft ready by Oct’: Ladakh chief secy as UT seeks Article 371 safeguards

Breakthrough in talks with MHA on legislative powers: Ladakh grps
NEW DELHI: Ladakh chief secretary Ashish Kundra said on Thursday that the Union Territory is moving towards seeking constitutional safeguards for its local population under Article 371, along with the creation of a UT-level elected body with legislative and financial powers.Kundra said a meeting of the sub-committee was held at the ministry of home affairs on Wednesday with the leadership of the Apex Body and the Kargil Democratic Alliance from Ladakh. Discussions focused on incorporating a special provision under Article 371 to protect the interests of the local population.He said the next meeting is scheduled for October, with the administration hoping to have an advanced draft of the proposed Constitutional Amendment Bill ready by then.
What Ladakh is seeking
The proposed framework would include a Union Territory-level body elected directly through constituencies and vested with legislative and financial powers.The move comes amid demands for greater constitutional protection for Ladakh following its transition into a Union Territory.
Articles 371 contain special provisions for specific states. These provisions differ from one state to another but broadly seek to protect local political, cultural, social and economic interests.
Article 371-A, for instance, provides special safeguards for Nagaland. Articles 371-B and 371-C provide for special committees in the Legislative Assemblies of Assam and Manipur and similiarly other provisions are there for other states.If a new Article 371 provision is introduced specifically for Ladakh, it would be significant because Ladakh is a Union Territory rather than a state.The proposal would therefore require a constitutional arrangement tailored to a Union Territory, potentially making it different from the existing Article 371 provisions that primarily apply to states.

AI firms ‘begging to be regulated,’ feel ‘compelled to race’ toward deadly technology: Ex-Anthropic researcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:22:09 UTC
20:22:09 KST

A former Anthropic researcher who warned that the race to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence could threaten humanity said Wednesday that AI companies are genuinely seeking regulation but feel compelled to keep competing for fear of falling behind their rivals.
“These people are also completely genuine when they are begging to be regulated,” Jacob Coxon, 27, told CNN's Anderson Cooper.
“They find themselves in this scenario where they're compelled to race towards building a deadly technology, and they would love for some sort of international body to allow them to approach it at a reasonable pace,” he said.
Coxon, who resigned from Anthropic on Tuesday after previously working at OpenAI, drew widespread attention with a post on US social media platform X saying the two companies were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
The post had garnered 143 million views by Thursday. His remarks have also received support from other AI safety researchers.
Evan Hubinger, an alignment researcher at Anthropic, responded to Coxon's post on X by saying he personally estimated the risk of AI killing all humans at more than 10% within the next decade, while acknowledging that current models pose a low extinction risk.
In the CNN interview, Coxon sought to clarify that he does not believe existing AI systems are capable of causing human extinction.
“Right now, there's no risk of extinction,” he said. “The current models, the worst they can do is maybe hack into something, potentially cause a lot of damages in infrastructure, but they're not intelligent enough to outsmart us at the level that would lead to extinction.”
His concern, he said, is the speed at which those capabilities are advancing and what could happen if AI systems become capable of improving themselves.
“I think what's just crazy is to look at the rate of progress, and there is a very real possibility that in the immediate future ... next year, the year after, recursive self-improvement will happen,” Coxon said.
Asked how such a scenario could unfold, Coxon pointed to what he described as a real-world precedent.
"The precise scenario sounds a little bit like science fiction. It sounds like something that's not real, but I think it is frighteningly real, and it's easiest to understand it if you think about real things that happened two months ago," he said.
"Two months ago, OpenAI agents, AIs hacked into third-party infrastructure entirely of their own accord, and this was like a concentrated hacking spree that they carried out of their own volition. I think that if you extrapolate into the future the level of capabilities of these AIs, with the same independent volition, they could cause extreme havoc."
He described the most concerning possibility as AI being used to conduct AI research itself, allowing systems to progressively increase their own capabilities.
“The AI just gets smarter and smarter with no human involvement necessary,” Coxon said.
“A couple of years ago, these AIs were just about helping humans a little bit. They could give you suggestions. Now they're close to replacing them,” he said, adding that humans were still needed but that “quite plausibly within a year, we'll no longer need humans for doing research in many areas.”   
Coxon raised concerns before resignation
According to an NBC News report on Wednesday, Coxon had expressed similar concerns privately before his resignation in messages to Anthropic colleagues on the workplace platform Slack.
“I've recently become more concerned about the degree and imminence of this risk,” he wrote, according to the report, warning that without international coordination, superintelligent AI could pose a risk of human extinction.
He also said he planned to publicly criticize the industry while making clear that he did not blame individual Anthropic employees for the situation.
Coxon said he had initially intended simply to leave Anthropic rather than make a public intervention.
“I thought I can't be part of this anymore,” he told CNN. “I did not expect it to go this viral.”
Sen. Bernie Sanders has cited Coxon's post and renewed calls for Congress to act on AI regulation.
A recent NBC poll also found that 70% of American adults are more worried about AI than excited by it.

British banking giant Lloyds has declined a mortgage application from the mother of Leona Kamio, a pro-Palestinian activist jailed over a violent raid on an Elbit Systems factory near Bristol, according to an investigation by independent outlet Novara Media.
The report said the bank told Kamio's mother that her mortgage application had been reviewed but that its advisers did not feel “comfortable” supporting it at this time.
Lloyds also refused an attempt to transfer the assets into the name of Kamio’s sister and pursue the mortgage application through that route, according to the report.
It was also reported that Kamio herself had previously received a letter from the bank while in custody informing her that Lloyds was “unable to maintain a banking relationship” with her.
Kamio was one of four pro-Palestinian activists convicted over a raid on an Elbit facility in the Bristol area. The group caused approximately $1 million in damage and clashed with police officers who arrived at the site.
Footage of the incident released by British prosecutors last year showed participants carrying hammers and axes while wearing red overalls. Body-camera footage from one of the responding police officers showed a violent confrontation, including an individual raising a hammer and attacking a female officer.
Prosecutors said the raid had been “carefully planned.” Kamio and two other women were sentenced to six years in prison.
According to a separate report by Al-Quds Al-Arabi, Kamio’s mother said she runs a small business in South Wales and has been a longtime Lloyds customer.
She said her business had suffered over the previous two years as she devoted time and resources to campaigning for her daughter’s release from prison. The mortgage, she said, was intended to ease some of that financial pressure, and the bank’s refusal had dealt her a serious economic blow.
Lloyds rejected any suggestion that political views determine its decisions. 
“We do not close customer accounts or make lending decisions based on political or personal beliefs. Our decisions are based on relevant laws, regulation, account conditions or lending requirements. We’re unable to comment on individual cases,” a Lloyds spokesperson told Novara Media.

Space-based surveillance: Dhruva to get key systems worth €5m from Safran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:18:20 UTC
20:18:20 KST

French aerospace major Safran Space signed key contracts worth over €5 million with Indian space-tech startup Dhruva Space.
BENGALURU: French firm Safran Space, under contracts worth more than €5 million, will supply critical systems, including optical payloads, for satellites being built as part of India’s Space-Based Surveillance-3 (SBS-3) programme by Dhruva Space, a release from the French President’s Office has confirmed.The contracts, signed during the International Space Summit in Paris, cover communication systems, inertial navigation units, optical payloads and ground stations for the constellation, which is planned to be deployed between 2027 and 2030.SBS-3, a strategic project approved by the Cabinet Committee on Security, will comprise 52 satellites in low Earth and geostationary orbits and is aimed at providing the armed forces with persistent surveillance, secure communications and greater situational awareness across India’s land and maritime areas of interest.The programme marks an expansion of the private sector’s role in India’s strategic space capabilities. Of the 52 satellites, 31 are to be built by private industry, with the remaining 21 being built by Isro. The private-sector allocation has been divided among three companies: Antaris will build 15 satellites, while Pixxel and Dhruva Space will build eight each.Dhruva’s eight satellites therefore form part of the private-sector component of the larger SBS-3 constellation, rather than a separate constellation.
The programme is expected to improve the frequency with which strategic areas can be observed and strengthen India’s ability to monitor developments along its borders and across the Indian Ocean Region.The Safran contracts will give Dhruva access to a range of French technologies for the satellites and associated ground infrastructure. Safran said the cooperation illustrates the rise of Indian New Space and the ability of French industry to support the development of India’s sovereign space capabilities. The company also said the partnership could open the way to further cooperation under future phases of the SBS programme.The Paris summit also produced two other India-related announcements. French launch-services provider RIDE! signed an agreement to launch two satellites for TakeMeToSpace, an Indian company developing orbital data centres. The deal builds on RIDE!’s collaboration with Indian space companies, including the launch of a European atmospheric re-entry capsule aboard Isro’s PSLV.
Separately, French Earth-observation company U-Space and Indian company Axiscades signed a commercial cooperation agreement to explore the Indian microsatellite market, addressing both commercial and institutional demand.Together, the three announcements point to a widening India-France space relationship spanning strategic surveillance, satellite launches and commercial satellite manufacturing, with Indian private companies increasingly at the centre of the cooperation.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

From Al-Hudaydah to Mocha: Rapid developments reshape Yemen’s military map
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:18:04 UTC
20:18:04 KST

Yemen has seen rapid military developments along its western coast, changing control of key areas as the country continues to face one of the world’s worst humanitarian and economic crises.
Yemeni media reported Thursday that Houthi forces had reached the strategic Mocha port in southwestern Taiz province, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, after taking control of the Hays and Al-Khawkhah districts in southern Al-Hudaydah province.
The developments, if confirmed, would give the Houthis control over the entire Al-Hudaydah province on the Red Sea, strengthening their position along Yemen’s western coast and bringing them closer to the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Before the reported advance, Hays and Al-Khawkhah were controlled by government forces, particularly the National Resistance Forces led by Presidential Leadership Council member Tareq Saleh.
The developments are part of a rapidly escalating military confrontation between the Houthis and government forces, reviving concerns that the conflict could widen after years of relative calm.
The Houthis took control of Hays and Al-Khawkhah following the withdrawal of government forces from the two districts amid intense fighting, according to local sources.
The independent Al-Masdar Online website reported that Houthis had taken control of Hays and Al-Khawkhah in southern Al-Hudaydah, as well as large areas of districts in western Taiz.
It added that the group had reached Mocha port after government forces withdrew south toward Lahej province.
The strategic importance of Hays and Al-Khawkhah lies in their location along Yemen’s western coast. Control of the two districts could allow the Houthis to advance more rapidly toward areas of Al-Hudaydah and Taiz while opening new routes toward coastal areas near Bab al-Mandab.
Following the reported withdrawal of government forces from Hays and Al-Khawkhah, Houthi forces advanced toward the strategic city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast, near Bab al-Mandab.
Al-Masdar Online reported that the Houthis had reached Mocha port, while other Yemeni media outlets reported that the group had taken control of the city, coinciding with the withdrawal of government forces toward Lahej.
There was no official comment from the government or the Houthis on the developments in Mocha.
Mocha holds major military significance as it is one of Yemen’s closest cities to Bab al-Mandab, one of the world’s most important maritime passages linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and carrying ships traveling to and from the Suez Canal.
Earlier Thursday, the 2 December news agency, which reports on the government-aligned National Resistance Forces, quoted Saleh as ordering armed forces along the western coast to “reorganize their ranks.”
Saleh said the western coastal forces, including the National Resistance, Giants Brigades, Nation’s Shield forces and units from the Taiz military axis, had suffered significant casualties in recent days while confronting a Houthi offensive that he said was “planned by Iran.”
He ordered the formation of an alternative command center in a secure location to regroup the forces in consultation with the Arab coalition leadership and Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council.
According to the agency, joint forces had already established a command center south of Mocha in Taiz following Houthi “breakthroughs” across several combat fronts under heavy fire involving various types of weapons.
The media office of the government authority in Al-Hudaydah, meanwhile, said military units operating on the Hays front in southern Al-Hudaydah and western Taiz were being reorganized.
It said the move was part of a plan to organize deployments, redistribute forces, conduct a coordinated field operation and reorganize defense.
The Houthi advance along parts of the western coast came a day after government forces announced that they had captured large areas in Al-Jawf province in northeastern Yemen, near the Saudi border.
On Wednesday, the Yemeni army said in a statement that its forces had captured the Al-Mutahaffat area, Al-Masariya Hill and adjacent hills north of Al-Faraid Hill in the northern Al-Labanat Al-Olya area of Al-Jawf.
It said government forces had also taken control of earthworks and trenches stretching about 20 kilometers from Al-Duhaida positions through Al-Saara to Bir Al-Maraziq, east of Al-Hazm, the provincial capital.
The army said its forces were continuing military operations amid heavy human and material losses among Houthi fighters, claiming that several fighters had been captured or neutralized and others wounded.
It added that government warplanes had carried out targeted airstrikes against Houthi gatherings and positions, destroying several military vehicles and pieces of combat equipment.
Al-Jawf is strategically important because it shares a land border with Saudi Arabia and lies near the Houthi-controlled provinces of Saada, Amran and Sanaa. It also borders the oil-rich provinces of Hadhramaut and Marib, which are under government influence.
The developments come amid Yemen’s broadest escalation since 2022, when a UN-sponsored truce was initiated before the peace process stalled and military confrontations resumed in July.
The Houthis control most of northern and western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa and the provinces of Dhamar, Al-Bayda, Ibb and Al-Mahwit, as well as Al-Hudaydah and most of Hajjah and Saada provinces. They also control areas of Taiz, Lahej and Al-Dhalea.
Government forces and their allies, meanwhile, control the interim capital Aden in the south, as well as Al-Mahrah in the far east, Hadhramaut, Shabwa and Abyan, in addition to most of Lahej, Taiz and Al-Dhalea provinces.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Türkiye’s National Space Programme will involve research initiatives on developing and commercialising high-value satellite and space technology to expand domestic production capacity in this area.
Ankara also plans to establish the research infrastructure necessary to build next-generation railway technologies and eco-friendly propulsion systems to contribute to meeting net-zero emissions targets in transportation.
The MTP outlines new financial mechanisms to be introduced to evaluate, fund and commercialise local patents, trademarks and industrial designs.

The Houthis are testing the limits of Saudi restraint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:17:23 UTC
20:17:23 KST

The Houthis are testing the limits of Saudi restraint
Riyadh needs to restore deterrence without being pulled back into a prolonged Yemen war.
The renewed escalation in Yemen is no longer simply a Yemeni battlefield development. For Saudi Arabia, it is becoming a direct test of national security, economic resilience and the kingdom’s ability to prevent the wider regional war from spilling further across its borders.
The latest Houthi attacks have demonstrated this clearly. Missiles and drones have hit civilian and economic sites in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran, injuring dozens of civilians and causing fires and temporary disruption at energy facilities. The attacks came as fighting intensified in Yemen and around the western coast, while the Houthis continued to threaten maritime traffic in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.
Saudi Arabia therefore faces two interconnected threats: Attacks on its territory and attempts to disrupt the maritime routes on which regional and international trade depends.
This creates a difficult strategic equation for Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has spent the past several years trying to move away from direct military involvement in Yemen and towards diplomacy, de-escalation and support for a political settlement. A return to an open-ended war would contradict that strategy and impose unnecessary political and economic costs.
But restraint cannot mean accepting repeated attacks on Saudi territory.
A different security environment
The security challenge today differs considerably from the first years of the Yemen war.
Saudi Arabia has strengthened its air and missile defences, improved coordination between its military and security institutions and accumulated considerable experience in countering drones and ballistic missiles. It is therefore much better prepared to defend its territory than it was a decade ago.
Yet the Houthi threat has also evolved.
The group possesses a combination of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and increasingly sophisticated drones. Even when most incoming weapons are intercepted, relatively inexpensive systems can impose disproportionate defensive costs and create uncertainty around airports, industrial facilities, border communities and energy infrastructure.
This means Saudi security cannot depend on interception alone. No air defence system can guarantee a perfect shield indefinitely.
The strategic objective must therefore be deterrence: Convincing the Houthis that attacks on Saudi territory will impose costs greater than any political or military benefit they expect to obtain.
This does not necessarily require returning to the large-scale military campaign of previous years. Riyadh has more options today. These include intelligence operations, strengthening Yemeni government forces, improving border security, disrupting missile and drone supply networks and, where necessary, conducting proportionate operations against facilities directly involved in attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The distinction is important. Saudi Arabia does not need to choose between doing nothing and returning to a full-scale war.
The economic front
The economic consequences are equally important.
Saudi Arabia is one of the world’s largest energy exporters, which makes attacks on its oil infrastructure internationally significant even when physical damage is limited. The latest attacks affected energy facilities and contributed to renewed concern in already nervous global oil markets.
There is an apparent paradox here: Regional instability can push oil prices higher and temporarily increase Saudi oil revenues. But higher prices caused by war should not be confused with economic benefit.
Saudi Arabia’s economic strategy under Vision 2030 depends increasingly on stability, investment, tourism, logistics, technology and the development of major projects outside the oil sector. Persistent missile and drone attacks can raise insurance and transport costs and affect perceptions of regional risk even if the kingdom’s underlying economy remains strong.
The greater strategic concern is maritime security.
Saudi Arabia occupies a strategic position between two of the world’s most important energy corridors: The Strait of Hormuz to the east and Bab al-Mandeb to the west. Disruption of both routes represents a serious challenge not only for Saudi Arabia but for the global economy.
This is why the Red Sea dimension of the Yemen conflict is particularly important. Bab al-Mandeb connects the Indian Ocean with the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. A sustained Houthi ability to threaten shipping there would increase freight and insurance costs and potentially divert vessels around Africa.
Saudi Arabia, however, possesses an important strategic advantage: Its energy infrastructure is not completely dependent on the Gulf. The kingdom can transport significant quantities of oil through its East-West pipeline to terminals on the Red Sea. This provides an alternative to Hormuz and gives Riyadh greater strategic flexibility.
That advantage does not, however, eliminate Saudi Arabia’s exposure to insecurity elsewhere in the Red Sea, including around Bab al-Mandeb.
Protecting Bab al-Mandeb should therefore be understood not simply as a Saudi or Yemeni interest but as an international economic and security requirement.
Avoiding the Houthi trap
The greatest danger for Riyadh may be political rather than purely military.
The Houthis could benefit from drawing Saudi Arabia back into an extensive war. It would allow them to portray the conflict once again as a confrontation between Yemen and an external power rather than a struggle among Yemenis over the future of their state.
Saudi Arabia should avoid this trap.
Confronting the Houthis must remain fundamentally a Yemeni responsibility. The internationally recognised Yemeni government and its forces should carry the principal burden of confronting Houthi expansion on the ground, while Saudi Arabia provides political, economic, intelligence and defensive support.
This is particularly important on the western coast. If the Houthis consolidate their military position around strategic areas overlooking the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb, the consequences will extend far beyond Yemen.
The objective should not be to retake Sanaa through another large-scale air campaign or restart an indefinite regional war. It should be to prevent the Houthis from using military force to change the regional balance, threaten neighbouring states or threaten international maritime arteries.
Diplomacy backed by deterrence
Saudi policy is therefore likely to operate on several tracks simultaneously.
First, Riyadh will continue strengthening its air and missile defences and protecting critical infrastructure. Second, it can increase support for Yemeni government forces while avoiding unnecessary direct involvement in ground combat. Third, it will seek broader regional and international cooperation to secure the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.
At the same time, diplomatic channels should remain open.
Saudi Arabia has repeatedly demonstrated its preference for a negotiated settlement in Yemen. But negotiations are sustainable only when both sides believe that escalation carries unacceptable costs.
Diplomacy, therefore, must be backed by credible military power.
Saudi Arabia has strong incentives to prevent Yemen from becoming another permanent front in the wider regional confrontation. The kingdom’s economic transformation requires stability, while its geopolitical interests require secure borders, uninterrupted energy exports and freedom of navigation.
But the same logic that encourages restraint also places limits on it.
If attacks on Saudi cities, civilians and energy infrastructure continue, Riyadh will increasingly regard the issue not as intervention in the Yemeni civil war but as the defence of Saudi territory.
That distinction will shape what comes next.
Saudi Arabia does not need another prolonged Yemen war. Nor does Yemen. But avoiding one requires restoring deterrence while preserving the possibility of a political settlement.
The most effective Saudi strategy, therefore, is neither unlimited escalation nor passive restraint. It is calibrated pressure: Defend the kingdom, strengthen legitimate Yemeni institutions, protect the Red Sea, keep diplomatic channels open and make clear that attacks on Saudi territory will carry consequences.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

A plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was delayed by a Russian drone as he prepared to fly to attend a state funeral in Oslo, Moldovan and Norwegian authorities say.
Zelensky and his wife Olena were on the jet at Chisinau, Moldova's capital, ahead of Wednesday's funeral of Norway's King Harald V when the unmanned aircraft crossed over the Moldovan border.
The drone prompted an immediate airspace shutdown and Zelensky's plane was left on the runway for around an hour before it could take off.
The flight was only authorised after it was confirmed the drone had come down 160km (100 miles) away. Asked by reporters on Thursday, the Kremlin said there had been no threat to the jet.
Zelensky's plane had been due to take off at around 16:30 (14:30 GMT) from Chisinau International Airport.
But Moldovan government spokesman Dumitru Ciorici told the BBC that Moldova had closed its airspace after noticing a Russian drone had entered it from the direction of Ukraine.
"Three departures and four arrivals were delayed as a result," he added.
"After 17:20 (15:20 GMT), the authorities confirmed that the drone had come down and exploded... some 160 kilometres from Chisinau International Airport."
Zelensky and his wife arrived safely in Oslo on Tuesday evening, where he held talks with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and other officials about military aid.
They joined other dignitaries for King Harald's funeral before flying on to Iceland for a brief visit and then to Canada for further talks.
