Saudi Arabia’s ‘Muslim NATO’ faces its first trial by fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:32:01 UTC
19:32:01 KST

Saudi Arabia’s ‘Muslim NATO’ faces its first trial by fire
A massive attack by Yemeni’s Houthis on Saudi Arabia has become the first serious test for the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement – a defense pact between Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad established just a month ago. We’re no longer talking about a future security architecture in abstract terms. Rather, a very concrete question is being posed: What actions should Saudi Arabia’s allies undertake following a strike on its territory?
According to the Saudi-led coalition, Houthi missiles and drones struck civilian and economic targets in four southern cities. At least 73 people were injured, including women and children. Fires broke out at energy facilities and damaged utility infrastructure; operations at some enterprises were temporarily suspended. The Houthis claimed to have attacked Saudi Aramco facilities in Abha, Jizan, and Najran, as well as the King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait.
The city of Jizan is of particular significance. Its oil refinery has a capacity of around 400,000 barrels per day and is one of Saudi Arabia’s largest refineries; it primarily supplies the domestic market. Through this attack, the Houthis demonstrated their ability to achieve three goals: threaten the population, disrupt energy infrastructure, and cast doubt on Saudi Arabia’s reliability as a key oil supplier.
The geography of the attack is notable. Khamis Mushait is a vital military hub for Saudi Arabia, Jizan is an oil refining center and port, Najran lies near the Yemeni border, and Abha serves as the administrative center of the Asir province. It was a distributed operation targeting various sites and one of the largest operations launched against Saudi Arabia since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran on February 28, 2026.
The Houthis claim that the operation is a response to Saudi strikes on Yemen; they claim that 121 airstrikes were carried out over the preceding three days. Riyadh speaks of a dangerous escalation and a violation of sovereignty. The previous model of limited deterrence, established after the 2022 truce, has effectively ceased to function, and hostilities have once again spilled beyond Yemen’s borders.
This brings up the delicate issue of the Mecca Agreement. The document was signed on August 7, 2026 by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan; its publicly stated formula clearly implies that an armed attack on any one of the three states is considered an attack on all. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan even likened this arrangement to Article 5 of NATO. However, an impressive-sounding collective defense formula does not automatically imply a functioning military mechanism.
The full text of the agreement has not been disclosed publicly. It is thus unclear who determines whether a specific incident constitutes an attack that triggers mutual obligations, whether the assistance is automatic, and who would command the designated forces. The first meeting of the joint political-defense committee took place on August 31. The parties agreed to establish a secretariat in Riyadh and began discussing joint exercises, military interoperability, and defense production. While the political commitment has been proclaimed, the framework for its implementation is still taking shape.
Even NATO’s Article 5 does not require all allies to automatically enter into war; each state takes whatever measures it deems necessary. In the case of the Mecca Agreement, the scope for interpretation is likely even broader. Assistance could entail intelligence sharing, the strengthening of air defense systems, arms supplies, and the deployment of specialists – but not necessarily joint strikes on Yemen.
The reaction of the allies confirms this interpretation. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif described the Houthi attack as “cowardly,” condemned it “in the strongest terms,” and declared unwavering solidarity with the leadership and people of Saudi Arabia. The Turkish Foreign Ministry also issued a strong condemnation, affirmed its support for Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and demanded that the Houthis immediately cease their attacks. However, neither country has publicly announced the convening of an emergency committee, heightened military readiness, or the provision of military aid to Riyadh in response to the new strike.
This does not mean that the agreement has failed. Collective defense is not limited to an immediate retaliatory strike, especially if the affected state has refrained from requesting specific assistance. Riyadh may currently be more interested in discreet cooperation regarding intelligence, missile launch detection, and counter-drone measures than a conspicuous entry of its allies into the war.
However, relying solely on rhetoric will not be sustainable in the long run. If the attacks persist, members of the alliance will need to define the threshold at which the principle of ‘an attack on one is an attack on all’ takes on practical meaning. Otherwise, the Houthis and other regional forces will receive a signal that the pact does not alter the cost of exerting military pressure on Saudi Arabia. For any defense alliance, this poses a greater risk than limited military damage: Deterrence only holds as long as a potential adversary believes that the commitments will be backed by action.
Ankara and Islamabad have reasons to avoid direct involvement in the Yemen campaign. Despite close military ties with Riyadh, Pakistan seeks to maintain a working relationship with Iran; its parliament refused to send troops to Yemen in 2015. Türkiye is also reluctant to transform the agreement into an anti-Iran bloc or risk being dragged into a protracted conflict.
A phased response is therefore the most likely scenario. It will likely start with consultations, followed by the strengthening of Saudi air defense capabilities, intelligence sharing, and the supply of anti-drone systems. Pakistan may provide specialists and additional personnel, while Türkiye can offer drone technology, electronic warfare capabilities, and munitions. Joint strikes would only be considered in the event of continued attacks, heavy casualties, or major disruptions to oil exports, and would require a separate political decision.
Following the strikes, the price of Brent crude approached $99 per barrel, although the initial surge remained within the 2% range. While the market does not yet view the damage as critical, it is reacting to multiple sources of risk. On September 4, Iran and the US targeted each other’s oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Houthis are intensifying pressure on shipping around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Before the war, around one-fifth of global oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz. A simultaneous threat to two key shipping routes could rapidly alter the relatively calm outlook of traders.
For the signatories of the Mecca Agreement, the attack does not serve as a trigger to automatically enter the war; rather, it is a test of their ability to devise a unified course of action. Condemnation by Sharif and the Turkish Foreign Ministry represents only the initial level of the response. It now remains to be seen whether the joint committee will be convened, whether Riyadh requests assistance, and what would happen in the event of a follow-up strike.
If political statements are followed by consultations, the strengthening of air defense capabilities, intelligence sharing, and the coordination of joint actions, the Mecca Agreement will acquire real, practical meaning. However, if the practical response is limited to rhetoric about a ‘cowardly attack’, the reputational gains derived from the August summit will quickly evaporate. The Houthis struck more than just Saudi targets; they effectively tested whether the alliance exists beyond the text of the joint communiqué. Currently, there is no definitive answer to this question – and there is a feeling that none may come.

"The Americans can exert influence, but they are not the only ones doing so. The Europeans exert influence in a different way. And there are contradictions between them here," Patrushev said when asked whether Washington could influence Kiev to enter peace talks.

Heat not seen ‘for the last 100,000 years’ – climate monitor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:30:42 UTC
19:30:42 KST

Heat not seen ‘for the last 100,000 years’ – climate monitor
Global heat hit an all-time high in August, with temperatures averaging 16.96C worldwide, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Western Europe suffered its hottest summer on record, as heatwaves, drought, and wildfires battered the region.
August 2026 was 1.65C hotter than the 1850-1900 average, a period commonly used as the benchmark for temperatures before large-scale industrial warming, Copernicus said on Thursday. It was the hottest August in records dating back to 1940 and effectively matched July 2023, the previous all-time monthly high, with less than 0.01C separating them.
“Humans haven’t seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years,” Samantha Burgess of the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, told AFP. Copernicus records extend back to 1940. Scientists use evidence including ice cores, tree rings, and corals to reconstruct temperatures further in the past.
The record followed an exceptionally hot summer across Western Europe. France, the UK, and Belgium all recorded their hottest summers; France endured 53 heatwave days and received almost 40% less rainfall than normal, making it the country’s second-driest summer since 1959.
The extreme heat also triggered a sharp rise in mortality. France registered an estimated 5,764 excess deaths from all causes during the June 17-July 2 heatwave – 36% above the expected level in affected areas, according to Sante publique France. Another 1,243 excess deaths were recorded during heatwave periods from July 3-22.
The combination of scorching temperatures and scarce rainfall hit crops and transportation. Germany’s grain harvest fell an estimated 7.3% year-on-year, with the authorities blaming heat and drought, while falling water levels on major rivers including the Rhine disrupted shipping.
France announced more than €1 billion ($1.16 billion) in emergency aid for farmers as tens of thousands of farms faced financial difficulties.
Dry vegetation fueled wildfires across the continent. More than 647,000 hectares had burned across the EU by early September, nearly twice the 20-year average for that point in the season, according to the European Commission’s Joint Research Center.
Oceans outside the polar regions reached their joint-highest monthly sea-surface temperature, extending a three-month run of record warmth. Scientists attribute the long-term warming trend primarily to human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, while natural phenomena such as El Niño can further boost temperatures in the short term.
UN climate chief Simon Stiell called the latest records “the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction,” warning that extreme heat will continue while coal, oil, and gas are burned. Long-term global warming is currently around 1.4C above pre-industrial levels.

Houthis seize key Yemen city near Bab el-Mandeb Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:30:13 UTC
19:30:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Houthis seize key Yemen city near Bab el-Mandeb Strait
The Houthis have seized the strategic Yemeni port city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast, government sources said on Thursday, marking a major development in the renewed fighting as tens of thousands have been displaced across the country.
Three Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Houthi forces had entered Mocha and taken control of the coastal city, while local sources told The New Arab that large numbers of residents were fleeing towards the southern city of Aden.
The takeover comes after weeks of escalating Houthi attacks on Mocha and its port and amid a broader offensive by the Iran-backed group across western Yemen.
Mocha is strategically important because of its location on Yemen's western coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and one of the world's most important maritime trade routes.
The city's capture could therefore have wider implications for security around the strait and commercial shipping through the Red Sea, as fighting intensifies across Yemen's western coast.
The Houthis launched a major offensive in Hodeidah and Taiz provinces last week aimed at advancing towards Bab al-Mandab, prompting government-aligned forces to mount counterattacks and expand operations elsewhere in the country.
Mocha had already come under repeated Houthi missile, drone and explosive-laden boat attacks in recent weeks.
The city's port suspended all commercial and maritime operations in mid-August after it was struck by more than 25 Houthi missiles, according to information provided by sources.
The attacks caused civilian casualties and damaged facilities and property, with material losses estimated at around $16 million.
The takeover coincides with an escalation in fighting along Yemen's western coast, particularly in southern Hodeidah and western Taiz, where government and allied forces have been carrying out military movements and withdrawing from several positions.
Yemeni government forces withdrew overnight from Hays district in southern Hodeidah as military units operating around Hays and western Taiz began a process of reorganisation and redeployment, military and local sources said.
It remains unclear how many troops withdrew from Hays and Al-Wazi'iyah or where they have been redeployed. Military sources said the movements were part of preparations for a coordinated field operation.
Tareq Saleh orders western coast forces to regroup
Tareq Saleh, deputy chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, said on Thursday that government forces on the western coast had suffered heavy losses in recent days while confronting the Houthi offensive.
Saleh said forces had been ordered to regroup and establish an alternative command centre in a secure location in consultation with the Saudi-led coalition and the Presidential Leadership Council.
Military media affiliated with Saleh's National Resistance said the joint forces had established a command centre south of Mocha following Houthi breakthroughs on several fronts under heavy fire.
The forces involved in the western coast fighting include the National Resistance, the Giants Brigades and Nation's Shield forces, alongside units from the Taiz military axis.
Saleh accused Iran of planning, supporting and participating in the Houthi offensive through what he described as its "various tools", without providing further details about Tehran's alleged involvement.
Iran has rejected accusations that it is interfering in Yemen, saying this week that it supports the country's unity and territorial integrity and a Yemeni-led dialogue based on a UN-backed roadmap.
Meanwhile, military media sources reported air strikes on Houthi positions in Al-Tuhayta, Al-Salif and Kamaran Island in Hodeidah province.
The National Resistance's military media also said the Houthis had targeted Zuqar Island with two ballistic missiles.
The latest developments come amid the most significant escalation on several Yemeni fronts following years of relative calm. Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but clashes resumed in July and have since widened.
Fighting has also spilled across the border into Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh accusing the Houthis of targeting Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan with ballistic missiles and drones. Saudi authorities said this week that recent Houthi attacks had wounded at least 73 people.

Everything New You Can Do With Siri AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Siri made its debut on the iPhone in 2011, five years ahead of Google Assistant and 11 years before ChatGPT would open up to the public. Despite the head start, Apple's voice AI has been comprehensively overtaken in recent years, and made to look rather primitive compared to the many generative AI rivals it’s now up against.
With the launch of iOS 27, Apple and Siri are fighting back. There's a new name—Siri AI—and a host of new capabilities that are coming to your iPhone.
These are the new features that you'll be able to make use of once iOS 27 appears on your handset, if you're running the iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max or later (including, of course, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo). Only these latest phones have the necessary on-board silicon to meet the higher AI processing demands.
Get More Personal Context
You'll notice when Siri AI arrives that it spends some time indexing everything on your iPhone. That's so it can dig deep into your texts, emails, calendars, and whatever else you have stored on your phone (everything is kept on-device though—nothing gets sent back to Apple).
It means you can ask natural questions about text conversations, email interactions, and appointments—"What day is my work appraisal happening?" for example, or "Where did I say I'd meet Mom?"—and get informed, personalized answers back, based on what's already stored in your apps.
This works for photos and videos as well. Open up the Photos app and you're able to ask Siri AI to show you all the pictures of your pet, or the images you took on your last vacation, or all the photos of trees you've collected, via simple, conversational prompts.
Ask About Anything on the Screen
Siri AI knows what you're looking at while you're using your iPhone—perhaps even better than you do. Whereas before you would've had to take a screenshot and give it to Siri to look at, now you can just ask.
So if you're on the web in Safari, you can say "Hey Siri" and then get it to summarize the text onscreen or identify a landmark in an image in an online article. You can ask what certain options mean in Settings, or look up more details about a game you're thinking about downloading from the App Store.
The same sort of visual processing is available through the iOS Camera app too: Just switch to Siri mode using the selector by the shutter button, and ask Siri AI about anything that's in view (nutritional information about an item on a menu, for instance).
Write and Edit Text Anywhere
The old Siri could generate text for you, but it offloaded the job to an integrated ChatGPT plug-in. With Siri AI, no third-party help is needed, and you can use it for things like text messages and emails.
Just call up Siri AI by saying "Hey Siri" or tapping on the Write with Siri link, then tell it what you want to say or describe the edits you'd like it to make. You can instruct it to make your messages sound more or less formal, to expand or shorten sections of text, or to turn quick notes into full paragraphs and sentences.
You retain final approval over what's written, and can continue to make manual or AI-generated edits as you go. Siri AI lets you review all the changes and jump backwards and forwards through your different revisions.
Do More Inside Your Apps
Not only can Siri AI access more information pulled from your apps, it can now take more actions inside these apps. You’re able to create calendar events or switch playlists just by talking or typing to the digital assistant.
Some of this was already possible with the earlier incarnation of Siri, but now you can go deeper and do more inside your apps, and you should be able to use a wider range of natural language prompts to get stuff done—just as if you were talking to a real human assistant you'd handed your phone over to.
You might see some suggestions for actions pop up as well—so if someone texts you a date and time, you’ll see Siri inviting you to create a calendar event. Over time, deeper hooks into third-party, non-Apple apps should show up too.
Get at All Your Chats With the Siri App
For the first time, Apple's digital AI assistant has its own app. Launch it from the home screen to access your Siri AI conversation history and sync your queries and requests across different Apple devices.
Compared to the likes of Claude, Gemini, or ChatGPT, this is something Siri AI has been sorely missing, and it gives you another way of launching chats with the assistant: Open up the dedicated app rather than invoking it with a voice command.
Also, look out for what Apple calls "broad world knowledge" in the new Siri AI. Roughly translated, stand-alone queries about the history of Rome or how to fix a leaky faucet should bring up more informed, complete responses in the app.
Customize Siri’s Pace and Expressivity
This final tip needs even more computing resources, so it’s only for the most powerful devices—the 2026 iPhones, as well as the iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, and iPhone Air—as far as iPhones go.
The actual feature is being able to adjust the tone, speed, and what Apple calls the "expressivity" of Siri AI's spoken responses to you. In other words, you can tweak the personality of the assistant to some extent, as well as switch between voices.
To find these new options, open up Settings on your iPhone and tap Siri. You can customize Siri AI in other ways from this same screen, including changing the AI’s default voice and choosing how long to keep chats stored in your history.

EU floats idea for using Russia's frozen assets that would ease Belgium's concerns
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
13:30:00 EEST
19:30:00 KST

EU floats idea for using Russia's frozen assets that would ease Belgium's concerns
Europe has put forward a new proposal for using Russia's frozen assets to support Ukraine, seeking to address Belgium's concerns over the legal risks it could face from such a move.
Source: an article by European Pravda; Heorhii Tykhyi, spokesman for Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs in a comment to European Pravda
Details: One of the alternative approaches to using Russia's frozen assets to support Ukraine, currently being discussed within European expert circles, is to change not only how Russian money is used, but also where it is held and which institution is responsible for its custody.
This concerns the possibility of moving Russian assets out of the Euroclear depository in Belgium and entrusting them to a new custodian under EU control.
This idea also has Ukraine's support – Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs says it has passed on to Brussels its own vision of how this could be implemented.
Quote from Tykhyi: "Ukraine's Ministry of Finance has already put forward a specific proposal to the European side. It concerns creating an EU-level mechanism to which these funds could be entrusted. The decision on their actual use for Ukraine's defence, resilience and recovery needs would then be made collectively, with distributed responsibility across all EU member state governments."
More details: If a new EU structure or banking institution replaces Euroclear as custodian, legal responsibility, along with the Russian funds, could shift to the pan-European level. In that case, it would be the EU, not Belgium, that would have to respond to lawsuits or demands for the return of funds, which would broadly address the concerns the Belgian government has cited in its objections to the reparations loan.
However, for now, the EU views this idea as a theoretical possibility rather than a ready-made plan.
A legal and financial mechanism for the transfer that would remove the risks from the Belgian government has not yet been worked out; accordingly, there is also no draft legislative proposal from the European Commission.
To determine whether the idea is feasible and politically acceptable, the European Commission would need to set out a legal basis for transferring the assets, choose or propose a financial structure to manage them, define the instrument's model, rules and governance arrangements and clarify how any potential losses or liability would be shared if courts were to rule in Russia's favour.
Background: The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has proposed a way to transfer frozen Russian assets to Ukraine on the basis of two rulings by the European Court of Human Rights.

Deputy Minister Artur Harazim opens Arctic Council meeting

Deputy Minister Artur Harazim opens Arctic Council meeting
08.09.2026
On 8 September, Undersecretary of State at the MFA Artur Harazim opened the Warsaw Format Meeting. It is an annual meeting of the Arctic Council, a platform for cooperation among the eight Arctic states, indigenous peoples' organisations, and observer states, which aims to promote cooperation in the Arctic region. This year, the Council is chaired by Denmark.
Opening the meeting in Warsaw, Deputy Minister Artur Harazim highlighted the Arctic’s ever-increasing importance in the current geopolitical situation. He also pointed out that the processes taking place in the Far North affect other regions of the world. He noted that Poland has significant research potential allowing it to support efforts to better protect the natural environment of the Arctic.
The meeting was co-chaired by Arctic Ambassador Kenneth Høegh of Greenland, who presented the Danish chairship’s activities to date, whose priorities include sustainable development of the Arctic and support for the people living in the Far North.
The participants also listened to a presentation by Ambassador for Arctic Affairs Helen Eduards from Sweden, which will take over the chairship of the Arctic Council in May 2027.
Observers representing non-Arctic states and various organisations described their involvement in the activities of the Arctic Council working groups focusing on, for example, emergency situations, conservation of Arctic flora and fauna, and the protection of the Arctic marine environment. The participants were also presented with the latest information on investment in infrastructure for the study of Arctic regions.
***
The Arctic Council was established by the Ottawa Declaration in 1996. Poland was one of the first countries to be granted an observer status in 1998. This year’s meeting brought together over 80 participants.

WATCH Russian drone destroy Ukrainian MiG (MOD VIDEO)
A Russian long-range drone has destroyed a Ukrainian MiG-29 fighter jet shortly after it landed at an airfield outside Kiev, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said, releasing footage of the strike.
The aircraft was hit at Vasilkov airfield in Kiev Region, according to the ministry.

Türkiye aims to expand its position as global logistics hub with new projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:25:26 UTC
19:25:26 KST

Seda Tolmaç
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Türkiye plans to accelerate transport processes and reduce exporter costs by making trade and logistics infrastructure more efficient under its Medium-Term Program (MTP) for 2027-2029, as it aims to become a global logistics hub connecting Asia, Europe, the Middle East and Africa.  
The three-year economic roadmap highlights efforts to develop alternative and resilient trade routes across Türkiye’s east-west and north-south axes amid recent regional conflicts and supply chain issues.
Ankara will boost the capacity and competitiveness of international transport networks, specifically the Middle Corridor and the Development Road project.
Plans are underway to strengthen connections along the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars and Kars-Igdir-Aralik-Dilucu railway lines, alongside the Zangezur Corridor. These upgrades will diversify and expand rail transport capacity from the Caspian Basin through Türkiye and then to European markets.
Meanwhile, planned improvements to the Hejaz Railway in the south will facilitate uninterrupted global transport links connecting Türkiye with the rest of the Middle East.
At the same time, the Istanbul Northern Railway Crossing will become a critical junction by connecting freight from the Middle Corridor, the Development Road and the Persian Gulf directly to Europe.
Türkiye will cement its central role in global trade by establishing an uninterrupted and high-capacity railway connection, integrating ports, rail lines and roadways.
The MTP outlines other efforts to develop stronger connections between these corridors and logistics centers, organized industrial zones, production plants, airports and border crossings to boost the share of rail in overall freight transport, hence expanding Türkiye’s intermodal transport capacity.
These efforts will also strengthen Türkiye’s competitive edge in international trade and its potential as a global logistics hub.
Ankara aims to improve its overseas logistics distribution networks initiative to integrate more local firms into global supply chains and establish the necessary infrastructure for end-to-end global deliveries to be completed quicker and at lower costs.
The three-year economic roadmap also prioritizes easing Türkiye’s foreign dependence on critical inputs and technologies while outlining plans to develop early intervention capabilities and alternative supply chains against potential risks due to geopolitical shocks or trade measures.

====================================================================================================

The Muslim families fighting for burial space in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:23:57 UTC
19:23:57 KST

Breadcrumb
Newham's burial crisis is forcing Muslims to ask: Where will we bury our dead?
Standing with clipboards in hand outside a mosque in the East London borough of Newham stood two volunteers from the Newham Muslim Burial Association (NMBA), asking mosque-goers about their experiences burying their loved ones.
Admittedly, not part of the typical Friday Prayer routine, but that didn't stop people from giving these volunteers their time of day.
The volunteers were there to deliver the hard truth to those listening: Newham is predicted to completely run out of burial space by 2032.
As expected, alarm bells were raised. Many were shocked to hear this for the first time; others saw it as an opportunity to voice their dissatisfaction with the entire burial process.
From cost to accessibility to unmet faith needs, it was clear that this issue required urgent attention. And it got urgent attention from the NMBA.
The Newham Muslim Burial Association, established in 2023, is a grassroots community organisation advocating for better burial provisions for Newham residents, covering land availability, accessibility, affordability and faith-sensitive needs.
"Newham has never had a community organising initiative like this, built from scratch and on a voluntary basis," one NMBA spokesperson said.
"The alternative was watching a crisis unfold right in front of us," she continued. "We couldn't sit back and wait for the local authorities to do something. We had to take matters into our own hands."
It started with a listening campaign in April. Volunteers visited mosques, conducted online surveys, and generally spoke with people.
The consensus could not have been more telling — 86% of respondents said burial provisions for Muslim communities were insufficient, while 93% said the average £4,000-£5,000 cost of a burial plot was unaffordable.
Behind these percentages are real families with real experiences.
One Newham resident said that "the local authorities are very oblivious to the needs of the Muslim citizens, who are already economically very poor," adding that many even "get into debt due to the high costs of burials."
Another resident said the high cost meant they had to bury their loved ones in the Gardens of Peace cemetery, a significant distance from where the family lived, making visits to loved ones far more difficult than they needed to be.
Grieving families don't deserve extra financial burdens at an already distressing time, as one resident put it: "The average Newham resident doesn't have that kind of money at hand, especially when deaths are completely unexpected."
The NMBA's mission was to bridge the gap between Newham's decision-makers and the people who felt the consequences of those decisions. This did not mean making empty promises, but a genuine determination to achieve material outcomes.
The wins start rolling in
After months of lobbying, the group finally saw its first major success in March.
Newham Council granted £750,000 to the NMBA to support local burial provisions for the coming financial year, and the council promised to work closely with the NMBA and local mosques to develop a long-term plan.
This is an undeniable "positive step" in the right direction, but the Chair of the NMBA, Kamran Qureshi, still cautioned that "we need a sustainable, multi-year strategy."
He added: "We cannot afford to put a sticking plaster on a systemic issue."
His words highlight that this sum of money doesn't signify the end of the fight, but rather indicates that their efforts weren't going to waste.
An NMBA spokesperson said, "The council will still need our help to turn this money into something tangible," showing how this issue will always be grounded in community action and collective organising.
In April, the local mosque, Masjid al-Humera, voluntarily donated £115 to the cause, showing that when a community cares, it will show up in whatever capacity it can.
Then, in June, an even more significant step was taken.
Dignity Group, which owns the East London Cemetery, agreed to provide 250 new burial spaces for Newham's Muslim community at a site in Plaistow. They have also expressed willingness to offer an additional 600 spaces if demand is particularly high.
Not only did the NMBA secure the much-needed plots of land, but it also built relationships with key organisations and placed faith-based community needs at the forefront of decision-making to facilitate inclusive and sustainable burial provisions.
The Muslim Council of Britain has commended the NMBA, saying, "Muslim communities organising to meet local needs is what a healthy, engaged society looks like, and it's exactly the kind of civic participation we want to see more of across the UK."
Quantity of burial space isn't the only issue the NMBA is advocating for; the quality of these spaces is equally important in ensuring they fulfil the faith-sensitive needs of Newham's Muslim community.
Some of these requirements include using virgin (previously unused) land for burial plots, orienting graves towards Mecca, and providing on-site ritual facilities.
Over the next 12-year period, an estimated 13,652 burial plots will be required in Newham, with at least 10,452 needing to be on virgin ground, primarily to serve Muslim and Jewish faith requirements.
The numbers are certainly alarming. But what the Newham Muslim Burial Association has shown is that this crisis doesn't mean Newham residents have no choice but to watch the clock until 2032; instead, they can organise right now within their communities to help make the changes they need to see.
As Green councillor Ibrahim Alom puts it: "For us, this isn't about the council deciding everything from the top down. It's about working alongside organisations like the NMBA and listening to residents to develop solutions that are practical, respectful and supported by the community."
A campaign run by volunteers, starting with a stack of surveys outside a mosque, can move a council and a private cemetery operator in the same year.
"What we've been able to achieve so far with the model of community organising shows that people will engage in issues that they care deeply about," one NMBA spokesperson said.
"This is not the end. We will continue to lobby until we see consistent, tangible outcomes."
It takes one conversation
One volunteer shared a touching story of her experience engaging with locals. One Friday, she walked into the packed women's section of a local mosque, waiting for prayer to begin, hoping to speak with people and raise awareness about this issue.
She was met with an unexpected obstacle: a language barrier. But she tried nonetheless. She managed to find one woman she could speak to about the crisis, who then translated it for the other women in the room.
That group translated it further until everyone understood it in their own language. Before long, the room was buzzing with women talking about their experiences with the burial process, confiding in each other about how difficult it is, and coming to the collective conclusion that this was a problem.
She said that this experience made her realise that "in this diverse community, there may be multiple languages, but one in common is the language of seeing and understanding injustice and inequality."
The chatter, the discussion and the open dialogue are what get things moving.
They helped Newham residents realise that this was an issue and that action was needed.
People engaged in whatever way they could, and for a grassroots community organisation like the NMBA, that was enough to get the ball rolling.
Majidah Chowdhury is a student and freelance journalist based in London

SC seeks UP govt response on plea challenging MLAs, MLCs’ pension, perks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:22:56 UTC
19:22:56 KST

Supreme Court agrees to hear plea on pension to MLA, MLCs
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday sought responses from the Uttar Pradesh government and others on a plea challenging provisions of a 1980 law that provide pension and other facilities to sitting and former MLAs and MLCs in the state.A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta issued notice on the petition challenging a May verdict of the Lucknow bench of the Allahabad High Court, which had dismissed the plea against the constitutional validity of the provisions.The top court posted the matter for hearing after four weeks.
Plea questions benefits to legislators
The petitioner, Lok Prahari, had challenged provisions of the Uttar Pradesh State Legislature (Members' Emoluments and Pension) Act, 1980, arguing that the state legislature had effectively made itself the “judge in its own cause” by granting benefits to its sitting and former members.The plea contended that the benefits were “manifestly arbitrary” and contrary to the constitutional principle that public office is meant for public service and not personal gain.The High Court had noted that the law provides sitting and former MLAs and MLCs with salary, allowances and other facilities. It also extends pension, family pension, free travel, medical facilities and other amenities to their spouses, family members and companions.
What petitioner argued
The petitioner contended that these provisions go beyond the powers conferred on state legislatures under Article 195 of the Constitution.Article 195 deals with the salaries and allowances of members of state Legislative Assemblies and Legislative Councils. According to the petitioner, it does not specifically provide for pension, post-retirement benefits or facilities for family members and companions.
The High Court, however, had held that the challenge was essentially based on a policy disagreement rather than any demonstrable constitutional infirmity.It observed that the constitutional scheme does not prevent a legislature from making provisions for pension, allowances or allied benefits for its members, including former members.While dismissing the plea, the High Court had said there was no constitutional bar on the state legislature enacting measures of social security for its current and former members.

US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers, 3 linked to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukrainian official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:21:57 UTC
19:21:57 KST

US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers, 3 linked to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukrainian official says
The U.S. military destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers on Sept. 8, three of which have ties to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said in a comment shared with the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) on Sept. 9 said its forces struck the five vessels in response to attempts by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to target a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles.
The five vessels were the Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, as well as the Derya near Iran's Kharg Island. U.S. forces instructed the crews to abandon the vessels before striking them, CENTCOM said.
Three of the tankers, the Kaviz, Charminar, and Riesco, have direct links to Russia's shadow fleet and have been involved in transporting Russian oil, Vlasiuk said.
The Kaviz had called at the Russian ports of Ust-Luga and Novorossiysk and transported Russian oil, according to Vlasiuk. He added that the vessel had repeatedly switched off its Automatic Identification System (AIS), which ships use to broadcast information including their location and identity.
According to Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), the Kaviz was previously affiliated with Fractal Marine DMCC, a company sanctioned by the U.K. for servicing Russia's energy sector and identified by HUR as a key operator of Russia's shadow fleet. HUR also lists the tanker as sanctioned by the U.S., Ukraine, the EU, Switzerland, the U.K. and Canada.
The Charminar had previously called at the Russian ports of Ust-Luga, Primorsk, Vysotsk and St. Petersburg, Vlasiuk said.
HUR lists the Charminar as having been involved in exports of Russian crude and petroleum products and links the vessel to Fractal Marine DMCC. The vessel has also been linked to a shipping network associated with Iranian oil trader Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani, who trades in both Russian and Iranian oil, Vlasiuk said.
The third vessel, the Riesco, has likewise transported Russian and Iranian crude and petroleum products, including through ship-to-ship transfers with sanctioned vessels, according to HUR. The tanker has been under U.S. sanctions since November 2025 and Ukrainian sanctions since February 2026.
CENTCOM published footage showing the Riesco sinking in the Gulf of Oman following the strike.
Russia's shadow fleet is a network of vessels used to move sanctioned Russian oil around the world, at the same time obscuring ownership to avoid Western restrictions. HUR's register had identified more than 1,400 such vessels as of May 2026, many of them aging ships sailing under third-country flags.
The fleet has become a crucial source of revenue for Moscow, with estimates suggesting it carries about 75% of Russia's sanctioned oil and helps generate income used to fund the Kremlin's war against Ukraine.

Türkiye sets eyes on quantum, space tech growth with new research incentives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:21:39 UTC
19:21:39 KST

Zeynep Duyar
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Ankara prepares to overhaul its research and development (R&D) incentives to foster the development of critical technologies, especially targeting space and quantum areas, to reduce the country’s foreign reliance, according to its three-year economic roadmap. 
The Medium-Term Program (MTP) covering 2027-2029 aims to strengthen the Turkish technology ecosystem through targeted investments and entrepreneurship to meet the sector’s rapidly evolving requirements through state funding for existing R&D centers, tech development zones and business incubators.
The roadmap outlines the need to fund early-stage tech startups with massive potential to become unicorns, or companies with a valuation of $1 billion.
Plans are underway to maintain a specialization model to help large-scale private R&D centers and technoparks focus on developing innovative solutions in emerging fields, with state research funding directed toward deep technologies including cybersecurity, autonomous systems, quantum computing, hypersonic systems and next-generation materials.
Ankara will also support the fields of nanotechnology, biotechnology, sensors, chips, batteries, nuclear and renewable energy technologies, as well as blockchain and robotics.
The MTP plans to establish strategic collaborations among research institutions, universities and private-sector companies working in these fields.
Türkiye’s National Space Program will involve research initiatives on developing and commercializing high-value satellite and space technology to expand domestic production capacity in this area.
Ankara also plans to establish the research infrastructure necessary to build next-generation railway technologies and eco-friendly propulsion systems to contribute to meeting net-zero emissions targets in transportation.
The MTP outlines new financial mechanisms to be introduced to evaluate, fund and commercialize local patents, trademarks and industrial designs.
The government will use a university-industry collaboration model to fund specialized research facilities, product-focused platforms and state-of-the-art testing labs.
Türkiye aims to seek global research collaborations in strategic technologies to cement the global footprint of its domestic ecosystem and expand its overall development capacity.

Tens of thousands of Hasidim have already arrived in Ukraine to visit the grave of their spiritual leader in Uman. The largest influx was recorded over the past three days, while the main entry is currently taking place through the borders with Poland, Romania, and Moldova. Andriy Demchenko, spokesperson for the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine, told a UNN journalist more about the situation at the border.
Details
The pilgrims began arriving back in late August. Currently, according to the spokesperson, the exact total number of Hasidim can be determined only based on border crossings.
The arrival of Hasidic pilgrims in Ukraine began as early as the 20s of August. Every day, either several hundred or several dozen pilgrims were entering, meaning there had been no such massive influx since then. However, the past three days, September 7, 8, and 9, saw the largest number of people enter Ukraine so far. For example, 13,700 Hasidic pilgrims entered Ukraine yesterday, while the total for Monday and Tuesday was 11,600
Overall, since the organized groups began arriving in Ukraine, border guards have recorded the arrival of tens of thousands of pilgrims.
We are referring to organized groups of Hasidic pilgrims in this statistic. If someone is traveling separately, or if we cannot say that they are traveling directly to Uman, then they will not be included in this statistic. Therefore, we can speak only about those groups that we record at the border. Since the 20s of August, more than 31,000 Hasidic pilgrims have already entered Ukraine
At the same time, no extraordinary situations related to the arrival of pilgrims have been recorded at the border so far, although some Hasidim were nevertheless denied entry into Ukraine for various reasons.
Fortunately, there have been no unusual situations related to the entry of Hasidic pilgrims during this period. As citizens of foreign countries, Hasidic pilgrims cross our border in accordance with the legislation governing border crossings by foreigners. If they do not meet certain criteria, they may also be denied permission to cross the border. In total, 13 Hasidic pilgrims were denied entry into Ukraine
The largest influx of pilgrims traditionally occurs in the several days before the start of the celebration of the Jewish New Year, known as Rosh Hashanah. Hasidim come, in particular, to Uman to visit and pay their respects at the grave of their spiritual leader, Tzadik Nachman of Breslov, who was the great-grandson of the founder of Hasidism. Before his death, he bequeathed that he be buried precisely in this place and that his followers come to his grave specifically during the celebration of the Jewish New Year.
The largest influx of Hasidic pilgrims occurs three to four days before the beginning of their New Year. This year, the celebration begins on September 11 and ends on September 13, so, in fact, there will still be such a massive influx today, while starting tomorrow, the entry of Hasidic pilgrims into Ukraine will drop almost to zero
The route most frequently used by pilgrims to enter Ukraine has also changed, and, according to the spokesperson, pilgrims are currently using the Polish and Romanian routes most actively.
Until Monday, September 7, Hasidic pilgrims crossed the border both through the border with Moldova and through the border with European countries, but before Monday, the preference was primarily for the route from Moldova. Since the seventh, there has been a larger influx through European countries, with Poland and Romania being the borders they are choosing most actively. If we are talking about the entire border, 13,000 people per day does not constitute a heavy load on the crossing points
Photographs of long lines of pilgrims at the Polish-Ukrainian border, in particular near the Medyka–Shehyni crossing, have also appeared online, Andriy Demchenko says. At the same time, border guards note that such footage does not always show the real situation along the entire border, as queues may quickly disappear after an organized group has passed through.
If an organized group was brought to the border by bus, got off and joined the queue for the pedestrian crossing, one can take a photo showing that there are huge queues there. But this queue will disappear within a fairly short period of time, and it will no longer be there—until the next bus brings another group of similar Hasidic pilgrims.
This year, Ukraine expects approximately 40,000 pilgrims to arrive; however, a more precise figure can be determined only after the main influx has ended. For now, on the eve of the celebrations, the border continues to receive organized groups.
According to various forecasts, I saw that there would be at least 40,000. If today is as active as yesterday, then, of course, the number of Hasidic pilgrims entering Ukraine will exceed 40,000. We will be able to give the exact number tomorrow.

India to press for digital currency payment system at BRICS summit, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:19:19 UTC
19:19:19 KST

India is pushing to link central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) across BRICS nations for cross-border payments at a summit later this week, despite political and technical hurdles that could limit progress, two sources familiar with the discussions said.
India is chairing BRICS this year, with leaders of the bloc set to meet in New Delhi on September 12 to 13.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) proposed linking the countries' official digital currencies to facilitate cross-border trade, Reuters reported in January.
The BRICS grouping includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
The proposal to link CBDCs would be a part of the agenda for the leaders' meeting, the sources said, although the limited adoption of digital currencies globally could complicate implementation.
They did not want to be identified due to the sensitivity of the issue and because they are not authorised to speak to the media.
Emails sent to India's external affairs and federal finance ministries and the RBI were not answered.
Political, technical challenges
India's proposal will build on the 2025 declaration at the BRICS summit in Rio de Janeiro, which pushed for interoperability between members' payment systems to make cross-border transactions more efficient.
Any move towards linking CBDCs, however, is likely to face significant challenges.
Previous discussions within BRICS on creating shared payment mechanisms have made little headway, underscoring the difficulties of integrating financial infrastructure across a diverse group of countries.
Strained relations between countries, such as Iran and the UAE, will remain a sticking point, with the UAE having cut financial ties with Iran, one of the two sources said.
India has also been reluctant to deepen financial connectivity with China, the second source said, adding that such arrangements would require deeper trust between the neighbours.
India stalled Alipay+'s proposal to link with the country's instant payments system for cross-border transactions over national security concerns due to its Chinese links, Reuters reported.
Currency-swap arrangements would also be needed to help manage trade imbalances before any CBDC linkage could become operational, the source added.
Dollar alternative?
BRICS nations have previously explored alternatives to dollar-based payments, including a proposal by Brazil for a common currency for the group, though the plan never advanced.
US President Donald Trump had warned the bloc against such a move by threatening to impose high tariffs.
India has no interest in replacing the dollar, and linking official digital currencies is aimed at making cross-border payments easier and faster, the second source said.

Russia’s new shelling tactics deepen suffering in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:19:17 UTC
19:19:17 KST

Russia’s new shelling tactics deepen suffering in Ukraine
Ukrainians are losing more sleep, shopping for food is becoming harder and travel is often fraught with risk and delays.
Kyiv, Ukraine – When Olena Krakovska is at work selling tools for manicures from a small shop on the basement floor of a shopping centre in central Kyiv, she doesn’t hear or see much.
“I’m already in a bomb shelter. Air raid or not, I’m at work,” the 42-year-old single mother of two boys told Al Jazeera.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump, Putin hold ‘frank’ phone call as US restarts Ukraine deal efforts
- list 2 of 4Cluster munitions kill, wound over 1,000 globally in 2025
- list 3 of 4At least eight people killed in Russian attacks across Ukraine
- list 4 of 4In maps and charts: Russian and Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets
Outside there are regular wailing air raid sirens, red-and-white explosions of Russian drones hit by Ukrainian interceptors, gong-like thuds and white plumes of smoke swelling in the sky.
Falling debris, from tiny metal pieces to larger fragments of fuselage, flop in the wind and come down with the sour stench of gunpowder.
But when Krakovska is at home, the air raids rattle her senses and nerves.
“There’s been too many recently. My brain isn’t functioning, my movements are uncoordinated,” she said.
Since mid-August, Russian air raids in Ukraine have become longer, more frightening for residents and more frequent as part of Moscow’s new tactic aimed at “terrorising our people, our cities and our villages far more intensely,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 6.
Between June and early August, there were five air raids a week with a combined duration of 2.3 hours, according to a calculation by the UA.news web portal. In the third week of August, their number rose to 12 and their duration to 7.9 hours, and in the fourth week, 34 over 23.2 hours.
Early September brought a brief lull – Russia stopped shelling Kyiv for three days when United States negotiators visited Moscow and Kyiv.
But on Monday, shelling resumed with a six-hour air raid, killing five, wounding 35 and causing several fires.
Each raid involves fewer drones and missiles, but the timing is unpredictable, keeping hundreds of thousands awake all night and paralysing all walks of daily life.
They interrupt office hours, business meetings and school lessons, traumatise people and cause long traffic jams. They also turn commutes on public transport into hours-long ordeals.
Stoicism, a macabre sense of humour and ingenuity keep Ukrainians optimistic.
“There’s no way out, only when you’re in a coffin,” Krakovska quipped.
That’s a phrase she heard from her great-grandmother Serafima, who survived the 1932-33 Holodomor famine and the 1941-43 Nazi occupation of central Ukraine.
“She saw things that were way worse than what we’re living through,” Krakovska said.
What worries her during her working hours is not the air raids but the schooling of her sons Bohdan, 12, and Volodymyr, 10.
Their academic year began on September 1, but after two days spent in the airless school basement-turned-bomb shelter, she decided that they should study online, at home, in front of laptops.
But video games are just a click away, and the boys can barely focus on what their teachers say.
“They don’t socialise with friends, don’t play outdoors. They bicker. They pay less attention to their classes and homework,” she sighed.
Her daily habits have changed, too.
Krakovska lives on the left bank of the Dnipro river that bisects Kyiv and is up to a kilometre (0.62 miles) wide.
She used to spend 45 minutes getting to work by subway listening to music, scrolling through social media or reading e-books.
But Kyiv authorities stop the movement of subway trains across the Dnipro during air raids – and crowds of frustrated commuters spend hours in subway stations or nearby.
One day in late August, Krakovska, like hundreds of other exhausted people, spent almost three hours waiting for the train inside a station.
She kept checking the Telegram channels that report the progress of air raids, worried about her phone’s dying battery and her sons’ safety.
Her shopping habits have also changed. She no longer idles in supermarkets looking for discounts – Russian attacks have destroyed several warehouses, leading to some food and medicine shortages.
“You still can buy anything, but you need to spend more time looking,” she said.
These days, she quickly buys food from small vendors next to the shopping mall or her apartment building.
One of them is Olha Bondar, 49, who owns a tiny fruit and vegetable stand in an underground pass.
She has begun to earn a bit more – but the war consumes every extra kopeck she makes.
She and her son Vadym fled Volnovakha, an eastern town with a pre-war population of about 20,000, days before it was occupied by Russian forces in 2022.
Most of Volnovakha lies in ruins, including her grandfather’s house where she grew up playing with her siblings and cousins, weeding beds of beets and tomatoes and throwing Colorado potato beetles into a tin can with gasoline.
The black and orange beetles “look like St George’s ribbons,” one of Russia’s main ideological symbols now ubiquitous in occupied Ukrainian regions, she said with a grimace of disgust.
Some of her relatives have not left because of their pro-Moscow sympathies.
“They blame Kyiv and the West for all the death, destruction and squalor around them,” Bondar said with a shrug.
She does not mind the air raid sirens as long as she gets text messages from her 24-year-old son who volunteered to enlist in 2023 and serves in northern Ukraine.
“I hear his voice or read his texts – and nothing else matters,” she said, before weighing a kilogramme of velvet-blue plums.
She lives in a rented one-bedroom apartment. But more affluent Kyiv residents have fled for the suburbs, renting or buying houses with wood stoves, wells and cool, dark basements to store food.
“We just can’t find a house, they don’t let people with pets in, and we have two fox terriers,” Roman, a software engineer who withheld his last name because his main client is a defence company, told Al Jazeera.
He and his partner Alisa, a yoga instructor who switched to online lessons, feel stranded in their two-bedroom apartment on the eighth floor of a nine-storey building.
After recently enduring a 3.5-hour traffic jam, Roman prefers to talk to his colleagues and clients on Zoom.
He also said his mental health is affected; he has started taking antidepressants and sleeping pills.
“Otherwise I just lie awake listening and thinking, listening and thinking,” he said while his dogs rummaged in the grass near his apartment building.
“And his tossing and turning drives me nuts,” Alisa quipped.
But they keep adapting and thinking ahead because the coming winter will bring more strikes on energy infrastructure and exhausting blackouts.
“We got used to things we’d only seen in horror movies,” she said.

The Institute of Journalism at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv recognized Bohdan Nahaylo for his contribution to independent journalism and for bringing the truth about events in Ukraine and around the world to wider audiences.
Kyiv Post Editor-in-Chief Bohdan Nahaylo has received an award from the Institute of Journalism at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv.
The award was presented during a ceremony marking the start of the new academic year. Nahaylo was recognized “for his contribution to the development of independent Ukrainian journalism and for spreading the truth about events in Ukraine and around the world.”
Bohdan Nahaylo is a British-Ukrainian journalist, author and former UN diplomat with decades of experience covering Ukraine and international affairs.
He took the helm of Kyiv Post in December 2021, shortly before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. By mid-2022, under Nahaylo’s leadership, Kyiv Post had expanded its offering with a fully fledged Ukrainian-language edition, providing Ukrainian-speaking readers with exclusive translations of selected content from the English-language newsroom as well as coverage of the day’s most important developments.
Throughout Russia’s full-scale war, accuracy and rigorous fact-checking have remained among Kyiv Post’s core editorial principles. Under Nahaylo’s leadership, the newsroom continues to operate from Kyiv, covering the war as well as Ukraine’s political, economic and social developments, while explaining the Ukrainian context to international audiences.
Nahaylo has consistently emphasized that Ukraine’s interests are best served not by propaganda, but by professional journalism — verified facts, thorough documentation, balanced analysis and active engagement with international audiences.
“Bohdan’s steady leadership during wartime, his deep historical knowledge and his commitment to safeguarding editorial independence have been instrumental in Kyiv Post’s continued work. This recognition from one of Ukraine’s leading journalism institutions acknowledges a professional career dedicated to factual reporting and journalistic integrity,” said Kyiv Post CEO Luc Chénier.
For Kyiv Post, the recognition of its Editor-in-Chief is also an opportunity to underscore the importance of independent Ukrainian journalism during wartime. As an English-language Ukrainian news outlet serving an international audience, Kyiv Post reports on Ukraine directly from Kyiv every day, helping strengthen Ukraine’s voice in the global information space.
About Bohdan Nahaylo
Bohdan Nahaylo is Editor-in-Chief of Kyiv Post, a British-Ukrainian journalist, author and former UN diplomat. Over the course of his career, he has worked with Amnesty International, British media organizations, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and the United Nations. He has served as Editor-in-Chief of Kyiv Post since December 2021.
About Kyiv Post
Kyiv Post is a Ukrainian English-language news outlet founded in 1995. It covers Russia’s war against Ukraine, politics, business and the economy, society and international affairs for a global audience.

Bayeux Tapestry goes on display at sold-out London exhibit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:18:00 UTC
19:18:00 KST

Bayeux Tapestry goes on display at sold-out London exhibit
September 10, 2026
The Bayeux Tapestry exhibition in London opened Thursday to much fanfare, in what British newspaper the Times has dubbed "Tapestry-mania," with more than 100,000 tickets already sold.
The tapestry is on loan from France, and comes after years of diplomacy, with the move being seen as a symbol of close ties between Paris and London. It is thought to be the first time the tapestry has gone on display outside of France.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the tapestry's loan a "return," while King Charles III hailed the move as a "precious symbol of trust at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations."
The work is believed to have been made in England nearly 1,000 years ago before finding its way to Bayeux, now located in the French region of Normandy.
Two previous attempts to loan the Bayeux Tapestry to the UK were unsuccessful. Once was in 1953 for the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, and again in 1966 for the 900th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings, which is depicted on the tapestry.
What is the Bayeux Tapestry?
The Bayeux Tapestry is a 70-meter long artwork, which is thought to be incomplete, depicting the Norman conquest of England in 1066.
Norman forces led by William the Conqueror were able to defeat and dethrone King Harold Godwinson in a campaign culminating in victory at the Battle of Hastings. The tapestry famously depicts Harold being shot in the eye with an arrow, as he is said to have died — admittedly in what modern historians believe is likely a myth or artistic exaggeration.
This conquest was a crucial contributing moment in the establishment of what would become England and later the British Empire and the UK. It was the last of several successful foreign invasions of England in a millennium, and turned out to be the last one for a millennium.
The conquest also added the final core ingredient, French, to the linguistic melting pot that produced the modern English language.
The embroidered cloth, which has brief Latin titles captioning its 58 scenes, is widely accepted to have been made in England as a tribute to William after his victory. It was then transported to his family home in Normandy.
The Bayeux Tapestry will be on display at London's British Museum until next July.

Türkiye’s exports to Asia-Pacific countries increased 18.6% year on year to $5.7 billion in the first eight months of the year, while the country’s total exports rose 4% to $185 billion over the same period, according to the Turkish Exporters’ Assembly (TIM). 
China received the most Turkish exports bound for the Asia-Pacific region, accounting for $2.5 billion, marking a surge of 35.1% year on year.
South Korea followed with $480.2 million, marking a 15.8% surge, Japan with $423.8 million and an 11.8% jump, Indonesia with $365.5 million and a 15.2% increase, and Pakistan with $361.6 million, posting a 2.2% uptick.
Singapore saw the highest increase in Turkish exports, with a 154.2% surge compared with the same period last year, reaching $324.5 million.
Singapore was followed by Brunei, with a 147.6% rise in Turkish exports totaling nearly $3.1 million, while Turkish exports to Laos rose 82.7% to $5.8 million and to Cambodia by 49.1% to $22.2 million.
The total Turkish exports to the country’s largest export markets in the Asia-Pacific region, namely China, South Korea, Japan and Indonesia, reached $3.8 billion in January-August.
Turkish exports to 14 Asia-Pacific countries increased while declining in six.
Mining products led exports during the first eight months of the year, growing 39.1% in exports to the region and reaching $1.72 billion.
Chemical products and goods followed with $983.9 million, and textiles and raw materials with $408.3 million.
Istanbul was the largest province by Turkish exports to Asia-Pacific countries in the first eight months of the year, accounting for $4.1 billion of the total, followed by Ankara with $1.3 billion, Izmir with $366.1 million, Elazig with $202.8 million and Kocaeli with $192 million, the data showed.

Trump's war cascades into a multifront battle for regional order

Breadcrumb
Trump's war cascades into a multifront battle for regional order
Iran has widened its war in the Gulf. Israel, meanwhile, continues its war in the Arab Levant and is also preparing for a greater role in the Gulf.
Tel Aviv is openly declaring that it will continue its war against Iran and its regional axis, while Benjamin Netanyahu continues to speak of bringing down the Iranian regime. Tehran, weakened and in retreat across parts of the Levant, is seeking to expand its influence in the Gulf, not only through the Strait of Hormuz but also by opening a new front around the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
It has already laid the groundwork through a series of military operations against Gulf states and appears to be preparing for further action if the US blockade continues and military strikes persist.
The world is holding its breath. Donald Trump is threatening to strike Pickaxe Mountain, the heavily fortified nuclear facility near Natanz. Netanyahu, meanwhile, continues to say that Israel is ready to carry out further operations against Iran as Tehran seeks to restore its nuclear programme.
Israel is working to provoke Iran further and draw it into a renewed war. Netanyahu appears to see escalation as the main route through which to fight his electoral battle, and therefore prefers to continue military operations in pursuit of achievements that could improve his political standing.
What Netanyahu wants is a renewed war stretching from Lebanon to Syria, alongside renewed confrontation between the United States and Iran. He is also seeking a greater Israeli role in the Gulf, particularly in the Yemen war.
Israeli reports point to concern in Tel Aviv that the Houthis could consolidate control over Bab al-Mandab and gain greater influence over shipping in the Red Sea. The Israeli military has also conducted exercises in Eilat simulating naval warfare.
Redrawing West Asia for good?
What the United States is doing amounts to redrawing the map of the Middle East, and of a significant part of the wider region. Israel, for its part, repeatedly says that it has already changed the Middle East and intends to continue doing so.
The shared US-Israeli objective is to draw the states of the region further into Israel’s orbit and into the Abraham Accords. Israel will seek to impose this through military pressure, whether in Lebanon, Syria or later on other states, including Gulf countries.
Saudi Arabia is particularly important in this regard, as Trump continues to push for it to join the Abraham Accords.
Lebanon, meanwhile, remains under sustained military and political pressure aimed at pushing it in the same direction.
This cannot be separated from remarks by the Israeli president about his ambition to meet the Lebanese president, visit Beirut and announce a peace agreement. Nor is it different from US statements that openly point towards an eventual peace agreement between Lebanon and Israel.
The framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel is increasingly being presented as the basis for governing that relationship, with Hezbollah’s disarmament across Lebanese territory treated as a central condition.
In this way, Washington is effectively giving Israel political cover to remain militarily active until Hezbollah is disarmed.
The US position coincided with Israel’s destruction of tunnels at Ali al-Taher, north of the Litani River, a clear indication that Israeli military operations may continue in other areas.
Netanyahu himself said that the Israeli army had destroyed tunnels around Beaufort Castle and Ali al-Taher, adding that there would be further operations.
Against this backdrop, the region appears to be approaching another moment of explosion.
It may be delayed, or it may erupt at any moment, particularly as Iran studies the options available to it and considers how to respond to the tightening US blockade, the strikes it is facing and the escalation in Lebanon.
In Yemen, Iran has moved towards an escalation through its allies, with the aim of strengthening control over Bab al-Mandab.
This has come alongside advances by the Yemeni government in other provinces as it seeks to tighten pressure around Sanaa and weaken the Houthis.
Iran’s moves in Yemen therefore constitute one of the most important tests of the Mecca security arrangement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.
Dealing with the situation in Yemen will require renewed activation of the international coalition established by Saudi Arabia to protect navigation through Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea.
Israel is likely to watch from the sidelines initially and wait for an opportunity to impose itself as a central player there, whether through security and intelligence cooperation or through direct military power.
But that would come at a high political price: first through a security agreement with Saudi Arabia, and then through a political agreement, peace deal or normalisation.
Israel as the region's policeman
What Israel wants is clear: to become the “policeman of the region” and the effective successor to US predominance from the Gulf to the Arab Levant.
Israel is presenting itself as a state capable of guaranteeing the security of regional governments and protecting them, on the basis that such protection requires alliance with Israel and acceptance of its conditions.
Israel also wants to demonstrate that the Mecca arrangement, or any other security or defence agreement, cannot provide Saudi Arabia or other regional states with an alternative source of military strength.
Turkey and Pakistan did not intervene militarily in support of Saudi Arabia in the past, have not done so now and may not do so in the future.
Israel, which is increasingly fighting over strategic routes, corridors and crossings, is also unlikely to accept a Turkish military presence around Bab al-Mandab or Turkish intervention in a campaign against the Houthis.
Israel is seeking to widen the war across the region.
It wants to show that it alone is capable of confronting Iran and its allies, and through that confrontation impose itself as an essential party in any regional equation involving the Arab Levant, the Gulf or the Eastern Mediterranean.
This is what Israel has been working towards for years.
It has built partnerships and strategic alignments around the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly with Cyprus and Greece, while also seeking to connect these arrangements to the Gulf.
The same logic is visible in the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, or IMEC, which links India to Europe through the Gulf and the Eastern Mediterranean.
Israel wants Saudi Arabia and Egypt to become part of this wider strategic architecture, while gradually drawing Lebanon and Syria into it as well.

Caravaggio’s “Magdalene in Ecstasy” at the Italian Embassy in Berlin
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:49:57 CEST
18:49:57 KST

Italy is included for the first time in the official program of Berlin Art Week, with a project that brings together an Italian 17th-century masterpiece and one of Europe’s most important contemporary artists. The exhibition, organized by the embassy in collaboration with Offsite Arts and curated by Tjioe Meyer-Hecken and Felipe Schwager, brings Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio’s *Magdalene in Ecstasy*, painted around 1606 during the dramatic years of his flight from Rome, to Germany for the first time. The painting is paired with a new work commissioned for the occasion from Belgian sculptor Berlinde De Bruyckere, an artist who for decades has explored the body, vulnerability, transformation, and religious iconography through materials such as wax, fabric, wood, and metal. The project establishes a dialogue spanning over four centuries of art history, connecting different artistic languages around universal themes such as ecstasy, suffering, desire, and the metamorphosis of the body. During the exhibition’s opening, attended by representatives from institutions, the cultural world, and the art scene, Italian Ambassador Fabrizio Bucci said: “We have spent the last year rethinking what an embassy can be in a city like Berlin: not just a place that represents its own country, but a space open to culture.” “Italy’s artistic heritage is not something to be displayed behind glass. We want to bring it into the present through new encounters, new interpretations, new forms of expression, and, where possible, new creations,” Ambassador Bucci emphasized.
                                    
                                       
				Today, the exhibition will be the centerpiece of Berlin Art Week’s Featured Night, followed by public viewings by reservation through September 25.
                                    
                                       
				“Caravaggio x Berlinde De Bruyckere” is the centerpiece of a broader program organized by the embassy around Berlin Art Week, which includes the exhibition marking Maurizio Cattelan’s return to Berlin twenty years after he co-curated the fourth Berlin Biennale. This is the Italian artist’s first major solo exhibition in Germany, organized as part of the “Preis der Nationalgalerie 2026” award he received. 
Participation in Berlin Art Week is merely the latest in a series of initiatives through which the embassy is transforming its spaces into a true cultural hub, strengthening dialogue with some of the most established institutions in the German art scene—particularly in Berlin—and the Italian art scene.

Govt sends letter to EU for budget flexibility for defence, energy spending
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:42:11 CEST
18:42:11 KST

Premier Giorgia Meloni's executive
has sent a letter to the European Commission to initiate the
procedure to use the national escape clauses under which EU
allows greater budget leeway for investments in defence and
energy, government sources said on Friday, confirming a report
by La Repubblica.
                                    
                                       
				Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti briefed Meloni's cabinet on
the letter on Thursday, the sources said.
                                    
                                       
				The original escape clause, brought in last year following
Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, gave member States the
option of running extra deficit of up to 1.5% of GDP for three
years for defence investments only.
                                    
                                       
				But Meloni's government successfully lobbied the European
Commission to allow for extra spending on energy investments too
after the Iran war led to a spike in fuel prices.
                                    
                                       
				In August Giorgetti said the government would request the
maximum level of flexibility for energy security of 0.6% of GDP
and 0.9% for defence.
                                    
                                       
				Under pressure from US President Donald Trump, Italy and its
NATO allies have pledged to increase defence and security
spending up to 5% of GDP.
